Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:44:05 CET
11:44:05 KST

By Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology as he attended an exhibition and demonstration of unmanned aeronautical technology, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
The firepower demonstration following the exhibition involved tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
The display highlights Kim’s push to modernise North Korea’s armed forces by using drones and artificial intelligence as Pyongyang draws lessons from its forces’ experience in Russia’s war against Ukraine and from other global conflicts.
KCNA photographs showed unmanned aerial vehicles bearing the North Korean Air Force’s emblem at the exhibition attended by Kim and some of his generals.
Another series of images showed what appeared to be an unmanned aerial vehicle crashing into a military vehicle on a hill and exploding in a ball of flame, which KCNA said was part of a weapons demonstration during the exhibition.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
According to KCNA, Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea in building modern armed forces, KCNA reported.
Kim has made repeated calls for the development of drones and AI in the military. According to state media, Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024 and oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025. In September 2025, he called AI a top priority in modernising weapons.
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid Moscow in its war against Ukraine, and gained battlefield experience in drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
North Korea is transforming its military with drones and AI, drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.
By showing a comprehensive display of weapons, North Korea is trying to “shut off the possibility of dialogue or negotiations” with South Korea, Lim said.
(Reporting by Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim; Editing by Nia Williams, Jamie Freed and Ed Davies)

====================================================================================================

John Turturro Gives a Career-Best Performance in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:44:04 UTC
11:44:04 KST

To paraphrase the old-school comedian Rodney Dangerfield, a pickpocket in 2020s New York gets no respect. Almost no one carries much cash anymore, and credit cards are useless unless you’re willing to commit fraud. What’s a poor guy with crackerjack observational skills and exceedingly dexterous fingers supposed to do when he can’t even pay for his diner breakfast with his morning’s earnings?
That’s where John Turturro’s Harry Lehman finds himself in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, writer-director Noah Segan’s charming, nimble, and affecting drama about a guy who has seen his city, and his world, change drastically during his lifetime. For Harry, a typical workday involves boarding the subway and identifying the easy targets. In his soft, elegant tweed coat—a garment he might have bought 20 or 30 years ago, maybe at Barneys, when the dough was really flowing—he swirls through New York, his vision attuned to checked-out, earbud-wearing Wall Street dudes, or women who allow their purses to dangle precariously. He sees what others miss, though he’s living in a world where no one pays any attention to their environment. It’s a lonely life.
But there’s a bright spot in Harry’s world: Though his wife, Rosie (Karina Arroyave), has been stricken with an unnamed ailment and can neither move nor speak, his days revolve around her. He cares for her tenderly, as best he can, talking to her, laughing with her. At one point he puts Odyssey’s 1977 sequins-and-stardust disco hit “Native New Yorker” on the stereo and dances for both of them, in a kind of disco-salsa shuffle, his arms whirling as if the breeze itself were his dance partner.
Rosie’s care costs money, which means Harry needs to hustle harder than ever. Watches can still bring in the bucks, as long as they’re not fake. And to unload those, Harry has a close pal and longtime co-conspirator, the wily, wisecracking pawnshop owner Ben (Steve Buscemi). Ben will also take stolen phones, though they’re troublesome: they need to go to a guy in Chinatown, Kelvin Han Yee’s Frank, who knows how to scrub them, after which they’re packed into a container and shipped off to god knows where. When Harry boosts a USB crypto wallet from a brazen young criminal and spoiled rich kid, Dylan (Will Price), Ben has no idea what to do with it—plugging it into his circa-1995 desktop personal computer sends the machine into a tailspin. So he sends Harry downtown to see Frank—whose front is a herb shop, though it seems less like a front than a side hustle—and that’s where Harry’s troubles really begin.
The Only Living Pickpocket is part drama, part comedy, part thriller. It’s also a movie about a man reckoning with his past: We may warm to the sight of Harry caring so lovingly for Rosie, but there’s much more to his story, as we learn. And you can’t always tell where the movie is headed; its beats are wriggly, unpredictable. Until recently, writer-director Segan has worked mostly as an actor, often with director Rian Johnson (he appeared in Brick, Looper, and the Knives Out movies), and he has directed one previous feature, the 2022 horror movie Blood Relatives. The pickpocketty lightness of touch he shows is remarkable for a fledgling director.
It doesn’t hurt that he’s got Turturro as a star. In the early part of his career, as a favorite of Spike Lee and the Coen Brothers, Turturro, with his tightly coiled, jack-in-the-box energy, always looked like he might blow at any moment. But he’s become much subtler, and sexier, over the years. in the underappreciated 2013 comedy Fading Gigolo, which he also wrote and directed, he played a foxy florist who becomes a classy male escort, servicing sultry hotties (Sharon Stone, Sofia Vergara) before falling for a lonely Hasidic widow (Vanessa Paradis). Suddenly, he was a leading man, and a hot one.
Turturro still has some of his old combustibility; you occasionally catch an air of menace behind that snaggle-tooth smile. But he now has more softness, more range, and the performance he gives in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is one of his finest, as well as one of the best of the year. In the first section of the film, you believe Harry is just a guy whose glory days have passed: He belongs to a dream New York, that of the 1970s and ‘80s, of strobe-lit dance clubs and independent cinemas seemingly on every block. (Cinematographer Sam Levy, who also shot Frances Ha and Lady Bird, is in tune with the old New York nestled within the current one; he captures the city, from the Bronx to Chinatown, in all its shabby-shiny glory.) At one point, Harry suggests to Rosie that the two hunker down for the evening and watch an old movie, maybe something with Barbara Stanwyck; he comes from a generation that was used to looking toward its past as well as its future.
The city wasn’t a safe place in Harry’s younger days—but we’re talking about something other than physical safety, a kind of creative vitality that, if you were attuned to it, could rub off on you like glitter. Harry still has some of that sparkle, but it’s tempered by melancholy, the aftermath of little mistakes and big ones he’s made along the way. Turturro captures all of it—and shows how Harry intends to do right by those he’s harmed—with the kind of lived-in ease you earn, if you’re lucky, over the course of a career. Whirling through the city in that tweed coat, he’s like Fred Astaire breezing through an obviously fake white-cardboard Venice or descending a staircase from nowhere. The grit of the city is his glamour, its noise his music. It’s all his for a song, or a watch deftly separated from its owner’s wrist. His city is a tough place and, as Odyssey sang, he should know the score by now. But at least he knows the dance steps, because as much as New York may change, those never do.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said late Thursday that a vessel was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
"UKMTO has received a report of an incident 25NM Northeast of Khasab, Oman in the Strait of Hormuz. A third party has reported that a vessel transiting outbound is on fire, the cause is unknown at time of report," the agency said in a statement.
The status of the crew, extent of damage and potential environmental impact remained unknown.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO whilst authorities investigate," the statement added.
The incident comes amid rising tensions between Iran and the US about navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy and commodity supplies.
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the strait, but its implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continued to escalate.

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
October 30, 2026
The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.
The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.
Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.
What is the complaint against Roundup?
Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.
The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.
Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.
The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.
What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?
The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.
"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement.
"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.
The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."
The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption

Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption
Elias Antonio Saca confessed to diverting over $300m in public funds during his presidency and took a plea bargain.
Elias Antonio Saca, the former president of El Salvador, has been released after serving a 10-year prison term for corruption.
Saca, 61, arrived at court to formally report his release on Thursday after fulfilling the terms of a plea deal in which he confessed to diverting and laundering more than $300m from public funds during his 2004 to 2009 administration.
His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits.
Arrested at son’s wedding
Saca was first arrested during his son’s wedding in 2016 and was sentenced to five years for embezzlement and another five years for money laundering in September 2018.
A plea bargain allowed Saca to avoid a potential 30-year prison sentence.
In 2019, the former president was found guilty of offering $10,000 to a court employee to obtain information about a case against him, though a judge determined the second sentence to be part of his existing 10-year term.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
During the initial trial, prosecutors said Saca appropriated funds from the state budget for himself and others, including taking more than $7m for his former party.
Saca was also ordered to repay $260m to the state. He is one of four Salvadoran presidents who have faced corruption charges, including his successor Mauricio Funes, who escaped to Nicaragua in September 2016 and died there in 2025.

Final vote results in Israel set up weeks of uncertainty about who will govern

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Final vote results in Israel set up weeks of uncertainty about who will govern
Leo Sands, Johnatan Reiss and Ephrat Livni
- Israel’s final election count left Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc on 53 seats and the main opposition on 48, so neither can form a government alone.
- President Isaac Herzog will choose who gets first chance to build a coalition, likely Gadi Eisenkot, as parties face weeks of talks, complaints, and possible legal challenges.
- The vote followed the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack and exposed deep division over Netanyahu, Arab parties, and the risk of another long political deadlock.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – The final vote count in Israel’s election, released early on Oct 30, confirmed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition nor the main opposition alliance won enough votes to form a government.
The result sets the stage for weeks of jockeying and political uncertainty.
Netanyahu’s Likud party and its hard-right allies won 53 seats in Parliament, not enough to meet the 61-seat threshold for an outright majority.
The final count, from Israel’s Central Elections Committee, showed Netanyahu’s alliance was down from the 64 seats it won in the last election, in 2022.
The main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who had led in opinion polls for months, won 48.
Two Arab parties secured 19 seats, their highest-ever number of seats.
The results are subject to potential “minor corrections” in coming days before they are submitted to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Nov 4, the committee said just after midnight.
Herzog will decide who he thinks has the best shot at assembling a majority and ask that person to try to form a government.
Herzog has said he will consult with party leaders after formally receiving the vote count next week.
The final seat tally will be formalised on Nov 4, and the political parties will be able to file complaints and legal challenges until Nov 18.
Herzog is likely to offer Eisenkot the first chance to form a government, said Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, a non-partisan research group.
Based on Israeli law, and past elections, the party leader who receives the most recommendations from the other leaders who consult with the President is generally given priority, he said.
The election was widely considered a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, and his government, the most hard-right in Israeli history.
It was also the first vote since the Hamas-led attack on Oct 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history, that ignited the devastating war in the Gaza Strip.
Voter turnout was the highest since 1999, but despite widespread public anger over Netanyahu’s refusal to take responsibility for preventing the Oct 7 attacks, the Jewish-led opposition parties failed to secure enough seats to immediately oust him.
Netanyahu outperformed expectations, playing on voters’ fears of Arab political power and potential security threats to win the most votes.
Eisenkot had presented himself as a foil to Netanyahu throughout the campaign, arguing that the Prime Minister was pushing the country toward authoritarianism and destroying its international standing.
Netanyahu’s edge in Parliament presents Eisenkot and his ideologically diverse bloc with a difficult choice: Seek an alliance with Arab parties to topple him or join forces with Netanyahu in a potential unity government.
The process to form a government could be bitter and drawn out, lasting weeks if not months.
Once Herzog selects a candidate, that person has 28 days to negotiate with other factions to try to assemble a governing majority.
A 14-day extension to the deadline can also be requested.
If the first candidate fails, the President can task up to two others to try to form a government.
If they also fall short, new elections will be held.
Herzog, however, said on Oct 28 that everything possible must be done to avoid another election.
Historically, it has typically taken between 20 and 100 days to form a government, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
A number of scenarios have been floated, in addition to a national unity government.
Another is that the opposition bloc reaches out to the Arab parties, whose strong showing could make them major players in the negotiations for the next government.
But most Jewish parties, including those in the opposition bloc, are not keen on that approach.
Many Israeli Jews have long objected to including Arab parties – especially those that are unwilling to back Zionist positions – in any governing coalition.
Both leaders could also try to get parties or individual lawmakers to defect from the rival bloc.
Since the Oct 7 attack, views towards Arab parties have hardened.
Netanyahu repeatedly invoked the spectre of Arab voters throughout his campaign, accusing them of “trying to steal the elections” and galvanising his right-wing base with racially charged language.
For his part, Eisenkot has largely declined to say whether he would partner with Arab parties, but he has said that none of them meet his conditions for joining forces as potential coalition allies.
A deadlock in political negotiations would suit Netanyahu, analysts say, as he would remain caretaker prime minister until the next government is formed.
For many voters, the election result threatens an uncomfortable prospect: A return to the political deadlock that paralysed Israel between 2019 and 2022, when voters headed to the polls five times.
While many supporters of Netanyahu are relieved that he still has a chance to retain power, others who had hoped for his decisive defeat have felt crushed by the possibility of a political stalemate. NYTIMES

Drone attack reportedly kills worker at Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A drone attack on Oct. 29 reportedly killed an employee of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on X.
The victim was reportedly a welder working at the plant's centralized repair workshop, according to the United Nations nuclear watchdog.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that attacks on nuclear plant personnel are unacceptable and violate the agency's Seven Indispensable Pillars for Nuclear Safety and Security during armed conflict.
Grossi renewed his call for maximum military restraint around nuclear facilities to prevent the risk of a nuclear accident.
The IAEA did not specify whether the attack was carried out by Russian or Ukrainian forces, or provide further details.
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, located in the city of Enerhodar in southern Ukraine, is Europe's largest nuclear power plant. It has been under Russian occupation since the start of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The plant has repeatedly faced threats to nuclear safety, including drone attacks, disruptions to external power supplies, and incidents affecting plant workers.
On Oct. 3, the IAEA reported a series of drone attacks that damaged transformers at the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant, threatening the nuclear facility's external electricity supply.
In August, a drone explosion at a bus stop used by plant personnel killed one person and injured 15 others, according to the IAEA.
The agency has maintained a permanent monitoring presence at the Russian-occupied facility since September 2022 over concerns of the risk of a nuclear accident.
The reported death at the nuclear plant came on the same day Russian forces launched multiple missile and drone attacks against the Ukrainian-controlled city of Zaporizhzhia, injuring at least 14 people, including a child, according to Ukraine's National Police.

- The protests reflect wider anger over a social and economic crisis. Experts say young people feel ignored, while the government has promised aid and future plans for under-30 workers.
AI generated
ROME - School and university students are to rally in several Italian cities on Oct 30 to call for more funding for schools and support for housing, with security forces preparing for possible clashes.
Students have been protesting for weeks, setting up tent camps and occupying schools to make their demands heard, matching similar movements across the border in France.
The Italian protests have taken place alongside those of truck drivers and farmers over the spike in fuel prices and the cost of living, as well as rising defence spending.
“On Friday, we expect a massive mobilisation of students, who will block and empty schools,” Laura Teresi, 18, from Rome’s Cavour high school, a spokesperson for the OSA student movement, told AFP.
“We will take to the streets to denounce the rearmament policies of (Prime Minister Giorgia) Meloni’s government and the rising cost of living, which is weighing ever more heavily on families, workers and students,” she added.
The students will also protest against the “endless budget cuts to teaching,” Teresi said.
Officials are worried about a repeat of the violence on Oct 17 and 18 in Milan, the country’s economic capital, where groups of young people set cars on fire and looted shops.
‘Malaise’
On Oct 30, the radical left USB union has called for a general strike.
“The broader Italian and European context is marked by a crisis and a social, economic and cultural malaise affecting different segments of society and different regions,” said Rosario Forlenza, professor of contemporary history and political anthropology at Rome’s Luiss University.
“The younger generation (is)... a generation that is under-represented politically, that sees political leaders’ attention focused elsewhere and therefore lives in a situation of precarity, social distress and even a lack of a future,” Forlenza said.
In response to the youth protests, Meloni’s hard-right government has eased rules on detaining minors and toughened laws on public gatherings.
The government also last week agreed on a €175.2 million (S$250 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
Measures in favour of young people and families are also planned in the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties, such as an annual bonus of €2,500 for workers under 30.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general... who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Meloni said at a press conference on Oct 28, stressing that these measures were “not for those who smash windows”.
Psychologist and psychotherapist Matteo Lancini said part of the problem was schools themselves because they were “totally disconnected” from young people’s needs.
“What we need are schools that change radically, schools that are not designed around adults’ pension systems,” Lancini said at a meeting with the foreign press in Rome.
Instead, “everyone eases their conscience by saying it’s social media’s fault”, he said. AFP

How Trump could interfere in US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

How Trump could interfere in US midterm elections
- Trump’s team may try to affect the US midterms by challenging voter lists, pressuring officials, and sending more federal monitors. Critics fear this could scare voters and disrupt voting.
- Officials also fear federal agents could seize ballots or records during the count, which may slow results and fuel fraud claims. Courts have mostly blocked such legal moves so far.
- After voting, Trump could try to block certification or challenge Democratic wins, but experts say federal law limits this power. Legal teams are ready to fight any interference.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – State officials who run US elections are bracing for further intervention by US President Donald Trump’s administration in next week’s midterms – fearing federal authorities could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block unfavourable results.
Trump, whose Republicans face an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and urged his party to “nationalise” voting in at least 15 places.
The White House says it is protecting election security, and many of the feared scenarios remain hypothetical. The US Constitution gives the president no direct role in running elections, and federal courts have so far rebuffed the administration’s main legal challenges.
Here are the key potential flashpoints:
Before election day
1. Voter eligibility
The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain their voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens. It has lost more than two dozen of those cases.
It has also demanded that ballots be set aside from about 20,000 people in California and more than 400 in Washington state whom it suspects are non-citizens.
A federal judge rejected the California request on Oct 28, saying it would wreak havoc on an election already underway. Washington state has also refused the demand.
Studies have repeatedly found non-citizen voting to be exceptionally rare.
2. Pressure on officials
The Justice Department has warned election officials in every state that they could face prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to vote.
And Trump on Oct 27 offered US$1 million (S$1.3 million) for information leading to a voter fraud conviction, without giving details.
At polling stations
1. Federal monitors
The Justice Department plans to send around 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states – its largest deployment ever.
Monitoring is a decades-old practice, but Democrats and voting rights groups fear monitors could intimidate voters.
The department says they will be unarmed, barred from interfering with voting and drawn from neither the FBI nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
2. Immigration agents and troops
Advocates fear ICE operations near polling stations could deter voters in immigrant communities.
The administration says it is not planning operations targeting polling places, although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents could serve warrants there.
Trump has declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act, which allows the president to deploy troops at home.
A Civil War-era law bars troops and armed federal agents from polling places, and legal experts say an emergency declaration would not give the president power over elections.
Counting the votes
1. Seizing election materials
Federal agents could seek warrants or subpoenas for ballots, voting machines or records – potentially disrupting the count.
In January, the FBI seized ballots and other 2020 election records in Fulton County, Georgia, a focus of Trump’s false claims that he won that year.
Election officials warn that similar action during an active count could undermine safeguards tracking how ballots are handled.
2. Challenging the count
Trump could allege fraud involving mail-in ballots, voting machines or votes counted after election night, fuelling demands for recounts or attempts to halt counting.
But the US Supreme Court ruled in June that states may count mail ballots postmarked by election day that arrive afterward, and courts can intervene against unlawful disruption.
After election day
1. Blocking certification
The Justice Department has sued Alaska to delay certification of its Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, citing a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who it says is trying to confuse voters, which he denies.
Trump said he ordered the lawsuit.
Experts say federal law does not allow the department to block certification, which courts can compel officials to carry out.
2. Challenging Democratic victories
Trump could pressure state officials to dispute results, as he did after losing the 2020 election.
Experts warn unresolved disputes could also delay the seating of newly elected lawmakers in January.
But courts have repeatedly upheld states’ authority over elections, and Democrats and voting rights groups have assembled legal teams to fight any interference. AFP

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition won the most seats in the general election but fell eight short of a parliamentary majority, final results showed Friday. Arab party groupings emerged as potential kingmakers, while allegations of foreign interference threatened to complicate efforts to form a government.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp finished ahead of the opposition but remained well short of a majority, final results from Israel's general election showed Friday, setting the stage for tough coalition talks or potentially another vote.
Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with his Likud party remaining the largest faction with 27 seats.
The opposition bloc, led by centrist Gadi Eisenkot, secured 48 seats.
The results from the Central Elections Committee also cemented the emergence as potential kingmakers of the Arab party groupings Raam and the Joint List, with the two winning a combined 19 seats.
The fragmented outcome sets the stage for difficult negotiations to form a government that could last weeks, with no single bloc able to reach the 61-seat threshold needed and the prospect of another election remaining if talks fail.
The final tally came after Netanyahu's camp spent Thursday amplifying unproven allegations that Arab-Israeli groups received foreign funding to influence the vote, accusations rejected by both Arab-majority lists and Qatar.

Intelligence data: How many Su-34 fighter-bombers has Russia lost, and how many remain in service?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:29:00 UTC
11:29:00 KST

Intelligence data: How many Su-34 fighter-bombers has Russia lost, and how many remain in service?
This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, according to Ukrinform.
As the agency notes, such losses are quite significant for the aggressor country’s aircraft fleet, as its restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation. By way of comparison: the number of Su-34s destroyed is equivalent to approximately 2.5–3 years of their production, based on an estimated production capacity of 14–18 aircraft per year.
As of October 22, according to intelligence data, the Russian Federation’s Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34s of various modifications in service, including the upgraded Su-34M (Su-34NVO).
It is emphasized that the sheer numbers of the Russian Su-34 fleet do not fully reflect its actual combat capability. Such an assessment must take into account a range of factors: the technical condition of the aircraft, the number of trained crews, the intensity of operation, maintenance capabilities, and the ability to replace losses.
According to the Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR), the Su-34s deployed in the war against Ukraine are one of the key components of the enemy’s strike aviation. The use of these aircraft as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the aggressor country to expand its capabilities for striking ground targets, particularly in areas of active combat operations and in settlements near the front lines.
Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernize the Su-34, seeking to maintain the size of its air fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes. The potential for further expansion of this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components, and the ability of the aggressor country’s military-industrial complex to compensate for losses.
Serial production of the Su-34 is concentrated at the V.P. Chkalov Novosibirsk Aviation Plant, which is part of the United Aircraft Corporation of the Russian Federation. The production capacity of this facility allows for the manufacture of approximately 14–18 aircraft of this type per year.
The priority is the production of modernized Su-34Ms, which feature improved onboard equipment and expanded capabilities for the use of airborne weapons. The modernization is intended to enhance the aircraft’s effectiveness, taking into account combat experience gained during the war against Ukraine.
At the same time, production resources are divided between the needs of the Russian military and export orders. In particular, part of the production capacity is dedicated to fulfilling a contract to supply Su-34ME aircraft to Algeria. This places an additional strain on the production system, forcing Russia to balance replenishing its own air fleet with fulfilling international contractual obligations.
“However, between October 22, 2025, and October 22, 2026, 22 new Su-34s were delivered to the Russian Aerospace Forces. This figure exceeds the estimated annual production volume by 14–18 aircraft,” the Main Intelligence Directorate reports.
Intelligence data indicates that during the initial phase of the full-scale invasion, the Russians used the Su-34 primarily to bomb ground targets with unguided aerial bombs, including the FAB-250, FAB-500 M-62, and the concrete-piercing BetAB-500. The use of such weapons required the aircraft to fly close to their targets, which increased their vulnerability to Ukraine’s air defense systems.
At the same time, the enemy began using the Su-34 as a platform for the Kh-31 and Kh-59 guided air-to-air missiles, as well as, in some cases, the Kh-35U anti-ship missiles to strike ground targets.
As noted by the Main Intelligence Directorate, fundamental changes in Russian aviation tactics occurred with the widespread introduction of aerial bombs equipped with a standardized guidance and correction module. The combination of the Su-34 with relatively inexpensive UMPC kits became one of the key factors in the aggressor country’s buildup of its strike aviation capabilities.
These guidance and correction modules enable Russian invaders to convert significant stockpiles of conventional aerial bombs into guided munitions suitable for use from a distance, thereby reducing risks to the carrier aircraft, as the Su-34s can remain outside the engagement ranges of certain Ukrainian air defense systems.
The use of Su-34s in Russia’s “scorched earth” tactics leads to large-scale destruction of infrastructure, civilian casualties, and the forced displacement of survivors from frontline communities.
According to intelligence data, the Russian aircraft manufacturing industry remains dependent on a complex supply chain for electronic components, high-tech equipment, and specialized materials. Of particular importance are components for avionics, navigation systems, communications equipment, and electronic warfare systems, as well as industrial and measuring equipment necessary for the manufacture of modern aircraft.
International sanctions are hindering Russian manufacturers’ access to certain critically important technologies. Under these conditions, the aggressor country continues to use schemes involving intermediary entities, third countries, and alternative import channels to meet the needs of its military-industrial complex.
“In this regard, intensifying sanctions pressure on Russia remains a pressing issue. Specifically, this involves the ability to block mechanisms for circumventing sanctions, strengthen export controls, and restrict Russian companies’ access to critical production technologies for the Russian aircraft manufacturing industry—technologies that allow Moscow to continue its genocidal war against Ukraine,” the Main Intelligence Directorate states.
As reported by Ukrinform, in October, the Russian army suffered record casualties on the front lines.

Dream cruise derailed as fuel crisis puts pressure on global operators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Australian passengers in financial limbo after Odyssey cruise ship runs out of money
In short:
Australian retirees are among passengers caught up in a luxury cruise ship's financial crisis.
Soaring fuel costs have been blamed after the vessel became stranded in Cambodia.
What's next?
Anxious passengers are waiting for answers about the ship's future and whether they will get their money back.
A Queensland woman has handed over $63,500 from her superannuation for a dream retirement at sea — only to watch it unravel before she even stepped onboard.
Lisa McKay was weeks away from joining the luxury residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey when she discovered passengers had been forced off the vessel in Cambodia after it ran out of money.
The former teacher said she feared she would never see her money again after paying for a voyage she hoped would transform her retirement.
"This was going to be my trip of a lifetime," Ms McKay said.
"I don't have that money to waste and lose. It's just been devastating, absolutely devastating."
On Tuesday, more than 200 passengers were told to pack their bags during a scheduled stop in the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville, with the company no longer able to cover the costs of operating the cruise.
The US ship set sail from Belfast in 2024 on a three-and-a-half year round-the-world voyage, promising residents visits to 425 destinations across 147 countries.
"Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement.
Brisbane passenger Rina Cavazza is among those left scrambling to find accommodation and make arrangements to leave Cambodia after being forced off the ship.
Ms Cavazza, who paid $170,000 to live aboard the Odyssey, still had 18 months remaining on her voyage when passengers were told to disembark.
She is now staying in a local hotel and is making arrangements to return to Brisbane.
"It's been a sad time for many," Ms Cavazza said.
"We have had no word and no idea what is happening. I just know that this is our last day of access to the ship and I'll have one opportunity to go back and collect my belongings."
Questions about finances
The bulk of passengers onboard the Florida-based ship were from the US and Canada, according to the Cambodian government.
Some had sold their homes to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars for the years-long cruise, marketed as an alternative to retirement options.
Ms Cavazza said passengers were asked for funds to help pay for fuel, as far back as February and again, just before docking in Cambodia.
"Some people paid hundreds of thousands of dollars extra to help out with fuel," Ms Cavazza said.
Ms McKay, a former Brisbane school teacher, said she used her superannuation to pay for the trip via a direct bank transfer, and was due to board in Kuala Lumpur on November 15.
She said she had concerns about the company's finances after reading negative comments online and raised them with a booking agent, before paying.
In messages seen by the ABC, the booking agent said she "wouldn't be working for them if [she] thought they were in trouble" and that if the ship could no longer operate, the "company would arrange another ship".
"My chances of getting my money back [are] very, very slim," Ms McKay said.
"Travel insurance doesn't cover boutique ships."
Sign of things to come
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said monthly fuel costs per cabin had averaged about $US1,800 but were now $US6,000 to $US8,000 in parts of Asia, due to the ongoing war in Iran.
"The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," it said.
It is not the only cruise company feeling the fuel crunch.
The world's largest cruise operator, Carnival Corporation, said higher fuel prices had added about $US150 million to its 2026 outlook.
The company recently announced it was halving its fleet in Australia next year.
Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.
Royal Caribbean said its fuel costs rose 27 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, from $US279 million to $US355 million.

The Centre is seeking detailed records from three Delhi medical institutions as an expert panel reviews summer and winter vacations for govt medical colleges faculty.An expert committee constituted by Union health ministry to examine vacation and academic/on-duty leave arrangements for Central Health Service (CHS) teaching doctors had held its first meeting on Aug 31, according to official documents.The ministry sought information from Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, ABVIMS and Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, and Lady Hardinge Medical College and its associated hospitals. Institutions must also provide monthly data on outpatient attendance, admissions, ICU occupancy and surgeries for 2024-25 and 2025-26.The committee will assess whether the existing 50% faculty roster ensures uninterrupted patient care and whether vacations affect undergraduate and postgraduate teaching, examinations, research and academic administration.Sources alleged that some doctors combine vacations with academic leave and child care leave (CCL), extending their absence from work. These allegations could not be established from the official documents and require documentary verification and a response from those concerned.
Sources also questioned whether faculty in certain central govt medical colleges face vacation and administrative rules that are not applied in the same way at institutions such as AIIMS, PGI and UCMS. The extent of any differences in the applicable rules remains to be established.The ministry is also seeking details of outcomes from academic/on-duty leave, including research publications, grants, new projects, teaching initiatives and clinical skills acquired. The committee is gathering data to assess the existing arrangements.

Ukrainian units conducting long-range strikes were instructed to suspend new missions against Russian refineries after completing operations already underway.
The decision came amid mounting tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Washington increasingly frustrated by Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy sector as diesel prices reached record highs.
The reported suspension has not been independently confirmed.
Trump sought a 30-day halt to refinery strikes
According to the WSJ, Trump’s adviser Jared Kushner pressed Ukrainian officials to halt refinery attacks for 30 days as a gesture of appreciation for Washington’s diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war.
Kyiv sought assurances that Russia would reciprocate by suspending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure or that Washington would provide additional Patriot air defense missiles.
Neither proposal produced a breakthrough, the report said.
European allies also encouraged Ukraine to exercise restraint, amid concerns about rising fuel costs and further deterioration in relations between Kyiv and the White House.

The pressure intensified after Trump publicly criticized Zelensky earlier this month, calling for Ukraine to replace its president and demanding an end to strikes on Russian oil facilities.

The remarks came as Trump announced an arrangement to increase purchases of Russian diesel and ease sanctions affecting Moscow.
The developments raised concerns in Kyiv that Washington was reducing economic pressure on Russia while demanding restraint from Ukraine.
Russia continues striking Ukrainian cities and energy facilities
The reported pause comes as Moscow continues its campaign of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure, raising fears of widespread power and heating disruptions ahead of winter.
Russian forces launched another wave of attacks on Thursday, Oct. 29, killing civilians and damaging infrastructure across several Ukrainian cities.
In Dnipro, a Russian drone struck a crowded railway platform, killing at least 14 people. Additional attacks struck Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, while a late-night ballistic missile strike on Kyiv killed at least one person.
The continued bombardment highlights the absence of a reciprocal arrangement under which Russia would halt attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in exchange for Kyiv suspending strikes on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has repeatedly defended its long-range drone campaign as a means of disrupting Russia’s war economy and responding to Moscow’s attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have enabled strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting refineries and other energy facilities far from the front lines.
The campaign has become an important tool for Kyiv to impose economic and logistical costs on Russia despite its smaller military and limited access to Western long-range weapons.
Ukraine’s dependence on US support complicates its position
The Journal reported that Ukraine’s reliance on American military assistance, intelligence-sharing and communications technology has made Kyiv vulnerable to pressure from Washington.
The deterioration in relations coincided with restrictions on Ukraine’s use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which temporarily disrupted some Ukrainian drone operations and air defense capabilities before service was restored.
Ukraine also depends on US-supplied Patriot air defense systems and interceptors to protect cities and critical infrastructure against Russian ballistic missiles.
According to the Journal, the dispute has further weakened Ukrainian confidence in Washington’s commitment to supporting Kyiv.
Midterm elections and US peace efforts
The timing of the reported suspension coincides with the final days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, when high fuel prices have become a sensitive domestic political issue for the Trump administration.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising diesel prices, although energy analysts point to the war in Iran and broader disruptions to global oil markets as the main drivers of the surge.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the suspension could last beyond the elections.
The reported pause raises questions about why Ukraine is being pressed to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities while Moscow faces no comparable pressure to stop its relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

New Sydney rail line opens to commuters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:07:52 CST
11:07:52 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The final stage of a major Sydney rail project opened to commuters on Friday morning after nine years of construction, connecting the city's southwest suburbs to the northwest.
The first service on the Southwest Metro line departed Bankstown Station, 16 km southwest of central Sydney, at 4:31 a.m. local time on Friday, making 10 stops at new stations on the way to connecting to the Metro City Line, which opened in 2024, at Sydenham in the city's inner-west.
The completion of the new line means that driverless trains can travel directly along 66 km of track from Bankstown to Tallawong, 36 km northwest of central Sydney, via the CBD and a tunnel under the Sydney harbor.
Construction on the project began in 2017 and cost 23 billion Australian dollars (about 16.2 billion U.S. dollars), up from an initial estimate of 11.5 billion AUD.
Services on the new line will operate every four minutes during peak commuter hours, every five minutes outside those times on weekdays and every 10 minutes on weekends and evenings.
A further expansion of the new underground metro network connecting the major population center of Parramatta, 20 km west of central Sydney, to the CBD is expected to open in 2032. ■

New Zealand voter enrolment rate falls below previous election levels
China
Unknown Publisher

10:07:47 CST
11:07:47 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 3.8 million people have enrolled to vote in New Zealand's 2026 general election scheduled for Nov. 7, with the provisional enrolment rate at 93.6 percent, below the final rates recorded in the previous two elections.
The Electoral Commission said on Friday that the enrolment rates were 94.7 percent in 2023 and 94.1 percent in 2020. The final rate for this year's election will not be confirmed until after voting ends.
The provisional enrolment rate for people aged 18 to 24 was 74.2 percent, up from 53.9 percent at the end of July and close to the 76.7 percent recorded in 2023, the commission said in a statement.
Among voters of Maori descent, the provisional enrolment rate was 85.9 percent, with 603,968 Maori voters enrolled, up from 567,012 in 2023, according to the commission.
Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said the figures showed awareness of the new requirement to enroll before voting began. He said the commission would review its efforts to increase enrolment and report back to parliament after the election.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National Party is seeking a second term after taking office in 2023, while Labor, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, is campaigning to return to power amid public concerns over the cost of living, economic growth, jobs and public services.
Meanwhile, 309,876 people cast advance votes in the first three days of voting, which started on Monday, up from 235,515 in the same period in 2023, the commission said.
More than 2,300 voting places are expected to operate nationwide on election day. Official election results are scheduled to be declared on Nov. 27.
New Zealand citizens or permanent residents aged 18 or above, who have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in their life, are eligible to vote in the election, according to the commission. ■

Hackers exploit PHP flaws to seize servers in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:06:26 UTC
11:06:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan was among the targets of a recent hacking campaign that exploited PHP flaws to seize servers, according to a new report that says the operation bears signs of a nation-state effort.
Israeli AI firm Dream released a report Monday detailing how an AI-assisted campaign in October identified and took full control of 25 Palo Alto Networks firewall and management servers across Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and the US. The report said the selection of targets indicated “potential nation-state adversary efforts,” adding that the four countries are China’s primary geopolitical rivals.
The campaign exploited PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP that prompted Taiwan’s Administration for Cyber Security (ACS) to call for software updates across government agencies and businesses last week. The vulnerabilities in the programming language allow attackers to execute code remotely without authentication.
In the latest campaign, 22 compromised firewalls across the four countries were left with hidden backdoors that allow return access and are “ready for exploitation at any time.” Three servers in a US government-affiliated environment were singled out for deeper intrusion.
Taiwan’s ACS said Friday that companies have been fixing their systems and updating PHP in light of the critical flaws.
Dream did not attribute the activity to a specific actor but pointed out that the operation ran on China Standard Time and that the attackers used FOFA, a Chinese search engine, to find targets.
The report also found signs that hackers used AI tools while developing code, including an installation of Claude Code and settings configured for the Chinese language models DeepSeek and Kimi.
The findings follow what experts said may have been the first known end-to-end autonomous cyberattack against Taiwan’s government systems using AI. Dream, which exposed that operation in August, said at the time that evidence “points to a Chinese-language operator.”

====================================================================================================

Loving someone with dementia is hilarious and heartbreaking in new show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Before I Forget celebrates humour, aging and Blak matriachy on the main stage
As Kamarra Bell-Wykes's mother's dementia worsened, the playwright began developing what would eventually become Melbourne Theatre Company's latest play, Before I Forget.
The Yagera/Badtjala/Butchulla theatre-maker's mother was Jeanie Bell, a prominent Aboriginal linguist and academic who played a critical role in language reclamation. She has since passed, but her presence looms large in the play.
"Sometimes I could just hear mum talking to me as I was writing," Bell-Wykes tells ABC News.
The story centres on three women: Faith (Roxanne McDonald), based on her mother; Faith's daughter Karma (Melodie Reynolds-Diarra); and her granddaughter, Hope (Tyallah Bullock).
The names poetically hint at their character arcs and mirror the intergenerational connection between Bell-Wykes, her mother and her daughter.
Translating personal truth into fiction
Bell-Wykes brought together a trusted team of creatives on stage and behind the scenes to add a familial feel to the production. McDonald, who plays Faith, knew Dr Jeanie Bell and translated some of her mannerisms into the character.
"When you're an actor, you study people, whether you do it in a conscious or unconscious way," says McDonald.
"Jeanie just embodied the community and took everyone in. I just remember her laugh. It brings back all these beautiful fond memories back for me."
Bell-Wykes also has long-standing friendships with Reynolds-Diarra and frequent creative collaborator Carly Shepherd, who is the assistant director.
She candidly admits directing was a "black-mirror experience"; she had to be well past her grieving process to enter that metaphorical and physical space.
Despite the play grappling with death, Bell-Wykes found ways to inject humour into the dialogue; her mother's larger-than-life personality provided ample material for laughs.
"Particularly for Blackfullas, humour is a natural part of our communities, our lives. We use it as a survival mechanism; we are naturally funny people," Bell-Wykes remarks.
"Dementia is a hilarious, heartbreaking disease."
The challenge was to navigate how much of her own personal truth to embed into the characters and stories, and what aspects to dramatise, while still making it feel authentic.
"How do you protect the people that are passed and are still alive, while also telling a good story? It's been a very slow, careful process," Bell-Wykes says.
Matriarchy, motherhood and preserving legacy for future generations
Jeanie Bell's significant legacy in preserving Aboriginal language is imbued through integrating Butchulla and Gubbi Gubbi dialogue in the play.
Reynolds-Diarra describes the impact of Dr Bell's work on future generations with admiration, ensuring the community could proudly speak their language on Country again.
"She was more than just the typical matriarch of the family; she was also preparing her community with tools that could help them in the whiter societies," says Reynolds-Diarra.
"My mum's legacy does exist in a written form, and I have been reconnecting with my matriarchal knowledge through the process of this play," Bell-Wykes shares.
Since colonisation, Aboriginal women have been essential to keeping families together and on Country, which can also be a source of intergenerational trauma.
When mothers pass away, families can drift apart. Grandmothers also play a pivotal role in raising children, with Bullock, McDonald and Reynolds-Diarra noting the influence this had on their upbringing.
"I think within that direct lineage from the grandmother to the grandchild, there's something that's passed down specifically through that; I suppose it's the strength," says Reynolds-Diarra.
"Even with my mum being passed away, she is now teaching me language and teaching my daughter," says Bell-Wykes.
Bullock notes the role that Elders play in communities, particularly in relation to younger generations — represented in the character of Hope.
"It's taking authority of your culture and actually embodying it, finding ways that you've grown up knowing about it, but then taking courage and steps to actually go beyond that, follow your ancestors," says Bullock.
An Indigenous play with a universal story
Caring is a core part of the story, and the cyclical nature of it. How do you care for the ones that once cared for us? Despite the play focusing on an Aboriginal family, the universal themes of mothers and daughters, as well as loss, will connect to audiences from all walks of life.
"This play is about our daughters becoming our mothers and our mothers becoming our daughters. But that's also part of our kinship systems. Our grandmothers come back as our grandchildren … even though our little ones are there to learn from us, they are also there to teach us," says Bell-Wykes.
Loading...
"This is a universal story about love and acceptance and forgiveness; of death, and celebrating the lives that we have and always taking that knowledge with us."
Bell-Wykes responds directly when asked how her play will take audiences on an unforgettable emotional journey.
"Get 'em laughing, punch 'em in the guts."
Before I Forget is at Melbourne Theatre Company until November 28.

WASHINGTON – Nearly nine in 10 Americans believe government corruption is widespread – a consensus Democrats hope to capitalise on as voters make up their minds on whether to keep billionaire Donald Trump’s Republicans in power.
Former president Barack Obama has hammered the message home in recent days as he stumps for Democratic candidates in must-win states, hoping to flip control of Congress.
Trump “is very much focused on enriching himself and his family and his cronies”, Obama told a rally on Oct 28 in Georgia.
“The guy has made billions of dollars while in office.”
“We have never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this,” Obama added, echoing a speech he made days earlier in Michigan, another swing state.
Ray La Raja, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, said Democrats’ goal with such anti-corruption rhetoric is partly about “energising the base” of steadfast Democrats to make sure they vote.
But it also aims to create a “narrative to get those swing voters, those persuadable independents” who are generally upset about the economy, to “come out” on Nov 3.
Some Republican voters also “might be so demoralised, they won’t show up”, La Raja added.
Who’s to blame?
Democrats head into the midterm elections with high expectations, as the party of a sitting president historically loses seats – Trump’s approval ratings are at record lows – and there is broad discontent over high prices.
Meanwhile, a Gallup poll released in September showed 89% of Americans believe there is widespread government corruption in the United States – 10 percentage points higher than in 2025 and the highest level in 20 years.
The spikes in perceptions of corruption were most elevated among Democrats, according to the poll.
La Raja said that the most important issue for voters, always, is economics, and most people now believe those conditions are not good.
“And they’re looking for why. Who’s to blame for this? And corruption is one of those narratives that works,” he said.
Democratic leaders hope to funnel that anger at soaring gas and grocery costs toward Trump, while highlighting, like Obama did, that the president’s net worth has risen by billions of dollars since he began his second term.
“There’s a direct link between the unbelievable levels of corruption and the continued rise in the cost of living,” Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, said in September.
Trump has also repeatedly accused his political opponents of wrongdoing, though his attacks primarily focus on alleged election fraud.
He has denied any conflicts of interest or that he has been involved in his family’s business deals since taking office.
Watergate?
Nonetheless, he openly blurs the lines between government and personal business – a prime example being the choice of his own golf resort to host an upcoming G-20 summit.
He has also faced scrutiny over his historically high number of stock trades, contracts being inked by his family around the world, and the peculiar gift of a free luxury jet by Qatar to be used as Air Force One.
But none of the scandals with whiffs of corruption have so far triggered sensational backlash comparable to the Watergate saga, which led to Richard Nixon’s resignation in 1974.
Could Trump be getting a pass due to his businessman background, or are there deeper shifts in how the public and media perceive alleged corruption?
Trump’s vice-president, J.D. Vance, remarked that had such a scandal as Watergate occurred nowadays “it would be like a 12-hour news story”.
“The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy,” the likely 2028 presidential contender added. AFP

European Council President António Costa speaks alongside Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney during a roundtable with business leaders at the EU-Canada Summit in Montreal on Oct. 29, 2026. | Christopher Katsarov/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing.
Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals.
“Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa.
Advertisement
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.
“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.
Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.
But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.
A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Advertisement
Diplomatic balance
Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues.
Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations.
The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision”
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas signs the EU-Canada Host Country Agreement with Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand in Montreal on Oct. 29, 2026. | Christinne Muschi/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end.
By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.”
Advertisement
The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects.
Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.”
AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy.

New York state police to take over sexual assault complaints at Cornell

By Daniel Trotta
Oct 29 (Reuters) - New York state police will take over future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University, Governor Kathy Hochul said on Thursday, in the latest fallout over the university’s handling of an alleged gang-rape on campus.
The announcement follows widespread criticism of the university’s conduct in the case and questions about why no criminal charges were filed after a woman identified only as Jane Doe said she was raped by members of a Cornell fraternity.
New York state police and Cornell University signed an agreement that sexual offense complaints, which normally fall under the jurisdiction of campus police, will be referred to state police for criminal investigation unless otherwise requested by the accuser, Hochul said in a statement.
“When someone reports sexual assault, they deserve to be heard, treated with compassion, and know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated,” Hochul said in her announcement.
Referring to the Jane Doe allegations as “horrifying,” Hochul said: “Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them. We cannot afford to let them down.”
Hochul previously named Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to reopen the criminal investigation into Jane Doe’s complaint, and a committee of Cornell’s board of trustees appointed former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a review of the university’s response to sexual assault claims.
NO CONFIDENCE VOTE UNDERWAY
Jane Doe said she was drugged and gang-raped during a visit to the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, according to a civil lawsuit filed this year.
Fraternity members pressured her to take ketamine and sexually assaulted her over several hours while she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit alleges, naming seven former students.
Attorneys for the fraternity members have denied the allegations. Some of the attorneys have said the sexual activity was consensual, while others have disputed their clients’ participation in the events described in the lawsuit.
Although Cornell expelled or disciplined several of the students involved in the incident, no criminal charges were filed.
The lawsuit triggered widespread criticism of the university in Ithaca, New York, with students, alumni and advocates calling for greater transparency about how the school handles sexual assault claims.
Cornell’s Faculty Senate is currently moving forward with a vote of no confidence against the university administration. About 135 members of the governing body can vote on the non-binding resolution from Friday until November 6, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.
“The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution reads.
(Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, California; Editing by Tom Hogue)

Trump DOJ issues subpoenas in California noncitizen voting probe, escalating pressure campaign
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:50:28 CET
10:50:28 KST

By Andrew Goudsward
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration has demanded records from California as part of a criminal investigation into alleged voting by noncitizens – escalating its battle with the largest US state ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.
The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received federal grand jury subpoenas last week seeking information about the agency’s methods for detecting “unlawful voting by aliens” and preventing such ballots from being counted, according to copies of the subpoenas seen by Reuters on Thursday.
The Trump Justice Department has heaped pressure on California over alleged noncitizen voting, filing a civil lawsuit against the state and sending a series of letters this month warning election officials that they risk criminal exposure if they do not verify voters’ citizenship status.
The subpoenas also seek records related to Los Angeles County’s response to those letters, according to the documents.
The demands are part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration to identify cases of voter fraud, raising concerns among Democrats and other critics that Trump could use the issue to sow doubt about the results of the election, which will determine control of Congress.
“At every step, the US Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach,” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement on Thursday. “Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”
It was not immediately clear if Logan’s office was the focus of the investigation.
LEGAL BATTLE
Though studies have repeatedly shown that voting by noncitizens is rare and has no impact on election results, the Trump administration has intensely focused on the issue.
The Justice Department has charged 156 immigrants with voting or registering to vote unlawfully in a pre-midterm push, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters on Thursday. The agency has used subpoenas to state and local election officials to build such cases.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the latest subpoenas but said that California and the federal government “agree that noncitizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law.”
On Wednesday, a federal judge rejected a Justice Department request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from a list of 20,000 voters the administration alleges are likely noncitizens. The DOJ has appealed the ruling.
Lawyers for California have questioned the reliability of the Trump administration’s immigration data and argued that the federal government does not have the authority to intervene in its elections.
Under the US Constitution, states administer elections and not the federal government.
Before ruling against the DOJ, US District Judge David Carter told agency lawyers at a hearing on Tuesday that the “court believes that it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately.”
(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Stephen Coates)
