Reddit shares sink on weak sales guidance and plans login requirement test as Google search traffic shrinks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:01:02 UTC
08:01:02 KST

Reddit plans to require all users to create official accounts to access the social media platform, marking a major departure for the site known as "the front page of the internet." 
The company revealed the change Thursday as part of its third-quarter earnings, in which it beat on the top and bottom lines, but provided weak fourth-quarter sales guidance. The company's shares dropped over 15% after its numbers were released.
Here's how the company did compared with LSEG estimates:
- Earnings per share: $1.40 vs. $1.35 expected
- Revenue: $895 million vs. $878 million expected
Reddit CEO Steve Huffman told CNBC in an interview that the company's shrinking search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to the "shift to AI mode and AI overviews." The traffic decline played a big role in Reddit's planned efforts to require people to become logged-in users.
A previous Google search update designed to surface "authentic" content from internet forums helped Reddit grow its user base over the past few years, but the search giant's continued push on AI overviews and related chatting features has negatively impacted referral traffic.
"I think fundamentally that relationship between Google and the rest of the internet is evolving, and so for us, this means a continued focus on our core users that come to Reddit directly," Huffman said.
Previous Google algorithm changes would "kind of come and go," Huffman said, but the company's AI efforts represent "a fundamental shift in how the Google product works, from being a traffic driver to whatever's going on now."
The CEO didn't provide any specific timing on when Reddit plans for the platform registration change, saying only that implementing it through the site would involve a lot of complexity. The company will begin testing in the fourth quarter outside of the U.S.
He said that Reddit is still determining what parts of the service logged-out users will be able to see, and will iron out the details as part of its upcoming testing.
Reddit said that daily active uniques, or DAUq, rose 12% year-over-year to 130.3 million in the third quarter, trailing Wall Street estimates of 133.7 million. U.S.-specific DAUq dropped 2% year-over-year to 50.7 million, which was below analyst projections of 53.5 million.
Huffman said that "search referral traffic is down meaningfully in this quarter" and that the trend will continue in the fourth quarter.
He said that Reddit is continuing its effort to make its platform "a daily habit" for users. "So that's where our focus is: growing those app users and logged-in users," Huffman said.
Reddit, which derives the bulk of its overall sales from online advertising, is able to monetize logged-ln users better than logged-out users, because those registered users are more active and valuable to advertisers itching to deliver more targeted ads.
"The vast majority of our revenue comes from our app users and logged-in users are direct traffic, and both of those are up Q. over Q. and so that's where our focus is," Huffman said.
The company's third-quarter sales grew 53% year-over-year, marking an end to the eight-straight quarters of revenue growth eclipsing 60% that it reported in July as part of its second-quarter earnings.
Reddit said that fourth-quarter sales will come in a range of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, which was below Wall Street estimates of $1.05 billion.
"It's still a strong guide," Huffman said about its revenue guidance. "We are still growing at an industry leading rate, and that's despite the headwinds from search referrals."
Reddit's third-quarter average revenue per user, or ARPU, came in at $6.87, which was higher than the $6.50 that analysts were expecting.
The company's "other revenue" segment, which includes its data-licensing business, jumped 35% year-over-year to $48 million in the third quarter. Reddit's two biggest data-licensing partners are OpenAI and Google.
Huffman said that Reddit remains "in negotiations" with Google over its data-licensing agreement, and said that it is "only going to do a deal that makes sense for Reddit," if it chooses to continue the partnership.
"I think there's a lot of strategic considerations that goes into that," Huffman said.
Huffman called the required registration plan a "big change" for himself, considering he "grew up on the open Internet."
"Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me, I've been holding that line," Huffman, a Reddit co-founder, said. "I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work."
Huffman later expanded on the significance of AI's impact on Reddit's user growth in an earnings call with analysts, and explained that the company plans to continue spending on marketing efforts intended to offset search-referral declines. 
"This is a consequential time for Reddit, and this period does remind me of about 11 years ago when I came back to the company," Huffman told analysts, referring to when he rejoined Reddit in 2015 following it's then-chief Ellen Pao stepping down. "We had a lot of conversations then about what is Reddit and what is Reddit for, and what is our place in this ecosystem. And we've been having those conversations at Reddit recently." 
"Reddit's mission is to create community and belonging for everyone in the world, and while there's overlap between Reddit and other players in the ecosystem, whether we're talking about social media or AI search, fundamentally, Reddit is communities and conversations," Huffman said.

Youth theatre raises more than $68k to carry forward 50-year legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Sydney theatre Shopfront Arts Co-Op has empowered young people for 50 years
Joining Shopfront Arts Co-Op changed Paul Capsis's life.
Fresh out of high school, the writer and performer — known for the 1998 movie Head On — was dragged by a friend to watch a show at the youth theatre in southern Sydney in 1983.
Seeing performers his own age on stage was "remarkable", he recalls.
"It was a magical experience," he says. "I was like, 'What have I been missing out on all these years?'"
After the show, Shopfront's co-founder, director Errol Bray, invited him to get involved in its upcoming production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
The theatre became a refuge after Capsis's difficult school years.
"I was severely bullied," he says. "You start to think that is how the world is going to be outside."
At Shopfront, Capsis began writing and performing in his own shows, created in collaboration with other young people in the company.
"It was a major thing to be with people that liked me," he says. "We laughed and we performed and we hung out.
"It was healing after my horrific years at high school."
The youth theatre that shaped Capsis's life turned 50 this month.
Over the past five decades, it has kick-started the careers of artists including Olivier Award-nominated performer Trevor Ashley, former Sydney Theatre Company artistic director Andrew Upton, and playwright Hilary Bell.
It also continues to empower young people as performers, writers and decision-makers, and has also been acknowledged by the wider industry at the Sydney Theatre Awards.
Making big things happen
One of its award-winning shows, The Lies We Were Told, created with Australian Theatre for Young People, was remounted at the Sydney Opera House this month in celebration of the company's 50th anniversary.
It followed a youth conference, featuring Heartbreak High star Thomas Weatherall and musician Dobby, and a 50-hour act-a-thon fundraiser, which aimed to raise $50,000 for the theatre. It raised more than $68,000.
The act-a-thon was a fitting tribute to the company's punk past, not only bringing together alumni with the current ensemble, but replicating its successful fundraiser of 1978.
That year, to avoid eviction, the young people of Shopfront resolved to buy the building and raised a $43,000 deposit through an act-a-thon, raffles and government support.
It is a history Shopfront's Young Leader, Liv Tsigaropoulos, who works as a conduit between the theatre's staff and young people, knows well.
When she was in Year 9, she made a mini documentary about the theatre for the National History Challenge, which won her the national Democracy Matters award.
By then, she had already been part of Shopfront for a couple of years, having started when she was 13.
Now 19, she's thrilled to be a custodian of the company during its anniversary year.
"It's the best time to be Young Leader," she says.
"It's such a full-circle thing. I remember reading about the act-a-thon when I was doing my research."
The performance of The Lies We Were Told is part of that full-circle feeling; Tsigaropoulos auditioned for that show when she first joined Shopfront in 2021.
"Since that, I never left, and they could never get rid of me," she says.
Over her six years with the theatre, she has participated in its drama workshops, made short films, learned about technical production, and joined one of its five advisory panels.
For Tsigaropoulos, the special thing about being part of the theatre is the lengths it will go to bring a young person's ideas to life.
She recalls how that gave her the "confidence to stand by [her] ideas".
"In a space like Shopfront, you can say a crazy, big, unrealistic or impossible goal, and the Shopfront staff make it happen," she says.
"You're gonna see your words expressed on stage, what you think expressed on stage, and that's so special … People watch it and laugh and cry."
For example, she suggested she start a show stuck outside.
"It was so silly," she says. "I was like, 'I've missed the show.'
"It's small things I think are funny or cool and would want to see. Getting that put in a show is really fulfilling."
Now, it is up to her as Young Leader to help make those things happen for the next generation of young people.
"The only thing more beautiful than [your idea being brought to life] is working at Shopfront, and a young person tells you an idea, and you make it happen," Tsigaropoulos says.
The next 50 years
The money from the fundraiser will help Shopfront keep bringing young people's ideas to life at a time when funding for arts companies can be precarious.
It is something Shopfront knows all too well, having lost multi-year funding from the federal government alongside many youth arts companies in 2016, and again in 2021.
Shopfront is currently receiving funding from Creative Australia and Create NSW.
The money raised will also help the theatre stay open to everyone, through scholarships and free tickets to performances.
"We never turn young people away if they can't afford it," Tsigaropoulos says.
"We'd rather lose money and let a young person come for free and get to experience Shopfront."
Capsis recalls his own fundraising efforts for Shopfront, standing on a box outside Hurstville Station, singing Janis Joplin.
"We're raising money, we're making shows, and that became my blueprint," he says.
"The big world of professional theatre and musical theatre didn't see me as somebody they wanted, so I made my own work."
It was his training ground, which saw him tour shows to the UK and Canada, and sing on stage for the first time.
"Some people go to NIDA [National Institute of Dramatic Art] and they do three years intensive," Capsis says. "I did Shopfront theatre one night a week and every weekend."
It also helped him make connections, including with Hilary Bell and Julian Meyrick, who collaborated on his award-winning one-man show about his Maltese grandmother, Angela's Kitchen.
"It all comes from Shopfront," he says.
For Capsis, what sticks out is how the theatre empowered him and the young people around him.
"I think it's extremely important young people have a place to voice how they feel, and to learn," he says.
That centring of young people may be what's behind the longevity of Shopfront Arts Co-op, Australia's longest-running and only youth-owned and led theatre company.
"[That longevity is] a testament to all the people who have ever come through Shopfront and the determination, the belief they have in amplifying young people's voices, and that has stayed at its centre since the very beginning," Tsigaropoulos says.
She adds empowering young people remains important, even if they don't want to pursue careers in the arts.
"We're not an acting school pumping out mini DiCaprios and Margot Robbies," Tsigaropoulos says.
"[But] it gives a lot of people a place where they feel they belong and feel welcome and feel accepted."

US agency votes to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:56:00 UTC
07:56:00 KST

US agency votes to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics
- FCC votes to bar Chinese labs from testing US electronics, including phones, cameras and computers, over national security concerns and lack of reciprocal access.
- Chair Brendan Carr said 82% of electronics were tested in China in 2025, and warned labs could expose sensitive data, admit insecure gear, or steal intellectual property.
- The ban starts in December 2028. It adds to wider US action against Chinese tech, including restrictions on drones, routers, and firms such as Huawei and ZTE.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Oct 29 voted to bar all Chinese labs from testing electronic devices including smartphones, cameras and computers for use in the US, expanding a previous agency action targeting Beijing.
The FCC said it will prohibit test labs and certification bodies in countries including China that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based test labs. The FCC prohibitions are slated to take effect in December 2028. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said that in 2025, 82% of electronics were tested in China, which does not have an agreement with the US.
“These labs are a critical gateway into American communications infrastructure – and their privileged role gives them access to sensitive and confidential information about electronic products often months before the devices enter the market,” Carr said, adding they could “allow insecure gear into the US market, disrupt communications networks, or even steal intellectual property”.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In 2025, the FCC banned testing of US electronics by labs owned or controlled by the Chinese government, and several dozen labs were barred.
About 4% of all electronic devices are tested in labs inside the US, Carr said.
Separately, the FCC streamlined its approval process for devices tested in US labs or labs from countries not posing national security risks.
This is the latest move by Washington to crack down on China over technology issues and equipment.
In December, the FCC banned the import of all new models of Chinese drones and also has banned imports of new models of Chinese-made consumer routers, the boxes connecting computers, phones and smart devices to the internet.
In July, the FCC voted to bar sales of devices in the US that contain key hardware from Chinese companies deemed to be national security risks.
The FCC maintains a list of firms, including Chinese telecom company Huawei and ZTE, whose equipment is barred for sale in the US due to national security concerns.
In June, the FCC banned the import of more equipment from a group of Chinese manufacturers including Huawei and ZTE and has proposed to ban the import of most military-grade drones. REUTERS

NCLT, NCLAT hijacked by corporate affairs ministry: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:55:05 UTC
07:55:05 KST

SC slammed the corporate affairs ministry for "completely hijacking" NCLT and NCLAT, citing infrastructure failures, large vacancies and contractual hiring that undermine the tribunals' autonomy.
New Delhi: In an outburst sure to embarrass the govt, Supreme Court Thursday slammed the ministry of corporate affairs for “completely hijacking” the two most important quasi-judicial financial adjudicatory bodies – National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the appellate NCLAT.The stinging remarks came from a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing petitioners who have been complaining for the last few months about the shoddy infrastructure, lack of support staff and large vacancies hampering the work in NCLT, which in the financial year 2024-25 had approved resolution plans worth Rs 55,000 crore. The tribunal adjudicates corporate civil disputes, company law violations and insolvency proceedings.“The system, the tribunals, we are compelled to observe, has been completely hijacked by the ministry of corporate affairs. That is the problem. And that is impinging on the autonomy of these institutions. These are the things we must look into. The ministry wants to have a complete whip over these tribunals. That is what is most unfortunate,” said the CJI.The bench has sought detailed proposals on infrastructure and staffing from the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT in four weeks.
Contractual employees harassing judicial members, let past and present staff go: SC
Appearing for NCLT Bar Association, senior advocate Sanjiv Sen said the roofs of certain floors in the building housing NCLT are collapsing and have become unusable. A large number of posts of judicial and technical members are lying vacant, he said, adding that the most unfortunate part is that out of 320 regular posts in NCLT, 253 are vacant.At this juncture, senior advocate Meenakshi Arora said the ministry has outsourced recruitment of contractual employees to a foreign firm and that could jeopardise the integrity of the important financial adjudicatory body. She said the existing contractual employees have already rendered service for eight years and must not be displaced.CJI Kant said, “We are not approving contractual recruitment of employees. It must be done through the Union Public Service Commission or Staff Selection Commission.” When Arora said termination of contractual employees must be stayed, the bench said, “We will not do any such thing at the behest of contractual staff. We would like to give full autonomy to the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT on this issue. The only thing is how soon it should happen.”The CJI said, “Contractual employment means backdoor entry. In Bombay for instance, I know how these contractual employees ran away with original files and FIRs had to be registered. They do not care about the judicial members or technical members. Some technical members are still manipulating certain things.”
“But these contractual employees are harassing the judicial members. So let the past and present contractual employees go. Let the autonomy of recruitment be with the president of the tribunals.... The heads of these tribunals are the most suitable persons to assist us in suggesting ways and means to smoothen and strengthen the day-to-day functioning of these two important tribunals, including requirements of land and buildings and safekeep of records.”

Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:46:19 UTC
07:46:19 KST

Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Oct 29 - El Salvador's deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, is the first major overseas test of President Nayib Bukele's anti-gang tactics.
Around 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were in Haiti as of Wednesday night, a security official told Reuters. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said these would for now be capped at 2,500. Yet authorities have not clarified the troops' command, or rules of engagement, fueling concerns of more risks to civilians in a country with a long history of harmful foreign interventions.
Bukele billed the deployments as a rescue mission for four aircraft technicians who were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. They have been missing since they jumped from a burning vehicle during the ambush in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.
Haitian and Salvadoran authorities have said the troops' main mission is to rescue the missing technicians. But the deployment's size - matching in 10 days what the UN-backed force struggled to deploy over more than a year - has prompted questions over whether the soldiers could be part of a broader and longer-term operation.
On Thursday, Bukele said the deployments were nearly finished and his government was covering 90% of the costs.
Bukele, in office since 2019, won huge popularity at home with tough-on-crime policies, including a gang crackdown that relied heavily on mass incarceration. Other governments have sought to replicate his approach, despite rights activists' warnings over due process and innocent deaths.
Bukele would, however, likely encounter a profoundly different security environment in Haiti, analysts warned, as institutions have been whittled down by corruption and faltering funds, prisons are vastly overcrowded, the judiciary paralyzed and many gang recruits are underage.
"This could help increase support for Bukele if this helps his narrative of being an anti-gang force in the region and delivering results," said Maria Fernanda Arocha, an analyst at conflict monitoring group ACLED.
"We don't know if this will bring the results he is expecting."
A CID Gallup poll on Wednesday showed 86% of Salvadorans approved of the Haiti mission, though 82% also expressed concern for their countrymen.
In El Salvador, security analysts said they were cautious of a risky mission without a formal agreement, UN backing, or support from the Shield of the Americas - a US-led anti-crime coalition the Trump administration launched earlier this year.
POINTS TO ESCALATION
Haiti's unelected leaders have since 2022 called for international forces to help fight heavily-armed gangs that have expanded their influence beyond the capital and are responsible for massacres, gang rapes and widespread extortion.
But successive UN-backed missions were slow to deploy, leaving a fractured security response. Haiti hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince to fight the gangs, which nonetheless continued to make gains.
Sam Vigersky, a policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he believed the UN-backed mission - renewed for just six months in September - was under pressure to produce results but the Salvadorans' arrival signaled more chaos.
"The overall security picture is not pointing towards one of stabilization, it's pointing towards one of escalation," he said.
Since the October 18 ambush, the area has been the site of continuous armed clashes. A security official said operations there were largely run by Haitian police.
Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a security expert at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said residents were skeptical of yet another foreign intervention and had reported heavy gunfire, drone strikes and possible civilian deaths.
He said he was not aware of humanitarian corridors to help people escape: "The gang leaders do not want people to leave the area because they probably want to use them as shields and make sure the population actually slows operations against them."
Washington has not publicly supported the mission but a US military official said Pentagon C-130s helped it deploy.
Irwin Stotzky, a rights expert at the University of Miami, said the US administration, which ended immigration protections for about 350,000 Haitians, has reasons to be invested.
"We've got to make it appear as if it's safe to send 350,000 people back to Haiti, when they actually are in great fear of their lives," he said. REUTERS

Starbucks Q4 revenue falls 4.5 pct, net income surges 408.8 pct
China
Unknown Publisher

06:46:00 CST
07:46:00 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. coffee giant Starbucks reported Thursday that its revenue fell 4.5 percent year on year to 9.14 billion U.S. dollars in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, while net income surged 408.8 percent, partly reflecting a sharp decline in restructuring and impairment costs.
According to the company's financial results for the 13-week quarter ended Sept. 27, net income attributable to Starbucks rose to 677.2 million dollars from 133.1 million dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share increased to 0.59 dollars from 0.12 dollars, while non-GAAP adjusted earnings per share rose 53.8 percent to 0.8 dollars.
Operating income jumped 256.5 percent to 991.8 million dollars from 278.2 million dollars a year earlier, while operating margin expanded to 10.8 percent from 2.9 percent.
Starbucks said the decline in quarterly revenue was primarily attributable to the conversion of its retail operations in China to a licensed joint venture model.
Global comparable coffeehouse sales rose 7.2 percent, driven by a 5.2 percent increase in average ticket and a 1.8 percent rise in comparable transactions.
In North America, comparable sales increased 7.9 percent, including a 7.7 percent rise in the United States. Revenue from the North American segment grew 6 percent to 7.33 billion dollars.
The international segment recorded a 37 percent decline in revenue to 1.31 billion dollars, largely reflecting the restructuring of Starbucks' China operations. International comparable sales increased 0.9 percent.
Starbucks opened a net 303 new coffeehouses during the quarter, bringing its global store count to 41,607 at the end of September.
For the full fiscal year 2026, Starbucks reported revenue of 37.91 billion dollars, up 2 percent from the previous year. Net income attributable to the company rose 36.1 percent to 2.53 billion dollars, while diluted earnings per share increased to 2.21 dollars from 1.63 dollars.
Looking ahead, Starbucks expects revenue to decline approximately 1 percent in fiscal 2027, primarily reflecting the transition of its China operations to the licensed joint venture model.
The company projects approximately 4 percent growth in North American comparable sales and plans to open a net 1,200 new coffeehouses worldwide. ■

Indian man suspected of faking Bondi Beach mass shooting injury to receive victim compensation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:44:20 UTC
07:44:20 KST

Australian police in New South Wales announced Wednesday that a 46-year-old man had been arrested and charged with allegedly attempting to defraud authorities by fabricating an injury sustained in the Hanukkah terror attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach.
He is suspected of doing so to obtain substantial financial compensation intended for victims of the attack.
According to a police statement, the man falsely claimed that he had been injured in the shooting on December 14, 2025, in which 15 people were killed. He subsequently filed fraudulent compensation claims. The amount he sought has not been disclosed.
The Australian newspaper The Daily Telegraph identified the suspect as Simaxwell Cyril, an Indian citizen who claimed he had been struck by shrapnel during the attack. However, he is suspected of having fabricated the injury.
The Australian federal and New South Wales state governments operate a special assistance program for victims of the massacre. Under the program, eligible victims wounded by gunfire or shrapnel can receive a one-time payment of 35,000 Australian dollars, plus recognition grants and assistance covering medical expenses and financial losses.
The suspicions against Cyril came to light by chance during an investigation by detectives from the New South Wales Police Homicide Squad into police actions during the attack.
This investigation is separate from the terrorism investigation targeting the perpetrators of the massacre. While gathering evidence, detectives became suspicious that Cyril had provided a false account of his injury and used it to submit compensation claims.
Police arrested Cyril on Tuesday morning at a police station in Parramatta, western Sydney. He was charged with offenses of “publishing false or misleading information to obtain a benefit” and “making a false representation that resulted in the commencement of a police investigation.”
He was released on bail on restrictive conditions and must appear at Parramatta Local Court on November 18.
Cyril expected to be deported from Australia
However, his legal troubles did not end there. According to The Daily Telegraph, after his release on bail, Cyril was arrested by Australian immigration authorities on suspicion of remaining in the country beyond the expiration of his visa.
He was transferred to the Villawood Immigration Detention Centre and is expected to be deported from Australia.
The allegations prompted strong reactions within Australia’s Jewish community, which is still grappling with the aftermath of the attack. Alex Ryvchin, co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, condemned the alleged attempted fraud. He told the Nine Network that diverting police resources to investigate false claims when the community needs protection from security threats is an “abhorrent act that we should all condemn.”
What is the Bondi Beach massacre?
The massacre took place on December 14, 2025, when two attackers, a father, Sajid Akram, 50, and his son, Naveed, opened fire on hundreds of people attending a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi Beach.
Fifteen people, aged between 10 and 87, were killed, and approximately 40 were injured. The father was shot dead by police, while his son was wounded, arrested, and charged.
Meanwhile, a further hearing in the case against Naveed Akram, now 25, took place Wednesday, as the alleged compensation fraud case came to light. Akram faces 78 charges, including 15 counts of murder, 43 counts of attempted murder, and committing a terrorist act.
Judge Karen Stafford granted the prosecution’s request to postpone the hearing until February 2027 to allow time for consultations with victims and their families to be completed.
Police clarified that the investigation into the suspect accused of compensation fraud would not affect the proceedings against Akram.

Senior officials told N12 that the case is unlikely to lead to an indictment and that the suspects explained the source of the money in question.
Abbas denied involvement in alleged Qatar-linked election interference
Earlier on Thursday, Abbas denied claims that he was involved in a separate, alleged election interference scheme via Qatar, saying he backs an investigation into the matter and claiming that Netanyahu employs Qatari agents.
"Ra'am welcomes the decision of Central Elections Committee (CEC) Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspicions of an attempt to improperly influence the elections through foreign funding," said Abbas. "And to Abu Yair [Netanyahu], who employs Qatari agents in his office, we have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he is conducting against Arab citizens: 'There will be nothing, because there is nothing.' Unlike you, with us this is the truth and not another lie."
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) launched an investigation into suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voting in Arab communities.
The investigation, begun following a directive issued by Sohlberg, was initiated amid "severe suspicions... regarding improper influence through foreign funding by entities acting against Israeli interests during the elections," the Shin Bet stated.
Jonah Davidov and Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

True Zionists should welcome Arab participation in Israel’s government - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:43:28 UTC
07:43:28 KST

Israel’s Arab citizens have given our country an extraordinary democratic opportunity. Their turnout in this election should be a source of national pride. Bringing willing Arab partners into government could strengthen our democracy, help repair our society, and change how Israel is seen around the world.
Millions of Israelis went to the polls, including thousands who flew home to vote. Their commitment deserves our respect. After years of war, loss and division, our citizens deserve leaders prepared to use the opportunity they have created.
In these pages on October 12, I argued that politicians who exclude Arab citizens from government because they are Arab hand Israel’s enemies a weapon. The election has made that question immediate. Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan now face a decision whose consequences extend far beyond the formation of another coalition.
With counting still underway, the reported result gives Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats, the Zionist opposition 48 and the Arab parties 19. These numbers do not constitute a governing agreement. They demand serious negotiations among those who believe our country needs a different government.
Not welcoming Arab voters would make mockery of equal citizenship
Our Arab fellow citizens sought change through Israel’s democratic institutions. We should welcome their participation and recognize its significance. Celebrating their votes while refusing to consider their representatives as governing partners simply because they are Arab would make a mockery of equal citizenship.
Eisenkot, Bennett, Lapid and Golan: each of you has asked Israelis to trust you with our future. You now have a responsibility to examine every credible path to a government that can defend the country, restore its institutions and serve its citizens. Campaign pledges cannot relieve you of the duty to exercise judgment.
I write as an Israeli who believes in the Jewish state and fears for its future. I respect those who have carried the burden of defending it, including leaders with whom I disagree. I ask them now to challenge the prejudices that prevent us from building a stronger country.
There must be clear obligations for every governing partner. Each must reject terrorism, respect democratic institutions, and undertake to protect Israel and its citizens. Apply those standards equally to Jewish and Arab parties, then negotiate over the differences that remain.
Some differences may prevent agreement. A party’s policies or conduct may make cooperation impossible. But being Arab cannot be a disqualification, and no leader committed to Israel’s founding promise should defend such a position.
In 1948, as our country faced war for its survival, Ben-Gurion proclaimed a Jewish state committed to equal political rights for all its citizens. The Declaration of Independence called on Arab inhabitants to participate in building the state and its institutions. These commitments belong to the core of the Zionist dream.
True Zionists should have the confidence to honor them. A Jewish state in which Arab citizens share responsibility for governing fulfills a promise made at its birth. Excluding them because of their identity betrays it.
Bennett and Lapid have already governed with Ra’am, and Arab ministers have already served Israel. They know cooperation is possible and understand its difficulties. The task now is to build an agreement in which willing Arab partners exercise meaningful authority and accept the responsibilities that accompany it.
Arab leaders must also be prepared to compromise. Those seeking a place in government must help develop a workable program and accept responsibility for difficult decisions. They cannot expect their partners to take political risks while declining to take any themselves.
The international consequences could be profound. Palestinian citizens of Israel already elect representatives to our parliament in competitive national elections. Seeing those representatives exercise authority in the government of the Jewish state would provide a powerful answer to those who insist that Zionism necessarily means racial exclusion.
A cabinet in which Jewish and Arab ministers govern together would confront that claim with an uncomfortable reality. These would be Arab citizens making decisions, directing ministries and sharing responsibility for Israel’s future. Their authority would come from the same democratic process as that of their Jewish colleagues.
That would directly challenge the allegation that Israel’s Jewish identity makes equal political participation impossible. It would not resolve the conflict in the West Bank and Gaza or settle accusations concerning Israeli rule there. Those questions require decisions of their own, and our argument gains strength when we are precise about what shared government would demonstrate.
Netanyahu, extremists does not get to define Zionism
Netanyahu and his extremist partners have repeatedly weakened that argument through rhetoric that treats Arab political participation as a threat. When they suggest that a government supported by Arab votes lacks legitimacy, they give substance to the very charge of exclusion that Israel’s defenders are asked to rebut.
They do not get to define Zionism for the rest of us. Their insistence on distinguishing between the legitimacy of Jewish and Arab votes violates the equality promised at Israel’s founding. We should reject that rhetoric openly and build a government that gives practical effect to our principles.
The first test would be what that government delivers. Organized crime terrorizes Arab communities and weakens the state. Housing, education, public services and confidence in the police demand sustained attention. Jewish and Arab ministers who tackle these problems together would begin repairing the relationship between citizens and their government.
This could be the fastest credible way to begin restoring Israel’s standing after years in which the current government has deepened our divisions and damaged trust in our institutions. A new coalition alone will not repair that damage. A government that shares authority and addresses neglected social problems would show that the country has begun to change.
It would be the political equivalent of pressing Control-Alt-Delete on a system that has become stuck. The problems would remain, but we would have a chance to make government function again, with different partners and a renewed commitment to the citizens it serves.
Such a government could also improve the conditions for diplomacy with Saudi Arabia. Riyadh’s demands concerning Palestinian statehood would remain, and Arab participation in our cabinet could not substitute for addressing them. Yet a government prepared to build trust with Arab partners at home could bring greater credibility to negotiations abroad.
For Israelis, and for Jews defending Israel around the world, this would be a change worth fighting for. We could point to a Jewish state whose Arab citizens help govern it, with shared obligations and real authority. Our answer to those who deny the possibility of such a state would be visible in the government itself.
Eisenkot and his colleagues should begin serious negotiations now. Establish common obligations, test where agreement is possible and bring willing Arab partners into government. Our voters have created an opportunity to renew Israel’s founding promise. Those who claim to defend that promise must now act on it.
Jeremy M. Levin is an Israeli-American physician-scientist and biotechnology executive, an elected member of the American Zionist Movement and a participant in the most recent World Zionist Congress. He is a former CEO of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries and former chairman of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says ties to company under spying probe were ‘normal’

- Huang said Nvidia checked its GPUs and found no illegal shipments to China, which is barred from buying Nvidia’s powerful AI chips under US export rules.
- The case shows rising US-China tech tension, which has cut Nvidia off from China sales and led to more export probes and smuggling claims.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Nvidia’s Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the chipmaker’s dealings with Megaspeed International were “normal and not unusual” following a New York Times report that one of the Singapore-based firm’s executives is under investigation for spying on behalf of China.
Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed’s officials was proper, and the chipmaker has checked to ensure that Megaspeed didn’t illegally send its artificial intelligence processors to China, Huang said in an interview on Oct 29. That country is barred from buying Nvidia’s powerful AI chips – known as graphics processing units, or GPUs – under US export rules.
“We’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one,” he said in the interview. “And I think the US government also has as well.”
The remarks follow a Times story that the US government is investigating an executive from Megaspeed for allegedly providing information to the Chinese government. Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, has previously been pictured with Nvidia’s leader on social media, and the story reports that she may have been serving as a Chinese agent aiming to evade chip export controls.
In the interview, Huang said that his interactions with her were typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. She’s no longer with Megaspeed, he said.
“Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang said. The CEO said he hadn’t been informed by the US government of its suspicions about Huang Le.
The growing geopolitical rivalry between the US and China has led to increasing clampdowns by Washington on exports of key American technology. That has cut off Nvidia from a lucrative source of revenue in China, the largest market for chips.
The company has received some latitude to ship a limited amount of older AI-related products to the Asian country under the Trump administration. That approval hasn’t resulted in a material amount of shipments, at least in part because Beijing has sought to limit the deliveries itself in an effort to foster its own chip industry.
Nonetheless, the restrictions on exports have led to investigations and charges of smuggling of Nvidia’s best products to China – something the company has said is an insignificant issue. Megaspeed is one of a group of companies that Bloomberg News and others have reported may have tried to illegally divert shipments of chips intended for data centers outside of China into that country. Why are Israelis surprised Arab voters showed up? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:38:53 UTC
07:38:53 KST

Oops. Look, there are Arabs in Israel.
Israelis woke up on Oct. 28 to realize that the Arab vote could change the picture, and many of them reacted as if they had only just discovered that Arab citizens live here. The Joint List and Ra'am won 19 seats between them, up from 10 in the outgoing Knesset, on an Arab turnout of about 80%. Those are the facts. The surprise is the story.
This is not new. Israelis have always had a talent for not seeing the Arabs who live among them. In May 1967, weeks before the Six-Day War, when Jordan ruled East Jerusalem, Naomi Shemer wrote "Jerusalem of Gold" for the Israel Song Festival. Looking across the border at the Old City, she described its market square as empty. It was not. Arab Jerusalemites lived there, traded there and prayed there. They simply were not in the song.
Amos Oz once told Shemer as much. The square was not empty, he said, and "we are not alone in this land." Shemer answered with a marriage analogy: another man's presence does not make a wife any less yours. The others are not denied. They are simply noticed only when they seem to threaten what is "ours." The rest of the time, they are scenery.
Arab citizens make up about a fifth of Israel's population. Nearly half of Israel's pharmacists are Arab, and Arab nurses and doctors fill hospitals and clinics across the country. We trust them with our bodies. We rarely think of them as voters.
Part of it is the way we live. Most Jews and Arabs in Israel live in separate towns, send their children to separate schools and, until university or the hospital ward, rarely share a room. Part of it is language. Arabic is the mother tongue of one in five Israelis, yet only about 10% of Jewish Israelis understand some Arabic. And part of it is the words we use. In Hebrew, Arab citizens are "the sector" (HaMigzar) or "the minorities," terms that keep them at a polite distance. Arab towns make the evening news when there is a murder, rarely when there is a vote.
None of this belongs to the right alone. In fact, the surprise was loudest among those who see themselves as liberal, open and democratic.
Israel's center-left likes to think of itself as the camp of coexistence. It praises the Arab doctor in the COVID ward and speaks warmly of a shared society. But when it comes to power, it keeps Arab citizens at arm's length. Its leaders ruled out Arab partners in advance and, in the words of a TheMarker analysis this week, dug their own pit by turning their backs on Arab voters. The Arab parties reached out. So far they have been ignored.
For much of the center-left, the Arab public is not a partner but a reservoir: votes that should turn out against Netanyahu, quietly, and then disappear from the conversation. Arab citizens are welcome to tip the balance, as long as they do not ask for a seat at the table. TV presenter Lucy Aharish put it bluntly on her program: “In the last elections, the Israeli center complained that the Arabs didn’t show up and so brought the extreme right-wing government to power. Now that they have shown up, the parties reject them.” When Arab citizens turned out in force, many liberal Israelis were as taken aback as anyone. They had hoped for help. They got a public with its own parties, its own leaders and its own demands.
Israel's founders saw it differently. The Declaration of Independence, signed on May 14, 1948, by the 37 members of the People's Council, calls on the state's Arab inhabitants to take part in building it "on the basis of full and equal citizenship and due representation in all its provisional and permanent institutions," as Naama Lazimi recalled. On the right, Ze'ev Jabotinsky went further. In The Jewish War Front, published in 1940, he wrote: "In every Cabinet where the Prime Minister is a Jew, the vice-premiership shall be offered to an Arab, and vice-versa." The founders of the Labor movement's state and the father of the Israeli right agreed on this much. It is their heirs who are surprised.
To be precise, Arab citizens have always voted. In Israel's first decades, turnout was even higher than today, reaching 90% in 1955, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, but under military rule those votes went mostly to Mapai and its affiliated lists, not to parties of their own. In the last 20 years, Arab turnout has never come close to this year's 80%. What is new is not that Arabs vote, but that they voted as a public with a voice of its own.
That is the paradox. For years, right and left alike have asked whether Arab citizens are integrating into Israeli society. This week they did the most integrated thing a citizen can do: they stood in line at a polling station, in an Israeli school, and dropped a ballot into an Israeli box. And that is what startled us.
There are real arguments to be had with some of the parties they voted for, as there are with many parties. But an argument with a party is not the same as discomfort with its voters.
"The Arab citizens are not guests in the country," Nimrod Dvir, founder of the Darkhenu movement, wrote in Ynet this week. That this still needs to be written, by a liberal, to liberals, says it all.
The “market square” was never empty. It was full in 1967, it is full today, and on Oct. 27 its people showed up in numbers that made them impossible to overlook. We can keep acting surprised every few years, or we can finally look at the square as it is.

Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:36:06 UTC
07:36:06 KST

Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86
Stewart died in Los Angeles after battling Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died on Wednesday in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement on Thursday.
Although best known for his film and television roles, Stewart spent much of his career onstage, performing Shakespeare and other classics.
His career included performances as Claudius and Macbeth, a one-man adaptation of “A Christmas Carol”, and West End and Broadway productions of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” alongside longtime friend Ian McKellen.
Stewart earned some of the best reviews of his career for his 2007 portrayal of Macbeth, including his only Tony Award nomination. The Times of London described his Macbeth performance as “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour”.
“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told the Associated Press news agency in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”
From working-class Yorkshire to Shakespeare
Raised in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
He joined an amateur drama group at 12 and, as a teenager, memorised Shakespeare for fun. A scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School helped launch his acting career.
Stewart, who developed alopecia at a young age, had been bald since he was 19.
His childhood was also marked by domestic violence. His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
Stewart later became a patron of Refuge, a charity supporting survivors of domestic abuse.
From Shakespeare to Captain Picard
Stewart spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, playing everyone from Mark Antony and Henry IV to Shylock and Oberon.
“People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?'” he told the AP. “Telly?”
He eventually left and appeared in the 1981 film “Excalibur”. In 1987, shortly after performing in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, he was offered a role in a science fiction series.
“I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail,” he said.
But “Star Trek: The Next Generation” ran for seven seasons and 178 episodes. Stewart became known worldwide as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, whose command, “Make it so”, became one of the show’s best-known lines.
Stewart also played Professor Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men, beginning with the 2000 film “X-Men”. He returned to the role in several sequels, including 2017’s “Logan”, alongside Hugh Jackman as Wolverine.
Stewart died just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series, which aired from 1966 to 1969.
Queen Elizabeth II knighted Stewart in June 2010. He also served as an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.

World’s largest crypto exchange investigates suspected multibillion-dollar hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:30:10 UTC
07:30:10 KST

World’s largest crypto exchange hit by cyberattack
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has estimated the impact of a cyberattack at approximately $6.3 billion, saying hackers may have exploited an employee’s compromised laptop to carry out unauthorized withdrawals.
In an update on Friday, the company said its preliminary investigation suggested that an attacker had gained access to a service container through a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, allowing unauthorized withdrawal transactions to be submitted.
Binance said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B. We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far,” the exchange said in a statement.
The company stressed that customer funds were safe and said it would publish a detailed technical report once its investigation was complete.
As an immediate precaution, Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while conducting security checks. It also revoked the affected address authorization and enlisted law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover funds and identify those responsible.
The incident follows reports of suspicious transactions involving billions of dollars in digital assets transferred from wallets linked to Binance on Thursday.
Blockchain researchers initially estimated the outflows at $2.77 billion across five blockchains. Binance subsequently confirmed that $2.54 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
Stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle and Ripple were among the companies that moved to freeze assets linked to the suspected attack.
The suspected attack comes amid a series of major cryptocurrency thefts this year. In September, hackers stole approximately $388 million from the Bitget exchange, while attacks on the Drift Protocol and Kelp DAO platforms in April resulted in losses of roughly $285 million and $292 million, respectively. In February 2025, suspected North Korean hackers stole approximately $1.5 billion from Bybit in what was widely described as the largest cryptocurrency heist on record at the time.
Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to violating US anti-money-laundering laws and stepped down as head of the exchange as part of a settlement that saw Binance agree to pay $4.3 billion in penalties. He subsequently served a four-month prison sentence.
US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025. The White House defended the decision, claiming he had been unfairly prosecuted under former President Joe Biden as part of a broader crackdown on the cryptocurrency industry.

An armored capsule instead of an open platform: Ukraine develops an evacuation module for the Murakha UGV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:25:10 UTC
07:25:10 KST

Ukrainian company Robotic Complexes is developing CASEEVAK, an armored module that lets the Murakha unmanned ground vehicle carry wounded soldiers off the battlefield, the company told Militarnyi on 28 October. The casualty rides in a closed capsule with ventilation, heating, lighting, and a first-aid kit, and side and rear doors let medics load and reach the soldier from any side.
Drones that can fly long distances pose a threat to both wounded soldiers and the crews evacuating them, making transportation the main challenge, said Ukrainian military medic Daryna Boiko, The Independent reported. Developers are looking for new ways to counter this threat. The current Murakha model is being equipped with passive anti-drone protection elements, the developers say.
An armored capsule that keeps the wounded connected
After a wounded soldier is loaded onto an evacuation platform, it is important not only to transport them to a safe location but also to protect them and monitor their condition during transit.
The module is built around a closed armored capsule made of 3.5 mm-thick Armox 500T steel with an inner lining of HDPE 1000, the media outlet reports. Side and rear doors allow the wounded to be loaded from different directions and accessed during evacuation.
To enable the operator to monitor the person inside and maintain contact with them, the capsule is equipped with a camera with day and night channels and two-way audio communication. The system can be controlled via ELRS, LTE, Starlink, or fiber-optic communications. Militarnyi reports that even if the capsule is detached from the main platform, it retains two independent communication channels.
The developers are also working to integrate vital-signs monitoring systems intended to provide medical personnel with information about the wounded person’s condition during transport.
An electric platform and protection against FPV drones
The evacuation module requires a platform capable of carrying it as it moves through dangerous areas. The Murakha is equipped with two electric motors, delivering a combined torque of 1,600 N·m, and a 35 kWh battery. The system’s stated range is up to 80 km, according to the media outlet.
Another area of development is protection against drones. Measures intended to protect the system include net launchers and electronic warfare (EW) equipment. However, work on a protective cage against FPV drones is still ongoing, according to the report.
The company has already conducted ballistic tests of the armor steel at a distance of 50 meters, using ammunition of various calibers, Militarnyi reports.
The Murakha-Mini logistics platform
The same company previously developed the Murakha-Mini logistics platform. Ukrainian military personnel began using it on the front line to deliver equipment, provisions and other supplies, Militarnyi reported on 24 October 2025.
The UGV can carry up to 250 kg and travel up to 40 km on a single charge, the media outlet reported. During one combat mission, it transported 150 kg of cargo and towed a six-metre platform carrying another drone and provisions, covering 16 km in one direction, Militarnyi reported.

Amazon posts negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion, holds 2026 capex unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:24:49 UTC
07:24:49 KST

Amazon shares plunged more than 6% in extended trading Thursday after the company reported disappointing third-quarter results and ballooning negative free cash flow, reflecting its swelling AI investments.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $1.89 vs. $1.96 estimated
- Revenue: $201.94 billion vs. $202.31 billion estimated
Wall Street was also looking at other key revenue numbers:
- Amazon Web Services: $45.98 billion vs. $45.29 billion, according to StreetAccount
- Advertising: $19.64 billion vs. $20.82 billion, according to StreetAccount
The company held steady on its capital expenditure forecast for 2026, saying it continues to expect spending will reach $220 billion this year.
Tech's hyperscalers have been on a blistering spending run to meet the surge in demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, but signs have begun to emerge that the capex splurge is moderating. Earlier this week, Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion.
CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with investors that the company expects to "spend meaningfully more in 2027," and that Amazon has a "clear line of sight to attractive financial returns."
The aggressive AI spending has eaten into Amazon's cash flow. The company posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve month period, a swing of 386% year over year. In the prior quarter, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion.
The company said the shortfall was primarily due to an increase in purchases of property and equipment as a result of AI investments.
Capital expenditures reached $77.3 billion during the quarter, ticking up from $35.1 billion one year earlier, and coming in well above analysts' estimated $58.7 billion, according to FactSet.
Amazon said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to be in the range of $240 billion and $247 billion. The midpoint of its guidance was below Wall Street's expectations of $244.5 billion, according to LSEG. The fourth quarter is typically one of Amazon's biggest by revenue, due to the peak holiday shopping season.
Sales in Amazon's cloud segment soared 39% year over year to $45.98 billion. That topped the consensus forecast for $45.29 billion and growth of 38%, according to StreetAccount.
Jassy highlighted AWS acceleration in the earnings release, saying the company expects revenue growth rates of "over 40%" next year and in 2028. He added, "Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working."
Jassy told investors on the call that he expects AWS will be a $1 trillion revenue business in the next five to 10 years.
Amazon is facing pressure from Wall Street to show that its AI investments are lifting its revenues. The company pointed to growing traction for Bedrock, its AI model marketplace, along with its Trainium and Graviton AI chips.
Jassy said Amazon's chips business "continues to grow triple-digit percentages year over year." He added that the company plans to make its Trainium chips available externally "late in 2027," assigning a timeframe to comments Jassy made earlier this year suggesting such a move.
Third-quarter net income came in at $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, vs. $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year ago. The company said the decrease was driven primarily by a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain from its investment in the AI startup Anthropic, which was recorded in the 2025 third quarter.
While the AWS segment continues to hum along, results weren't as bright in Amazon's retail business, which remains its largest unit by revenue, or its advertising segment.
Online sales gained 2% year over year to $68.47 billion, which fell short of analysts' projected $69.68 billion, according to StreetAccount. It marked a slowdown from one year ago, when sales increased nearly 10%.
Advertising revenue rose 11% year over year to $19.64 billion. That missed StreetAccount consensus estimates of $20.82 billion.
Both units were impacted in part by Amazon's decision to pull its annual Prime Day sale forward in several countries from its typical third quarter timeframe into the second quarter so as to not conflict with the FIFA World Cup in July.

Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
October 29, 2026
German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.
Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.
Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.
Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.
He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.
"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.
"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."
Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.
Two Grand Slams in 2026
Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.
The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.
But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.
Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

Chinese scientists are less satisfied with their jobs than researchers in any other major country, according to a survey that also found they are more optimistic about their careers than their counterparts in the United States and Britain.
Only 51 per cent of the 157 respondents from China said they were satisfied with their jobs, according to the survey published this month in the British scientific journal Nature, down 24 per cent from 2018.
The survey drew 3,882 respondents from 133 countries, across a variety of disciplines, academia and industry. Because respondents chose to take part, the results cannot be taken as representative of all Chinese scientists working across disciplines, regions and types of institutions.

MOSCOW, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Russia supports any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, President Vladimir Putin said late on Thursday, adding the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners.
Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin said Russia was prepared for a potential war with Europe, though it did not want one.
“We support any steps…we support any actions aimed at restoring full-fledged and complete relations with European countries,” Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders.
“First of all, we are ready, but we want no war with Europe. And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal — to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.”
Putin said Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere had been right to make the call despite criticism from some European capitals that the two were breaking ranks by initiating contact with Moscow.
He said Russia wanted no impediments to navigation in the Baltic Sea and added that restricting communication could lead to a situation similar to that in the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the US-Iranian conflict in February.
“Does someone want the same situation in the Baltic as in the Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz?” Putin said. “I don’t know. We don’t want that, but we will respond to any challenge.”

Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:18:00 CET
07:18:00 KST

By Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology as he attended an exhibition and demonstration of unmanned aeronautical technology, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
The firepower demonstration following the exhibition involved tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
The display highlights Kim’s push to modernise North Korea’s armed forces by using drones and artificial intelligence as Pyongyang draws lessons from its forces’ experience in Russia’s war against Ukraine and from other global conflicts.
KCNA photographs showed unmanned aerial vehicles bearing the North Korean Air Force’s emblem at the exhibition attended by Kim and some of his generals.
Another series of images showed what appeared to be an unmanned aerial vehicle crashing into a military vehicle on a hill and exploding in a ball of flame, which KCNA said was part of a weapons demonstration during the exhibition.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
According to KCNA, Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea in building modern armed forces, KCNA reported.
Kim has made repeated calls for the development of drones and AI in the military. According to state media, Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024 and oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025. In September 2025, he called AI a top priority in modernising weapons.
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid Moscow in its war against Ukraine, and gained battlefield experience in drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
North Korea is transforming its military with drones and AI, drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.
By showing a comprehensive display of weapons, North Korea is trying to “shut off the possibility of dialogue or negotiations” with South Korea, Lim said.
(Reporting by Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim; Editing by Nia Williams, Jamie Freed and Ed Davies)

El Salvador frees ex-President Saca after 10-year corruption sentence
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:17:46 CET
07:17:46 KST

By Gerardo Arbaiza
SAN SALVADOR, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Elias Antonio “Tony” Saca, a former Salvadoran president imprisoned for corruption, was released on Thursday, his lawyer said, standing alongside the politician as they exited a courthouse.
Saca, 61, served a reduced 10-year sentence after pleading guilty to diverting and laundering more than $300 million from the state budget during his 2004-2009 administration.
His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits. “The 10 years were completed,” Machado said.
“We have come to the court to formally report the release. This was requested just yesterday.”
Although Saca was sentenced in 2018, his prison term was backdated to 2016, when he was arrested during his son’s wedding. A plea deal allowed Saca to reduce a potential 30-year sentence.
Saca is one of four Salvadoran presidents to have faced corruption charges, although the other former leaders avoided the prospect of jail time. Mauricio Funes and Salvador Sanchez Ceren fled to Nicaragua, and Francisco Flores died before his trial could begin.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
In 2014, after his expulsion from the party, he sought to return to the presidency with the Grand Alliance for National Unity (GANA), but the Supreme Court ruled his candidacy unconstitutional.
Prosecutors had alleged that Saca diverted state funds for personal use and to benefit his allies, including by funneling large sums of money to his party. Saca was ordered in separate civil proceedings to repay millions of dollars to the state.
(Reporting by Gerardo Arbaiza; Writing by Raúl Cortés Fernández and Diego Oré; Editing by Daina Beth Solomon)

Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:16:51 UTC
07:16:51 KST

Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
An Icelandic web company, FlokiNET, has defended the data’s publication as satisfying a ‘legitimate’ public interest.
The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has asked an Icelandic web hosting company to take down a site with information about tens of thousands of its employees.
On Thursday, the Icelandic company FlokiNET posted a letter it received from the cybersecurity firm ZeroFox, on behalf of DHS.
The letter accused FlokiNET of violating its terms of service by publishing a “stolen” employee dataset and asked it to “remove or disable” the information.
“The content is live and places more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm,” the letter said.
FlokiNET said the letter concerned one domain, icepi.cx, which has compiled information about employees from a range of DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Those agencies have come under intense scrutiny since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign in 2025.
But the Trump administration has often refused to identify DHS agents involved in specific operations, citing safety risks.
Though FlokiNET said it refused to comply with DHS’s request, it noted that the website’s registrar ultimately suspended the domain. The employee information has since moved to a different domain.
In a statement posted online, FlokiNET defended its decision not to remove the site.
“Federal officers carrying out an enforcement programme are not private individuals while they are carrying it out,” the company said. “The public has a legitimate interest in knowing who is doing that work, under whose authority, and in which office.”
The database was first posted online on Wednesday by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a group that showcases leaked government data.
In the past, DDoSecrets has released emails from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as well as information from the Israeli Ministry of Justice and police departments in the US.
A hacker group calling itself the “Department of Peace” has claimed responsibility for obtaining and sharing the DHS data.
Since the database was first published, other groups have spread the information elsewhere, including on sites like icepi.cx. As a result, the information is unlikely to be entirely scrubbed from the internet.
The Trump administration, however, has taken an aggressive approach to online platforms purporting to contain information about ICE employees and other agents involved in immigration operations.
Last year, for instance, the US Department of Justice pressured tech giants like Apple to remove apps that track ICE agents, including one called ICEBlock.
The move sparked backlash from Democrats and free-speech advocates, who argued that the public has a right to report on ICE’s movements.
“Blocking access to these apps at the request of the federal government raises the distinct possibility that Apple is working with government to violate its customers’ First Amendment right to record and report on the activities of their government,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin wrote in a letter last year, asking Apple to review its decision.
Immigration agents, meanwhile, have taken several steps to conceal their identities during operations, including wearing face masks or street clothes.
That lack of transparency has spurred criticism from human rights groups and immigration advocates, who argue that they have little recourse to pursue allegations of excessive force or impropriety during ICE raids.
Since Trump was sworn in for a second term, at least 25 people have faced gunfire from immigration agents. Six of the shootings have resulted in deaths.
Other cases have involved alleged violations of civil liberties – including unlawful arrests and racial profiling – as well as controversial tactics like car ramming and tackling.

Although Saca was sentenced in 2018, his prison term was backdated to 2016, when he was arrested during his son’s wedding. A plea deal allowed Saca to reduce a potential 30-year sentence.
Saca is one of four Salvadoran presidents to have faced corruption charges, although the other former leaders avoided the prospect of jail time. Mauricio Funes and Salvador Sanchez Ceren fled to Nicaragua, and Francisco Flores died before his trial could begin.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
In 2014, after his expulsion from the party, he sought to return to the presidency with the Grand Alliance for National Unity (GANA), but the Supreme Court ruled his candidacy unconstitutional.
Prosecutors had alleged that Saca diverted state funds for personal use and to benefit his allies, including by funneling large sums of money to his party. Saca was ordered in separate civil proceedings to repay millions of dollars to the state. REUTERS
