Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded
- Sebastian Herrero survived a Spain train crash on Oct 28 near Seville, where another train hit his and 69 people died.
- He described the scene as “devastating”, with burnt-out carriages, injured passengers and bodies being pulled out after the crash.
- The accident revived safety concerns after a January crash on the same line, and Herrero said those responsible must “take responsibility”.
AI generated
MADRID – When his train drew to a halt, Sebastian Herrero thought the stoppage was due to a fallen overhead line, a problem that has increasingly beset Spain’s high-speed railway network in recent years.
But concerns about arriving late at his destination were suddenly interrupted when he found himself flying through the air and landing face-first on the seat opposite as another train slammed into the back of his.
Herrero, 46, was on his way on Oct 28 to Seville from Madrid on an early-morning train operated by Iryo when a train operated by state-owned Renfe ploughed into it, sending its final three carriages careering down a raised embankment in a crash that killed 69 people.
Herrero and others in his carriage escaped by scrambling down the embankment and crossing a fence into a field. Looking back, he realised the extent of the accident for the first time.
“The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded.
“What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were,” Herrero said in an interview in Seville.
Herrero, who said he feels “born again” after surviving the disaster, was fortunate that his carriage was near the front of the train, but the impact still left many passengers with broken arms or noses.
Dilemma after January crash
The crash followed another accident that killed dozens in January and involved the same rail companies on the same line near the town of Adamuz.
It has revived a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, Europe’s longest and – until recently – a source of pride for Spaniards.
Herrero remembers people asking him after the Adamuz accident whether he felt safe taking the train.
“I remember when the Adamuz thing happened because I spent a month and a half thinking about lots of things, as I had to drive there and the roads aren’t exactly in the best condition either,” he said.
“Petrol isn’t at its cheapest right now, far from it, and flying isn’t an option. So for many of us who have that connection between Seville and Madrid and whose lives depend on it, you can’t see any other solution.”
For many of the people of different nationalities and backgrounds involved in the Oct 28 accident, the prevailing feeling was one of indignation.
“It is high time for whoever is responsible to take responsibility,” Herrero said.
“I don’t know whether it is up to the courts to say so, or whether it is up to politicians, or whether it is for the Spanish people to decide, but what is clear is that it is unacceptable for this to happen and it is inconceivable that it could ever happen again,” he added. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Neptunes successfully destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers, used by Moscow to launch unguided and guided aerial bombs (KABs), in Russia’s Volgograd region on Thursday, Oct. 29.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft, which can also carry missiles of various types, at the Marinovka airfield, near the settlement of Oktyabrsky. This was initially reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Several minutes later, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the report, noting that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes during the day. In one of the strikes, a launcher for Russia’s Iskander ballistic missiles was hit as well.
The Su-34, a two-seat long-range strike derivative of the Su-27 fighter, was originally developed in the 1990s, but was only brought into service in 2014.
It is described as Russia’s main aircraft launching KABs on Ukrainian cities nationwide, capable of carrying up to 8 tons of munitions, with an estimated value of each jet at about $50 million.
Such bombs remain one of Russia’s most destructive weapons against Ukrainian cities near the front line. Earlier on Thursday, three KABs struck an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, injuring at least 13 people.
Throughout the day, at least 20 people were killed and 109 wounded in Russian attacks on Ukraine nationwide, with several types of weapons used, including ballistic missiles and first-person-view (FPV) drones.
Putin Says Nordic Leaders Were Right to Call Him, Despite EU Criticism
Second strike on Su-34 in two weeks
The Marinovka airfield, located about 400 kilometers (249 miles) from Ukraine, has previously been targeted by Ukrainian Defense Forces in 2025 as well, as it hosts a squadron of Su-34s.
Overnight Oct. 14-15, Ukraine struck six Russian Su-34 bombers with a Neptune missile strike, at another military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. The attack targeted Borisoglebsk airfield and also destroyed equipment used to support flight operations
Originally designed to destroy warships, Neptune is a domestically developed Ukrainian Cruise missile. In April 2022, its ground-based system sank Russia’s shadow fleet vessel, the Moskva.
Since then, Ukraine has upgraded the missile for strikes on land targets deep inside Russia, with the new version capable of reaching targets up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) away.
Zelensky warns of fresh ballistic attacks
During the same remarks, Zelensky said Ukraine had obtained intelligence that Russia was preparing fresh ballistic missiles.
He called on partners to provide interceptor packages for Patriot air-defense systems, of which Ukraine is facing a critical shortage. “We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
The appeal follows similar warnings during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, where he described Patriot missiles as Ukraine’s most critical shortage, urging Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Ahead of winter, Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as early as Oct. 15, due to limited deliveries from allies.
For Ukraine the PAC-3 is among the very few weapons capable of deterring Russia’s ballistic missiles. Russian Iskander-M, for example, is a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead that is strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.

EU considering Canada as ‘associate member’, Ursula von der Leyen says, despite internal opposition
- The EU and Canada are exploring a closer deal that could be an “association without accession,” but the term “associate member” was left out of the joint declaration.
- Ursula von der Leyen said both sides want deeper work on AI, climate, energy, security and Arctic defence, with talks to continue until next year’s summit.
- Canada wants closer EU ties to cut US dependence under Mark Carney, but the plan may upset Donald Trump and still needs work on rules, cables and supply chains.
AI generated
MONTREAL - European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Oct 29 the EU and Canada continue to explore Canada becoming the union’s first “associate member,” a term so divisive among member countries that it does not appear in a joint declaration.
The European Union and Canada aim to deepen cooperation on AI, climate, energy and security, von der Leyen said, in a speech at a Canada-EU summit in Montreal.
The associate member term, which Germany and several other EU countries oppose, has no legal meaning.
“Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession,” von der Leyen said.
“We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before.
“We can work on everything, from AI and climate to energy or security,” she said.
Canadian and EU leaders, however, dropped the idea of associate EU membership from their joint declaration, seen by Reuters, agreeing instead to an “ever closer association.”
The declaration, which officials plan to make public on Oct 30, said work to define the Canada-EU relationship would continue until another summit next year.
Canada seeking to reduce US dependence
Deeper ties to Europe are part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
Von der Leyen first floated associate membership for Canada six weeks ago, prompting a rebuke from countries that argued they could not agree to a concept that had no legal status and had not been fleshed out, diplomats said.
Three EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they were surprised von der Leyen continued to use the “associate member” term, since the declaration deliberately excluded it.
Speaking later at the summit, European Council president Antonio Costa said the idea of associate membership for Canada was “audacious,” but that he shared von der Leyen’s ambition.
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an associate member, including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.
Carney said the term for Canada’s new relationship with the EU is insignificant.
“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he told reporters.
“What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthens Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects, AI,” Carney said.
Canada and the EU were both trying to find an effective response to the geopolitical threats Trump has posed, said Mark Manger, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs at the University of Toronto.
“Canada and the EU both are now in this position where the most important ally they relied upon is suddenly not behaving like an ally anymore,” he said.
Manger said Canada and the EU have an enormous opportunity to expand their relationship, but that it would take time to address regulatory inconsistencies, build new undersea cables linking Canada to Europe and secure common supply chains, some of the objectives mentioned in the joint declaration.
The declaration also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.
Von der Leyen called for deeper cooperation between the EU and Canada on Arctic security.
“When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbours and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the European Union and Canada,” she said.
“We have to act and change our strategic posture and, together with like-minded partners like Canada, stand up for these values.”
Later on Oct 29, Carney will meet with European business leaders before hosting a dinner with EU leaders. REUTERS

Admiral Bauer: If Russia attacks, Alliance will fight back to break enemy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:10:00 UTC
04:10:00 KST

Admiral Bauer: If Russia attacks, Alliance will fight back to break enemy
Admiral Rob Bauer, former Chair of the NATO Military Committee, expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event organized by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"Ukraine has to fight this war in a certain way because it was limited by the U.S. and other Western nations in the use of certain weapon systems or not allowed to use some of them. So NATO is not going to fight exactly the same way as Ukraine is fighting the Russians," Bauer said.
He explained that in the event of an attack, the Alliance would deploy its air force and navy and launch long-range precision strikes against Russian territory.
"This is something that Ukraine is now doing more and more with weapon systems that it has developed yourself. As you were limited at the outset, you started to work on the drones. So in a way, the drones were your answer to a limited amount of artillery ammo. The fact that you are successful in that area now is a testament to the fact that you found an answer to the fact that you were not supported as we should have supported you," the admiral said.
Even Ukraine's possession of a certain number of F-16 fighter jets cannot match the capabilities of a full fleet of strategic bombers, F-35s, F-22s, F-15s, F-16s and other assets available to the Alliance, Bauer said.
He added that the Alliance's regional plans are fully aligned with the tasks at hand.
"General Grynkewich, NATO's SACEUR, talked about this at a forum in Warsaw just a couple of weeks ago. His message was that Article 5 is ironclad and that the U.S forces in Europe will fight within NATO to first block the Russians, then blunt them if necessary, and if it takes longer, to break them. We are talking about the industrial complex and the logistics support of a longer war that we will have to break, as Ukraine is doing now with Russia, with its refineries and everything else," the admiral said.
Asked whether he believed all NATO allies would have the political will to repel an aggressor, Bauer said: "General Grynkewich would never have been able to say this in Warsaw if it hadn't been exclusively approved by the White House."
In Bauer's view, this was "a message from President Trump to NATO: America is with NATO, article 5 is ironclad, and the regional plans are in place."
He also explained that if intelligence indicated Russia was building up its forces and the Alliance knew which direction they might try to advance in, "the battle groups can be strengthened from 1,000 to 5,000, to a brigade size in different nations."
"At the political level, these plans have already been agreed, so at a certain stage, within those plans, certain things are going to happen," the admiral said.
He added that the situation had been different in the past, when many of these measures would have been debated, with questions raised about whether they were necessary.

How Many Su-34 Fighter-Bombers Does Russia Have Left? Ukraine’s Intelligence Has the Figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:05:45 UTC
04:05:45 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Many Su-34 Fighter-Bombers Does Russia Have Left? Ukraine’s Intelligence Has the Figures
Russia continues to produce and modernize its Su-34 fighter-bombers despite significant losses sustained during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with approximately 140 aircraft of this type remaining in service as of October 22, 2026, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The Su-34 fighter-bomber is a key component of Russia’s strike aviation capabilities, particularly due to its use as a platform for launching guided aerial bombs against ground targets, including Ukrainian frontline positions and settlements near active combat zones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, Russia’s Aerospace Forces currently operate approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft of various configurations, including the upgraded Su-34M, also designated Su-34NVO.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 fighter-bombers, while another seven aircraft have sustained damage, Ukrainian intelligence reported.
These losses represent a substantial reduction in Russia’s fleet of fighter-bombers, particularly given the time, financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation required to manufacture replacements.
HUR estimates that Russia’s current production capacity stands at approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually. At that rate, replacing the 43 aircraft destroyed since February 2022 would require roughly 2.5 to three years of production.
Despite these losses, Moscow continues to manufacture and upgrade the aircraft in an effort to maintain its operational fleet and sustain the intensity of missile and bomb strikes against Ukraine.
However, according to Ukrainian intelligence, Russia’s ability to expand its Su-34 fleet remains dependent on several factors, including available manufacturing capacity, access to technological components, and the defense industry’s ability to compensate for aircraft losses.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Su-34 fleet has also faced threats at the airfields where the aircraft are stationed. On October 23, Ukrainian forces carried out a missile strike against Russia’s Baltimor military airfield in Voronezh, a major base for Su-34 fighter-bombers, according to the Exilenova+ OSINT community.
Preliminary reports suggest that the attack targeted aircraft parking areas and the grounds of the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University, located immediately adjacent to the airfield.

Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal Fails to Lower US Prices as Fuel Costs Rise

Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal Fails to Lower US Prices as Fuel Costs Rise
The diesel agreement announced by US President Donald Trump and the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has so far failed to lower diesel prices in the United States, with average prices instead rising slightly, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 28.
According to data cited by the Journal from the American Automobile Association, the average US diesel price reached $6.35 per gallon on October 28, up from $6.28 when Trump announced the agreement on October 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deal was presented as a way to bring additional Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets, but analysts remain skeptical that the volumes will be large enough to materially ease prices, the Wall Street Journal noted.
Last week, a tanker carrying more than 300,000 barrels of Russian diesel departed the port of Primorsk. The vessel initially listed New York as its destination before later changing its status to “for orders,” indicating that no final unloading port had been confirmed.
Analysts cited by the Journal also questioned whether Russia would be able to export the promised volumes because of the poor condition of its refineries and existing export restrictions.
Even if those shipments materialize, the planned volumes would represent only a small share of the shortfall in the global diesel market. Russia is expected to ship slightly more than 100,000 barrels per day this month and around 125,000 barrels per day in November, according to the Wall Street Journal.
By comparison, Russia exported roughly 800,000 barrels of diesel per day in 2025, underscoring the gap between the volumes discussed under the current agreement and the scale of Russia’s previous exports.
The diesel agreement is facing legal challenges in the US. Rep. Jamie Raskin warned that American companies importing Russian fuel could face fines of up to $1 million and prison terms of up to 20 years, arguing that the administration’s sanctions waiver cannot override a congressional ban on Russian energy imports.

Netanyahu's party pushes baseless election fraud claims amid losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:05:00 UTC
04:05:00 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party escalated unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud Thursday, accusing Arab-led parties of manipulating the vote with possible foreign backing as final results were expected to strip his coalition of its parliamentary majority.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the emerging results of the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset. Final vote results were expected Thursday evening.
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!” it said, claiming - without evidence - that the alleged election interference was "aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government.”
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar - a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based Palestinian resistance group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous.”
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. "They are doing this because they lost,” he said.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties.
The projected outcome of the results was expected to show both Netanyahu's bloc of religious and nationalist allies and his more secular and socially liberal opponents falling short of a parliamentary majority required to form a new government. The Arab parties would hold the remaining seats and could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within the week. Israeli law requires election results to be certified by Nov. 4.
Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab Israelis of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.
On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public - and against the Arab public in particular.”
"Netanyahu is working to steal the election,” the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.
The head of the Arab-led Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.
President Isaac Herzog called it a "sensitive moment” and called for a full investigation. He warned that "we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
With nearly all of the votes counted, Israeli media projected 53 parliament seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 48 seats for Eisenkot’s bloc and 19 for Arab-led parties.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, incursion.
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step - something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.

Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:04:17 UTC
04:04:17 KST

Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.
The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.
Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.
Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.
“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.
One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.
In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.
Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.
Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.
Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.
Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.
There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.
The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.
The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

‘Arab voice doesn’t count’: Jewish Israeli blocs reject Palestinian support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:02:33 UTC
04:02:33 KST

‘Arab voice doesn’t count’: Jewish Israeli blocs reject Palestinian support
Palestinian voters could decide Israel’s future, but its political class refuses to accept their mandate.
Few certainties have emerged from Israel’s parliamentary elections. The diverse coalition of Israel’s self-styled ‘Zionist’ opposition remains short of a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud appears to be the largest party, but its electoral bloc has not secured enough seats to form a government.
What is not in doubt, however, is the surge in turnout from Palestinian citizens of Israel, which has established Arab parties as a pivotal bloc in the parliament, potentially one able to determine which of the rival camps forms a government, if either is willing to work with them.
Anger over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and what analysts have described as the overt racism of its governing coalition helped drive Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in large numbers.
An estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters in Israel turned out for Tuesday’s election, marking a surge in participation by a community that accounts for about 21 percent of the population.
The turnout has given the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining who forms the next government.
However, rather than acknowledge that groundswell of support, Israel’s leading politicians have sought to either delegitimise their vote – attributing it to foreign interference – or somehow cast Palestinians exercising their democratic right as an “attempt to steal the election”.
Arab votes don’t count
Framing the result as a bid to secure the “Islamisation of Israel”, Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party has gone so far as to call on Israel’s internal security service, the Shin Bet, to investigate the possibility of foreign election interference into the large-scale Palestinian turnout. In doing so, they appear to have thrown the legitimacy of the Arab vote into question and tainted any future attempt by the opposition to ally with the Arab parties.
Despite denouncing Netanyahu’s government as corrupt, incompetent and damaging to Israel’s international standing, much of Israel’s Jewish-led opposition has remained reluctant to embrace the support of Palestinian parties to remove him from power.
The left-wing Democrats have been the likeliest to cooperate with the Palestinian parties, while other opposition figures have either resisted such an alliance or stopped short of rejecting allegations that foreign actors helped engineer the surge in Palestinian voter turnout.
On election night, former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid ruled out sitting alongside Palestinian parties in government, despite having relied on their support during their brief 2021–22 government.
On Thursday, another leading member of the opposition, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian parties. He said he would sit alongside “neither Bibi nor Tibi”, using Netanyahu’s established nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List – as a stand-in for the wider Palestinian bloc.
“It was clear from campaigning that there was going to be a large turnout,” said Orly Noy, who stood for the Palestinian-dominated Balad party. “The [governing] coalition had shown there were no red lines in Gaza and Palestinians in Israel sensed they might be next. People also just couldn’t face another term of soaring crime and a police force headed by [far-right National Security Minister] Itamar Ben-Gvir.”
“What few rights Palestinians had have been slipping away since October 7. The last tool they had in their toolbox – the only thing they had that was equal to everyone else – was their vote, so they used that in massive numbers, but even that now seems to be being undermined and delegitimised,” she said.
With all ballots counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu Jewish opposition bloc has 48. However, with the 19 seats held by Palestinian parties, the majority in parliament is against Netanyahu.
“Why are the opposition and the press even thinking of this as a three-way split? In any other rational democracy, people would be framing this as an overwhelming victory for the opposition and a rejection of Netanyahu, but we’re not doing that,” Noy said.
“Instead, we’re hearing elements of the opposition talking about joining with Netanyahu in some kind of National Unity government. That’s both a measure of how racist these parties are, when they won’t align with Arabs to form a majority, as well as how profoundly undemocratic they are,” she said.
Different visions
Political differences do exist between an opposition that deliberately frames itself as Zionist and a Palestinian minority whose claim to equal national and civic rights is seen by some as a rejection of that. But underlying that disagreement is a fundamentally different vision of Israel’s future, according to political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg.
“Given that much of Israel’s mainstream politics rests on the assumption of Jewish supremacy, I think it’s understandable that the Arab vote is seen as a challenge,” he said of a sentiment that many argue has been state policy since the 2018 Nation State Law, which enshrined the right to national self-determination as exclusive to Jewish people.
“There are very different ideas at play of what it means to be a citizen of Israel and of how Israel should be governed and for whose benefit,” he said. “These are fundamental differences, of course they are, but they can’t disguise the racism underpinning all.”
“They want to form a government with only Jewish voices,” said Mauricio Lapchik, Hebrew campaign director for the Joint List. “If the numbers of these results were in a different country, in a democratic country, I think it would be crazy to think that they will not be able to say that they won the elections, having this majority. But only in Israel, because the voice of the Arabs do not count as the voice of the Jews, we cannot talk about a victory.”

Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was subject of investigation into leaking information about Iran and Ukraine.
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the director of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, for what the Pentagon says is severe misconduct. The move comes amid reports that the US had warned its allies of a possible renewal of strikes against Iran.

“Sylvia is the subject of an investigation for leaking classified information about the Iran war, the war between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” the official added.

The official said Sylvia was the Defense Department’s chief military planner but “was not a central planner for the Iran war”. “That is the responsibility of CENTCOM [Central Command] and its commander, Admiral [Brad] Cooper,” the official said.
Sylvia’s firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran.
He is the second person to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the J5, under Hegseth. His predecessor was forced to retire in October last year.
“Sylvia failed three polygraphs which questioned him about leaking classified information,” the Pentagon official said while accusing Sylvia of putting national security at risk.
“Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” he concluded.
There is no immediate replacement for Sylvia, according to an official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to The Associated Press news agency.
Before arriving at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led.
His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valour, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat.
Sean Parnel, assistant to the defense secretary for public affairs, said earlier on Thursday in a post on X that “the Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” He did not refer specifically to Sylvia.
Sylvia is the latest senior Pentagon official whom Hegseth has accused of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests.
President Donald Trump has promised to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said he would do so after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

EU governments helpless as energy prices soar to four-year highs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:00:41 UTC
04:00:41 KST

LUXEMBOURG — Europe’s energy ministers are running out of ideas to protect citizens from surging energy prices as winter approaches.
But at a summit in Luxembourg on Thursday, they were clear on one thing: Demanding voters cut back on power use is not an option.
European gas prices soared above €100 per megawatt-hour on Wednesday for the first time since 2022, as last-minute panic-buying to fill European gas reserves added to supply pressures linked to the war in the Middle East.
Advertisement
But at the Thursday summit, EU energy ministers broadly acknowledged that both Brussels and national capitals had run out of ideas to contain price pressures.
“We’ve exhausted most of our short-term options,” said one senior European energy official, granted anonymity to offer a candid perspective. “What’s left is really crisis management.”
For the past year, government attempts to cushion price rises with renewables schemes, windfall taxes and costly fuel subsidies have ultimately failed to contain anxieties that have since boiled over into widespread protests across the continent.
“The EU and member states don't have a magic wand to make the price increases go away,” Irish Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, told reporters. “There's a lot of measures that have been taken already in the short term. What today is about is actually seeing how we can move to more sustainable measures.”
But even crisis management is proving politically difficult. Despite calls by EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen earlier this year to encourage consumers and businesses to cut energy use, European ministers are reluctant to make such a move official policy.
“I don't want to see that we will limit people,” said Mika Nykänen, the state secretary to Finland's energy ministry. Instead, he called for policy designed to “change behavior” and reduce energy consumption less painfully. “Industry does it naturally. Normal households, normal families — they sometimes need encouragement,” he said. “For instance, subsidies to invest in the energy efficiency of houses, windows.”
Advertisement
Demand reduction “has an impact on industry, it has an impact on business, and in a difficult situation, it could be the way to do that. But it does not … solve the long-term,” Polish Secretary of State for Energy Wojciech Wrochna told reporters.
High prices “will regulate demand by itself,” Swedish Energy Minister Ebba Busch told reporters.
Fossil fuel subsidies
Such was the opposition to demand reduction measures on Thursday, Jørgensen — who was at the summit warning of a "difficult" winter of soaring fuel prices ahead — gave up even proposing it, focusing instead on subsidies. He reluctantly accepted that such subsidies could include fossil fuels as well as clean alternatives, but urged that they be "targeted and temporary."
Since the war started, governments have paid €18 billion for tax relief on fossil fuel products, including a controversial move by Rome earlier this month to reduce the impact of gas prices on electricity costs.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned national leaders against this tendency, urging them at a summit this month to keep policies temporary and targeted to avoid inadvertently increasing fossil fuel demand and distorting the EU single market, according to two EU diplomats familiar with her comments.
That remains a point of contention among EU leaders, with some, including Greece, calling for greater fiscal space to increase energy subsidies while others warn of the dangers of subsidizing fossil fuels.
Advertisement
“Our concern is to make sure that we don't create conditions where different member states go very far in different national decision-making,” said Lithuanian Energy Minister Lukas Savickas in a separate interview.
Jørgensen did not respond to POLITICO's question at a subsequent press conference when asked whether new fiscal flexibilities were being considered.
Other ideas have gone by the wayside. Von der Leyen rejected calls by countries to establish an EU-wide tax on windfall profits of oil and gas companies at this month’s summit, the diplomats cited above said even as European oil companies like Shell, TotalEnergies and Repsol rake in their biggest profits since 2022.
Member countries also questioned the value of a Commission proposal to coordinate the purchase of energy supplies. Such a scheme would work in theory but be hard to implement for “big players” with established supply chains, Wrochna said.
Neither has the EU’s commitment to hastening the release of strategic crude oil and diesel reserves earlier this month — in response to what EU officials described as U.S. “blackmail” — done much to ease fuel costs.
Even so, the EU's commitment will now include over 40 million barrels on top of the 10 million pledged by Paris, France's economy minister Roland Lescure told reporters on Thursday.
Advertisement
A parallel push to delay methane monitoring requirements — a plank of the EU's 2024 Green Deal that industry argued was poorly designed and would disrupt supplies — also had no impact on prices.
Slow pay-off
To be sure, measures designed to lower electricity prices and encourage consumers to switch away from imported fossil fuels are starting to work, with soaring sales of heat pumps and electric vehicles in Europe this year. "There's no silver bullet, but when you add all of these things up, it can actually matter," said Jørgensen.
But even longer-term efforts to encourage the switch to cleaner energy are facing backlash as countries resist ceding power to Brussels.
One example is a Commission proposal to make electricity bills more affordable and speed up electrification, including by ensuring electricity is not taxed more heavily than natural gas. Member countries pushed back against the proposal’s taxation provisions on Thursday, arguing that Brussels is overstepping EU treaties requiring that tax changes be approved unanimously, risking higher costs for households and industry.
Busch, the Swedish energy minister, said the proposal’s taxation provisions went too far, warning it would face “a lot of pushback” from countries concerned about EU interference in national tax policy.
Germany and Poland also raised concerns about the proposal’s potential impact on industry and national tax systems, while Italy warned that changing tax rates could make energy more expensive rather than encourage electrification.

Oldest known Mars rock is a ‘Rosetta stone’ for the Red Planet’s watery past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:59:44 UTC
03:59:44 KST

In 2022 a group of nomadic meteorite hunters discovered a strange stone in the Sahara Desert. Called Teghaza 001, initial analysis by experts showed it was a meteorite from Mars. Now new research reveals it’s the oldest ever found, and it’s revealing more about the Red Planet’s complex history.
Scientists fortunate enough to get their hands on samples of the space rock have been analyzing tiny pieces of Teghaza for years to better understand exactly what it is and when it formed. The new paper, published today in Science, identifies it as a piece of Mars’s crust that’s at least 4.1 billion years old, from a time when that world was warmer, wetter and more Earth-like.
“We’re holding a piece of a rock that’s dated even before the oldest Earth rock—a piece of Mars that’s so ancient, it existed when life had just started on Earth,” says Yang Liu, lead author of the study and a planetary scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Several hundred Martian meteorites are known. All of them got here by giant impacts that have pelted Mars for eons, occasionally blasting bits of the planet into space, some of which by chance fall to Earth. Most are relatively young, each revealing little more than a snapshot from the most recent 600 million years or so of Mars’s 4.5-billion-year history. The only other known intact ancient sample, a meteorite discovered in Antarctica in the 1980s, is just 10 million years younger than Teghaza.
When Liu received a piece of the rock from the team at the University of New Mexico that initially analyzed it, she was tasked with studying its manganese, an element that can help scientists discern whether an ancient rock was ever exposed to water and oxidation. But soon she noticed the presence of zircons in the meteorite—tough crystalline minerals that can endure in rock for billions of years and contain radioactive isotopes that can be used for ultraprecise dating. The zircons, Liu realized, made Teghaza very special. In the exhaustive work that followed, she and her team isolated zircons and other minerals from small scraps of their precious samples, pinning down the meteorite’s chemical composition and dating its elements to the early days of Mars’s history.
Teghaza, they found, is an igneous rock that formed from slowly-cooled magma and was once a piece of the planet’s crust. Comparing ratios of certain elements in the meteorite to those measured by orbiters for larger swaths of the planet’s surface, Liu and her team found the closest matches within the rugged, crater-pocked terrain in Mars’s southern highlands, a region thought to be among the world’s most ancient.
Pinpointing the possible sites where Teghaza was launched by a giant impact on its fateful journey to Earth is a feat all its own, but the meteorite’s chemical composition shows something even more enlightening.
As detailed in work from Liu’s team published earlier this year, some of the minerals in the meteorite have been aqueously altered—a sign that liquid water once percolated through Mars’s ancient mantle and crust. And careful analysis of remnant hydrogen trapped inside Teghaza shows that even when the rock formed, more than 4.1 billion years ago, the planet was already well on its way to losing most of its atmosphere, growing cold and transitioning to its current freeze-dried state. Taken together with the results in today’s paper, Liu says, all this reinforces how Mars’s mantle is likely more heterogeneous and complex than many planetary scientists have long assumed.
Liu’s research on Teghaza is ongoing; her team “has only scratched the surface,” she says, of the insights the meteorite might hold.
A clearer understanding of Mars’s deep past can also inform our own. Mars and Earth formed in similar ways, with giant magma oceans that cooled into cores, mantles and crusts. Because of its tectonic activity that continuously buries, melts and recycles the planet’s crust across geological time, Earth’s surface does not preserve many (if any) samples from its primordial youth—but Mars is different, as its geophysical tumults ebbed long ago.
One reviewer of the paper called this meteorite “the Rosetta stone of Mars,” Liu says, because it may be able to tell the stories of planets across the solar system.
“We’re hoping to start using Mars to compare and contrast and to understand what makes a planet habitable for life,” she adds.
There’s much still to learn about this meteorite’s mysteries, says Anya Udry, a planetary scientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who was not involved with the Science study. But truly understanding the full story of Mars requires more than gathering additional impact-imported fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth; what’s necessary is more visits to the world itself.
“Mars is a complex planet, and this meteorite is really cool, but we don’t know exactly where it came from, so this is really another example of why we need to bring back samples,” she says.

AFRL Plans to Award $30M for Cislunar Project Starting Next Spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:57:37 UTC
03:57:37 KST

The Air Force Research Laboratory plans to launch its latest technology challenge next month—a project meant to speed up development of systems that can operate beyond geosynchronous orbit.
SpaceWERX is leading the effort, dubbed Cislunar Prime. The space innovation hub is looking for commercial capabilities that could put the Space Force on a faster path toward cislunar operations in three focus areas:
- space domain awareness
- cislunar communications
- positioning, navigation, and timing
The tentative plan, according to an AFRL spokesperson, is to officially announce Cislunar Prime in December, solicit proposals in January, and begin awarding contracts next spring. The program has $30 million to fund 15 direct-to-phase-two Small Business Innovation Research contracts worth $2 million each.
The Space Force defines cislunar as the region of space past GEO and extending to the moon and beyond, hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and 1,728 times the volume of space complained within GEO. Conditions there present challenges for satellite operations like PNT and SDA, given its distance from the Earth and its unstable trajectories.
Speaking Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Advanced Programs Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy said because of these dynamics, the Space Force needs a better understanding of how to operate in cislunar space.
“Space is often described as hard and difficult and a fight that we’re not seeing,” he said. “But I would characterize cislunar as even harder and more difficult, and we really don’t see what’s going on in that arena.”
The Space Force has a handful of active projects exploring cislunar operations, including AFRL’s Oracle program, which plans to launch its first satellite in December—a pathfinder for efficient cislunar mobility, navigation, and space domain awareness. Over the past year, the service has signaled it plans to ramp up cislunar research and development activities, driven in part by China’s plans to establish a presence beyond GEO and on the moon.
Purdy said the Pentagon’s posture toward cislunar operations and planning has shifted significantly over the past year. He cited President Donald Trump’s December 2025 executive order that emphasized the importance of cislunar operations, as well as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine’s acknowledgement of cislunar as a “warfighting domain” during AFA’s Air, Space, and Cyber Conference in September.
Now, the service is looking to quickly fund satellites and software that could be ready for operations as soon as 2029, Purdy said. Beyond Cislunar Prime, the Space Force and its newly established Cislunar Coordination Office have two forthcoming requests for information—the first focused on existing cislunar hardware and software that could fly in the next two to three years, and the second for AI and autonomous processing capabilities.
“We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.”

Germany and Ukraine test armed ground robot for frontline deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:56:57 UTC
03:56:57 KST

Remote-controlled and heading for the front lines. ARX Robotics and the Ukrainian company ROBONEERS report completion of the first major system tests.
A German and a Ukrainian defence company have tested an armed ground robot for use by Ukrainian forces, with the first systems due to be integrated and delivered by the end of 2026.
The cooperation agreement was signed in early October during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's state visit to Kyiv, in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Before the end of 2026, the first robotic vehicles fitted with the new weapons modules are expected to be ready for deployment and delivered in line with the needs of Ukraine's armed forces.
How the new system works
It's known as GEREON. Built by ARX Robotics, the unmanned vehicle provides mobility and power and can carry out reconnaissance using cameras and sensors.
It can be fitted with the SABER weapons module, built by Ukrainian company ROBONEERS, which is mounted on top and provides remotely operated fire support for attack and defence capabilities. The companies say this allows soldiers to operate the system from a safer distance.
Unarmed versions of GEREON are already being used for a range of tasks in Ukraine. They can transport supplies, evacuate wounded personnel, support electronic warfare, carry out reconnaissance and counter drones. The platform can also be adapted for combat missions.
The companies say the aim is to create one flexible robotic system that can be quickly adapted for different frontline missions.
The SABER weapons module is also customisable, allowing soldiers to fit different weapons depending on the mission, from rifles to grenade launchers.
ARX says GEREON is the largest fleet of Western-built unmanned ground vehicles currently being used in Ukraine.
Maximilian Wied, CFO and co-founder of ARX Robotics, said: "Modern land forces need combat platforms that can be quickly adapted to different missions, integrate new technologies and work seamlessly with existing systems."
ROBONEERS says its robotic systems have already been used in more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014.
The two companies are already cooperating in other areas. They have set up a joint venture to expand production of another unmanned ground vehicle, the Rys Pro, in Germany and Ukraine. The companies are targeting production of more than 1,000 units in its first year.
German defence minister to visit tech company Helsing
Artificial intelligence is also a focus for German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, who is visiting defence technology company Helsing at its headquarters in Munich.
The visit will focus on the company's latest products and AI capabilities, alongside meetings with management, employees and the works council.
Helsing was founded in 2021 and has grown rapidly into one of Europe's most prominent defence technology companies.
It develops artificial intelligence and software for military systems, including technology designed to add AI capabilities to existing platforms such as tanks, submarines and fighter jets.

Wallaby 'incredibly proud' as brother represents Australian Deaf Rugby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:54:52 UTC
03:54:52 KST

Wallabies star Charlie Cale proud as brother Jack represents Australian Deaf Rugby
For as long as he can remember, Wallabies back-rower Charlie Cale has always been able to rely on his older brother Jack.
Growing up in Sydney's northern suburbs, they would often team up together against the eldest of the Cale boys, Sam, in fierce backyard rugby battles.
Even when it came to studying during their school years, Charlie knew Jack was in his corner.
"He helped me with a lot of my schoolwork," Charlie fondly tells ABC Sport.
"There's been a few exams … he's helped me in a lot of ways, actually.
"That's the best thing about Jack. He's always been there for me and anyone else that has needed him.
"He's one of a kind."
Jack's encouragement is repaid by the support he receives from Charlie and Sam, who both keenly follow his career with the Australian Deaf Rugby (ADR) men's squad.
Last Tuesday night in Sydney, Charlie proudly presented Jack, Australia's vice-captain, with his official team tie ahead of the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which begin in Tokyo this weekend.
Australia's men's and women's squads are among the favourites to emerge triumphant once the tournament concludes on November 3.
Jack is grateful to have Charlie and Sam's backing as he juggles rugby commitments with his job as a lawyer.
"It's always been really helpful having two brothers to go through a rugby career with," says Jack, who has played for Eastwood (Shute Shield) and Mosman (Subbies) at club level.
"We're always checking in with each other, trying to watch each other's games.
"Charlie, even with the limited time he gets outside of training with Brumbies and Wallabies squads, is always trying to watch our games as well."
On the international stage
Jack's introduction to deaf rugby came out of the blue.
"In late 2022, I got a phone call from an old coach of mine on a Saturday morning," says Jack, who had played colts and grade rugby in Sydney by this stage.
"He gave me a call and said, 'Mate, there's this deaf rugby trial happening down at Hunters Hill.'
"Of course, I didn't know what he was talking about as I hadn't really heard anything before.
"I went down there and ran around in a bit of a sevens trial, for maybe 20 or 25 minutes.
"I didn't think I'd actually played that well. I didn't touch the ball that much.
"I came off the field and I wasn't sure what to expect."
A letter arrived in the mail a few months later in early 2023, informing Jack he was selected in the ADR men's squad for the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which were being held in Córdoba, Argentina in April of that year.
There was one small problem, though.
Jack found out about his selection during the club rugby off-season, meaning he was not exactly at peak fitness.
"I had to get myself fit pretty quickly without any rugby training, which was a bit of a struggle," Jack laughs.
Jack worked his way back into shape and seamlessly joined the Australian line-up, which he helped lead in his vice-captaincy role.
They made the final, gallantly losing 20-5 to Wales, while Australia finished third overall in the women's competition.
In Tokyo, the men's squad faces England, Japan, Hong Kong China and Italy in the pool stage, with the top three advancing to the knockout rounds of the tournament.
Australia is one of six teams in the women's draw, where it plays Fiji, England, Wales, New Zealand and a combined Barbarians team in a single pool.
Each will progress, with the two top-ranked teams moving directly to the semifinals.
Having avoided Wales in the men's round-robin matches, Jack considers England to be Australia's main threat in the preliminary phase.
"You've obviously got to go match by match," Jack says.
"It's important to get through the pool stage as well as we can and then the mindset obviously shifts to the knockout stages.
"I'd consider us in the better pool for the opportunity to do that."
Embracing challenges
To participate in World Deaf Rugby tournaments, players must have an average bilateral hearing loss across both ears of at least 40 decibels.
The level of hearing loss varies from player to player in the Australian teams, which illustrates to Jack the importance of non-verbal communication during matches.
"I stepped into this environment where nothing was said on a rugby field," he says.
"It was a bit of a challenge to get used to that.
"But I also really enjoyed that challenge, being able to communicate with some of those guys whose hearing is a lot more affected than mine is."
As much as Jack loves playing alongside his Australian teammates, he also gets a kick out of facing them in club rugby.
On one such occasion last year, he and Australian captain Tim Anstey opposed each other when Mosman met Newport in the NSW Subbies competition.
"It's pretty awesome playing against someone like that, who you now travel with on international tours," Jack says.
"But it's also surreal finding out that someone you might have been playing rugby against is also partially deaf and had the same struggles as you growing up, and you're now representing your country with them.
"It's pretty cool."
While Jack relishes every chance to represent Australia, spreading the message of inclusivity is just as important to him and everyone involved in deaf rugby.
ADR states its goal is to give every deaf and hard-of-hearing athlete the opportunity to play the game, regardless of their experience level.
"We want to find as many deaf or hard-of-hearing rugby players as we can," Jack says.
"It's really just word of mouth within deaf and hard-of-hearing communities."
Jack's family is also firmly behind the cause.
"I've got a lot of respect for this [ADR] program," says Charlie, who has played six Tests for the Wallabies.
"It gives these guys a platform and opportunity they may have lacked growing up.
"We know how much it means to Jack and therefore it means a lot to us."
Family support
Charlie got up early in the morning to watch Jack play at the world titles in Córdoba three years ago.
But a friendlier time zone will make it easier for him to follow his brother's progress in Tokyo.
"I don't think I've missed a game," Charlie says.
"I've woken up at 2am or 3am. I love watching him play."
As he did in Córdoba, Jack will have his devoted mum and dad, Sue and Tim, barracking from the sidelines in Tokyo.
The Cale parents do everything possible to watch their three sons play rugby.
"I don't think our mother has missed a rugby game of ours in God knows how many years," Jack says.
"Dad is always on the phone, straight after games, checking in with us and seeing how we've gone."
Just as he helped Charlie all those years ago with his schoolwork, Jack knows he can also depend on the support of his family.
"We're incredibly proud of him," Charlie says.

Sybiha said the European leaders initiated the call in coordination with Kyiv. Its main purpose was to convey Ukraine’s message: Along with proposing an in-person meeting between the leaders, Ukraine also called for a ceasefire.
“We want this meeting and are ready for it. In all likelihood, only a meeting between Zelensky and Putin can change the dynamics of the negotiations. Zelensky is ready to discuss the most difficult and sensitive issues, including territory,” Sybiha said.
Stubb’s office had previously said the purpose of the call was to “convey Ukraine’s position on the upcoming peace talks in Abu Dhabi directly to President Putin.” Helsinki provided no details.
Putin’s conversation with Stubb and Støre was his first contact with European leaders who support Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.

Putin says Russia is ready for war with Europe

- Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is ready for war with Europe but does not want one, warning there would be no winners.
- He spoke in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, responding to European plans to be ready to repel a Russian attack by 2030.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is “ready” for a war with Europe but does not want one, and warned that a conflict between them would leave no winners, responding to European warnings that Moscow could be able to attack NATO by the end of the decade.
Putin made the remarks at a press conference in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, held jointly with the African Union’s chairman, Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, The Moscow Times reported, citing Interfax. He was asked about his recent phone calls with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and said Russia supports any steps to restore full relations with European countries, either with the European Union as a whole or one by one.
“Many are talking about preparing for war by 2030. First of all, we are ready, but we do not want any war with Europe. If they want to prepare, let them prepare,” said Putin.
He added that Europe had not managed to inflict a “strategic defeat” on Russia and was unlikely to do so by 2030, according to TV Rain.
“If things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that,” Putin said.
Putin also referred to tensions in the Baltic Sea, asking whether anyone wanted the region to end up like the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, and said Russia did not want that but would respond to any challenge. He did not name any country or describe what kind of response he meant.
The 2030 date Putin cited matches the timeline European governments have set for rearmament. EU states aim to be able to repel a Russian attack by 2030, and several European officials have warned that Russia could rebuild enough military strength to strike a NATO member before then. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and the head of Germany’s armed forces, Gen. Carsten Breuer, have said Russia could be capable of a large-scale conventional attack on NATO territory by 2029, and a classified German intelligence and military analysis reported in 2025 said Moscow was preparing the conditions for a conventional war against NATO, with the Baltic states a possible target. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said Europe should be prepared for a possible major conflict with Russia as early as 2027.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected those warnings, and Putin has long said Russia has no plans to attack NATO countries. In December 2025, he said that if Europe “suddenly wants to wage a war with us and starts it, we are ready right away,” Fox News reported, while also saying Moscow did not seek war with Europe. European leaders, for their part, say Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, shows why they need to rearm.
Putin’s latest comments came two days after his calls with Stubb and Støre, which European officials have not described in detail. Neither Finland nor Norway, both NATO members that border Russia, had publicly responded to Putin’s remarks by Thursday evening.

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
October 29, 2026
European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.
"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.
But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
What's on the agenda for the summit?
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

Trains in Europe are getting safer despite recent tragedies in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:49:16 UTC
03:49:16 KST

Europe's trains are actually getting safer, despite recent tragedies in Spain
Spain was once regarded as a world leader in rail systems, but after suffering two of its deadliest train incidents in over a decade this year alone, questions have emerged.
The country has commenced three days of mourning after at least 69 people died, and dozens more were injured, after two high-speed trains collided just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday.
A computer system failure saw six trains stopped on just over 60km of track between Madrid and Seville, while another was manually given clearance to move, according to Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
What are the recent incidents in Spain?
Spain's high-speed rail network, operated by state-owned RENFE, is among the largest in the world, second only to China.
In January, 46 people died on the same rail network after two high-speed trains carrying around 400 passengers collided.
It was the first fatal incident along Spain's dedicated high-speed rail lines since its opening in 1992.
According to European Union data, rail fatality rates in Europe have decreased over the last decade, and last year recorded no fatalities or major accidents.
However, a series of accidents in 2023 saw a spike in those numbers.
Between 2022 and 2024, Spain recorded some of the lowest fatalities per million train kilometres in Europe.
University of Sydney's Rico Merkert, who specialises in European transport systems, said isolated incidents shifted people's perception around safety.
"There are so many trains, including high-speed trains, operated or run each and every day in Europe. There are millions of people travelling on those trains," Professor Merkert said.
"One incident is catastrophic and really not good and very tragic in terms of the number of fatalities.
"But statistically speaking, it's still safe due to the large volumes of passengers using trains and high-speed trains every single day in Europe."
He added that the European Train Control System (ETCS) prevented trains from reaching excessive speeds and could recognise when there was potential for a collision.
"The problem with the accident that happened [this week] is that there was a signalling sort of failure,"
he said.
"There was a system issue, so it broke down, and it's not quite clear whether that ETCS system was actually operating at all or partially unavailable. It looks like that system failure caused manual operations or signalling."
How does train safety in Europe compare?
A report into railway safety from the European Union found Australia, South Korea and the EU were among the safest railway systems between 2020 and 2024.
It also looked into passenger fatalities and found Japan was the safest, with no fatalities recorded.
Professor Merkert said it was difficult to compare Australia's rail system to Europe, because it does not have high-speed trains.
"[It] is not comparing apples with apples … high-speed trains are between 250 and 300 kilometres an hour, and you simply don't have those trains operating here in Australia," he said.
The report into railway safety said the gap in passenger fatality rates between Europe and Japan would be difficult to close in the medium term.
Professor Merkert said that was due to Japan's long tradition of running high-speed rail safely and efficiently.
"Similarly, China, they had a few incidents themselves, but overall again, the number of trains that they're operating and the number of people using those trains without having any accidents is quite remarkable," he said.
He said overall railway systems were safe, but once automated, additional safety procedures were required.
"There needs to be manual safeguards and governance structure in place that prevent things like what has happened [this week], and that simply seems to not have occurred,"
he said.
