Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:48:14 UTC
03:48:14 KST

Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is stirring up trouble at home during a controversial trip to Montreal, turning what should have been a straightforward trade mission into a petty argument over Canada’s fictional “membership” in the bloc.
The EU mandarin traveled to Montreal for the 21st annual EU-Canada summit on Thursday, with her tail between her legs. A month after unilaterally promising Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney “associate member” status of the bloc, she was reportedly forced to scrub all mentions of the term and downgrade her offer to one of an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada.
When the summit closes on Friday, both sides will issue a revised joint statement that reads: “We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” according to a draft seen by Policito.
Why was the text changed?
Von der Leyen reportedly gave neither the EU’s vast bureaucracy, nor its members’ wary leaders, any warning before she told Carney in front of the European Parliament that she “would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union.”
Unilateral decisions and boundary-overstepping are von der Leyen’s calling cards, as her fellow Eurocrats have repeatedly complained to the press. “Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” an unnamed diplomat told The Guardian on Wednesday. The widespread anonymous briefing to various mainstream European media made it clear that France, Germany, Greece and Italy had forced von der Leyen to adopt the new, watered-down terminology.
Ursula goes rogue
In her first speech in Montreal on Thursday, von der Leyen refused to adopt the new, sanitized wording. After noting that “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography,” she insisted that “we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. Our idea is simple: it is an ‘association without accession’.”
Whatever form Friday’s communique will take, von der Leyen has evidently chosen to disregard the concerns of the EU’s largest member states for the sake of her own personal project. However, the difference between both statements is purely rhetorical.
What does ‘associate member’ mean anyway?
Neither “Associate member” nor “ever closer association” are defined anywhere in EU law.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz attempted to define “associate membership” in May when he suggested that it be granted to Ukraine. Under his proposal, Ukraine would participate in European Council meetings without voting rights, send representatives to the European Parliament, receive more EU funding, and become party to the EU’s mutual defense clause.
The proposal was rejected by Kiev, with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky arguing that this kind of ‘membership-lite’ would leave his country “present in the European Union, but voiceless.”
“Ever closer association” is an even more meaningless term, lifted straight from ‘Ever Closer Union’, a hagiography on EU integration by the bloc’s court historian, Desmond Dinan. Writing in 1994, Dinan argued that “European integration is a good thing,” and the phrases he used – “ever closer union” and “pooling sovereignty,” for example – have since become staples of EU speeches and press releases.
US President Donald Trump ridiculed von der Leyen’s word games last month, calling the concept of associate membership “laughable,” and threatening to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if the EU-Canada proto-alliance ever harmed US interests.
Carney – who plainly insisted last month that Canada is “not looking to become a member of the European Union” – responded diplomatically to the intra-EU squabbling. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” he said ahead of the summit. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
However, Von der Leyen’s “membership” promise and the subsequent retraction has undermined Carney in front of his opponents. In a social media post on Thursday, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre described the concept of “associate membership” as “theater,” and dismissed the summit as “yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more."
How long will this theatre go on? While Canadians can’t afford food and homes, Mr. Carney has distracted for months with big talk about “Associate Membership” with Europe. Now, Europe has rejected it. For the next two days, we will be distracted again from the cost-of-living crisis with wall-to-wall media coverage on yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more. No one’s mortgage or grocery bill will come down. We already have a free trade deal with Europe, Mr. Carney. Get the 9 countries who have not ratified it to do so. And get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out.
— Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) October 29, 2026
What does von der Leyen actually want?
Von der Leyen has far more riding on this summit than Carney. While the EU needs energy, minerals, and Canada’s geographic clout in the Arctic, Canada only needs to diversify some of its trade away from the US – which accounts for around 72% of its exports and 46% of its imports – in order to hedge against Trump’s tariffs and trade restrictions. At present, the EU accounts for less than 6% of Canada’s exports and 12% of its imports.
🛬 Touchdown in Montréal 🇨🇦 Rarely have I looked forward to a Summit this much. An ocean separates Europe and Canada. Yet we have never felt closer. We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as Associate Member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further. With an Alliance for the Future, we will stand together and respond to a world of growing rivalries. Montréal, we’re about to write a new chapter in our shared history.
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 28, 2026
Although the agenda is wrapped up in the language of “shared values” and “respect for the rules-based international order,” Brussels’ priorities in Montreal are clear: the energy-starved EU needs access to Canada’s resources.
According to Euronews, the latest draft of the joint declaration includes a promise to “assess opportunities for long-term energy connectivity,” including the supply of Canadian liquefied natural gas to the EU. Remember that in July 2025 von der Leyen personally pledged to Trump that bloc members would buy $750 billion worth of US energy by the end of 2028, in a trade deal that was widely seen as one-sided.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne has also announced that Ottawa and Brussels intend to sign an agreement on the supply of critical minerals including lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The EU currently controls less than 4% of the world’s supply of these minerals, which are vital in the production of electric vehicles and missiles – both of which the EU intends to increase.
The Europeans also intend to sign defense production and technology-sharing deals, to squeeze cash out of Canada for the bloc’s increasingly stretched €90 billion loan package for Ukraine, and deepen involvement in the Arctic, according to the summit agenda. As the EU set out in its updated Arctic Strategy’ earlier this month, Brussels intends to increase its military presence to challenge Russia in the north, and plans to literally redraw the map of the region to increase its meager Arctic claims, and to pursue closer ties “with like-minded partners,” including Canada.
To challenge Russia in the Arctic, the EU likely has its eyes on Canada’s polar-trained military and its 20-strong icebreaker fleet, compared to the ten such vessels spread across the 27-member bloc. None of these icebreakers are nuclear powered, and even if they were to operate on joint Arctic missions, they would be outnumbered and outclassed by Russia’s fleet of 43, eight of which are nuclear powered
However, any hope von der Leyen may have had of securing preferential single market-style trade deals with Carney have apparently been dashed. According to AFP, the “associate member” version of the joint statement included an “explicit goal of deeper financial market integration.” The new, “ever closer association” communique has replaced this with a promise by both sides to “limit potential negative effects on each other.”
Von der Leyen’s unforced error
Whether von der Leyen will, by virtue of repetition and against the will of four EU member states, invent an “associate membership” is immaterial. The concept is a legal fiction, and by insisting on the word “membership,” the European Commission president set herself up for an entirely avoidable clash with the French, Germans, Greeks, and Italians.
It’s very interesting to see the Commission president goes so defiantly against the position of Germany — the biggest member state and her home country — on an issue that, as of now, remains strictly theoretical.
— Jorge Liboreiro (@JorgeLiboreiro) October 29, 2026
The argument over the statement’s wording has overshadowed the summit, but the geopolitical reality remains unchanged: the EU needs Canada’s energy supplies to keep its economy afloat, Canada’s money to prop up its Ukraine project, and Canada’s geography to legitimize its Arctic expansion. For these, it doesn’t matter how the deal is dressed up.

'They know exactly what they're doing' — What Russia gains from a ceasefire in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:47:26 UTC
03:47:26 KST

Why did Russia agree to the Oleshky ceasefire?
An aerial view of Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, Ukraine in a photo published on Sept.16, 2026. (Dmytro Lubinets / Telegram)
Moscow's consent to a temporary ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky seems like a long-overdue and welcome concession from a country that has repeatedly rejected or violated ceasefire proposals during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
So why is the Kremlin so on board with Oleshky? Experts, as well as information from Oleshky itself, suggest Russia's motives go far beyond addressing the humanitarian catastrophe it created itself.
Instead, the highly publicized ceasefire brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump presents several opportunities for Moscow to manipulate facts on the ground, an international audience, and — crucially — the White House, all as it positions itself ahead of a new round of peace talks.
"They know exactly what they're doing," John Foreman, a former U.K. defense attache in both Kyiv and Moscow, told the Kyiv Independent.
The propaganda opportunity
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.
Military analyst Vasyl Pehno said on Oct. 27 that Russia had created the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and is now presenting itself as "heroically rescuing civilians."
The evacuation of residents from Oleshky provides the Kremlin with the opportunity to convince the world that Ukrainians under occupation would rather live in Russia than go back to Ukraine.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Footage broadcast by Russian state media channel TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
read also
The political gains
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XVI, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
The first lady facilitated the ceasefire arrangement after she learned about the crisis during the United Nations General Assembly week, her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 28.
He added that her involvement in the Oleshky ceasefire was "wanted very much" by Putin, something Foreman said has obvious political motives.
"Allowing Melania to take the credit bolsters their credentials to the MAGA base as peacemakers before the midterms," he said.
Foreman argued that the temporary truce could help placate Trump, while he blamed Ukraine for blocking the peace process, Foreman added.
"The same Kremlin approach for the diesel deal, agreeing to three-way talks, and releasing a hostage in return for pausing new sanctions," he added, saying each time Russia gains something substantial without "conceding anything significant."
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow wants to give Trump another opportunity to claim he has helped stop a war.
Russia is unlikely to violate the ceasefire this time, he said, not out of concern for civilians, but because the Kremlin would not want to jeopardize its relationship with Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Despite this, the Beckman is adamant that Russia is acting in good faith.
"It's my understanding and my belief in being very close to all of these negotiations and knowing all of the parties for a long time, that everybody, the Russians included, is working in good faith," Beckman said.
"It's understood that this is a humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and these elderly people need to be saved."
read also
Crisis beyond Oleshky
While the Kremlin agreed to the Oleshky ceasefire, it remains silent about the dire humanitarian situation across other occupied territories.
Daria Rabinovitsch, co-executive director at Helping to Leave, an organization that helps civilians leave the occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that calculating how many settlements are isolated is nearly impossible due to broken communications and missing internet access, but at least three other areas are known to be suffering from isolation.
These include the Kinburn Spit, settlements in the Polohy District of Zaporizhzhia Oblast where drivers refuse to go, and Enerhodar, where access has become hazardous due to intense air attacks along transport routes.
Such enclaves frequently appear when the front line shifts and Russia gains more territory, Rabinovitsch said. In some places, Russian military personnel relocate residents from active combat zones deeper into occupied lands, she added.
While the ceasefire might facilitate temporary relief efforts in Oleshky, it leaves systemic problems facing Ukrainians under Russian control unaddressed.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
"Oleshky is not the only community on the temporarily occupied territories that is experiencing a humanitarian catastrophe, and while we are happy and hopeful for the people there, we know that this evacuation will not resolve the systemic problems facing Ukrainians in the Russian occupation," Rabinovitsch said.
According to Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the initial 30 hours of the ceasefire proceeded without incident. While Kherson Oblast had a brief chance for respite, Russian forces continued striking other Ukrainian regions and killing civilians.
As Lubinets headed to Oleshky on the morning of Oct. 29, Russian troops attacked the railway station in Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, with a jet-powered drone, killing at least 13 people.

2026-10-29
18:47:12 UTC
03:47:12 KST

Australian-made Bluebottle drones to patrol Fiji's waters for drug traffickers
Fiji's hundreds of islands and vast maritime territory make it difficult to detect drug traffickers.
Intent on accessing lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand, smugglers from the Americas use the island nation as a Pacific transit point.
"Our biggest challenge is our waters are too big," Fiji's Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said.
"We don't even have eyes on it, let alone have the capability to affect anything on it."
But a new fleet of uncrewed maritime surface drones could help level the playing field.
The 7.4-metre-long Australian-made Bluebottles can remain at sea for up to six months, while using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious activity.
Powered by a retractable solar sail that can harness the sun and wind, they also have an underwater flipper that converts the boat's rocking in the waves into forward motion.
Mr Tikoduadua said the Bluebottles would help Fiji capitalise on its limited resources.
Traffickers are known to use yachts, fishing vessels, freight ships and even semi-submersibles, known as narco-subs.
Fiji's navy, meanwhile, operates just two large patrol boats, RFNS Savenaca and RFNS Timo, both Australian-donated Guardian-class vessels.
The RFNS Timo replaced a previous vessel, the RFNS Puamau, which ran aground during its maiden voyage in 2024.
'Virtually impossible to detect'
Australia is donating the drones and training as part of a $600 million package for the Pacific-wide Waqa Moana maritime security initiative to counter illicit drug trafficking.
The money will also fund new Australian Federal Police programs and regional surveillance support.
Fiji's first drones are expected to start arriving next year, but the total number has not been made public, with Mr Tikoduadua saying they wanted to "keep drug dealers guessing".
Australian Minister for Defence Industry and Pacific Island Affairs Pat Conroy earlier this month said the Australian Navy had 15 Bluebottles, most of which monitored the country's northern coastline, with orders in for another 40.
"They are virtually impossible to detect unless you get very close to them," he said.
An Australian company, Ocius Technology, designed the Bluebottles and operates them from a military base in Darwin.
Ocius chief growth and market development officer Rob Brezniak said the vessels could be fitted with high-tech surveillance sensors, including infrared cameras, radar and sonar to detect submarines.
He said they relayed intelligence to a team of human operators via satellite, with AI helping to filter the data and flag potential threats for a faster response.
"A government can then task an asset like a crewed vessel to approach," he said.
Mr Brezniak did not expand on how the AI technology made its assessments, saying "a combination of things helped it make an informed decision".
He also declined to disclose the individual cost of the drones, however the Australian government said its contract with Ocius to deliver the 40 drones was worth $176 million.
In Fiji's case, Mr Tikoduadua said Fijian personnel would control the Bluebottles and configure them to monitor surface vessels, with a detection range of up to 30 nautical miles (55.5km).
He said intelligence would be transmitted to human operators at the Vuvale Maritime Essential Services Centre (MESC), an Australian-funded security hub near Fiji's capital Suva which houses Fijian agencies including the navy, police and fisheries.
Mr Tikoduadua said the gathered information could be shared with partner countries and organisations if a vessel left Fiji's jurisdiction.
"If we need partner navies to come take a look, or a commercial vessel to take a look, it gives us that flexibility," he said.
Levelling the playing field
Mr Tikoduadua has seen the Bluebottles in action.
New Zealand recently deployed two to Fiji during a four-week joint operation.
Associate Professor Jose Sousa-Santos, convenor of the Pacific Regional Security Hub at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, said officials reported the unmanned drones detected more than 100 illegal fishing vessels, many of which had switched off their transponders.
"They did exactly what they were supposed to do," he said.
"They were supported by the New Zealand Air Force and when they identified vessels that raised red flags, they were able to contact the RNZAF to provide further surveillance coverage."
Mr Sousa-Santos said the Bluebottles had the potential to disrupt trafficking operations if they were positioned in zones smugglers regularly operated in.
"It would force them to move to other trafficking routes which might not be as safe or profitable," he said.
A new frontier
Steve Symon, who chaired New Zealand's Ministerial Advisory Group on Transnational, Serious and Organised Crime, said the Bluebottles were a valuable tool.
But he feared the region's size meant they could only be effective if deployed in large numbers.
He added the crime syndicates would probably adapt.
In the short term, Mr Symon said traffickers could rely more heavily on cargo ships and corruption within ports if surveillance drones made their operations more difficult.
But it might only be a matter of time before traffickers started using similar drones, he said.
Criminal syndicates had a powerful incentive to adapt because of the huge demand for illicit drugs in Australia and New Zealand, he said.
"The reason why these [Bluebottle] drones are so good is because they are solar-powered and you can send them out for months at a time.
"But we'd be naive to think organised crime isn't going to be ready adopters of the same technology."
Sharing with Australia
Mr Tikoduadua said data the Bluebottles collected would be shared with partners, including Australia.
Mr Conroy said Australia needed to work with Fiji to stamp out the illicit drug trade, which meant "working together in a coordinated way in terms of intelligence gathering, intelligence sharing and interdiction".
Australian officials did not say whether the Bluebottles in Fiji would be used for anything beyond detecting drug traffickers and illegal fishing, such as monitoring foreign military vessels.
Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor of defence and security at the University of Western Australia, said she did not believe the drones would have wider strategic implications for Australia's defence.
"Fiji and Australia have a significant defence partnership and we would already share significant information about what is happening in our maritime domains," she said.
"So the employment of Bluebottles to support collection of that kind of information would not be any different to, I suspect, what's already in place."

Ukraine and NATO's Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding that opens up new opportunities for the joint development and testing of technologies, as well as for deepening cooperation between Ukraine's and NATO's innovation ecosystems.
According to the Alliance's press service, the document was signed on Thursday, October 29, at NATO headquarters.
The press release explains that the partnership is based on the principle of reciprocity. "Ukraine has developed an extraordinary innovation ecosystem while confronting the realities of modern conflict, rapidly testing, adapting and improving technology under the most demanding conditions, as a result of Russia's war of aggression. DIANA offers an established pathway connecting innovators with NATO's defence and security expertise and infrastructure," the statement reads.
The Memorandum also lays the foundation for further cooperation, "helping Ukrainian innovators navigate NATO requirements, explore testing opportunities and tackle barriers to scaling promising technologies." "For NATO, closer cooperation could broaden the community of innovative suppliers and technologies contributing to the security of the Alliance, while strengthening the industrial base on which collective security depends," NATO said.
NATO said that at a time when "Allies need both to replenish critical capabilities and build a stronger, more innovative industrial base for the future, DIANA's model is designed to connect promising companies with real defence and security problems and create pathways for technologies to move towards operational capability."
Commenting on the signing, Acting Managing Director of DIANA Jyoti Hirani-Driver said: "This Memorandum of Understanding is a beginning. A door is opening. Now our job is to walk through it together. We have an enormous amount to learn from Ukraine."
The signed agreement is the first of its kind between DIANA and a NATO partner. "[The agreement] marks a practical step towards strengthening mutual security through innovation. It also builds on the broader NATO-Ukraine cooperation across their innovation ecosystems, which has developed significantly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine," the press release notes.

EU pressure on Antigua's 'golden passport' trade threatens budget cushion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:46:17 UTC
03:46:17 KST

EU pressure on Antigua's 'golden passport' trade threatens budget cushion
CASTRIES, St Lucia, Oct 29 - Antigua and Barbuda's likely move to end its citizenship-by-investment program under European Union pressure threatens a vital revenue stream for the island nation and could test the future of Caribbean "golden passport" schemes, analysts said.
The issue exposes a vulnerability across the Caribbean, where several small economies have built government revenues and luxury developments around demand for passports valued partly for the access to Europe they provide.
Prime Minister Gaston Browne said this month Antigua would “very likely” commit to phasing out its citizenship-by-investment program after the EU gave Antigua and four other Eastern Caribbean nations until November 12 to agree to close their schemes by June 1, 2028.
The EU says the programs pose security risks by allowing foreigners with few ties to a country to obtain citizenship and visa-free entry to the Schengen area, a key selling point for passport buyers. Countries that keep the schemes risk losing that access.
The EU had initially requested the June 2028 phase-out in letters sent to Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis and Saint Lucia in June. Under a revised EU visa-suspension mechanism, operating an investor-citizenship program can itself provide grounds for suspending visa-free access, though the suspension is not automatic.
The programs, which require investments starting at $200,000, grant foreign applicants citizenship and a passport, rather than temporary residency, typically in exchange for contributions to state funds or investments in approved projects.
Buyers have included nationals of China, Russia and Middle Eastern countries who would normally need visas to enter the EU, and applicants generally have not been required to live in the Caribbean to obtain citizenship. Demand from Americans has grown since 2020, according to Kristin Surak, a London School of Economics professor who researches investment migration.
Citizenship-by-investment inflows in 2023 equaled about a fifth of the combined GDP of the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union, a group of eight Caribbean economies that share a currency and central bank, according to a 2025 International Monetary Fund paper.
The IMF estimated in a paper published in 2025 that direct investment in projects tied to the passport programs was so large that it represented between 100% to 170% of all foreign direct investment officially recorded across the five countries with such schemes.
'EXISTENTIAL FISCAL QUESTION'
Schengen access has traditionally been an important attraction for buyers of Caribbean citizenship-by-investment passports, and losing it could reduce their value while affecting ordinary citizens too, said Surak.
A suspension could force hotels and other developments financed through passport sales to seek fresh capital, delay construction or abandon projects altogether, analysts said.
The immediate stakes are high for Antigua, where citizenship sales are the government’s largest source of non-tax revenue, according to C. Justin Robinson, director of the University of the West Indies Five Islands Campus.
The government collected about $58 million from the program in 2025 and budgeted $44.4 million for 2026, or roughly 7% to 11% of recurrent revenue, he said.
Ending the program would erase more than half of Antigua’s projected primary surplus this year, Robinson estimated.
The consequences could be even greater elsewhere.
In St Kitts and Nevis and Dominica, where such inflows have at times exceeded 10% of GDP, suspension could pose what Robinson called an “existential fiscal question.”
Antigua's experience could also test how aggressively Brussels is prepared to use access to Europe as leverage over citizenship policies beyond its borders. The EU also withdrew Vanuatu’s visa-free access in 2024 over concerns surrounding its investor-citizenship scheme. REUTERS

Taxing Wealth Makes Sense, But It Won’t Fix Our Economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:43:38 UTC
03:43:38 KST

In June, Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire when SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq. Now, the U.S. midterms are here, and wealth taxation is on the ballot.
Californians are set to vote on Proposition 40, which would take 5% of fortunes above $1 billion, once, and send nine-tenths of the revenue to fund California’s Medicaid program. A swarm of Silicon Valley billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, has spent more than $333 million campaigning against the potential tax, warning it will backfire and push the wealthy to flee the sunshine state.
Such reactions are not new. Even the income tax once looked like an assault on property. The Supreme Court struck one down as unconstitutional in 1895, and it took the 16th Amendment in 1913 to make it ordinary. Taxes on great fortunes may travel the same road and become unremarkable within a decade. Plus, research indicates that the wealthiest households often pay lower effective tax rates than the people who work for them.
I support Proposition 40. But it is not sufficient in addressing the underlying economic issues at hand.
A wealth tax like Proposition 40 tries to recover a share of value long after that value has been created, compounded, and defended. By then, the money has lawyers. Which is why the origins of this extreme wealth matter, now that the prospect of redistribution has so agitated the people holding it.
To understand how these systems work, think of the iPhone. As I argued in my book The Entrepreneurial State, the iPhone's foundational technologies came from public research: the internet, GPS, the touchscreen, and the voice recognition behind Siri. Speech understanding research at Carnegie Mellon, MIT, and Stanford Research Institute was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) in the 1970s. Researchers then spent two more decades on language and learning systems no company would finance, because the payoff lay thirty years out.
Or think of Google. The search algorithm that made Brin's fortune grew out of a National Science Foundation project at Stanford.
And then there’s SpaceX, whose listing made Musk a trillionaire, took $396 million from NASA to develop the Falcon 9 and the Dragon capsule, then $1.6 billion to fly cargo to the space station and $2.6 billion to fly astronauts. The world’s richest man was also the biggest political donor this election cycle, spending $366 million supporting Republican causes.
Other people see them as tech bros. I see them as a brologarchy. They surfed off publicly financed research to earn enormous rents, and continue to profit off of them through what I call “algorithmic rents”: returns from owning the platforms, data, and models the rest of us must pass through, and manipulating what our “attention” sees.
None of this takes anything away from the entrepreneurs. Turning a research program into a reusable rocket is hard. The public carried the risk in the years when these technologies had no market and no buyer. The state carries the blame: for not setting out, in the contracts, the terms of that initial investment and a fair share of the rewards for the risk the public took.
The Department of Energy made the asymmetry explicit in 2009, issuing two near-identical loan guarantees to two of Musk’s companies: $465 million to Tesla and $500 million to Solyndra. Solyndra, a now-bankrupt solar panel manufacturer, collapsed two years later, and the taxpayer absorbed the loss and the political damage. Tesla, by contrast, succeeded. Under its loan agreement, the government held warrants it could exercise only if Tesla failed to repay on schedule; Tesla repaid nine years early and the warrants lapsed. The public took the downside on one deal and wrote itself out of the upside on the other.
Economists call this socializing risk and privatizing reward. It describes a contract drafted without the confidence to ask for anything.
NASA once had that confidence. In the early 1960s, it moved Apollo contracts from cost-plus-fixed-fee to incentive contracts tying a contractor's fee to cost, schedule, and performance, setting terms rather than writing blank checks. More recently, the CHIPS and Science Act attached conditions to $52.7 billion of semiconductor funding, covering where plants get built and what jobs they create.
I believe those conditions did not go far enough. Wage standards covered laborers and mechanics rather than every worker, and affected communities got no formal seat in the decisions. But the principle is American, recent, and bipartisan. Public money can come with terms.
This is called “pre-distribution,” shaping how value is created and shared at the outset, rather than waiting for the tax code to repair the damage, and it is a crucial principle for making capitalism work for us all.
But establishing this kind of capitalism requires that we commit to another principle: access for all and reward sharing. If the public carries the risk, it should hold a claim on the reward. In practice, that means equity stakes in companies built on public loans, royalties on patents from publicly funded research, and a public fund that recycles the returns into the next round of risk. The United States has started to embrace this philosophy in its semiconductor infrastructure funding. It could do the same for our public investments in artificial intelligence, and those contracts are still being written.
These principles address our broader capitalist system and create a different framing from universal basic income, which many tech billionaires are quite fond of. A basic income leaves the origins of their fortunes untouched, treats wealth as given, and asks only for a transfer, which is why it can be endorsed without conceding anything. A citizens' dividend changes the logic, because it pays out on the grounds that the public helped create the value in the first place. That is a debt owed directly, not only through the tax code. And we know it is possible. Alaska has paid its residents a dividend from oil revenue since 1982.
None of this is an argument for voting against Proposition 40. California's billionaires should pay, and the state's health system needs the money. But a one-time levy collected decades after the fact is a costly way to claim a return that could have been written into the contract at the start. Redistribution settles old accounts. Pre-distribution can redesign an economy from the outset for more inclusive, sustainable growth.
It matters that we act now. The next fortune is being built right now, on public research, with public money; we should make sure it serves the common good.
An economy is not weather, a natural phenomenon that cannot be designed differently or more fairly. It is a set of contracts, and we are the ones who write them. We can write them for an economy designed with people and for them, one that shares the knowledge and the rewards along the way. The common good economy provides the principles through which to achieve this.

Egyptian man who fire-bombed pro-Israel rally in Colorado pleads guilty to federal hate crimes - media
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:43:07 CET
03:43:07 KST

By Keith Coffman and Steve Gorman
DENVER, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The man who lobbed gasoline bombs at a pro-Israel rally last year in Colorado, setting fire to several people including a woman who later died from her burns, pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal hate-crime charges, the Associated Press reported.
Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, an Egyptian national, is already serving a life prison term for his guilty plea in May to more than 100 state charges, including first-degree murder.
Soliman pleaded guilty to nine counts of hate-crime offenses and three explosives charges in federal court in Denver on Thursday. The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty, the AP reported.
Soliman has admitted tossing two Molotov cocktails at people taking part in a peaceful rally in downtown Boulder on June 1, 2025, staged to express solidarity with hostages seized by Hamas militants who stormed into Israeli villages from the Palestinian enclave of Gaza on October 7, 2023.
Prosecutors said Soliman also used a makeshift blowtorch fashioned from a spray bottle during his attack. He yelled “Free Palestine” as the gasoline bombs he lobbed at the crowd burst into flames outside a municipal courthouse in the heart of Boulder’s popular Pearl Street shopping district.
Soliman had disguised himself as a gardener as he approached the rally and had carried a crate containing 16 more gasoline bombs that went unused, according to prosecutors.
‘ENEMY IS ZIONISM’
Authorities in Colorado identified 29 victims, including 14 who were burned or injured while fleeing, and 15 who were close enough to be considered targets of attempted murder. One victim, 82-year-old Karen Diamond, died of her injuries later that month. Her husband suffered severe burns and survived.
The firebombing came amid heightened tensions over the 2023 Hamas raid and Israel’s war of retaliation in Gaza, which sparked a surge in anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim hate crimes across the US and a wave of pro-Palestinian protests that many Israel supporters branded as antisemitic.
Admitting his guilt in state court nearly six months ago, Soliman denounced his own crimes as contrary to “the teachings of Islam” and said he bore no ill will toward Jewish people. He went on to lament the “thousands of families who have lost their families in Palestine and Gaza,” and said the “enemy is Zionism.”
A public defender who spoke on Soliman’s behalf before he addressed the court in May said her client “felt overwhelmed for the suffering of the world and acted on that impulse.”
According to affidavits filed in court by prosecutors, Soliman told investigators after his arrest that he wanted to “kill all Zionist people” and had planned his attack for a year, but delayed going through with it until after his daughter had graduated from high school.
Soliman, who lived with his wife and five children in Colorado Springs before his rampage, also has asserted that his family members were unaware of his intentions.
The family was taken into immigration custody in June 2025 after his arrest and transported to a detention facility in Texas. They were held until a court-ordered release on April 23, 2026, more than 10 months later.
The children and their mother, who subsequently divorced Soliman, were re-arrested on April 25 of this year just after returning to Colorado. They were freed again when attorneys intervened a day later, according to court documents.
Court records entered at about the time that Soliman reached a plea deal with federal prosecutors earlier this month showed that he had withdrawn motions seeking to preclude any further attempts at removing his family.
(Reporting by Keith Coffman in Denver; additional reporting by Andrew Hay in New Mexico; writing and additional reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; editing by Donna Bryson and Sanjeev Miglani)

By Mayela Armas and Deisy Buitrago
CARACAS, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday the United States has suggested the country hold presidential elections next year, a timeline she has previously supported, in her first substantive remarks since returning last weekend.
Machado’s return to Venezuela risks straining her ties with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid. Maduro is facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Washington has said Machado, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, has every right to be in Venezuela, but Trump has also praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez. The Trump administration supports negotiations between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups which do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement on overhauling Venezuela’s electoral council and top court before the next elections.
Machado thanked Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their roles in Maduro’s ouster and said the relationship between the two countries is one of mutual respect and in both nations’ best interests.
“Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that makes clear that presidential elections will be held in 2027,” Machado said, adding she would ensure that all eligible Venezuelans can cast ballots in any future election.
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Rubio has previously said he expects Machado to support the talks.
At a press conference in Caracas, Machado avoided responding when asked about Trump’s comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, and this week, that Venezuela could become the 51st state.
Machado has cultivated Trump as an ally for years.
The opposition leader added she was pleased Rodriguez, in remarks earlier in the day, had also backed elections and that those who help the country transition back to democracy will need guarantees. Machado said a transitional justice process, a truth commission and a revamp of state security forces are necessary.
Machado, 59, returned to Venezuela on Sunday after several failed attempts this year. She was barred from running in the 2024 election but her proxy roundly won, according to tallies provided by the opposition at the time. Venezuela’s institutions, however, backed Maduro.
CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
Venezuela needs transparent contracts, open bidding for public deals and international arbitration to ensure investors and the Venezuelan people receive the most from future investments, Machado said.
Rodriguez’s interim government has signed deals with a variety of companies interested in oil, gas and mining with support from the US. They include a deal between North American Blue Energy Partners and the US government to export production from 17 Venezuelan fields.
Machado said NABEP’s contract, which she has not seen, “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” especially because of the company’s CEO Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt has been investigated in the United States, Spain and Switzerland, including for money laundering, but never indicted.
“I want to emphasize something to all those investors who are looking at Venezuela today, or who have entered Venezuela in recent times: every legally signed contract will be honored,” Machado said, adding some contracts could be “changed to new terms that we will offer, which will be much better.”
The country needs a deal with the International Monetary Fund to establish how the country will manage its huge debt load and attend to urgent humanitarian needs, Machado said.
POLITICAL PRISONERS
Machado, who lived in hiding for more than a year before leaving the country as many of her close collaborators were detained, said releasing political prisoners is key to restoring democracy.
Venezuela’s opposition and human rights groups have said for years the government uses detentions to stamp out dissent. The government has denied holding political prisoners.
Legal rights group Foro Penal says 322 political prisoners are incarcerated in Venezuela, and more than half of them have not been convicted. Some 11,000 people are under other restrictions such as house arrest.
Foro Penal is focused on ensuring “the destruction of the repressive apparatus,” especially regarding the new top court, the immediate and full liberation of political prisoners, the overturning of repressive laws and setting up an eventual truth commission, its vice president Gonzalo Himiob told Reuters this week.
Rodriguez said earlier on Thursday that more than 9,000 people have been released or had legal restrictions withdrawn under a limited amnesty law.
On Monday, Machado visited her lawyer Perkins Rocha, who was arrested after the 2024 vote and held for 18 months in Caracas’ Helicoide, where advocates and former inmates have alleged torture takes place. Rocha remains under house arrest and had his amnesty request rejected.

The school will become a gymnasium, but the students will stay: Parliament changed the rules for upper-secondary education
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:41:01 EET
03:41:01 KST

The school will become a gymnasium, but the students will stay: Parliament changed the rules for upper-secondary education
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament allowed students at a two-year upper-secondary school to complete their studies at their own institution even after its reorganization. The law will remain in effect until the end of the 2027/2028 academic year.
Members of Parliament allowed upper-grade students to complete their education at their schools even after their status changes. The decision concerns students studying under the two-year upper-secondary school program and is intended to ensure continuity of the educational process during the implementation of the specialized upper-secondary education reform. UNN reports this, citing the Verkhovna Rada and the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine.
Details
On Thursday, October 29, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in the first reading and as a whole Draft Law No. 15082-d, which introduces amendments to the Law of Ukraine “On Complete General Secondary Education.” A total of 265 Members of Parliament voted in favor of the decision. The document stipulates that students who are obtaining specialized upper-secondary education within the two-year upper-secondary school program in the 2026/2027 academic year will be able to complete their studies at the same institution to which they were admitted or transferred.
This primarily concerns current tenth-graders who are studying under the 2011 State Standard. They will have the opportunity to complete the 11th grade at their school and receive a certificate of complete general secondary education, even if the institution changes its type and becomes a gymnasium by that time. In particular, if a school is reorganized from a lyceum into a gymnasium, students will be allowed to continue studying under the existing two-year program until its completion.
If the educational institution is merged with another one, students will be able to complete their studies at the institution that becomes its legal successor.
How the new mechanism will work
To implement the provisions of the law, its authors provided for a temporary simplification of the licensing procedure for general secondary education institutions. This concerns schools that, as part of the reform, are being reorganized or reprofiled as gymnasiums, but in which upper-grade students continue to study under the two-year program.
According to the Ministry of Education and Science, such institutions will be able to obtain or reissue a license to conduct educational activities at the specialized upper-secondary education level under a simplified procedure. To do so, the institution’s administration must submit a relevant application to the licensing authority. The authorized body must issue or reissue the license within 10 business days without carrying out the standard licensing procedure.
At the same time, the law provides a mechanism to prevent delays in this process. If a decision is not made within the specified period, the license will be considered issued or reissued automatically. The validity of such documents will be limited until the end of the 2027/2028 academic year.
Why it became necessary to adopt the law
The need for legislative changes is linked to the upper-secondary school reform, which envisages Ukraine’s transition to a 12-year system of general secondary education. Under the new model, students will obtain specialized upper-secondary education in grades 10–12 at academic or vocational lyceums. At the same time, gymnasiums will provide basic secondary education, meaning education primarily in grades 5–9.
To implement the reform, communities are gradually forming a new network of educational institutions, determining which schools will operate as lyceums and which will become gymnasiums.
However, this transition created a problem for students who had already begun studying under the old two-year program. In particular, after a school’s status changed, its ability to continue educating students in grades 10–11 could be restricted. As a result, some upper-grade students faced the prospect of transferring to another educational institution just one year before receiving their certificate of complete general secondary education.
Back in September, Member of Parliament Iryna Borzova drew attention to this problem, noting that thousands of parents, children, and teachers were awaiting a decision that would allow current tenth-graders to complete their studies at their schools. The relevant parliamentary committee considered the legislative initiatives and prepared a revised Draft Law No. 15082-d, which was supported by lawmakers.
Will the decision affect the transition to 12-year education?
The Ministry of Education and Science emphasizes that the adoption of the law does not change the timelines for implementing the specialized upper-secondary education reform.
Therefore, from September 1, 2027, new tenth-graders studying under the New Ukrainian School program will have to switch to a three-year model of specialized secondary education. It provides for education in grades 10, 11, and 12, with the opportunity to choose a specialization and study individual subjects in greater depth in accordance with their educational interests.
At the same time, students who are already studying under the two-year program will be able to complete it without switching to the new model.
The Ministry of Education and Science also clarified separately that lyceums participating in the pilot implementation of the specialized secondary education reform from September 1, 2026, will continue to operate in the format in which they began the academic year.
Context
The reform of upper secondary school is one of the stages in implementing the New Ukrainian School. It provides for the separation of basic and specialized secondary education, the creation of a network of academic lyceums, and a gradual transition to three-year education in the upper grades.
From September 2027, the new model is expected to be launched for students entering the tenth grade. The first mass graduation of twelfth-graders under this system is expected in 2030.
Reminder
Earlier, the Ministry of Education explained what exactly the reform of upper secondary school changes.

Texas Republican group seeks to block certification of state’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:40:01 UTC
03:40:01 KST

Texas Republican group seeks to block certification of state’s election
Republicans in a Texas county have filed a lawsuit asking for ballots in the state’s midterm races to be hand-counted.
Days before the United States’ pivotal midterm elections, a Texas group affiliated with the Republican Party has asked a federal judge to stop certification of the state’s upcoming election results.
In a lawsuit filed on Tuesday, the Potter County Republican Party and its chairman, Daniel Rogers, claim potential election interference by artificial intelligence (AI) or “malicious actors” that could compromise the results of next Tuesday’s elections in Texas.
The plaintiffs, who are asking for a hand count of every ballot from every precinct in the state before election certification happens, allege voting machines have components inside made by China that would allow them to be manipulated.
“If a component is tampered with during manufacturing, it could serve as a point of entry for unlawful and malfeasance hackers, allowing for the possibility of synchronized attacks across multiple election machines and jurisdictions,” the lawsuit read.
The legal challenge comes as several polls show Democrat James Talarico narrowly leading his Republican challenger, Ken Paxton, in Texas’ all-important US Senate race that could ultimately decide which party controls the chamber after November 3.
The Talarico and Paxton campaigns and the Potter County Republican Party did not immediately return requests from Al Jazeera for comment.
The legal complaint does not specify if any voting machines in Potter County, or elsewhere in Texas, have been compromised. The plaintiffs acknowledged in their filing that no previous election in the county was “altered” by a third party, arguing that the possibility of vote manipulation by AI makes the state’s election safeguards easily compromised.
“The real likelihood of a clever and undetected hack by recently developed AI programs, which conceal their activity to avoid detection, reinforces the need for a full verification based on hand-counting of all paper records or ballots in all Texas precincts, prior to certification of the federal results,” they wrote.
State law in Texas already requires hand-count audits in elections where electronic tabulators are used. But the plaintiffs argue that does not go far enough.
“The paper record or ballot provides an independent verification mechanism only if election officials actually compare a complete hand count of all of the paper records or ballots,” the filing said.
The lawsuit also claims US “adversaries”, such as China, Iran and Russia, are capable of accessing election systems.
US President Donald Trump in July declassified documents that, he claimed, showed Chinese interference in the US 2020 presidential election, reviving his attacks on US elections despite no evidence that Beijing impacted the vote he lost that year.
Last week, the US Department of Justice also sought to block certification of an election, claiming, in Alaska, that an independent candidate with the same name as the state’s Republican Senator up for re-election is running in order to mislead voters.
Alicia Pierce, a spokeswoman for Texas’s Secretary of State, whose office administers elections in the state, said it “does not plan to comment on the lawsuit at this time”.

ATO and ASIC feared data was sent offshore in 2025, internal emails reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:39:55 UTC
03:39:55 KST

ATO, ASIC feared data breach by supplier VIQ Solutions a year before it was public
In short:
Internal emails between the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) and the Australian Tax Office (ATO) show a potential data breach by VIQ Solutions was investigated in 2025.
The concerns about the integrity of ATO and ASIC data, occurred approximately one year prior to the ABC revealing family court and Federal Court data was sent offshore by VIQ Solutions.
What's next?
Investigations into the court data breach are ongoing.
Australia's corporate watchdog failed to alert other government agencies about concerns that transcription service VIQ Solutions had sent potentially sensitive work offshore, documents released under Freedom of Information (FOI) have revealed.
Sensitive data from courts and federal government agencies is forbidden from being stored or processed offshore due to potential hacking and national security risks.
Internal emails between the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) and the Australian Tax Office (ATO) exposed concerns that preferred government transcription provider, VIQ, had potentially offshored sensitive data, almost a year before the ABC first reported a court data breach by the same company.
The emails also show that ASIC, which was responsible for managing the relationship between VIQ as a preferred provider and government agencies, ignored an ATO request to assess whether other agencies had been impacted and instead left it up to VIQ.
The alarm was first raised around March 2025 when VIQ sent an email to the ATO that included a hyperlink to a transcript that was "available for download" from a site in the United Kingdom.
An assistant director at the ATO sent an email to both ASIC and VIQ stating:
"This appears to indicate the [sic] VIQ Solutions is already allowing customer data to be shared, accessed or used outside of Australia. This is of serious concern to the Australian Taxation Office."
The ATO and ASIC advised staff to stop using VIQ for transcription services until they had more information.
"We have requested that VIQ conduct an investigation and confirm that our data has not been sent overseas. We are also not utilising VIQ until the investigation is complete," an ASIC project coordinator wrote in an email chain that included ATO staff.
"If you haven't already, you may wish to request that a similar investigation is also completed for the ATO," the project coordinator wrote.
In the days that followed, concerns were raised about the integrity of the information being provided by VIQ in response to the potential breach.
"We have found some potential inconsistencies in VIQ response to date and more impacts the more questions we ask," an ATO director wrote.
By early May, VIQ had provided a report to ASIC about the potential breach. Based on the report, ASIC determined the incident was a "near miss" and that none of its own data had been compromised.
But there was no independent investigation into any other agency using the service.
An email from a project coordinator at ASIC on May 12, 2025 stated:
"Recently ASIC became aware of a potential data breach after Evidence Support Panel provider, VIQ, was thought to have sent ATO data processing offshore… This incident was determined to be a near miss, and we will work with VIQ to ensure that any risk mitigation and process improvements are implemented to ensure ongoing security."
The concerns about the integrity of ATO and ASIC data, occurred approximately one year prior to the ABC revealing family court and Federal Court data was sent offshore by VIQ Solutions.
Shortly after the court data breach became public, VIQ Solutions was put into administration and eventually shut down. Investigations into the court data breach are still ongoing.
Emails show that in March 2025 an ATO director raised whether other agencies might be affected and later questioned whether ASIC would assess any broader impact.
An ASIC staff member responded saying this would be discussed after its own investigation. The emails do not show whether this was carried out.
The ABC asked both the ATO and ASIC if either department raised the offshoring incident with any other government agencies who used VIQ at the time.
The ATO said it "reported the incident to the relevant panel manager", who is the person responsible for managing any potential breaches and assessing risks to the Commonwealth.
ASIC said it had taken "appropriate action" and that "VIQ was responsible for notifying agencies affected under any separate arrangements".
At least 13 government agencies used VIQ Solutions before ASIC removed the company as an approved supplier from AusTender on March 19, 2026.
Shadow Attorney General Senator Michaelia Cash said the growing concerns about data integrity needed investigating.
"It’s astounding this issue continues to grow but the Attorney General keeps her head in the sand," Senator Cash said.
"The Coalition has called for an investigation co-ordinated by the Attorney General that stretches across all government agencies.
"This latest example only reinforces the need for such an investigation to assure Australians our national security has not been compromised."
In July, an administrators' report from McGrath Nicol — who stepped in when VIQ Solutions went into voluntary administration — found the data breach "adversely affected" the company's ability to secure tender opportunities.
The administrators also found that the directors of VIQ Solutions may have breached their duties by "not acting with care and diligence".

A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:39:43 UTC
03:39:43 KST

Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”
Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”
Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.
The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.
According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third-party website.
WIRED is declining to name the third-party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but the National Institute of Standards and Technology has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.
The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”
Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology,” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”
Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.
While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”
Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”
Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.
But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.
But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air-gapped systems.
“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.
Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.
As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time-consuming and difficult to vet.
“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture and architectural issues that we see in other code.”
The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.
There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top-secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open-source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.
This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

Israeli soldier charged with spying for Iran in exchange for cryptocurrency

An Israeli soldier has been charged with spying for Iran and providing sensitive military information in exchange for cryptocurrency, The Times of Israel reported Thursday, citing Israeli security authorities, Anadolu reports.
A statement from Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet, police and military said the soldier was arrested in September following an investigation into suspected espionage activities on behalf of Iranian intelligence operatives.
Military prosecutors filed an indictment Thursday, charging the soldier with passing information to an enemy with intent to harm state security and maintaining contact with a foreign agent.
The investigation found that the soldier had maintained contact with Iranian intelligence operatives for approximately one year, during which he allegedly provided sensitive information about his military unit’s activities, the army’s operational readiness and military call-ups.
The information reportedly included details about his call-up following the outbreak of the war with Iran earlier this year.
Prosecutors said the soldier also shared information about military bases and their coordinates, as well as photographs of missile interceptors, military vehicles and US refueling aircraft stationed at an Israeli airport.
Authorities said he provided Iranian operatives with information about fellow soldiers and commanders, knowing that the intelligence agents might attempt to recruit them for espionage.
The investigation also found that the soldier shared access to a Telegram group used by young Israelis preparing for military service, which an Iranian operative subsequently joined.
Prosecutors said the soldier knowingly maintained contact with an Iranian handler and received cryptocurrency payments in exchange for the information.
The Iranian operative allegedly instructed him to install encrypted communication applications and offered to purchase him a mobile phone and a pistol.
The two also reportedly agreed to use coded language and prepare a cover story in case Israeli security forces discovered their activities.
The soldier was offered $200,000 to travel to Iran, according to prosecutors.
An Israeli military court extended his detention until Nov. 12, although authorities are seeking to keep him in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings.
The case comes amid heightened tensions between Israel and Iran following the outbreak of the war earlier this year.
