Netanyahu’s stalemate and the liberal fantasy of a new Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:34:21 UTC
03:34:21 KST

Open any of Israel’s liberal newspapers, or the Financial Times, or the New York Times, and one finds the same thing: the commentary on Israel’s elections arranges itself into a narrative of possible redemption. When the interpretive community that shapes opinion in the metropolitan centers speaks of the ‘struggle for Israel’s soul’ and the possibility of a new Israel arriving through the ballot box, the elections become an occasion to push a frame that attempts to ‘redeem’ the irredeemable. How is one to concede the crimes and still make room for the persistence of the settler colonial slaughter in Palestine?
Since the outset of this year, a politics of ‘redemption’ has been pushed with vigor. Many of you will have read The New Yorker (one of the worst liberal magazines in its treatment of Palestine, though the others are hardly better), which lent its pages to officials in the Biden administration who salvaged themselves through a formula of ‘good intentions, bad decisions, and missed opportunities’. It is a non-apology of a very familiar kind in the Palestinian experience: the only apology we have heard from the mouths of Zionist leaders is ‘We are sorry you forced us to kill you’. Intentions are pure, a site from which innocence can be retained even when Biden and his administration labored overtime to provision all the equipment, diplomatic cover, bombs, and financial aid necessary for a genocidal campaign in Gaza to proceed for roughly a year and a half, during which he was in a position to leverage American power to stop it.
The non-apology arrives on the condition that it costs nothing: when those who backed genocide and made it possible are no longer in a position either to be held accountable or to stop the killing machine. The Israeli version follows the same logic. The ‘anti-Netanyahu change bloc’ is presented to us as a reasonable alternative, more fluent in the idiom of Western capitals, and better equipped to draw over Israel’s persistent cruelty the veil of ignorance on which the smooth operation of Western liberal support has historically depended. Seen through the prism of the liberal intelligentsia in the West, this is a necessary change: one that might wean Israel from perpetual war and return it to diplomatic and political arrangements, restoring it to the community of ‘legitimate’ states as a country guilty of nothing worse than questionable moral decisions. Decisions that remain redeemable and ultimately can secure Israel’s long-term future if it is willing to return to its old pragmatism, expand and withdraw, kill and bank in concessions.
Indeed, much is granted to the loose collection of parties in Israel’s opposition that agree on three things. First, a push against the right-wing religious takeover of the state’s bureaucracy and its attempt to remake the legal order that has been one of the salient features of Israel’s religious Zionist right-wing. Second, a vigorous hatred of Prime Minister Netanyahu, who has outsmarted them and held onto power for the past twenty years, pulling one trick after another to sustain his hold over Israeli politics. Third, the need to redefine the relation to Haredi and Orthodox community in a manner that would integrate them into Israel military machine and economy. As for the Palestinians, they can look forward to the same policies, the same day-to-day crimes, and the same massacres in Gaza, but now under a government granted a renewed license for its effort to bury Palestine because it is simply not Netanyahu’s.
What the change bloc offers is better management of the same system. It will lean more on the courts and the army to do the same job that the settlers have taken up with a sense of super-impunity in the West Bank. It is also more likely to renew the fighting in Gaza and to push the U.S. toward another round of war with Iran. It will present itself as a more credible partner for ‘normalization’ agreements that can rescue Israel from itself and from its doctrinal tilt toward embracing ‘pariah status,’ at least at the level of rhetoric. It will also offer an excuse to Western capitals that do not really want to sanction Israel and are looking for any ‘fig leaf’ to rationalize the persistence of their failure to act.
Israel’s so-called liberals, no less implicated in the structures of power, have always preferred the idiom of moderation to the blunt vocabulary of their rivals on the right. The liberals kill and perform the theatre of moral complexity. They massacre and take pleasure in possessing the capacity to utter words of guilt. They chuckle at the crimes they committed in closed rooms and in archives that only open up decades later. The substance is the same, and for all the talk of a struggle for Israel’s soul, it has been, and will remain, rotten to its core. They differ only in rhetorical strategy, and the right’s candid avowal of what the state actually does is seen by the Eisenkots as stupidity, a failure in the management of appearances.
The entire media complex around Israeli political centrism predicted a sweeping victory for its center, a narrative that wove together an infalted spin on the extent of animosity towards Netanyahu (way more popular than Haaretz would have you believe), the credentialism of the opposition leader as former chief of staff of Israel’s military with a son killed in Gaza, and the brains behind Israel’s deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure as a means to pressure and defeat resistance movements (The Dahiya Doctrine). This was the man who would unseat the Prime Minister and dethrone the king of a state so accustomed to Netanyahu that its politics has shrunk to the person himself, the polity mistaken politics for a personality. The results have produced a stalemate, with Netanyahu’s coalition coming out first with about 53 seats to around 48 for Gadi Eisenkot’s coalition. Netanyahu, declared defeated the day before, rose once again to sustain a fighting chance.
Elections and the illusion of rescue
One of the most talked-about shifts in this round of elections is the extent to which Palestinian citizens of Israel participated in the vote. Turnout among Palestinians was estimated at 80 percent, which broke the 1999 record. The Palestinian community, which makes up around 21 percent of the population and whose participation is a matter of political contestation, voted at much lower rates in previous rounds, somewhere between 40 and 60 percent. The jump in turnout should be read principally as a desperate attempt both to unseat the right-wing government and to return to a semblance of normalcy in everyday life between the river and the sea. In a tragically ironic twist, it is a desperate attempt to secure a colonial reality that is less invested in obscene forms of violence and more capable of masking it through a slow-grinding process. As a tactical intervention, it is also meant to offer Israel’s opposition a clear path towards securing a government, one in which they would have to grant some concessions to Palestinian citizens of Israel, largely on issues pertaining to everyday life and on the issue that has exhausted Palestinian political communities: the willful lack of policing that has permitted the rise of organized crime in Palestinian towns and villages inside Israel, with strong indications of Israeli intelligence sanctioning it.
Both the Joint List and Ra’am are projected to win a record number of seats, around 19. That showing compounds a problem that has already produced repeated political stalemates. Israeli politics has become so polarized around the figure of Netanyahu, and has shifted so far to the right through demographic and ideological change, that the two dominant blocs can neither govern together nor secure a majority on their own. The opposition, a largely weak collection of forces, is also incapable of truly embracing an overt political coalition with Arab parties. It is caught between its hatred of Netanyahu and its utter disdain for any political embrace of Arab parties, both in principle and out of fear that such an embrace would entail a tacit empowerment that might also push Israel towards compromises on national grounds. So the things Israelis casually fear are a Palestinian state or equal political, economic, and civic rights.
It is not a shock, then, that one of the first cynical moves by the Netanyahu-led coalition has been to invoke foreign interference in the elections, and the role of Qatar, Turkey, and the “Muslim Brotherhood” in shaping the outcome through “bribes” and influence operations, which, it claims, explain the strong showing of the Arab vote in the current electoral round. Right-wing Israeli media already call it “Ra’amgate,” a reference to Ra’am, the list led by Mansour Abbas and affiliated with the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement. Abbas, in recent years, moved to break many of the political taboos around Palestinian participation in Israeli elections, situating himself as a pragmatic leader, devoid of nationalist sentiment and interested in full civic and economic rights within the horizon of the Israeli state as it stands. Despite the many concessions, both symbolic and material, he is still treated as a “suspect” and as having a hidden agenda by many pundits and Israeli political operatives. What motivated Netanyahu, who is himself implicated in a Qatar bribery scandal through assistants who worked in his office, was to muddy the waters of any possible coalition that would see Abbas working with the opposition to unseat the Prime Minister.
But the Arab vote in Israel and its strong showing at the polls tell a different story. They speak to the sense of brokenness that has defined politics outside Gaza, and indeed in Gaza itself. The incapacity to muster an active form of resistance, and the daily assault on Palestinian life in the West Bank, in Jerusalem, and within Israel itself, have propelled a cruel push towards a protest vote built on the hope both of ousting the “Kahanist” forces from Israeli politics and of returning to a pre-October 7 sense of normalcy. It is cruel because it comes on the heels of symbolic concessions and amid the weakness of Arab political movements, which have been left wrecked as political forces and without a material and political social base. It is also cruel because it carries a sense of “cruel optimism,” in which voters know all too well that the Zionist forces on the ballot disagree on much but agree on who is on the menu – the Palestinians. But it is the desperation of the “at least” logic that stands out: at least a new government will curtail some settler excess, show more pragmatism in economic relief, and take more steps towards fighting crime. In other words, it is a symptom of a society that has lost much of its capacity to solve its own problems and is hanging its wager on forces that share the same desire to eliminate.
It is also cruel because the rise of Israeli opposition will only help whitewash Israel, sanction diplomatic relief, postpone sanctions, and open a window for the deepening of Arab normalization. It is cruel because, in the moment, it is also one of the few avenues of a cruel form of hope.

New study challenges what we thought we knew about Long COVID
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:33:14 UTC
03:33:14 KST

in brief
- Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, leading to knock-on effects.
- Australia has a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs in NSW, Victoria, SA and the ACT.
New research from the United States suggests Long COVID may have affected fewer people for less time than previously thought.
Using refined data collection methods, a team from Stanford University has found that people suffering from chronic COVID-like symptoms may have been misdiagnosed or the illness overreported.
According to the Australian government, Long COVID is defined as contracting COVID-19 and experiencing symptoms for a period of at least 12 weeks afterwards.
But researchers said no clinical test exists for Long COVID, making it difficult to track its prevalence accurately.
They stress that people who were wrongly assumed to have Long COVID may still have experienced debilitating symptoms that could have been caused by other illnesses.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"These findings indicate that Long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought," said co-author Steven Goodman, professor of epidemiology and population health in the Stanford School of Medicine.
The Australian government predicted there would be more than 1.3 million cumulative historical Long COVID cases nationwide by the end of 2023 and suggested between 5-10 per cent of people who contract COVID-19 still have symptoms after three months.
How was the research done?
The Stanford researchers reviewed 4.4 billion health insurance records from more than 244 million Americans and say they found a flaw in previous studies.
Older research compared people who tested positive for COVID-19 with people who were never diagnosed or tested.
The issue is that people who are more likely to test also have more records of various health issues, which can create a biased association between those health issues and COVID-19.
Professor Jure Leskovec, another author of the study, explained these discrepancies may substantially overestimate the range and duration of health effects attributable to COVID-19.
"Our new study design found 98 per cent fewer Long COVID-attributable outcomes between four to 12 months after infection compared with conventional approaches applied in the same dataset," he said.
"This doesn’t mean Long COVID is 98 per cent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID."
By focusing only on patients who tested positive or negative, the researchers believe they have produced a more accurate picture of COVID-19's long-term health effects.
Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News refining our understanding of Long COVID is vital for supporting people with the illness.
"We need to make sure that we continue to look into Long COVID, manage those people, try and find tests and obviously also therapies to try and improve their situation," he said.
Difficulties with diagnoses
No diagnostic test exists for Long COVID, and Griffin explained that the criteria some experts use have shifted over time.
It's suspected there could even be different forms of Long COVID, further complicating both diagnosis and treatment.
"It's a complex constellation of symptoms that can involve pretty much every organ system in the body," Griffin said.
The disease can also manifest differently in people or be confused with other illnesses with similar symptoms.
In the worst case, some patients may have their symptoms dismissed or discounted because there is no reliable test.
"They may see some clinicians who say that they don't have anything wrong with them or that it might be due to something else or perhaps it's psychological and not an actual condition relating to their COVID infection."
Experts warn against losing sight of long COVID
Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, which could mean inadequate resources are directed toward the condition.
"For a short period of time there were some resources deployed to help address that. But then I think in more recent times, a lot of those have been wound up," Griffin said.
Australia has only a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs.
Dozens more of these clinics and targeted support programs have been discontinued since the height of the pandemic.
Experts said scientists worldwide will keep improving their understanding of the COVID-19 pandemic, both to better understand its impact and to prepare for future public health emergencies.
"COVID-19 had been one of the worst pandemics we face, but it certainly won't be the last. We can take the opportunity to reflect, see how we can be better prepared, and I guess also continue to manage COVID well," Griffin said.
Scrutinising and refining statistics is therefore part of building population wellbeing and resilience.
Leskovec said: "These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them."
"On the other hand, for data scientists, earlier Long COVID studies might need to be revisited with better controls. Our approach could improve those and future population-health studies."

Houthis say Saudi strike kills 12 as blasts heard in Riyadh

Breadcrumb
Houthis say Saudi strike kills 12 as blasts heard in Riyadh
Yemen's Houthis on Thursday said 12 people were killed in Saudi strikes on residential areas in Taiz province, while explosions later rocked Riyadh.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government have exchanged daily attacks since a years-long truce fell apart over the summer.
In the Saudi capital, AFP correspondents heard at least eight explosions as authorities warned the city was "under a hostile aerial threat" in a phone alert.
Saudi civil defence issued warnings for "potential danger" in Riyadh, Kharj and the southern city of Najran that were lifted shortly afterwards.
The Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport that forced its shuttering for two weeks as flagship events were cancelled - threatening the kingdom's economic diversification plans.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in Yemen since hostilities resumed, with more than 275,000 displaced, according to United Nations figures.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement Thursday shared by the group's Saba news agency.
On Wednesday, at least 14 people were killed in Saudi strikes on a petrol station and market, according to the Houthis, while the group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding civilians.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.
Yemen has been reeling from war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.

US proposes Venezuela elections for 2027, opposition leader Machado says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:31:27 UTC
03:31:27 KST

US proposes Venezuela elections for 2027, opposition leader Machado says
CARACAS, Oct 29 - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday the United States has suggested the country hold presidential elections next year, a timeline she has previously supported, in her first substantive remarks since returning last weekend.
Machado's return to Venezuela risks straining her ties with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid. Maduro is facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Washington has said Machado, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, has every right to be in Venezuela, but Trump has also praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez. The Trump administration supports negotiations between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups which do not include Machado's Vente Venezuela movement on overhauling Venezuela's electoral council and top court before the next elections.
Machado thanked Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their roles in Maduro's ouster and said the relationship between the two countries is one of mutual respect and in both nations' best interests.
“Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that makes clear that presidential elections will be held in 2027,” Machado said, adding she would ensure that all eligible Venezuelans can cast ballots in any future election.
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Rubio has previously said he expects Machado to support the talks.
At a press conference in Caracas, Machado avoided responding when asked about Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, and this week, that Venezuela could become the 51st state.
Machado has cultivated Trump as an ally for years.
The opposition leader added she was pleased Rodriguez, in remarks earlier in the day, had also backed elections and that those who help the country transition back to democracy will need guarantees. Machado said a transitional justice process, a truth commission and a revamp of state security forces are necessary.
Machado, 59, returned to Venezuela on Sunday after several failed attempts this year. She was barred from running in the 2024 election but her proxy roundly won, according to tallies provided by the opposition at the time. Venezuela's institutions, however, backed Maduro.
CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
Venezuela needs transparent contracts, open bidding for public deals and international arbitration to ensure investors and the Venezuelan people receive the most from future investments, Machado said.
Rodriguez's interim government has signed deals with a variety of companies interested in oil, gas and mining with support from the US. They include a deal between North American Blue Energy Partners and the US government to export production from 17 Venezuelan fields.
Machado said NABEP's contract, which she has not seen, "evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," especially because of the company's CEO Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt has been investigated in the United States, Spain and Switzerland, including for money laundering, but never indicted.
“I want to emphasize something to all those investors who are looking at Venezuela today, or who have entered Venezuela in recent times: every legally signed contract will be honored," Machado said, adding some contracts could be "changed to new terms that we will offer, which will be much better."
The country needs a deal with the International Monetary Fund to establish how the country will manage its huge debt load and attend to urgent humanitarian needs, Machado said.
POLITICAL PRISONERS
Machado, who lived in hiding for more than a year before leaving the country as many of her close collaborators were detained, said releasing political prisoners is key to restoring democracy.
Venezuela's opposition and human rights groups have said for years the government uses detentions to stamp out dissent. The government has denied holding political prisoners.
Legal rights group Foro Penal says 322 political prisoners are incarcerated in Venezuela, and more than half of them have not been convicted. Some 11,000 people are under other restrictions such as house arrest.
Foro Penal is focused on ensuring "the destruction of the repressive apparatus," especially regarding the new top court, the immediate and full liberation of political prisoners, the overturning of repressive laws and setting up an eventual truth commission, its vice president Gonzalo Himiob told Reuters this week.
Rodriguez said earlier on Thursday that more than 9,000 people have been released or had legal restrictions withdrawn under a limited amnesty law.

The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:30:28 UTC
03:30:28 KST

British politics is still polarised around Brexit, although 10 years on from the referendum, the terms of debate are very different. Or they should be. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has moved discussions of European solidarity from the realm of abstraction to a matter of urgent defence partnership. Donald Trump’s presidency in the US, marked by scorn for European democracies and indulgence of Vladimir Putin, has undermined confidence that Britain can rely on any “special relationship” with Washington.
Under these circumstances, it would be absurd to deny that a reappraisal of Brexit is in order. The prime minister acknowledged this in his speech at the Labour party conference last month, calling for a national conversation about the future relationship with every option, including rejoining, on the table. The Eurosceptic opposition are having none of it. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accuses the government of stirring division by raising the European question. She told MPs this week that Labour should thank the Tories for the Brexit deal they negotiated.
The Tories and Reform UK like to remind Andy Burnham of comments he made when campaigning in Makerfield earlier this year for the seat that became his launchpad to reach No 10. Mr Burnham said that rerunning the old Brexit arguments was “the last thing we should do right now”. That can be made consistent with his current position in the sense that an exact rerun of the 2016 debate would indeed be pointless, which is why something different, more future-facing, is being proposed instead. Mr Burnham’s critics see that as sleight of hand to conceal a flagrant change of line. But the distinction between relitigating outdated arguments and engaging with present realities is a vital one.
The Tory position, shared with Reform, contains no audit of Britain’s foreign and economic policy interests. It is based on ideology and fear of confronting the facts that such an evaluation reveals. Brexit has made Britain poorer and diminished its influence on the world stage. The public know this all too well, as evidenced by opinion polls indicating majority support for a closer EU relationship.
Mrs Badenoch’s position is also disingenuous, given her commitment to pull Britain out of the European convention on human rights. That would pointlessly reopen some of the most fissile Brexit arguments because of the ECHR’s codification in the Good Friday agreement for Northern Ireland.
A phenomenon that Mrs Badenoch and Mr Burnham have observed, but respond to differently, is that voters have no desire for a return to the poisonous political atmosphere of the immediate post-referendum period. The Tory leader uses that aversion to justify her lack of a strategic concept for Britain’s future relationship with its continental neighbours. The prime minister’s approach is to sound ecumenical, saying that he aspires to national consensus on the best way forward, while sounding vague about his personal preferences.
That ambiguity has given the opposition cause to accuse the prime minister of conspiring to undo Brexit, but it has also dissolved some of the taboo around discussion of much closer models of reintegration with the EU, which is a necessary condition for a healthier fact-based debate. That isn’t a conversation the Conservatives want to have, but for the prime minister to share in their denial would be, as he has said, a dereliction of duty.

Iran says four tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
At least four tankers have caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's armed forces said Thursday, a day after the US military said it had cleared key routes through the waterway.
"Over the past 24 hours, three violating oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking mines while attempting to pass through the unauthorised southern route of the Strait of Hormuz," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement.
The vessels had "switched off all their radar and navigation systems" and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said.
It was not immediately clear when the incidents occurred or which flags the tankers were flying.
Later Thursday, Iran's army reported that another tanker had caught fire east of the strait.
"A tanker that was illegally operating in a restricted and dangerous area east of the Strait of Hormuz was damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines, rendering it unable to move," the army said in a statement carried by state television.
The British maritime agency UKMTO, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a ship on fire in the strait.
"Regional authorities have identified the vessel as a dhow, which was involved in a maritime security incident, igniting a large fire onboard causing the dhow to list and sink," it said.
"The crew have been safely evacuated."
In recent weeks, Iran has reported multiple vessels striking sea mines, prompting US Central Command (CENTCOM), which runs military operations in the region, to reaffirm on social media its insistence that all mines in "primary transit routes" have been cleared.
On Thursday, Hossein Mohebi, the spokesman for the IRGC challenged the claim, saying: "Prove your Hormuz mine-clearing claim with independent evidence, not statements!" in a post on X.
Since the outbreak of the war on 28 February, Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
The United States has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait. On Sunday CENTCOM said it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.
Iran considers ships using the southern corridor near the Omani coast unauthorised.
In their statement on Thursday, the Guards said "the IRGC Navy states that the unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz is mined, and that vessel owners and crews are responsible for transiting these routes and should not pay attention to CENTCOM's delusions on social media".
The IRGC also said it had captured a US reconnaissance drone, in a separate statement.
"The IRGC Navy announced that its electronic warfare unit had successfully captured a US MQM-170 drone during an offensive operation in the western Strait of Hormuz," the statement said.

Following Hamas’s 2023 invasion on Oct. 7, USCIRF said that the Houthis transferred Marhabi to a prison ward with extremists who threatened him. A 10-day prison strike eventually saw the Houthis relocate him to solitary confinement.

Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:29:09 UTC
03:29:09 KST

President Tokayev outlined the country's priorities for the coming year in his annual address, urging the government to accelerate energy and construction projects, while criticising inefficiencies in public policy.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a long-term national uranium reserve and faster progress on building two nuclear power plants (NPPs) in his annual state-of-the-nation address on Wednesday.
“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year, and to sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement with the goal of launching construction of the Moyynkum NPP as soon as possible,” he said.
Tokayev highlighted that nuclear energy is one way to achieve an electricity surplus, which he described as essential for digitalising the economy and integrating artificial intelligence into all areas of public life.
He also criticised the government over inefficient energy management and corruption schemes in the sector. During winter shortages, Kazakhstan buys electricity from neighbouring countries at high prices, only to sell it back at much lower rates in summer.
“It’s a rather simple sort of ‘business’, and one that has persisted for decades. I’m assured that this is standard practice in the energy sector,” Tokayev said.
He added that such practices had also led to the deliberate obstruction of power plant construction and commissioning in several regions.
Logistics hub 'historic opportunity'
Tokayev opened his address by pointing to an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical environment, which he said “did not exist even during the Cold War."
Growing vulnerabilities along maritime routes, he argued, were increasing the importance of overland transport corridors.
“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.
He pointed to the construction of the Aral-Caspian Highway, which began in August. The project is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route by 1,000 kilometres and reduce cargo delivery times to three days.
The Bakty–Ayagoz railway line is scheduled to launch next year. It will establish a third railway crossing with China and increase freight capacity by 20 million tonnes.
Tokayev said Kazakhstan needed to move beyond its role as a transit country and become an organiser of international freight flows.
He called for developing domestic logistics operators, creating distribution centres, and digitising the transport sector, while also instructing the government to focus on air transit and road infrastructure.
Address in numbers
According to the IMF's forecast, Kazakhstan's GDP will exceed €350 billion this year, making it the world's 47th-largest economy. GDP per capita is expected to surpass €17,000.
The industrial sector now accounts for more than 14% of GDP. Tokayev attributed the growth to efforts to diversify the economy.
Small and medium-sized businesses contribute 40% of GDP, while their share of fixed capital investment has approached 70%.
Kazakhstan's gold and foreign exchange reserves, combined with the National Fund's assets, have exceeded €110 billion. Tokayev said the country should use these resources to modernise infrastructure and improve living conditions across its regions.
Domestic bank assets have surpassed €130 billion, while savings accounts have reached a record €94 billion. Around 78% of these savings are held in the national currency, which Tokayev cited as a sign of the tenge's growing value.
The president designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, calling on parliament to prioritise building and modernising public infrastructure, including roads, airports, hospitals and cultural centres.
The regions plan to build around 70 medical facilities and 50 educational, sports and cultural facilities. The National Fund is expected to allocate approximately €12.8 billion for these and other infrastructure projects by the end of 2029. Nearly €3 billion of that amount is earmarked for social projects over the next four months.
Tokayev also highlighted the country's demographic profile, noting that Kazakhstan has around seven million children, accounting for 34% of the population. More than 237,000 children have special educational needs.
Tokayev said the sector grew nearly 6% last year, with total output reaching almost €30 billion.
The address followed Kazakhstan's Day of the Republic and came as the country prepares to mark the 35th anniversary of its independence.

ADL-Boundless study finds simple messaging aids American in identifying online antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:28:36 UTC
03:28:36 KST

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Center for Antisemitism Research (CAR) and educational organization Boundless released a new research study on Thursday that reveals that a brief message reminding young Americans that hatred of Jews is broadly rejected can significantly improve their ability to recognize and report online antisemitism.
Jonathan Greenblatt, ADL CEO and National Director, stated that "young people are encountering antisemitism online every day, and too often they don't recognize it for what it is." Greenblatt added that "this research shows that something as simple as reminding people that hatred of Jews is not accepted by most Americans can move them to recognize it and speak up. That is a practical, scalable tool for educators, platforms and community leaders."
The study, entitled “Bridging the Gap: What Young Americans Miss About Online Antisemitism,” was conducted to examine how young adults interact with hateful online content and to test which educational approaches effectively influence recognition and reporting behavior.
The study surveyed 7,499 Americans aged 18 to 44 nationwide between July 9 and July 17, using the opinion research firm Cint. The sample encompassed 3,043 participants from Gen Z (ages 18 to 29) and 4,456 Millennials (ages 30 to 44), alongside 3,229 Democrats, 2,319 Independents, and 1,951 Republicans.
Participants were randomly assigned to read one of six short educational messages addressing antisemitism, ranging from neutral factual definitions and personal narratives, such as a story about a mother named Maya encountering a swastika near a school, to historical explanations of scapegoating, social norming, and broader prejudice, or to receive no message at all, before evaluating real examples of social media posts.
Many young adults struggle to identify antisemitic content, study finds
The evaluated social media post examples included classical antisemitic tropes, such as religious slurs referencing the ‘synagogues of Satan,' right-wing posts targeting officials with treason accusations over alleged Israeli allegiance, and contemporary rhetoric concerning Israel and Zionism from both the political left and right. The study also included non-ideological material and a racist control post featuring memes about Black achievements to measure false positives.
The findings show that many young adults struggle to identify antisemitic content even when it is overt. Among the untreated control group, between 22 percent and 29 percent disagreed that classical antisemitic posts were antisemitic. That difficulty increased when encountering contemporary antisemitism expressed through hostile language about Israel and Zionism, where disagreement rose to between 32 percent and 37 percent.
The study also measured participants' willingness to take action by reporting harmful material to social media platforms, finding that baseline readiness to report offensive posts was generally lower than overall recognition rates.
To explore and test whether brief educational prompts could bridge the gap between spotting hate and taking action, the study evaluated six different interventions. Most messages produced little measurable change. However, the social norming message, which emphasized via survey data that 82 percent of Americans want online antisemitic hate speech removed and 77 percent want government action, yielded statistically significant improvements in both the ability to spot offensive material and the willingness to report it to platforms.
Compared with individuals who saw no message, those who read the social norming intervention were 6.1 percent more likely to recognize a contemporary nonpartisan antisemitic post and 5.6 percent more likely to report it. The intervention also led to a 6.9 percent increase in understanding offensive right-wing contemporary posts and a 5.9 percent increase in reporting classical left-wing antisemitism.
“The impact of a short message that most Americans reject antisemitism was moderate, but when you consider how quick and easily scalable such a message is, this result is groundbreaking,” said Matt Williams, Vice President of the ADL Center for Antisemitism Research. “Moving the needle 6 percent on recognizing and reporting antisemitic content doesn't seem like much for a room full of people, but think of what a 6 percent reduction across millions could bring about.”
Study identifies generational differences
The study also highlighted generational differences in how young adults respond to online hate. While Millennials were somewhat better than Gen Z at spotting antisemitic posts, Gen Z respondents who successfully identified antisemitism were more likely to report it, at 77 percent compared to 68 percent for Millennials.
Williams told The Jerusalem Post that while the data surfaced this distinct generational contrast, determining whether younger users view reporting toxic content as an expected baseline duty while older users see offensive posts through the lens of free expression remains a question for further study.
The study also identified distinct patterns among political Independents. When presented with a disinformation awareness message explaining how antisemitism uses scapegoating and conspiracy theories to manipulate public anger, Independents showed an 11 percent increase in recognizing classical right-wing antisemitism and about a 10 percent improvement in understanding contemporary antisemitism from both political sides. Furthermore, the research found that Democrats and Republicans were equally likely to recognize antisemitism regardless of whether it originated from their own political side.
Based on these results, the report outlines several key actionable recommendations for educators, platform developers, and community leaders going forward.
The authors stress that initiative leaders must prioritize recognition above all else, cautioning that young adults cannot respond to or report online antisemitism if they fail to recognize it in the first place. Interventions must also specifically focus on training individuals to identify contemporary forms of antisemitism, particularly when expressed through language surrounding Israel and Zionism.
At the same time, organizations should avoid relying solely on generic educational content or emotional appeals, as brief exposures to standard informational text or perspective-taking narratives failed to yield significant shifts in behavior.
Furthermore, funding and strategic outreach should actively invest in scalable social norming campaigns and expand testing around disinformation awareness, as reinforcing that antisemitism is broadly rejected by the public proved to be the single most effective tool for driving action, while teaching media manipulation techniques showed unique promise among political Independents.
Interventions must be tailored by the target audience to account for distinct demographic gaps, addressing Gen Z’s primary challenge with content recognition alongside Millennials' action gap when deciding whether to report toxic posts.
Aviva Klompas, Co-founder and CEO of Boundless, told The Jerusalem Post that future efforts must look beyond simply documenting abuse. "We want to move beyond pointing out that antisemitism is a problem and figure out what actually works to address it," Klompas said. "When people see antisemitism online, particularly in posts with thousands of likes or shares, they may assume those views are widely accepted. One of the most important findings is that reminding people that social media doesn't necessarily reflect public opinion, and that most Americans reject antisemitism, can make a real difference."
Klompas further stated the need for adaptive strategies, telling the Post, "We also want to keep exploring how to build resilience to manipulation and disinformation. Our findings among political Independents suggest that helping people recognize the techniques used to spread antisemitic conspiracy theories may be particularly effective. Perhaps the broader lesson is that we need to question our own assumptions about what works. Just because a message resonates within the Jewish community doesn't mean it will persuade the audiences we're trying to reach. We need to test our approaches, learn from the evidence, and be prepared to adapt."
Addressing practical applications for technology platforms, Williams informed the Post that the ADL "continuously talk with and share our research with social platforms," while also exploring ways to operationalize findings independently.

Lithuania has agreed to introduce universal military conscription for young men starting in 2032.
This decision was adopted by the Lithuanian State Defense Council, according to LRT.
According to President Gitanas Nausėda, 2032 was chosen as the start date for the changes so that there would be enough time to invest in adequate facilities for a larger number of conscripts and in the training of instructors.
“We have decided that universal conscription will be introduced starting in 2032,” Nausėda stated after the council meeting.
He added that women will continue to be able to serve in the military on a voluntary basis.
Currently, more than 5,000 young men are drafted into the armed forces each year.
Nausėda noted that after the introduction of universal conscription, the plan is to draft approximately 7,500 young people annually. This figure takes into account the demographic situation, as well as the fact that some young people are exempt from military service due to health reasons.
He added that it is also necessary to balance conscripts’ military service with the retraining of reserve personnel so that both processes proceed at the appropriate level.
“I believe this is the optimal approach,” the head of state noted.
He also reported that the State Defense Council has agreed to expand the range of service options. In particular, conscripts may be allowed to train as drone operators, assist the State Border Guard Service, or serve as firefighters.
Partial conscription was reinstated in Lithuania in 2015 amid escalating threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea.
Earlier, the United States resumed deploying troops to Lithuania. With the arrival of another 200 American service members on October 27, nearly one-third of the new U.S. contingent will be stationed in the country.

The Guardian view on online harms: Ofcom is failing at its job | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:25:27 UTC
03:25:27 KST

One thing is clear following last week’s report from the media regulator, Ofcom: the mammoth task of protecting children from online harms has barely begun. Campaigners said that they were dismayed but not surprised that the proportion of children viewing harmful content has stayed the same despite a raft of measures in the Online Safety Act designed to protect them. Research showed that high-priority material including pornography and self-harm, as well as a broader category covering bullying, abuse and the promotion of violence, continued to be encountered regularly in the nine months after new safety duties came into force.
The regulator found that personalised feeds were the main way that such content was presented, and noted that such feeds show different material to boys and girls. Suicide and self-harm content were more commonly seen by girls and children with special educational needs or disabilities. In a grim irony, Ofcom’s report appeared one day after a coroner in Norfolk ruled that suicide imagery viewed on TikTok “may have played a significant part” in the decision by a 14-year-old girl to take her own life in May.
This is a deeply concerning situation. Significant resources went into the UK’s online safety bill on the understanding that, after two decades during which tech companies had been granted extraordinary freedom over the terms of their engagement with citizens, democratic control was being reasserted. Silicon Valley’s reckless disregard of children’s safety and wellbeing convinced the public, and then parliament, that action was needed. Yet three years after the bill passed, Meta, TikTok and X are all engaged in legal challenges against Ofcom and appear to believe that their interests should trump the law.
Andy Burnham’s government needs a step change in how it treats big tech, which currently differs little from its predecessor. Lisa Nandy held on to her job as secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport; a ban on social media accounts for under-16s is due to come into force in spring 2027. Ministers want the UK to take a tougher approach than Australia, a pioneer in preventing online harm, and are looking at proposals requiring photo ID for teens to access sites.
But the new age limit and other safety rules can only work if the regulator is capable of enforcing them. And the Ofcom report was not encouraging. In evidence to MPs about the lack of a “safety culture” at social media companies, Ofcom’s chief executive, Melanie Dawes, sounded far too tentative. Whistleblowers have been making similar points more forcefully for years.
The Online Safety Act was never meant to be a once-and-for-all law. The pace of technological change – above all, the rise of AI – made further legislation inevitable. But searching questions must be asked about a situation in which a new law has led to no benefits at all for the user group – children – that it was designed to protect. As the Guardian has argued previously, ministers should have imposed a duty of care and made businesses accountable for improvements, rather than simply obliging them to follow a code.
Accountability remains too easily evaded at the top of tech. Executives should face a greater risk of criminal penalties for serious failings. Expressions of disappointment are no substitute for action. Regulators and ministers have the powers to secure change. They need to demonstrate an appetite for using them.

No seat at the table: Israel’s post-election message to its Palestinian citizens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:25:17 UTC
03:25:17 KST

Israel’s dilemma over its identity as a state couldn’t be clearer, and its leaders have set their priorities straight after the long-awaited election day on Tuesday. According to the Israeli Central Elections Committee, some four million Israeli citizens cast their vote, representing around 77.7% of voters, the highest turnout in over 20 years. Described as the most heated in Israel’s history, the 2026 elections centered around one question: Should Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stay in power?
As of Thursday morning, after counting nearly 90% of votes, the Netanyahu camp takes the prize, with 55 out of the 120 seats in the Knesset, followed by the opposition camp with 49 seats, and the Arab Palestinian parties with 19 seats, the most seats won by Palestinian citizens of Israel in the state’s history. Neither the Netanyahu camp nor the Eisenkot camp has reached the 61-seat majority required to form a government, and the Arab camp seems to be the key to solving the deadlock. However, the majority of the Eizenkot camp refuse to ally themselves with Palestinians, despite fiercely wanting to oust Netanyahu. This makes the achievement of the Palestinian vote essentially irrelevant, despite representing 20% of Israel’s population, and leaves the central question of forming a new government unresolved.
There are multiple possible scenarios ahead, and somebody will have to make some strategic concessions with deep political implications for the identity of Israel. The coming weeks may be the most politically significant since Israel’s establishment in 1948 — for Israel as a state, for its Palestinian citizens, and for Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who remain subject to Israel’s rule, despite not having citizenship. In order to understand the significance of this political moment, and the possible scenarios to come, we need to look back at the elections process within a larger context.
Voting on what?
Israelis voted on Tuesday for the first time since the October 7 attacks in 2023, widely considered as the largest security failure in Israel’s history, for which Netanyahu, under whose watch it happened, hasn’t taken any responsibility. But it is also the first vote sinceIsrael unleashed a genocidal military campaign on Gaza, which has earned a world-wide concensus for the crime of genocide, including a charge from a UN special investigation commission, all major international human rights organizations, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and Israel’s leading human rights group, B’Tselem. The Gaza genocide has turned global opinion against Israel, pushing it into an unprecedented political isolation. Meanwhile, neither its official stated goal of destroying Hamas, or its unofficial goal of expelling Palestinians out of Gaza, has been achieved.
Under Netanyahu’s government, Israeli settlers in the West Bank have launched their largest ever offensive, ethnically cleansing more than 100 rural Palestinian communities and attacking the heart of Palestinian towns, which invited international condemnation and even sanctions, albeit limited, on Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
It is also the first Israeli election since Israel’s two-round war with Iran, which has seen Israel receiving missile strikes like never before, wear out the U.S. deterrence in the region, giving Iran full control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz, boosting its position in the region, and deepening the U.S. opposition to Israel’s influence in American politics, including amongst the Republican party. Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s own promise of “regime change” in Iran has become a distant dream.
This election also arrives with a backdrop of Netanyahu’s campaign to change the decades-old established state institutions in Israel, giving the extreme ideologically-driven para-state pro-settler movements a way into controlling state institutions, and concentrating power in the executive branch, polarizing Israeli society along ideological and social identity lines. The peak of this crisis culminated in 2023, with the mass protests in Israel against Netanyahu’s attempt to diminish the power of the Israeli Supreme Court, shortly before the October 7 attacks. Moreover, the Tuesday vote comes in the midst of the unresolved Haredi drafting crisis, as the religious ultra-orthodox Jewish community demands to put its exemption from military drafting into law, while more Israelis demand that Haredis serve in the army like the rest, especially with the exhaustion of reservist forces, and the Israeli army’s crisis of manpower. In an attempt to maintain support from both sides of the crisis, Netanyahu dragged it on until the very end of his term.
By opening multiple fronts of war, deepening Israel’s military presence in Lebanon, and escalating campaigns on Palestinians in the West Bank, Netanyahu succeeded in keeping Israel in a constant state of emergency, fostering a ruthlessnationalist war-time atmosphere. Last week, media reports revealed that Israeli war planes were sent to the edge of Iran’s borders, in an attempt to provoke a new round of fighting, which would have forced the postponement of the elections. According to reports, the Israeli army’s Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir refused to go through with an attack on Iran at Netanyahu’s demand, setting a new precedent in the dynamic between the army’s chief and the Prime Minister. If he stays in power, Netanyahu has promised new military offensives in Gaza, in the West Bank, and against Iran.
Netanyahu’s setback
Two main camps are confronted. On the one hand, the Netanyahu camp includes his Likud party and other smaller right-wing, nationalist, religious, and anti-Arab parties, such as the far-right Jewish Power party led by Itamar Gvir and the far-right Religious Zionism party led by Bezalel Smotrich. On the other hand, the opposition anti-Netanyahu camp is led by former chief of the Israeli army staff, Gadi Eizenkot, and his Yashar party. Eizenkot himself is considered to be center-right, institutionalist, and pragmatic, joined by other key figures of the Israeli opposition: Avigdor Liberman, leading the Israel Beitenu far-right party, representing Russian-origin Jewish Israelis, Neftali Bennet, former Prime Minister, leading the B’Yachad far-right pro-settlers party, Yair Lapid, running the Yesh Atid center-right secular party, and Yair Golan, running The Democrats party, described as the left of the Zionist spectrum, secular, institutionalist, and pragmatic.
Shortly after voting posts closed at 10:00pm local time, media estimations showed that the opposition camp, led by Gadi Eizenkot, had won a majority of votes, making up between 52 to 54 seats out of the 120 seats in the Knesset, followed closely by the camp of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with 49 to 52 seats.
Netanyahu’s Likud party, the main force in his camp, was estimated to have won 24 to 25 seats, becoming the largest single party, followed by the Yashar party, led by the main opposition leader, Eizenkot, with 21 to 24 seats. Netanyahu’s main allies in his now-expired cabinet, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, were estimated to have won seven and six seats respectively. However, without the required majority, Netanyahu appeared to be far from forming a cabinet and staying in power. Although Eizenkot’s camp, with less ideological common ground, appeared to have come on top, it didn’t reach the required majority either.
The surprise of the night came from the two Arab lists, representing the Palestinian minority, who, according to initial estimates, won 17 to 18 seats, far more than their goal of 15 to 16 seats prior to the voting day. These seats were won by two forces. First, the Joint Arab list, including the Palestinian nationalist, liberal, pro-citizenship Balad party, whose leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, quit the race in early October to avoid being disqualified by the Israeli Supreme Court, the Ta’al nationalist pro-citizenship Palestinian party led by Ahmad Tibi, and the Hadash anti-Zionist Arab-Jewish leftist party. This alliance was estimated to get 11 seats. Second, Ra’am, representing a branch of the conservative Islamic movement led by Mansour Abbas, which was estimated to have won six to seven seats.
The voting rate in the Palestinian community in Israel reached 80% according to Palestinian media outlets in Israel, a historical voting rate unseen since the mid-1990s, securing the highest number of seats for Arab parties in the history of Arab representation in Israel. The high Palestinian turnout affected how the vote-to-seat ratio is calculated, making it impossible for either of the two main camps to reach the 61-seat majority and positioning Palestinian representation in the Knesset as a key player capable of determining who forms the next Israeli government. However, in the hours that followed, this numerical victory proved not to be a guarantee of Palestinian citizens of Israel’s capacity to influence Israeli politics.
In the early hours of Tuesday night, Palestinians celebrated in the headquarters of the Joint Arab List in Nazareth, where the head of the list, Yousef Jabarin, said in a speech that “our people sent Ben-Gvir home.” Jabarin later told the media that the Arab parties’ priority was to oust Netanyahu’s government and ensure that “there will be a change in policies, not only in faces.”
In Tel Aviv, Israeli opposition supporters also celebrated at the headquarters of Eizenkot’s campaign. The opposition leader offered what was described as a victory speech, saying that Israelis “had demonstrated that they lost trust in Netanyahu.” Eizenkot called upon the Israeli security forces to “remember that Netanyahu is now the head of an interim cabinet, and no longer the Prime Minister,” in a clear call to refuse any attempt by Netanyahu to start a war with Iran in the remaining transition weeks of his term. Netanyahu, for his part, remained silent until 3:00 am, when he declared, from the Likud party’s headquarters in Jerusalem that his party was the largest, and called for a “right-wing, strong, government,” and that Israel must “not form a government with anti-Zionist Arab parties.” Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s allies, including foreign minister Gideon Saar and finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, dismissed the opposition celebrations as premature.
In 2022, Netanyahu formed the government which ended its term on Tuesday, the 6th that he has led so far, with a 68-seat coalition in the Knesset. For years, Netanyahu has been seen as the sole leader of the overwhelmingly growing Israeli right and far-right camp. For him, falling short of securing a stable majority and forming a government is a clear setback. Despite this, his chances of staying in power proved to be far from over, after the official vote count began to be published on Wednesday morning. The first announcements indicated a comeback of Netanyahu’s camp on top, with 54 seats, with Eizenkot’s camp falling to 49, and later 47 seats. By Wednesday night, 77% of votes had been counted, confirming Netanyahu’s camp as the largest block in the new Knesset, although still short of the 61-seat majority required to form a government. Arab lists, for their part, were announced to have won up to 19 seats, making them the determining factor.
The final result is yet to be announced on Thursday night, after counting the votes of Israeli serving soldiers and foreign diplomatic missions, which take longer to register due to a special procedure. These make up more than 600,000 votes, representing 10 to 12 seats, which could change the entire equation. Given that these votes do not include Palestinian citizens, they are expected to go to both Netanyahu’s and Eizenkot’s camps, probably along the same lines as the other votes.
The Arab dilemma
The Arab lists, representing the Palestinian national minority in Israel, have established themselves as the determining factor, sharing the same goal as Eizenkot to put an end to Netanyahu’s 18 years in power. All of Eizenkot’s allies have expressed their willingness to oust the current Prime Minister, and they have the chance of doing that by building an alliance with the Arab lists. However, Eizenkot’s allies, except for Yair Golan, have pledged not to form a government with Arab support.
The Joint Arab List’s leaders have stated that although they wouldn’t join a government coalition, they are ready to provide an Eizenkot-led government with a “safety net” by supporting it with their vote of trust, without joining the coalition or subscribing to all its decisions.
The Ra’am Palestinian party, led by Mansour Abbas, on the contrary, is ready to join an Israeli government. It even has a Jewish candidate on its list, Yoav Segalovitz, a former Knesset member for Lapid’s Yesh Atid party, now occupying the second slot of Ra’am’s list, under Abbas himself, just to make it easier for the Israeli opposition to make an alliance with Ra’am, without having to put an Arab face in the cabinet. By all measures, the Israeli opposition has the possibility of ousting Netanyahu and ending his political career. It is only a difficult choice because it requires some form of alliance with the Palestinian component.
This is a difficult choice, because of the overwhelming anti-Arab sentiment in Israel, growing since before October 7, 2023. Since 2015, Netanyahu has referred to the Arabs’ participation in elections as a “national security threat,” arguing that Arab citizens “have 22 other Arab countries.” In 2015, on election day, Netanyahu addressed his supporters, warning that “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls,” and repeated the same threat last Tuesday. To the exception of Yair Golan, and non-Zionist Jewish leaders who are part of the Arab lists, Israeli opposition leaders never pushed back against Netanyahu’s logic. None of them attacked him for discriminative or inflammatory language, nor did any of them take the advantage to come out as more moderate or morally higher. Opinion polls, and Tuesday’s voting results have shown that bigotry against “the Arabs” is the most unifying political message in Israel.
Accepting an alliance with Arab lists would mean a loss of public support and, therefore, instability for the incoming government. Eizenkot, Lapid, and Bennet have stressed that they want to form a Zionist government, which means the exclusion of both Arab and Haredi parties, the latter of which are considered non-Zionist for religious reasons. However, without the support of Arab lists or Haredis, Eizenkot’s camp remains unable to form a government, as is Netanyahu.
What’s next?
There is no possible scenario ahead in which the solution to the current political deadlock in Israel comes from Netanyahu’s camp. It is monolithic, fanatic, and laser-focused on an extremist agenda on domestic issues, Palestinians, and surrounding countries that Netanyahu refers to as “Greater Israel.” For this camp, any cooperation with Arab lists is not only a political taboo, but also an accusation that it throws at its opponents to discredit them.
At the same time, there is no possible scenario without any concessions. The opposition camp, at least, has obvious concessions to choose from: accepting Netanyahu’s continuity in power, or accepting cooperation with the Arab lists. If Eizenkot and his allies lean towards Netanyahu, the current Prime Minister might have to drop his alliance with the Haredis and begin drafting them into the Israeli army.
These concessions might come in the form of one of four scenarios. The first of these scenarios is the ousting of Netanyahu, if Eizenkot, with the support of at least one of his allies, Yair Golan, decides to cooperate with Arab lists, especially the Joint List, by accepting their offer of a safety net. This would allow Palestinian candidates to discuss the terms. Among these are, according to statements made by the head of the Balad party, Ahmad Tibi, changing the speaker of the Knesset for a more moderate one, drafting legislation to improve the conditions of Palestinian citizens of Israel, especially in terms of house demolitions and fighting organized crime, and de-escalating tensions in the West Bank and Gaza.
The second possibility is a unified government between Netanyahu and Eizenkot’s camp, making Palestinian citizens and the seats that they won completely irrelevant. The Haredi community might find itself sidelined as well. This scenario is the one favored by the Trump administration, according to Israeli media reports, which said that Trump is planning to mediate between both Israeli camps to form a stable government that can participate in a possible upcoming round of war on Iran. In this scenario, Palestinians’ hopes of de-escalating the situation in Gaza and the West Bank, and improving conditions for Palestinian citizens of Israel, would all fade away.
The third scenario is the continuity of the political deadlock, and setting a new date for elections, which would be in March. This would give Netanyahu at least five more months n power, during which he can start a new war with Iran to boost his popularity and force a war-time atmosphere on his opponents, and go further in the escalation in the West Bank. The Israeli president Yitzhak Herzog, who is tasked with choosing who receives the delegation to form a government, said that he wants to prevent this scenario.
The fourth and final scenario is that Netanyahu would use the remaining time he has as interim Prime Minister to start a war with Iran, possibly after the US midterm elections, when such a war would be more favorable for the US president. This would impose a war-time state of emergency in Israel, in which Eizenkot and other opposition leaders would find themselves forced to join a national unity war government under Netanyahu.
As it stands today, one thing has been made clear: Despite the fact that the anti-Netanyahu camp has won an overwhelming majority, a feat that should make the path to a post-Netanyahu government clear, this is not the case, and the only reason is that this camp includes a major Arab, Palestinian component.
The incapacity of the Israeli opposition to form a government with Arab lists immediately stems only from the anti-Arab sentiment in the Israeli political scene and society. This is despite Palestinian citizens of Israel showing every possible flexibility, asking for nothing more than recognition of their status as a national minority as equal citizens. In the case of Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, he even stated his disposition to recognize the Jewish character of Israel. But it is for their Palestinian, Arab identity that Netanyahu has delegitimized any political cooperation with them, without any significant pushback from his opponents.
In practice, Israel is clearly defining itself as a democracy only when its Palestinian citizens are made absent, and that despite being the original, indigenous people of their own country, they are still not allowed a seat at the table.

‘A clear alliance’: Nations accused of undermining science at UN nature talks
- Four countries, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil, are accused of weakening UN biodiversity science at COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia.
- The dispute centres on whether nations should “welcome” or only “take note” of two IPBES reports on nature, climate and the economy.
- Delegates and experts warn this could set a harmful precedent and leave nature policy without a strong scientific base.
AI generated
YEREVAN - Political tensions are mounting in the final days of the United Nations biodiversity talks with a handful of countries accused of trying to weaken the science that underpins global nature policy.
The growing feud over the role of science has alarmed veteran negotiators and follows recent efforts by fossil fuel-reliant nations to delay reports by the IPCC, the global authority on climate change.
“The same thing is happening here as what is taking place with the IPCC,” said a French government delegate at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
The delegate requested anonymity to discuss ongoing negotiations.
The delegate said four countries – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil – were frustrating progress.
The pushback is directed at two scientific assessments by the UN-backed IPBES biodiversity panel on the overlap between the nature and climate crises and the economic forces driving them.
Nearly 200 nations were due to agree how these landmark findings should guide efforts to protect nature but some countries “did not want to acknowledge them”, the French delegate added.
A negotiator from another developed nation told AFP these four countries were also leading this push.
“There is a clear alliance of Russia, Saudi, Argentina and, to some extent, Brazil, all working together to try to water down IPBES reports, not welcome them, or use them as bargaining chips in other negotiation items,” the negotiator said on condition of anonymity.
Setting precedent
Much of the dispute boils down to a few paragraphs of text in a draft agreement and whether countries should “welcome” or “take note” of the IPBES findings.
The latter phrasing is considered far weaker in the language of UN negotiations, where every word is closely scrutinised.
The current draft was “a text without ambition”, said the French delegate.
“If we no longer have a scientific basis to work from, then everything we discuss here is merely a matter of opinion,” the delegate added.
Academics and civil society activists at COP17 have already issued a joint statement of concern at the state of negotiations.
When approached by AFP in Yerevan, IPBES chair David Obura declined to comment as the talks were still ongoing.
Although the summit is due to end on Oct 30, a number of outstanding matters – including around the science – remain unresolved.
The dispute echoes a growing pattern in consensus-based global negotiations, where oil-producing countries are accused of frustrating efforts to tackle fossil fuels, plastic trash and other environmental harm.
Climate science has long been a flashpoint and the IPCC is currently deadlocked, as countries including Saudi Arabia and India push to delay publication of its next set of benchmark reports on global warming.
In an unprecedented decision in 2025, a crucial summary of the Global Environment Outlook, a flagship UN scientific report, was torpedoed as nations rowed over fossil fuels.
“We’ve pretty much always seen IPCC reports being politicised...,” said the negotiator from the developed country.
“But in the biodiversity world they’ve been much less contentious until the last few years, and this COP in particular.”
“They’re never easy, no decision is. There’s always nitpicking over language – but it’s gotten far worse.”
Bethan Laughlin, a senior policy specialist for the Zoological Society of London who observed the COP17 negotiations firsthand, said the trend was worrying.
“The point really isn’t this particular text, although it is highly significant. The point is the precedent it sets,” she told AFP in Yerevan. AFP

Finland launches criminal probe of suspected environmental damage by Google
The US tech giant is investing $15bn in a huge new data centre project in northern Finland.
Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland.
The project is part of a $15bn deal announced last month by Alphabet’s Google to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe.
Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a local subsidiary of Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos, before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed.
“We are investigating whether the company’s operations have breached the Water Act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told the Reuters news agency on Thursday, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine.
Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation, and a Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.
Tree felling prompts local anger
Videos and photographs showing the scale of the forest clearance at the site of the data centre, and Google’s initial reluctance to address the issue in the days after the news broke, have prompted widespread anger in Finland, where there is a high level of respect for the natural environment among the public.
“All the outrage and dismay directed at Google, I can very much share that, especially when we are talking about the parent company valued as the third-largest in the world,” Finnish Green MP Oras Tynkkynen told Al Jazeera. “There is just no excuse. You have to know the legislation of the country you are operating in; you can afford to hire the best legal experts to help you navigate the local legal requirements.”
Finnish authorities ordered Google to stop work at the data centre site at the start of October, and the latest information from the police highlights shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the site.
Tynkkynen called Google’s actions “unforgivable”, but cautioned that while the anger being directed at the US tech giant was justified, it was also diverting scrutiny away from legacy Finnish forestry companies, which he says are “by far the biggest contributors to biodiversity loss in this country”.
What is Finland’s appeal for data centre construction?
Finland’s cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe’s main destinations for data centre investments in recent years.
Finland, similar in size to Germany – but with one-seventh of the population, less than six million people – has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States.
AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 percent in Finland’s electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said.
Google’s planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.
Supporting Google’s plan, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in September that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns that it would suck up energy and push up power prices.

US Jews urge Israel opposition to partner with Arab parties
Unknown

2026-10-29
