Beskrestnov: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot interceptor missiles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:24 EET
02:54:24 KST

Russia is producing ballistic missiles in volumes that exceed the global production capacity for Patriot interceptor missiles, stated Serhiy Beskrestnov (Flash), an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies.
"Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the number of Patriot interceptor missiles produced globally to counter them," he told reporters on Thursday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia continues to manufacture Iskander and S-400 missiles, with production capacities in these segments exceeding current requirements. Furthermore, Russia has partially shifted production away from Kinzhal missiles toward ballistic missiles, Beskrestnov noted.
He emphasized that the increase in Russian ballistic missile production exacerbates the shortage of interceptors. He added that this imbalance is further compounded by the introduction of missiles from North Korea and Iran.
Beskrestnov noted that countering this threat requires an increase in the global production of PAC-3 interceptor missiles. At the same time, this process faces limitations, and scaling up production volumes takes time.

Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:52:25 UTC
02:52:25 KST

The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”

Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:51:20 UTC
02:51:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
The Horn of Africa is where strategic maritime corridors, fragile states, and regional ambitions converge - and it is emerging as a new front in Middle Eastern geopolitical competition.
Israel’s 26 December 2025 recognition of Somaliland’s independence added new dimensions to these tensions, intersecting with Turkey’s expanding military, economic, and diplomatic footprint in Somalia and broader partnerships across the Horn of Africa.
From Turkey’s perspective, Israel’s Somaliland move and its broader regional engagement challenge Ankara’s strategic interests. Tel Aviv, for its part, views Somaliland as a potential gateway to projecting influence near Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen and along one of the world’s most important maritime corridors.
Somaliland’s longstanding quest for international recognition risks becoming further entangled in the rivalries of Middle Eastern powers, transforming a local sovereignty dispute into a wider contest over the future of Red Sea security.
As Turkey and Israel deepen their engagement, and other external actors pursue their own agendas, the Horn of Africa might end up an increasingly crowded arena of geopolitical competition. The implications for regional stability could be serious.
Israel's Somaliland gambit and the rivalry with Turkey
Situated alongside busy maritime routes, the Horn of Africa links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, occupying a position of much geostrategic importance.
Egypt, Iran, Israel, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) increasingly view the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding territories as a single security environment. Instability in one part of this interconnected region can disrupt commercial shipping, threaten energy security, and intensify rivalries among states far beyond its shores.
Israel’s decision to recognise Somaliland’s independence and to invest in deeper ties with the self-declared breakaway republic is very much about securing a strong position in a territory situated in close proximity to Yemen.
This land can provide Tel Aviv with the means to closely monitor Houthi activity, improve intelligence collection, and strengthen surveillance of maritime routes that have become increasingly vulnerable to disruption.
“Israel’s interest in the Horn of Africa is not new but has sped up amid regional shake-up in the aftermath of [7 October 2023],” Dr Burcu Ozcelik, Senior Research Fellow for Middle East Security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
“Israel sees Somaliland mainly through a defence cooperation lens, and as a possible staging ground for future offensive military activity against the Houthis. The strategic value of access near Yemen for Israel spans intelligence, surveillance, and potentially military operations,” she added.
Ankara and Tel Aviv’s rivalry and maritime security interests are “mutually reinforcing” motivations, argued Cameron Hudson, an independent analyst with expertise on African peace, security, and governance, who previously worked on Africa at the Central Intelligence Agency, State Department, and the US National Security Council.
“They are two sides of the same coin and cannot be disaggregated,” he told The New Arab.
However, Omar S. Mahmood, a Senior Analyst for Somalia and the Horn of Africa at International Crisis Group, offers a more qualified interpretation. He suggests that the immediate motivation for Tel Aviv is mostly related to security, while competition with Ankara is a secondary consequence, not necessarily the driving force.
“I don’t think Israel’s relationship with Somaliland is driven by a broader rivalry with Turkey per se. But there are local ramifications as Somaliland itself is seeking external allies as it is uncomfortable with growing Turkish military support to Somalia, viewing it as a potential future threat,” explained Mahmood in an interview with The New Arab.
“So, in this sense the middle powers can get drawn into supporting opposite sides in local rivalries, even if that was not the primary factor driving their engagement in the first place,” he added.
Turkey's foothold in Somalia
Turkey’s presence in Somalia is a product of many years of sustained investment and political commitment.
In 2011, Somalia faced a devastating famine which claimed approximately 250,000 lives (half of them children) amid an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. At that time, Mogadishu did not have many reliable partners around the world.
That was when Ankara’s engagement with the country gained momentum, beginning with humanitarian assistance and reconstruction before developing into a much wider relationship across multiple domains, from investment to military training and security cooperation to state-building.
Central to Turkey’s military partnership with Somalia has been its TURKSOM facility in Mogadishu. This training establishment has been at the heart of Turkish efforts to help build up the Somali government’s ability to fight al-Shabaab.
Ankara and Mogadishu signed a 10-year defence agreement in 2024, extending their cooperation into naval development and the protection of Somalia's coastline, alongside growing Turkish interests in maritime security and offshore oil and gas exploration, underscoring Turkey’s stakes in Somalia achieving greater stability.
Bilateral ties also strengthened when Somalia sought international support following Ethiopia's agreement with Somaliland concerning access to the sea in exchange for recognition - a deal which infuriated officials in Mogadishu.
Ankara subsequently helped mediate between Somalia and Ethiopia, illustrating how Turkey’s influence has gone beyond military and economic cooperation and entailed effective regional diplomacy.
In late 2025, Turkey joined many other countries around the world in strongly denouncing Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Ankara feared that recognition of the breakaway republic gravely threatened Somalia’s territorial dignity.
Turkey also has concerns about the potential creation of openings for external actors to establish a presence for themselves in territories situated near maritime routes where Ankara has vested interests.
Rather than reacting with an immediate escalation of its military presence, Ankara seems to find its most effective response to be based on reinforcing its relationships and institutions that serve to underpin Turkish influence in Somalia. This measured approach appears to be aimed at protecting the investments which Turkey has made in the country without setting Ankara up for any overt confrontation with the Israelis in Somalia.
However, Ankara’s efforts to preserve its position in Somalia could have unintended consequences. Somaliland may interpret deeper Turkish-Somali security cooperation as a threat to its political ambitions, prompting Hargeisa to seek stronger external backing and, in the process, potentially deepening regional tensions.
The Emirati factor
No analysis of Turkish-Israeli competition in the Horn of Africa is complete without taking stock of the UAE’s role. Abu Dhabi’s support for Somaliland, even if short of formal recognition, places the UAE broadly on the same side of this sovereign dispute as Tel Aviv.
The UAE has vast strategic and commercial interests across the Red Sea, giving Abu Dhabi high stakes in the Horn of Africa’s evolving security order, while its normalised relationship with Israel continues to be an important feature of the Middle East’s geopolitical landscape more than six years after the Abraham Accords’ signing.
On the other side, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, and other regional actors have expressed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, a position that connects their interests in the Horn of Africa to their wider security cooperation in the Middle East.
Hudson sees the UAE and Israel as a “powerful and mutually reinforcing duo in the Red Sea” which are both willing to challenge established power structures and intervene in disputes in the Horn of Africa to further their national interests at the region’s expense.
“They are happy to pick winners and losers, unsettle established power dynamics, and actively intervene in regional politics and conflicts in ways that benefit them even if that means unsettling regional dynamics,” he told The New Arab.
Hudson contrasts this with “Turkish or Saudi efforts to stabilise and reinforce established power dynamics as a way of limiting destabilising outside influences.”
Clearly, Abu Dhabi’s role is important not only due to Emirati ambitions but also because external backing can make local leaders less willing to compromise by reducing the perceived costs associated with confrontation.
The local stakes of a wider geopolitical contest
Despite the growing involvement of Middle Eastern states in the Horn of Africa, and the risks of this region becoming more of an arena for external competition, it is necessary to note that Somalia and Somaliland are not passive actors victimised by a giant game of geopolitical chess.
Both have agency and are actively seeking non-African partners to strengthen their positions and advance their political objectives.
For the government in Mogadishu, Turkey's military, economic, and diplomatic support is critical to strengthening state institutions, improving security, and protecting Somalia’s territorial integrity.
Meanwhile, Somaliland has long sought international recognition and has strong incentives to cultivate relationships with countries such as Israel and the UAE, which might advance that goal or at least provide greater protection against perceived threats.
In this sense, “you have a layer of local rivalries that now intersect with regional rivalries, creating a potentially dangerous situation,” explained Mahmood, who emphasised that this permits “Horn of Africa actors to take on more maximalist, aggressive and less compromising positions, knowing that [they] have…external support to fall back on.”
Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, Israel, and maritime targets have done much to help explain why regional powers see the Horn of Africa as increasingly important to their foreign policy calculations.
As Houthi-Saudi hostilities escalate, Riyadh is focused on growing stronger security partnerships with regional actors, while governments in the Horn of Africa are likely to view closer cooperation with the Kingdom as a way to secure higher levels of assistance and bolster their own military capabilities. Meanwhile, the conflict in Sudan adds new layers of complication as it draws regional actors into overlapping security and political calculations.
Yet a greater military presence does not necessarily translate into greater stability. While competing powers expand their security footholds with the aim of countering one another, mistrust can deepen, territorial disputes can intensify, and local actors will probably pursue greater support from external powers.
Therefore, the Horn of Africa is increasingly likely to become exposed to conflicts in and around the Red Sea even if not directly involved in their initial escalation. Within this context, heightened insecurity means that further militarisation of the Red Sea risks undermining, rather than enhancing, security.
An evolving security arrangement around the Red Sea
On 7 August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement - a trilateral alliance which is defensive in nature and aimed at containing the chaotic instability unleashed by the war centred on Iran.
This security configuration has potentially significant implications for the balance of power around the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. It was hardly surprising that the leadership in Mogadishu hailed the pact in the immediate aftermath of its announcement, especially given Somalia’s close ties with the three signatories and shared threat perceptions of Israeli aggression.
For Somalia, the pact’s significance extends beyond its endorsement and raises important questions about regional realignments and Ankara’s position in the Horn of Africa within the wider context of an emerging security architecture.
Escalating Houthi-Saudi hostilities prompt a broader recalibration of regional security alignments, bringing Turkey and Pakistan closer to Saudi Arabia through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. For Ankara, this partnership offers an opportunity to connect its longstanding presence in Somalia with a wider strategic role in Gulf and Red Sea security.
Dr Ozcelik told The New Arab that the hostilities have “crossed red lines that were deemed unthinkable not long ago,” setting in motion a realignment among Riyadh’s allies. Ankara’s growing institutional engagement with the Kingdom therefore extends beyond diplomatic rhetoric, highlighting a more formal commitment to regional defence and security cooperation.
There are implications of this emerging Turkish-Saudi alignment for the rivalry between Ankara and Tel Aviv. As Dr Ozcelik stressed, Ankara is “institutionalising its partnership with Saudi Arabia beyond rhetoric and through defence commitments, minilateralism, and regional diplomacy.”
This closer Turkish-Saudi relationship will not escape Israeli strategists’ attention, particularly as Ankara expands its regional security role while Riyadh remains firm in its support for Palestinian statehood.
In Dr Ozcelik’s assessment, these parallel developments risk “fuelling a greater gulf between Israel and Turkey,” further complicating an already tense relationship that has significantly deteriorated since 7 October 2023.
While commentators sometimes toss Somalia around as a possible Mecca Joint Defence Agreement candidate, Hudson considers formal Somalia membership in the pact unlikely in the near term. He noted that Somalia remains a recipient of security assistance rather than a country capable of contributing meaningfully to a mutual defence arrangement.
“Given the high level of instability still emanating from Somalia, external countries would be foolish at this point to enter into a mutual security agreement with them now. Somalia can’t provide for its own security, let alone contribute to the security of others,” Hudson told The New Arab.
Similarly, Mahmood does not expect Somalia to formally join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. But he does think Mogadishu is likely to deepen security relations with the pact’s three signatories, noting that this is a development already underway. “Somalia prefers to align with this bloc of countries and sees them as a future source of support as it continues to build up its military capabilities,” he observed.
The risks of an expanding geopolitical contest
The internationalisation of the Horn of Africa’s political disputes and security crises entered a new chapter after Israel became the first UN member-state to officially recognise Somaliland ten months ago.
What started as a dispute over Somaliland’s recognition and Somalia’s territorial integrity has transformed into a larger contest over maritime security, military access, and regional influence.
A dangerous risk is an exacerbating security dilemma in which competing alliances deepen mistrust, undermine compromise, and expose the Horn of Africa to conflicts originating elsewhere.
Preventing further escalation will require Middle Eastern powers and their regional partners to exercise restraint while recognising that lasting stability depends on addressing the disputes that drive Somalia and Somaliland to seek competing external allies.

Egyptian man who fire-bombed pro-Israel rally in Colorado pleads guilty to federal hate crimes
DENVER, Oct 29 - The man who lobbed gasoline bombs at a pro-Israel rally in Colorado last year, injuring several people including a woman who later died, pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal hate-crime charges, the US Department of Justice said.
Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 47, an Egyptian national, is already serving a life sentence for his guilty plea in May to more than 100 state charges, including first-degree murder.
Soliman pleaded guilty to nine counts of hate-crime offenses and three explosives charges in federal court in Denver, according to the DOJ. The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty.
The plea deal asks that Soliman be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years. Soliman will be sentenced on January 7.
"The defendant admitted that he committed the attack because of the actual or perceived Jewish religion and Israeli national origin of the group he targeted," the DOJ said in a statement.
David Kraut, a federal public defender listed as Soliman's lawyer, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Soliman has admitted tossing two Molotov cocktails at people taking part in a rally in downtown Boulder on June 1, 2025, held in solidarity with hostages seized by Hamas militants who stormed Israeli villages from the Palestinian enclave of Gaza on October 7, 2023.
Prosecutors said Soliman yelled "Free Palestine" as the gasoline bombs he lobbed at the crowd burst into flames outside a municipal courthouse in the heart of Boulder's popular Pearl Street shopping district.
Admitting his guilt in state court nearly six months ago, Soliman denounced his own crimes as contrary to "the teachings of Islam" and insisted he bore no ill will toward Jewish people. He went on to lament the "thousands of families who have lost their families in Palestine and Gaza," and said the "enemy is Zionism."
Authorities in Colorado identified 29 victims from the attack, including 14 who were burned or injured while fleeing and 15 who were close enough to be considered targets of attempted murder. One victim, 82-year-old Karen Diamond, died of her injuries later that month. Her husband suffered severe burns and survived.
The firebombing came amid heightened tensions over the 2023 Hamas raid and Israel's military assault in Gaza, which sparked a surge in anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim hate crimes across the US and a wave of pro-Palestinian protests that many Israel supporters branded as antisemitic. Pro-Palestinian protesters reject accusations their support of Gazans amounts to antisemitism.
FAMILY'S IMMIGRATION DETENTION
According to affidavits filed in court by prosecutors, Soliman told investigators after his arrest that he had planned his attack for a year, but delayed going through with it until after his daughter had graduated from high school.
Soliman, who had lived with his wife and five children in Colorado Springs, also has asserted that his family members were unaware of his intentions beforehand.
The family was taken into immigration custody in June 2025 after his arrest and transported to a detention facility in Texas. They were held until a court-ordered release on April 23, 2026, more than 10 months later.
The children and their mother, who subsequently divorced Soliman, were rearrested on April 25 of this year just after returning to Colorado. They were freed again when attorneys intervened a day later, according to court documents.
Court records entered at about the time that Soliman reached a plea deal with federal prosecutors earlier this month showed that he had withdrawn motions seeking to preclude any further attempts at removing his family. REUTERS

UN rapporteurs warn of &#8216;scholasticide,&#8217; erasure of truth in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:50:20 UTC
02:50:20 KST

UN special rapporteurs on Thursday warned of the systematic destruction of education and the media in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Anadolu reports.
During a briefing by the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People at UN headquarters in New York, Farida Shaheed, the rapporteur on the right to education, said the world continues to witness “scholasticide, the systemic and systematic obliteration of education, which has been horrendous in Gaza.”
She said that “98% of the schools and all 13 universities have been destroyed,” adding, “Almost 21,000 Palestinian students have been killed. A classroom of children every day during the war on Gaza.”
Saying that the destruction aims to uproot Palestinian society, Shaheed said: “Scholasticide is multigenerational; it aims to dismantle the very foundation of Palestinian society, erase their history and destroy a sense of collective self.”
She said 13 libraries, the central archives of Gaza holding 150 years of history, 195 heritage sites, 227 mosques and at least three churches were also destroyed or targeted.
In the occupied West Bank, Shaheed said, “Last September, 10 out of 48 schools were demolished in East Jerusalem.”
She noted that some schools had to close after failing to obtain licenses, which often depend on curriculum changes that delete references to Palestinian history and culture.
“In the first half of the year, there were 224 security incidents, which affected 152 schools, 20,450 students, and at least 859 educational personnel,” she said. “Settler violence has also displaced at least 1,700 children from school.”
Francesca Albanese, the rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, addressed the briefing virtually and said her latest report examines the role of the media.
“Since October 2023, Israel has killed nearly 300 journalists and media workers in Gaza,” she said.
She said when witnesses are silenced, “the crime is not only committed; it is concealed, and impunity becomes part of the plan.”
Albanese said more than 74,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, which “has the highest number of child amputees per capita in the world.”
Pointing to the ceasefire announced last year, she said, “I wish I could tell you the so-called ceasefire had brought relief. It has not,” she said, adding that more than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since it was announced.
Albanese said thousands of Palestinians were forcibly displaced from Hebron in the West Bank after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to destroy the neighborhood of those behind the Oct. 23 checkpoint attacks.
“Gaza might be the breaking point, not because of the United Nations’ lack of tools, but because its members chose not to use them,” she said. “It is not too late.”
Urging states to act, she said: “Suspend arms transfer and trade that sustain unlawful occupation and genocide. Fund and protect UNRWA. Protect the journalists.”
“History will ask what each of us did. Let our answer not be that we just watched,” she added.

Ukraine should not agree to limits on size of its armed forces – Admiral Bauer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Ukraine should not agree to limits on size of its armed forces – Admiral Bauer
He made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event hosted by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"I think there's two elements that are extremely important when it comes to a just peace. One is that Ukraine remains a truly sovereign state, which can decide its own future and its alliances. And that means credible Armed Forces. That means the ability to run the country as the people of Ukraine want. All these demands from Russia that there shouldn't be credible Armed Forces in Ukraine are unacceptable," Bauer said.
He added that, second, there must be credible means of deterring the aggressor from invading again.
"People often talk about security guarantees, but there should be credible deterrents to make sure that Russia understands that, if they try again, they will fail," the Dutch admiral said.
In his opinion, unless these two conditions are met, it is highly unlikely that Ukraine will be able to accept any peace settlement proposal.
He believes that even territorial concessions could form part of a settlement, but only if the two conditions outlined above are met.
"Also, it's not about giving away lands. You could say that you are accepting that you have no control over these territories, but you're not accepting that they are Russian. No de jure recognition. It's only accepting the situation only to end the war," he said.
At the same time, drawing on the experience of the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Bauer believes it is unlikely that anything short of a mechanism as close as possible to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty would be an acceptable option.
Speaking about the security of the entire European continent, the admiral also said that Ukraine must genuinely become "part of our security in the larger sense, when it comes to Europe."

Prediction market operator Polymarket is investigating a string of well-timed and profitable trades on Israel's election this week, according to a Bloomberg News report on Thursday.
Shortly before polls closed on Tuesday, hundreds of newly created accounts placed bets on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu retaining his position and his Likud party winning the most seats, according to the report.
The report said those trades quickly became profitable- and together some of the accounts already cashed out over $100,000 - after some exit polls showed that Netanyahu’s party had won more seats than early reports suggested.
Many wallets have significant gains that have not yet been realized, the report said.
Prediction markets face growing scrutiny over potential insider trading, with platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi reporting a surge in suspicious activity amid a sharp increase in trading volumes. Reuters reported in May that Polymarket had seen a significant uptick in trades flagged as suspicious this year.
Polymarket investigates suspicious betting activity linked to Israeli election
Polymarket is reviewing dozens of newly created wallets that traded on the election, its internal investigative team told Bloomberg.
Data analysis firms Polysights and Bubblemaps have also flagged the activity as suspicious and are investigating, the report said.
The findings are not conclusive, and it can be difficult to distinguish potential insider trading from original research or lucky bets, Bloomberg reported.
Representatives for Polymarket and Polysights did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Bubblemaps said its analysis shared with Bloomberg was recent and that it had no further updates.

IDF soldier indicted for allegedly spying for Iran, leaking sensitive military intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:49:36 UTC
02:49:36 KST

A soldier has been indicted for providing information to Iran, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police, and the IDF Spokesperson's Unit, announced in a joint statement Thursday.
The soldier was arrested in September in a joint operation by the Shin Bet, the Ayalon District Police Investigations Unit, the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID), and the Defense Ministry's security authorities.
The official charges filed by the prosecution are providing information to the enemy with intent to harm state security, providing information for the benefit of the enemy, and contact with a foreign agent.
The soldier's alleged espionage activities involved encrypted communications, coded messages, cryptocurrency payments, and a cover story designed to conceal his contact with Iranian intelligence. His handler also reportedly offered him a substantial financial incentive to travel to Iran.
According to investigators, the soldier maintained contact with Iranian intelligence operatives for approximately a year, fully aware of whom he was communicating with. During that period, he allegedly disclosed sensitive information about his unit's activities, IDF operational readiness, and emergency mobilizations, including details of his own call-up at the outbreak of Operation Roaring Lion.
IDF soldier allegedly shared military base coordinates, photos of US aircraft with Iran
The information he allegedly provided included the locations and coordinates of military bases, along with photographs of interceptor missiles, military vehicles, and US refueling aircraft stationed at an Israeli airport.
Investigators also found that the soldier supplied his handler with personal information about fellow soldiers and commanders in his unit, despite knowing that the Iranian operative intended to use those details to recruit additional individuals for espionage.
In exchange, the soldier received payments through cryptocurrency wallets, following instructions from his Iranian handler.
The investigation further revealed that the soldier gave his handler access to a Telegram group called "Kal Bakrav," which serves Israelis preparing for military service. The Iranian operative subsequently joined the group.
The handler also instructed the soldier to install malicious communications applications that would allow them to exchange encrypted messages. He reportedly suggested that the soldier purchase a basic mobile phone and a handgun.
IDF soldier, Iranian handler allegedly used coded messages and cover story to evade detection
To avoid detection, the two allegedly agreed to communicate using coded language and devised a cover story in case Israeli security authorities uncovered their activities.
The Iranian handler also offered the soldier $200,000 to travel to Iran, according to investigators.
A military court extended the soldier's detention until November 12, 2026.
In their joint statement, the Shin Bet, Israel Police, and IDF described the case as an extremely serious threat to national security and urged the public to remain vigilant against suspected foreign intelligence recruitment attempts.
"We call on the public to exercise the utmost vigilance. Any suspicious approach by an unidentified individual, request to provide information, or offer of payment in exchange for 'services' must be reported to the security authorities," the agencies said.
The security agencies added that they would continue working to prevent espionage and terrorism and pursue legal action against individuals suspected of assisting enemy operatives or endangering Israel's security.

02:49:34 KST

Israel extradited Alexander Block to the United States early Thursday to face charges over the alleged theft of about USD 2.8 million in digital assets from cryptocurrency platform Nomad, the State Attorney’s Office announced.
Block, an Israeli-Russian citizen formerly known as Alexander Gurevich, was transferred to American authorities after extensive legal proceedings in Israel, including an unsuccessful Supreme Court appeal and a subsequent request for a further hearing.
The case concerns allegations that he exploited a security flaw in August 2022 to obtain digital tokens - without depositing the assets that were supposed to back them - and then moved the proceeds between digital wallets to conceal their origin.
According to the Supreme Court judgment, US authorities indicted Block in the Northern District of California in August 2023 on eight counts involving computer offenses, transferring stolen property, and money laundering. The US requested his extradition in December 2024.
Block was arrested at Ben-Gurion Airport in May 2025 while preparing to travel to Russia. He had changed his surname from Gurevich to Block and obtained a passport in his new name shortly before his arrest.
Block identified flaw in crypto platform, withdrew about 2.8m in tokens
Nomad, the cryptocurrency platform, operated as a bridge between blockchain networks, allowing users to lock digital assets on one network and receive corresponding tokens on another.
According to the American extradition request, Block identified a flaw that allowed him to bypass the check confirming that the original assets had been locked. Prosecutors allege that, after testing the vulnerability, he withdrew about USD 2.8m. in tokens on August 1, 2022, without supplying the corresponding assets.
He then allegedly converted the tokens into other cryptocurrencies and transferred them between wallets to obscure the source of the funds.
The Jerusalem District Court approved his extradition in July 2025. His appeal challenged whether the alleged conduct constituted criminal offenses under Israeli law and whether the evidence was sufficient to support extradition.
Block argues transactions used Nomad functions
Block argued that the transactions used functions available within Nomad’s automated system and that the public record of blockchain transfers undermined the money-laundering allegations.
The Supreme Court rejected those arguments, holding that exploiting a programming flaw could constitute unlawful computer intrusion, even where the software technically permitted the action. It also explained that publicly visible transactions did not necessarily identify the people controlling the wallets or rule out efforts to conceal the source of funds.
The State Attorney’s Office said Supreme Court President Isaac Amit subsequently rejected his request for a further hearing. Thursday’s transfer was coordinated by the prosecution’s International Department and the Israel Police’s operational coordination and Interpol units.

"There is no such thing as a humanitarian gesture in Iran. It's like the trucks going to Hamas. When you want to help the other side's poor, they interpret it as you not wanting to destroy them. To this day, we are still sending trucks and money to Hamas."

The aircraft was involved in Operation Althea. The causes of the accident still have to be established.
An Italian helicopter taking part in an EU peacekeeping operation has crashed near the town of Brčko in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The European Union's EUFOR military mission confirmed the CH-47 Chinook helicopter had crashed on Thursday afternoon. A spokesman said four crew members had been killed and 11 were injured.
A spokesman for Brčko hospital, said three of the 15 crew members on board the helicopter were killed in the crash and a fourth died in hospital.
"Twelve people were brought to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person died from his injuries in hospital," said the spokesman, Salih Ibrahimbegovic.
EUFOR also said no civilians had been injured and no civilian infrastructure, property or vehicles were damaged in the crash.
The crash happened in Gorice, about 180 kilometres (110 miles) northeast of Sarajevo.
"As a result of this crash, a number of EUFOR personnel tragically lost their lives, and others were seriously injured," EUFOR said in a later statement.
Bosnia's Defence Ministry said "it is not possible to issue further statements, while awaiting more precise information, above all about the state of health of the personnel".
EUFOR has urged people not to spread unverified information or disinformation and to rely on official channels for updates on the incident.
Brčko district mayor Siniša Milić said three people had died and 12 had been injured, with one of those injured in a critical condition.
"All have been treated in a hospital in Brčko. Medical staff are on alert," he said.
Further details about those on board and the cause of the crash are expected to be released once the authorities have completed their investigation.
EUFOR’s roughly 1,200-strong mission has operated in Bosnia since 2004, when it took over from NATO. It works under a UN Security Council mandate to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of the peace agreement that ended the 1992–95 war.

Senior US general fired, accused of leaking classified information
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:47:05 CET
02:47:05 KST

By Phil Stewart
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired US Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner on the Pentagon’s Joint Staff, over accusations he leaked classified information to the public, officials said on Thursday.
Sylvia’s firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth’s sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth’s effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior US general has “got problems.”
“We’re very much looking for leakers, and she’s going to have big problems, long-term problems,” Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
KEY POSITION
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top US military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the US Army’s 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the US military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called “another little Epic Fury.” The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal US military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That’s the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: “Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it.”
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia’s 32 years of service, saying “we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances.”
“Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further,” the spokesperson said.
(Reporting by Phil Stewart; additional reporting by Ryan Jones; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)

Israel's election results are in: How a government is formed or new elections are triggered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:41:57 UTC
02:41:57 KST

Israel's Central Elections Committee completed the vote count Thursday, leaving the country facing a familiar political dilemma: Neither of the main blocs has secured the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Despite the inconclusive results, political consultations are already underway, with parties on both sides seeking to assemble a governing coalition and avoid another election. The next stage will place President Isaac Herzog at the center of the process, as party leaders prepare to recommend their preferred candidates for prime minister.
How does Israel form a government after an election, what happens if the first candidate fails, and when could voters be sent back to the polls?
Step by step: What happens after Election Day?
The first step is the official publication of the election results by the Central Elections Committee in Reshumot, Israel's official gazette. Under the law, the committee has eight days from Election Day to publish the results, making Wednesday, November 4, the final deadline.
The 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, exactly two weeks after the October 27 election. But the race to form a government will begin before the new parliament formally convenes.
Once the Central Elections Committee submits the official results to President Herzog, he will summon representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset to the President's Residence. Each party will recommend the lawmaker it believes should be tasked with forming the next government.
Herzog is expected to begin consultations on Wednesday, November 4. The meetings are expected to continue Thursday and could extend into Friday.
Under Israeli law, the president has seven days from the publication of the official election results to complete consultations and assign the task of forming a government. If the results are published on November 4, that gives him until November 11, although he may make his decision earlier.
The president generally gives the mandate to the lawmaker he believes has the strongest chance of assembling a governing coalition. In most cases, that is the candidate who receives the largest number of recommendations from parliamentary factions.
The first attempt: 28 days, with a possible extension
The first lawmaker entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to complete coalition negotiations and present a government.
The president may grant additional time, but extensions cannot exceed 14 days in total, giving the candidate a maximum of 42 days.
If the candidate fails, Herzog has two options. He can assign the task to another member of Knesset, potentially the leader of the opposing political bloc, or inform the Knesset speaker that he sees no prospect of forming a government.
A second candidate would receive 28 days to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
The last chance: 61 signatures in 21 days
If the president concludes that no candidate can form a government, or if the second candidate also fails, a final parliamentary mechanism comes into play.
A 21-day period opens during which at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a specific member of Knesset who has agreed to accept it.
If the required majority of lawmakers signs such a request, the designated candidate receives 14 days to form a government.
If that effort also fails, or no candidate secures the necessary 61 signatures within the allotted period, the Knesset is automatically dissolved and Israel heads to another election.
For now, the election may be over, but the political contest is far from settled. The coming weeks will determine whether the parties can negotiate a coalition capable of securing the Knesset's confidence or whether Israelis will once again be asked to return to the ballot box.

What Ceuta’s border crisis reveals about Frontex’s role in European security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:39:29 UTC
02:39:29 KST

A rare visit by Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia to Ceuta earlier this month has brought renewed attention to a migration crisis that continues to strain the Spanish territory on North Africa's Mediterranean coast, nearly three months after an unprecedented influx of migrants from Morocco.
Around 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta in late July, with humanitarian organisations estimating that at least 141 people died during the crossings.
Although most migrants have since left, thousands remained in the territory in October, many sleeping rough as local authorities struggled to provide shelter and essential services.
The royal visit, the first in nearly two decades, also came amid renewed tensions between Spain and Morocco, which maintains a longstanding sovereignty claim over Ceuta.
The crisis has exposed the pressures facing one of Europe's most sensitive external borders, where migration management still relies heavily on physical deterrence, cooperation with neighbouring countries, and emergency measures.
But Ceuta is neither an isolated incident nor an exception. It raises a broader question about the European Union's approach to border management: How does the bloc control its external frontiers, and who is accountable for the machinery behind them?
Part of the answer lies in the dramatic evolution of Frontex, the Warsaw-based European Border and Coast Guard Agency.
Over the past two decades, Frontex has evolved from an agency that primarily coordinates member states' border operations into a heavily funded institution with its own armed standing corps and expanding surveillance capabilities.
Yet, this technological militarisation has not delivered structural stability.
Its expanding use of aerial surveillance and cooperation with third-country authorities have also raised concerns about indirect pushbacks at sea and the division of legal responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Investigations into alleged pushbacks, oversight failures, and the agency's response to maritime emergencies have intensified scrutiny of whether Europe's expanding border security system is compatible with its fundamental rights obligations.
The rise of Frontex
As European integration deepened, migration and border management increasingly became matters of security policy.
The 1992 Maastricht Treaty marked an early step towards intergovernmental cooperation on migration, while the 1997 Amsterdam Treaty established the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice (AFSJ) as a central element of EU policy.
The 1999 Tampere European Council summit subsequently laid the foundations for the Common European Asylum System (CEAS).
Population movements following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the EU's eastward enlargement and the September 11, 2001 attacks further reinforced the association between migration, terrorism and border security.
Although a 2001 German-Italian proposal for a joint border police force stalled over concerns about national sovereignty, the 2003 Thessaloniki summit agreed to establish an operational mechanism to manage the EU's external borders.
The Council subsequently established Frontex under Regulation (EC) No 2007/2004, based on Articles 62 and 66 of the EC Treaty. Headquartered in Warsaw, the agency began operations on 1 May 2005.
Initially responsible for coordinating border operations among member states, conducting risk assessments and providing training, Frontex has gradually evolved into a large operational border force with armed personnel.
Its budget, approximately €6 million in 2005, has grown to more than €900 million annually, while successive regulatory changes, notably Regulation (EU) 2016/1624 and Regulation (EU) 2019/1896, have expanded its powers.
Under the 2019 regulation, Frontex aims to reach an operational capacity of 10,000 personnel by 2027, comprising 3,000 statutory Frontex staff and 7,000 personnel contributed by member states.
Equipped with uniforms, operational equipment and the authority to carry firearms under specified conditions, the standing corps represents a significant departure from the agency's original coordinating role.
Europe's expanding border security framework
The EU's increasingly security-oriented approach to migration was further reinforced by the adoption of the New Pact on Migration and Asylum in 2024.
The pact introduced a seven-day screening procedure at the EU's external borders, along with accelerated asylum and return procedures for certain applicants.
Under the framework, some asylum seekers may be treated as not having formally entered EU territory while their applications are processed, raising concerns about access to asylum procedures and legal safeguards.
The pact also expanded the Eurodac biometric database, lowering the minimum age for collecting fingerprints and facial images from 14 to six.
Its solidarity mechanism allows member states to contribute through relocation, financial payments or other forms of support, while the broader framework places greater emphasis on cooperation with third countries in managing migration.
Yet as Frontex's operational powers have expanded, questions have persisted over who bears responsibility when alleged rights violations occur.
The agency operates alongside national border authorities, creating a complex division of responsibilities between Frontex, host member states and other participating countries.
While national authorities retain responsibility for many operational decisions, Frontex provides personnel, surveillance capabilities and intelligence support.
Critics argue that this arrangement can complicate efforts to establish responsibility for alleged violations and make it more difficult for affected individuals to seek legal redress.
Pushbacks and the accountability question
Investigations by European oversight bodies and journalists have raised serious concerns about Frontex's involvement in unlawful pushbacks and how it handles evidence of alleged rights violations.
A European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) investigation found that then-executive director Fabrice Leggeri and senior agency officials were aware of illegal pushbacks carried out by the Greek Coast Guard in the Aegean Sea.
The investigation documented failures to report incidents and attempts to conceal evidence of alleged violations, including deleting records and diverting surveillance flights. It also raised concerns about interference with the agency's fundamental rights monitoring mechanisms.
Leggeri resigned in April 2022. The European Parliament subsequently refused to grant discharge for Frontex's 2020 budget, citing concerns over the agency's management and accountability.
Questions about Frontex's responsibilities also emerged following the Adriana shipwreck off the coast of Greece in June 2023, in which hundreds of migrants and asylum seekers died.
An investigation by the European Ombudsman found shortcomings in Frontex's response to maritime emergencies and raised questions about its ability to act independently when vessels are in distress.
The agency detected the overcrowded vessel by aerial surveillance before it sank, but the disaster exposed gaps in communication, coordination, and responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Such controversies have fuelled calls for greater oversight and, in some cases, the agency's dismantling.
The Abolish Frontex movement, a coalition of civil society organisations and activists across Europe, has campaigned to abolish the agency, citing alleged rights violations, biometric surveillance, and its role in enforcing restrictive border policies.
Frontex's growing reliance on aerial and satellite surveillance, alongside its maritime operations, has raised concerns that its border-monitoring practices could facilitate interceptions that circumvent international maritime law and search-and-rescue obligations.
Operating from bases in Malta and Pantelleria, unmanned aerial vehicles developed by Israel Aerospace Industries and Elbit Systems, alongside the EU's Copernicus satellite network, are used to detect migrant boats in the Mediterranean.
Critics argue that surveillance information can be shared with the Libyan Coast Guard or Tunisian authorities rather than civilian rescue organisations, enabling third-country forces to intercept migrants and return them to countries where they may face abuse.
Because such interceptions can occur without direct physical involvement by EU personnel, questions have emerged about whether Frontex is facilitating what critics describe as “refoulement by proxy”.
Human Rights Watch has accused Frontex of complicity in abuses against migrants intercepted and returned to Libya, raising concerns about the agency's responsibilities under the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face serious threats to their safety or fundamental rights.
The paradox of fortress Europe
Events along Ceuta’s perimeter and unmanned patrols tracing the central Mediterranean are two sides of the same coin.
On the periphery, frontline states rely on ad hoc physical barriers, bilateral appeasement of authoritarian transit regimes, and immediate pushbacks.
Meanwhile, at the institutional core in Brussels and Warsaw, billions of euros continue to pour into an autonomous surveillance and security architecture designed to insulate the European mainland from the human reality at its gates.
As Frontex marches toward its 2027 goal of a 10,000-strong armed standing corps under the codified framework of the 2024 New Pact on Migration and Asylum, the central paradox remains unresolved.
Advanced surveillance drones, automated biometric screening, and outsourced interception do not eliminate the root causes of forced displacement; they can instead shift difficult questions of legal responsibility into a fragmented jurisdictional space.
Unless subject to enforceable judicial oversight by the Court of Justice of the European Union, independent scrutiny by civil society, and uncompromising operational transparency, Frontex will remain what the Ceuta crisis so starkly laid bare: a multibillion-euro “security illusion” that continually undermines the foundational human rights norms upon which the European Union was built.

Syria: Flash floods kill four, collapse bridges, roads
At least four people, two of them children, have been killed after sustained heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in six provinces across Syria, local media and authorities reported on Thursday.
Heavy rain on Wednesday left at least three bridges out of service in the eastern province of Deir ez-Zor, while key roads have also been damaged.
The flooding has disrupted water supplies, while authorities shuttered schools in Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, and Hasakeh on Thursday amid the storms.
Hundreds of families have been forced to leave their homes and the displacement camps where they reside in recent days.
Emergency teams have evacuated at least 375 families from three displacement camps in Raqqa province and have rescued 15 people who were trapped in their vehicles, the state-run SANA news agency reported.
Hospitals, schools, and bakeries have been affected by the flooding while disaster management teams have warned people about the risk of drowning.
Rescue teams were sent to the village of Kasrat Surour after a drainage crossing collapsed and left over 100 families surrounded by floodwater.
The flooding has caused major disruptions to traffic, including on the Aleppo-Raqqa highway.
Syrian army helicopters have been deployed across the country to help those who have been stranded.
The flooding has had far-reaching impacts, with telecommunications disrupted in Deir ez-Zor due to damage caused to fibre optic cables on the Homs-Deir ez-Zor and Aleppo- Deir ez-Zor routes.
The minister of emergencies and disaster management, Raed al-Saleh, has urged residents in eastern governorates to remain in their homes unless absolutely necessary, and to steer away from low-lying areas.
He has also called on people to refrain from trying to cross flooded roads, which comes as rescue teams grapple to deal with the situation.
Syria has been battling thunderstorms, hail, and strong winds in recent weeks, with the meteorological directorate warning that the storms and lightning are set to continue.
Syria was last hit with flooding in May, affecting scores of farmers during harvest season and destroying important wheat, barley, cotton, and vegetable crops.
The flooding in Aleppo and Idlib affected over 19,000 people and damaged over 3,400 shelters.

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:37:16 EET
02:37:16 KST

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Kyiv • UNN
Stroke symptoms occur suddenly: call 103 or 112 immediately. In Ukraine, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are covered by the NHSU.
On October 29, the world observes World Stroke Day—a disease that can cause disability or death within minutes. Its first signs are sometimes mistaken for fatigue or stress, resulting in precious time being lost. UNN explains how to recognize the symptoms, help the affected person, and receive free treatment in Ukraine.
Details
The World Stroke Organization’s campaign in 2026 is being held under the slogan Every Minute Counts ("Every minute matters"). Its aim is to teach people to recognize the danger in time and call emergency services.
What a stroke is and why it occurs
A stroke is an acute disruption of cerebral blood circulation. Without sufficient oxygen, brain cells begin to die. Consequences may include impaired movement, speech, vision, memory, and coordination. An ischemic stroke occurs because a blood vessel is blocked by a clot and accounts for the majority of cases. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a vessel rupturing and bleeding. Treatment for these conditions differs, and it is impossible to determine the type based on external signs: urgent diagnosis using CT or MRI is required.
Contrary to everyday myths, a stroke does not occur only in older people. If a young person has problems with high blood pressure, heart disease, heart rhythm disorders, diabetes, or vascular damage, they are just as likely to suffer a stroke as older patients.
How many strokes are recorded in Ukraine and worldwide
According to WHO estimates, 11.9 million new strokes occurred worldwide in 2021. Approximately one in four adults is at risk of experiencing a stroke during their lifetime. In addition, stroke is one of the leading causes of death and disability both in Ukraine and in most countries worldwide.
According to the Ministry of Health, 128,075 Ukrainians were diagnosed with a stroke in 2024. A statement by the Kyiv Regional Military Administration dated October 29, 2026, says that more than 90,000 cases of acute stroke were treated in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year. In turn, Ministry of Health expert Professor Yuriy Flomin reported that 68,116 hospitalizations for acute stroke were recorded during the first half of 2026. The share of hospitalizations at facilities with a contract with the National Health Service of Ukraine increased from 86% in 2021 to 96.5% in the first half of 2026.
Speaking about strokes in Ukraine, it is worth emphasizing that, despite the war, access to specialized care for people suffering from this condition is improving. According to the data cited by Flomin, thrombolysis was used in 18% of hospitalizations for ischemic stroke during the first half of 2026, while mechanical thrombectomy was performed in 3.7%. CT, MRI, or angiographic examinations were recorded in 98.1% of hospitalizations for acute stroke.
How to recognize a stroke: five warning signs that should not be ignored
Signs of a stroke usually appear suddenly. Ukrainian doctors advise remembering them using the acronym MOZOK, where
-  M - speech. The person speaks unclearly, confuses words
or does not understand the other person; 
-  O - face. The corner of the mouth droops, and the smile becomes
asymmetrical; 
-  Z - dizziness. Balance and
coordination are impaired; sometimes a sudden, very severe headache occurs; 
-  O - eyes. Vision suddenly deteriorates, and objects appear double; 
-  K - limbs. An arm or leg becomes weak or numb,
more often on one side of the body. 
You can also ask a person suspected of having a stroke to smile, repeat a sentence, and raise both arms. Difficulty performing even one of these actions is a reason to call an ambulance immediately.
A severe headache, vomiting, or sudden drowsiness also requires attention, especially if it occurs simultaneously with other signs. Sometimes the symptoms disappear quickly. This may be a transient ischemic attack—a short-term disruption of blood flow to the brain that warns of the risk of a stroke. Even if the person feels better, emergency examination is necessary.
How to recognize a stroke: Ukrainians reminded of dangerous symptoms28.10.24, 15:57 • 13579 views
First aid for a stroke: what to do before medical professionals arrive
First of all, you should immediately call 103 or 112. The dispatcher needs to be told the address, the symptoms, and that a stroke is suspected. It is also important to remember when the person was last known to be well, as the choice of treatment depends on this.
Until the medics arrive, ensure that the person remains calm and loosen any tight clothing. If the patient is conscious, help them assume a comfortable position. If the person is unconscious but breathing normally, place them on their side. This is done to prevent stomach contents from entering the lungs if the patient begins to vomit. This position also reduces the risk of choking on their own saliva.
If normal breathing is absent, begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation according to the dispatcher’s instructions.
A person suspected of having a brain hemorrhage or thrombosis of the brain’s blood vessels must not be given water, medication, or food. Because of impaired swallowing, they may choke. Aspirin is particularly dangerous among medications. It can harm the person because it thins the blood. This is life-threatening in the case of a hemorrhagic stroke.
Before the medics arrive, prepare the person’s documents, a list of the medications the patient takes, and information about any comorbidities so that dispatch to the hospital is not delayed because of this.
How to receive free stroke treatment in Ukraine
Acute stroke care is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program at hospitals that have the relevant contract with the NHSU. In August 2026, the service reported that there were 179 such facilities.
Free services include an examination by a neurologist, a CT or MRI scan, tests, round-the-clock monitoring, medications, inpatient treatment, food, and early rehabilitation. When indicated, thrombolysis (dissolving a clot with medication), mechanical thrombectomy (removing a clot through the blood vessels), or neurosurgical intervention is performed. The treatment method depends on the type of stroke and when the symptoms began. Thrombolysis is possible only under certain conditions and within a limited time, and it is not used in cases of hemorrhage.
According to international recommendations, emergency neuroimaging should be performed as soon as possible. In Ukraine, the standard provides for aiming to perform a CT or MRI scan no later than 30 minutes after the patient is admitted. The NHSU emphasizes separately that patients should not have to pay for a CT or MRI when a stroke is suspected as part of inpatient care. You can clarify the list of facilities or complain about demands for payment by calling 16-77.
Who is at risk and how to prevent a stroke
The main risk factor in this situation is high blood pressure. It may cause no symptoms while gradually damaging the blood vessels. Smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, alcohol, and heart rhythm disorders are also dangerous.
To prevent stroke, the WHO recommends monitoring blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol; not stopping prescribed treatment; quitting smoking; limiting salt and alcohol; and eating more vegetables and fruit. At least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week is beneficial if there are no contraindications.
For heart rhythm disorders, a doctor may prescribe medications to prevent blood clots. However, taking such medications without medical supervision is dangerous.
Ukraine also has the "Health Screening 40+" program for the early detection of risks, while under the "Affordable Medicines" program, certain medications can be obtained free of charge or with a co-payment.
Life after a stroke: is recovery possible?
Although many strokes still end in the patient’s death at home or in hospital, many patients overcome this condition with the help of medical professionals and survive. However, the consequences of the illness may include impaired movement, speech, memory, or swallowing, as well as anxiety, fatigue, and depressive symptoms. Some patients require long-term—and sometimes lifelong—assistance from others. The prognosis depends on the severity of the stroke, the timeliness of treatment, and rehabilitation.
Rehabilitation begins as soon as the patient’s condition allows. A physical therapist, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and psychologist help restore movement, communication, and self-care. The process may take months and requires family support.
After discharge in Ukraine, a person may receive inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation, as indicated. At facilities that have a contract with the NHSU, it is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program. A doctor refers a patient for an inpatient course; transfer from another facility is also possible. The sessions are tailored to each individual: one person may need to learn to walk again, while another may need to restore swallowing or the ability to form words. It is important for relatives to help the person follow the specialists’ recommendations, but not to force them to do exercises beyond their capabilities.
To prevent a recurrent stroke, it is necessary to monitor blood pressure, glucose, and cholesterol and follow the doctor’s instructions. Unfortunately, a stroke cannot always be prevented. However, knowing the signs of a stroke according to the B.E.-F.A.S.T. formula, promptly calling 103, and managing risk factors can help save lives and reduce the likelihood of severe consequences.
Let us remind you
The Ministry of Health warns that recently more and more middle-aged people have been suffering strokes: as of 2019, more than 62% of stroke cases occurred in people under the age of 70.

Russia still hasn’t found an effective way to curb VPNs. Now officials are considering limits on all foreign internet traffic.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:36:19 UTC
02:36:19 KST

Russia still hasn’t found an effective way to curb VPNs. Now officials are considering limits on all foreign internet traffic.
What happened?
On October 27, Forbes reported that Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is considering routing all foreign internet traffic through TSPU filtering equipment (TSPU is the Russian acronym for “technical means of countering threats”), effectively separating the Russian internet from the global internet at a technical level.
The measure could primarily affect people who use VPN services to bypass blocks. The plan is to cap the amount of foreign data each user can consume. The proposed limit is not yet known.
Several sources told Forbes about the proposals, which will likely be included in a bill to overhaul the telecommunications industry. The authorities have been preparing changes to telecommunications laws since the spring and are discussing specific proposals with major industry players. The Digital Development Ministry stressed that all the proposed measures “are being examined, but it is premature to say which will make it into the final amendments or in what form.”
Haven’t there been proposals like this before?
Not quite. First, in the spring, the Digital Development Ministry wanted to limit foreign traffic only on mobile networks. Now, the proposal apparently also covers home internet connections.
Second, the earlier plan called for telecommunications providers themselves to identify and limit foreign traffic. The ministry asked them to charge users extra if they used more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data a month. BBC News Russian reported that each additional gigabyte would have cost 150 rubles. Now, the ministry plans to impose the restrictions itself using TSPU equipment.
What would the authorities gain from this?
The Digital Development Ministry intends to use this approach to combat VPNs that allow users to bypass Russian internet blocks. These services are generally based abroad, as are most of their servers. So when users connect to one of these VPNs, all their traffic becomes foreign traffic, even when they visit Russian websites.
VPN services could try to rent servers inside Russia to get around the data cap. But this summer, the authorities banned Russian hosting providers from serving them.
There are also plans to create a register of violators who have used servers in Russia to run VPNs. If caught bypassing blocks, they will be barred from signing contracts with hosting providers in Russia for a full year. In other words, using Russian hosting infrastructure will become even harder in the future.
But for now, too much about the proposal remains unknown, Sarkis Darbinyan, a digital rights lawyer and expert at RKS.global, told Meduza:
It’s unclear what exactly the ministry will consider a foreign domain, whether there will be exemption allowlists, and what will happen once the quota runs out: disconnection, slower speeds, or an extra charge. These details will determine whether the measure specifically targets VPNs or affects everyone.
How does the ministry plan to identify foreign traffic?
We don’t know. Most likely, by IP address. Since 2019, Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, has required Russian holders of autonomous system numbers, which identify networks, to report their network addresses and notify the agency of any changes within three business days. Roskomnadzor can use those addresses to determine whether a given data packet came from Russia or abroad.
But under this approach, even people who don’t use VPNs could find that some traffic from Russian websites is technically classified as foreign. Much depends on whether individual components of a webpage — fonts, images, or videos — load from foreign sources and exactly how the data is routed. Even traffic from a site with an IP address registered in Russia can pass through nodes abroad. This could happen, for example, because of the particular terms of traffic-exchange agreements between telecommunications providers or because traffic takes alternative routes during network outages.
How would TSPU equipment limit an individual user’s foreign traffic?
We don’t know this for certain, either. The difficulty is that TSPU equipment filters data packets that don’t explicitly identify the user they belong to. Only the source and destination IP addresses are visible. That information is not enough to limit a particular person’s foreign traffic: Different subscribers can use the same IP address at different times.
Telecommunications providers, however, have the missing information. In the spring of 2025, they were required to give Roskomnadzor comprehensive information about their subscribers, including their assigned IP addresses and the number identifying the specific TSPU device through which each user’s traffic passes.
Since December 2025, telecommunications providers have been subject to fines of 300,000 to 500,000 rubles for each failure to provide this information.
If the ministry’s proposal is adopted, how will it affect ordinary Russians?
For now, we can only speculate. But requiring all foreign traffic to pass through a filter that tracks quotas would clearly make it easier to slow and ration that traffic. This would be another major step in the authorities’ campaign against independent VPNs, and users of those services would be hit hardest, Darbinyan said. Besides finding a working VPN, they would have to decide how best to use their allotted gigabytes of foreign data, choosing between videos, games, social media, and other sites and services unavailable in Russia.
Darbinyan said there could be several other consequences:
- There will be problems with updates. Updates for iOS, Windows, and games can run to tens of gigabytes. A single file could eat up a month’s allowance. “And then,” Darbinyan said, “if you can’t afford an extra international data package, you’re stuck without up-to-date software.” That creates an additional risk: Devices without updates are more vulnerable to scammers and malware, both of which are proliferating with the AI boom.
- Developers, IT workers, and remote workers will suffer. Using GitHub, Docker Hub, cloud services, Zoom, and Microsoft 365, or working with foreign clients, means using lots of foreign data. “For freelancers, students taking international online courses, and scientists, the restrictions will become an obstacle to their work. Online gaming will probably become a pastime only for the wealthy, who can afford to pay for extra gigabytes, since gaming requires enormous amounts of data,” Darbinyan told Meduza.
Still, Darbinyan believes the authorities are unlikely to impose a strict, very low cap on everyone at once:
Technically, it’s very difficult, and politically, it’s costly — because it would upset users opposed to the government as well as businesses, the IT industry, and gamers. Most likely, they’ll start with mobile networks, a generous cap, and extensive allowlists, then gradually tighten the restrictions.
This measure is also unlikely to make foreign services disappear entirely. The aim, apparently, is to make access to foreign services inconvenient, slow, and expensive so that people switch to Russian alternatives on their own, rather than to cut off access to everything abroad.
