Polls do not dictate the winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

Amid the fervor of an election campaign, many treat poll results like a report card, scrutinizing every percentage-point change and growing anxious or panicking when numbers fluctuate. Some notice wide discrepancies between polls conducted by different organizations and question whether the methodology is flawed or the figures have been manipulated.
However, all of this is unnecessary. Polls are, after all, merely sample surveys — the real winner would ultimately be determined by each vote cast on election day.
In the past few years, polling has faced a fundamental problem: Few people answer landline calls, and many no longer have landlines at all. Yet local election polls often rely on landline numbers to identify a respondent’s location and confirm whether they live within the electoral district, which leads to insufficient coverage. That makes sampling impossible.
Even among those who still have landlines and are willing to answer, figuring out how to weigh their responses to accurately reflect the views of an entire electorate has become a major challenge for pollsters.
Imagine that only one person in a particular age group answers the phone. If that person’s views are weighted to represent the entire age group, any difference between their opinion and that of other voters could cause a dramatic shift in the overall results of the poll.
That is why polls should be taken with a grain of salt. There is no need to be discouraged by polls, and those who are in the lead certainly should not become complacent. Polls do not decide elections — votes do.
With less than one month until election day, candidates should not get carried away or disheartened by poll results. To achieve victory, they should make the most of the remaining time, work pragmatically to win votes and ensure that every vote is counted.
Some voters fixate on the polls while others dismiss the results as an illusion; some rush to interpret the numbers and others get into arguments or demand that the campaign teams of the candidate they support respond in specific ways.
As others descend into chaos, we should stay calm, take time to reflect on our chosen candidate’s strengths and think carefully about how to communicate those strengths to our friends and family — and even those we have only just met. We should engage with them sincerely, explaining why they need to vote and why they should vote for the candidate we are supporting.
One of the most important reasons for this is that China is always closely watching Taiwan’s elections. Election results reflect public sentiment and morale in Taiwan.
In Taipei, for example, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) — who advocates for resilience — would deal a serious blow to China’s will to wage war.
That is because China can only afford — and wants — a quick and decisive victory; otherwise, it risks the collapse of its regime. The more Taiwanese demonstrate their resilience and determination to resist, the more carefully China must weigh its options before acting and the less likely it is to launch a war.
While some candidates scramble to cover up their deeply flawed public image, dismiss unfavorable polls as illusions and spend their days cooped up at home “analyzing” poll results, we should put the polls aside for now. Whether the numbers favor us or not, the election outcome would be determined by actions.
There is no need to get emotional over poll numbers; instead, we must focus on steadily winning one, two or even 10 more votes each day. When the day’s work is done and you go to sleep, you can feel at peace knowing you have met your goal.
Each person’s small efforts, day after day, all add up to something much greater. The victory that ultimately matters most is the one achieved on election day.
Tommy Lin is chairman of the Formosa Republican Association and director of the Taiwan United Nations Alliance.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Daniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks.
“I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says.
By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing.
Photo: AP
“I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape,” she says.
In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realized she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodeling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.
“I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says.
The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure.
But after the consultation, she decided to trust her surgeon. Cesin had already paid for flights and taken three weeks off from her job as a sales director. The next day she was anesthetized, and her surgeon used an ultrasound to locate the ribs, made six small incisions in her back, and inserted a vibrating tool to create greenstick fractures — an incomplete bone break — on each rib. When she came to she was wearing a black corset with small knobs on each side that she could tighten to her preferred measurements.
The recovery has been uncomfortable. It was initially hard to stand or lie down without help, and there was soreness from the incisions. The first week, Cesin barely slept.
“Your body doesn’t get used to any position, so every hour I would wake up.”
But the worst part has been eating while wearing her corset, which must remain on for 23 hours a day; this causes acid reflux. Despite her discomfort, when we speak six weeks after her surgery, she is pleased with the eight centimeters she has shaved off her waist.
Cesin is one of a small but growing number of women choosing to fracture their ribs for an hourglass shape. To achieve this look, women previously underwent riskier rib removal techniques, which reduce the protective bone barrier for the liver and spleen.
Kazbek Kudzaev, a plastic surgeon in Russia, realized in 2017 that he could achieve similar aesthetic results when he moved the ribs with a drill until one side fractured, then bound the body in a corset while they healed. Since his discovery, surgeons in countries including Colombia, South Korea and France have refined the technique. Today, it takes about an hour and is performed under general anesthesia as a day-surgery treatment.
NON-INVASIVE PROCEDURE?
It is touted as a noninvasive procedure, but many of the women I interviewed described feeling as if they had been “hit by a bus” after surgery. And there are serious risks. These include standard surgical complications, such as allergic reactions to the anesthesia, blood clots, wound infections and seromas (pockets of fluid that build up under the skin). But also more specific dangers, including a collapsed lung, known as a pneumothorax; and a haemothorax, where blood collects in the space between the chest wall and the lungs. Both of these are potentially fatal.
Sandip Hindocha, a consultant plastic surgeon at the Private Clinic on Harley Street in London, is skeptical about the procedure.
“If a patient came to my clinic and said this is what I want to do, I’d be asking the question: ‘Why do you want to do that? And why do you want to make such a permanent change to your body?’”
He references a paper published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, which states that between 2018 and 2024, out of 2,351 patients who had rib remodeling, there was an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent.
“That’s not a small number,” he says. “If we did a breast augmentation, you wouldn’t expect a complication rate like that.”
The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), doesn’t endorse the procedure. Former president Nora Nugent points out that it is relatively new, “with limited data available on long-term results and it requires advanced body contouring skills as well as the ability to treat any potential complications. It may be something that UK/BAAPS plastic surgeons bring into their practices in due course but it is not available at the moment.”
The procedure isn’t typically offered to cisgender women over the age of 40, because of the increased chance of them having osteoporosis, which can cause the bones to fully break rather than fracture. Another complication for patients is that gaining weight can cause your body to change shape again, so pregnancy can affect the results. The procedure “needs to be done with a surgeon who has a lot of experience in it,” says Hindocha. “Maybe a surgeon that also does chest wall reconstruction.”
In the UK, plastic surgeons are advised to give patients a cooling-off period of at least two weeks to weigh up the risks and potential consequences of having any procedure. But Hindocha worries that patients are sometimes opting for rib remodeling with less time for reflection, despite the permanence of the change.
“If you put an implant in and later you don’t want it, you can, worst case scenario, remove it,” Hindocha says. Whereas the ribs are “a structural, rigid part of you that you cannot reverse.”
WAISTLINES THROUGHOUT HISTORY
Throughout history, waistlines have expanded and shrunk. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing and tight-lacing became a symbol of beauty for the “leisure class” (the restrictive garments made physical labor impossible). The engineered hourglass shape fell out of fashion in the 1920s, but made a comeback with Marilyn Monroe, before slender, androgynous frames gained popularity from the 60s to the 90s. In the 2010s, the extreme curves of the Kardashians became the defining silhouette.
In recent years, tinier, waif-like frames have become popular on TikTok and Instagram, but a highly defined waist is also considered desirable. This is thanks, among other things, to the multibillion-dollar shapewear industry; global access to Instagram and filters; and easily streamed online workout videos that focus on creating a slim, hourglass silhouette through targeted training. But now there are adverts on social media for permanent surgical options too.
In July, 10 Australian influencers, who have made names for themselves globally on shows including Married at First Sight and Below Deck, prompted headlines with a trip to Bali. They were there for a brand collaboration with a rib recontouring practice called Snatched Waist. The clinic they visited looked more like a spa than a surgeon’s office and, post-surgery, the influencers were soon lounging by the pool, showing off their narrow waists on Instagram.
Not everyone is sunbathing in a bikini after the procedure. When Sophia woke up from her rib remodeling procedure in November last year, she expected to be transferred to her Beverly Hills hotel room, a little sore but ready for recovery. Instead, she was surrounded by emergency medical technicians, who were putting her on to a stretcher to take her to hospital by ambulance. The next thing she remembers is lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to an electrocardiogram and an intravenous drip.
A CT scan showed Sophia had suffered a pneumothorax: 25 percent of one of her lungs had collapsed. She was put on oxygen and monitored for six hours before being released. Although she had signed all the consent forms for the procedure, “it was completely shocking to me,” she says.
For at least a month, Sophia had a deep pain in her lung and some shortness of breath. She had to return to the hospital after some fluid build up, but eventually started feeling better. The pain from the surgery itself subsided after about three weeks: coughing and sneezing was no longer agonizing. And she was able to return to her office job and hike in her corset at the weekends.
Sophia is transgender and chose the procedure to feminize her body, by narrowing her torso, which she felt was too wide. She began consultations for the procedure in August last year, with the surgeon planning to fracture ribs 10, 11 and 12. But by the time of her surgery in November, the surgeon felt confident he could achieve better results by going even further up the ribcage, ultimately operating on five ribs on each side. Sophia knew this would increase her risk of a pneumothorax, but was willing to take the chance.
“I didn’t start transitioning until I was 47 and I feel as if I’m playing catch up, because I’m so old, and testosterone was running rampant all those decades,” she says. “That’s why gender-affirming procedures are really important to me.”
’IT WAS A BIT UNDERWHELMING’
The final results weren’t what she had hoped for though. “It was a bit underwhelming.”
Last month, she went for a second round of rib remodeling with Leif Rogers, a different surgeon in Pasadena and Beverly Hills, California. Rogers removed cartilage from the anterior side of her ribcage on ribs three to 10. On rib four, he cut sections out and secured them with titanium plates and screws. Sophia had a breast augmentation at the same time, as the inframammary incisions were already open. When she e-mails to update me a week and a half after her second surgery, although there has been no collapsed lung this time, she says: “Recovery has been significantly more painful, and I am experiencing more shortness of breath.”
Despite the risks, Rogers expects skeletal remodeling to take off: that includes rib remodeling, clavicle shortening and pelvic widening.
“Versions of it have existed for quite some time,” he says. “Limb lengthening and shortening has been around for a long time. Of course, we change the bony skeleton of the face all the time, but other than that we haven’t changed the torso very much. The changing of the skeleton of the body is a little bit newer, as for a long time people used to just put their hands up and say: ‘Too bad, this is the way you’re built.’”
So why now?
“The techniques have got way better. And there’s marketing for it out there.”
In the US, he says, medical insurance often covers the procedure for transgender patients, “because they consider it a medical condition to have gender dysphoria. And I think on top of that, it’s just social media. Social media makes everything explode.”
Rogers says the Kardashians have been highly influential.
“I think Kim was part of why we wanted a big butt, and then she lost a lot of weight, so everyone wants to be like Kim, right?”
In 2022, Kim Kardashian attended the Met Gala after losing a considerable amount of weight, in a sparkling dress once worn by Monroe. Her slender figure coincided with a growing movement towards thinness, a rejection of the body positivity movement of the 2010s, and the advent of the Ozempic era, when the diabetes drug became popular as a weight-loss treatment. A controversial 2022 New York Post article was headlined: “Bye-bye booty: Heroin chic is back.” On TikTok, people had begun measuring their waists using A4 sheets of paper, phones and Apple headphone wires, showing off their Barbie-like proportions.
“We have always done very demanding things for beauty,” says Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and author of the 2018 book Perfect Me, who mentions foot binding and extreme corsetry. “But they were always about adornment. I think what’s different with the global ideal now is that increasingly things are becoming normalized and naturalized. We’re seeing things that are purely about adornment being recategorized as health and hygiene, and then they become invisible, and if you don’t do them you start to look abnormal,” she says. “It becomes about standard presentation.”
As we move from a text-based culture to a visual culture, increasingly, “who we are is how we look,” she says, “and that is a form of identity that is a massive and dramatic change, but one that’s snuck up on us, that we don’t talk about enough. So the visual is becoming the dominant way of presenting ourselves, being ourselves and thinking about ourselves.”

Pakistan reverses Taiwanese airlines ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

The first Taiwanese commercial aircraft since restrictions were lifted flew over Pakistan yesterday morning following an abrupt U-turn by authorities to approve permits that were briefly revoked due to Islamabad’s “one China” policy.
EVA Airways (長榮航空) Flight 65 from Taipei to Vienna entered Pakistani airspace at about 3:30am local time, Flightradar24 tracking data showed.
All other Europe-bound EVA Air and China Airlines (華航) flights that departed late on Wednesday night into early yesterday morning opted to use Russian airspace, or go via India.
Photo: EPA
The airlines had been forced to detour, including flying over Russia, since Sunday, after Pakistan shut its airspace to Taiwanese carriers, citing support of Beijing’s “one China” policy.
However, just hours after Bloomberg News reported the move, Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority hastily renewed the permits for the Taiwanese carriers.
They would now be allowed to fly through Pakistani airspace until March 27 next year, documents dated on Wednesday showed.
EVA Air declined to comment, while China Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
No country had previously said it would deny all Taiwanese carriers use of airspace.
Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) yesterday said that the Cabinet “deeply regretted” Pakistan’s brief closure of its airspace to Taiwanese airlines.
“We deeply regret Pakistan’s behavior, including pandering to China by compromising flight safety, disregarding international rules and reality, undermining our national sovereignty, and politicizing and weaponizing airspace,” Lee said when asked about the issue at a Cabinet news conference.
“The Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign country. It and China are not subordinate to each other. This is an undeniable, objective fact and the status quo in the Taiwan Strait,” she said.
A Ministry of Transportation and Communications official said that the access period coincided with the International Air Transport Association’s winter schedule, and that an application for continued access would be filed for the summer schedule that follows.
The ministry would remain in close contact with the airlines about any changes in airspace access, the official said.
“We suspect China [was] behind this,” Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) told Bloomberg Television.
“China Airlines and EVA received a notice from the Pakistan authorities that they will lift the ban, but only temporarily ... until the end of the winter,” Chen said.
“We condemn Pakistan, and if China is behind this, I think that is a very bad practice to use its leverage over the countries in the global south to do that,” he said. “I think that gets in the way of the safety of the passengers and the smooth operation of the global supply chain.”
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) told reporters that “as far as we are aware, there are no obstacles for residents of the Taiwan region to travel internationally.”
In April, the Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permits for President William Lai’s (賴清德) flight to Eswatini, forcing him to postpone the trip.
At the time, Taiwan blamed “intense pressure” from China for the revocation.
“China now learned that this could be an effective way to block our airspace access and therefore sort of further isolate Taiwan,” Chen said. “We see this is the discovery that they can weaponize the airspace assets.”
Many like-minded countries had assisted Taiwan over the airspace closure, he said.
“We are afraid that this might be a practice that spreads to other global south countries,” he said. “I think that is a major concern for not only for Taiwan, but also for other countries in the region and beyond.”

AI rise could fuel China invasion threat: Palantir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

Palantir Technologies Inc’s head of defense Mike Gallagher on Wednesday warned that advances in artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities have made it more compelling for Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to seize control of Taiwan.
Gallagher, a former Republican member of the US Congress who led a House of Representatives committee focused on US strategic competition with China, said that Taiwan’s importance to AI development has grown to the point that Xi might need to act on Beijing’s designs toward the nation — especially in light of the competition between the US and China to dominate the technology.
“The logic of Xi Jinping sacrificing enormously to take Taiwan is getting more compelling,” Gallagher said at a defense policy event in Indiana with US Senator Jim Banks.
Photo: Bloomberg
Chinese embassy in Washington spokesman Liu Chang (劉暢) said in a statement later on Wednesday that Beijing “brooks no external interference” and suggested the US “act prudently” on Taiwan.
“The Taiwan question is China’s internal affair,” he said. “Stronger cooperation between enterprises on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in semiconductors and other fields is the right path toward mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.”
As Taiwan is the home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), it makes it a chokepoint that China could exploit to halt US progress in AI technology if authorities in Beijing found the US was gaining too much of a lead, Gallagher said.
“If China takes Taiwan, they will control TSMC or disable TSMC — they will have the ability to hold the rest of the world economically hostage,” said Gallagher, who left Congress in early 2024 and joined Palantir later that year.
While some prominent US officials have previously warned that China was seeking the capability to invade Taiwan by next year, the US has backed away from that projection, including in March with an intelligence assessment that concluded an invasion “would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure.”
Even so, China has stepped up patrols by its coast guard off Taiwan’s east coast, highlighting the risk that a blockade would pose to global supply chains in the event of a Chinese invasion.
The patrols add to the regular military drills conducted by Chinese forces in the region.
Palantir plays a critical role in the US military as a key provider of technology for the Pentagon, including its Maven Smart System, which uses AI for surveillance and targeting.
During his remarks, Gallagher said that companies in Silicon Valley have increasingly talked about the inflection point where AI models begin to improve themselves, calling it the kind of super intelligence that could get China’s attention, characterizing it as being on par with the development of nuclear weapons.
“If that is true, that we’re at an inflection point, and this technology is a game changer on par with the advent of nuclear weapons in the 1940s,” he said.

Samsung raises spending to 60% after AI chips sell out

16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

Samsung Electronics Co plans to increase spending more than 60 percent this year after selling out of high-end chips for next year, yet its stock fell after the company failed to outline plans to share ballooning profits.
The world’s largest maker of memory chips expects capital expenditure to jump to 84.4 trillion won (US$63.1 billion) this year, targeting market share from SK Hynix Inc. and Micron Technology Inc.
However, chip-division operating income fell about 2 percent shy of estimates and the company withheld plans for future shareholder payouts until January.
Photo: Bloomberg
While Samsung’s semiconductor profits surged 15-fold — reflecting a severe shortage of storage for servers and smartphones — investors had expected more after SK Hynix soundly beat expectations a day prior. Samsung let the market down after its smaller rival announced total new payouts of US$45 billion.
Longer-term, the world’s biggest memory maker is trying to mobilize its financial resources to catch up in securing lucrative long-term contracts, particularly for the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) essential for Nvidia Corp’s accelerators.
Samsung sees the next-generation of such advanced chips — to work with Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform — as a once-in-a-decade chance to catch up to SK Hynix.
“Samsung is also lifting capex by around 60 percent this year, so until it spells out how this windfall gets split between new capacity and shareholders, there’s a genuine question mark over how much actually comes back to investors,” eToro lead analyst for Asia Pacific Josh Gilbert said. “That turns January into a must-deliver moment.”
Samsung yesterday reported that group-wide net income also missed estimates.
While earnings are bounding ahead, the shortfall versus expectations coincides with growing doubts about the extent and durability of the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom, as well as Samsung’s ability to sustain higher margins.
The company has secured 10 long-term supply agreements with key customers, executives said.
However, while SK Hynix said its HBM was sold out through 2029, Samsung said its HBM was sold out only through next year.
Appetite for AI linchpins like Samsung and SK Hynix had waned in the past few weeks after a series of setbacks for neoclouds like CoreWeave Inc, specialist developers of AI data centers.
While hyperscalers including Meta Platforms Inc and Amazon.com Inc are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into infrastructure, questions persist over whether and when those investments would generate sufficient returns to justify the spending.
Samsung needs to demonstrate progress in advanced memory such as HBM4, where competition with SK Hynix remains intense. Samsung tripled HBM4 sales in the third quarter over the prior three months, and said it plans to start mass production of the next-generation HBM4e in the first half of 2027.
Samsung Electronics’ sales and operating profit could rise sharply this quarter, as the company expects DRAM and NAND bit demand to rise more than 15 percent sequentially, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Masahiro Wakasugi said.

Samsung also announced additional shareholder returns for this year.

‘Spogomi’ sport to come to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

The Ministry of Environment and the Nippon Foundation Spogomi Federation yesterday agreed to introduce the litter collection sport “Spogomi” to Taiwan.
The agreement was signed by federation president Max Tamazawa and Rotary International District 3522 director Lung Ming-tao (龍明道) at a news conference held at the ministry.
Tamazawa said Spogomi is an innovative sport combining athletics with environmental protection, created by federation executive director Kenichi Mamitsuka in 2008.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
It incorporates exercises into litter collection, under the philosophy that cities and the ocean would become cleaner as Spogomi contests are held, he said.
As about 80 percent of marine debris comes from land, removing garbage from urban environments help prevent waste from flowing into the sea, Tamazawa said, adding that that is an important issue for Taiwan and Japan given that both are surrounded by waters.
People of any age, gender and nationality can participate in Spogomi, he added.
The sport is expected to help people see environmental issues as personal problems and opportunities to take action, he said.
The first Spogomi World Cup was held in Tokyo in 2023, Tamazawa said, adding that the federation was established in April last year to further promote the sport.
Spogomi World Cup contestants played in teams of three and collected litter in a designed area — which was announced on the day of the contest — within 1.5 hours, he said.
Scores were calculated based on the types and weight of the collected garbage, Tamazawa said.
Spogomi is not just about collecting as much litter as possible, he said, adding that team strategy and teamwork spirit matter more.
Taiwan’s participation is expected to help expand the sport’s influence, and promote international cooperation and exchanges in environmental protection, Tamazawa said.
He also thanked the ministry and Rotary International for helping to promote Spogomi.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said he expects Spogomi events to be held nationwide over the next year.
A Spogomi Team Taiwan would be selected through national tryouts for the Spogomi World Cup in Japan in October next year, he said.
“The goal is to shape Taiwan’s environmental actions into a fresh force driving international exchanges,” Peng said.
Spogomi combines the English word “sport” and the Japanese word “gomi,” which means “rubbish.”

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:40 UTC
01:42:40 KST

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the US for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40 percent since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20 percent over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out US$2.4 trillion from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
Photo: EPA
AI stocks account for over 40 percent of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60 billion yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy — including technology — meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group.
She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centers. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics — also known as embodied AI — as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” Wang said.
Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from Dec. 1, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as US$100 billion.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping (習近平), China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilizing policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk,” Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:40 UTC
01:42:40 KST

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned on Sunday after nearly a year away, would walk a tightrope as she seeks the elections her supporters want without running afoul of a US-backed negotiation process between the interim government and other opposition groups.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Washington has said she has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised Acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that does not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
The talks, which have continued this month, would remake the electoral council and top court ahead of eventual elections. Both bodies are staffed by ruling party loyalists and backed ousted president Nicolas Maduro in a disputed 2024 presidential election, despite tallies published by Machado’s movement that showed her candidate had won. The US military captured Maduro in January.
Illustration: Mountain People
Machado supporters, tens of thousands of whom swarmed her caravan between Barquisimeto and Caracas on Sunday, waving flags, chanting her name and festooning her with rosaries, are eager for elections and call her the next president. She has said a presidential vote should happen next year.
Machado’s team did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked whether Machado would participate in the negotiations, Rodriguez said she hoped the dialogue would lead those who called for sanctions against the country — a common ruling party critique leveled at Machado — to feel remorse. Rodriguez added that the talks offer a chance for all voices to be heard.
“I hope both the dialogue and the program for democratic coexistence and peace can provide a space where all voices can be heard, where voices seeking the good of the country can be heard,” the acting president said during a visit to a military hospital in Caracas, where she urged politicians to concentrate on serious issues and not put on a “show.”
Although Machado cultivated Trump as an ally for years, he said last month it was too soon to consider democratic elections. On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of her return plans, although a person briefed on her movements disputed that.
Machado’s eagerness for a vote could “short-circuit” the relationship with the US and its three-phase stabilization, recovery and transition plan for Venezuela, political risk consultancy Pder y Estrategia head Ricardo Rios said.
“The idea [at the negotiations] is to hold a regional election before a presidential election. She will probably push for electoral guarantees and for a presidential election to be held as soon as possible,” Rios said.
However, much remains to be defined before voters cast ballots.
“What guarantees does the ruling sector have to leave power [if it is defeated],” Rios asked. “That still needs to be defined in order to make this viable, because otherwise, no matter how popular she is, it complicates matters.”
Machado’s safe return was a direct outcome of the negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a longtime champion of Machado, said on Sunday, adding he expects all political actors to support the talks.
Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held, he told reporters on Monday. He did not provide an estimated date for elections.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” Rubio said. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
The EU echoed that sentiment, saying on Monday authorities and all political actors should advance “an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue towards free and fair elections.”
The negotiations would lead to a top court being in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US Department of State official said earlier.
“The reception [Machado] got yesterday will only reinforce the tendency to demand instant results,” International Crisis Group senior analyst for the Andes region Phil Gunson said. “Not only might that provoke a reaction from government hardliners, but it could — if successful — produce a political rupture instead of a peaceful transition, with inadequate post-electoral guarantees and a potentially ungovernable country.”
The opposition included in the talks, led by Dinorah Figuera, a lawmaker elected in 2015 to the last Venezuelan legislative body recognized by the US, said Machado’s return was a significant step in the US plan.
“Her role is also tied to how she interprets the signals from the US, which has called for reconstruction and reconciliation. She has to be an ally in the negotiations,” ORC Consultores managing director Oswaldo Ramirez said.
“Rubio sent a clear message,” he added. “I don’t see her trying to torpedo the negotiations. She can’t stray outside the lines.”

The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Again, that’s no disrespect to any of them. That’s the last thing I want to do, but today I feel like I’m the best catcher in the world.”
Contreras became the eighth catcher voted the World Series Most Valuable Player (MVP) after lifting the Milwaukee Brewers to their first World Series championship.
Photo: AFP Warning: Excessive consumption of alcohol can damage your health
Leader of the small-market Brewers, the 28-year-old hit .381 while guiding his pitching staff, throwing out four attempted base stealers and winning 10 of 13 appeals in the first Series with the Automated Ball-Strike challenge system. He had a run-scoring double during Milwaukee’s clinching 4-1 victory in Game 5 on Wednesday night.
“He’s our pit bull. You don’t just walk up and pet him. There’s a chance you get nipped,” manager Pat Murphy said.

“My brother is my role model. I don’t have a lot of friends. He’s my friend,” William Contreras said. “If I have something to ask somebody, I ask Willson.”
William Contreras teared up when asked about Venezuela, his home country. He was on Venezuela’s team that won its first World Baseball Classic (WBC) in March, although he was 0 for 13 with no RBIs.
He and teammates Jackson Chourio and Antonio Senzatela joined Americans Alex Bregman and Luke Gregerson of the 2017 Houston Astros in winning the WBC and World Series in the same year.
“It means everything because that’s the first time Venezuela guys win the WBC and the World Series,” William Contreras said. “It’s history, history for my country. I love Venezuela. It’s my country.”
He joined Gene Tenace (1972), Johnny Bench (1976), Steve Yeager (cowinner in 1981), Darrell Porter (1982), Rick Dempsey (1983), Pat Borders (1992) and Salvador Perez (2015) as catchers to win the award.

“Think about what he’s achieved, and he’s disappointed his numbers aren’t better,” Murphy said. “He’s disappointed that he isn’t Gold Glove.”
Contreras was best at leveraging baseball’s robot umpires, leading MLB with 185 challenges and 105 overturns during the regular season. He won 22 of 33 in the post-season.
“It’s not magic,” Contreras said. “I think it’s the experience of playing every day throughout the season.”
He batted .444 with a pair of solo homers in the Division Series against the San Diego Padres, hitting a tiebreaking, seventh-inning drive in the opener and another homer in Game 3. He batted .357 with one homer and three RBIs in the Championship Series sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
“I told him before the game: You will be the MVP of the World Series,” Murphy said. “People recognized what that kid did for us. There was no doubt in my mind. Yeah, he’s special.”

While this plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
Photo: Reuters
Final results were expected soon after about 500,000 absentee ballots are counted from military personnel, diplomats, people in prisons and hospitals, and others.

One of the Arab parties, the Joint List, late on Wednesday said that there was an “unprecedented show of strength” and the Jewish voters “willing to swim against the tide of racism.”
It said it was open to political cooperation.
Netanyahu’s Likud party, despite receiving the most votes, has accused the Arab-led parties of stealing the election and asked the election committee to investigate.
The election committee has said the number of reported irregularities in the election was low.
Israel’s president next week is to task someone to form the next government.
It has traditionally been the leader of the party with the most votes, but that is not required.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year.
On Wednesday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog signaled that he wanted to avoid that step — something Eisenkot has said as well.

Taiwan is stepping up efforts to issue details and maps depicting locations where Chinese warships and coast guard vessels operate.
“We are staying vigilant about their activities,” Wu said. “The simultaneous threat to Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines is obvious.”
Photo from National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu’s X page
The remarks accompanied a map he posted on X showing the locations of 53 ships, 34 of them navy warships, including the aircraft carrier Liaoning.
The carrier and its accompanying battle group were positioned to the east of the Philippines, with other formations off Taiwan’s east and southeast, along with three off the southern coast of Japan, the map showed.
Wu published a similar map on X in May.
The defense ministries of China, the Philippines and Japan did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Wednesday, Japan’s Ministry of Defense said it had tracked three Chinese warships and a coast guard ship a day earlier as they passed through the narrow Osumi Strait off Kyushu Island and into the Pacific.
This month, China’s Ministry of National Defense said the Liaoning was engaged in a routine training exercise not directed at any specific country.
China’s ties with Japan and the Philippines have tanked in the past few months. It has been upset by Japanese support for Taiwan, while embroiled in an increasingly bitter standoff with Manila in the South China Sea.

Warship activity signals Beijing ambitions: analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

Recent Chinese naval activity beyond the First Island Chain reflects the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) ability to conduct coordinated operations across the western Pacific and signals Beijing’s strategic ambitions, analysts said yesterday.
The assessment follows reports of Chinese naval movements stretching from southern Japan to Taiwan and the Philippines, reported separately by National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) and by Japan’s Joint Staff Office.
Lin Ying-yu (林穎佑), an associate professor at Tamkang University’s Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies, said the PLA had integrated naval forces from its northern, eastern and southern theater commands.
Photo: AFP
Its naval operations should be viewed not as separate activities by individual theater commands, but as part of a broader “First Island Chain theater,” with interconnected vessel movements reflecting an overall operational plan for the First Island Chain, he said.
Citing information from Japan’s Joint Staff Office, Lin said the Liaoning aircraft carrier strike group passed through the Miyako Strait and sailed east of Taiwan toward the Philippine Sea.
The movement indicated that China’s focus remained on the South China Sea, where Beijing was using a form of “gunboat diplomacy” to pressure Manila, Lin said.
Lin said the attention on China’s aircraft carrier should not overshadow other advanced warships, particularly the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer seen in the operation, which he described as a measure of the Chinese navy’s combat strength.
Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌), an associate research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said that PLA Navy activity had three political implications.
The activity was a response to the US-Japan Keen Sword 27 exercise, held on Monday last week to yesterday on Japan’s southwestern islands, and to a Wednesday meeting in Cebu between US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi, Shu said.
The two officials agreed to strengthen defense cooperation along the First Island Chain linking Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines, he said.
Shu added that the naval activity was also a response to a US Army guide calling for regional forces to mobilize on the first day of an Indo-Pacific conflict and identifying China as a “pacing threat.”
On the military front, Shu said the Liaoning aircraft carrier is deployed at sea annually, but the scale of China’s naval forces involved this time was significant.
He said China was using routine exercises to build its ability to operate beyond the First Island Chain and gradually develop carrier strike group capabilities modeled on the US Navy.

More than half of Taiwanese use AI tools, survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

Just more than half of Taiwanese adults have used generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in the past six months, a Fair Trade Commission (FTC) survey released yesterday showed.
OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini account for more than 90 percent of the tools used and nearly 40 percent said they paid for AI services.
The survey was conducted from May 6 to 28, and collected 1,079 valid responses from Taiwanese aged 18 and older who had used generative AI tools in the previous six months.
Photo: Bloomberg
The FTC identified three key trends: widespread use of multiple AI platforms, growing adoption of paid subscriptions and a tendency among users of free services to switch to competing tools when quality declines.
ChatGPT was the most widely used, accounting for 87.9 percent of respondents, followed by Gemini at 67.8 percent and Anthropic’s Claude at 8.9 percent, it found.
Asked to identify their primary AI tool, 56.6 percent chose ChatGPT and 34.6 percent went with Gemini, the survey said.
The most common reasons for using AI were learning (56.5 percent) and work-related tasks (55 percent), while 47.2 percent said they chose a platform that best met their needs, it found.
Of the 39.8 percent of respondents that used paid AI services, nearly 70 percent paid out of pocket, the survey found.
Half of the subscribers spent between NT$500 and NT$1,000 per month, and 76.3 percent said they would keep their subscriptions even if prices rose 10 percent, it added.
Among the 60.2 percent of respondents who use free AI services, 89.5 percent said they do not pay for subscription as the free version was sufficient, the survey found.
If the quality of free services declined, such as lower usage limits or slower response times, 76.7 percent said they would switch to another free platform, while 15.5 percent said they would upgrade

Economy in boom mode for 10th month, NDC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

Taiwan’s economy remained in boom territory for a 10th consecutive month last month, as surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware continued to drive growth despite an increasingly high comparison base, the National Development Council (NDC) said yesterday.
The economy’s monitoring indicator climbed to 41 last month from a revised 40 in August, marking its 10th consecutive month at levels that signal a boom — the longest such streak in records dating back to 1984.
That reflects a structural shift driven by AI investment, with Taiwan’s semiconductor industry and extensive network of suppliers helping spread the gains beyond major chipmakers, NDC Department of Economic Development Director Chen Mei-chu (陳美菊) said.
Photo: CNA
“AI demand continues to grow despite an increasingly high comparison base,” she said.
The nation’s integrated supply chain gives it an advantage over economies that rely more heavily on a handful of large manufacturers, such as South Korea, Chen said.
Expansions by major companies have also boosted business for small and medium-sized enterprises, while the robust market positions of local chipmakers have given them greater pricing power.
Global cloud service providers are projected to spend about US$957 billion on capital expenditure this year, with the figure forecast to exceed US$1.5 trillion next year, TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) said.
Taiwan is well placed to capture a large share of that spending because its manufacturers supply the chips, components and equipment needed to build AI infrastructure, Chen said.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), the world’s largest contract chipmaker, plans to spend US$60 billion to US$64 billion this year, with total capital investment from this year through 2028 expected to exceed that of the preceding three years.
The AI boom is also creating opportunities for traditional industries, with demand growing for materials used in electronics manufacturing and machinery for Taiwanese companies expanding production overseas, Chen said.
Suppliers of copper foil, circuit-board substrates and specialty chemicals are benefiting from the expansion, while overseas factory investments by Taiwanese manufacturers are supporting exports of machinery and conventional industrial equipment.
The leading indicators, which gauge economic prospects over the next six months, rose 0.56 percent to 104.69. Four components increased: the floor area of building starts, the export-order trends index, manufacturing business sentiment and stock prices.
The coincident indicators, which track current economic conditions, edged up 0.01 percent to 105.21, supported by higher turnover in wholesale, retail and food services, stronger exports and longer overtime hours in the industrial and services sectors.
The NDC expects sustained global investment in AI infrastructure to continue supporting Taiwan’s exports of electronics and information and communications technology products.
Capital spending by domestic semiconductor, memory and substrate manufacturers, as well as investment by foreign companies in Taiwan, should provide additional support, it said.

Sales at the brands in mainland China fell as much as double-digits in August and last month compared to the same period a year ago, two research firms surveyed by Bloomberg that track industry data said. 5G services on high-speed rail inconsistent: test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Although high-speed rail passengers can access 5G services during transit, mobile reception and Internet connectivity remain unreliable along certain sections of the route due to gaps in coverage, a test by the Consumers’ Foundation and the Telecom Technology Center found.
The test, conducted on March 18, covered the entire high-speed rail route for express and all-stop trains during peak and off-peak hours.
Representatives of the three major telecoms — Taiwan Mobile, Far EasTone Telecommunications and Chunghwa Telecom — assessed mobile Internet connectivity by using new Samsung phones to download and upload files of identical sizes to their respective HTTP servers.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
The download and upload speeds were measured and transmitted to the center’s data server.
Operators also used mobile phones to call a fixed audio source on their respective networks, with consistent call durations and intervals.
Chunghwa Telecom recorded the highest average download and upload speeds, at 159Mbps and 39.21Mbps respectively, the results showed.
Taiwan Mobile recorded an average download speed of 144.65Mbps and an upload speed of 31.19Mbps, while Far EasTone averaged 122.27Mbps for downloads and 36.01Mbps for uploads.
All three operators delivered better download and upload speeds at underground stations in northern Taiwan, including Taipei, Banciao (板橋) and Nangang (南港) railway stations, where relatively comprehensive infrastructure was in place, the foundation said.
Download speeds were generally faster in Chiayi County, while upload speeds were higher in Kaohsiung, it added.
Download and upload speeds were unstable in tunnels in Hsinchu and Miaoli counties, it said.
Chunghwa Telecom had access to 5G services for 92.86 percent of the test time, followed by Taiwan Mobile at 90.22 percent and Far EasTone at 85.3 percent, it added.
In some sections, including Tainan’s Yongkang District (永康) and Miaoli County’s Zaociao Township (造橋), 5G was unavailable, leaving passengers with access to 4G services only, it said.
All three operators also experienced voice-call disruptions during the test, particularly when trains passed through tunnels, the foundation said.
The results indicate that 5G coverage along the high-speed rail route needs improvement, it said, adding that passengers could experience poor Internet connectivity and interrupted calls when trains pass through tunnels or challenging terrain without additional equipment to strengthen signals.
“Given that consumers pay higher monthly fees for 5G services, they should reasonably expect stable, continuous, high-speed Internet access,” the foundation said. “However, the test showed that high-speed rail passengers frequently had to switch between 5G and 4G on their mobile devices, put up with unstable signals or rely solely on 4G in certain sections of the journey.”
“There is an obvious gap between consumer expectations and actual experience,” it added.
Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp said it signed a memorandum of understanding with the three telecoms in March to improve telecommunications quality along the line.
The operators would replace 369 base-frequency repeaters along the route with remote radio heads, increasing the number of units deployed to more than 2,200, it said, adding that the upgrade is scheduled for completion by the end of next year.
Once completed, it is expected to enable passengers to make uninterrupted voice calls, browse Web sites and stream videos without losing connection, the company said.

Palestinian parties could redraw Israel’s political landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.
In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority,” but the real outcome looks as if it would be far more complex than that.
The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old would be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis would not so easily be sidelined and ignored.
The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied. Although the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority.
If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israeli President, Isaac Herzog discretion over whom he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role.
Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. However, to do so he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List). They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election.”
However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.
Negotiations with the Joint List, with 11 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian-Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organization.
Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.
“Laying down conditions won’t work with the Joint List,” Shbita said. “We will negotiate as equals because we need each other.”
In the absence of an agreement with one or both of the Palestinian groupings, it is possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.
It would be an unstable solution, making another election more than likely. That would provide Netanyahu the opportunity to rally support among conservative Israeli Jews and claim to have been vindicated in his campaign slogan, “the Right or Palestine,” which rhymes in Hebrew.
Netanyahu has looked beaten before over his three decades at or near the top, and staged a comeback each time with the aid of his unparalleled tactical skills as a dealmaker. No one is yet ruling out another breathtaking political escape, but this time, if he does bounce back, he would owe his resurrection to his avowed political enemies for dropping him a lifeline rather than make historic compromises across Israel’s deep racial divide.
Speaking from the Joint List victory party in Nazareth in the early hours of Wednesday, one party official said: “The Zionist opposition will have to choose between supremacy and building democracy.”

Judge rejects vote suit
A federal judge on Wednesday rejected a Department of Justice request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens. District Judge David Carter said that “eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This court declines to be a party to such process.” Prosecutors for the department said they would appeal the decision. It sued election officials in the state earlier this month, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on voter rolls. It had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. California mails ballots to all 23 million registered voters. Court filings show that more than 500,000 ballots had already been processed by this week. First Assistant Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on social media following the ruling that citizens were being disenfranchised. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials,” Essayli wrote. “This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution. Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later. It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots.”

EDITORIAL: Airports are not an election gambit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:32 UTC
01:42:32 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Oct. 8 announced a plan to remove Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) and use the space to build an artificial intelligence (AI) park. The announcement came less than two months before the nine-in-one local elections, and the most fiercely contested Taipei mayoral race.
Plans to relocate the airport is not a new idea. Most former Taipei mayors and mayoral candidates have presented plans to remove or transform it.
Unlike former Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) mayors Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) and Hau Lung-bin’s (郝龍斌) plans to transform the airport into a regional business airport, or Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) mayor Chen Shui-bian’s (陳水扁) proposal to move it to Greater Taipei’s suburban districts, Chiang proposed that the airport be completely decommissioned and transformed into an AI park, which would house an AI industrial cluster, residential facilities and green parkland, aiming to host 200 enterprises and accommodate 35,000 residents.
However, as a civilian-military airport, Songshan shoulders multiple missions, including connecting international and domestic routes, providing transportation services for outlying islands and eastern Taiwan, and being a resource node in the national defense system. If the airport could be easily removed without a proper replacement, all previous proposals would have been completed years ago.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare said the number of residents in outlying islands seeking medical treatment and emergency care in Taiwan proper totaled 38,651 last year. There are nine medical centers within a half-hour drive from the airport, making it a crucial medical and emergency transit center for these residents.
Although Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport and the High Speed Railway have taken over major international and domestic transportation duties, Songshan airport remains a vital transportation hub for domestic, outlying islands, cross-strait and northeast Asian flights.
The airport is also part of regional military protection, anti-decapitation defense, and disaster response and rescue. Amid rising cross-strait tensions, the Ministry of National Defense has repeatedly said that plans to relocate or transform the airport should prioritize military missions and national defense resilience.
Chiang’s plan is to transfer Songshan airport’s traffic to the Taoyuan airport, which is set to complete its third terminal and runway construction around 2033. However, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said that would severely impact the capacity and efficiency of the Taoyuan airport, and that the new terminal and runway are being built to meet rising international traffic demand, not domestic transportation.
Shifting outlying islands’ air transport to Taoyuan would also greatly inconvenience residents from those areas and could even lead to medical delays.
Politicians and residents of outlying islands and even KMT members have voiced their objections to Chiang’s proposal. A TVBS poll showed that 41 percent of respondents opposed the plan, while 31 percent supported it.
Tech leaders have also questioned the feasibility and benefits of Chiang’s proposal. Pegatron chairman Tung Tzu-hsien (童子賢) publicly opposed the plan and suggested that AI parks be built in areas with greater potential for power and land expansion, such as the Danhai New Town (淡海新市鎮), instead of the congested Taipei area.
There is no need to sacrifice a city’s airport for AI development. Major international metropolitan cities generally retain or build secondary airports near their city centers, such as Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and Seoul’s Gimpo Airport, to accommodate international business exchanges.
The Executive Yuan in 2023 also approved a “Songshan International Airport 2040 Master Plan,” designating it as a key capital metropolitan business airport, and formulating a “Taoyuan-Songshan” dual-airport model in which the two airports would complement each other — serving business aviation and providing alternate transportation during contingencies.
Chiang’s plan has been criticized as an election stunt. Ironically, during a Taipei legislative by-election in 2023, Chiang slammed then-DPP candidate Enoch Wu’s (吳怡農) proposal to relocate Songshan airport, calling it “a hasty proposal for election.” Now, Chiang has not only suggested the same idea, but also brought it up at the last minute. He had never submitted a proposal about transforming the airport to the central government during his nearly four-year tenure as mayor.
Given the wide-ranging impact of relocating the airport, the issue needs a thorough assessment and discussion. It should not be hastily brought up as a hollow campaign promise.
Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

The good news is that the US is engaged in both races, which will also benefit US allies and partners in Asia, including Taiwan. Taiwan’s AH-64E Apache attack helicopters have been grounded for inspections following a US technical notification about gearbox risks, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said yesterday.
Speaking briefly to reporters before a legislative committee hearing, Koo said the army would deploy AH-1W SuperCobra attack helicopters and OH-58D reconnaissance helicopters to carry out readiness missions during the inspection period.
He did not elaborate on the inspection requirements or how long the Apaches would remain grounded.
Photo: Lee Jung-ping, Taipei Times
According to a US Army Public Affairs release issued on Oct. 2, the US Army has ordered an immediate, temporary pause in flight operations for AH-64E Apache helicopters equipped with Improved Drive System (IDS) transmissions.
The pause would remain in place while required inspections and corrective actions are completed, the release said.
Meanwhile, a May report by Defense One, citing an internal US Army safety document, said an investigation had indicated that the AH-64E’s IDS transmission could experience an internal failure that could lead to loss of tail rotor thrust, electrical power and hydraulics.
The report said the root cause was still under investigation.
Taiwan took delivery of 30 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters from the US in five batches, with the final six arriving in 2014.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Wednesday said that he is his country’s rightful leader after fleeing to the US to start a self-imposed exile.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday won a runoff election, defeating Bolsonaro.
“I am the elected president and the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny,” Bolsonaro wrote on X, slamming “electoral fraud.”
Photo: AP
“I will lead the opposition from here,” he said.
In a subsequent statement, he said he is the “leader,” rather than “president.”
Bolsonaro, 45, touched down earlier on Wednesday in a private jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami.
Rogerio Marinho, the leader of Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party in the Brazilian Senate, told reporters in Brasilia that he was in “solidarity” with the former candidate, describing him as a “political exile.”
However, he distanced himself from Bolsonaro’s statement, and refused to back up Bolsonaro’s claims of electoral fraud.
“The Liberal Party cannot make that claim,” he said. “There is no evidence of that.”
Bolsonaro “is an expression of the right in Brazil today ... he calls himself a leader and it’s true: he’s a leader,” Marinho told reporters.
US President Donald Trump said that Brazil’s election was “very strange,” but told reporters he “won’t get involved” in Bolsonaro’s claims.
Details of how Bolsonaro, who was accompanied by his wife and daughters, made it to US soil are still emerging.
He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering. With his parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports, but left anyway, reaching the US via Argentina and Ecuador.
A police source told reporters that Bolsonaro’s Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, Italian documents showed.
The US Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared “with applicable immigration laws and procedures.”
The travel ban was issued by Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Lula, who won Sunday’s election with 51.8 percent of the vote, called Bolsonaro’s departure a “shameful” act.
“A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide,” he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration on Tuesday.
However, Brazilian police on Wednesday said that he was not considered a fugitive.
The most high-profile fraud case against Bolsonaro in Brazil centers on the unreleased biopic Dark Horse starring US actor Jim Caviezel as Bolsonaro’s father, Jair.
In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately US$24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil’s biggest-ever fraud cases.
In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the film’s financing, and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency.

Operators reassure public that trains can fail safely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) and Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) yesterday said their train safety systems are designed to automatically bring trains to a stop when they detect abnormal conditions.
They made the comment following a deadly collision in Spain on Wednesday, when a high-speed train struck another train that had stopped on the tracks, killing at least 69 people.
Spanish Minister of Transport and Sustainable Mobility Oscar Puente said the railway control center had allowed a train to resume service despite a red signal, describing the decision as “incomprehensible,” foreign media reported.
Photo: AFP
TRC president Feng Hui-sheng (馮輝昇) said the company’s railway safety office had obtained information about the accident in Spain and was reviewing its own safety protection mechanisms.
Taiwan’s railway signaling system is designed to fail safely, meaning that a system failure should cause it to default to a safe state, Feng said.
If a train stops, the signal governing the section behind it would display a danger indication, instructing following trains to stop, in accordance with safety procedures, he said.
The following train’s protection system would also activate automatically to slow the train and bring it to a stop, while train personnel would get off and carry out standard operating procedures to protect the train from behind, he added.
“Please rest assured that Taiwan Railway will rigorously implement its safety protection mechanisms. An incident like the one in Spain would not happen here,” he said.
THSRC said that its system, like Japan’s Shinkansen bullet train system, was designed according to the principle of failing safely as well.
The railway operators said high-speed trains are monitored by an automatic train control (ATC) system that continuously monitors their speeds.
When the system detects an abnormality, loses a signal or encounters a signaling failure, it automatically applies emergency brakes to ensure safe train operations and protect passengers, they said.
The ATC system continuously calculates the maximum permitted speed based on the position of the train ahead, the route set by the control center and other track conditions, the operators said.
If a train exceeds its permitted speed, the system automatically reduces its speed to prevent overshooting the limit or getting too close to a train ahead, they added.

The digitally democratic campaign of Puma Shen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:26 UTC
01:42:26 KST

Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign — officially called “The Taipei Current” (洋流) in English, also referred to as the “Ocean Wave,” as the third character in Shen’s name, yang (洋), means “ocean” — has leveraged digital and Internet tools. Rather than using them as one-way channels, his team has combined social media engagement, gamified organizing, online-to-offline mobilization and the organic spread of subcultural memes to drive an unconventional campaign model that has culminated in the “Ocean Wave” of support.
The campaign has broken through echo chambers and attracted record-breaking digital traffic. Media personality and politician Jaw Shaw-kong’s (趙少康) YouTube interview with Shen earlier this month attracted a live audience of more than 140,000 at its peak and amassed more that 1.1 million views within 24 hours. This six-fold surge showed that Shen has caught the attention of many pan-blue and centrist voters, demonstrating his ability to break out of his bubble.
Shen has also gamified his campaign efforts. In line with the nautical theme of the “Ocean Wave,” supporters are able to enter the “crew room” through Shen’s Line account to obtain a digital “crew ID card,” which unlocks maps and campaign information, giving young people a sense of involvement that keeps them participating. When tickets for front-row seats at the campaign headquarters’ inauguration rally became available for reservation, more than 50,000 people applied immediately, generating as many as 400 clicks per second. Within 30 seconds, all spots were filled, demonstrating the campaign’s extraordinary online rallying power.
Shen has tactically timed “online-to-offline” pop-up events, announcing speeches and appearances at markets on social media with only about an hour’s warning. That helps prevent die-hard supporters from traveling across districts to participate in multiple events, and yet, Shen draws hundreds or even thousands of people each time. It is a strategy that converts online buzz into physical gatherings, while giving local voters priority access in their own areas.
Shen has also leveraged social media, with his follower count on Threads surpassing 620,000 and his impressions reaching 56.1 million over the past 30 days. Among Taiwanese political figures, this puts him behind only former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文). He has been known to reference Naruto and One Piece to connect with younger audiences. When Shen’s campaign team reportedly confiscated his phone to encourage him to rest for half an hour, he still ended up in a livestream’s chat room engaging with the public from his computer.
Lastly, there has been supporter-driven promotional content for Shen, and the spread of the so-called “Ocean Current Economics” (洋流經濟) — a term that emerged to describe the phenomenon of supportive night market vendors selling out. A digital version of the official Soon Daily (順報) campaign magazine has been available for readers to download and share online. Supporters chased designs that resembled the blue floral shirt Shen was wearing at a campaign event in Kaohsiung last month, and cosmetic retailers reportedly sold out of the South Korean face mask he mentioned in a livestream earlier this month. Each viral instance generated further organic exposure.
Shen has moved beyond the traditional model of paid advertising and unilateral communication toward a digital-social ecosystem characterized by high engagement, gamification and online-offline integration. This has been the key to his ability to sustain high levels of public attention, and attract centrist voters and younger audiences.
Hsu Chi-hsiang is an immigration professional.
