Netanyahu ally offers Eisenkot path to PM, demands Haredi draft exemption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:12:33 UTC
00:12:33 KST

One of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's longtime ultra-Orthodox allies is considering a dramatic political shift, offering to support opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot as Israel's next prime minister in exchange for legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service. The proposal comes as Israel's election count nears completion, with neither political bloc securing the 61 seats needed to form a government.
A senior United Torah Judaism official confirmed to ynet on Thursday that the party intends to propose supporting a government led by Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, on the condition that legislation granting military draft exemptions be advanced.
"Gadi has the option of forming a government with Netanyahu, but then Netanyahu would be prime minister and he would be a senior minister," the official said. "We are offering him the premiership. That's better than being No. 2 or going to another election."
The proposal signals a possible break between United Torah Judaism and Netanyahu, whose right-wing and religious alliance has relied on the ultra-Orthodox party for parliamentary support. It also underscores the political leverage the party hopes to gain from an election that has left neither major bloc with a governing majority.
The obstacle, however, is substantial. During the election campaign, Eisenkot identified mandatory military or national service as one of his conditions for potential coalition partners, directly conflicting with United Torah Judaism's demand for draft exemptions.
Even with United Torah Judaism's projected seven seats, Eisenkot's current bloc would control only 55 of the Knesset's 120 seats, six short of a majority. Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, is projected to win six seats, but no agreement involving the parties has been announced.
The proposed arrangement could also face resistance from Eisenkot's existing political partners, particularly Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Liberman, who has opposed forming a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds 53 seats as 99% of votes counted
The political maneuvering comes as Israel's Central Elections Committee announced Thursday afternoon that 99% of votes had been counted, with no change in the balance between the main parliamentary blocs.
According to the latest figures, Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and the two Arab parties a combined 19, leaving both major political camps short of a majority.
Netanyahu's Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 21 and the Beyachad (Together) party with 12.
The Joint List is projected to receive 11 seats, while the Arab-led Ra'am party and the Democrats are each projected to receive eight. United Torah Judaism, Yisrael Beiteinu and Otzma Yehudit are each on seven, while Shas and the joint Religious Zionism-Zehut list are each projected to win six seats.
The Reservists and Economic Party remains below the electoral threshold and is not currently projected to enter the Knesset.
Double-envelope count completed, but results remain unofficial
Earlier Thursday, the Central Elections Committee announced that counting had been completed for the special double-envelope ballots, a voting procedure used by soldiers and others voting away from their designated polling stations.
The committee said results had been entered from 12,644 polling stations, representing 5,589,836 votes. Of those, 5,564,764 were valid and 25,072 were invalid.
The final batch of double-envelope ballots, representing 24,713 votes, had been transferred for data entry and verification. Their results will be published only after those procedures have been completed.
The committee emphasized that the figures remain provisional and that official results will be published Wednesday, November 4, following an additional election integrity review.
The preliminary outcome leaves Israel facing complex coalition negotiations, with United Torah Judaism's potential offer introducing another possible route to a government led by Eisenkot. Whether he would consider compromising on military service legislation, or secure enough parliamentary support even with the ultra-Orthodox party's backing, remains unresolved.

ECB's Lagarde resigns early so she can speak freely on topics beyond monetary policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:11:44 UTC
00:11:44 KST

ECB's Lagarde resigns early so she can speak freely on topics beyond monetary policy
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Thursday she had decided to step down eight months before her term was due to expire so that she can speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy.
Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019 and previously headed the International Monetary Fund. Her term would otherwise have run until October 2027.
"There is never a good time to leave," Lagarde told a press conference. "But it's embedded in the governance of the ECB that presidents, board members have to leave because they cannot be up for renewal."
Lagarde said the decision to leave early was driven by a wish to engage on issues outside the ECB's mandate.
"I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters," she said.
She noted that ECB officials are bound by strict rules of neutrality: "We have an obligation of neutrality, we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy," Lagarde said, adding that the mandate is "the price we pay for being independent."
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. "I'm interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation," she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, Lagarde said she believed she had something to contribute beyond central banking. "There are things that I can say — whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position," she said.
Lagarde sought to reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank's operations. "A process has already started to identify my successor," she said, adding there were "plenty of excellent candidates — much better than me, actually."
She dismissed concerns about continuity. "Don't worry about decision making in limbo — no, absolutely not," Lagarde said. "The institution is solid, strong, like a rock, and it will continue being so." REUTERS

As Delhi-NCR braces for Diwali celebrations, concerns over firecracker emissions and worsening air pollution put the spotlight on the festival’s environmental cost.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday said it was not inclined to impose a complete ban on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR, but warned authorities against pushing it to take a "very harsh stand" by failing to enforce its orders on the ground.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale said repeated judicial directions would serve little purpose unless authorities ensured compliance, stressing that air pollution affected "every living being"."We are not inclined to completely ban but don’t push us to take a very harsh stand," the bench said as reported by news agency PTI. The Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati outlined measures taken by the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) to tackle pollution.“There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed.The court said the matter was not adversarial and called for serious action and cooperation from all stakeholders to regulate the use of firecrackers.“Every year we are trying to balance it out but unless there is cooperation from everyone, it can’t be done,” the bench said, adding that the concerned officers must be present on the ground to monitor implementation.
The bench also suggested roping in prominent personalities, including sportspersons, to spread public awareness about the harmful effects of firecrackers.Bhati told the court that the Delhi government had drawn up an extensive plan to tackle the pollution season. Measures scheduled to come into effect from November include curbs on older vehicles and construction and demolition activities, along with staggered office timings.
The Centre informed the court that internal consultations on the use of barium in firecrackers were still under way. Bhati sought three weeks to complete the process, and the bench said it would consider the issue after that period.The Supreme Court was hearing two petitions, including a suo motu case on air pollution in the National Capital Region covering firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management. The other petition seeks a ban on the manufacture of firecrackers.

====================================================================================================

How Europe Is Defying Trump by Rallying Around the ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:03:32 UTC
00:03:32 KST

As the Trump Administration forges ahead with its campaign to dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC) “brick by brick,” Europe is publicly showing a steady stream of support for the institution.
The E.U. last week awarded the court and its officials the Sakharov human rights prize, commending “the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice.” The prestigious recognition came after former ICC judge Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay on Oct. 9 was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize—an honor long coveted by President Donald Trump. Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, acknowledged the award was intended to send a “message to those who are attacking, undermin[ing]... the international rules-based system.” Hours after Pillay’s win, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping new sanctions against the ICC. While previous U.S. sanctions had targeted the institution's prosecutors and judges, the new measures were aimed at “cutting off [the court’s] resources” by severing U.S. transactions with the court.
Experts warn that the sanctions could have “extremely disruptive” implications for the court, especially in regards to financial support for case work, travel to the U.S. for judges, and the core functions of the institution itself. “Leaving the political dimension to one side, the rule of law and the just resolution of disputes depends, to a large extent, on the body in question having all available evidence,” says Nabil Khabirpour, an affiliated lecturer in E.U. law and jurisprudence at Cambridge University. “Organizations that are involved in working with witnesses, both on the ground and within the legal infrastructure, are likely to be affected.”
The latest sanctions, which were announced with a six-month initial grace period, are part of a broader push by the Trump Administration to dismantle the institution it accuses of unfairly targeting the U.S. and Israel. The Trump Administration has staunchly criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and former investigations into the actions of American soldiers in Afghanistan. The ICC is recognized as the world’s highest criminal court. It draws its jurisdiction from the Rome Statute, a treaty that went into effect in 2002 and is ratified by 125 countries. Neither the U.S. nor Israel is a state party to the Rome Statute, and therefore they do not recognize the jurisdiction of the court.
Trump has long complained that the ICC oversteps its authority and should not claim jurisdiction over U.S. citizens. He amplified his campaign against the organization at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, taking time out of his 45-minute speech to publicly call on “all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution, immediately.” He said the U.S. is “opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the ICC” and “will never allow U.S. service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us.”
His call to action was swiftly rejected by European leaders.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, shortly after the speech, said: "We will, of course, not be doing that." In an interview with Germany's Deutschlandfunk radio station, he described the court as "an important institution” and said the issue is "one of the areas where we do indeed have to acknowledge a regrettable difference in policy from the U.S. Administration."
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten also defended the ICC, asking how can anyone “possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?”
“I believe there can be only one response,” he continued, in his own U.N. address. “To say: 'hands off' the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.” The remarks drew loud applause from attending delegates.
Similarly, European Council president Antonio Costa stressed that the E.U. stands “firmly behind” the ICC and argued it’s “unacceptable to threaten or attack the International Criminal Court, its officials, and its staff.”
The European Union as an organization has since strongly criticized the U.S. sanctions against the ICC. In a speech on Oct. 20, E.U. policy chief Kaja Kallas said the most recent “misguided” measures were “against” European interests.
“The U.S. has already adopted individual sanctions, including against nine judges and the chief prosecutor of the ICC. The latest U.S. announcement [on Oct. 9] to impose institutional sanctions puts the entire court at risk,” she argued, adding that Brussels will use the next six months "to open dialogue and look for solutions.”
European lawmakers call for “concrete” action against U.S. sanctions
The European Commission’s choice to take time to consider how to counter the U.S. sanctions has fallen short of what many European lawmakers have called for.
Several leading MEPs, including Germany's David McAllister, chair of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and France's Mounir Satouri, chair of the Subcommittee on Human Rights, issued a public statement on Oct. 9 calling for the Commission to activate a legislative shield referred to as the “blocking statute,” which would essentially prevent E.U. firms from complying with U.S. sanctions.
“The European Union must now demonstrate unwavering solidarity with the ICC and its personnel—not only with words, but also with concrete acts,” the leading Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) said in a joint statement. “The European Commission must immediately trigger the E.U. blocking statute, shielding the court and European actors from the extraterritorial reach of these sanctions. Europe must stand firm in defence of international law and the rule of law."
This request was bolstered as 58 MEPs reportedly sent a letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen for the Commission to activate the measure.
According to the Commission, the purpose of the European Union’s blocking statute is to “protect E.U. operators from the extra-territorial application of third country laws.” The blocking statute came into force in 1996 in direct response to the U.S. sanctions against Cuba. The aim of the measure was to protect economic operators within the E.U. from the effects of such extraterritorial sanctions, according to the Norton Rose Fulbright law firm. As such, the blocking statute shields European economic operators from the application of the U.S. legislation and sanctions specified in the Annex to the E.U. blocking statute. More recently, the E.U.'s updated blocking statute entered into force in response to U.S. sanctions on Iran after the U.S. withdrew from the nuclear agreement in 2018.
Kallas has expressed an openness to the measure, but also advised caution when delivering her statement on European support for the ICC. “We should keep all options on the table. If we use the blocking statute, we have one shot and we should do it well. So, it should be well prepared," Kallas said, urging companies “not to over comply” with the sanctions, as they are not yet in effect.
ICC prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told the Guardian last week that some ICC staff are already facing "banking difficulties," despite the grace period before the sanctions come into effect. Khan said the banks were “over complying” to minimize risk amid uncertainty over the scope of the measures. She said the court's work has not been hindered.
TIME has reached out to the ICC for comment.
If the E.U. were to activate the blocking statute, it would be a “very important gesture” that could show the Trump Administration how “Europe is serious about protecting the court and that it is prepared to take real steps in that direction,” says Sergey Vasiliev, a professor of international law at Open University Netherlands. But he warns that some may view it as a “very extreme or radical measure, that could perhaps anger the Trump Administration even more” at a time where U.S.-Europe relations are already strained.
Meanwhile, some ICC officials have suggested alternative measures in an effort to mitigate the expected impact of the U.S. sanctions. Osvaldo Zavala Giler, the court's registrar, told Politico that “comfort letters” could be sent out, reassuring firms that they needn’t comply with the U.S. measures.
But Vasiliev argues that this “will not necessarily solve the problem, because businesses are expecting clear assurances of protection… the only such assurance can be provided by the actual triggering of the blocking statute.”
Could the ICC row further escalate U.S.-Europe tensions?
Relations between Europe and the U.S. have been under increasing strain since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Trump has introduced various waves of tariffs on international trading partners, and has threatened further levies on the E.U. and member states in response to divisive issues.
When Trump’s pursuit of acquiring Greenland as a U.S. territory reached a critical point in January, Trump threatened to tariff European countries that opposed his campaign—a move that earned him strong rebuke from within his own party.
Last month, when von der Leyen invited Canada to work toward becoming the European Union’s first “associate member,” in what she described as an “urgent” reimagining of partnerships, Trump again threatened economic pressure. He called the proposal “laughable” and threatened to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if such an idea were to go ahead.
The Trump Administration has also clashed with its NATO allies. Earlier this year, Trump refused to rule out leaving the alliance over Greenland disputes, and since the start of the Iran war, the President has hit out at NATO countries for refusing to get actively involved in the conflict.
Should Brussels and Washington continue to clash on the ICC sanctions, “this could risk accelerating certain destabilizations, such as what we've seen with the trade wars,” says Khabirpour. International organizations will ultimately stand to suffer if the two remain at odds, he adds.

Two men suspected of having carried out an attempted attack on Starlink infrastructure in Lithuania are in custody in Germany, Lithuanian authorities said on Thursday.

Infrastructure by satellite internet provider Starlink, which is vital for air defence operations in Ukraine, has been repeatedly targeted in Eastern Europe in recent weeks.
Earlier this month, unknown individuals used Molotov cocktails and flammable liquids to try and set fire to Starlink equipment stored by a company in Lithuania, with authorities suspecting Russia was behind the attack.

Briginas said on Thursday that those thought to be responsible for the failed attack had no links to Lithuania.
The two men, who he said hold German-Turkish and German-Serbian citizenship and live in Germany, travelled to Lithuania on the eve of the incident and immediately left the country again after attempting to carry out the attack, according to the police chief.
They are currently in custody in Germany due to an European arrest warrant issued by Bulgaria, he said.
Briginas said the two individuals are also suspected of links to similar attacks in Poland and Bulgaria, adding that further people had been arrested in Poland.
A fire broke out at a Starlink ground station in Poland in September, with Warsaw also suspecting Russian sabotage. Starlink antennas have also been set on fire in Bulgaria.

Starship plans software changes to improve delivery robots' safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Starship plans software changes to improve delivery robots' safety
Safety improvements to the autonomous delivery robots on Estonia's streets will be primarily software-based, said Starship Technologies, after one of its machines was involved in a collision with a bus earlier this week.
A bus and a delivery robot collided in Tallinn on Monday evening, injuring several people after the driver braked sharply to avoid an accident.
Tallinn Transport (TLT) board member Andrei Novikov said the accident occurred during rush hour, when it was dark outside. A moving object suddenly appeared in front of the bus. "I don't know whether the bus driver was immediately able to understand whether it was a delivery robot, an animal or, for example, a cyclist," he noted.
He said the bus driver acted correctly by hitting the brake. Novikov added that, judging by the camera footage from the bus (see below), the "consequences would have been much worse" if the stop had been more sudden.
Novikov said that once the bus had stopped, the first thing the driver did was ask the passengers whether anyone needed help and whether an ambulance should be called. No one in the passenger compartment indicated that an ambulance was needed.
The driver then called TLT's control center and reported the situation. The driver asked what to do next. Together, they decided to continue operating the route, as the damage to the vehicle was minimal, none of the passengers needed an ambulance, it was rush hour and remaining stationary could have obstructed traffic throughout the area.
Passenger files health complaint
Novikov said, after the collision, the bus driver did not want to continue his working day because of his emotional state. He was sent home and a replacement bus driver took over. TLT has now filed a police report. Later, TLT received a complaint from a passenger concerning their health condition.
Lauri Potsepp, a board member of the Estonian Motor Insurance Bureau, said a bus driver is liable for damage caused to others by the bus regardless of fault. Therefore, if a person falls on a bus because the bus brakes sharply, the passenger can claim compensation from the bus's motor insurance provider, regardless of who caused the accident.
"Once the insurer has compensated for the damage, it will be determined who caused the accident, meaning what each of the drivers should have done to prevent the accident," Potsepp explained.
If it turns out that the accident was caused by the delivery robot or its operator, the motor insurance provider may seek reimbursement from the robot's owner for the compensation paid to the victims.
Potsepp added that, in addition to personal injuries, people's belongings may also have been damaged in such a situation. For example, clothing or a phone.
If a person does not know which insurer to submit a compensation claim to but knows the bus's registration number, they can find the insurer on the Motor Insurance Bureau's website.
"If they don't know the registration number, they can send an email to the Motor Insurance Bureau. We will determine who they can claim compensation from and direct the customer there," Potsepp said.
Robots move autonomously
Pepe Aaviksoo, head of operations at Starship Technologies, said the company is currently conducting an internal investigation to find out exactly what happened during the accident. Once the company has completed its assessment, it will share the information with the public and the police.
However, Aaviksoo could already say which improvements need to be made to prevent such situations. "The robot is largely a software-based machine, and the improvements are primarily software-based," he explained.
Aaviksoo said that, generally, the robots move autonomously. However, there are cases where a robot is connected to an office-based team, which takes over control if necessary. This is done either for safety reasons or because of a specific incident.
The office team then assesses what happened in the particular situation. However, Aaviksoo explained that robots are not constantly monitored. "This is simply not physically possible or economically sustainable, because we have several thousand robots around the world," he explained.
Yesterday, it was reported that the Robot left the scene of the accident. But Aaviksoo disputes this version of events. "After the robot was involved in the incident, it contacted the back-office team, whose task was to move the robot off the road to a safe location," he explained.
This meant that the robot had to move away from the middle of the road, and it waited by the curb. "From our perspective, the situation was clear, as indicated by the fact that the bus left the scene and we did not detect any rescue vehicles or police at the scene," Aaviksoo outlined.
The robot remained at the scene for approximately 10 minutes, he said.
Not all risks can be ruled out
Aaviksoo explained that although robots independently cross intersections every day, not all risks can be ruled out. "Just as a pedestrian, cyclist or driver cannot be absolutely safe," he said.
Aaviksoo added that this is an inevitable part of traffic, and the company's task is to do everything it can to ensure that its robots move safely in traffic.
Maria Pashkevich, head of the Transport Administration's Road Safety Department, said that specific traffic and safety requirements have been established for delivery robots in Estonia. For example, when crossing a road, a robot must ensure that it is safe to do so, comply with the obligation to give way and must not endanger other road users.
Pashkevich explained that in the event of a traffic accident, the robot's operator or user must ensure that the robot comes to a stop and does not pose any further danger to other road users.
If a person has been injured or killed in a traffic accident and the robot's operator is able to recognize this, for example through a camera, the operator or user must notify the Emergency Response Center and act according to the instructions received.
Pashkevich said that no traffic accidents involving delivery robots and resulting in human casualties have so far been registered in the Transport Administration's traffic accident information system.
"Although this does not mean that dangerous situations or such traffic accidents have not occurred," she added. For example, some incidents may not have been reported to the police.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Cooperation between Russia and Africa should become an instrument of peace, development and shared prosperity, Burundi’s President and African Union Chairperson Evariste Ndayishimiye told TASS in an interview on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

TEL AVIV, October 29. /TASS/. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party remains in the lead following the October 27 parliamentary election, with 97.3% of ballots counted, according to preliminary figures released by the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
Likud is projected to win 27 seats in the 120-member parliament, followed by Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s main opposition rival Gadi Eisenkot, with 21.
The bloc comprising Likud and the far-right and Orthodox parties that support Netanyahu and make up the current governing coalition also retains its lead. It is projected to secure 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition. Arab parties are set to win 19 seats, although neither Likud nor the opposition is expected to be willing to form a coalition with them.
The CEC is expected to complete the vote count by the end of October 29 and publish the final results no later than November 4. Once the results are available, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset before tasking one of its members with forming a new governing coalition.
A coalition needs at least 61 Knesset seats to form a government, a threshold no political bloc has yet reached. The leader of the party with the most seats usually becomes the candidate for prime minister. However, the president may also task a politician whose party did not win the most votes with forming a government if that politician can assemble a coalition.
The first candidate will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible two-week extension. If that attempt fails, the president will give another lawmaker two weeks to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
If no lawmaker succeeds in forming a stable coalition, new elections will be called after 90 days. Netanyahu will continue to lead Israel’s government until a new cabinet is sworn in.

The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.
Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.
Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.
Core Security
Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.
Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.
But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.
Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.
Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.
Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”
Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.
But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

Britain will reduce ‘unsustainable’ welfare costs, Finance Minister Healey says

AI generated
LONDON – British finance minister John Healey said the government would reduce spending on welfare benefits as he sought to address one of the big public spending challenges that remain after his first budget announcement.
“We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts,” he said in an interview with the BBC.
Healey made no commitment on when welfare spending would fall when asked whether it would happen before the next election, which is due no later than mid-2029.
Speaking later to reporters, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was “working flat out” to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible.
Healey’s tax and spending plans offered some short-term support for households hit by the surge in energy prices caused by the US-Iran war, financed partly by higher taxes on banks, savers and landlords.
But the budget did not address long-term questions such as how to raise defence spending to 3% of economic output, offset inflation’s impact on public spending and tackle the growing welfare bill, which includes pensions as well as support for people deemed too ill to work.
Spending on welfare is set to cost more than 11% of economic output in 2026.
The opposition Conservative Party and some bond investors say that reveals a lack of will in Burnham’s Labour Party to lower borrowing.
However, markets reacted broadly favourably to Healey’s budget and 10-year government borrowing costs touched a one-month low on Oct 29.
Tackling youth joblessness
Healey focused on the problem of unemployment among young people.
“This system is unsustainable,” he said. “I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters (who) have been written off.”
Healey said the government would help young people out of work who would be required to take opportunities on offer.
Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said that approach might save money “but it’s much more uncertain than just directly cutting entitlements or eligibility and it’s likely to give you savings over a longer timeframe, if you do deliver savings”.
A government review into young people out of employment, education or vocational training and another into the disability benefits system are due to be published in November.
Healey drew criticism from the left-leaning Resolution Foundation think tank for spreading too thinly his flagship spending measure – a £100 (S$170) reduction in energy bills for 20 million households to offset some of the sharp increase in bills caused by the US-Iran conflict.
“Even those families receiving help (will be) facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock,” its chief executive Ruth Curtice said.
Typical energy bills this financial year are set to rise to £1,750 a year after government support, 4% higher than after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the think tank said. REUTERS

Banks and healthcare firms are outbidding tech for software talent, major recruiter says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:59:38 UTC
23:59:38 KST

Banks, healthcare companies and other non-tech employers are outbidding tech firms for software engineers as demand for AI skills rises and layoffs reshape the talent market, according to new research by recruitment giant Randstad.
Healthcare and life sciences firms are paying up to 17% more for software engineers than tech companies, while banking is offering 13% more, per the research, which surveyed 1,100 business and technology decision-makers in 11 countries, including the U.S., U.K., France, Germany and Japan, and drew on 20 million job postings and roughly 100 million candidate profiles.
"These businesses see massive potential in AI, realizing business cases that they were not able to realize before," Sander van 't Noordende told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
"We've seen a massive investment wave in the technology sector ... now that wave is shifting towards businesses looking to find the benefits of AI."
The research also found that job postings requiring AI capabilities grew fivefold over the past year.
Tech layoffs reshape hiring
Meanwhile, 55% of non-tech organizations surveyed said they were recruiting workers following tech-sector layoffs.
U.S. tech companies announced 165,925 job cuts in the first nine months of 2026, a 54% jump from the same period in 2025, per data published by consultancy Challenger, Gray & Christmas on Oct. 1.
Microsoft recently said it's offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees. In June, Oracle said its workforce had shrunk by 21,000 in a year. Meta began layoffs in May, affecting 10% of its workforce, or around 8,000 jobs.
In February, Jack Dorsey's payment company Block laid off more than 4,000 employees, nearly half of its workforce.

Expert: NATO aware Russia may attempt to attack Alliance territory
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023–2025), made these remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“here is real concern that Russia could miscalculate again and commit aggression against the Alliance, so there is a willingness to make certain changes,” said the former head of the Alliance’s Nuclear Planning Staff Group.
He is convinced that NATO and its allies are prepared to continue deterring any aggression. The expert emphasized that NATO allies do not currently assume that Russia will cease to be a threat in the near future; it will likely remain a threat for a long time to come.
The expert noted that there is currently a great deal of mistrust toward Moscow, along with the realization that Russia may act irrationally; therefore, one cannot be certain that Russia will not repeat the major strategic miscalculation of 2022 and attack NATO.
“The decision will be made in the Kremlin. NATO, the West and Europe can only be prepared for such a development… I hope the Kremlin will continue to be extremely cautious. I do not think Russia will want to take that risk in the future… An attack on NATO would be much more difficult and much larger in scale, given the geography and capabilities involved,” the expert noted.
In his view, an understanding of the risks should deter the other side and prevent conflict—and, more importantly, the use of nuclear weapons.
At the same time, Stokes acknowledged that there are scenarios that raise concerns that “such a scenario is possible.” He explained that the Kremlin might “seriously consider” the possibility of using nuclear weapons if Russia found itself in a conventional war with NATO and began to lose, lose key territories, or felt that the regime itself was under threat.
“This is a difficult balance: we must defend the Alliance against any aggression while ensuring that Moscow does not perceive this as a strategic defeat,” noted the former NATO director of nuclear policy.
He believes that one of the key elements in avoiding such a scenario is communication—both public and diplomatic, particularly through informal channels.
As previously reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky believes that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin will not risk using nuclear weapons because he could lose his allies.

The chairman of Israel’s Central Elections Committee, Noam Sohlberg, has asked domestic intelligence service Shin Bet to investigate allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday’s election, The Times of Israel reports.
In a letter to Shin Bet chief David Zini, Sohlberg said he had been informed of serious suspicions that foreign actors acting against Israel’s interests had sought to influence the election through funding.
Sohlberg, who is also a Supreme Court judge, stressed that he could not confirm the basis of the suspicions but believed they required a thorough investigation. He did not identify any countries or provide further details.
Citing Hebrew-language media, The Times of Israel reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party alleged that money from Qatar and Turkey had reached groups encouraging Arab citizens of Israel to vote.
No evidence has been presented to substantiate those allegations or implicate Arab party leaders.
Likud has also claimed that Arab parties “stole” the election through bribery, threats and document forgery. The Central Elections Committee rejected accusations of electoral fraud in comments to Channel 12, according to The Times of Israel.
The claims come amid indications of unusually high turnout among Arab voters. Al Jazeera reported that Channel 12’s exit polling put turnout among Palestinian voters at around 80 percent, which would be a record.
With nearly 95 percent of votes counted, the Joint List and Ra’am were on course to win a combined 19 seats, up from 10 in 2022.
The two Arab parties could play a pivotal role in negotiations to form a government, with neither rival bloc appearing able to secure a majority without them.

Police announce stop-and-search zone for Copenhagen derby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:56:00 UTC
23:56:00 KST

Copenhagen Police will introduce a stop-and-search zone around Parken on Sunday, 8 November, when FC Copenhagen face Brøndby IF in a match classified as high risk.
The zone will be in force from 06:00 to 20:00 across parts of Østerbro, including Trianglen, Blegdamsvej, Jagtvej, Østerbrogade, Svanemøllen Station and Strandboulevarden.
Within the zone, police can stop and search people without suspecting them of a criminal offence. The measure is intended to prevent unrest surrounding the derby.
Police Inspector Peter Dahl said officers hoped for a festive and peaceful day, but would be deployed in large numbers given the fixture’s history.
“We will also be present in large numbers so that we can intervene if there should be signs of unrest brewing,” he said.
Police have also instructed FC Copenhagen to keep Brøndby supporters inside Parken for up to an hour after the final whistle. The aim is to separate the two groups of fans and prevent confrontations after the match.
Copenhagen Police warned that penalties for certain offences committed in connection with a football match can be increased by up to 50 percent. These include offences involving drugs, weapons and fireworks.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre says he had a “good conversation” with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen on Wednesday after she criticised his joint phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Frederiksen declined to comment further when asked about the matter later that day at Amalienborg in Copenhagen.

ECB holds rates, but economist sees hikes this year
The European Central Bank kept its key interest rate unchanged on Thursday, while warning that rising energy prices pose a growing risk to inflation.
“Although the full consequences of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has so far remained largely stable, and wages at present show no significant reaction,” the ECB said in a statement.
The decision follows rate increases in June and September.
Tore Stramer, chief economist at the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said uncertainty surrounding French public finances and a broader rise in market interest rates had given the ECB room to pause.
However, he cautioned that further increases remained a possibility.

The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.

Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.

Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.

Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.

ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.

“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:55:55 UTC
23:55:55 KST

Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
