Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Japan Advances Deep-Sea Mining as Support for a Moratorium Grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:52:00 UTC
23:52:00 KST

Thousands of meters below the ocean surface, where no sunlight has ever reached, lies a world long imagined as a barren dark plain. But in its soft sediment and across the mineral-crusted rocks that litter the bottom, life has been unfolding for millions of years. Corals that count their age in millennia, creatures so unhurried in their growth that a single disturbance can erase what will never return. It is among the last wilderness left on Earth, and one of the least understood. And yet, this barely charted world is already becoming an arena for the global race for mineral resources.
The deep-sea world has metals such as rare-earth elements, cobalt, and nickel – which are essential for a wide range of technologies including smartphones, electric vehicles, and wind power generation. According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), more than 30 exploration contracts have been signed with various countries for the seabed in international waters, and this trend has been accelerating in recent years.
In February 2026, Japan became the world’s first country to successfully and continuously retrieve rare-earth mud, sediment rich in critical minerals, from a depth of 6,000 meters. It happened aboard a ship almost 2000 km away, off Minamitorishima, the country’s easternmost island. For Japan – which relies on China for about 90 percent of its supply of rare earths, and which experienced a halt in exports from China in 2010 – this success sparked nationwide excitement as a major step toward breaking free from dependence on China.
The international community, though, is beginning to move in a different direction: moratoria on deep-sea mining. Even though the industry is still only in the test phase, calls to slow its advancement have already emerged. This is because the effects of extraction on the marine environment remain largely unknown. Even for polymetallic nodule mining, in which metal-rich rocks are collected from the deep ocean floor – a prospect that has been studied for decades – caution is growing. Yet Japan is pushing ahead with an unprecedented form of deep-sea mining.
As the first country to have continuously retrieved rare-earth mud from such depths, and as a member of the ISA, Japan is in a position to influence the future of the maritime order.
Critical Minerals Made-in-Japan From the Deep Sea
In Japan, research and development related to the exploitation of rare-earth mud at Minamitorishima is being conducted as part of the “Establishment of a Maritime Security Platform” initiative – a maritime component of the Strategic Innovation Promotion Program (SIP), a large-scale research program led by the Cabinet Office.
Japan depends on China for approximately 90 percent of its rare earth imports. But in 2012, China banned rare-earth exports to Japan in response to territorial disputes. That sparked an ongoing quest to diversify Japan’s supply chains – and, ideally, homeshore extraction and refining.
The discovery of mud containing rare-earth elements in the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) waters near Minamitorishima turned the deep sea into Japan’s hope, according to Professor Yasuhiro Kato of the University of Tokyo, who made the discovery.
“If we can develop the resources we’ve found, such problems [surrounding rare earths] will disappear. I believe this has truly become a hot issue in the industrial sector,” said Professor Kato.
In February, Japan conducted the world’s first successful continuous recovery of rare-earth mud from the seafloor at a depth of 5,569 meters to the ship’s deck. As part of a large-scale research program led by the Cabinet Office, this project aims to conduct demonstration tests at a rate of 350 metric tons per day by February 2027. The objective is the industrialization of rare-earth mud from Minamitorishima starting in 2028.
For the Japanese government, this is a matter of resource security. The Cabinet Office frames the Minamitorishima project as a national strategy to reduce dependence on any single supplier and secure a stable resource base.
Global Calls for a Pause in Commercial Deep-sea Mining
At the same time, a growing chorus of calls to slow down on commercial mining is evident in the international community. Forty-six countries, including those in the EU, the Pacific Islands, and Africa, are calling for a moratorium or suspension of deep-sea mining.
These calls largely concern mining on the high seas. But some countries have gone further, halting activity even in their own waters. In March 2025, Portugal became the first EU country to ban deep-sea mining, enacting a law that will remain in effect until 2050. Even Norway, the first in the world to approve commercial deep-sea mining, has shifted its policy in response to political pressure, announcing it would suspend mining plans until 2029. At the 2025 United Nations Ocean Conference (UNOC), French President Emmanuel Macron called for a moratorium as “internationally essential,” while the U.N. secretary general warned, “We must not turn the deep sea into the ‘Wild West.’”
However, these calls do not completely rule out future development. Rather, they represent a movement urging countries to wait a little longer to explore deep-sea resources and eventual commercialization.
Beyond governments, more than 77 corporations and financial institutions, including Google, Samsung, Volvo, and BMW, have pledged not to source minerals from the seabed.
Behind these calls lies a deep uncertainty about what deep-sea mining would actually do to the ocean, from sediment plumes and noise to the long-term fate of ecosystems that science has barely begun to map. What unites the countries urging restraint is a single conviction: that too little is yet known to proceed.
If mining advances in the Pacific deep sea, the effects could reach the dinner table in Japan directly. Japan consumes roughly a quarter of the world’s tuna, and for Pacific bluefin tuna in particular, it accounts for about 80 percent of the global catch and consumption.
At a time when much of the world is making concerted efforts toward decarbonization of the economy in response to climate change, the possibility that deep-sea mining could potentially release more carbon into the atmosphere troubles some scientists. This is because seabed sediment is one of the Earth’s largest and longest-lasting carbon reservoirs, having locked away organic carbon for thousands to millions of years. Disturbing it, scientists warn, risks releasing that stored carbon back into the ocean and the atmosphere.
Little Is Known About the Impact of Rare-Earth Mud Mining
Professor Jeffrey Drazen of the University of Hawai‘i, who co-authored a paper on the ecological impacts of deep-sea mining published in Nature Communications in November 2025, warned about the commercial expansion of seabed mining, “When a factory is built and its smokestacks begin to emit smoke, for the first few years no change is visible in the surrounding forest,” he said. “It is only ten years later, when the trees begin to wither, that we realize how severe the damage is.”
Deep-sea mining, he explained, follows the same pattern with one key difference. Once disturbed, the deep seafloor does not recover easily, because it operates on a timescale utterly unlike that of the surface. Life in the deep grows exceedingly slowly, and some organisms live for thousands of years. Set against the roughly 30 years it is said to take a Japanese forest to regenerate after logging, the timescale of the deep sea is orders of magnitude greater.
“The natural environment of the deep sea recovers slowly, and in some cases, recovery may be impossible,” Drazen noted.
In the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), a stretch of the Pacific deep sea extending south from Hawai‘i, test mining in the 1970s removed nodules – rounded lumps of hardened minerals – from the seabed, leaving furrows spaced eight meters apart. According to a study published in Nature in March 2025, when revisited 44 years later, those furrows at the site were still clearly visible. While some organisms came back, large sessile animals such as corals and sponges barely returned. The study concluded that the visible physical impacts would persist “for at least many decades.”
Professor Kato, who leads the development effort, thinks that the environmental risks are being overstated. Noting that the impacts of manganese nodule mining have been studied since the 1980s, he said, “Those who have actually carried out such tests have a sense that the impact is, in reality, quite limited.”
Much of this knowledge, however, concerns the mining of manganese nodules, which has half a century of accumulated research, dating back to the 1970s. The rare-earth mud that Japan is pursuing is different: it involves sucking up vast quantities of the thick sediment, and the research into the environmental impacts of its extractions is even scarcer than for nodules.
Commercial-Scale Environmental Assessments Are on a Different Scale From Testing
In response to these environmental concerns, the Cabinet Office’s Strategic Basic Research Program (SIP) and JAMSTEC have been conducting environmental monitoring tests in parallel with the mining operations. During tests off of Minamitorishima between January and February 2026, researchers recovered rare-earth slurry using a mining system adapted from oil and gas drilling technology and designed to minimize environmental impacts from sediment plumes.
Field operations, such as exploration and mining trials, are primarily carried out by the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC). The tests involved deploying methods developed by SIP Ocean, which have since become ISO international standards, to help monitor environmental changes during mining operations and document the condition of the seafloor prior to extraction.
Hiroyuki Yamamoto observed these operations firsthand as project leader of the Marine Environmental Impact Assessment System Development Project Team, which evaluates the environmental impacts of deep-sea resource development. He draws a sharp distinction between two things that are easily conflated: JAMSTEC’s monitoring technology and tools to detect changes on the seafloor, and the actual evaluation of what commercial-scale mining would do to the ecosystem. SIP, he said, has built the former, not the latter.
“SIP hasn’t done an impact assessment. Developing monitoring technology and conducting an impact assessment are two different things. Once you say you’re going to mine on a commercial basis, you have to run the calculations at that scale – and that hasn’t been done yet,” said Yamamoto.
The reason, he explains, is that such an assessment requires modeling at a commercial scale that does not yet exist while the project is still in a test phase. The implication is striking: a project the government says could reach commercial production by 2028 has not yet been assessed – and by its own lead scientist’s account, cannot yet assess – what mining at that scale would do to the deep sea.
The rare-earth mud layer on Minamitorishima was formed approximately 34.5 million years ago. Once the deep seafloor is disturbed, recovery takes at least many decades, if not longer. However, the reality is that there is currently no long-term monitoring program in place to observe this recovery process.
The Cost Wall Facing Commercialization
While some are calling for rare-earth commercialization on Minamitorishima within the next few years, Yamamoto had this to say in response to expectations of Japan’s goal of commercialization by 2030: “What SIP is doing in its surveys isn’t suited for commercialization. Extraction of 350 metric tons a day is simply impossible. Even if it were possible, whether it would be commercially viable is a separate issue. I think it will take time.”
While the recent test by the research vessel Chikyu lasted only a few days, commercial mining would require the vessel to remain at the same site for months. Minamitorishima is far from the mainland, and the mud lies deep. The round trip and the work at such depths cost an enormous amount. “More than 10 million yen (over $65,000) disappears every day,” Yamamoto said. “Even while the ship sits still, the thrusters run constantly, to hold it in position.”
The problem is that even with massive investments, the amount of rare-earth elements that can be extracted is extremely small. Based on the results of the current trials, there appears to be no prospect of Japan being able to meet this demand on its own. There remains a significant gap between the amount of resources lying on the seafloor and the ability to extract them economically.
The pull of commercialization endures, as rare earths are indispensable to modern life. The medium-to-heavy rare earths said to be abundant in the Minamitorishima mud are the ones whose supply China monopolizes. Even with a wide gap between the resources lying on the seafloor and the ability to extract them economically, hopes for development run deep.
Researchers in the field are unanimous that Japan cannot realistically reach commercial production by 2030. So even if commercial mining were formally suspended until then, experts like Tanaka say there would be no real loss. That time could instead be used to refine monitoring technology, work through the unresolved problems, and engage directly in shaping the international rules, and to bring national legislation into line with UNCLOS as well.
And yet Japan will not support a moratorium.
Japan’s motivations are not simple. Julie Klinger, who studies rare earth supply chains at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, sees several calculations entangled here.
“It is for multiple reasons. The instability of dependence on China is real. There is also the matter of alliance management. The October 2025 U.S.–Japan Framework for Securing the Supply of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths explicitly links Japanese mining investment with U.S. defense supply chains,” she explained.
“And there is also the tech demonstration aspect as well. Japan’s tech and engineering breakthroughs in relation to seabed mining and exploration are themselves of very high value, scientifically, diplomatically, and potentially as a high-value export.”
Why does Japan cling so tightly to a 2030 commercialization that researchers themselves call impossible? Securing resources, managing an alliance, showcasing technology – with all of these entangled factor, the answer may lie not in the rare earths themselves, but in the geopolitics that surround them.

- Revenue: $2.53 billion vs. $2.54 billion expected
Restaurant Brands reported third-quarter net income attributable to common shareholders of $542 million, or $1.54 per share, up from $315 million, or 96 cents per share, a year earlier.
Excluding certain noncash items, the company earned $1.10 per share.
Net revenue rose 3.1% to $2.53 billion.
Across all of its restaurants, the company reported same-store sales growth of 3.8%. Restaurant Brands has reported same-store sales growth above 3% for the past five quarters.
While the broader industry saw traffic soften in the third quarter as gas prices stayed high, Restaurant Brands said it has not seen any significant changes in consumer behavior.
"The environment, from what we see, has been relatively stable over the last couple of quarters and even into recent months," Restaurant Brands CEO Josh Kobza told CNBC.
Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. The burger chain's home market is in the middle of multiyear turnaround, with a focus on improving its food and restaurants.
"The plans we've put in place over the last several years are working, and we're going to keep executing against them," Restaurant Brands Chair Patrick Doyle said on the company's earnings conference call. "Burger King has delivered over four years of industry outperformance, and now we've seen three consecutive quarters of truly exceptional results."
After improving the quality of its Whopper earlier this year, Burger King turned its attention to its nuggets and sauces.
"Nuggets and sauces, frankly, we knew for a while that there was an opportunity," Kobza told CNBC. "We've heard it loud and clear from our guests."
Since Burger King relaunched its nuggets on Sept. 1, with 100% white meat chicken, sales have shot up more than 35%, Kobza said on the earnings call. More core menu items will get an upgrade next year.
Tim Hortons reported same-store sales growth of 1.8% in Canada, its home market. In July, the coffee chain launched a line of matcha drinks, bringing more customers to its locations during the sleepier afternoon hours.
Popeyes was once again the laggard of Restaurant Brands' portfolio. The fried chicken chain's U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%.
In recent quarters, Popeyes has struggled as other chicken rivals have lured its customers away with discounts. Restaurant Brands is trying to stage a comeback with improved restaurant operations and a focus on its core menu.
Restaurant Brands previously forecast that Popeyes would return to same-store sales growth in the second half of 2026, but Kobza said on the earnings call that the company now believes it will take longer, although traffic is improving. The return of Popeyes' $6 Big Box promotion in September boosted sales less than expected, according to Kobza. Plus, the chain has scaled back its wings to refocus on its core menu items, hurting sales in the short term.
The company's international business saw same-store sales growth of 3.9%, fueled by its Burger King locations.

Under Sanctions, Russia Turns to Africa With Plans to Relocate Industrial Production
Russia is ready to move part of its industrial enterprises to Africa, Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced on October 29, The Moscow Times reported the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This fully corresponds to Russia's interests, especially today, when numerous sanctions are being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises," Putin stated at the Russia-Africa forum. He described the investment potential of Russian companies as "fairly high" and added that "there is work to be done here."
Putin stressed that investments in African countries must be "reliable and protected." Plants would then operate "regardless of the foreign policy situation," he explained.
He was responding to Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who argued that Africa must go beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods.
"We must develop our own industrial potential, modernize our agriculture, strengthen our energy infrastructure and logistics routes, and invest more in research and technology development," Ndayishimiye told the forum. He emphasized that Africa should become "a real market for production and sales" rather than remain a consumer market.
A day earlier, Putin told 22 African leaders, including those of Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and Mali, that Russia had achieved "impressive results" in high technology. He said Moscow was ready to share its know-how with its "African friends." Competitors "have to catch up with us in some areas and copy our developments," he emphasized.
Russian ministers and state companies have since set out their own offers. Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov announced that Russian companies were ready to manufacture goods in African countries under industrial cooperation.
"The main message we bring to Africa is: let's ensure sovereign development together," he stated. Reshetnikov proposed cooperation in pharmaceuticals and IT solutions. Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov expressed readiness to develop automobile manufacturing in partnership with African partners.
Rosatom proposed building floating nuclear power plants in coastal African countries. "As a starting step, a source such as a floating nuclear power unit could be a good entry point to both solve their tasks and join the nuclear club," a representative of the state corporation explained.
Russia's largest liquefied natural gas producer, Novatek, offered African countries its own production technology, proven on Arctic projects. Aluminum giant Rusal signed a memorandum with Ghana on a joint venture to mine and process bauxite, the raw material for aluminum.
Moscow's push into African markets follows steep losses in its traditional energy trade since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gazprom has lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union, with Russian gas exports expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021.
Exports are projected to fall to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028 once the EU gas embargo takes effect, a level last seen in the second half of the 1980s. Efforts to offset the losses through a major new supply deal with China have stalled over pricing, leaving talks on the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline suspended.

Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

- Category
- World
Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Russia has begun using an Arctic maritime route dating back to World War II to export grain for the first time, Reuters reported on October 28. The move comes as Moscow seeks alternatives to traditional shipping corridors through the Black and Baltic Seas amid growing security risks stemming from its war against Ukraine.
To address these difficulties, Russia has been redirecting grain shipments from its southern agricultural regions to Baltic Sea ports, offering subsidies for rail transportation. At the same time, Moscow has begun exploring the Arctic as an alternative export corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 28, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport and Demetra Holding, one of Russia’s largest grain trading companies, announced that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain, transported from the country’s main agricultural regions, was being loaded onto a vessel at the port.
According to Reuters, the vessel is expected to carry approximately 28,000 metric tons of wheat from Murmansk to Casablanca, Morocco.
Located nearly 2,000 kilometers north of Moscow, near Russia’s border with Norway, Murmansk offers access to international waters. The port also has historical significance, having served as a major entry point for Allied supplies delivered to the Soviet Union during World War II.
“At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said in a statement.
The development comes as Russia increasingly relies on Baltic Sea ports to maintain its grain exports.
According to Reuters, Russia exported approximately 1.2 million metric tons of grain through Baltic ports in September alone, accounting for more than 60% of its total seaborne grain shipments that month.
To accommodate the growing volumes, Russian companies have been converting port terminals previously used to handle fertilizers and coal into facilities capable of processing grain exports.
Russia has permitted grain-carrying vessels to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, temporarily authorizing departures from the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
Citing three sources familiar with the situation, Bloomberg reported that the clearance was issued on October 26, with at least one vessel having already crossed the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea.

Researchers develop AI tool to identify bacterial DNA in soil
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:49:12 CST
23:49:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Israeli researchers have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can identify bacterial DNA in tiny genetic fragments found in soil, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said Thursday.
Researchers extract DNA from soil samples to study the microorganisms living there, but identifying the source of many genetic fragments remains difficult.
The tool, called BBERT, is an AI model designed to process highly fragmented DNA/RNA sequences as short as 100 DNA letters and learn patterns in bacterial DNA, the university said in a statement.
In their study, published in Nucleic Acids Research, the researchers showed that the tool can identify bacterial DNA, including genetic material that can't be matched to existing reference databases.
The tool helps distinguish bacterial DNA from that of other organisms and identify fragments containing protein-making instructions, they said.
In tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from non-bacterial DNA with around 90 percent accuracy, identified protein-making fragments with 88 percent accuracy and their correct reading frames with 96 percent accuracy.
Tested on 1,969 publicly available soil DNA datasets, the tool identified many fragments that existing methods had left unclassified.
The researchers said that the tool could help uncover previously overlooked genetic information and better understand the diversity of life in soil. ■

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde attends a press conference at the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany, Oct. 29, 2026. The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday that it would leave its key interest rates unchanged. (ECB/Handout via Xinhua)
FRANKFURT, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday that it would leave its key interest rates unchanged.
The interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will remain unchanged at 2.5 percent, 2.65 percent and 2.9 percent, respectively.
Rising energy prices are posing upside risks to the inflation outlook but underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far, the ECB said in a press release.
"The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth."
Inflation in the euro area surged in September to 3.8 percent from 3.2 percent in August, hitting a three-year high. The rise in inflation has been driven largely by higher energy prices, according to data released by the European Commission.
The ECB has hiked interest rates twice this year, pushing the interest rate on the deposit facility up to 2.5 percent from two percent.
The ECB insists that it is "well positioned" to navigate the current elevated uncertainty and will still continue to follow its data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determine its future monetary policy stance.
The ECB is scheduled to publish its latest edition of the staff projections in December. ■

DAMASCUS, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- At least four people, including two children, have been reported dead amid heavy rainfall and flash floods across several Syrian provinces, while hundreds of families have been forced to leave displacement camps, local media and authorities said Thursday.
Syrian state-run newspaper Al-Thawra reported that two children drowned in separate incidents in the northern province of Raqqa and the eastern province of Deir al-Zour.
Another man, identified as Ali al-Salem, died after being swept away by floodwaters in the al-Buassi area west of Raqqa's Tabqa city, according to the report.
Syria's emergency and disaster management authorities also reported one death in a traffic accident in western Raqqa countryside.
Meanwhile, emergency teams had evacuated about 375 families from three flood-affected displacement camps in Raqqa countryside and rescued 15 civilians trapped in vehicles, according to state news agency SANA.
Floodwaters rendered seven bridges, culverts and unpaved roads unusable, and emergency crews pumped water from more than 150 homes and public facilities, including hospitals, schools and bakeries, according to the emergency and disaster management authorities.
In Kasrat Surour, the collapse of an earthen drainage crossing left more than 100 families surrounded by floodwaters, prompting emergency rescue operations.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a Britain-based war monitor, also reported extensive flooding in displacement camps, including Washokani and al-Talae in northeastern Hasakah province, where dozens of tents were inundated and families lost bedding, blankets and food supplies.
The Observatory said floodwaters disrupted traffic on several roads, including sections of the Aleppo-Raqqa highway, while heavy rainfall damaged homes and temporary shelters in other parts of northern Syria.
Education authorities suspended classes Thursday in public and private schools across Hasakah, Raqqa and Deir al-Zour as the severe weather continued.
Emergency teams remained deployed in affected areas, with authorities warning residents to avoid flood-prone areas and waterways. ■

Finnish news agency STT to end news services after 139 years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:49:00 CST
23:49:00 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Finland's national news agency STT announced on Thursday that it will shut down its news and photo services by the end of March 2027, ending 139 years of journalistic operations amid prolonged financial difficulties.
STT's board confirmed the decision after completing legally mandated negotiations with employees. The closure is expected to eliminate 89 positions, including 68 journalism jobs. In addition, 30 fixed-term employment contracts or framework agreements will end.
STT said its news and photo services would continue operating until March 31, 2027. Its press release distribution business, which employs seven people, would remain operational.
The agency attributed the closure to years of financial losses and a lack of shareholders' commitment to sustain and develop its operations. Previous cost-cutting measures had failed to restore financial viability.
Its financial situation worsened when Sanoma, Finland's major media group and STT's principal shareholder, stopped using the agency's services at the beginning of 2026.
STT CEO Kimmo Laaksonen described the closure as "a great tragedy for Finnish society as a whole," noting that the agency would mark its 139th anniversary on Sunday.
The Finnish government had earlier pledged 1.05 million euros (about 1.17 million U.S. dollars) in financial assistance to STT. However, the funding was never disbursed, and the Ministry of Transport and Communications suspended preparations for the subsidy in September pending a decision on the agency's future.
Founded in 1887, STT is one of the world's oldest national news agencies. The closure will leave Finland among the few European countries without a national news agency.
The Union of Journalists in Finland has warned that the loss of STT could weaken access to reliable information, particularly in regional and local media, which depend heavily on the agency for national and international news coverage.
The union said regional news outlets would face higher costs or reduced news coverage as they seek alternatives to STT's services. It also warned that the closure could threaten the survival of other struggling media organizations. ■

YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has made significant contributions to advancing negotiations at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), from pre-conference dialogue in Kunming to the ongoing global review of collective progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan told Xinhua.

"A majority of parties have submitted their national reports, laying an objective foundation for the assessment. Available evidence shows the world is far from reaching the 2030 targets," he said, noting that the first-ever global review of collective progress towards the KMGBF in Yerevan is of critical importance because it will clarify how close the world is to achieving its goals and identify implementation gaps.
Beyond the negotiations, China took the lead in establishing the Kunming Biodiversity Fund in 2021, contributing its own resources to help developing countries strengthen their conservation capacity. Officially launched in 2024, the fund offers new opportunities and helps turn decisions made at COP meetings into tangible results, he said.
Matevosyan said China and Armenia are already cooperating on national parks and protected areas.
"I had the honor of visiting China's Botanical Garden and China's Elephant Park during the Kunming Dialogue. My team and I met many scientists and specialist protected-area managers in China. The success of COP17 will not end on Oct. 30, as Armenia will hold the COP presidency for another two years, he said.

Orders grew even faster than sales, with the Arlington, Virginia-based defense electronics maker booking $1.64 billion in new funded orders in the three months ended September 30. That gave it a book-to-bill ratio of 1.5x, meaning it took in $1.50 of new business for every dollar of revenue it recognized, and the company said both figures were its strongest since it became a public company four years ago.
Funded backlog, which counts work that customers have placed on contract with money already committed but that the company has not yet delivered and booked as revenue, reached a record $5.64 billion. That figure is up 21% from $4.68 billion a year earlier and continues a steady climb through 2026, from $4.7 billion at the end of March and $5.1 billion at the end of June.
“These results reinforce a strategy that is working — investing ahead of demand, in both differentiated capability and capacity, to help our customers maintain overmatch and enable us to scale when the mission requires it,” said John Baylouny, President and CEO of Leonardo DRS.
Net earnings rose 60% to $115 million, or 43 cents per diluted share, from $72 million, or 26 cents, a year earlier, although a lower tax bill accounts for part of that increase. Operating earnings grew 25% to $116 million, while the income tax provision fell to $1 million from $15 million, and the company now assumes a full-year tax rate of 13%, down from 16.5% in its previous outlook.
Adjusted EBITDA, a measure that excludes interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and one-time items, rose 27% to $149 million, with the adjusted margin widening to 14.0% from 12.2%. The company credited program execution, a more profitable mix of work and higher volumes for the improvement.
The Advanced Sensing and Computing segment, the larger of the company’s two units, grew revenue 14% to $659 million on the strength of tactical radars and space sensing programs, while booking just over $1 billion in orders and lifting its operating margin to 8.6% from 7.8%. Demand for its radars has continued into the fourth quarter, after the company won a place on a $500 million counter-drone radar contract from Joint Interagency Task Force 401 in mid-October, although that figure is a ceiling for orders the company must still compete for rather than guaranteed work. On the space side, the U.S. Space Force in September selected Leonardo DRS to further develop sensor technology intended to detect, track and target fast-moving threats.
The Integrated Mission Systems segment, which includes electric power and propulsion work for naval vessels as well as force protection programs, grew revenue 12% to $428 million. Its operating margin climbed to 15.0% from 12.5%, even as the company increased spending on internal research and development. Much of that naval business rests on the U.S. Navy’s Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine program, for which Leonardo DRS holds contracts worth more than $3 billion to supply electric drive propulsion components, and in September the company also announced it would build the electric propulsion system for South Korea’s next-generation KDDX destroyer.
The quarter extended a run of growth this year, after Leonardo DRS reported first-quarter revenue of $846 million in May and second-quarter revenue of $913 million in July.
The new 2026 outlook calls for revenue of $3.95 billion to $3.985 billion, up from a prior range of $3.90 billion to $3.975 billion, along with Adjusted EBITDA of $545 million to $555 million and adjusted earnings per share of $1.50 to $1.53. Based on the $2.825 billion the company has recorded through September, the revenue range implies fourth-quarter sales of roughly $1.13 billion to $1.16 billion.
Cash generation was weaker in the quarter, with operating cash flow of $96 million and free cash flow of $61 million, down from $77 million a year earlier, as more money went into working capital. For the first nine months, free cash flow was negative $28 million, an improvement from negative $149 million in the same period of 2025.
Cash on hand fell to $294 million from $647 million at the end of 2025, largely because the company repaid $191 million of borrowings over nine months, cutting long-term debt to $165 million from $321 million and leaving nothing drawn on its credit facility at quarter end.
The board declared a quarterly dividend of 9 cents per share, payable November 25 to stockholders of record on November 12, and Leonardo DRS repurchased 288,633 shares for about $12 million during the quarter. Italy’s Leonardo S.p.A. owns 71.38% of the Nasdaq-listed company, according to the parent group.
The updated guidance excludes the pending purchase of Raft LLC, a McLean, Virginia-based developer of mission software that fuses data from multiple sensors, which Leonardo DRS agreed in July to buy in an all-cash deal valued at $450 million. The company plans to fund the purchase with cash on hand and borrowings under its revolving credit facility, and its third-quarter results already included $4 million in deal-related costs.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, pending regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

KABUL, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Afghanistan marked a strategic milestone this week with the opening of its first specialized mining exhibition, a platform designed to spotlight the nation's substantial mineral resources, attract domestic and international capital, and accelerate the shift toward value-added processing.

From southern Kandahar, a zinc oxide producer employing 60 workers highlighted its mineral extraction operations in Afghanistan's mountainous terrain. Welcoming the specialized event, he noted that transforming raw gemstones into finished products generates substantially greater value within the country. "We hope to establish contacts with other traders and show them that we have the capability to produce these kinds of products in Afghanistan," Esmatullah told Xinhua.

The purpose of holding this exhibition is to showcase the country's mineral products and take an effective step toward fostering cooperation and coordination among domestic and foreign investors, Hanafi said. ■

Climate change to cut rice, maize, sugarcane output in Southeast Asia: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:48:22 CST
23:48:22 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Climate change is projected to reduce production of key crops across Southeast Asia, with rice, maize and sugarcane facing declines, according to a study released on Thursday by the Singapore Food Agency and the National University of Singapore.
The ASEAN Agri Climate Impact Twenty study projects average rice production to decline by 3 to 5 percent between 2025 and 2044, while maize output could fall by 5 to 6 percent and sugarcane production by 1 to 4 percent.
In contrast, cassava production is projected to increase by 16 percent, while soybean output could rise by 11 to 13 percent.
"More favorable average projections for some crops do not mean that they are free from climate-related risks. Production could still be affected by variability in climate conditions in any particular year including extreme heat, heavy rainfall or drought in an unfavorable year," the report said.
Very strong El Niño events could reduce average crop production across the region by up to about 10 percent, the study found. Rice and rain-fed farming systems are generally more vulnerable to such events.
Overall, Southeast Asia is expected to experience rising temperatures, more frequent and prolonged heat waves, and increasingly variable rainfall, potentially disrupting water availability, planting schedules and crop yields. ■

Feature: Chinese hospital ship brings relief to Ghanaians
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:48:22 CST
23:48:22 KST

by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- For nearly a year, Eugene Amartey Annan, a young Ghanaian engineer, has endured the pain of living with a hernia. This condition occurs when an internal organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot or opening in the surrounding muscle or tissue wall, most commonly in the abdomen, groin and testicles.
The condition became severe to the point that Annan found it difficult to work, with the cost of treatment for a local Ghanaian worker quite prohibitive.
But a change came when the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Ghana's eastern port of Tema on Oct. 23 for a friendly visit and medical mission, the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the West African country.
On Monday, the medical team successfully operated on Annan in the theatre.
Speaking with Xinhua at the recovery ward on the military hospital vessel, Annan added that although he felt a little pain the day after the surgery, some pain relievers given to him had made the pain subside, and he was hoping to be discharged soon.
Annan lauded the medical workers on the vessel for their efficiency and professionalism, thanking them for the free medical care. "They pamper us so well that any illness will vanish. They are bringing China to Ghana."
Meanwhile, Sophia Annan, mother of the 45-year-old engineer, who came in to attend to her son at the recovery ward, also had a taste of the benevolent and efficient medical service provided by the personnel on board the vessel, who treated her hypertensive condition and eye problem free of charge.
"Whatever you ask them, they have the patience to answer you. The service provided here is free and we didn't pay anything," Sophia Annan said.
She added that the military medical personnel from China handled the patients with utmost care and empathy, serving them with food, toiletries, and dental care products.
Besides Annan and his mother, thousands of Ghanaians also received free medical care from the medical personnel on board the Auspicious Ark. Among these was Kingsford Adjei, 30, a student of the University of Cape Coast, who underwent surgery on board the huge Chinese naval hospital ship to correct a fracture sustained during a football game in January.
Adjei had to discontinue treatment due to the high cost of surgery, and had to discontinue his part-time job and depend solely on his mother for upkeep. But on Monday, medical personnel onboard the Chinese Navy hospital ship carried out free surgery on his right leg, and he was recovering in the ward when Xinhua visited.
"Right now, everything is successful; I'll go back to school again and do everything by myself. Thank you. They shouldn't stop. They should keep on doing it. Maybe there are people who didn't receive the opportunity now. Therefore, if they keep on coming, many people will benefit," he pleaded.
Moreover, many others also visited with gynaecological issues, dental issues, and everyday health issues, such as fevers, among others.
Among other visitors were those who also reported to the ophthalmology unit of the floating hospital, where they received treatment and care for age-old eye problems. Among these was Nicolas Senam Nanevie, a 48-year-old Ghanaian teacher, who had suffered eye problems with blurred eyesight since childhood, with spectacles hardly improving his condition.
Nanevie was diagnosed with glaucoma, which he was told was not fully developed for surgery, and he had been applying eye drops for temporary relief. However, when the 48-year-old teacher visited the Chinese naval hospital ship on Sunday, he was booked for surgery on Monday.
"I've been asked to visit a local eye clinic after 10 days to have the stitches removed. I am so happy and grateful," Nanevie told Xinhua.
Huang Zhen, an ophthalmologist at the eye center on the navy hospital ship, told Xinhua that an average of 200 people have visited the center daily with different eye problems since the ship arrived in Ghana last Friday.
"Most of the eye problems they came with are presbyopia, cataract, glaucoma, and others. Many patients need cataract and glaucoma surgeries, and this time we have many cataracts and glaucoma," Huang said.
She praised the Ghanaian volunteers working with the Chinese medical personnel for their efficiency and support. ■

Joint Statement on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) Sanctions North Korea Cyber security Joint statement On : October 29th 2026 The text of the following statement was released by Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union. Throughout October and today, the European Union (EU) and the governments of Australia and the United States have implemented sanctions to target the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities, and actors involved in unlawful DPRK-Russia cooperation. Their actions represent their efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s ability to support its unlawful development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missiles, and to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation. These designations build on detailed reporting published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which monitors and reports on DPRK’s non-compliance with UN Security Council resolutions in the absence of the UNSCR 1718 Committee Panel of Experts, whose mandate renewal was vetoed by Russia in 2024. The MSMT’s first and second reports outlined the DPRK’s unlawful military cooperation with Russia, along with cyber-enabled IT worker fraud, both of which serve to fund Pyongyang’s unlawful weapons programs. In September 2026, the MSMT released its third report detailing the DPRK’s deployment of overseas workers to generate revenue for its WMD and ballistic missile programs. The MSMT will continue to monitor, expose, and report on attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions by the DPRK. The MSMT and EU reaffirm our commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK, calling on it to abandon its unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs, and taking action to counter DPRK attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions. We continue to strongly support the implementation of all DPRK-related UN Security Council resolutions. We call on all UN Member States, and especially permanent members of the Security Council, to fully implement these resolutions.

FIFA expects a record $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:07 EET
23:42:07 KST

FIFA expects a record $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup
Kyiv • UNN
FIFA expects around $5 billion from tickets and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup — five times more than in Qatar. The tournament was attended by 6.81 million fans.
FIFA is expected to receive around $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality services at the 2026 World Cup — more than five times what it earned at the tournament in Qatar four years ago. UNN reports this, citing The New York Times.
Details
FIFA President Gianni Infantino previously announced that this year's World Cup, co-hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, generated $15 billion in revenue, $2 billion more than expected.
This means that one-third of this revenue came solely from ticket sales and hospitality services, although the $5 billion figure is part of an ongoing audit, so it could be slightly higher or lower.
The 2026 World Cup included 40 more matches (104) than Qatar (64), while ticket sales and hospitality services at the 2022 tournament generated $929 million in revenue.
The governing body of world football was widely condemned for its ticketing policy at this year's tournament, introducing dynamic pricing for the first time and also receiving a 30 percent commission on any resale.
One consequence of FIFA not allowing a traditional secondary ticket market in the United States and instead permitting resales only through its own platform was that it prevented money from going to advertising intermediaries and, as the governing body says, from being reinvested in world football.
The initial prices announced before the tournament were the highest in World Cup history, with tickets for the final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, United States, on July 19 starting at $4,185 — seven times the price of the cheapest ticket for the 2022 final in Qatar.
In response to what they called "sky-high" prices, Football Supporters Europe and Euroconsumers, a consumer protection organization, filed an official complaint with the European Commission. FIFA has consistently defended the prices, pointing out that any revenue generated from ticket sales will ultimately be reinvested back into football, and also noting that they reflect the North American market, where it is not uncommon to pay hundreds of dollars to attend sporting events.
However, following widespread negative reaction, they introduced a limited number — 1,000 tickets priced at $60 — for each of the 104 World Cup matches.
FIFA emphasized that the tournament was attended by "an unprecedented 6.81 million fans" and that the "attendance rate" was "99.7 percent across all matches."
"The revenue generated by the tournament will provide unprecedented resources for FIFA's member associations to invest in the game, such as supporting the development of men's, women's and youth football across all 211 FIFA member associations every day of the year," a FIFA spokesperson added.
"As announced earlier this month following the FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, the FIFA administration presented the FIFA Council with a proposed initiative called the \"FIFA Surplus Solidarity Program\", which envisages using part of FIFA's reserves to more than double the level of planned funding for the 2027–2030 period to $6.35 billion," the statement said.

The net profit of Russia’s “PhosAgro” fell by 37% in the third quarter of 2026 — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
PhosAgro’s net profit in the third quarter of 2026 fell to $156 million. Costs rose by more than 30%, while debt reached $4.5 billion.
Net profit of one of Russia’s largest fertilizer producers, "PhosAgro," fell by 37% in the third quarter of 2026, to $156 million, while production costs and debt are rising. This is reported by Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, reports UNN.
Details
Over the nine months, gross profit fell by 27%, to $1.7 billion, while net profit declined by approximately 67%, to $389 million. The cost of production rose by more than 30% year-on-year. Sulfur and sulfuric acid, which are essential for producing phosphate fertilizers, became more expensive: about $503 million was spent on them in six months
According to available information, the company sells mainly for export, particularly to India, Brazil, and African countries, and therefore depends on global prices, demand, and delivery costs.
Last year, it produced 12.2 million tonnes of products for more than 100 countries, but large volumes do not generate profit if selling prices lag behind costs
At the same time, the company’s debt is also increasing. In particular, according to the intelligence service, debt at the end of the third quarter amounted to about $4.5 billion, 11% more than at the end of 2025.
Last year, capital expenditures amounted to about $836 million, while free cash flow was only $253 million. If profit continues to decline, modernization will have to be financed through loans.
A similar picture can be seen throughout Russian industry: large production and export volumes are increasingly failing to translate into profit

Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
A Ukrainian man living in Monaco has been charged in connection with the death of Antoine de Massy, a relative of Prince Albert II, the ruler of the wealthy European principality.
The 42-year-old suspect, whose identity has not been disclosed, has reportedly lived in Monaco for three decades. Prosecutor General Stephane Thibault announced a judicial investigation on Wednesday.
According to local media, the Ukrainian national has been charged with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger. He denies wrongdoing and has been remanded in custody.
De Massy, 29, whose father is a first cousin of Prince Albert II, was found dead on Sunday evening after apparently falling approximately 13 meters from an elevated section of the coastal Boulevard du Larvotto into a garden behind a luxury residence.
The former competitive tennis player was reportedly last seen alive overnight Saturday into Sunday, leaving a nightclub apparently intoxicated and accompanied by another man. His family alerted authorities when he failed to attend a gathering, triggering a search that led to the discovery of his body in the secluded garden.
Thibault said CCTV footage showed the suspect accompanying de Massy along Boulevard du Larvotto. The Ukrainian national was arrested on Monday, although it remains unclear whether he was the man who reportedly left the nightclub with the victim.
Earlier this year, Monaco, known as a haven for millionaires, was rocked by a bombing targeting Ukrainian-born businessman Vadim Ermolaev, who was injured alongside members of his family.
The alleged bomber was identified as a Ukrainian woman who was later found dead in her home country, reportedly killed by her handlers. Investigators identified the suspected masterminds as an active operative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, and an unofficial agent of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Both are now in Ukrainian custody.
Kiev portrayed the bombing as a profit-driven crime carried out by rogue agents. However, one suspect claimed the operation had been authorized by the Ukrainian state as a legitimate act of war against Russia.
The case resurfaced this week when former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said the Monaco bombing “echoed” an alleged Ukrainian intelligence plot against him that Austrian law enforcement had thwarted.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine for Vienna last month and was subsequently dismissed by parliament after a subordinate was accused of running a protection racket on his behalf. The Austrian authorities confirmed the arrests of suspected Ukrainian intelligence operatives in early October.

- A Saudi Defense Ministry photo from King Khalid Air Base appears to show a Bahraini F-16 squadron pilot and a Pakistan Air Force member, analysts said.
- Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Pakistan have not commented on the image or confirmed any Bahraini deployment to the base.
A photo released by Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry from a visit by its top military officer to King Khalid Air Base in the kingdom’s southwest appears to show a Royal Bahraini Air Force fighter pilot and a member of the Pakistan Air Force at the base, open-source analysts at OSINTWarfare pointed out in a post.
Gen. Fayyadh Al-Ruwaili, chief of the general staff, visited military units in the southern region, units deployed along the border with Yemen and military commands in Khamis Mushait and Jazan, where he received briefings on operational missions, the Saudi Defense Ministry announced. The ministry’s statement did not mention any foreign personnel, and neither Bahrain nor Pakistan has commented on the image.
According to OSINTWarfare, the photo shows a Bahraini officer with the rank of major wearing the patch of the Royal Bahraini Air Force’s 1st Tactical Fighter Squadron, known as the Desert Falcons, on his right shoulder. The squadron flies F-16C/D fighters from Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain and is responsible for defending Bahraini airspace, and the analysts said it has not previously been publicly known to have taken part in operations abroad. A Pakistan Air Force member can be seen in the background, identifiable by his uniform, they added, though the image does not show whether the personnel are deployed to the base, how many are there or what aircraft, if any, they brought.
King Khalid Air Base sits outside Khamis Mushait in Asir province and is the main Royal Saudi Air Force hub for the southern border with Yemen, an area that has been under fire this autumn as Houthi missile and drone attacks in September struck targets in Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait and Saudi Arabia resumed its air war against the Iran-backed group.
Bahrain sent F-16s to fight alongside Saudi Arabia when it joined the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis in 2015, and on Dec. 30 that year a Royal Bahraini Air Force F-16 crashed in Jazan province while flying for the coalition, with the pilot surviving. Bahraini officials did not say at the time which squadron the aircraft belonged to.
Pakistani fighter and support aircraft arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base in the Eastern Province in April under the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement the two countries signed in September 2025, and a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times this month that Pakistan Air Force jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthis. Analysts estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to the kingdom, including air force and army air defense units.
Britain said on Oct. 20 that Royal Air Force Typhoons will fly defensive patrols over Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye is preparing to send personnel under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, pending approval by its parliament.
Saudi Arabia and Bahrain have not said whether Bahraini F-16s are operating from King Khalid Air Base or flying missions over Yemen.

Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
According to a Ukrinform correspondent, this was stated during a briefing by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President.
“Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the world produces ‘Patriots’ to counter them. In other words, this balance looks very strange. If we add North Korean missiles to this, and the missiles produced by Iran, then we realize that global production of anti-ballistic missiles—such as the PAC-3, for example—needs to be increased. But there are currently problems and limitations, and while the Pentagon is trying to increase these production volumes, it’s difficult to do so,” Beskrestnov noted.
He noted that Ukraine could obtain licenses to manufacture anti-ballistic missiles, but the problem lies in the backlog for their components.
To address the shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Ukraine is requesting that missiles be provided on loan, which it would later return once it begins domestic production; however, due to the unstable global situation, European partners are unwilling to agree to such a move. For its part, the U.S., which has a sufficient supply of PAC-3s, is very limited in how many it is willing to provide.
“These missiles are in the United States, and there’s a stockpile there—some say 3,000, others 4,000; there are 5,000 missiles in the U.S.—and to protect Kyiv, for example, where the ‘Patriot’ system is deployed, through the winter, we need about 4–5% of the U.S. stockpile. That’s a very small portion. And we’re asking the U.S.: ‘Give us this, because the Russians will destroy our infrastructure,’ but this requires a political decision. A decision from the U.S. government. They could give us these missiles—it wouldn’t affect their own defense, because, as I’ve already said, it’s literally 4 percent. But they won’t. We’re receiving a very small number, and we see what’s happening now. I actually believe this is our number one problem,” Beskrestnov noted.
According to the adviser, the situation on the front lines is currently stable, and Ukraine will be able to withstand the enemy even in the event of additional mobilization in Russia. At the same time, the biggest problem today is urban warfare and the enemy’s intention to completely destroy Ukraine’s economic potential.
“Even if they mobilize an additional 300,000 people, that solves nothing. We’ll simply produce more FPVs and field more crews to attack the Russians. We’re already facing the problem that our troops aren’t meeting their targets because there simply aren’t that many Russians to begin with. It sounds very strange, but it’s true. In other words, we understand that the war has changed,” the adviser noted.
According to him, the enemy is destroying infrastructure, bridges, and warehouses in order to cripple Ukraine’s economy.
Beskrestnov emphasized that the enemy is currently stockpiling missiles and “Shahed” drones to continue attacking critical infrastructure. Kyiv will be the primary target, as the capital is a symbolic city for the Russian occupiers.
“Kyiv is a symbolic place for our enemy. They understand that the government is here, and they understand that the international community is watching Kyiv. That is why they want to attack Kyiv specifically,” the adviser emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine currently needs an aid package consisting of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from Europe and several other countries; subsequently, the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program will become operational, and contracts with Germany for the procurement of the relevant interceptors will take effect.

Inflation is accelerating, the economy is slowing: what decisions the NBU and ECB made and how they will affect Ukrainians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:29:20 EET
23:29:20 KST

Inflation is accelerating, the economy is slowing: what decisions the NBU and ECB made and how they will affect Ukrainians
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU raised its rate to 16.5% due to inflation and pressure on the hryvnia. The ECB left rates unchanged amid energy risks.
October 29 can confidently be called a day of important monetary decisions: two major financial regulators immediately announced their resolutions. The economic well-being of Ukrainians depends on them: the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and the European Central Bank (ECB). The NBU raised its key policy rate to 16.5%, while the ECB left its rates unchanged. In addition, both regulators highlighted the risks stemming from rising energy prices. What other key decisions did the financial regulators make, and how will they affect the daily lives of Ukrainians? UNN reports.
Why the NBU decided to raise its key policy rate
Until October 29, 2026, the key policy rate stood at 16%. The regulator now seeks to curb price growth, support hryvnia savings, and reduce pressure on the foreign exchange market. The NBU hopes that a higher rate will help support hryvnia savings and encourage banks to increase deposit yields.
In addition, as the financial regulator emphasizes, declining exports and the consequences of Russian attacks have increased pressure on the hryvnia. Therefore, the NBU expects higher returns on hryvnia savings to help stabilize the foreign exchange market.
Inflation in Ukraine exceeded the NBU's expectations: why did this happen
In September 2026, consumer inflation in Ukraine accelerated to 10% year-on-year, while core inflation, which reflects more persistent price changes, stood at 8.8%. According to the National Bank's estimates, the trend continued in October. The main reasons were higher fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East and Russian strikes on warehouses and logistics facilities. This increases business costs and intensifies price pressure on consumers.
The inflation forecast for 2026 was (raised, - ed.) to 12.5%. According to the NBU's estimates, the consequences of shelling alone will add about 0.7 percentage points to annual inflation.
For 2027, the NBU forecasts inflation of 7.3%, driven by an expected decline in oil prices and the effects of monetary policy. A return to the target of 5% is expected in 2028.
The NBU also took into account the risks of increased budget spending on defense and reconstruction, a labor shortage, and pressure on wages. At the same time, the regulator warns that a deterioration in the security situation could cool consumer demand and partially restrain inflation. The blocking of ports could lead to a short-term decline in purchase prices for certain products.
National regulator downgrades forecast for Ukraine's economy: what to expect next
Along with its decision on the rate, the NBU revised its assessment of economic dynamics. According to the regulator's preliminary calculations, real gross domestic product contracted by 0.5% in the third quarter compared with the same period last year. The reasons were the blockade of ports and Russian strikes on industry and logistics. Metallurgical and ore-producing enterprises suffered the greatest losses; the situation also deteriorated in other sectors.
For 2026, the NBU forecasts a 0.4% contraction in GDP and estimates the negative contribution of shelling at 1.9 percentage points. In 2027, the economy could grow by 0.4% according to its forecast, provided logistics improve; in 2028, it could grow by 2.2% if security risks decline. Growth will be supported by investment in the defense sector and infrastructure recovery.
What will happen to Ukrainians' deposits and loans
The change in the key policy rate will not affect the terms of all deposits and loans currently held by Ukrainians. At least, this will not happen immediately. Each bank will make such decisions independently and gradually.
The NBU notes that small banks were the first to respond to previous decisions. Recently, large institutions have also begun reviewing rates on hryvnia deposits. Ukrainians themselves continued to increase their hryvnia deposits and investments in domestic government bonds.
Lending has not stopped, however. According to the NBU, in September, the volume of net hryvnia loans to businesses increased by more than 32% year-on-year, while lending to households rose by 38%. The regulator also announced four packages of changes aimed at supporting lending to the defense industry, the energy sector, agriculture, and trade.
A moderate increase in the key policy rate is a balanced decision that makes it possible to maintain a balance between controlling inflation and supporting the economy
At the same time, the NBU forecasts that the rate will remain at 16.5% until the second quarter of 2027, but allows for a review if risks change.
International assistance for Ukraine: what is happening with it and why it remains important
In the third quarter, Ukraine received less international assistance than expected, primarily due to delays in reforms. The laws passed by parliament in October should help unblock funding from the EU and the IMF.
The NBU's forecast for 2026 envisages approximately $50 billion in direct budget support and more than $32 billion under the defense component of the Ukraine Support Loan program. For 2027, $52 billion and $37 billion, respectively, have been allocated. Under this scenario, Ukraine's international reserves are expected to exceed $62 billion in 2026–2027.
However, the NBU warns that official Kyiv may receive financial support unevenly. At the same time, the risk of delays has decreased somewhat recently following Ukraine's fulfillment of some of its obligations to partners and earlier signals regarding financing for next year.
What decisions did the European Central Bank make
On the same day, the ECB Governing Council left all three key interest rates unchanged. The deposit facility rate is 2.50%, the rate on main refinancing operations is 2.65%, and the marginal lending facility rate is 2.90%.
The ECB explained the pause by citing uncertainty. Higher energy prices threaten to accelerate inflation and slow economic growth, while the full impact of the energy shock has not yet emerged. According to the ECB, underlying price pressures remain relatively stable, and wages have so far not responded significantly to the energy shock. Financing conditions have tightened since the previous meeting.
The Governing Council is not committing in advance to any specific path for interest rates
The ECB's target is inflation of 2% over the medium term. However, future decisions will depend primarily on new data, forecasts, and risks.
At the same time, the ECB continues to gradually reduce its portfolios of securities purchased under the APP and PEPP programs: proceeds from maturing securities are no longer being reinvested. In addition, the ECB remains ready to use the available instruments if instability in financial markets hinders the transmission of its monetary policy across all euro area countries. In particular, a special transmission protection instrument has been provided for this purpose.
How the decisions of the two regulators differ
The NBU raised its rate amid accelerating inflation and risks to the hryvnia. The ECB left rates unchanged to assess the consequences of the energy shock for the euro area. However, it is not correct to directly compare Ukraine's 16.5% rate with the ECB's 2.5% deposit facility rate as indicators of borrowing costs. These are different instruments in different economies, with different inflation targets and risks.
For Ukrainian depositors, the key consequence of the NBU's decision may be continued support for hryvnia deposit rates. For borrowers, the cost of new loans will depend on banks' terms, while for businesses, the restoration of logistics, access to financing, and the security situation will also be important.

Russia has found a World War II-era route in the Arctic for grain — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Russia has found a World War II-era route in the Arctic for grain — media
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is sending its first shipment of grain through Murmansk amid the blockade of Black Sea trade. About 28,000 tonnes of wheat are headed to Morocco.
Russia has, for the first time, turned to an Arctic shipping route dating back to World War II to export grain, amid the fact that Russia’s war against Ukraine has halted trade in the Black Sea, while officials warn of risks in the NATO-controlled Baltic Sea. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Russia, seeking to retain its key grain customers in the Middle East and Asia, has sought to redirect exports to Baltic Sea ports by subsidizing rail transportation from the fertile southern regions, but has also been considering opportunities in the Arctic.
The Murmansk Commercial Seaport and the Demetra holding company, one of the country’s largest trading firms, said on Wednesday, October 28, that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain from "key agricultural regions" was being loaded onto a vessel.
Murmansk, located nearly 2,000 km north of Moscow, near the border with Norway, can be reached through neutral waters. Allied convoys used the port during World War II to deliver goods to the Soviet Union.
"At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport is rapidly opening an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers," the port said in a statement.
According to shipping data and a market source, about 28,000 metric tons of wheat are to be loaded in Murmansk onto a vessel bound for the port of Casablanca in Morocco.
Russia has redirected its trade mainly to Baltic Sea ports, which handled 1.2 million tons in September, accounting for more than 60% of all grain exports by sea. Companies are repurposing fertilizer and coal terminals to handle grain.
Some Kremlin officials, the publication writes, have warned of risks from potential hostile actions by European NATO member states in the region. All countries with access to the Baltic Sea, except Russia, are NATO members.
Turkey, an importer of grain from Russia, led efforts to establish a ceasefire and restore supplies in the Black Sea, but Russia said it was no longer interested in a new Black Sea grain deal.

European Commission rejects Baltics' €500 million anti-drone request
The European Commission rejected an appeal from the Baltic defense ministers for €500 million in additional support for drone defense for the eastern flank, suggesting they borrow the money instead.
The ministers from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania sent the request at the end of September.

The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument was launched last year and provides €150 billion in favourable loans for defense procurement across the EU.

Türkiye will continue working to deepen cooperation with Turkic states across all fields, drawing on longstanding fraternal ties, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday ahead of a summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara.
Fidan made the remarks on US social media platform X following a meeting of OTS foreign ministers held ahead of the leaders’ gathering, which is being hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
“I hope the summit we will hold tomorrow under the hosting of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will bring blessings to the Turkic world,” Fidan said.
He added that consultations rooted in traditions inherited from previous generations would strengthen solidarity and help member states achieve shared objectives.
Ankara summit to focus on unity and cooperation
The summit, scheduled for Thursday and Friday in Ankara, is being held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.”
According to the organisation, the gathering will bring together the leaders of member states, senior representatives from observer countries and the OTS secretary general to discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation, among other issues.
The meeting is expected to provide an opportunity to review existing partnerships and explore ways to expand collaboration across the Turkic world.
Five member states, several observers
Established in 2009 as the Turkic Council, the organisation adopted its current name at its eighth summit in Istanbul in 2021.
Its five members are Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus and the Economic Cooperation Organization participate as observers.
Fidan’s remarks underscore Ankara’s commitment to strengthening ties within the organisation and advancing cooperation based on shared history, cultural links and common goals.
