Germany seeks new head of state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Germany seeks new head of state
October 29, 2026
Wanted: A new head of state — female, male, or other. Requirements: German citizen, entitled to vote, minimum age 40. Please apply as soon as possible! Availability starting January 30, 2027; job starts March 19, 2027.
This is not an official job posting, but Germany's federal government is indeed looking for someone to fill the nation's highest office. Having already served two terms, current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is no longer eligible for another, leaving the position open for a successor. Many feel that it is time for Germany's first-ever female head of state.
"The person should have a certain level of public recognition, be politically unbiased, capable of bringing people together, approachable and a reasonably good [public] speaker," political scientist Ursula Münch told DW.
In Germany, a federal parliamentary republic, the president serves as head of state and a representative of the country as well as someone who embodies moral authority for the nation. Unlike in the US, France, or Russia, the president does not wield extensive political power or direct government affairs.
Steinmeier was nominated by his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), in 2009. However, once elected via a convention of parliamentarians and state electors, a president-elect has to suspend their party membership in order to serve in the office apolitically. This time, it is Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the senior partner in the coalition government with the SPD and the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which has the right to nominate a candidate.
Political scientist Münch said that "the three parties must agree on a person who is acceptable for all three." Since the convention that will select Steinmeier's successor is currently controlled by these three parties and their delegates, it is very likely that whomever Merz nominates will be elected.
Will Germany soon have its first female president?
"Well, I would really like it to be a woman this time. We've had 12 male federal presidents since 1949 — it's about time for a woman. But if the right man were to be nominated, I'd be fine with that too," said Münch. According to an August survey conducted by the Forsa polling institute for the RTL television network, about 74% of German respondents say they don't care whether it's a man or a woman. Another 19% explicitly want a woman, while 5% prefer a man.
Ilse Aigner, president of the Bavarian State Parliament in Munich, appears to have a good chance. Aigner is a member of the smallest party in the coalition, the Bavarian CSU, and is considered a unifying figure. She also has experience in government in Berlin, having served as agricultural minister at the federal level. She enjoys strong support within her Bavarian CSU party, whose leader Markus Söder recently said: "It would be tremendous if she became federal president."
Even members of the opposition Greens and the SPD are full of praise for Aigner's candidacy. "What are we actually waiting for? Surely Ilse Aigner has long since secured a majority across party lines?" asked SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch recently. However, Merz, who is friends with Aigner, has remained tight-lipped so far — possibly also because Aigner is not a member of Merz's party, but rather of its smaller sister party, the CSU.
Several female presidential candidates
Other potential successors from the CDU membership have been mentioned: Bundestag President Julia Klöckner, former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Education Minister Karin Prien. Hesse's state premier, Boris Rhein, is also a possible candidate. In recent days, another name has been making the rounds: lawyer Ines Claus, who serves as CDU's parliamentary group leader in Hesse and deputy party chair at the federal level — and is largely unknown.
However, rumors that she would be nominated were swiftly shot down by the chancellor. Sources close to Merz emphasized that he has so far "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal." There are "a number of suitable" options, sources added.
The president is elected every five years by the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments. Among them are also prominent figures from the spheres of culture, science, sports and society. The candidate who receives more than 631 votes goes on to assume office. The governing parties — the CDU/CSU and the SPD — have a combined total of 682 votes, a comfortable majority.
Presidential role key amid polarization and crisis
The office of the president is often underestimated as merely a ceremonial role. Yet, as an authority standing above the political parties, this person wields considerable political, legal and moral influence. This is especially true in times of political polarization and international crises. While the president does not govern like a chancellor, he or she represents Germany both at home and abroad.
"From a constitutional perspective, the federal president is enormously important. For example, in a political crisis, he could decide whether it makes more sense to dissolve the Bundestag or to advocate for a minority government," explained political scientist Münch. In addition, he reviews and signs laws proposed by politicians.
What happens next?
The federal chancellor and CDU chairman has an interest in an orderly process, say sources close to the government. The "first milestone" will be the meetings of the CDU Presidium and Executive Board on November 9. Until then, discussions will be held with the state chairpersons of the CDU and the CSU. Sources made it clear that the SPD and the Greens will also be consulted, "since the election of the federal president should have broad support across the democratic spectrum."
That is how political scientist Münch sees it: "I still consider the question open, with a slight edge for CSU candidate Ilse Aigner." But there could still be a real surprise, she added.
This article was originally published in German.

U.S. military trains on palletized SUADS anti-drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:21:42 UTC
23:21:42 KST

- U.S. soldiers and airmen trained on Trust Automation’s RD-SUADS, a self-powered counter-drone system that fits on a standard 463L military cargo pallet.
- RD-SUADS runs four days on its diesel generator and belongs to the SUADS family ordered under a $490 million U.S. Air Force contract.
U.S. Army soldiers and U.S. Air Force airmen at Grafenwoehr Training Area in Germany are training on the Rapidly Deployable Small-Unmanned Air Defense System, or RD-SUADS, a palletized counter-drone system built by Trust Automation of San Luis Obispo, California, as they test how training across services can sharpen the response to drone threats, U.S. Army Europe and Africa said on social media.
Photos released with the post show the troops working with the system, which the counter-drone news account Counter Unmanned Systems identified as RD-SUADS. The Army did not say which units are taking part, how long the training will run or whether the system will be fielded with units in Europe. Grafenwoehr hosted a similar effort in February, when U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa ran its Joint Multi-Domain Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems Operator Course with soldiers, airmen and Marines to assess opening the course to more services.
RD-SUADS is the air-transportable member of Trust Automation’s Small-Unmanned Air Defense System family, designed to detect, track, identify and defeat small drones at bases and deployed sites. The company built it to be shipped and set up quickly without relying on local power.
“Promoting combat agility, this C‑sUAS is a self-contained, self-powered system that fits within a 463L pallet, enabling easy transport via military aircraft. Equipped with an integrated diesel generator with standalone operational capacity for four days between refueling. Additionally, the shore power interface allows sites with power infrastructure operate the system utilizing standard DoD generator connections and base power connections,” Trust Automation said.
The 463L pallet is the standard cargo pallet used by U.S. military transport aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17, so the system can be loaded and flown in with the same handling equipment as other air cargo. The SUADS family also includes a fixed-site tower version for permanent bases and an expeditionary version sized to travel as checked baggage and fit in larger SUVs. The U.S. Department of War’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 lists the systems in its 2026 counter-small drone quick reference guide, noting they can host several electronic warfare capabilities to defeat small drones without firing a shot.
Radar is a central sensor. In April, Echodyne said its EchoShield radar had been chosen as the primary radar for SUADS, with RD-SUADS carrying up to four of the units, after the U.S. Air Force awarded Trust Automation a $490 million contract to develop, prototype and produce counter-drone systems through 2030. That contract is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity deal, meaning the U.S. Air Force can order systems in varying numbers and configurations over its life, and Echodyne’s radar now feeds all three SUADS versions.
The system has already been tested with the U.S. Army. Trust Automation said in October that SUADS completed a U.S. Army operational assessment during a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California, where it detected and engaged drones at roughly 2 to 6 km (1.2 to 3.7 miles), with coverage reaching about 7 km (4.3 miles) in favorable conditions. In that configuration, the system combined radar and electro-optical and infrared sensors with the NINJA and DroneBuster electronic attack systems.

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
October 29, 2026
This article contains descriptions of rape, exploitation and sexual assault. Reader discretion is advised.
Sadio Konimba had hoped for a better future. The 26-year-old had lost her husband and was left alone with her child in Bamako, the capital of Mali.
When an acquaintance told her about the possibility of reaching Europe via the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau, she decided to make the journey. She left her 6-year-old daughter behind with relatives for the time being.
Konimba says she was invited to the country's capital, Bissau, with the promise of work and better chances of eventually continuing on to Europe.
She was told the journey from Bamako to Bissau would cost between 100,000–125,000 CFA francs (roughly €150-€190, or $170-$210), which she paid. She had only intended to stay temporarily in Guinea-Bissau, but when she wanted to return to Mali, her money was not refunded.
"I had to pay a large sum of money," Sadio told DW, adding that instead of the prospects she had been promised, she was confronted with a very different reality.
According to Konimba's account, men from Senegal offered to repay the money she had paid if she "worked" for them. When she realized what that meant, she refused and demanded her money back. To this day, she has received nothing.
Jane, a 21-year-old woman from Sierra Leone, recounted how she was subjected to an attempted rape and other abuses at the hands of a criminal network. She told French news agency Agence France-Presse they even tried to force her into prostitution.
Sadio and Jane are among dozens of victims of a suspected human trafficking ring that was dismantled by police following an operation in Guinea-Bissau on October 21. The intervention followed complaints from victims who had reported abductions and fraud.
In a written statement to DW, the criminal investigation police said that more than five suspects had been arrested.
Trapped by fales promises
According to police, the network used a front company to lure people with promises of jobs and assistance with migration to Europe.
Around 70 people are believed to have fallen victim to the scheme. Most came from abroad, including Guinea, Mali, Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal. The suspected perpetrators allegedly charged victims between 400,000 and 700,000 CFA francs for each journey to Guinea-Bissau.
According to preliminary findings, the victims were held against their will in Bissau, subjected to pressure and forced to take part in fraudulent pyramid schemes. They were expected to recruit additional participants into the schemes through social media.
To make their operations appear legitimate, those responsible allegedly used false contact details for supposed offices in Canada, the United States and Portugal. Information from Interpol, the international police agency, helped investigators uncover the network, according to police.
Issa, a 23-year-old from Guinea, says he paid a smuggler 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,000). When he refused to recruit more people, he was allegedly threatened with death.
A growing criminal network
For Bubacar Ture, head of the Guinean League of Human Rights, the case is an alarming sign.
"As a human rights organization, we are extremely concerned about this phenomenon, which has now reached deeply troubling proportions," he told DW. In May, authorities rescued 60 foreign nationals during a similar operation.
Ture sees a link between the human trafficking problem and Guinea-Bissau's weak institutions. Criminal networks exploit these conditions to continue their activities, he said, noting that women are particularly vulnerable to human rights abuses.
The small Portuguese-speaking West African country has been plagued by political instability since independence in 1975 and is also known as a transit hub for cocaine bound for Europe.
Rescued, but still trapped far from home
A week after their rescue, the victims face a new problem: many lack the funds needed to travel back to Mali, Sierra Leone or elsewhere in West Africa.
Sadio Konimba is temporarily staying with an acquaintance in Bissau. Her friend told DW that Konimba had been deeply traumatized by what she had experienced. She had never imagined she could fall into the hands of a human trafficking network that might force her into prostitution.
Konimba herself does not want to discuss in detail what kind of work she was asked to do. Police confirm that women in such cases are often sexually exploited.
Konimba says she has managed to borrow around 75,000 CFA francs from acquaintances in recent days. But that falls short of the cost of her journey back to Bamako.
According to available information, Guinea-Bissau's migration and border authority, the Direcao-Geral de Migracao e Fronteiras (DGMF), also lacks the funds needed to finance the victims' return journeys.
Contacts have been established with the diplomatic missions of the countries concerned. But progress appears slow, and no concrete arrangements for their return have yet been announced.
Support systems falling short
Bubacar Ture criticizes the lack of protection available to victims.
"There are no public shelters for cases like these," he told DW, noting that private facilities have limited capacity, and psychological support and funding for temporary accommodation are also lacking.
The human rights advocate commends the criminal investigation police for taking action against the networks despite limited resources. At the same time, he calls for greater support.
"We make an urgent appeal to the government and international partners to provide adequate support to the judiciary, the police and the other institutions," he told DW.
For Konimba, one thing matters above all else now: returning to Bamako.
"Now I definitely want to go back to my mother and my daughter," she told DW. "Every day she asks me, 'Mom, are you coming home?' I tell her, 'I will come, I will come. Just wait a little longer.'"
But Konimba still does not have enough money for the journey. She is free, but for her, the struggle to rebuild a life with dignity has only just begun.

S.p.A., the company that owns it, had presented appeals against
the closure of the facility's hot area.

upheld a motion presented on health grounds by members of a
parents' association and a child with a rare genetic mutation
and said that activity at the hot area must stop within three
months unless all the asbestos on the site is removed and
measures to bring particulate emissions within safe limits are
taken.

the plant and the implementation of a plan to decarbonize it and
make it electric, with fears thousands of jobs could be lost.

board has tasked its president, Antonio Gozzi, to express an
interest in taking over the former ILVA steelworks with the
authorities on behalf of a consortium of Italian companies.
                                    
Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has not ruled out State
involvement.
                                    
Indian group Jindal, Czech group CE industries, and US-based
private investment group Flacks have also expressed interest in
buying the plant.
                                    
The Taranto factory, once Europe's biggest steelworks, has been
dogged by economic problems in recent years and linked to high
cancer rates in the Puglia port city.

CEO Lucia Morselli and former plant director Alessandro Labile
be put under house arrest over potentially cancer-causing
emissions from the factory in the 2022-23 period along with

for checks on strategic facilities.
                                    
ADI was put into State-controlled administration early in 2024
after ArcelorMittal's ownership of the group ended

The return of veterans to work requires systematic support, particularly from trade unions, says the head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Byzov
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:18:11 EET
23:18:11 KST

The return of veterans to work requires systematic support, particularly from trade unions, says the head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Byzov
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Serhii Byzov, spoke about how trade unions help military personnel and their families, facilitate the professional adaptation of veterans, and cooperate with employers to create proper working conditions.
The return of veterans to civilian work requires not only employers’ willingness to hire people with combat experience, but also systematic support — from physical and psychological recovery to workplace adaptation and the protection of labor rights. Trade unions can play an important role in this process by helping service members and veterans obtain the necessary support, find jobs, and protect their interests after employment. UNN spoke with Serhii Byzov, Head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, about how the trade union system is helping defenders return to working life.
Details
The FPU emphasizes that support for a veteran should not end after medical assistance has been provided or employment has been secured. It is important for a person to be able to return to professional activity, receive a decent salary, have proper working conditions, and be able to count on the protection of their rights.
The trade union’s main task is to help the veteran. After returning from the war, a person may need not only rehabilitation, but also support with employment, adaptation to civilian life, and the resolution of labor-related issues. Therefore, a trade union should be there not only when a problem arises, but also when a person begins a new stage of their life
From rehabilitation to returning to the workforce
One of the areas of support for service members within the trade union system is medical rehabilitation and psychological recovery. According to the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, nearly 50,000 service members and their family members received rehabilitation and psychological recovery services at the sanatorium and resort facilities of PJSC "Ukrprofozdorovnytsia" from 2022 to October 1, 2026. In addition, since the beginning of the full-scale war, more than 25,000 people have found shelter at the company’s facilities.
We had one case when a service member approached us after suffering an open traumatic brain injury and requiring further rehabilitation. The trade union helped resolve the issue of injury payments and payment for 21 days of recovery at a sanatorium in Myrhorod. After rehabilitation, the service member returned to his brigade and continued his service
At the same time, the return to civilian life for those leaving the service does not end with health recovery. The next challenge may be finding a job, changing professions, or adapting a former workplace to the person’s new needs.
According to the FPU head, the trade union helps service members who are forced to leave the service due to their health condition find employment through cooperation with the State Employment Center. Another area is cooperation with business representatives who can offer veterans jobs, decent pay, and opportunities for professional development.
For a veteran, it is important not simply to find a vacancy, but to have the opportunity to work in accordance with their skills and state of health. Therefore, support should begin with dialogue: clarifying the person’s needs, determining whether the employer is ready to adapt working conditions, and understanding what opportunities exist for this. Trade unions can help establish such cooperation so that returning to work is not a formality, but a genuine restoration of professional life
Protecting rights after employment
Finding a job is only part of the reintegration process. After employment, questions may arise regarding working conditions, workplace organization, pay, and interaction with management or colleagues. For veterans who have been wounded or have a disability, it may be necessary to create an accessible workspace or adapt their job duties.
Particular attention should be paid to psychological adaptation. After the experiences they have endured, veterans may find it difficult to work in a noisy environment, among large numbers of people, or under constant stress. However, people are not always ready to speak openly about such needs, fearing biased treatment.
As Serhii Byzov emphasized, in such situations, a trade union can represent an employee's interests in dialogue with the employer, help protect labor rights, and seek solutions that take into account the person's needs and the enterprise's capabilities.
Our task is to represent the interests of employees and help find solutions that take into account the needs of veterans and the enterprise's capabilities
Among the approaches to reintegration, Serhii Byzov mentioned individual support for veterans, mentoring by colleagues, flexible working hours, and access to psychological assistance. According to him, it is also important to prepare not only the veteran themselves for their return, but also the team — so that interaction is based on respect and understanding rather than stereotypes.
Why cooperation between trade unions and employers is important
As the European Business Association reported, a noticeable trend has emerged: Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and adapting veterans. In particular, businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, introducing retraining and adaptation programs, and in some cases creating special positions to support veterans.
However, businesses' willingness to employ veterans must be accompanied by systematic support. It is important for an employer to understand how to organize an employee's return, what state assistance opportunities are available, and how to respond to a person's needs without violating their rights.
Trade unions can complement businesses' efforts through the direct representation of employees. They can participate in discussions on the conditions for veterans' return to an enterprise, monitor compliance with labor guarantees, help resolve conflict situations, and contribute to ensuring that support programs work not only formally but also in practice
In his view, it is also important to develop partnerships between trade unions, employers, government institutions, and organizations that provide rehabilitation and retraining services. Such interaction makes it possible to combine various support tools — from restoring health to professional fulfillment.
One of the tools that can be used to formalize the relevant guarantees is a collective agreement. The FPU is working to include provisions concerning veterans in sectoral agreements and has developed a model section for collective agreements at enterprises. This includes, in particular, workplace adaptation, retraining opportunities, psychological support, and assistance with employment after leaving military service.
This approach makes it possible to move from situational assistance to clear rules under which an employee can count on support, while an employer can plan the necessary changes. At the same time, specific mechanisms must take into account the nature of the work, the veteran's state of health, and the enterprise's capabilities.
Veteran reintegration is a shared responsibility
The return of veterans to civilian working life requires consistent efforts at various levels. The state must ensure effective support programs, employers must create proper working conditions, and trade unions must represent employees' interests, help protect their rights, and promote social dialogue.
For the FPU, this area means an opportunity to combine practical assistance to service members and their families with work on the conditions in which veterans return to working life. After all, successful reintegration is not only about employment but also about the opportunity to work with dignity, safely, and without discrimination
Successful veteran reintegration is not only about the opportunity to find a job. It also means fair pay, safe conditions, respect for human rights, and the opportunity for professional development. That is why it is important that support for veterans not be limited to individual programs but gradually become part of labor relations and the everyday practices of enterprises.

Home prices fall and rents rise, both for the first time in three years

23:17:20 KST

High mortgage rates and concern over the broader economy have taken their toll on the housing market, freezing sales for the last few months. Now those issues are having an impact on home prices and rents.
The median U.S. home sale price fell for the first time in more than three years, according to a new report from Redfin, a real estate brokerage. The drop was just 0.1% year over year for the four weeks ending Oct. 25, but it follows three straight years of increases.
While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are roughly a full percentage point higher than they were one year ago. Higher rates are putting the typical homebuyer's monthly payment now at the second-highest on record, according to Redfin.
Pending home sales, which are a measure of signed contracts on existing homes, continued to fall in the past few weeks. A separate report from the National Association of Realtors showed these sales in September hitting the lowest level in 25 years.
New listings are also falling, now at the lowest level since the start of this year, according to Redfin. That is because sellers are losing their advantage as supply rises and buyers back away. They can no longer command the prices they want.
With the for-sale market stalled, more renters are staying put, and that finally has rents rising again. Median rent nationwide rose 0.1% in October, according to Apartment List. That is the first gain in over three years. While it is a tiny move up, it marks a turnaround after an oversupply of new units had rents falling.
"The vacancy rate is also gradually tightening, as the market transitions out of the soft conditions that have prevailed in recent years," wrote Chris Salviati, chief economist at Apartment List in the report. "Our newest market indicator tracking the concession rate continues to show signs of softness."
The national multifamily vacancy rate stood at 7% in October, remaining elevated compared to long-term norms, but continuing to decline after peaking earlier this year.
Rents are rising even in the Sun Belt markets, which had seen high vacancies for several years, due to robust construction. Austin, Phoenix and Tampa are finally starting to recover, although Phoenix, along with Las Vegas and San Antonio are still seeing the steepest drops. The San Francisco Bay area led the nation in rent growth, (+13.1% year over year), followed by San Jose, California.

‘Made in Vietnam’ Is Harder To Prove Than It Looks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

Transshipment has been a sticking point in the ongoing talks on reciprocal trade between Vietnam and the United States. Transshipment involves routing goods through a third country, often with minimal processing, to disguise where they were made. This has become especially sensitive as companies move production out of China to avoid U.S. tariffs. For those companies the challenge is no longer just finding new suppliers, but proving their products’ origin.
Apple is moving almost all final assembly of U.S.-bound iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and AirPods to Vietnam. Other examples of multinationals that have expanded their production in Vietnam include Samsung and Nike. Chinese firms themselves are also heavily investing in Vietnam, particularly in electronics and auto manufacturing. This is part of a broader shift. In a survey of more than 1,000 businesses, 43 percent had shifted outsourcing locations in 2025. These moves are driven by tariffs, as well as labor costs and supply chain diversification.
As a result of these changes, U.S. imports from Vietnam soared from about $38 billion in 2015 to nearly $194 billion in 2025. Local suppliers have multiplied throughout Vietnam, though the country still depends heavily on imported inputs.
Washington, however, suspects that some goods sold as “Made in Vietnam” are Chinese products that have been relabeled. In August, a White House report named more than 40 countries as presenting elevated risks for illegal transshipment. Vietnam was listed in “Tier 2,” which the report defined as countries that “combine significant illegal transshipment volumes with deeper integration into China-linked supply chains, input sourcing, manufacturing platforms, logistics systems, or regional rerouting channels.”
Companies are under increasing pressure to show that goods produced in their new locations are genuinely made there. Country-of-origin rules vary by product and trade regime, often depending on the origin of key inputs and whether local processing meets the applicable requirements. Obtaining this information often depends on relationships with local sub-suppliers. Unfortunately, visibility beyond first-tier suppliers is often limited.
Technology can play an important role in improving product traceability. DNA barcoding, isotope testing, and blockchain records are examples of technology that can be used to verify a product’s origin. DNA or isotope testing, for example, can provide evidence about a raw material’s physical origins, while blockchain can preserve records of transactions and custody. Effectively using those technologies, however, depends on relationships. Suppliers may need to agree to utilize the technologies, share records, provide samples, and identify their own sub-suppliers.
Even in established supply chains, these relationships can be weak. McKinsey’s 2025 supply chain risk survey found that 95 percent of the surveyed companies had visibility into their first-tier supplier risks, but only 42 percent had visibility that extended deeper into the chain. Regular contact with second-tier suppliers was relatively limited, in part because direct suppliers were reluctant to facilitate those connections. Relocation can further obscure supply chain visibility. Relationships with local sub-suppliers will need to be developed, and this will take time.
With the increased focus on transshipment, buyers should treat traceability as a part of the decision to relocate. Complex products can make this challenging; a laptop, for example, can contain hundreds of components sourced from around the world. Buyers should prioritize the components that are the most consequential in determining origin, and build relationships that encourage suppliers to be open about their own suppliers. In turn, suppliers that can document where their components originate will be better placed to attract orders and investment.
Governments have a larger role to play. Vietnam is already tightening checks on origin fraud, but more is needed. Programs linking foreign manufacturers with local component providers would deepen the domestic supply base and help build the local relationships that traceability depends on. The Vietnamese government could also incentivize the creation of shared reference databases that help firms verify component origins. In addition to strengthening Hanoi’s position in talks with Washington, this could reassure investors that Vietnam’s origin claims will withstand scrutiny.
Washington must uphold a clear definition of illegal transshipment and its expectations on local content. Blunt or uneven enforcement risks penalizing genuine Vietnamese production. This could push investment to countries that face less attention and, in doing so, undercut the United States’ supply chain diversification strategy.
Transshipment concerns are turning product traceability into an economic and geopolitical imperative. This will have implications for market access, tariff exposure, and broader relations between Hanoi and Washington. Yet tariffs can also push production to new locales where companies have thin relationships. Just as governments are demanding more visibility, companies may lack the supplier relationships to provide proof of origin.
Shipping a product through Vietnam does not, by itself, make it Vietnamese in origin. A “Made in Vietnam” label will mean little if the firm behind it cannot convincingly identify the inputs to its product. Technology can be used to help produce that evidence, but investments in supplier relationships are what will make it work.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Oct 29, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders, who accused him of incitement.
The allegation represents an escalation of anti-Arab rhetoric by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Oct 27 effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main Jewish rivals.
Israeli election officials said on Oct 29 that there was a probe into fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not “systematically compromised”.
Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.
Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.
Election officials were expected to finish tallying votes later on Oct 29, in a tightly fought election that has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.
With nearly 93% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Parliament.
Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, with 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no realistic path to power without broad Arab backing, an option Eisenkot has so far ruled out.
However, Eisenkot’s camp could also try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside, without including them in a governing coalition.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud; Arab parties call it incitement
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout, and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote”.
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan said they were suspected of attempting to bribe voters to cast ballots for the Arab-dominated party Ra’am, which has Islamist roots.
On Oct 29, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.
Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran”.
Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar later denied.
Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said on Oct 29 that his party was not involved in the reported suspicious conduct and urged a full investigation. He said that Netanyahu was on an incitement campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens.
“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.
In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity”.
Israeli President: ‘We must not tarnish an entire community’
After vote tallying is completed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, relied on Abbas’ Ra’am party. But Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
Eisenkot called for an investigation that would protect election integrity but said Netanyahu was exploiting the suspicions to “spread chaos”.
He said in a statement that Netanyahu’s aim was to “challenge the official election results, in which the Israeli public voted against the government”.
Herzog said the allegations must be investigated.
“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said in a statement. REUTERS

“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.

One of those killed was a foreign national while the other two were Turkish, he added.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses described hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near a car park collapsed, sending up a huge cloud of dust.
The area was closed to the public after the collapse, according to local reports.
Rescue workers and excavators operated through the night under powerful floodlights before concluding the operation.
“As of now, all our operations have been completed. We have finished all checks and inspections,” governor Kok said in an updated statement.

In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no injuries were recorded.
Turkey’s culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.

“Overuse by tourists and some vandalism have been reported and some incompatible structures have been introduced,” it said on its website.

In 2022, two Spaniards were killed and three others injured when their hot-air balloon crashed in high winds.

Finland launches third Pohjanmaa-class corvette
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:14:38 UTC
23:14:38 KST

- Finland launched the third Pohjanmaa-class corvette at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the four new warships in the water.
- All four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will replace seven older Finnish Navy ships.
Finland launched the third of its four new Pohjanmaa-class corvettes at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the Finnish Navy’s largest warships in decades in the water, the Finnish Navy said.
The ship was moved out of the construction hall at the Rauma Marine Constructions shipyard on Finland’s west coast, where fitting out will continue afloat. The Navy said all four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will enter service in phases, and it has said it expects to take the ships into service between 2027 and 2029. The Navy did not say when the third ship will begin sea trials.
“The launch of the third vessel shows the progress of long-term and persistent work. This is an extensive undertaking that brings together the Navy’s future capability, domestic industrial expertise and close cooperation between different parties,” said Rear Adm. Tuomas Tiilikainen, commander of the Finnish Navy.
Construction has picked up pace across the four hulls. The first corvette, whose construction began in 2023, was launched in May 2025 and is now being fitted out. The second was launched on May 21 this year, less than a year after its keel was laid. Rauma Marine Constructions laid the keel of the third ship and started production of the fourth in January, putting all four under construction at the same time, and the fourth ship’s keel followed in July.
The corvettes are being built by RMC Defence, a subsidiary of Rauma Marine Constructions, for the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command under a program known as Squadron 2020. At 117 m (384 feet) long with a crew of about 70, the ships are the largest surface combatants the Finnish Navy has ordered since its coastal defense ships of the 1930s. Each is designed to stay at sea for 14 days and has a range of about 3,500 nautical miles.
The Pohjanmaa class combines several jobs that the Finnish Navy now spreads across older vessels. The four corvettes will replace seven ships: the four Rauma-class missile boats, the two Hämeenmaa-class minelayers and the minelayer Pohjanmaa, retired in 2015, whose name the new class carries. Each corvette carries anti-ship missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow surface-to-air missiles in a vertical launcher, a 57 mm gun, torpedoes for anti-submarine warfare and rails for laying sea mines, an important task in the shallow, mine-friendly waters off Finland’s coast.
The ships also have ice-strengthened hulls so they can operate year-round in the northern Baltic, where the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Bothnia can freeze in winter, and they are fitted with composite ballistic armor to protect key areas. The Navy said the corvettes will give it new capability to defend Finnish waters and operate within NATO, which Finland joined in 2023.
The Navy plans to keep the Pohjanmaa class in service into the 2060s. The first ship is due to be handed over to the Navy in 2027, with all four in service by 2029.

A brewery with a 270-year history is closing in the Czech Republic due to falling demand for beer
Kyiv • UNN
Velké Březno will cease production due to falling demand and rising costs. The Březňák brand will be moved to other Heineken breweries.
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, will cease production after nearly 273 years of operation amid falling demand for beer and rising costs. At the same time, the Březňák brand will be preserved, while its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries. Bild reports, UNN writes.
Details
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, located in the town of the same name in the north of the country, is ceasing production. Beer has been brewed at the company’s current site since 1753, while the history of brewing here dates back to 1606. As Robert Kičina, a representative of Heineken Czech Republic, told Ústecký deník, production was gradually reduced throughout 2026, and the remaining capacity will now be permanently shut down.
At the same time, the Březňák beer brand produced by the brewery will not disappear. Its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries, to which the Czech brewery has belonged since 2008. The logistics and sales divisions will remain at the former site. The reasons for the production shutdown include declining beer consumption in the Czech Republic, as well as rising energy and raw material prices.
Breweries in Germany are experiencing similar problems. In 2025, beer consumption in the country fell by almost 6%, and sales continued to decline in 2026. Amid falling demand and price competition, companies with decades-long histories are closing. For example, the Eichbaum brewery in Mannheim stopped production on September 30 after nearly 350 years of operation, while the 165-year-old Rupp brewery in Lower Saxony faced bankruptcy.

Israel elections: What the record tally by Arab parties means for Zionist politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:13:23 UTC
23:13:23 KST

Arab parties, which are mostly supported by the Palestinian citizens of Israel, received a resounding victory in the October 27 election, changing the balance of power in the Knesset.
With roughly 90 percent of ballots counted as of Thursday, the two main Arab-led parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – are on track for a combined count of 19 seats.
Their total is nearly double the previous count of 10 and well above the 2020 record of 15 seats.
According to the latest tally, Netanyahu’s right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc is expected to win 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is set to bag 48 seats.
Neither Zionist bloc is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The projected 19 seats give the Arab-led parties significant leverage in coalition negotiations, but they do not guarantee a place in government.
It creates an opportunity for the two Arab parties to assert their democratic credentials in a country where Palestinian Israelis have long been treated as second-class citizens.
The community, which lives in separate towns, consists of the people whose ancestors stayed put during the Nakba, the mass expulsion of over 750,000 Palestinians following the creation of Israel in 1948.
The level of discrimination against Palestinian Israelis, who now make up roughly 20 percent of the country’s population, has risen dramatically since the October 7 attacks three years ago.
Towns dominated by the Palestinian Israeli community saw a significant shift in voting patterns. Their turnout hit 80 percent, the highest in decades.
They voted in large numbers because of deep frustration with the most right-wing government in Israel’s history and its far-right ministers, who have vowed to “Judaise” parts of Israel populated by Palestinian Israelis.
Experts say Arab parties made electoral gains despite Netanyahu’s campaign strategy, which centred on delegitimisation of Arab political participation in coalition-building.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has already claimed that the election was “stolen by Arab parties” that “support terror and the elimination of the Jewish state” through bribery, threats, violence, forgeries and the use of illegal software.
Main members from both Zionist blocs have said they wouldn’t include Palestinian Israelis in a coalition.
Ferit Belder, associate professor of international relations at Istanbul’s Marmara University, tells TRT World that opposition leaders largely deferred the question until after the vote to avoid the political costs of “normalising” Arab politics in the first election after October 7, 2023.
“Despite their electoral success, it is not guaranteed that the Arab parties will be able to translate this success into concrete gains and become part of the ‘legitimate circle of coalition-building’,” he says.
The Central Election Committee’s moves against Arab parties – left to the Supreme Court to resolve – further underscored the reluctance of Zionist parties to defend legitimate Arab participation, he adds.
Ozgur Dikmen, a scholar of Jewish politics, tells TRT World that Zionist politicians are more likely to frame the Palestinian Israeli gains as an element of insecurity and threat.
In a possible new cycle of elections, as seen between 2018 and 2022, such an “Arab threat” narrative would remain a useful tool for the right, he says.
A political force to reckon with
Numbers show the Zionist blocs’ dependence on Arab parties to reach a majority, raising the political costs of exclusion.
Gokhan Cinkara, director of Necmettin Erbakan University’s Global and Regional Studies Application and Research Centre, tells TRT World that the election results mark a significant turning point in Israeli politics.
He says the Arab parties have become a political force that can no longer be ignored.
“Anyone seeking to form a government will have to engage with the Arab parties in some way,” he says.
The two Arab parties approached the election with different strategies.
Ra’am, under Mansour Abbas, insisted on formal coalition membership to address the concerns of the Palestinian Israeli community.
Ra’am also joined the 2021 Bennett-Lapid government. Its integrationist approach and moves, such as placing former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz on the Knesset candidate list, already positioned the party as a potential coalition partner.
The Joint List, a union of communist Hadash, secularist Ta’al, and nationalist Balad groups, offered only external support for any anti-Netanyahu government in exchange for concrete improvements: stronger action against violence and crime, better housing, and the rollback of discriminatory policies of Netanyahu’s government.
Dikmen says that the chances of “formal inclusion” of Arab parties in the coalition remain limited.
It might be slightly more possible for the Eisenkot bloc to accept a coalition supported by the Arab parties, particularly with figures such as Abbas willing to serve as supporting partners, he says.
“I do not think it would be very realistic to expect seeing a Palestinian-Israeli minister,” Dikmen says.
Belder notes that the main task for the Arab parties is to convert their Knesset seats into material improvements in the daily lives of the Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Abbas of the Ra’am party has long argued that parliamentary presence without executive power confines the parties to the “world of slogans”, Belder says.
In the Knesset, a larger and more confident Palestinian Israeli caucus can at least be expected to reshape debates on equality and minority rights, even if fundamental arguments over the character of the state remain largely unchanged.
Dikmen points out that since December 2022, the Ministry of National Security under far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir has made serious reductions in the security budget of Palestinian Israeli-majority towns, contributing to skyrocketing crime rates – one of the drivers of the high turnout.
“I think such a reaction would reflect itself in the attitudes of Palestinian members in the Knesset,” he says.
Belder anticipates that far-right efforts to undermine judicial authority and policies that harm Palestinian Israelis’ daily lives – performative home demolitions and the humiliation of residents under Ben-Gvir – can be reversed or restricted.
Settler violence in the occupied West Bank might also come under closer government scrutiny, he adds.
Cinkara notes that the Arab parties will play an important role in advancing opposition priorities, including the election of the Knesset speaker and the allocation of committee seats.
“The key challenge for the Arab parties will also be to offer their voters practical policies,” he adds.

‘I fear for my family’: Berlin mayoral candidate’s leaked messages expose Hamas ties, spark uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:11:13 UTC
23:11:13 KST

Berlin has been engulfed in political turmoil since the Sept. 20 local elections. Although the radical left-wing Die Linke party won the election, all its attempts to form a left-wing coalition with the Greens and the Social Democrats have stalled amid revelations of antisemitism within the party and ties between many of its members and radical Islamist figures and leaders of Arab crime families in the city.
A new report published Thursday morning by the German newsmagazine Der Spiegel has exposed another dimension of the relationship between Germany's radical left and extremist Islam. According to the report, Elif Eralp, Die Linke's leading candidate for Berlin governing mayor, openly acknowledged that she and her family live in fear of Hamas supporters within her party. 
The controversy began with a mistake rooted in an outdated and questionable practice in German journalism, under which interviewees insist on reviewing and revising their quotations before publication.
Eralp, who had been interviewed by Der Spiegel, also asked to review her quotes before they appeared in print. After receiving them, she returned a revised version to the magazine.
But Eralp and her aides failed to notice that the document they sent back to Der Spiegel still contained their internal correspondence discussing the changes they wanted to make. On Thursday morning, that correspondence became the magazine's lead story and a major issue on Germany's political agenda.
In the exchanges, Eralp acknowledged that she and her family were personally afraid of becoming entangled with Hamas supporters associated with the party. She even tried to remove a reference to one of them, citing police advice not to publicly identify specific crime families in Berlin.
"My husband and I don't want to name specific people. We're both afraid of these people," she wrote.
Eralp's spokeswoman explained in the correspondence that they could not delete part of the interviewer's question, only portions of Eralp's answers.
Eralp responded in what could be interpreted as considerable alarm:
"But what am I supposed to do now? It was a mistake to agree to this interview in the first place. Until now, we were talking about people involved in organized crime. Now we're talking about people with connections to Hamas. I can't put myself and my family at risk for Der Spiegel. What do we do now? Cancel the entire interview?"
The Berlin Die Linke leader continued:
"Until now, when incidents came up, including the one involving Ibrahim Ibrahim (a member of an umbrella organization associated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine who appeared at the party's election victory celebration in Neukölln), I condemned them in general terms. But now we're talking about condemning an individual by name."
Even the center-left joins the criticism: 'Supporters of terrorism and antisemitism are deeply entrenched in the party'
Der Spiegel's revelations triggered an uproar across Germany's political establishment.
"Berlin needs a mayor who can stand up to extremists and doesn't give the impression that they are dictating what she can say before she has even been elected," said Christopher Förster, a conservative member of Berlin's state parliament. "If she can't do that, she cannot be elected to the position."
Another member of the Berlin parliament, Burkard Dregger, said: "Anyone who gets involved with Hamas criminals and their supporters in Berlin should not be surprised when they now demand payment for their support during the campaign."
Kristin Brinker, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) parliamentary group in Berlin, also criticized Eralp.
"If even the most senior politician no longer feels safe, how are ordinary Berliners supposed to feel? Especially considering that they don't have personal security guards to protect them," she said.
Stefan Evers, the conservative candidate for governing mayor, added in a statement to the German newspaper Bild:
"Thursday's revelations deepen the serious concerns about a left-wing government in Berlin. How is Elif Eralp supposed to protect the safety of millions of residents as mayor if she herself is afraid of the Islamist connections within her own party? The warning signs can no longer be ignored, and it is not too late to act."
Michael Müller, a former governing mayor of Berlin, said Eralp's remarks "mean that Berlin's mayor would be vulnerable to blackmail. We need to acknowledge that clearly."
Criticism also came from the left side of the political spectrum.
Martin Hikel, the center-left Social Democratic district mayor of Berlin's Neukölln borough, said: "When someone allows themselves to be constrained in this way, it only shows how deeply these forces, which glorify terrorism and antisemitism, are entrenched in the Left Party."
At midday Thursday, during the inaugural session of the city legislature, Eralp responded to the revelations and sought to contain the damage.
"I won't let anyone intimidate me. I've made that clear. It's only natural to worry about your family," she said.
Daughter of Turkish immigrants draws support from pro-Gaza voters
Eralp, 45, is the daughter of Turkish immigrants who fled their country because of political persecution. She studied law and has worked extensively on immigration, discrimination, racism, asylum seekers and equal rights, including during her time at the United Nations.
Her success story as a member of a minority group and the progressive policies she advocates led some to dub her "Berlin's Mamdani" even before the September elections, when she emerged as Die Linke's candidate for governing mayor.
One of her campaign slogans played directly on that comparison: "From New York to Berlin, the left is back."
However, as in Mamdani's case in the United States, antisemitic and anti-Israel sentiment within Die Linke has intensified considerably under Eralp, particularly among the party's younger members.
Eralp has tried unsuccessfully to contain the major controversies sparked by the behavior of some party members. But in Berlin in 2026, displays of antisemitism do not appear to be driving voters away.
Eralp has to tread carefully on issues involving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the war in Gaza. Her party has taken a clear position on the issue, formally adopting in June the claim that Israel is committing genocide.
At the same time, Eralp has spoken out against extremist incidents, including a party gathering in Neukölln that ended with participants chanting "Death to the IDF." She has also pushed for an internal investigative committee to prevent the party from being tainted by antisemitism.
On the other hand, Eralp cannot afford to abandon the party's unequivocal support for Gaza, given the importance of Muslim voters and young supporters who helped propel Die Linke upward in the polls, largely because of its anti-Israel policies.
This summer, Eralp found herself posing for campaign photographs with activists who declared that "the Palestinian liberation movement will not end until Tel Aviv is in Palestinian hands."
Earlier this month, additional details emerged about Eralp, revealing that until just a year ago, she had been a member of Rote Hilfe (Red Aid), an organization whose motto is "The ends justify the means."
The organization provides legal and financial support to people convicted of crimes, provided their actions were motivated by left-wing ideology.
Many Germans had already raised concerns about the party's ties to Arab criminal clans and its desire to reduce police funding and presence.
Now, many voters are questioning whether Eralp's past involvement with an organization that supports violence or turning a blind eye to the law in pursuit of its goals could prevent her from becoming Berlin's democratic, law-abiding leader.

Polish army will soon receive first delivery of EU-funded vests and helmets
Poland's defence company Maskpol will deliver the first batch of bullet-proof vests and helmets ordered under the EU's defence funding programme SAFE, a deputy defence minister has said.
On Wednesday, at the Maskpol Protective Equipment Company's plant in Konieczki in southern Poland, which is part of the Polish Armaments Group, Cezary Tomczyk took part in a presentation of the first batch of equipment manufactured for the Polish Army under contracts funded by the SAFE instrument. Over the coming days, tens of thousands of new helmets and vests are due to be delivered to Polish military units, including those stationed in the east of the country.
“This is the first time that equipment from the SAFE mechanism has been supplied directly to Polish Army soldiers by Maskpol,” said Tomczyk during a press conference at the factory. In his view, this is a “turning point” in the process of army modernisation.
Tomczyk announced that by the end of 2026, 17,000 KKZ-01 type vests and 20,000 HBT-02 type helmets will be delivered. He added that the total value of the contract for the supply of individual equipment for soldiers from Maskpol under the SAFE programme is PLN 1.5 billion (EUR 340 mln).
Referring to the individual soldier equipment modernisation programme Szpej, conducted since 2024, Tomczyk said an audit carried out that year showed that only about one third of Polish soldiers had equipment that was up to the highest NATO standard.
He said that the number of composite helmets in the armed forces is set to rise from 84,000 at the start of 2024 to 350,000 by the end of 2026; while the number of bulletproof vests will increase from 60,000 to 180,000.
Under the SAFE programme, the MASKPOL company will deliver to the Polish Armed Forces 300,000 HBT-02 helmets and 50,000 KKZ-01 bullet-proof vests. (PAP)

‘Genocide’ and ‘apartheid’: Harvard's hometown backs divestment from IDF suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:07:48 UTC
23:07:48 KST

The city home to Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) moved Wednesday to promote divestment from companies supplying weapons and technology to the Israel Defense Forces.
The City Council of Cambridge, a university city of approximately 123,000 residents near Boston, narrowly approved a resolution calling on municipal employee pension funds to stop investing in companies involved in what the measure described as the "genocide, apartheid and occupation of Palestinians."
Among the companies identified were Israeli defense contractor Elbit Systems, U.S. technology company Palantir and aerospace giants Boeing, Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace.
The vote followed a heated debate, after council members spent six hours at an earlier meeting hearing testimony from residents. When the vote was postponed at that meeting, audience members shouted, "You are all complicit in genocide" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."
The approved resolution calls on the city to develop its own list of companies that municipal pension funds could use when considering divestment. A separate proposal to extend the boycott to companies involved with the IDF through municipal procurement contracts, rather than investments alone, was also narrowly defeated.
A compromise over the BDS movement
The original proposal was introduced by City Council member Ayah Al-Zubi, a Harvard graduate. "This is the worst atrocity of our lifetimes, and we are invested in it," she said during the discussions. "I don't want blood on my hands, and none of us should."
Al-Zubi argued that while the United States imposes sanctions on countries such as China, Iran, Russia and Syria, it gives Israel a "blank check." Asked why she was singling out Israel, she replied, "I'm not making Israel look bad. I'm telling the truth."
Al-Zubi initially sought to adopt a list of approximately 100 companies compiled by the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), a Quaker organization, which had gained support among activists affiliated with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel.
Deputy Mayor Burhan Azeem, however, proposed a compromise: Cambridge would develop an independent list without formally adopting the BDS movement's platform. That version ultimately secured council approval.
According to Cambridge for Palestine, the activist group behind the initiative, the city's employee pension and benefits funds held approximately $24 million in investments in companies included on the original boycott list during fiscal year 2025. The group also claimed that Cambridge had spent about $4 million on contracts with companies supplying technology to the IDF and Israel Police.
The activists' list included three Israeli financial institutions, Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi and Israel Discount Bank, in which they estimated the municipal funds held approximately $660,000. The activists accused the banks of financing Israeli settlements.
One of the first companies on the list was Elbit Systems, which previously maintained offices in the area before leaving in 2024 following repeated pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
During one protest in 2023, nine demonstrators were arrested following clashes with police, even though the offices housed an Elbit subsidiary specializing in medical equipment development. Boycott activists portrayed the company's departure as a victory, while Elbit said the relocation was driven by business considerations.
The list also includes Palantir, the American software company that develops data analytics and artificial intelligence systems and works with security agencies, alongside major U.S. weapons manufacturers.
Broader boycott rejected over concerns for city services
The proposal to prohibit municipal procurement contracts with the targeted companies failed after Azeem, despite supporting investment divestment, voted against the broader measure.
He explained that such a restriction could undermine essential services and the city's ability to purchase equipment. During the debate, council members raised concerns that the proposed boycott could make it difficult for Cambridge to buy body cameras for its police officers.
Following the vote, pro-Palestinian activists shouted "Shame" at council members, while some left the chamber in anger.
The debate also divided the local Jewish community. Opponents warned that the resolution could fuel antisemitism and unfairly single out Israel. Jewish residents described fears about displaying their religious identity in public and incidents of harassment involving Jewish children at local schools.
Council members Denise Simmons and Patty Nolan also cited an incident in which an Israeli-owned business was vandalized with antisemitic graffiti while neighboring businesses were left untouched.
Simmons proposed applying a similar policy to companies implicated in war crimes around the world, rather than focusing on a single country.
Nolan warned that the measure was dividing the city and could attract unwanted attention from the Trump administration, which has already clashed with Harvard over allegations of discrimination and antisemitism.
Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, however, defended the initiative, saying it was about "corporate accountability and how Cambridge invests public funds," rather than religion or identity.
Jeremy Burton, executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Boston, criticized the resolution's use of the term "genocide." He nevertheless welcomed the council's decision to reject the broader commercial boycott and avoid formally adopting the BDS platform.
Pro-Palestinian activists celebrated the passage of the divestment resolution but expressed disappointment over the failure of the separate procurement proposal.
Harvard and MIT not covered by the decision
The controversy also reached Harvard's student newspaper, The Harvard Crimson, where an editorial supported divestment. Three members of the editorial board dissented, arguing that the City Council should focus on residents' needs rather than risk pension funds to make a political statement.
Despite the debate's proximity to two of the world's most prominent universities, neither Harvard nor MIT is a party to the decision. Both are independent institutions, and the Cambridge resolution does not apply to their investments or their relationships with Israel.
Cambridge is not the first municipality in the Boston area to consider such a move. In neighboring Somerville, residents supported a nonbinding referendum calling for divestment from companies linked to Israel.
But the Cambridge resolution carries additional symbolic significance because of the city's global reputation as a center of academia, innovation and the technology industry.

Deadly train disaster deepens political crisis in Spain
A deadly high-speed train collision in Spain has deepened a political crisis engulfing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government ahead of next month’s general election, as opposition parties demand accountability. The disaster, which killed at least 69 people, has sparked angry protests and calls for resignations.
The collision occurred near Urda in Toledo province when a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state railway company Renfe struck a stationary train. Audio recordings obtained by El Pais suggest controllers breached safety protocols despite repeated warnings from the stationary train’s driver. It was Spain’s second major railway disaster this year, following a collision near Adamuz in January that killed 46 people.
The tragedy has become a major issue in Spain’s election campaign, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
“Beyond technical responsibilities, we demand the assumption of political responsibilities. Out of responsibility and humanity,” Frente Amplio said in a statement on Wednesday.
The coalition, which includes parties allied with Sanchez’s government, called for an independent audit of the railway network, describing two deadly high-speed train accidents in one year as “unacceptable.”
The leader of the main opposition People’s Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, also demanded an immediate investigation into the state of Spain’s railways, but stopped short of calling for resignations.
“Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, what condition the tracks and safety systems are in,” Feijoo said.
Public anger spilled onto the streets of Madrid on Wednesday, where protesters clashed with police outside the Transport Ministry while demanding the resignations of Sanchez and Transport Minister Oscar Puente. Some demonstrators hurled flares and other objects at officers, who responded with tear gas.
Vox and its affiliated trade union Solidaridad staged a separate rally in central Madrid, where protesters carried a banner reading “Corruption kills.”
Sanchez has promised a thorough investigation, calling two such disasters in one year unacceptable. He has also pledged to strengthen railway safety while standing by Puente, according to El Pais.
The tragedy has added to the Socialist-led government’s troubles following parliamentary defeats and mass protests over soaring housing costs. Sanchez called early elections after parliament rejected key housing measures in September, with the vote scheduled for November 29.
