Why some men don’t flex when their manhood is challenged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:50 UTC
23:00:50 KST

Men who blend emotional openness and progressive gender attitudes into their sense of manhood appear to be less reactive when their masculinity is called into question, according to new research published in Social Psychology Quarterly. While men often respond to gender-related insecurities by exaggerating tough, dominant attitudes, men in this experiment who more strongly endorsed a flexible masculine identity showed less of that overcompensation. The findings suggest that how men react to challenges to their gender status depends in part on how they define manhood for themselves.
In sociology and psychology, the dominant cultural ideal of manhood in a society is known as hegemonic masculinity. In the United States, this traditional standard expects men to be physically tough, emotionally guarded, self-reliant, heterosexual, dominant, and strictly avoidant of anything considered feminine. Because meeting all of these rigid standards at all times is nearly impossible, many men experience their gender status as fragile and easily challenged. When a man feels that his manhood has been doubted, he may engage in masculine overcompensation, which is the tendency to exaggerate aggressive, dominant, or traditionally macho behaviors in an effort to prove his status to himself and others.
Psychological research has repeatedly shown how easily this defensive reaction can be triggered. For example, a 2008 series of experiments demonstrated that people widely view manhood as an uncertain social status that must be earned and can be easily lost through a single unmanly act. Building on that idea, a 2013 experimental study found that men who were falsely told they scored in the feminine range on a survey about gender identity reacted by expressing greater support for war, more negative attitudes toward gay people, and stronger interest in purchasing sport utility vehicles.
When men face doubts about their manhood, the effects can be physical as well as attitudinal, and individual differences shape how strongly they react. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2017, men whose masculinity was challenged tried to display physical toughness by administering higher voltages of electric shock to their own arms, especially if they already saw themselves as highly masculine.
Most research on masculine overcompensation has assumed that all men measure themselves against a single, traditional standard of toughness and dominance. In recent years, however, sociologists have documented the rise of what they call hybrid masculinity, a gender style in which men selectively incorporate traits typically associated with women or marginalized groups into their identity.
A man practicing hybrid masculinity might openly discuss his emotions, follow a skincare routine, show physical affection to male friends, or voice support for feminism and LGBTQ+ rights. The authors of a 2014 sociological review argued that adopting these traits allows relatively privileged men to create symbolic distance between themselves and traditional macho norms while still retaining their broader social status.
If hybrid masculinity gives men a way to feel secure in their gender identity without relying on rigid toughness, it raises the question of whether these men still feel compelled to act dominant when their manhood is challenged. Justin Huft, a PhD candidate in sociology at the University of California, Riverside, designed an experiment to test whether endorsing hybrid masculinity shields men from the tendency to overcompensate. Huft also set out to create the first survey tool designed to measure hybrid masculinity in statistical research.
“While there has been interesting work done on masculine overcompensation, it has largely depicted masculinity as a monolithic identity,” Huft told PsyPost. “This is inconsistent with some other work in the masculinities literature, which depicts multiple forms of masculinity. My aim was to explore how masculine overcompensation looks when accounting for another form of masculine identity.”
To test this idea, Huft recruited 988 heterosexual adult men living in the United States through the online research platform Connect. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 83, with an average age of about 40 years, and reported an average household income between $50,000 and $59,999 per year. Roughly 65 percent of the men identified as white, 15 percent as Black, 10 percent as Asian, 8 percent as Latinx, and 2 percent as another racial background. Politically, about 46 percent described themselves as liberal, 31 percent as conservative, and 22 percent as moderate, while 54 percent reported having a religious affiliation.
Before receiving any feedback, participants rated their baseline level of traditional masculinity. They also completed Huft’s newly developed 20-item hybrid masculinity questionnaire on a 5-point scale. Statistical testing showed that the new scale captured two closely related aspects of hybrid masculinity: progressive gender attitudes, such as supporting women’s and LGBTQ+ rights or agreeing that men can wear makeup, and emotional expressiveness, such as telling others when feeling sad, showing empathy, and expressing affection toward male friends.
Participants also answered questions measuring three concepts from sociological identity theory: how important being masculine was to their overall sense of self (known as identity prominence), how frequently they thought about their masculinity in daily situations like work or social events (known as identity salience), and how much they felt close friends and family viewed their masculinity the same way they did (known as identity verification).
For the experimental manipulation, participants completed items that appeared to evaluate their masculinity and were then given false feedback on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 represented feminine and 100 represented masculine. Men were randomly assigned to either a non-threatening group, where they were told that their answers placed them at the high end of the average male range, or a threatening group, where they were told that they scored at the high end of the average female range.
Following the feedback, participants completed a 21-item questionnaire measuring their agreement with traditional, dominant masculine norms on a scale from 1 to 7. This questionnaire assessed seven hallmarks of rigid manhood: emotional restriction, self-reliance, negative views of gay people, avoidance of femininity, placing a high priority on sex, desiring dominance as a leader, and valuing physical toughness.
Prior to receiving the false feedback, the two groups did not differ in their baseline traditional masculinity, measured with a separate questionnaire on which the sample averaged 5.08 out of 7. After the feedback was delivered, however, men who were told they scored in the average female range endorsed higher levels of rigid masculine norms, averaging 3.19 out of 7 compared to 2.97 out of 7 among men who were told they scored in the male range. That difference is small, about one-sixth of the typical spread in scores, but it indicates that the experimental threat triggered masculine overcompensation across the sample as a whole.
Huft then ran statistical regression models that controlled for baseline masculinity, identity importance, everyday awareness of masculinity, identity verification, religiosity, political conservatism, race, and household income. Even after accounting for all of those factors, receiving the masculinity-threatening feedback predicted a 0.17-point increase in dominant masculine norms in the baseline model, while scoring higher on hybrid masculinity was strongly linked to lower endorsement of those rigid norms overall.
When Huft tested how the two factors interacted, he found that hybrid masculinity moderated the impact of the threat, reducing the overcompensation effect by 0.23 points for each 1-point increase on the hybrid masculinity scale. In practical terms, men with low hybrid masculinity scores showed a larger increase in rigid, dominant attitudes after their manhood was questioned, whereas the gap between the threatened and non-threatened groups shrank toward zero among men who strongly endorsed hybrid masculinity.
Several background characteristics also predicted higher endorsement of rigid masculine norms regardless of which feedback participants received. Men who thought about their masculinity frequently in daily life, held more conservative political views, had lower household incomes, or identified as non-white tended to endorse traditional masculine norms more strongly.
The overall presence of a defensive reaction aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that threats to manhood heightened support for aggressive political and foreign-policy strategies, though that earlier work focused on political aggression rather than personal masculine norms and observed the effect among liberal men rather than conservative men. In Huft’s study, by contrast, men who scored high on hybrid masculinity tended to be more politically liberal and reacted less to the threat.
The new findings also stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which did not find an increase in conservative political views, support for war, or homophobia after a masculinity threat, though that study examined broader political and social attitudes rather than the comprehensive inventory of personal masculine norms used by Huft.
Huft offers two possible explanations for the buffering pattern found in his study. Men who embrace emotional openness and progressive views may have already loosened the tie between their sense of self-worth and traditional macho ideals, making feedback about feminine traits less upsetting, or they may draw on other aspects of their identity, such as emotional maturity or humor, to feel secure without needing to act tough.
While this flexibility appears to reduce aggressive overcompensation at the individual level, Huft cautions that hybrid masculinity does not automatically dismantle gender inequality in society. Instead, sociological theory suggests that blending softer traits into manhood can allow men to present themselves as modern and progressive while quietly preserving the social privileges associated with being a man.
“Masculinity isn’t just one thing,” Huft explained. “It contains different attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics. These different constellations of masculinity cause people to perceive and experience masculinity threats differently. This, in turn, creates different sorts of responses to masculinity threats.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because men who scored high on the new hybrid masculinity scale also tended to report that being masculine was less central to their overall identity, the questionnaire cannot completely untangle whether these men were strategically blending gender traits to maintain their status or whether they simply cared less about manhood altogether. In addition, the experiment could not capture why men adopted hybrid traits in the first place, such as whether they adopted those traits preemptively, in response to past challenges to their manhood, or for unrelated reasons.
Hybrid masculinity was also measured rather than assigned, so men who scored high on it differed from low scorers in other ways. Most notably, they tended to be much more politically liberal, and the study did not test whether political views shaped how men responded to the threat. The new scale has so far been tested in only this one sample, and the study did not report whether participants believed the false feedback.
The study also focused exclusively on heterosexual, cisgender men in the United States, meaning the findings cannot be generalized to gay, bisexual, or transgender men. According to hybrid masculinity theorists, the ability to adopt feminine or non-traditional traits without facing harsh social penalties is often easiest for white, middle-class, heterosexual men, so future studies will need to test whether hybrid masculinity works the same way across different racial and socioeconomic groups.
It is also possible that for men who pride themselves on being progressive and emotionally sensitive, being told they scored as highly masculine could actually feel like a threat to their progressive self-image, prompting them to distance themselves even further from traditional manhood. Finally, future research could explore whether men whose manhood is challenged try to restore their pride in areas outside of gender altogether, such as by emphasizing their career achievements or financial status.
The study, “Hybrid Masculinity as a Buffer against Threats to Masculinity,” was authored by Justin Huft.

Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

FM: Zelenskyy wants to attend Ukraine Recovery Conference in Tallinn
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants to participate in the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Tallinn next year alongside other world leaders.
Speculation recently circulated in the media that Ukraine's senior leadership would be unable to travel to Estonia for the conference at the end of January because of what is expected to be a difficult winter of war.
The minister said Zelenskyy and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) have already signed the personalized invitations to leaders for the event in January.
"And he certainly wants to participate here. And now we are moving forward. There is no longer any hesitation about whether the Ukraine Recovery Conference will take place here and at what level. It will be at the level of world leaders. And these leaders have been invited here to Tallinn by Ukrainian President Zelenskyy," Tsahkna said at the government's weekly press conference on Thursday.
However, his attendance will depend on the situation in Ukraine in January.
"So the aim is to do everything possible, including on Ukraine's part, to ensure that all world leaders, led by President Zelenskyy, participate here. But let's be honest, there are three months to go. This does not change our preparations and plans with Ukraine in any way," he added.
The foreign minister said the aim of the conference is to provide Ukraine with additional funding.
"We are not talking here about a few million that were promised or given to Ukraine – we are talking about billions and billions," he said.
Tsahkna said it is very much hoped Zelenskyy will be physically present at the conference, but if the situation in Ukraine is "so drastic by then" that the president cannot attend, it may help the conference meet its goal.
"The contributions will be even higher and there will be even greater commitment from other world leaders, because that would be a sign that the situation is indeed becoming very difficult," Tsahkna said.
The Ukraine Recovery Conference URC27 is scheduled to take place in Tallinn on January 28 and 29.

Russia’s Military Losses Hit All-Time Monthly High as Ukraine Reports Over 49,000 in October
Russian military personnel losses in October 2026 have reached 49,040 as of October 29, marking the highest monthly figure since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff reported that the previous monthly record was registered in December 2024, when Russian forces suffered 48,670 personnel losses.
With October still underway, Russia’s average daily personnel losses have reached approximately 1,750, according to Ukrainian military estimates.
The figures also indicate a substantial increase in Russian losses over recent months. In February 2026, Russian forces sustained an estimated 26,090 personnel losses, compared with 46,230 in September and 49,040 as of October 29.
“Why this matters: The rate of Russian personnel losses exceeds the military’s ability to replenish its units. Each month of the war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia’s armed forces,” the General Staff added.
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed or wounded more than 302,000 Russian military personnel since the beginning of 2026, averaging over 1,000 casualties per day in less than ten months, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 27.
March recorded the highest number of Russian personnel casualties from Ukrainian drone strikes, with 33,989 soldiers killed or wounded. April followed with 33,961 casualties, while February saw the lowest monthly total at 26,204.
Throughout the year, Ukrainian drone units have consistently inflicted tens of thousands of casualties on Russian forces each month. Monthly totals exceeded 30,000 in January, March, April, May, July, and September.
In September alone, drone strikes killed or wounded 32,739 Russian troops. During the first 25 days of October, Ukrainian forces recorded an additional 27,829 Russian personnel casualties from drone operations.
Overall, as of October 29, 2026, Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had reached approximately 1,584,910, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

Russia has around 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications — DIU
Ukraine

Russia has around 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications — DIU
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has around 140 Su-34s and continues to produce them. Since the beginning of the invasion, 43 aircraft have been destroyed and seven more damaged.
The Russian Aerospace Forces have approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service, which are the main carriers of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions. This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence, reports UNN.
Details
Su-34 fighter-bombers are one of the key components of the aggressor state Russia’s strike aviation in the war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the occupation army to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements
The intelligence agency notes that, despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernize Su-34s, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and preserve the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes.
At the same time, the ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components, and the ability of Russia’s defence industry to compensate for losses.
As of October 22, 2026, approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications, including modernized Su-34Ms (Su-34NVOs), are in service with the Russian Aerospace Forces
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has lost 43 aircraft of this type destroyed, while another seven have been damaged.
Such losses are quite substantial for the aggressor’s aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, significant financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation. For comparison, the number of destroyed Su-34s is equivalent to approximately 2.5–3 years of their production at estimated capacities of 14–18 aircraft annually
During Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, the role of the Su-34 in the aggressor’s strike aviation has undergone a significant transformation. At the initial stage of the invasion, these aircraft were primarily used to bomb ground targets with unguided aerial bombs, including FAB-250, FAB-500 M-62, and BetAB-500 concrete-piercing bombs.
The use of such weapons required approaching the targets, which increased the aircraft’s vulnerability to Ukrainian air defence systems.
At the same time, Su-34s began to be used as carriers of Kh-31 and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, as well as, in some cases, Kh-35U anti-ship missiles to strike ground targets.
We remind you
The Ukrainian Navy destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, while two more were damaged on the territory of Borysoglebsk airfield. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic frontline Su-34 bomber, which Russia began serial production of in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, the aircraft is the main carrier of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions.

Kazakhstan Tears Down Lenin Monument as De-Sovietization Efforts Expand Across Central Asia
Authorities in Kazakhstan have removed a monument to Vladimir Lenin from the village of Kushmurun in Kostanay region as part of wider efforts to reduce Soviet-era influence across Central Asia, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported on October 29.
The monument was dismantled at the request of the regional administration after local residents collected nearly 400 signatures supporting its removal. Previous attempts to remove it in 2015 and 2022 had failed after opposition from supporters of the Soviet legacy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The initiative group supporting the demolition linked Soviet rule directly to mass famine and political repression in Kazakhstan. Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service noted that estimates of deaths during the Asharshylyk famine of the early 1930s reach as high as 2.3 million people, nearly half of Kazakhstan’s population at the time.
Some researchers have described the catastrophe as the “Kazakh Holodomor,” drawing parallels with the Holodomor in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s intelligence service stated that the removal of the Lenin monument and growing public discussion of Soviet-era repression have unsettled Russian political strategists because they challenge Moscow’s narrative of a prosperous shared Soviet past.
Russia presents itself internationally as the legal successor to the Soviet Union. The intelligence service argued that renewed attention to the individual histories of former Soviet republics, including famine, repression, and forced political control, undermines the mythology surrounding the Soviet period.
Similar de-Sovietization processes have intensified elsewhere in Central Asia, although their form differs between countries.
In Kyrgyzstan, calls for broader decommunization and derussification have grown during 2026. Uzbekistan has been described as a regional leader in this process, while Tajikistan has emphasized national identity and historical memory.
Turkmenistan has pursued its own model centered on national sovereignty within an isolationist and neutral foreign policy.
Despite those differences, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service assessed that de-Sovietization, decommunization, and derussification efforts across Central Asia share a common objective of reducing dependence on and influence from Russia.
The trend contrasts with Russian efforts to revive Soviet symbolism in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Russian authorities in temporarily occupied eastern Ukrainian city of Luhansk promoted Stalin and Lenin imagery during a February 14 propaganda event, replacing traditional Valentine’s Day themes with Soviet symbols.

Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds

Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds
A majority of American voters believe Russian leader Vladimir Putin is deliberately delaying efforts to end the war in Ukraine, while nearly two-thirds support continued military assistance to Kyiv and stronger sanctions against Moscow if Russia refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war, according to the October Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll, conducted by HarrisX.
The survey, which polled 2,700 registered US voters between October 24 and 26, 2026, is part of one of the most consistent polling series tracking American public opinion on Russia’s war against Ukraine. Its regular measurements provide insight into how attitudes toward the war and potential peace negotiations evolve over time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest findings show that 68% of respondents believe Putin is stalling negotiations with the United States and Western countries rather than genuinely seeking peace, up from 61% in September. Only 32% believe the Russian leader sincerely wants to end the war.
Skepticism toward Putin extends across political affiliations, with 74% of Democrats and independent or other-party voters saying he is delaying negotiations, compared with 58% of Republicans.
By contrast, 61% of Americans believe Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy genuinely wants to end the war, while 39% think he is stalling negotiations, a slight increase from 37% in September.
Support for Zelenskyy’s stated intentions is particularly strong among Democrats, with 69% believing he is genuinely seeking peace. The same view is shared by 61% of independent or other-party voters and 52% of Republicans.
Beyond perceptions of the two leaders, the poll also indicates substantial bipartisan support for maintaining pressure on Moscow if it refuses to engage in peace negotiations.
According to the findings, 64% of Americans support continuing weapons assistance to Ukraine and imposing additional sanctions on Russia if Moscow refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war.
Notably, support for these measures is nearly identical among Republicans and Democrats, with 67% of Republican voters and 66% of Democratic voters backing continued military assistance and additional economic pressure under those circumstances.
The findings highlight an area of bipartisan agreement on US policy toward Russia’s war against Ukraine despite broader political divisions in the United States.
The survey also found growing support for direct US security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a potential peace agreement involving Ukrainian territorial concessions. Some 64% of respondents supported such an arrangement, compared with 58% in September.
However, American attitudes toward economic measures targeting Russia become more complex when domestic energy costs are taken into account.
According to the poll, 61% of Americans oppose the United States purchasing Russian oil and diesel fuel while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine, while 39% support such purchases. Opposition is particularly strong among Democrats, with 73% against buying Russian oil and diesel, compared with 64% of independent or other-party voters.
Republicans were more divided, with 54% supporting purchases of Russian oil and diesel fuel and 46% opposing them.
At the same time, 63% of respondents said they prioritize lower fuel prices over restricting Russia’s ability to finance the war, revealing a contrast between opposition to Russian energy purchases and concerns about domestic energy costs.
The findings come as diplomatic efforts to arrange further negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States continue.
A proposed trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi remains dependent on confirmation from Washington, although both Kyiv and Moscow have expressed their readiness to participate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists on October 28.
Zelenskyy explained that the timing of the talks, expected to take place in November, could be affected by Washington’s ongoing diplomatic engagement in the Middle East.

Macron accuses French far right of fomenting spread of racism

The attack last Friday, which left one dead and seven wounded, has unleashed a bitter debate over racism in French politics and the media as the country grapples with a broad set of social grievances, months ahead of a presidential election.
"There are political movements which have led to ... a kind of disinhibition of speech, an ambient racism," Macron told YouTube influencer Hugo Decrypte in a lengthy interview released late on Wednesday.

RN lawmaker Jean-Philippe Tanguy told TF1: "It's Macron who has run France for the past nine years. It's on his watch that antisemitism, homophobia and hate has spread through France. He is to blame."
'WORDS CARRY WEIGHT'
French politicians on all sides have traded accusations of racism in the wake of the killing of 26-year-old Pengo Bossio Wangi in Trappes, a culturally diverse town 20 km (15 miles) southwest of Paris.
Anti-terrorist prosecutors said on Thursday the 39-year-old suspect, named Kevin T, acknowledged during questioning seeking victims of "African or Muslim type". His belongings included a copy of Hitler's book "Mein Kampf" and stickers mentioning the RN — though he said he did not support any particular party.
RN senator Edwige Diaz this week doubled down on comments by Jordan Bardella, now the party's leader, who in 2021 called Trappes a "mini-Islamic state". She said there was nothing wrong in that description.
"We can speak of a somewhat toxic climate in which certain people are constantly portrayed as suspicious or illegitimate," said Zineb Alami, lawyer for Bossio Wangi's father.
"Words carry weight," she said.
Numerous politicians on the right, including Bardella, and media commentators have blamed the rioting and looting that took place after street protests this month on immigration, without giving evidence. At a march in memory of Bossio Wangi on Sunday, people in attendance blamed the media coverage for inciting racial hatred.
Macron's minority centrist government also stands accused of not doing enough to tackle the spread of racist and far-right attitudes in society.
"The normalisation of the ideas of the far-right extends beyond the National Rally into the ranks of the government," sociologist Solene Brun told Reuters.
Aurore Berge, the minister for gender equality and anti-discrimination, was urged in parliament this week to take back her comment last month that it was legitimate to discuss the "Great Replacement", a far-right conspiracy theory that has been invoked by perpetrators of far-right attacks around the world in recent years.
In addition to the Trappes attack, far-right activists looking for confrontations with protesters were spotted across more than a dozen French cities last week, according to authorities. REUTERS

Meloni introduces personalised number plates, urges Italians to be 'creative'
ROME, Oct 29 - Italy's government will allow motorists to personalise the number plates of their vehicles, in a revenue-raising move that follows the example of the Unites States, Britain and other countries.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced the measure on Wednesday as she unveiled Italy's 2027 budget law, the last before a general election due next year, describing the number plate initiative as a "colourful note".
"One will be able to indulge oneself more or less as one sees fit, obviously at a cost. Something tells me that Italians' creativity could shine here," Meloni said.
Personalised plates will cost about €600 ($669) for cars and €360 for motor-bikes, according to a decree.
A Treasury official declined to estimate how much revenue the government expects the measure to generate.
Italian car number plates are currently made of a string of two letters, three numbers and two letters. The extent to which motorists will be allowed to stray from the standard formula is unclear.
The reform has triggered a wave of memes and jokes on social media, amid concerns that personalized license plates could open the flood-gates to insults and profanities.
One meme showed Meloni dressed up as Marie Antoniette, holding a platter of licence plates and saying, "Let them eat personalised plates" - a play on the famous phrase by the 18th century French queen "Let them eat cake".
Some welcomed the measure, including taxi drivers, who said distinctive personalised plates could make it easier to identify legitimate operators and combat illegal services.
Opposition parties on the centre-left were less enthusiastic, saying the licence-plate initiative was a distraction from more pressing issues that budget failed to address.
"Meloni should know that Italians have already chosen their personalised plate, and it reads: 'Meloni, go away'," said Francesco Silvestri, a lawmaker from the Five Star Movement. REUTERS

Speaker Johari Abdul declared the budget passed by a majority voice vote after Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan wrapped up the debate, with no recorded tally of lawmakers voting for or against the bill.

88 pct of businesses starting to adopt tokenized money: DBS survey
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:56 CST
22:53:56 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A recent survey found that 88 percent of businesses were already deploying or piloting tokenized money use cases, DBS said on Wednesday.
The report surveyed 422 business leaders across 11 markets. The findings come as "businesses rewire business operations, treasury operations and financial management toolkits amid volatility and trade fragmentation," said DBS.
Among the expected benefits of tokenized money, 72 percent of respondents cited improved auditability and traceability, while 71 percent expected real-time cross-border payments. Other benefits included stronger internal controls and governance, and better treasury liquidity management.
Stablecoins were the most widely adopted tokenized instruments, used by 63 percent of respondents, followed by tokenized deposits at 53 percent and tokenized money market funds at 52 percent.
Meanwhile, 78 percent of businesses had diversified their reliance on traditional settlement currencies by gaining exposure to multiple currencies to support trade across different markets.
Only 2 percent were not considering alternative currencies, highlighting "a broader shift towards a more diverse monetary system in the future," said DBS. ■

Feature: Revving up dreams, Libyan woman builds career in engine modification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:55 CST
22:53:55 KST

TRIPOLI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop humming with engines in Mayah, 40 km southwest of the Libyan capital Tripoli, 25-year-old Rawan Abu Aisha is building a career uncommon for Libyan women -- turning a childhood passion for cars into a business modifying engines.
Growing up, Abu Aisha often watched her father work as a mechanic. "The workshop environment was familiar to me from childhood because I grew up watching my father work with cars," Abu Aisha told Xinhua.
"Over time, that interest became something I wanted to turn into a profession," she explained, saying the opportunity came through an entrepreneurship competition in Libya that invited participants to present innovative business ideas.
Drawing on her family background, she proposed modifying car engines to meet owners' specific needs. The idea became real when a customer agreed to an engine replacement. The project subsequently grew into a company established in 2022, whose primary business is modifying engines using its own custom-built units.
"My father's support and practical experience helped me take my first steps in this field," she said. "His encouragement gave me the confidence to develop my skills and turn an idea into a real business."
Her studies in entrepreneurship also equipped her with knowledge of business management, marketing and accounting, helping the company move beyond its technical roots toward a more structured management approach. What began as a business relying largely on customer recommendations later expanded its reach through an online presence and social media platforms.
According to Abu Aisha, the company's social media page has attracted over 50,000 followers, and demand for its services has grown so rapidly that her current team can barely keep up.
"The growing number of followers and the rising demand for our services show that there is considerable interest in what we do," she said. "Our next step is to expand the business and improve our ability to meet customers' needs."
Abu Aisha also hopes to partner with companies abroad, stressing the importance of long-term planning and continuous development.
"Building a sustainable business requires more than providing a good technical service," she said. "It also requires organized management, continuous improvement and a clear vision for the future."
While she believes social acceptance of women in the workplace has grown in recent years, Abu Aisha's greatest lesson from entrepreneurship is that young women must take initiative and pursue their ambitions, rather than let stereotypes dictate their choices.
"Women should not allow stereotypes to decide what they can or cannot do," she said. "They should be willing to try, learn and discover their abilities through practical experience."
For young women considering careers in mechanics, engineering or other nontraditional fields, her journey shows how personal interests can be turned into professional opportunities through determination, learning and hands-on experience.
"I want to continue developing the business and provide services that customers can trust," she said. "I believe that competence and expertise, rather than gender, should determine whether someone can succeed in a particular profession." ■

Across China: New study traces evolution of terrestrial animals on Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:45 CST
22:53:45 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new study has reconstructed the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, offering a clearer picture of how the unique fauna of Earth's "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.
The research, led by a team from the Chengdu Institute of Biology (CIB) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"Overall, the study deepens understanding of how mountain animal life evolves and provides a framework for studying how biodiversity forms in mountain regions worldwide," said Li Jiatang, a researcher at CIB.
Home to many species found nowhere else, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, covering about 3.07 million square kilometers and ranging in elevation from 88 to 8,848 meters, according to the researchers.
The plateau platform, the Himalayas and the Hengduan Mountains are the plateau's three major subregions.
Scientists have long been interested in how the plateau's tectonic history and monsoon systems shaped the evolution of local biodiversity. However, earlier studies mostly looked at plants or single animal groups, leaving the overall development of the plateau's land animals poorly understood.
To fill this gap, the researchers combined time-calibrated evolutionary trees covering more than 20,000 species across invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They then reconstructed the evolutionary history of 527 endemic terrestrial animal species on the plateau.
The study found that most of the plateau's endemic land animals did not arrive from elsewhere and then become new species. Instead, many evolved locally, splitting into new species right where they were, something scientists call in situ diversification.
The plateau was also a major receiver of species. The study found that animals moved in nearly twice as often as they moved out. The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau therefore played two roles at once: it was a place where new species formed, and a biogeographic sink that took in more species than it sent out.
The three subregions played very different roles. The Hengduan Mountains were the main source of local species formation, producing many new species. The Himalayas were both a source and a sink, producing new species locally and receiving species from elsewhere. The plateau platform produced very few new species locally, with most of its animal life coming from immigration, making it an important sink and a major receiver of species.
The researchers also examined how geology and climate shaped this evolutionary history. They found that a major climate transition about 34 million years ago marked the onset of sustained species diversification and biological exchange. However, the timing of these processes varied across the three subregions, reflecting differences in their uplift histories and monsoon systems.
The study also found a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern. By comparing animal evolution with plant studies, the researchers identified this pattern across the plateau and its subregions. Early-colonizing plant groups created suitable ecological niches, laying the foundation for later animal immigration and diversification. ■

The point of the initiative is that people with disabilities are not merely beneficiaries of inclusion policies, but active participants in professional, social, and cultural life. WINDHOEK, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has heightened disease surveillance and strengthened preparedness at points of entry following the spread of Ebola disease across several countries, although no suspected or confirmed cases have been reported in the country, the health ministry said.
In a public health update issued Wednesday evening, the Ministry of Health and Social Services said it was strengthening preparedness and improving healthcare workers' capacity to detect, report and respond to potential Ebola cases.
The measures follow the spread of an outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus, with cases reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya and Nigeria, raising concerns about cross-border transmission.
The absence of specific vaccines and treatments underscores the importance of early detection, effective surveillance and prompt medical care, the ministry noted.
It urged the public to practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with suspected or confirmed cases and seek immediate medical attention if symptoms develop following possible exposure. People with relevant travel or contact histories were advised to inform healthcare personnel.
It also urged the public to remain calm and rely on official communications from the ministry, the World Health Organization and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for accurate information.
The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared in the DRC on May 15, 2026, after cases were detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. As of Oct. 26, the DRC, Kenya and Nigeria had reported a combined 10,151 confirmed cases, including 4,930 deaths, according to data from the World Health Organization. ■

Antarctic sea ice loss disrupts ocean freshwater system: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:28 CST
22:53:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) has rapidly become saltier and denser as Antarctic sea ice loss reduces freshwater input, potentially affecting deep-ocean warming and sea levels, according to new research.
The AAIW, a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean, helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents. It plays a role in heat, freshwater and carbon redistribution around the planet, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study, published in Nature Climate Change, found that Antarctic summer sea-ice melt helped maintain the AAIW from 1995 to 2015. From 2016, Antarctic sea ice declined to record lows. Between 2016 and 2024, reduced freshwater input led the water layer to become saltier, denser and deeper.
The team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of about 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, along with satellite and atmospheric datasets.
Researchers said the last time the AAIW underwent a similar shift was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica. However, that transition took thousands of years, rather than two decades.
The researchers said changes in the AAIW could affect the ocean's ability to store carbon and push more excess heat into deeper waters, meaning existing models may underestimate deep-ocean warming and miscalculate regional sea-level rise. ■

Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:50:35 UTC
22:50:35 KST

From today, everyone in Flanders can check for themselves whether the planned Flemish reform of road tax will work out more favourably or not. The Flemish Government is launching a website where you can work out the difference between the old and the new tax yourself. If the new scheme works out cheaper, you can indicate straight away that you wish to switch. Anyone who does not wish to switch need not do anything.
Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
In 2027, the annual road tax (JVB) in Flanders will be reformed. For most vehicles, the Flemish government will use just two parameters: the car’s weight and its CO₂ emissions. “The lighter and cleaner your car, the less you pay,” is the message. For cars with a powerful engine (over 2400 cc), you’ll pay slightly more.
Anyone who wants to check for themselves whether the new road tax will be cheaper can do so from today via the website www.vlaanderen.be/vergelijker , but it will be handy to have somebody who reads Dutch on hand. The Comparison Tool makes the reform very clear.
How does it work?
To make a comparison, all you need is your number plate and your registration date. Simply enter these details into the new Comparison Tool and you’ll immediately see a comparison between your current road tax and the new rate.
If the new rate is cheaper, you can switch to the new system straight away. If the current rate is cheaper – which may be the case, for example, for cars with a powerful engine or older cars – then you don’t need to do anything, and you’ll remain on the current rate until you buy your next car.

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:46:27 CET
22:46:27 KST

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO
Meeting in Paris on Monday, 26 October, representatives of Europe’s five leading military powers reaffirmed their determination to strengthen Europe’s role in NATO’s collective defence. In response to the Russian threat, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom intend to step up their military and industrial cooperation while continuing their support for Ukraine.
Military and Industrial Cooperation to Strengthen NATO’s European Pillar
The E5 is a consultation framework bringing together the Defence Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. At their meeting in Paris on 26 October, hosted by French Minister for the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin, the five countries reaffirmed the need for Europe to shoulder greater responsibility for its own defence while preserving its strategic partnership with the United States. “Produce more, produce faster,” Catherine Vautrin urged, calling for stronger European industrial capabilities and the development of equipment suited to both current conflicts and future threats. Achieving this ambition will require greater interoperability between armed forces, greater control over strategic technologies and closer coordination of defence investment. Also attending the meeting, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas stressed the importance of translating defence spending into tangible operational capabilities while maintaining pressure on Russia through sanctions. European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, meanwhile, emphasised the urgent need to accelerate industrial contracts and equipment deliveries, particularly through EU funding mechanisms designed to strengthen Ukraine’s capabilities.
In their joint statement, the E5 members reaffirmed their determination to build a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO, notably by increasing investment in Europe’s defence industrial capabilities.
A Stronger European Commitment to Ukraine
Support for Ukraine was also high on the agenda. “We are fully committed,” Catherine Vautrin affirmed, stressing the need to preserve European unity in the face of intimidation. In their joint statement, the five countries identified Russia as the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security, citing its ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the growing use of hybrid attacks. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius shared this assessment, stating that Vladimir Putin has shown no genuine willingness to agree to a ceasefire. As Russian strikes continue to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population, European countries continue to provide tangible support, particularly in air defence.
For Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, this mobilisation directly serves Europe’s security interests: “Helping Ukraine is not simply about helping another country; it is about safeguarding our own future and security.” Polish Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski, meanwhile, emphasised the need to develop more affordable air defence systems and strengthen industrial cooperation with Kyiv. NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska also stressed the importance of air defence, calling on Allies to step up their support to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure as winter approaches. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting reiterated the UK’s determination to maintain economic pressure on Moscow and continue supporting Ukraine over the long term. The E5 members also reaffirmed the importance of countering Russia’s shadow fleet and their commitment to helping provide robust security guarantees for Ukraine once a ceasefire or peace agreement is in place.
A Common Response to Other Threats to European Security
Tensions in the Middle East were also discussed, particularly maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, two vital shipping routes for international trade and energy supplies.
Beyond these issues, the group plans to intensify dialogue between political and military leaders and strengthen cooperation between national defence industries. The next E5 meeting is scheduled to take place in Rome in March 2027, with the aim of continuing to translate this political alignment into tangible operational capabilities.

Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission due to its aggression and environmental damage. Kyiv called for the damage to be assessed and Russia’s participation to be limited.
The Ukrainian delegation prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship during the 47th meeting of the Commission on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution. This was reported by the Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine, writes UNN.
A state waging an aggressive war and harming the marine environment should not head the body responsible for its protection
In her statement, she added that the Ukrainian side is drawing attention to the significant environmental consequences of Russia’s aggression for the entire Black Sea region. Attacks on infrastructure, damage to wastewater treatment facilities, pollution of water and soil, and the destruction of protected natural areas are creating threats that extend far beyond Ukraine.
Thus, the coasts of the Black and Azov Seas, the deltas of the Danube and Dnipro rivers, as well as wetlands of international importance, are suffering from the hostilities. Pollution is spreading through the sea, and the consequences for marine ecosystems may persist for many years.
The Ukrainian delegation emphasized that Russia’s actions run counter to international law and lead to marine pollution, undermining the joint efforts of coastal states aimed at fulfilling their obligations under the Convention on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution (the Bucharest Convention).
It is noted that Ukraine called on the states parties to the Convention to provide a clear assessment of the actions of the Russian Federation and their environmental consequences, support the assessment of the condition of the marine environment and the damage caused by the war, and take joint measures to prevent further pollution.
Separately, the Ukrainian side raised the issue of the possibility of applying legal and procedural mechanisms to fully terminate Russia’s participation in the work of the Convention’s bodies. The relevant initiative is to be considered by the contracting parties.

Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:45:01 UTC
22:45:01 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority.
Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse.
However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed.
Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach
Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026
The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law.
In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine.
In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year.
Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison.
Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021.
In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims.
Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN.
A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers.
It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026
Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information.
On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.
In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.
In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.
The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.
The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.
In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

A Judicial Challenge to India’s Paternalistic Anti-trafficking Framework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:44:00 UTC
22:44:00 KST

For decades, India’s anti-trafficking framework has rested on a flawed assumption: that trafficking and prostitution are essentially the same thing. As a result, women trafficked through force or deception, women who remained in prostitution after being trafficked, and adults who say they engage in sex work voluntarily have often been put through the same legal process. The law has frequently failed to distinguish exploitation from agency.
In Prajwala v Union of India (2026), decided on May 29, 2026, by a bench of justices – J. B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan – the Supreme Court has attempted to address this problem. The judgment, arising from a petition pending since 2004, lays down a detailed Victim Protection Plan, calls for a comprehensive anti-trafficking law, and, most importantly, recognizes that the existing framework inadequately separates trafficking from voluntary adult sex work. The distinction may seem obvious, but Indian law has struggled with it for decades.
The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (ITPA) emerged from a period when prostitution was viewed largely through a moral lens, and its machinery of rescue, detention, and rehabilitation reflects that origin. Over time, it treated very different women in the same manner. A woman trafficked against her will, a woman trafficked years earlier who remains in prostitution, and an adult voluntarily engaged in sex work may all find themselves before the same magistrate under the same statutory process. The court now recognizes that the one-size-fits-all model is a serious problem.
Its answer is a threshold inquiry. If an adult rescued during a raid states that she is engaged in sex work voluntarily and does not wish to be institutionalized, the magistrate must first determine whether that choice is genuine before ordering rehabilitation or long-term custody. This may seem procedural, but it is a significant shift. It challenges the assumption that every woman found in a brothel cannot make choices about her own life and introduces respect for agency into a framework long dominated by paternalism.
The Victim Protection Plan builds on this logic. It governs every stage of intervention, from rescue to prosecution and reintegration. It rests on principles such as non-criminalization, informed consent, privacy, and individualized care, and bars punitive practices inside protective homes. It also strengthens Anti-Human Trafficking Units and legal aid through District Legal Services Authorities.
The most compelling aspect of the judgement is its emphasis on dignity. Justice Pardiwala repeatedly stressed that trafficking violates human dignity because it reduces human beings to commodities. At the same time, the court recognized that the absence of dignity often precedes trafficking. Poverty, homelessness, lack of education, and economic vulnerability make exploitation possible.
Drawing upon Articles 21 and 23 of the constitution, the court held that rehabilitation is not merely a welfare measure but a right. This matters because governments have traditionally treated rehabilitation as policy rather than entitlement. By locating it within constitutional protections, the court elevated rehabilitation from charity to obligation, one a survivor can enforce in court. A survivor denied shelter, counselling, skills training, or support can now approach a court as a matter of right, rather than plead for a favor.
The judgement built on Budhadev Karmaskar v State of West Bengal (2022), where the court had already invoked Article 21 to uphold the dignity of sex workers. Prajwala insisted that the dignity of trafficking victims and of voluntary adult sex workers must both be protected.
Trafficking remains a serious concern in India. A government report revealed that India recorded 2,135 human trafficking cases in 2024, with roughly 5,800 victims identified. Yet a persistent criticism of India’s anti-trafficking regime is that success is measured by raids and rescues rather than long-term outcomes.
We know how many people enter the system, but far less about what happens afterward. How many survivors receive meaningful rehabilitation? How many gain access to education, employment, and stable housing? How many are retrafficked? The judgement acknowledged these shortcomings but offered limited answers on implementation.
Another unresolved issue is autonomy. The court observed that sex workers can hold rights even without a recognized right to sex work. While the judgment protects adult sex workers from arbitrary detention and police harassment, it avoids asking whether consensual adult sex work itself deserves legal recognition. If an adult engaged in sex work voluntarily is entitled to dignity, liberty, and constitutional protection, why does the law hesitate to recognize his or her agency fully? The court may have sidestepped the question because the case centered on trafficking, but the tension remains.
There is also a question of voice. Critics note that sex workers’ collectives, whose lives the judgment most directly affects, were not heard in open court. A framework that depends on distinguishing coercion from choice will work only if those who live that distinction help design and monitor it.
Implementation is the other test. The plan’s promises of privacy, individualized care, and legal assistance will be delivered by district officials, magistrates, and shelter managers who have long worked within a rescue-first culture. Guidelines on paper change little unless training and accountability follow.
The judgement also raises a broader constitutional question. Invoking Article 142, the Supreme Court has effectively created a nationwide anti-trafficking framework that will operate until Parliament legislates. The court may have felt compelled to act after more than two decades, but judicial directions cannot substitute for legislative reform indefinitely.
Courts can lay down guidelines; they cannot build the shelters, train the police, or fund the legal aid those guidelines demand. A statute could also do what a judgement cannot: align the ITPA, the trafficking provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and child-protection laws into one coherent scheme.
Ultimately, Prajwala is as much a judgement about state failure as it is about trafficking. The court identified a flaw that has persisted in Indian law for decades, the inability to distinguish exploitation from agency, and laid the foundation for a more humane, rights-based framework. But without legislative action, institutional capacity, and sustained political commitment, even the most progressive judicial vision risks remaining on paper.
The Supreme Court has drawn an important line between trafficking and voluntary adult sex work. Parliament must now ensure that it becomes part of law and practice rather than another missed opportunity.

What a China-US AI Safety Channel Needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

The most concrete outcome from last month’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was an apparent agreement to set up a China-U.S. AI incident reporting channel. But even if either government proves willing to use this direct line or start sending data across the Pacific, they must first address a more pressing issue: U.S. and Chinese frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they would need.
In the U.S., no federal statute or regulation specifically requires AI companies to report safety incidents and dangerous capabilities to the government. Although some states have passed incident reporting laws, federal legislation – such as the AI Incident Reporting Act and the FRONTIER Act – has stalled in Congress. The industry is still largely regulating itself.
Moreover, while the White House Accord on Super Intelligence pledges to identify and remedy safety issues, it does not mandate notification to regulators or set reporting deadlines. The Trump administration’s separate Super Intelligence Force is developing government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and other AI incidents. But it is not a regulator, and its recommendations would need to be implemented through enforceable measures.
There is also a severe lack of funding for federal government testing and oversight. According to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index Report, U.S. developers last year released 59 notable AI models, while British developers released just one. Yet the main U.S. federal AI-testing agency, the Commerce Department’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), has an annual budget of only $15 million, whereas the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute (AISI) has a budget of almost $90 million.
Given that the White House Accord seems to envision frontier labs doing the bulk of safety testing themselves, it remains to be seen what role the government would play in validating such testing, and whether any government body would have access to sufficient compute to conduct its own testing.
Unlike the United States, China’s government doesn’t face political bottlenecks, and it has already built a significant regulatory structure, with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) recently calling for behavioral controls, model traceability, security testing, and safeguards against system vulnerabilities and loss of control. But there is still no Chinese equivalent to CAISSI – a specialized, centralized AI-safety body with a mandate. The government has plenty of authority over tech companies, but oversight is dispersed across the CAC, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the Ministry of Science and Technology, and other agencies.
Evaluating the risk of frontier AI models requires technical expertise and coordination among all the relevant Chinese government departments, including the security services. But some Chinese government agencies lack sufficient technical capacity, and many of the people with the deepest technical expertise sit in private research institutes with no authority to demand access to a company’s most advanced models, let alone inspect its internal logs or force it to make changes.
For now, the government has deployed officials from the CAC and NDRC to Chinese labs to discuss possibly gating the release of the most advanced models. But the authorities eventually will need to mandate internal safety-testing teams, access to sufficient compute, and pre-release testing of the most advanced models.
With the next Sino-American AI-safety dialogue scheduled for November, the United States and China should focus on what would make an incident reporting channel more likely to work. For its part, the U.S. government needs a transparent and mandatory policy for testing frontier models. Either the White House should disclose its current framework and make it binding, or it should work with Congress to pass legislation like the bipartisan FRONTIER Act. The federal government also needs to set rules for external audits of AI companies, giving auditors a clear mandate, reporting obligations, and meaningful independence (with auditors selected and paid by an industry body or government agency).
At the same time, the Trump administration needs to be more proactive in monitoring company compliance. It should use the Super Intelligence Force to review the current, flawed release process for the most advanced models, consider what to do about increasingly capable open-weight models, and begin moving toward an incident response mechanism that has teeth.
On the Chinese side, making the reporting channel operational would require closing the authority-expertise gap. The CAC could define safety expectations and reporting arrangements; technical bodies could develop and validate evaluations; the NDRC and other industrial agencies could weigh the effects on investment and diffusion; and the Ministry of Commerce would remain relevant to technology-transfer and export rules. With the United States empowering the Super Intelligence Force to conduct a thorough review of the U.S. government’s role, China should consider something similar.
China also needs to address its lack of evaluation capacity and access to sufficient compute across companies, evaluators, and government bodies. Rapid advances in Chinese open-weight models make this particularly important, because once model weights are released, developers have much less visibility into how their systems are being used or misused. The nascent Z.ai-Concordia framework is a potential template. It sorts models into three categories: green zone models that are safe to be fully released; yellow zone models that require a staged release, structured access for vetted researchers, or API-only hosting while weights are evaluated; and red zone releases that are suspended pending review.
AI safety is a global challenge. Addressing it depends on close and growing collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and a reporting channel for AI incidents is just a small step in the right direction. It will take the U.S. and Chinese governments a long time to reach binding, verifiable agreements. They cannot afford to be held up by failing to enact domestic reforms.
