Russian Help Would Make North Korea’s Missile-test Flurry Worse News
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

North Korea has conducted a flurry of missile tests in the past few weeks. One of the biggest concerns is that Russia may have helped. Advances in North Korean missile technology are unwelcome in themselves, but any Russian technical backing behind the effort would indicate a tightening of the Moscow-Pyongyang partnership – and greater potential for more North Korean advances.
There have been at least four sets of North Korean missile launches in the past few weeks. On September 20, North Korea tested a new missile, thought to carry a hypersonic warhead. According to a South Korean report, North Korea’s Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) provided no details of the missile tested, but wording on the photo caption released by the agency referred to the “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory.” So it is likely to be an “upgraded version of the Hwasong-11MA” hypersonic missile that North Korea first showcased in 2025. South Korean security analysts believe the Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 “combines a KN-23, or Hwasong-11Ga, missile body with a hypersonic glide vehicle-type terminal section.” They describe it as “a long-range precision-strike weapon designed to penetrate missile defenses through maneuverability while striking targets several hundred kilometers away.”
Two weeks later, on October 3, North Korea fired an intermediate-range missile into the waters off its east coast. According to the Asia-Pacific Security Magazine, the KCNA characterized it as another hypersonic missile test. The KCNA reportedly claimed that the missile had struck a target 1,000 km away, though both South Korea and Japan suggested a smaller range. The North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, also claimed that the missile could “maneuver at low altitude and incorporated unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities intended to complicate interception.” Maneuvering is a characteristic of a hypersonic missile. Kim also asserted the inability of Japan and South Korea to arrive at an accurate picture of the flight details, saying that “whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points.” More worryingly, she also described the missile as “strategic,” implying it was designed to deliver nuclear warheads.
About a week later, on October 12, North Korea reportedly launched multiple ballistic missiles of different types. The missiles were fired off its east coast, with at least one type flying more than 900 km, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.
And on October 14 came news, credited to the KCNA, about North Korea test-firing two kinds of submarine-launched cruise missiles. These appear to have been fired from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a submarine that was launched in 2023. There has been some skepticism about the capability of this submarine, but if this was the actual launch platform, this North Korean capability should be treated seriously. Previous underwater missile launches had been from a testbed rather than an operational submarine.
These launches raise concerns about how North Korea managed to make such rapid progress in missile technologies. Many security analysts have attributed North Korean progress to the closer relationship between North Korea and Russia. If they’re right, then we have more reason to expect rapid North Korean technical progress.
North Korea extended military assistance to Moscow following the invasion of Ukraine. In return, North Korea reaped economic benefits and access to military technologies. According to a South Korean think tank, Pyongyang’s arms sales and troop deployment generated more than $10 billion for North Korea, which is huge for a country whose GDP is around $27 billion. Most of this payment was in the form of sensitive military technology, weapon parts, or other materials. Studies also note that Russian companies Novator and Raduga could be assisting North Korea in further advancing the development of new cruise missiles of the Hwasal family.
Beyond missiles, North Korea appears to have gained access to other critical technologies from Russia. South Korea’s military has intelligence hinting at Russia supplying North Korea with submarine nuclear propulsion technology. South Korean Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back revealed this in the parliament’s Defense Committee hearing in October 2025. Although the South Korean intelligence has not yet been verified, there is a reasonable suspicion that Moscow may have supplied two or three propulsion sets from its own decommissioned nuclear submarines. Some reports have also indicated the possibility of Russia providing North Korea with submarine noise-suppression technology.
In addition, Russia is known to have shared drone technology with North Korea. But the growing concern is that Pyongyang could gain access to more advanced and sophisticated drones that could be AI-enabled and jet-powered, such as the Geran-5. Further, North Korea’s Geumseong series tactical attack drones bear a close resemblance to Russian (and Israeli) types, which raises the strong possibility of Russian technology transfers to North Korea.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

Details: According to DIU, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed since the start of the full-scale invasion, while another seven have been damaged.
DIU noted that these losses are significant for Russia's military air fleet, as replacing the aircraft requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources and specialised industrial cooperation.
"By way of a comparison, the number of Su-34s destroyed is equivalent to approximately 2½-3 years of production based on an estimated capacity of 14-18 aircraft per year," the intelligence agency explained.
DIU said Su-34 fighter-bombers were one of the key components of Russia's strike aviation in its war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the Russian military to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements.
"Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernise the Su-34, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes," the intelligence agency emphasised.
Meanwhile, according to DIU, Russia's ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components and the Russian military industry's ability to compensate for its losses.

Chien said investors should watch whether the quarterly moving average holds as support and how trading volume changes. Lower volume and easing selling pressure near that level could signal stabilization, while a break below it on higher volume could point to further losses and a prolonged correction.
He advised against aggressive buying, recommending stocks with strong third-quarter earnings and sound fundamentals. He recommended waiting for share prices to stabilize and trading volume to recover before gradually building positions to reduce exposure to a potentially prolonged correction.

Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:04:04 UTC
22:04:04 KST

Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.
- Share:
Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.
A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.
Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.
"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.
Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.
Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years
To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.
At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.
Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.
Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.
Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.
Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.
High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline
The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.
After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.
That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.
Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.
These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.
Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes
When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.
Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.
The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.
Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.
Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.
Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.
Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?
The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.
"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."
Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.
In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.
The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.
Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.
The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

Bulgaria Has EU’s Widest Rich-Poor Gap in Healthcare Costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:03:00 UTC
22:03:00 KST

Bulgaria has the European Union’s widest income-based gap in the share of people who consider medical care a heavy financial burden, with 42.5% of those in the lowest income group reporting this difficulty compared with 9.7% of the wealthiest according to Eurostat data for 2025.
The difference of 32.8 percentage points is the largest among EU member states, indicating a pronounced disparity in how households with different financial means experience healthcare costs.
Across the EU, 18.7% of people in the lowest income group said medical expenses placed a heavy burden on their finances, compared with 8.5% among those with the highest incomes. The resulting gap of 10.2 percentage points is more than three times smaller than Bulgaria’s.
Latvia recorded the next-largest difference between the two income groups, at 26.1 percentage points, followed by Italy at 22.5 points and Romania at 20.1 points. Spain had the smallest gap, at just 0.9 percentage points.
However, Italy’s figures show that financial pressure from healthcare expenses can also affect wealthier people. There, 25.1% of those in the highest income group reported a heavy financial burden, while the share in Poland reached 20.6%. In contrast, the figure was below 3% among the wealthiest residents of eight EU countries. The lowest proportions, at 1% or less, were recorded in the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia.
The figures distinguish between the overall level of financial hardship and the difference between income groups. Bulgaria does not necessarily have the highest proportion of people struggling with medical expenses across every income category, but it has the widest divide between its poorest and wealthiest residents, giving the issue a particularly pronounced social dimension.
Poverty further widens the gap
Eurostat data for 2025 also show a difference in the financial burden of medical care between people at risk of poverty and those outside that category. Across the EU, 19.1% of people at risk of poverty reported that healthcare costs placed a heavy strain on their finances, compared with 12.5% of those not at risk, a gap of 6.6 percentage points.
In Bulgaria, the difference reached 23.1 percentage points, the largest in the EU. Latvia followed with 18 percentage points, Romania with 16.8 points, and Italy with 13.3 points. Spain and Slovenia recorded almost no difference between the two groups.
Italy had the highest proportion of people at risk of poverty who reported a heavy financial burden from medical care, at 47.6%. Slovenia recorded the lowest share, at 5.6%. Among people not at risk of poverty, the figures ranged from 34.3% in Italy to 2.8% in Estonia.
The Bulgarian figures point to a concentration of financial pressure among people with limited incomes. Although the statistics do not establish what causes the disparity, they show that healthcare expenses affect income groups unequally.
Health difficulties also reflect social differences
The study also assessed difficulties with basic daily activities. Across the EU, 24.9% of people at risk of poverty reported moderate or severe problems with walking, compared with 16.9% of those outside this group, a difference of 8 percentage points.
Problems with memory and concentration were reported by 20.6% of people at risk of poverty and 14.5% of those not in that category, a gap of 6.1 percentage points.
These figures add to the picture of social vulnerability, as people with lower incomes more frequently report both limitations in everyday activities and serious financial difficulties in paying for medical care. The data do not establish a direct causal relationship between these circumstances but show that they occur within the same social group.
The study draws on the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) and covers 2025. Its target population consists of people living in private households, while those residing in institutions are generally excluded.
The comparison places Bulgaria first in the EU for the difference between the lowest and highest income groups in the share reporting that medical care represents a heavy financial burden. The 32.8-percentage-point gap highlights the role of income in access to affordable healthcare, as well as the challenges households face in protecting themselves financially against health-related expenses.

The grammar of political hate? How a single word choice predicts nastier Facebook comment sections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:50 UTC
22:00:50 KST

Subtle grammatical choices in political social media posts are linked to how much hostility users express in the comment sections below them. A large-scale analysis of Facebook discussions published in Social Psychological and Personality Science indicates that posts referring to political groups with nouns rather than adjectives, or making sweeping generalizations about a party, tend to attract a higher proportion of prejudiced replies. Although the effect of any single post is small, the findings suggest that everyday wording habits online could gradually contribute to political division.
Hostility between opposing party supporters, which social scientists call affective polarization, has risen in the United States and several other democracies. Affective polarization refers to the tendency for citizens to view members of an opposing political party with dislike and distrust while favoring their own political group. At high levels, this animosity can lead voters to treat political rivals as enemies rather than fellow citizens, a dynamic linked to eroding trust in democratic institutions.
Sorting people into “us” versus “them” naturally creates some group bias, yet the intensity of that bias depends heavily on a psychological concept known as entitativity. Entitativity describes the extent to which an observer perceives a collection of people as a unified, tightly knit whole rather than a loose assortment of individuals. Supporting this idea, a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 samples found that the more people view an outside group as a coherent entity, the more prejudice they tend to hold toward its members. In politics, research has indicated that believing partisans are fundamentally different kinds of people was linked to greater partisan hostility, through more blame and assumed malicious intent, whereas believing political views themselves are fixed was linked to less.
“In essence, perceiving a group as entitative makes group members appear more interchangeable,” study author Carsten W. Sander, a research associate at Humboldt University of Berlin who conducted the research at Universität Hamburg with co-author Juliane Degner, a professor of social psychology there, told PsyPost. “People then generalize one member’s behavior to the whole group, retaliate against one group member for offenses committed by another, and generally show more outgroup prejudice. We reasoned that this could also fuel political polarization, understood as growing prejudice toward the political outparty.”
Because national political parties contain millions of people, citizens cannot observe an entire party firsthand and instead rely on media and conversation to judge how unified the other side is. Beyond explicit statements about a group, grammatical structures can quietly signal uniformity. One such cue is whether a writer uses a noun label, such as “Senate Republicans,” or an adjective label, such as “Republican senators.” Using a noun defines a person primarily by a single group category, whereas an adjective treats party affiliation as just one trait among many.
Controlled experiments show that these grammatical distinctions shape how people judge unfamiliar or minority groups. For instance, a 2020 study of print news readers found that articles describing an ethnic minority member with a noun rather than an adjective led readers to express slightly greater prejudice toward that entire minority group, whether the story was positive or negative.
A second cue involves generic statements, which are broad claims attributing an enduring trait to a group as an abstract whole, such as “Democrats want climate action,” rather than non-generic phrasing like “some Democrats want climate action.” In a 2010 experimental study of children and adults, participants who learned about a fictional animal category through generic statements were more likely to treat its members as sharing the same underlying nature, though the effect was weaker in children.
Most evidence on noun labels and generic phrasing comes from laboratory studies involving fictional or unfamiliar categories. Sander and Degner wanted to test whether these subtle wording differences also influence hostility toward established political groups like U.S. Democrats and Republicans in real-world online conversations. The authors noted that the relative frequency of partisan noun labels in U.S. online news has risen substantially in recent years, raising the question of how such language plays out on social media.
To examine this in a natural setting, the researchers gathered public Facebook posts and comments through the Meta Content Library. They selected Facebook because it has a diverse American user base and frequently hosts text-based political discussions. After excluding posts in which party labels referred to institutions or events rather than people (such as “the Democratic Party” or “the Republican primary”), the final sample included 45,780 posts and 769,684 direct replies written by 391,386 unique users across 3,878 pages and profiles. News media outlets contributed the largest share of posts, alongside public figures, politicians, and government officials.
To analyze hundreds of thousands of messages, the authors fine-tuned five artificial intelligence models built on transformer architectures, which are machine-learning programs that process language by evaluating how words relate in context. They trained and tested these models on thousands of human-coded examples, supplemented for two of the models with 600 synthetic posts written in matched pairs that differed in only one feature. One model classified whether a post used a party label as a noun (such as “voting Democrats”) or an adjective (such as “Democratic voters”). A second model identified whether the post made a broad generic claim about a group as a whole or a non-generic statement limited by qualifiers or referring to a single past action.
To account for other factors that might provoke angry replies, the models also tracked whether each post referred to a single individual, a subgroup (such as “House Republicans”), or the broader party, and whether the original post itself expressed hostility toward a political party. A separate model evaluated all 769,684 comments to detect partisan prejudice, defined as dislike or negativity aimed at a political group or collective target (such as “Dems are the worst” or “Idiots!”), while excluding remarks aimed only at a single person (such as “I hate Biden”). The researchers publicly registered their hypotheses and analysis plan in advance.
The researchers then used multilevel statistical models to test whether the wording of a specific post predicted the proportion of prejudiced comments below it. Comparing different posts published on the exact same Facebook page allowed the analysis to account for unmeasured differences between pages and their audiences. Across all 45,780 posts, posts using noun labels received a higher proportion of prejudiced comments than posts on the same page using adjective labels. Before controls, the odds that any given comment expressed partisan prejudice were 1.39 times higher beneath noun-label posts than beneath adjective-label posts, an odds ratio that fell to 1.15 after controlling for post prejudice and whether the target was an individual, subgroup, or whole party.
In practical terms, on a typical Facebook page where 59 percent of posts used noun labels, the model predicted that 16.7 percent of comments under a noun-label post would express partisan prejudice, compared with 14.8 percent under an adjective-label post. That is an absolute difference of 1.9 percentage points, or a relative difference of about 13 percent. By contrast, a page’s overall average use of noun labels across all its posts was not a statistically significant predictor of comment prejudice after controls were added, which the authors interpret as a sign that commenters were responding to the wording of the specific post, though they caution that comparisons between pages are vulnerable to hidden differences.
For their second main analysis, the authors tested generic language across the 26,026 posts and 437,744 comments that referred to political groups or subgroups rather than specific individuals. Posts using party labels generically drew a higher share of prejudiced replies than non-generic posts, with an odds ratio of 1.22 before adjustments and 1.20 after controlling for noun usage, post prejudice, and whether the post targeted a subgroup or the broader party.
On a typical page where 29 percent of posts were generic, the predicted probability of a prejudiced comment was 22.2 percent under generic posts versus 19.2 percent under non-generic posts, an absolute difference of 3.0 percentage points or a relative difference of roughly 16 percent. At the page level, pages that posted generic statements more often actually drew somewhat fewer prejudiced comments once other factors were accounted for, a pattern the authors attribute to other differences between pages rather than to the wording itself.
In that second analysis, noun labels continued to independently predict higher rates of prejudiced comments alongside generic phrasing, indicating that each feature was linked to online hostility on its own. Supplementary analyses also showed that these patterns held true whether posts mentioned Democrats or Republicans. Even when comparing different comments written by the exact same user across multiple posts, noun and generic labels still predicted more prejudiced replies, which the authors interpret as a sign that the language affected how users commented rather than merely attracting already hostile users.
These findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in early 2024, which found that broad generic statements about political parties led people to perceive a wider ideological gap between Democrats and Republicans than statements containing qualifiers like “some.” That earlier research measured perceived ideological divides in survey experiments, whereas the new study indicates that generic phrasing is also linked to hostile expressions in real-world social media discussions.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because the study observed existing social media activity rather than randomly assigning different wordings to readers, it cannot establish with certainty that grammatical labels directly caused the increase in prejudiced replies. In addition, the study only captured whether someone wrote a hostile comment in the moment, leaving open whether noun or generic labels create lasting attitude shifts or briefly trigger existing frustrations.
“The key caveat is that the findings are observational,” Sander explained. “Features of the post content that we didn’t control for could be driving both the labeling and the prejudiced comments, so the results shouldn’t be read as showing that labels cause prejudice.” Still, he added, “our results and earlier experimental research are consistent with that possibility.”
The automated classifiers were also imperfect. In test data, the model that detected prejudiced comments caught about 73 percent of them, and about 68 percent of the comments it flagged were truly prejudiced, so some misclassification is likely.
Another caveat is that the statistical effects of a single post’s wording are small, and subtle cues from nouns or generic statements might be overshadowed by explicit news about party infighting or unanimous votes. At the same time, the authors propose that labeling habits could spread through social networks, as one person’s phrasing influences another’s, a possibility they say still needs testing. They also argue that even if a post only briefly nudges a few users to leave hostile replies, those comments remain visible on the page, where they could give other readers an exaggerated impression of how much the opposing party dislikes them.
“The effects were small: about 15% prejudiced comments under adjective labels versus 17% under noun labels,” Sander said. “If they turn out to be causal, though, they could nevertheless matter in practice: Labeling choices by high-reach news outlets could affect very large audiences, and small effects may accumulate as people read many posts over time.”
To test whether changing how parties are labeled actually reduces online hostility, the researchers hope to evaluate these wording variations in real-world trials over extended periods. “The next step would be an experimental replication, for example in collaboration with an online news outlet that would let us randomly vary the labeling in its social media posts, as this would allow us to establish causality,” Sander noted.
Future studies could also examine whether shifting toward adjective labels, qualifiers like “some,” or person-first phrasing such as “people who voted Republican” helps cool down political comment sections. Researchers might additionally test whether describing discrete past actions, such as “Republicans voted,” rather than permanent group traits, such as “Republicans are,” tempers partisan animosity.
The study, “Constructing the Enemy: Noun and Generic Party Labels Predict Partisan Prejudice in Social Media Comments,” was authored by Carsten W. Sander and Juliane Degner.

AI Foundations for Learners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Sara Davila directs students toward responsible and creative use of AI
Students today encounter AI across nearly every aspect of their learning, from search engines and writing tools to content recommendations and automated feedback. Students may rely on AI regularly without fully understanding how it works, what it produces, or what is sacrificed when there is no effort and the opportunity to reflect is lost. While these systems can support efficiency and access, they also introduce new challenges related to independence, authorship, and critical thinking. The challenge for educators lies in helping learners move from dependency and passive consumption to active, intentional creation.
Just as educators benefit from a framework to guide thoughtful use of AI, students also need structured support to develop responsible and effective practice. English language learners have distinct and unique challenges that can impact their overall interaction and satisfaction with AI tools. Language learners may rely more heavily on translation tools or prefer AI-polished and translated work over their own voice. Given how quickly AI has become embedded in everyday tools, from a WhatsApp chat to word-processing applications, providing guidance is critical to support the unique needs of language learners while building digital literacy, AI competence, and English proficiency.
The AI Competency Framework for Students
The AI Competency Framework for Students offers a way for educators to support our learners (UNESCO, 2024). Like the AI Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2024) this is not a scripted curriculum or a checklist of digital skills but rather a lens for learning that helps students build confidence, ethics, and agency as they navigate AI-enhanced environments.
The student framework consists of four dimensions:
1. A Human-Centered Mindset
2. Responsible AI Ethics
3. AI Techniques
4. AI Systems Design
Together, these dimensions create a path for student use of AI, helping learners navigate from understanding to autonomy. As students learn to use AI thoughtfully, responsibly, and creatively, they can explore how these tools can deepen their own learning and creativity without risking opportunities for growth and reflection.
1. A Human-Centered Mindset: AI as Assistant to Learning
The foundation of AI literacy for students is the understanding that AI is a tool developed by humans to support humans’ success, not as a replacement for human knowledge, ingenuity, or innovation. When learners understand this, they can begin to use AI as a partner in the learning process without shortcutting key opportunities to gain new skills and abilities.
A key aspect of the framework is how it can help focus on the importance of reflection for learning. In practice, this mindset means guiding students to ask reflective questions like:
- Is this tool helping me practice a skill or doing the work for me?
- Am I still thinking, analyzing, and expressing my own ideas?
In some ways, the goal is to help students understand how using AI tools can impact their own sense of ownership, critical thinking, and creativity. As research has shown, when AI is introduced into learning is a key component of success: too soon and the lack of effort leads to complete disengagement, where just-in-time AI can stimulate critical thinking and creativity (Kosmyna et al., 2025). When learners think first and use AI afterward, they retain more knowledge, demonstrate greater creativity, and engage more deeply with content. Timing and intention make the difference between cognitive support and cognitive erosion.
2. Responsible AI Ethics: Learning to Make Informed Choices
As students experiment with AI, they also need to understand its ethical dimensions. Responsible use begins with three essential questions:
- Does this help me learn?
AI should extend thinking, not replace it. Students can learn to evaluate whether a tool supports skill growth or short-circuits effort.
- Am I being honest about my work?
Academic integrity must adapt to the AI era. Learners should know how to acknowledge when they’ve used an AI tool, much like citing a source. This transparency reinforces ownership and ethical behavior.
- Am I protecting my privacy?
Students should never share personal information, school details, or sensitive data with online systems. Developing digital boundaries is now as essential as learning to write a thesis statement.
Discussing these principles in the classroom helps learners turn ethical considerations into tangible questions that support learner understanding and autonomy with AI tools. Further, discussing ethical uses of AI helps learners consider academic integrity, much like understanding the difference between paraphrasing and plagiarism. By framing AI use around learning, honesty, and privacy, educators help students build habits that extend beyond the classroom and into responsible digital participation.
3. AI Techniques: Building Skill Through Purposeful Practice
The third dimension focuses on developing the practical skills to use AI effectively. This is where students learn how to communicate with AI tools and choose the right one for a given task. This includes working with generative AI models like ChatGPT or Claude, as well as identifying common forms of AI embedded in everyday technologies that often go unnoticed.
For example:
- When revising writing, a student might use an AI grammar checker to find sentence-level errors.
- When exploring a new topic, they might use a research-focused tool like Google Search or Perplexity to locate and evaluate reliable sources.
- When practicing pronunciation, they might use a speech-based AI to listen, repeat, and self-assess.
Over the last two decades, a variety of AI tools have launched, working quietly in the background to shape tasks and decisions without drawing attention. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday technologies, students must learn not only how to use visible tools but how to recognize when AI is influencing their work in less obvious ways. When a learner accepts a suggested sentence in a Word document or changes a topic based on a search result, they may not realize that AI is informing their decisions and potentially changing their intended communication. As such, helping students be selective, intentional, and aware becomes a key component of AI literacy.
4. AI Systems Design: Creating and Developing AI
The final dimension of the student framework is creative and empowering. It introduces learners to the idea that interacting with AI does not have to be a passive experience, but rather, these tools can be used to build what our learners imagine. As students learn how AI responds to input, they begin to see that they can shape how it behaves, understand its limits, and eventually use it, adapt it, or even build their own to support their own interests and personal goals.
Supporting this dimension does not require teachers to become AI developers or technical specialists. Rather, it involves helping students recognize that AI systems are not fixed tools but evolving constructions shaped by human choices, assumptions, and priorities. As students begin to understand this relationship, they move beyond interacting with AI toward thinking about how such systems are formed, how they can be questioned, and how they might one day be shaped to serve human purposes more deliberately.
To support this development, teachers can guide students with simple but powerful questions such as:
- What am I asking this tool to do, and why?
- How does the way I interact with the tool affect the result I get?
- What decisions seem to be built into this system?
- How could this tool be adapted to better support my own goals?
- If I were designing this tool, what would I change?
These questions shift attention away from the tool and back to the learner’s thinking, helping students see how their decisions shape AI outcomes. Over time, this awareness allows learners to move beyond using AI toward influencing and adapting how it is used. This reinforces a critical idea: meaningful learning comes not from the power of AI but from students’ ability to direct, evaluate, and shape the tools they work with.
From Users to Creators: A New Model of Learning
When all four dimensions come together, students transition from consuming AI output to creating with AI. Their learning pathway mirrors the development of knowledge from understanding to complex creation.
- Understand — Grasp what AI is and how it works.
- Apply — Use AI purposefully to support learning tasks.
- Create — Design new ideas, projects, or systems using AI as a tool for innovation.
This evolution turns students into collaborators in their own education. They become thinkers who use AI to test hypotheses, refine arguments, and imagine possibilities. These are all skills that prepare students for a world where human intelligence and machine intelligence will coexist.
Ultimately, the AI competency frameworks for teachers and students empower educators to guide students toward critical resilience—the ability to use AI creatively without losing their own voice or agency. The goal is to support the development of thoughtful citizens who understand AI’s limits, question its authority, and shape its future responsibly. Our role as educators is to ensure that AI enhances, not replaces, the essential processes of thinking and learning. By modeling curiosity, critical judgment, and ethical awareness, we prepare students to use these tools with intention and independence.
References
Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y., Situ, J., Liao, X., Beresnitzky, A., Maes, P. (2025). “Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing task.” arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872
UNESCO. (2024). AI Competency Framework for Students. Paris, France: UNESCO. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000391105
UNESCO. (2024). AI Competency Framework for Teachers. Paris, France: UNESCO. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000391104

Sara has helped educators and learning organizations reimagine English programs through evidence-based curriculum design, practical professional development, and 21st-century approaches to teaching and learning. Sara is based in Chicago, working worldwide. Learn more at saradavila.com.

Hong Kong reveals findings of probe into deadly residential fire

HONG KONG, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government on Thursday released a report on the investigation into a major fire at the residential complex Wang Fuk Court, announcing accountability measures and follow-up reforms.
At a press conference, HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee apologized for the deadly blaze. The HKSAR government has decided which principal official should bear political accountability, he said, pledging to pursue criminal proceedings against those involved and the companies linked to the incident, and investigate relevant civil servants.
Based on the independent committee's report, the HKSAR government will undertake comprehensive reforms, including banning bid-rigging in building maintenance projects, establishing a building maintenance support and services bureau, setting up a central data system and overhauling the complaint mechanism, Lee said.
Lee also vowed to spare no effort in leading the government in resolving the problems and implementing comprehensive overhauls to ensure that no similar incident occurs again. ■

Economic Watch: Smart, green and service-oriented: Canton Fair mirrors new momentum in China's foreign trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:37 CST
21:59:37 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The 140th edition of the China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is showcasing smart, green and service-oriented products, with high-tech, customized and low-carbon debuts drawing global buyers and highlighting new opportunities for Chinese manufacturing.
Logistics robots, drink-making robots and pet-companion robots crowded the intelligent robotics area at the fair, which is being held from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4 in Guangzhou, capital of south China's Guangdong Province.
At the booth of Hangzhou Taixi Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., buyers lined up to try out a consumer waist-assist exoskeleton. Many overseas buyers held the handrail and shuffled forward, step by step, to feel how the device relieves pressure on their lower limbs.
It is the first flagship product to integrate its human-oriented physical AI technology roadmap, said company founder Liang Linchao. The device uses waist motors and sensors to detect movement and assist lower-limb mobility. Its weight has been cut to about 2 kg, and alongside a refined appearance, algorithms and gait plans tailored to elderly people and hemiplegic patients have been added.
The cluster of cutting-edge smart equipment reflects a broader push toward industrial innovation. At this fair, 64 percent of exhibitors have integrated the industrial internet and artificial intelligence into R&D and production, and new products accounted for 23.2 percent of exhibits, marking a record high.
"At today's Canton Fair, consumer electronics are the dominant category, and tech products such as new energy storage, embodied intelligence and smart healthcare are eye-catching, with many cutting-edge Chinese-made products making their debut," said Zhang Li, an official with the Ministry of Commerce.
Nearby, several European buyers closely watched the scrolling data at DSL Tech Group's booth. The AI-POOL low-chlorine intelligent pool system uses sensor probes to collect the pool's real-time indicators such as residual chlorine, pH level, turbidity and water pressure, and automatically coordinates pumps, disinfection units and sand-filter backwash systems.
Chen Meixiang, the representative of the company, demonstrated on her phone how users can receive alerts about water quality abnormalities from thousands of miles away. The system adjusts automatically, so staff no longer need to visit regularly to take samples and mix chemicals.
"Many overseas private pools used to rely on maintenance workers visiting once a week, and water quality would easily exceed standards," Chen said. These European clients are mainly pool operation and maintenance service providers, attracted by the system's ability to cut manual maintenance costs.
These technology-driven products are also reflected in trade data. Customs statistics show that in the first three quarters of 2026, China's total imports and exports of industrial robots, electronic components, computer parts and electrical equipment exceeded 10 trillion yuan (1.49 trillion U.S. dollars), up 58.9 percent year on year, driving overall import and export growth by 11.3 percentage points.
Liu Chun, president of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, said that driven by technological innovation and industrial upgrading, high-tech and high-value-added products are gradually becoming the main growth engine of foreign trade, pushing "China's smart manufacturing" toward the high end of global industrial and value chains.
This service-oriented approach is visible at the booth of Shandong Linuo Paradigma Co., Ltd., where sales staff explained tailored plans to buyers from different continents.
"Africa lacks power and is windy and dusty, so we cut costs and provide solar water-heating systems that are easy to install and run without electricity," a staff member of the company said. "The Middle East wants high quality, so we match energy-saving products with high-standard certification, and South Asia emphasizes large capacity and durability, so we strengthen system adaptability."
The company has set up agent systems and localized service outlets in markets of Belt and Road partner countries, combining Chinese manufacturing, German-partnered technology and global service into a competitive edge.
Beyond individual products, the latest edition of the Canton Fair also features a batch of prefabricated new products, including space capsules, portable integrated kitchens and modular homestay houses. Chinese suppliers are moving from selling parts to selling whole houses, and integrated overseas expansion is supporting a new growth path.
"By launching prefabricated building solutions for cultural tourism camps, we have attracted buyers from Australia, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia among other countries, and more than 300 have reached preliminary agreements. We will continue to use project meetings to deliver full-chain services from planning to design, construction and operation," said Jia Xuehong, planning and design director of Chongqing SUNDON Prefabricated Construction and Technology Co., Ltd.
More and more foreign trade companies are shifting from simply taking orders and shipping goods to building systems and exporting supporting services. At the fair, 36.5 percent of exhibitors have started a transformation of "product plus service."
For the first time, the trade services zone covers all 10 major categories of producer services, including logistics and warehousing, industrial design, overseas operation and maintenance, cross-border investment and financing and other supporting services, building a one-stop support platform for companies expanding overseas.
Yang Jie, secretary-general of the Guangdong Industrial Design Association, said that under an industrial design and R&D approach that runs through the whole life cycle and centers on consumer pain points, more and more Chinese companies are winning favor in more markets by integrating design into the early stages of development and coordinating it with technology to deliver innovative products and solutions.
Green products are another highlight. Amid the global energy transition, green products and low-carbon technologies have become highly sought-after in international markets. At the fair, exhibitor Xiamen HiTHIUM Energy Storage Technology focused on showcasing its flagship long-duration energy storage products, presenting stable and reliable long-duration power supply solutions to overseas buyers.
Wang Pengcheng, co-founder and CEO of the company, said more and more countries and regions are advancing energy structure transition, and the company hopes that through the Canton Fair, the "Chinese solution" for long-duration energy storage can be seen by the world, so that more countries have the option of using stable, green and affordable clean power.
China is enriching global supply with quality green and smart products and helping accelerate the global green, low-carbon and digital and intelligent transition. Over the past decade, China has provided more than 80 percent of the world's photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of its wind power equipment, effectively driving down the cost of global wind and solar power generation.
Commenting on the trend, Liang Yutian, associate dean of the Institute of International and Regional Studies, Sun Yat-sen University, said the concentrated display of new energy, energy storage equipment, green home appliances and other products reflects the global green transition forming new market demand. In the future, around the digital economy, green energy, smart manufacturing and low-carbon technologies, countries can further strengthen technological cooperation, industrial coordination and standards alignment to cultivate new international growth points.
From continuous breakthroughs in hard technology to complete solutions stepping into the spotlight, and green thinking embedded in products, the innovation vitality surging at the Canton Fair illustrates how China's foreign trade keeps cultivating new advantages and deepening its links with the world. ■

African health ministers urge enhanced readiness, solidarity as Ebola outbreak escalates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:26 CST
21:59:26 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- African health ministers on Wednesday joined the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) for an emergency meeting, calling for enhanced continental preparedness and greater solidarity to contain the expanding multi-country Ebola outbreak.
The virtual meeting on Ebola was held amid the rapid geographical spread of the ongoing outbreak of the Bundibugyo Ebola strain. The outbreak has surpassed 10,170 confirmed cases with a mounting death toll, with four African countries affected so far, namely the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria.
Addressing the emergency meeting, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said the Ebola outbreak has, over the past five months, grown from a national crisis into a continental health security test.
Emphasizing that "the main priority today in our continent is to stop Ebola," he stressed insecurity, complex humanitarian situations, a lack of medical countermeasures, and limited funding are compounding the crisis.
Kaseya said that the confirmed cases in the outbreaks have reached 10,172, with more than 4,932 deaths and a case fatality rate of 48.5 percent. Some 2,727 patients have recovered from the disease.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a message delivered on his behalf, stressed that "we are still facing an extremely serious and difficult outbreak."
"This outbreak in the DRC is not a single outbreak in a single place. It is many outbreaks across a vast and complex area, requiring a sustained response everywhere at the same time," he said.
He noted that recent measures taken by authorities in Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria demonstrate the continent's capacity to manage outbreaks when detected early and met with rapid responses.
Describing Kenya's response to the outbreak as a "whole-of-government and whole-of-society" approach, Patrick Amoth, director-general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health, stressed that the country's experience also points to gaps Africa must close.
He highlighted health workforce infections, the cross-border spread of cases bypassing surveillance and contact tracing, and Africa's reliance on uncertain donated medicines amid a lack of licensed vaccines or specific therapeutics as critical gaps.
He stressed that Kenya will keep travel and trade open and will not impose restrictions beyond what international health regulations and evidence require. He further noted that the country will share data, sequences, and lessons openly.
Echoing the sentiment, Ugandan Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi noted that the country's experience shows that transmission can be interrupted when countries act early and decisively.
"Uganda was affected by this outbreak and was able to interrupt transmission within our borders," he said. "Our experience should give us hope, but should also give us a sense of responsibility."
He noted that the outbreak's international dimension requires sustained attention. "The lesson is straightforward: when a public health emergency threatens several countries, our response must also become regional and continental."
Beyond the four affected nations, 10 other countries across Africa have previously been designated as high-risk, namely South Sudan, Rwanda, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Somalia. ■

Across China: Water-skimming motorcycle stunt puts rural county on tourist map
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:19 CST
21:59:19 KST

CHANGSHA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A water-skimming stunt challenge has turned a rural Chinese county into an unlikely destination for tourists and motorcycle fans, drawing nearly as many visitors during the event as its entire population.
Mayang, a county with 274,000 permanent residents in central China's Hunan Province, received 250,000 tourist arrivals when Zhang Xue rode a custom-built motorcycle across the Jinjiang River on Sunday, the latest stage in a 17-year effort to master the water.
Zhang, 39, rode 40.74 km across the river. The run, which included seven consecutive U-turns, was certified by Guinness World Records as the longest distance traveled by a modified motorcycle on open water.
In 2009, he tried to ride across the water on a rudimentary modified motorcycle and fell into the river four times, reaching no more than 20 meters.
Zhang said he never lost faith in the project, even when failure seemed routine. "Even if I failed, I would have no regrets. I enjoy the process."
Today, Zhang is better known as the founder of ZXMOTO, the motorcycle manufacturer he established in Chongqing in 2024. Its French rider Valentin Debise ended the 2026 World Supersport season as runner-up in the riders' standings, while the company finished third in the manufacturers' championship in its debut year.
The motorcycle used in Mayang, the MX450, was built on a standard frame and powertrain, and fitted with an amphibious skimming kit. A front steering sled acted as a water rudder, while the rear wheel's deep-tread tire was partially submerged in the river, generating thrust to propel the bike forward. The bike had to maintain sufficient speed to stay on the surface, making U-turns particularly risky.
"The challenge was not only technical but physical," said Deng Liansong, a research and development engineer at ZXMOTO.
Guinness World Records adjudicator Xiong Wen, who witnessed the attempt in Mayang, said the significance of the event went beyond the numbers. "It is inspiring to see one person's passion for motorcycles persist for so many years and finally be recognized by more people," she said.
Videos of the run spread quickly on Chinese short-video platforms, where related hashtags accumulated more than 2.3 billion views. Local officials said traffic at Mayang's highway toll stations rose about 21 percent as visitors arrived from other parts of Hunan, as well as from Guangdong and Chongqing.
Zhao Yazhou, a motorcycle fan from Zhengzhou in central China's Henan Province, drove 11 hours to watch the challenge. He said the experience felt far more powerful in person than on a screen.
During the event period, the county generated 125 million yuan (about 18.76 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue, according to Tian Haishan, deputy director of Mayang County's bureau of culture, tourism, radio and television. On the day of the challenge, around 80,000 people were present, he added.
Tian described the event as a high-profile example of rural cultural tourism breaking into mainstream attention. "Zhang's extreme challenge in his hometown was not just the birth of a Guinness record," he said. "It helped bring Mayang into the national spotlight."
Zhang, recently appointed as a cultural tourism ambassador for Huaihua City, used the event to promote iconic products from his home county of Mayang, which is administered by Huaihua City. His bike carried branding for Mayang's traditional brown sugar, as well as symbols of rock sugar oranges and dragon boats.
Exposure from his Superbike World Championship appearance in March helped sell out a year's inventory of the brown sugar in three days, Tian said.
Zhang said his resilience was shaped by the place where he grew up. "Different regional cultures influence a person's character," Zhang said. "My unyielding nature comes from this land. I chose to fulfill my dream here so that my hometown could be seen by the world." ■

Ukraine's parliament calls on world not to recognize Russia's State Duma 'elections'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Ukraine's parliament calls on world not to recognize Russia's State Duma 'elections'
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, 250 members of parliament voted in favor of the draft resolution, No. 16091.
"The purpose of the draft resolution is to clearly and unequivocally establish the position of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine that the elections of deputies to the ninth convocation of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation, and the composition of the State Duma formed as a result, lack democratic and political legitimacy," the explanatory note to the draft resolution states.
Under the resolution, the Verkhovna Rada appealed to the United Nations, the European Parliament, parliamentary assemblies and governments around the world, calling on them, in particular, not to recognize the legitimacy of the Russian State Duma elections or their results; not to treat the ninth-convocation State Duma as a legitimate democratic basis for confirming the representative character of the Russian authorities; and not to recognize the credentials of newly formed Russian parliamentary delegations.
The appeal also emphasizes that the electoral process in Russia took place amid the systematic shrinking of political space, persecution of opposition politicians, and restrictions on freedom of speech and the activities of independent media and civil society.
"A separate and fundamentally important violation of international law was the Russian Federation's holding of elections to its own state authority in temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The Russian Federation has no right under international law to extend its own 'electoral process' to the territory of the sovereign state of Ukraine or to use the results of such voting to form its state authorities," the resolution states.
As Ukrinform reported, Russia included the Ukrainian-controlled cities of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Sviatohirsk in the Donetsk region in one of its electoral districts so that local residents could vote in the "elections" to the State Duma.
The elections to the ninth convocation of the State Duma of the Russian Federation were held from September 18 to 20, 2026.

Russian forces hammer Ukrainian army’s transport infrastructure in past day — top brass

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian forces struck transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army and enemy deployment sites over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

Monumental building, silver coins discovered at medieval city Rusokastro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Monumental building, silver coins discovered at medieval city Rusokastro
Thursday 29 October 2026 13:09
Thursday, 29 October 2026, 13:09
PHOTO Regional History Museum in Burgas
Font size
A monumental building, 7.60 metres wide and of still unknown length, has been uncovered near the inner southern fortress wall. It is the latest archaeological discovery of the year made by archaeologists from Burgas at the medieval city of Rusokastro, the Regional Historical Museum in Burgas (RIM-Burgas) has announced.
The walls are 1.1 metres thick and built of stone bonded with abundant mortar. The inner surfaces of the building’s walls are heavily coated with pink waterproof mortar. This suggests that the structure was used as a water reservoir or a storehouse for food supplies. It most likely represents the ground floor of a building located in the city’s central quarter, with a second, residential floor presumed to have stood above it.
A large number of portable archaeological finds have also been unearthed, including silver coins minted under Bulgarian Tsar Ivan Alexander, Venetian silver grosso coins known as matapanes, copper coins and many other artefacts. These are now being cleaned in the restoration workshop of the Burgas museum.
Rusokastro is included on the list of priority national sites receiving state funding to support cultural tourism in Bulgaria.

Naval drones sink Greek container ship sailing from Israel off Bulgaria's coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:56:06 UTC
21:56:06 KST

A Greek-owned container ship chartered by Israeli shipping company ZIM sank in the Black Sea after being struck by unmanned surface vessels off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday, Bulgarian authorities said, in the latest attack on commercial shipping amid growing concerns over the spillover effects of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET was carrying 421 shipping containers from Haifa's Gulf Port in Israel to the Romanian port of Constanța when it was attacked while passing through Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, outside the country's territorial waters.
All 18 crew members, including 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were rescued and safely transported to the Bulgarian port of Varna.
The Bulgarian government said it had received advance warning of the attack, believed to be connected to the war between Russia and Ukraine, but was unable to prevent it.
Footage published by a Bulgarian news website showed one of the unmanned surface vessels approaching the container ship moments before impact.
The ship sustained severe damage in the attack and subsequently sank, according to Bulgarian authorities.
The identity of those responsible remains unclear. Initial assessments suggest the vessel was not targeted because of its connection to Israel, although investigators have yet to establish a motive.
The incident has heightened concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the western Black Sea, where attacks involving aerial and maritime drones have become increasingly frequent.
At least six vessels have been attacked by aerial or unmanned surface drones off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving approximately 25 people dead, according to reports. The attacks have raised fears that the conflict between Russia and Ukraine is increasingly threatening shipping routes beyond the immediate war zone.
ZIM confirmed that the damaged vessel was chartered by the company but was not part of its owned fleet.
"A small container ship carrying a limited number of containers, which ZIM charters but does not own, was struck by an unmanned surface vessel in the Black Sea," the company said in a statement.
"All crew members were safely evacuated, and the expected financial damage, according to a preliminary assessment, is minimal."
The company said it was working to secure a replacement vessel and maintain service to its customers.
"To the best of our knowledge, several similar incidents involving vessels in the area have occurred over the past month," ZIM added.
Oren Caspi, chairman of ZIM's workers' union, said the attack underscored the importance of maintaining Israeli control over the shipping company amid growing geopolitical instability.
"In a reality of boycotts and security threats, in a world of political instability, we must keep ZIM Israeli," Caspi said.
"Much remains unknown about this extraordinary attack, and we are still learning the details."
Although Bulgaria does not share a land border with Russia or Ukraine, its position on the western Black Sea places it along important commercial shipping routes connecting the region to major Russian and Ukrainian ports.
The Black Sea has become a key theater of the Russia-Ukraine war, with unmanned aerial vehicles and explosive-laden maritime drones increasingly used in attacks on naval and maritime targets.
Such incidents have become more frequent in recent months, affecting Eastern European countries and shipping corridors previously considered relatively secure.
At least 45 merchant vessels have been attacked over the past 12 months in parts of the Black Sea that had not previously been classified as high-risk areas, according to figures cited in the report.
The latest sinking highlights the growing risks facing civilian shipping in the region, where commercial vessels continue to operate amid an expanding threat from unmanned weapons.
While there is no indication that the CONTSHIP JET was targeted because of its Israeli commercial connection, the attack adds to concerns among shipping operators about the safety of Black Sea routes and the potential for further disruption to international trade.

Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

VW logs €5.86 billion Q3 operating loss on Porsche writedown
October 29, 2026
The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.
The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.
The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.
It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.
"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.
What were the main takeaways from VW's Q3 figures?
The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.
Here are some of the key Q3 figures:
- An operating loss of €5.86 billion, compared to €1.3 billion in same quarter last year
- It's the company's worst single quarterly loss since the height of the "Dieselgate" emissions scandal in 2015
- Sales revenue dipped 6.3% year-on-year, to €75.3 billion
- Deliveries to customers, unit sales, and unit production numbers all dipped by roughly 15% as the company starts to reduce production levels, trying to adjust to falling demand
And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:
- Sales revenue of €233.4 billion was broadly comparable to 2025's figure of €238.7 billion
- But vehicle unit sales, at 5.9 million, are 11% lower than 6.6 million last year — meaning the group is selling fewer cars, at higher prices
- The company's order intake for new cars rose 4% year-on-year, and by 39% for battery electric vehicles (BEVs)
- Operating profit lies at just €0.1 billion, compared with €5.4 billion a year ago
- But VW said 'special items' amounting to €8.7 billion primarily explain this massive dip
- Non-cash writedowns on Porsche assets worth €6.4 billion were the largest portion of this
How did investors respond?
VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.
Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.
By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.
What are VW's downsizing plans?
CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.
Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.
Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.
CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.
Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.
"That is not enough in the long term," he said.
As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.
This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

Police officers and rescue workers to see pay rises in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Police officers and rescue workers to see pay rises in 2027
The government has allocated €7.3 million to increase the salaries of rescue workers and police officers, mainly those who are "lower-paid frontline employees," Minister of the Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said on Thursday.
Speaking at the government's weekly press conference, he said rescue workers, police officers, border guards and emergency response operators at the Emergency Response Center are set to benefit from the funding boost.
"The government has allocated €7.3 million to our area of administration for pay raises. Salaries will increase in 3,764 positions from the beginning of next year," he said. In total, almost 8,000 people work in the ministry's area of administration.
"All of them deserve fair pay for their work. But the state's financial resources are limited, and this requires clear choices," Taro said.
"We are not distributing this additional money evenly as a percentage increase, but directing it primarily to lower-paid frontline employees," he explained.
Rescue workers will receive the largest pay raise, with their salaries increasing by €140 per month, Taro said. This means the minimum salary for a rescue worker will rise by nearly 9 percent and the average salary by 8 percent.
"This will bring the average salary of rescue workers to approximately 85 percent of the Estonian average. This is a necessary step forward, but it cannot be considered sufficient," the interior minister acknowledged. The average salary was €2,092 in 2025.
Taro said the minimum salary for a police officer will rise by 4.4 percent, the average salary of a patrol police officer will rise above the Estonian average, and the minimum salary of an emergency response operator at the Emergency Response Center will rise by nearly 5 percent.
He added that SMIT technicians and customer support specialists will also receive pay raises. "The pay raise will be €90 per month," Taro said.
"The pay raise also covers the immediate supervisors of frontline employees who themselves perform operational duties. Other managers' salaries will not increase. Salaries at the Ministry of the Interior will not increase," he said.

I followed the debate in the European Parliament over the past months, and I can say there seems to be a broad majority support for this landmark FTA. The benefits for both sides are so huge that I'm sure the European Parliament will give its support in the consent vote," added McAllister, who heads the Parliamentary committee that shapes and monitors the EU's common foreign and security policy.
McAllister also said the EU would particularly welcome progress on the investment protection agreement as it would strengthen the confidence of European investors in the Indian market, encouraging greater European investments and contributing to job creation in India. He said the FTA would allow India and the EU to work more closely on de-risking supply chains and reducing dependencies.If the FTA indeed is ready for signing by mid-December, Modi is likely to stop over in Brussels to ink the deal on his way back to India from the US G20 summit. I would definitely mention information sharing, research cooperation and cybersecurity. One element would be that we also invite India to participate in a closer cooperation with our European defense industry, because here we also have a joint interest," said the lawmaker."We in Europe, as part of our strategic sovereignty, want to reduce the dependence on one particular country, and I understand that the debate in India is very similar. You also want to step-by-step reduce your dependence, and I think this is a very good win-win situation for both sides," said McAllister.
Asked about India's position on the Russia-Ukraine war, McAllister welcomed the Modi government's diplomatic efforts to achieve a ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, Black Sea shipping, and the movement of grain."Any peace agreement must be just, sustainable and acceptable to both sides. It must also include absolute, concrete security guarantees for Ukraine that Putin (Russian president) is not able to repeat this unbelievable act of aggression and violation of international law. So, if India with its special relationship with Russia - and also India with its constructive relationship with Ukraine - can play any kind of role constructively, it would be welcome," he said, while praising Jaishankar's "constructive" role for peace.

One of Spadshchyna’s founders and its first president was Andriy Parubiy, who was elected speaker of the Verkhovna Rada over 2016-2019.
The Vasyl Kostyuk Charitable Foundation was founded in 2026. It supports initiatives in sports, spiritual development and patriotic upbringing.
Previously we reported that Vasyl Kostyuk supported the training of Ukraine’s national karate team and its participation in the junior championships in Poland, where Ukraine’s young karateka won a record number of medals.
