Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.

The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.

The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.

“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.

It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.

Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Israel’s Smart Shooter exports drone-killing weapon station to Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:55:40 UTC
19:55:40 KST

- Smart Shooter delivered the first batch of SMASH Hopper MG remote weapon stations to an integrator building a defense system for an Asian military.
- The systems will support counter-drone and ground defense, and Smart Shooter helped set up local installation and maintenance capability.
Israeli company Smart Shooter has delivered the first batch of its SMASH Hopper MG remote weapon stations to an unnamed integrator in Asia, which is building them into a defense system for an Asian military to shoot down drones and engage ground targets, the company said on social media.
Smart Shooter did not identify the country, the armed force or the integrator, and it did not say how many systems were in the first batch, what the contract is worth or when further deliveries will follow. As part of the project, the company also helped the customer set up local installation and maintenance capability.
The SMASH Hopper is a lightweight remotely operated weapon station that lets a soldier aim and fire from behind cover or from inside a vehicle, and the MG designation refers to the version configured for a machine gun. It uses Smart Shooter’s SMASH fire control technology, which tracks a moving target and releases the shot only when the computer calculates a hit, an approach the company built for hitting small drones that are hard to engage with ordinary iron sights or optics.
Earlier SMASH Hopper versions carried an assault rifle, including the configuration inside the company’s SMASH DOME portable counter-drone system, which pairs the weapon station with radar and optical sensors.
Israel Defense Forces units have used the SMASH Hopper for several years, Smart Shooter said in June, when Israel’s Defense Ministry placed a new order worth up to $2.5 million with delivery by the end of 2026. That followed a separate ministry contract in May for SMASH Hopper systems, spare parts and services, which Israeli media linked to the drone threat on the country’s northern border.
Most of Smart Shooter’s sales come from its rifle-mounted SMASH 2000L and SMASH 3000 fire control sights, which are used by U.S. forces, and in September the U.S. Army included the company’s U.S. subsidiary in a group of 10 counter-drone suppliers sharing $4.15 billion in contracts, with Smart Shooter receiving $150 million. The company says the SMASH family is also used in Britain, Germany and other NATO countries.
Smart Shooter described the Asian integrator’s system as a layered defense against threats in the air and on the ground, but it did not say which other sensors or weapons the system includes or when the armed force expects to put it into service.

The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance as it concluded its fifth plenary session, according to Xinhua News Agency.
The Politburo presided over the meeting. 
President Xi Jinping, who's also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered an important address, and a communique was issued after the session.
At the session, participants considered and adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance. 
Xi delivered explanatory remarks on the draft of the resolution.
The CPC Central Committee gave a highly positive assessment of the great achievements the Party has made in exercising full and rigorous self-governance in the new era, Xinhua reported.
"It was stressed that many favourable conditions are now in place for advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, while we also face many new circumstances and new issues in this endeavour," the communique said.
Profound changes in global, national and Party conditions have made the CPC's tasks of uniting and leading the people in safeguarding China's sovereignty, security, and development interests, of uniting and leading the people in promoting reform and development and maintaining social harmony and stability, and of maintaining its advanced nature and integrity even more formidable, it added.
Systematic plans for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance were also made at the session, according to the communique.
Strict management of officials is the key to full and rigorous Party self-governance, it noted.
"We will build up the ranks of high-calibre officials with firm political commitment, outstanding professional competence, excellent work conduct, and strict discipline," it added.
Party organisations at all levels play the principal role in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique, adding that it is therefore essential to systematically advance the development of Party organisations at all levels and in all sectors to strengthen their political and organisational functions.
"It was noted that taking integrated steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to commit corruption is both an important strategy for full and rigorous Party self-governance and a fundamental guideline for our fight against corruption," the communique said.
"We must take systematic steps to address both symptoms and root causes of corruption and adopt a holistic approach that combines severe punishment, targeted remedy, and effective prevention, carrying this fight through to the end."
Strengthening Party regulations and institutions represents a long-term, fundamental strategy for ensuring full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique.
The CPC Central Committee decided at the session that the Party will convene its 21st National Congress in Beijing in the second half of 2027 and stated that this congress, which is to be held at a critical stage for basically realising socialist modernisation and on a new journey toward the Second Centenary Goal, will be a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country.
The session elected Zhang Shengmin as a new Politburo member.

Residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's Kherson region, who wish to return to Ukrainian government-controlled territory after evacuation will first be transported to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar region, according to a ceasefire agreement reported by Fox News.
From there, they will be flown on a Russian Ministry of Defence aircraft to Gomel in Belarus before being transferred to Ukraine.
The evacuees travelling to Ukrainian-controlled territory will be accompanied by Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, two representatives of his office and two Ukrainian journalists.
Representatives of Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and members of the humanitarian mission coordination group will also travel with them to Belarus.
On Wednesday morning, both Lubinets and Lantratova announced that no ceasefire violations had been recorded during the 30 hours since the truce began in Oleshky.
Oleshky is located in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine's Kherson region.
The town remains under constant shelling, while residents who have stayed behind have been forced to survive for months without electricity or adequate medical assistance.
Food and medicine are in short supply, and roads leading into the town have been mined.
According to volunteers, approximately 1,500 people, including around 40 children, remain in Oleshky.
Including neighbouring villages, the total number of people in the affected area is estimated at approximately 6,000, including around 200 children.
Lubinets reported that the ceasefire in Oleshky began at 3 a.m. on 27 October.
The Russian Ministry of Defence confirmed that the ceasefire had been implemented.
The ceasefire is expected to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. on 1 November.

Arkhangelsk Region's national park studies waste movement in White Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:51:29 UTC
19:51:29 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 29. /TASS/. Experts of the Kenozersky National Park and the Onega Pomorie National Park in the Arkhangelsk Region studied how waste spreads across the White Sea, the Kenozersky National Park told TASS. The specialists launched buoys with a GPS tracker from different locations to watch the waste movement.
"To show clearly where the waste comes from and how it gets into the water area, authors of the project "The Sea is Disturbed" together with the Marlin‑Yug Company, and specialists of the Marine Observation Systems Laboratory in Sevastopol have produced buoys with a GPS tracker. The research buoys were produced for the first time. They are similar to those used by polar explorers when they observe ice drifts. The buoys were launched six times to demonstrate to the Arkhangelsk Region's residents optional routes the waste follows in the White Sea," the national park said.
Most waste enters the White Sea from Arkhangelsk, Severodvinsk and Novodvinsk. Waste on the shore is either fishermen's waste (gear, improvised buoys and floats), or urban waste (bottles, food packages), or the waste people leave on the beach (rubber slippers), as well as "bio-loading stations from urban sewage treatment plants" (black plastic cylinders with petals).
On every buoy, the specialists left contact information as well as notes stating that it is safe and is part of the study. The buoys' routes formed into a map of six paths of a plastic bottle conditionally forgotten on the shore. The first buoy, launched at a crowded beach on the Yagry Island, was washed onto the shores of the Solza River the next morning - it has covered 21 km. A local village resident picked up the buoy. The second buoy passed 243 km and sailed to the Onega Peninsula. It was about to be picked near the town of Lopshenga, but the wind changed, and the buoy was blown back to Severodvinsk, where it was reported by people working for the local ship repair company.
The third attempt was to send a buoy from the Mudyug Island. It reached the village of Kuya, but the tide swept the buoy out into the sea 511 km from the place where it had been launched. On the 20th day of the trip, the Solovki Museum-Reserve staff found it. Further on, it was released from the Bolshoy Solovetsky Island, sailed 136 km, and was thrown onto dry land. During the second launch, the Solovetsky buoy reached the Murmansk Region and returned to the island after a week of travel. Buoy movements in real time during all the missions were available online.
"The project has helped everyone to see clearly how in a matter of days, potential waste, left on the shore, travels tens and hundreds of kilometers and ends up in unexpected places," the project's authors noted. The project's research was supported by the Presidential Nature Foundation.

RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with "striking butterfly layout"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:51:09 UTC
19:51:09 KST

RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with “striking butterfly layout”
British studio RSHP has completed a 45-storey office skyscraper in Shenzhen, China, featuring two angled wings connected by a central core.
Called Hetao Alpha, the 212-metre-tall office building comprises a 37-storey east wing and a 44-storey west wing connected by a central core. The building sits on top of a mixed-use podium.
“The naturally ventilated office tower features a striking butterfly layout with fully glazed east and west wings,” the studio said.
Cantilevered bays extended from the central concrete core on the east and west sides to form the tower’s angled wings, which have 70,410 square metres of office space.
On every 12 levels, mega trusses located on refuge and service floors provide additional structural support.
The Hetao Alpha skyscraper has a fully glazed facade that, together with open floor plates, ensures unobstructed views of the cityscape for the office workers.
Curved double-height glazing at each of the wings’ four corners captures curated viewpoints of the Shenzhen Bay Wetlands to the west and the Hong Kong Mai Po Wetlands to the south.
Lifts are located on the north and south facades in the central volume. These were also fully glazed to offer panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.
“Centred around a concrete core with suspended corner bays, the tower minimises its perimeter structure, creating slender edges and expansive double-height views, forming the distinct structural system that defines the tower’s identity,” said Marco Tessaro, associate at RSHP.
Louvred panels on the facade and vents were incorporated into the glazing to create natural ventilation throughout the building while reducing energy consumption.
This was one of the methods used to help the project achieve China’s 3-star Green Building Evaluation Standard, which is equivalent to LEED Gold.
A six-level public podium is connected to the east wing, creating a roof terrace where half of the space is reserved for greenery.
The studio added extensive vegetation, a feature wall and water elements to improve biodiversity and help create a calm environment for socialising.
“The building’s natural ventilation, green rooftop spaces, and energy-efficient facade define a truly sustainable development that reduces consumption while enhancing wellbeing for both occupants and the wider community,” said Wenchao Zhou, associate at RSHP.
Mega triangular trusses on the podium roof help transfer the load of the east wing to the building’s central core.
Another viewing platform is located on the building’s west wing, which, together with the podium roof terrace, was designed to invite public visitors and private tenants alike to engage in outdoor activities such as observing migrating birds, a popular hobby for the locals.
According to RSHP, one of the challenges of the project was combining two separate briefs from different clients to create an uplifting mixed-use development as well as an office building with a bold and coherent architectural identity.
“Taking a holistic approach to the complex brief, RSHP’s design for Hetao Alpha has created an open and welcoming destination for work, retail, and leisure that achieves a bold architectural identity with a seamless transition between public and private space,” the studio explained.
The 13,640-square-metre public podium houses sports facilities, a library, retail, and a double-height arts exhibition space.
A passageway cuts through the north and south ends of the ground floor, helping to give the podium a floating look that reduces the perceived weight of the volume.
The entrance lobby for the office building can be found inside the podium. This double-height space is supported by a series of slim columns connected to the triangular trusses above on the podium roof.
A metro station was integrated into the basement, which also has a sunken plaza with retail stores.
“Spacious, open, and welcoming, the tower and podium integrate seamlessly to form an elegant composition that maximises connectivity with the wider public realm and the park to the east,” said Richard Paul, director of RSHP.
“With glazed office wings overlooking Shenzhen’s wetlands and a public podium offering diverse activity, the development achieves a serene, flexible environment that accommodates a wide range of uses,” he continued.
Elsewhere in China, RSHP has completed a 186-metre mixed-use skyscraper in central Shanghai, as well as a vast convention centre in Zhengzhou, with 16 exhibition halls connected by a mile-long elevated walkway

Kyiv residents are switching to scooters because the Southern Bridge is closed
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv residents cover the 4 km between Osokorky and Vydubychi on scooters in 10 minutes for 60–70 hryvnias. On foot, the journey takes up to an hour.
In Kyiv, local residents are using rental electric scooters and bicycles to travel between the Osokorky and Vydubychi metro stations via the Southern Bridge, which has been closed to cars following Russian strikes. A scooter ride costs 60–70 hryvnias. This was reported by the public organization "Passengers of Kyiv" on October 29, according to UNN.
Details
"Kyiv residents have increased their use of rental electric scooters between the Osokorky and Vydubychi metro stations. It is possible to cross the Southern Bridge, which is closed to cars, by electric scooter in 10 minutes, paying 60–70 hryvnias for the service. At the same time, walking this 4-kilometer distance can take up to 1 hour. Currently, on the bridge on the Vydubychi metro side, there are a couple dozen scooters belonging to Bolt and only one from Bike Now. A Bolt specialist was also working on site, replacing batteries," the post says.
In addition, according to the public organization’s observations, people have set up an improvised bicycle parking area nearby. In particular, owners leave their bicycles, locking them to parts of the fencing. Presumably, after the end of the workday, they use them to get home across the bridge.
"We spoke with some scooter users, and they were pleased with this fast and inexpensive trip. The popularity of this shuttle-like movement by scooter is also growing because of the safety of travel—as cars are not driving at high speed in the adjacent lanes. Therefore, bicycles and electric scooters are currently a convenient, fairly safe, and certainly more cost-effective way to travel between the banks of the city than taxis," the post says.
Under these circumstances, "Passengers of Kyiv" called on representatives of the Transport Department of the Kyiv City State Administration and Kyivavtodor to temporarily remove at least one section of the crash barrier, so that people who arrive by scooter would not be forced to climb over the high barriers and get dirty, and also to remove the garbage from the spiral staircase, which Kyiv residents have begun using actively.
Reminder
From October 27 to November 1, traffic on the Southern Bridge will be partially restricted while the road surface is being repaired. Traffic toward the left bank will proceed only in the first lane.

UK keeps 623 Boxer order and adds heavy wheeled recovery vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:49:21 UTC
19:49:21 KST

- The British Army will buy a heavy wheeled recovery vehicle to recover Boxers after dropping a dedicated Boxer repair and recovery variant.
- Minister Luke Pollard said the order of 623 Boxers is unchanged, with over 500 built in Britain, alongside 72 RCH 155 artillery vehicles.
The British Army will buy a heavy wheeled recovery vehicle to tow and recover damaged Boxer armored vehicles in the field, after the Ministry of Defence dropped plans for a dedicated Boxer repair and recovery variant, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard told Parliament, UK Defence Journal reported.
Pollard was answering Conservative lawmaker Ben Obese-Jecty, the member for Huntingdon, who asked how the Army would repair Boxers in the field with no repair and recovery version on order. The minister did not say which vehicle the Army will buy, how many it needs or when the purchase will be made.
“The Army will absolutely have the ability to recover and support Boxer vehicles on the battlefield, such as through the Boxer support variants and the wider force, including the Heavy Wheeled Recovery Vehicle which we will procure,” said Pollard.
The question followed the Army’s decision this month to scrap three planned Boxer variants, armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch, as part of work on the Defence Investment Plan. In an answer the day before, Pollard said the ministry had assessed the armored recovery module built by German firm Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft for the role and rejected it, concluding that a generic heavy wheeled recovery vehicle would be more useful and more affordable across the whole force. Until a new vehicle arrives, Boxers recover each other, with backup from the Army’s Support Vehicle (Recovery) trucks and the tracked Challenger Armoured Repair and Recovery Vehicle.
Boxer is an eight-wheeled armored vehicle built around a common drive module that accepts different mission modules, which lets one chassis serve as a troop carrier, ambulance, command post or weapons carrier. A dedicated recovery version would have carried a crane and winch on that same chassis, keeping pace with Boxer units and sharing their protection and spare parts. A wheeled recovery truck can serve every vehicle type in the Army, but generally with less armor than a vehicle built on the Boxer hull.
Pollard said the overall order has not changed.
“There has been no change to our order of 623 Boxer vehicles, of which over 500 are being built here in the UK, and we are buying 72 Boxer RCH Artillery vehicles,” said Pollard.
All 623 Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard at two British plants, Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land in Telford and KNDS UK in Stockport, and Team Boxer UK delivered the 100th British-built Boxer in June. Pollard said the work backs more than 1,000 British jobs. Ministers confirmed last week that a planned third batch of Boxers is no longer being pursued through the program.
The 72 artillery vehicles are separate from that total. The RCH 155 pairs a 155 mm remote-controlled howitzer turret developed by Krauss-Maffei Wegmann with the Boxer drive module already in British service, and Britain signed a nearly £1 billion contract for 72 of the guns in May. They will replace the AS90 tracked howitzers in the close support artillery role, a gap the Army has filled with Swedish-built Archer guns since giving its AS90s to Ukraine.

Smoke from this year’s Indonesian forest and peatland fires has inflicted an estimated 8 billion ringgit (US$1.97 billion) in welfare losses on Malaysia, contributing to an estimated 1,700 deaths and severely disrupting manufacturing, according to a report commissioned by the country’s leading industrial group.
The study, “The 2026 Fire Season and Transboundary Haze in Malaysia”, was conducted for the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM), as reported by the Malay Mail. Drawing on satellite data, air-quality monitoring and atmospheric modelling, the assessment tracked the impact of prolonged haze from July 1 to October 22.
Short-term exposure to fine particles from the fires contributed to an estimated 1,700 premature deaths – with a 95 per cent uncertainty interval of 1,300 to 2,300 – the report found, noting the figures reflect statistical models rather than individually confirmed fatalities.

Ukraine needs EU support to develop decentralized power generation – Kachka
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Ukraine needs EU support to develop decentralized power generation – Kachka
Ukraine's representative to the European Union, Taras Kachka, made the statement at a special event organized by the Kyiv Security Forum entitled "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe," held in Brussels on October 28, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"At the local level, we need EU support on this decentralized generation. This is the experience of Kharkiv and other cities and it is now expanding to small and big cities, including Kyiv as well. We need to have an energy system that when every particular house, multi-apartment house, could be autonomous in terms of energy supply if the grid is not working. That can help also small businesses to stay alive and the economy continue to be operating," Kachka said.
He described the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, operating within the Energy Community, as one of the most effective assistance mechanisms. The fund pools financial contributions and purchases the equipment Ukraine needs.
"We had over EUR 2 billion aggregated in this fund, and it is one of the most efficient. But every winter, we learn new lessons what we need to buy. And this always happens, because Russia is damaging more and more elements of the grids beyond what we've been able to protect. And we also invent new ways of protecting with concrete, with hiding something under the earth. It all costs," Kachka said.
At the same time, he noted that new power generation technologies, particularly in renewable energy, help maintain the balance of the energy system. These include small wind and solar power plants, batteries and energy storage systems. Ukraine is also attracting investment in these areas.
"But the bigger picture is that you need to be able to protect your energy system. So that's why anti-ballistic, anti-missile and anti-drone systems are extremely important, since you have no alternatives," Kachka said.
He said that despite the difficult circumstances, Ukraine's energy sector remains attractive to public and private investors. As examples, the diplomat cited projects supplying equipment to Ukrainian companies with support from the Danish government, interest in energy projects under the Ukraine Investment Framework, and increased involvement by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC).
Speaking about urgent needs, he stressed the importance of increasing fuel supplies for small generators used in residential areas and ensuring that equipment reaches Ukraine promptly.

"The court has ruled to find Tandyr Oleksii Vitaliiovych guilty of committing the criminal offense provided for in Part 3 of Article 286 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and to impose on him, under this article, a sentence of imprisonment for a term of 9 years, with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a term of 10 years," the judge announced.

Context
On the night of May 26, 2023, Judge Oleksii Tandyr, then head of the Makariv District Court of Kyiv Region, ran over and killed a National Guard serviceman at a checkpoint in the capital. The judge was detained at the scene.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office launched an investigation under Part 3 of Article 286-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The High Council of Justice granted the motion of the deputy Prosecutor General to consent to the judge's detention. Judge Tandyr was remanded in custody.
In August, the High Council of Justice decided to dismiss Judge Oleksii Tandyr from the Makariv District Court of Kyiv Region.
In January 2026, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of European standards of liberty and security in the case of former Judge Oleksii Tandyr. The Court awarded Tandyr 2,100 euros in compensation for non-pecuniary damage and 250 euros in legal costs.

Lagarde Announces Early Exit as ECB Begins Search for Successor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:45:06 UTC
19:45:06 KST

Eurozone Inflation Jumps to 3.8% in September
Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8% in September, above market forecasts and at its highest level since September 2023
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will leave her post on February 7, 2027, about nine months before the end of her eight-year term, the ECB announced Thursday, as the bank prepared to release its latest interest rate decision.
Lagarde notified the ECB’s Governing Council, which determines interest rates across the eurozone, and European Council President António Costa of her decision, according to the bank’s statement. The ECB did not provide a reason for her early departure.
“The Governing Council thanked President Lagarde warmly and gave her a long standing ovation,” the statement said.
Costa also thanked Lagarde for her work, praising her “dedication as President of the European Central Bank since November 2019”.
“To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay,” Costa said.
The European Council, which brings together EU leaders, will appoint Lagarde’s successor. Under EU rules, the appointment requires a qualified majority vote following a recommendation from EU finance ministers and consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council.
Lagarde, a former French finance minister and managing director of the International Monetary Fund, took over as ECB president in November 2019. Speculation about her leaving before the end of her term had been circulating for months.
No official explanation has been given for her decision, although speculation has linked an early departure to the possibility of allowing EU leaders to select her successor before French elections that could result in a far-right victory and influence the choice.
The announcement came ahead of a key ECB meeting expected to focus on France’s deteriorating public finances. The bank was widely expected to leave its deposit rate unchanged at 2.5% on Thursday, with Lagarde scheduled to speak to reporters after the decision.

An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics, who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

Cemvision selected for €27.5 million grant to build low-emission cement plant in Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:44:56 UTC
19:44:56 KST

Swedish company Cemvision’s RE-MENT project has been selected to receive up to €27.5 million in funding from the European Union Innovation Fund to establish a commercial-scale low-emission cement plant in Ventspils, Latvia. The project is one of only two projects planned in Latvia selected for funding under this call. The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) supported the company throughout the application preparation and funding acquisition process.
Under the RE-MENT project, Cemvision plans to establish a plant in Ventspils capable of producing up to 500,000 tonnes of cement annually with exceptionally low production emissions. The project aims to manufacture supersulphated cement (SSC), which can reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 90% compared with conventional cement production. Over its first ten years of operation, the project is expected to avoid more than 3.1 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions, while strengthening European industrial competitiveness and promoting the production of sustainable construction materials.
“Being selected among the projects supported by the Innovation Fund demonstrates that our technology is ready to move from the demonstration phase to industrial-scale production,” says Claes Kollberg, CEO of Cemvision. “This grant is a decisive step towards establishing our first commercial plant and demonstrating that Europe can produce the cement it needs from industrial residual materials while generating only a fraction of the emissions associated with conventional cement production. LIAA provided significant support in preparing our application, and we look forward to continuing our close cooperation with the Latvian government and local authorities to bring the plant project to fruition.”
Cemvision will now begin preparing the grant agreement with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). The agreement is expected to be signed between November 2026 and March 2027.
LIAA supported the company throughout the Innovation Fund application process, including organising information days in Latvia, facilitating access to expert knowledge, and providing guidance on programme requirements and funding opportunities.
“We congratulate Cemvision on securing support from the European Union Innovation Fund for the development of its plant in Ventspils. This funding reduces the project’s financial risks and helps move the planned facility towards implementation. Investments of this kind support the development of manufacturing in Latvia using innovative technologies and open up broader opportunities for our companies in European markets,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA).
Cemvision’s project is one of two projects in Latvia that have secured funding under this European Union Innovation Fund call. This demonstrates Latvia’s potential to develop internationally competitive industrial projects that attract foreign investment, create new manufacturing capacity and support the transition towards a climate-neutral economy.
The first Latvian company to receive support from the European Union Innovation Fund was Aerones. In 2023, the company was awarded a €4.4 million grant to scale up the production of robotic systems for repairing wind turbine blades.
“Latvia’s industrial growth requires not only new manufacturing facilities but also modern infrastructure and accessible, high-quality housing that helps companies attract employees. The renovation of existing housing stock and the construction of new factories create demand for high-quality building materials at competitive prices. Cemvision’s planned investment in Ventspils demonstrates how green technologies can become a competitive advantage for industry: lower emissions mean reduced exposure to fluctuations in CO₂ allowance prices. For Latvia, this represents an opportunity to produce modern construction materials both for domestic needs and for export. The Nordic market is strategically important for Latvia. Earlier this year, I led a Latvian business trade mission to Sweden to establish new business partnerships and encourage investment that supports the shared growth of the Baltic and Nordic region. The value of investments like this extends far beyond the factory itself – they generate orders for Latvian companies, create new jobs and bring in export revenues, strengthening the economy as a whole,” emphasises Viktors Valainis, Latvia’s Minister of Economics.
In 2027, LIAA, together with the Ministry of Climate and Energy (KEM) and the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK), plans to organise an in-person Innovation Fund information day. The event will provide Latvian companies with information about the Fund’s financing opportunities and application requirements. The date and registration details will be announced at a later stage.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Representation for the countries of the African continent in international organizations must be ensured, Russian President Vladimir Putin has stated.
He described the absence of African delegates among the permanent members of the UN Security Council as unjust.
"The world is changing, and Africa is changing; Africa’s role and significance are growing. As we have noted - and we fully agree with this - Africa’s role will only continue to increase. He called for acting with caution in this matter "on the basis of a broad consensus, so as not to destroy what we already have."
"As of now, humanity has no other universal instrument at its disposal - within the international community - comparable to the UN Security Council or the United Nations itself," he concluded.

Ukraine Targets Russia’s Only Plant Producing Key Chemical for Military Body Armor in Bashkortostan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:44:26 UTC
19:44:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Targets Russia’s Only Plant Producing Key Chemical for Military Body Armor in Bashkortostan
A Ukrainian drone attack reportedly struck the Bashkir Soda Company chemical plant in Sterlitamak, Russia’s Republic of Bashkortostan, on the morning of October 29, with thick white smoke seen rising from the facility.
According to Russian media outlet ASTRA, the strike occurred after authorities issued a drone threat warning across the region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Bashkir Soda Company is one of Russia’s largest chemical manufacturing complexes, producing a range of industrial chemicals, including soda ash, baking soda, polyvinyl chloride, hydrochloric acid, and dichloroethane.
The company is part of Roskhim, a major Russian chemical holding group.
Beyond its civilian industrial operations, the facility also manufactures materials used by Russia’s defense industry, including terephthaloyl chloride, a chemical compound used in the production of high-strength aramid fibers. The company is also listed in the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade’s classified register of defense enterprises.
The Bashkir Soda Company is reportedly the only producer of terephthaloyl chloride in Russia, making the facility a significant supplier of a chemical used in manufacturing protective military equipment.
Aramid fibers are widely used in the production of ballistic protection materials, including body armor, helmets, and other protective gear.
The reported strike follows another drone attack on a major Russian chemical facility just a day earlier.
On the night of October 28, a drone strike sparked a fire at the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, Russia’s Tula region. The facility is among the country’s largest producers of nitrogen fertilizers and has previously supplied chemicals to a manufacturer of military explosives.
Video footage published by the monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 28 showed flames at the industrial complex following the reported attack. An analysis of the available imagery suggested that the plant’s AM-70 ammonia production unit may have been struck.

“Turn Around While There is Still Time”: US Senator Demands Tanker Carrying Russian Fuel Reverse Its Course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:44:20 UTC
19:44:20 KST

- Category
- World
“Turn Around While There is Still Time”: US Senator Demands Tanker Carrying Russian Fuel Reverse Its Course
US Senator Richard Blumenthal has publicly urged maritime operators to redirect vessels carrying illegal shipments of Russian diesel fuel destined for American ports.
In a statement shared on social platform X, the lawmaker highlighted the movement of the Agioi Fanendes, a Malta-flagged tanker transporting approximately 40,000 metric tons of Russian fuel toward the Port of New York and New Jersey.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vessel departed a Russian terminal on October 22 and is scheduled to reach its US destination on November 7. Addressing the managing director of Greece-based Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited (EASTMED), Blumenthal demanded that the company alter the ship's course immediately.
The lawmaker dispatched a formal letter to EASTMED managing director Athanasios Martinos, establishing an October 31 deadline for the firm to supply critical operational details.
His inquiry demands full identification of the seller, buyer, charterer, insurer, terminal operator, and entity managing the subsequent distribution of the cargo.
Additionally, Blumenthal questioned whether the shipping firm had received guidance or instructions regarding this delivery from the US Department of the Treasury or other federal regulators.
Blumenthal stressed that discharging Russian refined oil products at American facilities violates existing federal law.
He cited the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act enacted in 2022, which explicitly bans the import of Russian energy goods into the United States.
Addressing General License No. 135 issued by the US Department of the Treasury, the senator insisted that administrative authorizations cannot supersede statutory measures passed by Congress.
He stated, “The President may have issued a license to facilitate this transaction, but only Congress can make it legally valid.” Warning maritime operators that administrative waivers will not clear them of liability, he added, “Turn around while there is still time. If you deliver the diesel, you will violate a very explicit law passed in 2022 that prohibits the importation of Russian fuel. No president can unilaterally override a law.”
Previously, it was reported that American businesses faced severe legal warnings after Representative Jamie Raskin cautioned that importing Russian diesel could lead to fines of up to $1 million and up to 20 years in prison, despite President Donald Trump’s fuel agreement with Moscow.
Raskin sent a letter to major industry groups, stating that the administration could not unilaterally override the federal import ban that Congress passed following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
He stressed that those who participated in the deal acted at their own risk, as statutory restrictions required congressional approval and specific conditions regarding Ukraine to be met before any energy ban could be lifted.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,560 Troops, 1 Aircraft in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,560 troops and another military aircraft over the past 24 hours, bringing its total estimated personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion to approximately 1,584,910, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 29.
The latest tally also includes one tank and five armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative estimated losses to 12,449 tanks and 25,614 armored vehicles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Another 25 artillery systems and four multiple-launch rocket systems were added to the total, raising estimated losses in those categories to 51,699 and 2,245, respectively. Air defense system losses remained unchanged at 1,727.
The General Staff also recorded the loss of one Russian aircraft, bringing the cumulative figure to 450. Helicopter losses remained at 356.
Four additional ground robotic systems brought that total to 3,036, while another 1,614 operational-tactical UAVs raised estimated drone losses to 587,409.
Cruise missile losses remained unchanged at 5,140, while Russia’s estimated naval losses stood at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 272 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost during the latest reporting period, pushing the cumulative total to 168,010. One additional piece of special equipment brought that figure to 4,860.
Fighting remained intense across the front, with 189 combat engagements recorded between Ukrainian and Russian forces during the past 24 hours.
Earlier, reports emerged that Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated that Russia’s offensive in eastern Ukraine would take years to achieve its objectives at the current pace.

US Delivers $7.9 Million in Demining Equipment to Ukrainian Sappers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:43:44 UTC
19:43:44 KST

- Category
- World
US Delivers $7.9 Million in Demining Equipment to Ukrainian Sappers
The United States has delivered a new batch of specialized demining gear valued at $7.9 million to the State Special Transport Service of Ukraine.
According to the US Embassy in Ukraine, humanitarian landmine clearance directly aligns with American security and economic interests by creating safe conditions for US businesses to operate on Ukrainian territory, Hromadske reported on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new shipment is designed to help Ukrainian sappers safely and effectively clear landmines, anti-personnel mines, and unexploded munitions across contaminated areas.
Large areas of the country remain heavily contaminated with explosive remnants of war following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The State Special Transport Service works alongside other national agencies to clear hazard zones. The US government has previously funded training programs and instruction for more than 2,200 sappers serving in the unit, as reported by Hromadske.
US-trained units from the agency have already made thousands of areas safe, restoring 1,764 square kilometers of land. During these operations, specialists have identified and neutralized more than 262,000 mines and explosive items.
Almost 23% of Ukraine's territory remains contaminated—roughly 128,000 square kilometers—and full clearance is expected to take at least a decade.
Explosive devices have killed or injured more than 1,358 people since 2022, among them 380 killed, and clearing a single hectare costs at least $1,400.
The contamination keeps growing even as crews clear it. Russian forces have stepped up remote mining of Ukrainian supply routes, dropping explosive charges and magnetic mines from drones around Chasiv Yar and nearby Kostiantynivka in the Donetsk region.
Ukrainian units there must scan and clear the roads before every logistics run, often flying reconnaissance drones ahead of the movement.

Ukraine Hunts Russian Tank Regiment HQ for Months—Then Two HIMARS Rounds Finish It
Ukrainian forces spent months tracking the command post of Russia’s 26th Tank Regiment before destroying it with two HIMARS strikes, Ukraine’s 33rd Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on October 29.
According to the brigade, Ukrainian reconnaissance teams monitored the site for several months, refined its coordinates, and waited until they fully confirmed the target.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Once the location was verified, HIMARS was brought in. Two munitions were enough to destroy the command post, the brigade said.
The aftermath was partly captured in intercepted Russian radio communications included in footage released by the Ukrainian unit.
In the recording, one Russian serviceman says those who survived the strike scattered “like rats from a sinking ship.”
Another responds that they should have relocated the command post earlier.
The 33rd Brigade said the site was destroyed, while the extent of Russian personnel losses is still being assessed.
Earlier, the 45th Artillery Brigade of the 11th Army Corps destroyed a Russian 9A316 transporter erector launcher and radar element from the Buk air defense system using an M142 HIMARS rocket system.

Paris shooting suspect admitted to targeting Muslims and Africans, prosecutor says
A shooter suspected of killing one person and wounding five others, including a child, last week in the town of Trappes, near Paris, admitted to targeting Muslims and Africans, France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor said. The 39-year-old was on Thursday charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A man arrested after a gun attack in the Paris suburbs, killing one person and wounding seven including a child, has admitted to "targeting individuals who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African", prosecutors said Thursday.
Last Friday, the 39-year-old, identified as Kevin T., opened fire with a submachine gun from a moving vehicle as he drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris. He was arrested later that day. Most of the victims were of foreign origin.
The attack came in an increasingly tense political climate, with presidential elections just six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls.
On Thursday, the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, said the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT).
Read moreSuspect in racist Paris shooting transferred to psychiatric unit, had drugs in his system
Earlier this week Kevin T. had contested the racist nature of the attack.
National terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters Thursday that Kevin T. now claimed he had chosen the location for his actions because it was "a hotbed for Islamists".
The suspect has been held in police custody, Christen said, noting that he had requested that he be held in pretrial detention.
'No regret'
Authorities initially said five people, including an 11-year-old child, had been wounded in the attack, but later revised the toll to seven injured.
Three victims were still in hospital Thursday, one of them in life-threatening condition.
Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French national of Congolese origin, was killed in the attack.
Kevin T. rejected suggestions he had "intended to kill children", but that he "might have been mistaken due to their size".
He stated that he "feels no regret", Christen said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The prosecutor noted the "very high level of preparation" behind the attack, including the acquisition in September of "several weapon components designed to enhance the tactical effectiveness of a Sten submachine gun, as well as a police armband and handcuffs".
Kevin T. denied any "terrorist intent", viewing his actions as "legitimate", the prosecutor said.
A search of the suspect's home had uncovered "weapons or weapon components, specifically a magazine, two pairs of brass knuckles, a steel bayonet, and a silencer", Christen said.
Also found were several books, including a Quran, a Bible, and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf, as well as stickers celebrating Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN) party.
'RN provided ideological ammunition'
Christen said the stickers bore slogans such as "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", but they were not produced by the RN party.
Kevin T. had told investigators he had designed them himself, then ordered them to be manufactured via Amazon.
The suspect told investigators he was neither a member of nor a sympathiser with any political party, Christen added.
According to a source close to the investigation, Kevin T. had become increasingly radicalised by far-right ideology over the past decade, blaming Arabs and Black people for "everything".
Romain Ruiz, a lawyer for one of the victims, said: "What this man's statements show is that the National Rally provided him with ideological ammunition, and that this ammunition is what came out of his gun on Friday."
Kevin T., who has four previous convictions, said he had suffered from psychological problems and had used drugs since the age of 13.
The attack has triggered protests against the normalisation of racist hatred.
In an interview on the YouTube channel HugoDecrypte on Wednesday, Macron suggested that "certain political movements on the far right" – including the RN and "those close to them" – had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".
RN lawmaker Jean-Philippe Tanguy retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.
Authorities banned a far-right, radical-leaning symposium on "remigration" – scheduled for Saturday in the suburbs of Paris – and a demonstration planned for Sunday in the capital.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The Bulgarian Navy has sent the corvette Reshitelny to the waters off Cape Shabla to sink the cargo shipKHORYV, which was struck by a drone and capsized in the Black Sea near Constanța on October 23, Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov told bTV.
The vessel is drifting southward without a crew or lights inside Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone, posing a serious hazard to other ships navigating the area.
Eftimov said worsening weather was complicating efforts to sink the ship.
“We attempted to sink it, and we are continuing today. The ship has proven to have a very robust structure,” the admiral said.
At around 10 a.m. on October 23, the KHORYV crew reported an explosion caused by an unmanned aerial vehicle near the Romanian port of Constanța. The strike caused the merchant vessel to develop a severe list before capsizing, although it remained afloat.
Thirteen people were aboard the ship: 10 Ukrainian citizens and three Azerbaijani citizens. One sailor died in the incident, while three others remain missing. Bulgarian sailors rescued the remaining crew members.
The Bulgarian Ministry of Transport has issued a warning to mariners instructing them to keep at least five cables between their vessels and the KHORYV.

Germany news: Merz says North Korea threatening Europe's freedom
