Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:06:25 UTC
19:06:25 KST

Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
- The Pentagon is treating freezer failures at US military bases as a suspected cyberattack. Investigators are working with Cyber Command, law enforcement, and French counterparts.
- At least six commissaries were hit in late August. In one case at Fort Huachuca, the freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food”.
- The case raises wider fears about hacked cold storage. A similar French attack hit over 350 sites, caused major food losses, and showed outdated controllers can be easy targets.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoilt food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter.
One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier in October.
Reuters was unable to ascertain how far along the Pentagon’s investigation was or whether it had reached any conclusions about what happened or who might be responsible.
When asked about the investigation, the Pentagon said that a unit of Cyber Command – the military’s cyber force – was “working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners”. It did not elaborate.
The US Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division said its Cyber Field Office was involved in the investigation and that it was working with French law enforcement to better understand “the refrigeration outages in Europe”.
The late August malfunctions in the United States affected at least six commissaries – on-base stores where military personnel buy their food – according to a Reuters review of the military bases’ contemporaneous Facebook posts and website updates.
In at least one of the cases, the freezers did not simply stop working; the cooling units’ temperatures were cranked up overnight, yielding mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning.
The Fort Huachuca, Arizona Facebook account explained on Aug 26 that its freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was ‘spoiled’”.
The spate of rogue freezer behaviour and the possibility of cyber-sabotage were first reported on Aug 28 by a recently created blog called Signal and Silence.
The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with the French were reported by the newspaper Stars and Stripes and Britain’s Daily Telegraph, respectively. The news that the investigators were treating the incident as a suspected hack was first reported by Reuters.
The French Embassy in Washington said it would have no comment.
French freezers fried
If confirmed to be a cyberattack, the refrigerator malfunctions would be another illustration of how vulnerable critical infrastructure – in this case cold storage – can be to hackers.
The French freezer cyberattack overrode the temperature controls on commercial cooling units in more than 350 establishments, leading to dramatic scenes as supermarkets’ frozen food aisles were cleared of spoilt merchandise.
The French hack involved cranking the temperature inside the units up rather than merely knocking them offline, similar to what happened in Fort Huachuca in Arizona. Some French refrigeration units had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire.
The French attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one supermarket owner estimated earlier in October.
The French cyberattack appeared to have been easy to pull off, experts previously told Reuters. The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran many of the stricken units, said that many of the devices were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in.
Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment.
Chilling hacks
Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants.
Earlier in 2026, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one”.
Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the US and elsewhere.
Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers.
In December 2025, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 900kg of meat.
The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems.
Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there.
“It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said. REUTERS

Trump confronts a new midterm battleground: South Carolina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Trump administration ties bid to block Alaska Senate certification to second Sullivan
ROCK HILL, South Carolina, Oct 29 - The US Justice Department filed a revised lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block certification of Alaska's election results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses narrowly, citing a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a candidate with the same first and last names.
The suit raises the prospect of a messy fight over a contest that could determine Senate control in next Tuesday's midterm elections.
Alaska is one of about 10 highly competitive races that will decide control of the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and a post-election dispute in Alaska could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks.
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also called for a state investigation into the allegations, after the Times reported that aides to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Senator Sullivan.
“They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” lawyers for the Justice Department wrote in their amended complaint, citing the Times report.
Peltola's campaign and its lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Justice Department's amended complaint.
Reuters has not verified the New York Times report.
Trump for years has sowed doubts about the fairness of US elections and even prior to the Times report had pushed the Justice Department to file a lawsuit seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying Peltola, a former congresswoman, if she were to win the election.
WAVE OF SUBPOENAS
The Justice Department issued more than 40 subpoenas and document preservation requests in its probe, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday.
President Donald Trump told reporters earlier on Thursday: "It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It's so unfair.”
As campaigning enters its final few days, the White House has shelved plans for Trump to appear on Saturday in Kansas, the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate campaign, a Republican campaign official said.
"I don't feel like I have to go to Kansas," Trump told reporters.
Instead, the president will participate in more than 20 virtual campaign appearances before Tuesday, a White House official said.
"These events give him the opportunity to highlight his accomplishments and expand his reach across the country," the official said.

Policing such behavior would open the door to the government investigating why candidates choose to run and why voters support them, she said. "To the extent that people are uncomfortable with two Sullivans, I would offer you're probably going to be uncomfortable with a really high level of government intrusion into our elections as well."

Fire broke out at a nuclear facility in the United States - no contamination detected
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina and was extinguished. One worker sustained minor injuries; no contamination was detected.
A fire occurred at the Savannah River nuclear facility in the United States; no contamination was detected after the emergency. Newsweek reports, UNN writes.
Details
Representatives of the Savannah River Site (SRS) said radiological surveys detected no contamination following a fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory on Wednesday evening, October 28, local time.
One employee sustained minor injuries and was taken to a hospital, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) told Fox News.
An emergency was declared at the facility at 5:07 p.m. local time at the site near Aiken, South Carolina, after a fire was reported at the Savannah River National Laboratory. The fire has since been extinguished, according to the latest SRS press release.
The latest social media update confirms that the emergency is "over."
As of 9:45 p.m. local time on Wednesday, October 28, the emergency had been terminated, and protective measures, including the site perimeter, had been removed.
Residents nearby had earlier been urged to monitor local television and radio broadcasts for any actions that state officials might announce.
What is known about the nuclear facility
According to the SRS website, the facility is part of the United States' national nuclear security facilities.
According to the website, it was built in the 1950s to produce materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily plutonium-239 and tritium. Five reactors were built there, along with two chemical separation plants, a heavy-water extraction plant, a tritium extraction plant, a nuclear fuel and target fabrication facility, and waste disposal facilities.

Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
October 29, 2026
A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.
The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.
Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.
This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war.
Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz
The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.
The status of the crew is unknown, and so far no information has emerged pertaining to damage or environmental impact.
Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.
Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.
Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.
US drone downed
The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.
The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.
The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.
Fears of new US strikes
The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.
A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.
As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.
If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.
According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

Powers Summit 2026 will bring together business leaders, industry associations, employer organizations, government ministers and representatives of all political forces in Bulgaria’s Parliament in Sofia on December 10, with discussions focused on the country’s economic and policy priorities after the elections.
Described by the media as “The Bulgarian Davos,” the annual forum has developed into an independent platform for direct dialogue between business, industry and government, aiming to turn discussions into concrete proposals and commitments.
This year’s agenda covers five main areas: Bulgaria’s transition after adopting the euro, with an emphasis on investment, competitiveness and productivity; artificial intelligence, technology, data and the state; energy, industry, infrastructure and independence; defense and security in the Black Sea region; and Bulgaria’s population, including health, education, talent and demographics.
Aniela Ruseva, executive director of Webit, said the end of the elections would not remove the major challenges facing the country. She stressed that the summit had consistently provided an independent setting for business and industry to develop solutions that the government must consider.
“Elections come to an end, but the major questions facing Bulgaria remain. Over the years, the Powers Summit has proven to be an independent venue where the business sector and industry can formulate concrete solutions - solutions that the government must hear and address,” Ruseva said.
She noted that experts representing all parliamentary parties and members of the executive branch had participated in the forum, regardless of which party held power at the time. According to Ruseva, this continuity distinguishes the summit by allowing discussions to produce practical solutions rather than remain exchanges of positions.
Under the forum’s traditional “The Authorities Listen” format, political representatives and members of the executive branch will respond directly to priorities identified by business and industry.
Powers Summit 2026 will take place in Sofia on December 10 under the call “Power, Listen! (Власт, Чуй!)”

Army still wants an armoured mortar but currently has no route
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:58 GMT
19:00:58 KST

The Army continues to require an armoured mortar capability and is looking at alternative ways of delivering it, including through the Heavy Protected Mobility programme, which remains in its concept phase with no procurement decision taken, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress had been made in procuring an armoured mortar capability, following an earlier answer on armoured fighting vehicle finance.
Luke Pollard said: “The Army continues to require an armoured mortar capability. Alternative delivery routes, including through the Heavy Protected Mobility (PM) programme are being considered. The Heavy PM programme remains in its concept phase, and no final procurement decision has been taken.”
An armoured mortar is a heavy mortar carried inside a protected vehicle and fired from within it. A battlegroup can put high explosive onto a target within a couple of minutes of the call and then move before counter-battery fire arrives. Dismounted mortar teams can do the first part but not the second, and in a war where drones find a firing position within minutes, the ability to shoot and drive away is valuable.
An armoured mortar variant had been expected to come through the Boxer programme, and the answer that prompted this question established that funding had been removed from part of the armoured fighting vehicle portfolio. Pollard said separately that the decision reflected “a broader reprioritisation of capability investment to maximise operational effect and affordability”. The Army still needs the capability and no route to it has been settled.
Heavy Protected Mobility is the programme intended to replace the Army’s ageing protected vehicles, and a concept phase is the earliest formal stage of a procurement, well before a competition, a contract or a date.

Only about half of social science findings held up when retested, major replication project finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:33 UTC
19:00:33 KST

A large-scale international project has found that roughly half of tested scientific claims across the social and behavioral sciences hold up when independent researchers attempt to repeat the work. The research, published in Nature, indicates that the challenges of verifying published findings are not confined to a single field, but rather extend across disciplines including psychology, economics, sociology, education, business, and political science. On average, the effects observed in the replication attempts were less than half as large as those originally reported.
In scientific research, a replication attempt involves testing the exact same question as a previous study using independent data to see if the original conclusion holds true. If a scientific discovery represents a genuine regularity in human behavior, independent researchers following a similar procedure or analyzing a fresh dataset should be able to observe a similar result. Repeating past studies helps verify whether an initial finding is reliable enough to inform public policy, education, or clinical practice.
Over the past decade, large-scale verification efforts have raised questions about how often published findings hold up under scrutiny. A 2015 replication project tested 100 psychology studies and found that only about one-third produced the original results, sparking widespread discussion about research reliability. Follow-up investigations soon tested other areas of study to see if the issue was unique to psychology.
Other fields showed a similar pattern. A 2016 study of laboratory experiments in economics found that 11 out of 18 studies produced a statistically significant effect in the same direction as the original. Similarly, a 2018 investigation of social science experiments published in top-tier general science journals found that about 62 percent repeated successfully, though the strength of the findings was cut roughly in half. Together with other replication efforts, these projects suggested that across hundreds of attempts, roughly half of well-powered replications produced a statistically significant result in the same direction as the original.
Researchers have proposed several systemic explanations for why many published findings fail to repeat. Academic journals have historically favored novel, positive discoveries over inconclusive or negative results, creating a publication filter where studies that happen to overestimate an effect by chance are the ones most likely to be printed. Small sample sizes, flawed measurement tools, and flexible data analysis practices can also produce false positives. At the same time, academic culture has often discouraged verification work; for example, a 2017 study found that only about 3 percent of psychology journals explicitly welcomed replication studies, while a third implicitly discouraged them.
Most prior verification projects focused on a single academic discipline or examined relatively small groups of papers. To determine whether the patterns seen in earlier efforts apply across the broader landscape of human behavior research, a massive collaborative team led by Andrew H. Tyner of the Center for Open Science, alongside senior colleague Timothy M. Errington and corresponding author Brian A. Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science and a professor at the University of Virginia, launched a systematic cross-disciplinary investigation.
Nosek also coordinated the 2015 psychology project and co-authored the 2018 analysis of studies in top general science journals. The new work was conducted as part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program, bringing together hundreds of researchers from 31 countries.
“This project was part of a larger research program called SCORE that involved thousands of researchers around the world and began in 2019,” Nosek told PsyPost. “We were investigating whether algorithms could predict the replicability of findings to support decision-making about what research is needed next to advance knowledge.”
The researchers began by gathering a random sample of 3,900 quantitative papers published between 2009 and 2018 across 62 journals representing six major disciplines: business, economics, education, political science, psychology, and sociology. To be eligible, a paper had to use real human data, ranging from individual participants to families, businesses, or political entities, and report a positive statistical result. From a pool of 1,500 eligible papers, the team matched specific scientific claims with independent research groups who had the expertise and resources to test them.
In total, the teams completed 296 replication attempts covering 274 unique scientific claims drawn from 164 published papers across 54 journals. For 98 of the papers, researchers collected brand-new data from participants, while for 66 papers, teams analyzed existing secondary datasets that had not been used in the original research. Across the subset of studies where standard correlation metrics could be calculated, the median sample size was 206 in the original papers and 545 in the replication studies.
To ensure the tests were fair and rigorous, the replication studies were designed to have high statistical power, meaning they used large enough samples to have a median 99.6 percent chance of detecting an effect as large as the one originally reported. Whenever possible, teams used the original study materials. Before any data were collected or analyzed, each study’s design and analysis plan went through an internal peer review process, which invited feedback from the original authors, and was publicly registered in advance on the Open Science Framework to prevent researchers from altering their methods after seeing the results.
The researchers first evaluated the outcomes using the most common yardstick in social science: whether the replication study produced a statistically significant result in the same direction as the original paper. In science, statistical significance means that an observed pattern would be unlikely if there were no real effect, typically using a threshold of less than a 5 percent probability. Because some papers had multiple claims tested, the authors calculated results both by weighting claims so each paper counted equally and by counting each claim individually.
When weighted by paper, 80.8 of the 164 papers, or 49.3 percent, produced results in the same pattern that met the threshold for statistical significance. Another 40.4 percent of the papers showed a null effect, meaning the result did not reach statistical significance, while 9.7 percent actually produced a statistically significant result in the opposite direction of the original claim. When looking at the 274 unweighted claims individually, 151 claims, or 55.1 percent, succeeded by this measure, while 35.8 percent showed a null effect and 8.8 percent went in the opposite direction.
Beyond yes-or-no significance thresholds, the researchers examined the magnitude of the findings, known as the effect size. To compare studies that used different statistical models, the team converted the results of 157 papers (representing 249 claims) into a standardized correlation measure called Pearson’s r, which runs from -1 to 1, where 0 means no relationship, 1 means a perfect relationship, and negative values indicate a relationship in the opposite direction. Across the original papers, the median effect size was 0.25, whereas in the replication studies, the median effect size dropped to 0.10.
This drop from 0.25 to 0.10 represents a 58.1 percent relative reduction in the correlation and an 82.4 percent reduction in shared variance, a measure of how much one variable explains another. Overall, 80.3 percent of the replicated papers (126 of 157) and 70.3 percent of the individual claims (175 of 249) yielded smaller effect sizes than the original studies. Some of this shrinkage is expected due to a statistical phenomenon called regression to the mean: because the researchers only tested positive published results, any original studies that happened to overestimate the true effect by luck would naturally be followed by smaller, more realistic estimates upon retesting.
“The basic finding is that establishing the replicability of published results cannot be taken for granted,” Nosek said. “The main practical implication is that this research exposes greater uncertainty in the published literature than we might recognize. Establishing credibility and verifying research claims is an effortful process and our assumptions about the strength and nature of a finding are sometimes incorrect.”
When the researchers broke the results down across the six academic disciplines, they found only modest variation, and the differences between fields were not statistically significant. Weighted by paper, the success rates were 42.5 percent in economics (10.2 of 24 papers), 47.2 percent in business (17.0 of 36), 49.0 percent in psychology (28.4 of 58), 51.1 percent in sociology (9.2 of 18), 52.0 percent in political science (7.8 of 15), and 63.1 percent in education (8.2 of 13). However, some fields contributed only a handful of papers, such as 13 in education, so their individual estimates are uncertain. Similarly, the year a paper was published between 2009 and 2018 did not have a statistically significant relation to whether it held up.
The team also compared studies that gathered brand-new data against those that analyzed existing secondary datasets. Both approaches succeeded at similar rates on the basic significance metric: 47.8 percent of papers using new data held up, compared to 51.4 percent of papers using secondary data. However, when looking at effect sizes, studies using new data saw their median effect size drop from 0.28 in the original work to 0.11 in the replication, whereas secondary data studies started with smaller original effects (a median of 0.13) and dropped only slightly to 0.10.
Because scientists disagree on the best mathematical way to define a successful replication, the authors also evaluated the data using 12 additional criteria, such as checking whether the replication result fell within the original study’s margin of error, or combining both studies in a meta-analysis. Across all 13 methods, the estimated success rate ranged from 28.6 percent to 74.8 percent, with a median of 49.3 percent. The highest success rate (74.8 percent) came from combining the original and new data together in a meta-analysis, a method that leans toward success because it bakes in the original positive data, while methods that penalized replication studies for finding either smaller or larger effects than the original study produced the lowest rates.
“These findings confirm and extend existing work on replicability, such as the ‘Many Labs’ studies,” Stephanie Zellers, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki who holds a PhD in psychology and was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “Many Labs projects aim to test the replicability of specific research findings using a multisite collaborative approach. This work extends beyond this approach by comprehensively testing a wider range of research findings across behavioral and social science disciplines. The authors used a systematic, representative, and random approach to identify claims for testing, though there was some non-random selection introduced by teams choosing to start a specific replication project.”
“I am quite confident in these results and that is due in large part to the transparent and nuanced reporting,” Zellers said. “I appreciated the detailed discussion of replication metrics – these methods of comparing an original result to the replication result in order to decide if the original result replicated or not. Our choice of metric influences what the answer means, when we ask the question ‘did this study replicate?’ They all have their assumptions, strengths and limitations, and I am more confident in these results because the authors used different metrics when possible.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. A single successful replication does not mean the original finding is beyond doubt, and no two studies in the social sciences are ever identical. Shifting a study to a new year, a new group of participants, or a different cultural setting can alter the outcome for legitimate reasons that scientists do not yet fully understand.
“Failing to replicate a finding does not mean that the original finding is wrong,” Nosek emphasized. “One possibility is that the original finding is a false positive or exaggerated. Other possibilities are that we made an error in the replication study, or that unrecognized factors influenced the finding differently between the original and replication studies.”
“These findings do not mean that social and behavioral sciences are only ‘correct’ about half of the time and should not be interpreted as such,” Zellers added. “Replication is not inherently a positive thing and lack of replication is not inherently a problem. Rather we should focus on the total body of evidence for a claim and critically evaluate uncertainty in the evidence alongside the context and boundaries of the effect.” She noted that “meta-research is not a scientific ‘witch hunt’ focused on debunking some specific claim via replication, it is an essential part of science that helps us understand and evaluate a whole body of evidence for or against some claim.”
In addition, the studies tested in this project were not a purely random slice of all social science. Although the initial pool of papers was chosen randomly, the final 164 papers were those that proved practical to repeat within the project’s budget, timeline, and researcher expertise. Resource-intensive studies were less likely to be attempted, and qualitative research and papers reporting null results were excluded from the start. The mix of fields also shifted: psychology made up about 24 percent of the original sample but 35.4 percent of the completed papers, while education and political science shrank in relative share.
“I would be interested to see a project that tests replicability in a broader group of journals, broader research results like null and qualitative findings, and in different time periods of published results,” Zellers noted. “These types of studies could help us understand drivers of replicability and unreplicability.”
The authors suggest that the core issue facing the social and behavioral sciences is not necessarily a lack of replicability itself, as cutting-edge research naturally involves taking risks on uncertain ideas that may not pan out. In their view, the challenge is overconfidence: treating a single published paper as established fact rather than preliminary evidence.
“I think the authors do a reasonable job in discussing the findings without any sensationalist language about disciplines in crisis or fields being ‘built on noise,’ however I would also caution against any misinterpretation that suggests we should not be concerned about these relatively low rates of replicability,” Zellers explained. “Replication does not prove an original claim true and unreplicability does not prove an original claim false, and so we should not interpret any single replication result as good or bad without more information. That said, the overall low rate of replicability in social sciences fields is concerning because it may stem from systemic issues in scientific publishing, like publication bias toward positive results and overconfidence in published claims.”
“I was surprised that most of the research community readily accepted these findings,” Nosek remarked. “Our prior systematic replication studies generated substantial, heated debate. There are still a variety of perspectives on the implications of these results, but there was much less heated rhetoric. I think that is a sign of progress?”
Future research could use the publicly available dataset to examine what predicts whether a study holds up. Earlier work along these lines, including research covered by PsyPost in 2022, found that the political slant of psychology findings was not associated with whether they replicated.
Nosek added, “Now that we have published several systematic replication studies, many research efforts are using the outcomes to advance various research questions such as: How do you decide whether a finding has replicated successfully? (Not a trivial question!) What factors cause increases or decreases in replicability? How prevalent are each of those causes? Is there an optimal replicability rate for different research circumstances?”
“Discovery science is often high-risk high-reward, resulting both in powerful new findings and many false leads,” Zellers said of investigating optimal replicability rates. “Replication science can help us identify which leads may be dead ends, as well as understand moderators and generalizability. We need both to create robust and impactful science, especially when translating our research claims into care, policy, and practice. What is the optimal balance between discovery and replication science to make the best use of increasingly limited financial resources in research?”
The study, “Investigating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences,” was authored by Andrew H. Tyner, Anna Lou Abatayo, Mason Daley, Samuel Field, Nicholas Fox, Noah A. Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

Halloween Is a Chance to Rethink Your Relationship With Fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Whether you’re watching a scary movie or tiptoeing through a haunted house, Halloween can stir up spooky feelings. A gory scene may force you to cover your eyes or jump out of your seat. What drives these reactions is fear, a powerful core emotion.
Being afraid can feel like getting stuck in your own horror show—your heart pounds, your pupils dilate, and you may gasp or scream. These reactions are not under conscious control; they’re rooted in biology. Like all emotions, fear plays an important role. It helps you survive and bolt for safety.
Halloween gives you a chance to experiment with fear. It’s a time when the fright is real, but the threat is not.
As psychotherapists who specialize in Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP), we know that being able to name and work with fear is good for health. Acknowledging your emotions makes you less likely to suppress or avoid them, drink too much, or become numb to what you’re feeling.
While these behaviors take the edge off temporarily, research shows that stuffing down your emotions can lead to mental-health concerns, such as depression and anxiety, which have become more common among U.S. children and adults in recent years.
If you’d like to safely explore your relationship with fear this Halloween season, here are five exercises we recommend.
Recognize fear in your body
Have you ever tried to outsmart fear? Perhaps you scolded yourself for being a scaredy-cat or tried to stop the feeling with logic. Messages from society and our families often promote a mind-over-matter approach, reinforcing the belief that we can think our way out of an emotion.
A healthier approach is to get out of your head and tune into your body. During a frightening moment, notice the telltale signs of alarm, like trembling hands, a racing heart, or feeling cold. These physical sensations are important messengers that clue you into what core emotions you’re experiencing.
Once you identify and name them, their intensity will likely diminish. It may sound like a small act, but research shows that putting language on your emotions can help regulate and tame distress.
Watch fear come and go
Gripping, painful emotions can seem permanent. But watching them come and go can remind your brain that even the most frightening experiences are temporary.
During a spooky scene, you may want to cover your face or turn away. Rather than immediately distracting yourself, approach the emotion with curiosity. Observe how fear builds, peaks, and eventually subsides.
Curiosity helps us embrace a sense of wonder. Research shows that a curious mindset can cultivate positive emotions and reduce worry.
Calm the scary feeling
When fright takes hold, breathing techniques like 4-7-8 breathing or box breathing can soothe your nervous system. Taking long breaths instead of shallow ones sends oxygen to your muscles, which can help relieve tension.
You can also practice what eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapists call “dual attention.” Keep your eyes glued to the frightening scene and stay with the sensations in your body as you take deep belly breaths. Research shows that belly breathing increases parasympathetic regulation of the heart through vagal pathways, helping the body settle into a calmer state.
Discover how fear makes you want to move
When a ghoul jumps out or a frightening sound catches you off guard, pay attention to what your body wants to do. Do you feel an urge to flee, freeze, duck, or reach for someone’s hand?
In AEDP, we call these “adaptive actions,” and they offer clues about how your nervous system responds to perceived danger.
All core emotions, including fear, have impulses—energy in the body that makes us want to take action. When someone responds to our emotions with shame instead of empathy, we learn to block these impulses, creating a pressure-cooker effect. This can lead to symptoms like insomnia, muscular tension, and rumination that can hurt your health.
Noticing fear’s impulses expands your emotional awareness and sets the stage for you to work through other core emotions with greater wisdom.
Notice how connection changes fear
Sharing a scary moment with another person can make it easier to tolerate. That’s because having someone by your side doesn’t just provide reassurance; it calms the amygdala, the brain’s emotional center, and helps you heal past wounds and traumas.
We recommend this experiment: Watch a horror movie alone, and then with someone you trust. Or visit a haunted house with a trusted friend or partner. Notice what happens when you share the experience.
A little emotions education goes a long way towards nurturing your well-being. By learning to stay with fear, you teach your brain that you can handle challenging emotions.
And when we know emotions aren’t something to fear, we’re better equipped to handle life’s challenges with authenticity, flexibility, and courage.

It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

BISMARCK, N.D. — In 1918, an offshoot of the progressive farmer-labor movement known as the Nonpartisan League swept into power in North Dakota, riding a populist groundswell of anger directed at big banks and industry barons in Minneapolis and Chicago.
The group was organized by former Socialist Party member Arthur C. Townley, a failed flax farmer who barnstormed the state in a borrowed Ford Model T calling for public ownership of key industries, including banks, mills and factories. By 1919, the state legislature authorized a state-owned and -operated bank.
Over a century later, the Bank of North Dakota still stands, and the state is reaping the benefits.
The Bank of North Dakota is the nation's only surviving state-owned and -operated bank. It has persisted as Great Plains politics has shifted from prairie progressivism to deep-red conservatism, and it now manages about $11 billion in assets while enjoying broad support from the state's current political leaders.
"I think it's weird, right? We're one of the most conservative states in the union, and we have this state-run bank that was started by first-generation Norwegian immigrants," North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong, a Republican, told CNBC. "I don't think we could set one up now, but I'm sure glad we have it."
In addition to Armstrong, the bank's present-day boosters include the state's U.S. senators, Kevin Cramer and John Hoeven — who is a former president of the bank, and former North Dakota governor and current Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. All are Republicans in a party where "socialist" is a pejorative on the 2026 campaign trail.
At its core, the Bank of North Dakota is a bank. It has a governance structure, holds the state's deposits and provides loans. But it is also a unique institution that melds the political and financial arenas to advance the state's industrial and economic goals. Those efforts can range from saving a coal plant on the verge of going belly-up to buying down interest rates on loans for agriculture, energy or housing.
"I've always said it's a very interesting concept; obviously it's a successful one up here," Don Morgan, the Bank of North Dakota president and CEO, told CNBC. "It's one that if you use it wrong, it could be a little bit dangerous. But if you use it right, it can be a really powerful financial tool."
The bank also stands as a vestige of the country's last populist socialist uprising, as the U.S. is now gripped by another ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The bank, which is in a state President Donald Trump won by more than 36 percentage points in 2024, has been used as an example by Democratic, progressive and democratic socialist candidates and lawmakers from across the country who are trying to expand public banking.
CNBC traveled to North Dakota to talk with leaders of the bank, which rarely grants such access to national media, and with state political officials and business leaders to learn how the country's only state-owned bank operates and about the interplay with the state it serves — and whether its century-old idea could support a new groundswell of state-run banks.
"For a long time people have scoffed at it — 'Oh, that's their experiment with socialism over there' — but I think it's important to note that we live in an era of populism," Cramer said. "Others have looked at it a little bit skeptically, but more recently they've looked at it and gone, 'You know, we could use a tool like that.'"
A foundation of populism
Roughly a dozen states have had state-run banks in the past, but the Bank of North Dakota is the only one operating today. Most failed by 1900, following the enactment of laws allowing private banks to issue notes backed by Treasury bonds or due to turbulent economic stretches.
Still, some politicians hope to use the Bank of North Dakota as an example and bring public banking back to the national conversation. And a wave of progressive populism could create an environment where policymakers return to public banks as a solution for a litany of economic ills.
Most public banking supporters are Democrats, including progressive democratic socialists who have surged in popularity after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was elected in 2025.
Mamdani, who was a New York State Assembly member from 2021-2025, cosponsored a bill in the assembly that would have allowed municipalities and local governments to stand up public banks. Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, who narrowly lost to Democratic nominee David Crowley in August, included a call for a state bank modeled on the Bank of North Dakota in her official platform. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a potential 2028 presidential contender, led a bill in Congress with Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., to make it easier for states to create public banks.
"We're populists, whereas in other parts of the country Republicans aren't as populist as they are conservative," Cramer said of one of the nation's most conservative states being emulated by democratic socialists. "It's somewhat natural that a more liberal political bent is attracted to this sort of experiment that's been going for 108 years in North Dakota that looks more appealing on the surface to the left than it might to the right."
Several Democratic-led states, meanwhile, have already taken steps to give public banking a try. One of those states is Washington, where a work group of officials is set to deliver an implementation plan to the legislature by mid-2027.
"I think the people deserve to be in control of their own tax dollars that they're putting forward," said Washington state Sen. Bob Hasegawa, a member of the work group who has spent years pushing for a state bank. Hasegawa said he began advocating for the idea after the 2008 financial crisis.
"We're allowing big Wall Street banks to use our tax dollars, leverage it, and make tons of money for their shareholders and themselves," he said. "And in the meantime, if we want to do anything like build a bridge or water system or whatever, we have to go back and sell bonds. So we're essentially borrowing what otherwise would be our own dollars back just so we can build infrastructure or finance other programs."
Massachusetts, New Mexico and California are also pursuing their own proposals to create public banks.
A monetary expert says public banking makes good sense in the design of the monetary system.
"For me, it came from a design perspective. Why don't we do this obvious thing? Why doesn't the public use the same power of banking that private institutions use?" said Christine Desan, the Leo Gottlieb Professor of Law at Harvard University, who teaches about the political economy of capitalism and the monetary system.
"The reason banks are such great lenders is that they operate in a network," Desan said. "In effect, the way a public bank would operate is it would be saying, we're just going to join the network; the public, the state of Massachusetts, will join the network, and then we'll have the same advantages in lending."
Skepticism from commercial banks
Major players in the banking industry aren't sold on public banking as a concept.
The American Bankers Association opposed eventual laws in California that allowed municipalities to set up public banks and set up state checking accounts for individual citizens. The group also opposed a ballot measure in Los Angeles that would have allowed the creation of a public bank.
"History has shown that public banks are a solution in search of a problem and present significant risks to taxpayers," ABA spokesman Josh Britton told CNBC. "America's banks are already highly regulated and well-capitalized and reliably serve communities, businesses, and state and local governments across the country, and misguided political interference would only harm consumers and the economy."
The state getting involved in banking decisions is also one of the greatest political risks facing public banking. A public bank could theoretically pick winners and losers based on the political bent of elected officials, disadvantaging some industries while advantaging others.
Morgan said strict prohibitions on competition with local financial institutions, along with a sound governance structure, could help other states set up public banks with as few pitfalls as possible.
"Our founding documents stating that we're never to compete with [North Dakota financial institutions] is a very powerful statement, because I've always said the minute we start competing with them, then our model falls apart," he said. "I believe any state can do it. But how you found it originally is critically important. That original governance framework is critically important."
Morgan noted the bank does "serve at the pleasure" of the North Dakota Industrial Commission and legislature and will follow them "as long as it does not jeopardize and move against our founding documents or jeopardize the safety and soundness of the bank."
Running the bank as a financial institution more than as a government institution serves as a "backstop that we can fall back on, because at the end of the day, we have to run the bank and protect the bank because we're protecting the state's deposits," Morgan said.
Morgan, who travels the country to speak with public banking advocates, said a public bank could serve its state in any way the state wants, so long as it is a bank first. Other states have proposed using the bank to fund new housing, finance infrastructure and reduce inequality.
"Your bank can do whatever your state wants it to do, as long as it does not get in the way of being a healthy bank," he said. "And then when you're ready, you can do those things that strategically align with your state, which will be different in every state of the Union."
A bankers' bank
Today, the bank of North Dakota acts as a "bankers' bank," backing small community banks in financing projects they may be too small to finance themselves.
The bank is helmed by the Industrial Commission, a government body created by the bank's founding statutes. The governor, attorney general and agriculture commissioner make up the commission, which acts as a board of directors for the bank. The bank also has an advisory board and an executive committee, the latter of which runs its day-to-day operations.
"I really attribute that governance framework to the 107-year history and why we're still around, [while] many other public banks have failed out up to this point," Morgan told CNBC at the bank's Bismarck headquarters.
Morgan said the bank's core business consists of participation loans, commercial real estate loans and agricultural loans. The bank also engages in other areas where the state's privately owned banks don't already compete, including offering direct student loans at a low interest rate for North Dakotans hoping to attend college.
It will also quickly stand up disaster relief programs. The bank pumped $500 million in loan support to farmers in 2026 amid challenges from Trump's tariffs, low commodity prices and high input costs. In decades past, it has gone further — selling foreclosed farmland back to families under asking price after the Dust Bowl and ensuring teachers got paid in full during the Great Depression.
The bank does not have a traditional deposit base of individual customers stashing their cash. In fact, the bank discourages individual deposits so as not to compete with the state's community banks.
Instead, the bank is the primary depository of state funds. Morgan said it draws its core deposit base from the general fund, a mix of state revenue from taxes and fees. The state legislature can then appropriate bank profits back into the general fund for the state's budget, or the profits can be used to fund the bank's investments to benefit the state's industries.
"We take that average balance of about $6.6 billion — that's our deposit base, our core deposit base," Morgan said. "We use those deposits [for the bank's operations], work through our 91 financial institutions in the state, do our participation loans, do our disaster loans, do our student lending, and then we make a nice healthy profit back to the general fund."
The state's other banks don't see the Bank of North Dakota as competition, according to Rick Clayburgh, president and CEO of the North Dakota Bankers Association. Instead, they view it as a tool that allows community banks to "punch above their weight class."
"I think if we were trying to create a state bank here in North Dakota today, our association would probably be opposed to it," Clayburgh said. "But the fact that we know what it is now and that it's developed over the 107 years, it is a wonderful tool for institutions."
Coal and data center funding
An example of the bank's investment activity — and one progressives might do differently — is found in McLean County.
There, in the middle of the rolling plains between Underwood and Washburn, Rainbow Energy Center's Coal Creek Station burns lignite coal to generate 1,151 megawatts of electricity per hour for roughly 1.7 million customers in Minnesota via a hulking transmission line. The plant employs about 200 people directly, and the coal mine next door employs hundreds more.
In 2020, however, the plant was on a much different trajectory. Its then-owner, Great River Energy, said the plant was losing money and that it planned to retire it by the end of 2022, replacing its generation with wind farms and natural gas.
Then-Gov. Burgum, a vocal supporter of coal, along with Cramer and Hoeven immediately demanded that Great River find a buyer for the plant and its accompanying transmission line, a tall order, as the country was moving toward renewable energy and coal's economic advantages were declining.
"It would have been a huge detrimental impact to this area," said Ethan Vaagene, the plant's director. "It was probably the worst feeling I've had in my life ... I still remember this day when the prior owner announced to all the employees that they were going to be closing the facility. It was a complete shock to all of us."
Burgum led an all-of-government effort to find a buyer. And while one did emerge, the complex financing of the sale would have proven difficult to execute without the Bank of North Dakota.
Morgan said the Bank of North Dakota was able to "quarterback" the complex sale of the plant and its transmission line from Great River to its eventual buyer, Rainbow Energy. Rainbow Energy Center bought the coal plant, and Nexus Line purchased the transmission line that moves the power to Minnesota. Both companies are affiliates of Rainbow Energy Marketing Corporation.
The deal included a financing package in which the North Dakota Transmission Authority sold bonds for the first time, netting $150 million in proceeds to fund a loan to Nexus Line to purchase the transmission line. The Bank of North Dakota purchased NDTA bonds through a $150 million Match Program loan, the bank's program that supports large-scale economic diversification projects.
The CEO of the company that bought the power plant said that without the Bank of North Dakota, the deal would not have materialized.
"I start all our meetings with the Bank of North Dakota [by saying] that we wouldn't be here today without you," Rainbow CEO Stacy Tschider told CNBC, standing on the coal plant's roof. "If I was going to go outside the state, it would be more difficult to basically get other banks' understanding because ... with prior administrations, there has been a war on coal."
After the bank's investment, Rainbow began expanding the plant's use.
CNBC toured the plant with Tschider and Vaagene. Tschider said he envisions the plant as a futuristic "energy park."
An example of the plant's evolution already exists. Underneath the soaring spires releasing steam from electricity generation, computers mining cryptocurrency hum away. Coal Creek now redirects the electricity it generates on site to mine bitcoin during periods of low grid demand to offset lost profits.
Tschider said the plant is in talks with artificial intelligence hyperscalers to build a data center directly next to the plant, bringing in more revenue. A smattering of anti-data center yard signs dot roads near Coal Creek, indicative of local opposition to the facilities that is plaguing the AI build-out nationwide.
"We're in the process right now of working with several hyperscalers," Tschider said, adding that he expects to begin construction over the next six months.
A stablecoin for the original populist
The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library, nestled in the canyons of the badlands in Medora, North Dakota, is built into the geography, jutting out of the land where a young Roosevelt visited seeking solace after his wife and mother died on the same day.
On the day CNBC visited the library, the Bank of North Dakota — which extended a $70 million line of credit to the library to begin construction while it awaited private financing, allowing it to open for the nation's 250th anniversary — was celebrating the launch of its first stablecoin there. Dubbed the Roughrider Coin, it will allow North Dakota's network of community banks to execute near real-time bank-to-bank transfers.
Roosevelt looms large over the ethos of North Dakota, and the library has big ambitions: It aims to host a presidential debate and serve as a national hub for conservation work in the U.S. Roosevelt also has the unique distinction of being the favorite president of modern political figures on both sides of the aisle for his populist, progressive appeal, trust-busting history and staunch nationalism.
The bank, in many ways, was a result of the movement in American politics that Roosevelt ushered in.
"The Bank of North Dakota has very deep roots in the state of North Dakota; [it's] very much tied to the prairie populist movement," said Robbie Lauf, the library's interim CEO. "That kind of happened after the Progressive Era, of which Theodore Roosevelt was one of the most important characters of a fundamental piece of American history."
Lauf, who previously worked in Burgum's office and in the office of former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, rejected any idea that the bank clashes with free-market ideals just because it was founded out of a prairie populist, progressive movement.
"Anywhere where agriculture and rural communities are formed, there's a deep populist heritage, and there's a misunderstanding of what populism means, as well," Lauf said. "What it really is trying to do is help us achieve self-determination as a region."
"It is anything but an embrace of any type of state ownership of means; it's a partnership with private enterprise," he said. "This institution does not work without private enterprises and private banks ... For me, that's deeply free market."
Asked about the bank's socialist roots, Morgan said the bank, whatever its roots, was simply a good idea.
"There's good ideas on all sides of the political spectrum," he said. "We get so hung up in the debate or the letter by your name or the title assigned to you. There are good ideas."

I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “completed” more than half of my existence on this mortal plane. A few days later, when I noted that my family has a mild history of diabetes, the app updated my age of death from 74 to 73.
And just like that, I lost a year.
I know I won’t live to be 100; people in my family generally croak in their early eighties. But was it possible to extend my lifespan by 10, even 15 years, with a hyperpersonalized plan? “You have two paths,” a message from the app exclaimed. “We are here to help you achieve the longer one.” I made an appointment with Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company has partnered with, and willingly gave Death Clock my blood.
There’s no shortage of products that aim to reshape our relationship to our bodies. My inbox overflows with emails from longevity zealots pitching the latest anti-aging fads: salmon sperm scalp injections, a platelet-rich plasma treatment “Hailey Bieber swears by.” It’s almost too much, this urge to cheat the natural order of time.
“That’s a fool errand,” Death Clock CEO Brent Franson tells me one afternoon. He says advocates like Johnson—whose mantra “Don’t Die” reads more like a rejected Nike slogan than a wellness-oriented affirmation—“have to be really careful about inferring immortality when you have something to sell. That’s a dangerous place to be. The reality is we’re all going to die. It’s a question of when.”
Over Zoom, all I can think about is what Franson is trying to sell me.
The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, meaning the future of health care may be shaped less by traditional treatment and more by personalized AI health services. With Doctronic, a HIPAA-compliant platform that works like a personal AI doctor, people can refill prescriptions without the need to see a human physician, while apps like Superpower and Lifeforce (similar to Death Clock) offer membership-based health insights and clinician-reviewed recommendations. Twin Health purports to create an AI replica, whatever that means, of a person’s metabolism. All of it is meant to help us live a little longer, though it’s unclear exactly how and at what cost.
Mike Ludkovski, a professor of statistics and applied probability at UC Santa Barbara whose research focuses on longevity analysis, says mortality awareness platforms like Death Clock “sell the illusion that individual lifespan is a linear process” that can be hacked. A 2024 Aging Cell study likewise suggested that an aging clock shouldn’t be treated as a measure of someone’s overall biological age. “Ultimately, individual-level triggers precipitating death are inherently random and will never be truly forecastable,” Ludkovski says.
I ask Franson if we’re actually getting healthier or just growing more anxious about being unhealthy. “I think both,” he says. “There’s a very unhealthy obsession with self-optimization—tracking everything, trying to control everything.”
Wasn’t Death Clock, in part, also guilty of that?
When the blood panels returned a week after I gave my sample, the results were mostly what my doctor had warned me about earlier this year. I’ve got borderline high cholesterol and blood sugar levels “creeping toward prediabetic range.” Shockingly, I have “optimal liver health” and normal cortisol levels. Videos from so-called wellness influencers had convinced me that a string of recent sleepless nights were the result of high cortisol, but, it turns out, the algorithm isn’t always right.
Based on my results, the app kept feeding me more tasks. Increase my vitamin D3! Schedule a DEXA scan for bone density! Discuss a prostate-specific antigen screening with a specialist! Despite Franson’s claim that he wants Death Clock to eventually be a replacement for primary care physicians, the app kept nudging me to discuss my results with a doctor.
Ultimately, I started to realize, tracking health data can only do so much. There is a belief, says Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime: Does Aging Suck, or Do We Suck at Aging?, that being able to measure something means it can also be managed. Death doesn’t work that way, she says, “so the measuring starts to serve a different need: the need to feel less afraid.”
Terry-Leonard is also the cofounder of the Center for Deeply Human Leadership, an independent research institute studying AI’s effect on brain health. She’s skeptical that consumer-facing longevity apps can lead to positive behavioral shifts on their own. “Facts don’t change minds,” she says. People understand that certain activities are unhealthy, but they do them anyway.
Keeping death in view is one of the oldest practices we have, and what seems to matter is whether a person feels they have the personal agency to make the necessary adjustments in their life. Researchers who study how thoughts of death shape health choices find that people move toward healthier behavior when they also have the confidence and resources to act, which not everyone does. “And without those,” Terry-Leonard tells me, “the anxiety tends to go into protecting how we feel about ourselves rather than into our health.”
While researching her book, Terry-Leonard found that older adults with more positive attitudes about aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer than those with negative outlooks. An app with a death countdown “can quietly teach us that aging is loss,” hindering longevity rather than promoting it.
In the month that I used Death Clock, this was the fact I couldn’t completely escape. I became a meticulous steward of my bodily functions, logging “daily habits” with the verve of an accountant manically calculating numbers just before tax deadline. In a single day I added 5.8 years to my life by earmarking that I’d completed at least 30 minutes of strength training, abstained from alcohol, brushed and flossed my teeth, gotten consistent sleep, spent time in the sauna, and drank more than eight glasses of water. But even as I labored to improve my death date, the clock was always there, counting down. It was an albatross that moved in a single, uniform direction: tick, tick, tick. Time became a burden I was being forced to optimize.
It makes sense that people are preoccupied with the very thing they are trying to escape. The need for control is addictive. But instead of assuaging my anxieties and questions about the great beyond, Death Clock only seemed to amplify them.
As the image of the life I want to build sharpens in my mind, a life that has already unfolded in deliciously unforeseen ways, I realize it has less to do with how I will make things happen and has everything to do with who I want them to happen with. Life isn’t about adding more time, but making it count when we can. I silenced Death Clock’s notifications on my phone and texted a friend: “Let’s meet at 7.”

Reencle Essential Review: Same Scraps, Lower Price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

There’s a new Reencle composter in town, and of all the features I thought I might miss from the trailblazing original Reencle Prime, I didn't think it would be the auto-close lid.
The overly sensitive opening sensor annoyed me at first, but I ended up not giving the Prime’s lid another thought during my nearly 1.5 years of use. In hindsight, this is a testament to its convenience. It even has a setting for it to auto-open. Walk over to the receptacle, it opens; dump your scraps in, it closes. Buttons and lids remain clean and untouched by dirty, slimy hands.
Reencle’s brand-new, lower-cost unit, the Essential, is pretty much the same as the Prime (which is still available), with a few small tweaks—updated looks, a larger shovel, and a lid you have to manually close and a button you have to press to open. The button and lid already dirty after only three weeks, but my family consistently forgets to push the lid closed, having grown used to the auto-close lids of both our trash can and our old Prime. At least a few days a week, I will be caught off guard by a constant beeping—the Essential letting us know its lid is still open.
Aside from that, the Essential delivers the same user-friendly, close-to-compost-producing experience as its older sibling, but for $150 less.
Compost in Progress
You may have heard of kitchen composters before, whether the Lomi, FoodCycler, or the original Reencle Prime. It’s a compelling fantasy: Food scraps go in the bin, and out comes ready-to-use compost.
Unfortunately, for all of these machines, it’s just that: a fantasy. Many of them (like Lomi and FoodCycler) simply grind and dry the scraps to create a material that looks kind of like dirt. Sure, it’s odorless and shelf-stable, but if you want to use it in your garden, you’ll need to mix it into potting soil at a very low ratio—like 1:10, or even 1:20 if you’re processing a lot of meat and dairy.
Reencle, meanwhile, actually uses thermophilic bacteria (including Bacillus and Actinomycetes) to break down the waste, resulting in a biologically active material that, while not ready-to-use compost, is at least part of the way there. There are a couple of other machines that also do this, and I’ve tried them, but they’re bulkier, pricier, and louder than Reencle—don’t discount the noise-polluting effects of an audible fan running 24/7, especially if you live in a small space. (Reencle’s large-capacity Gravity model was—and remains—the only food recycler/composter I’ve ever tested that was truly silent at all times.)
