Navantia UK raises apprentice target by half
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:25:48 GMT
18:25:48 KST

Navantia UK is increasing its commitment to recruit apprentices across its British yards from 500 to 750 by 2030, an announcement made as the Scottish Secretary and the defence industry minister visited the company’s yard at Methil in Fife, according to the company.
The apprentices will work on building three Fleet Solid Support ships for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary and will be ready to take on further projects for the Ministry of Defence.
Donato Martinez, chief executive of Navantia UK, said: “There is real momentum at Methil. We are investing in the yard, bringing in new work and recruiting more people. We also need to build the skills that will support the yard and our wider business in the years ahead.
“That is why we are increasing our nationwide commitment from 500 apprentices by 2030 to 750. It will give more young people the chance to build skilled careers in our industry and help us develop the workforce we need as the business grows.
“Methil has an important role to play in the future of UK shipbuilding. The investment being made here, the skills in the workforce and the opportunities ahead, including Programme Euston, give us a strong base to keep building from.”
Investment at Methil has reached £26.7 million since Navantia UK acquired the yard in January 2025, including a further £12 million announced this year for training facilities, machinery, infrastructure and new technology. The workforce has grown from 180 to 275 and 75 apprentices are now training at the site, including 21 who arrived this year, part of a company-wide intake of 121 joining 222 already employed across the four British yards at Methil, Arnish, Belfast and Appledore.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Government worked hard to secure the future of yards such as Methil as part of our commitment to Scotland’s industrial heartlands, and today with Navantia I’ve seen the difference that commitment has made. A busier order book, a growing workforce and a large increase in apprenticeships – this is what’s possible when government and industry work together.
“There are huge opportunities with the defence dividend that come from being part of the United Kingdom. I’m proud that the UK Government’s support for the sector is delivering skilled jobs and growth for communities right across Scotland. This is a new age of industrialisation for the UK, with Scotland at its heart.”
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Apprentices are at the heart of defence’s industrial base that keeps this country safe. These opportunities pave the way for the next generation, providing essential skills, training and experience while contributing to the security of the UK.”
Programme Euston, referred to by Martinez, is the Ministry of Defence programme for new floating docks at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, and the Chancellor confirmed that those docks will be built and delivered in British shipyards. The GMB union has argued that Methil should get the work.

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Estonia is set to become the first country in the world where people are invited to screening programs based on genetic data. Next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation for genetic testing to determine their individual breast cancer risk, regardless of whether or not they have health insurance.
Until now, women have been invited to breast cancer screening after their 50th birthday, but starting next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation so that each woman's risk of developing breast cancer can be calculated based on genetic data.
"If this risk is higher than usual – if the risk for these 40-year-old women is the same as it is for other women at the age of 50 – then including these women in screening earlier is justified. Starting mammography already at the age of 40," said Steven Smit, head of the biobank laboratory at the Estonian Genome Center.
Around 3,000 genetic variants are taken into account when calculating the risk. However, the study does not include BRCA gene mutations, which led actress Angelina Jolie to decide to have her breasts removed 13 years ago to prevent developing the disease.
"These are hereditary forms of cancer, which are assessed through separate tests as needed if there has been breast cancer in the family," Smit said.
There are almost 10,000 40-year-old women in Estonia, and invitations will be sent both to those who have already donated their genes to the Estonian Genome Center and to those who have not.
"The gene donors' data will not be checked automatically. The first step is still to go to the Health Portal and submit a declaration of consent there so that the data can be used in the healthcare system," said Krista Kruuv-Käo, head of preventive services at the Estonian Health Insurance Fund.
The same declaration of consent must also be completed by women whose data is not in the Estonian Genome Center. They will receive a referral to a laboratory to provide a blood sample.
It is also possible to put this service in place for other serious diseases, but the Health Insurance Fund does not consider this reasonable, as the state would not have the capacity to follow up on them.
"We are also analyzing how we could use genetic risk in the case of cardiovascular diseases to more precisely involve those people whose risks are higher in preventive measures," Kruuv-Käo said.
Currently, the Estonian Genome Center holds data on approximately one-fifth of Estonia's population, and no new gene donors are being accepted.
"The Genome Center would certainly be fully prepared for this, but at the moment there is simply no funding available for it. The Genome Center's general funding has also been reduced in recent years," Smit said.

Data centers, aerospace sectors offer new opportunities for Malaysian steel makers: official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:24:00 CST
18:24:00 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's iron and steel industry can seize opportunities to shift to higher-value production by supplying the automotive, data center, and aerospace sectors, Investment, Trade and Industry Deputy Minister Sim Tze Tzin said on Thursday.
The steel industry is transforming beyond its traditional focus on construction and infrastructure, with high-technology sectors opening up new markets for domestic producers, Sim told a press briefing on the sidelines of the 15th Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation (MISIF) Conference on the Status and Outlook of the Industry.
He said Malaysia's position as a major data center hub in Asia offered opportunities for the industry to supply products such as server racks, cables and wire harnesses and noted that at least one steel maker had informed him that it is diversifying into supplying server racks for data centers.

Sim also said that as the country's automotive sector expands and increased localization is implemented, there is a greater demand for locally produced automotive-grade steel. ■

Ischaemic heart disease remains Malaysia's leading cause of death
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:54 CST
18:23:54 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Ischaemic heart disease was Malaysia's leading cause of death in 2025, accounting for 18,001 deaths, or 13 percent of the total, the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) said on Thursday.
The disease was the leading cause of death among males, with 12,670 deaths, while pneumonia was the main cause of death among females, accounting for 7,684 deaths, DOSM said in a statement.
Ischaemic heart disease was also the leading cause of death among Malays and Indians, while pneumonia topped the list among Chinese and other Bumiputera communities.
Overall, Malaysia recorded 199,807 deaths in 2025, up 0.4 percent from 198,992 in 2024.
Of the total deaths last year, 138,507, or 69.3 percent, were medically certified, DOSM said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled 16 measures to make it easier for foreign businesses and professionals to operate in the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the world's largest FTP by area, with new policies covering energy trade, medical services and bonded business operations, according to a government circular made public Thursday.
Under the measures, foreign physicians legally licensed to practice medicine overseas may obtain permits to provide clinical diagnosis and treatment services in Hainan for up to three years, with extensions available in accordance with relevant regulations.
More convenient policies regarding work permits and stay and residence will also be introduced for foreign nationals.
The Hainan FTP, located in China's southernmost island province, launched island-wide special customs operations in December 2025, allowing freer entry of overseas goods, expanded zero-tariff coverage and more business-friendly measures as part of China's efforts to promote high-standard opening-up.
Overseas companies will be allowed to use bonded facilities at Hainan's liquefied natural gas (LNG) receiving terminals, while the FTP will be supported in conducting LNG futures delivery warehouse operations after LNG futures contracts are launched.
Other measures include promoting offshore trade, expanding the range of products eligible for bonded maintenance, facilitating the entry of eligible bonded remanufactured products into pilot free trade zones on the Chinese mainland, encouraging the use of the yuan in new forms of barter trade, and deepening the FTP's economic and trade cooperation with China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Bonded remanufactured products entering mainland pilot free trade zones will be subject to applicable import tariffs, import-related value-added tax and consumption tax. They must also meet all applicable technical requirements for equivalent new products and relevant regulations on remanufactured products, and be clearly labeled as such.
The circular also calls for improved insurance products and services in areas such as international transportation and bonded maintenance.
The latest measures come amid robust growth in Hainan's foreign trade. In the first three quarters of 2026, the province's goods imports and exports reached 285.44 billion yuan (about 42.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 49.8 percent year on year, while trade in services rose 11.7 percent to 56.95 billion yuan, according to data from Hainan's provincial commerce authorities.
Trade in maintenance and repair services more than doubled year on year to 3.31 billion yuan during the same period, according to the provincial commerce department. The trade mainly came from imports of aircraft materials and components and revenues from aircraft maintenance services.
The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in Hainan rose 38.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation.
The FTP measures are part of China's broader efforts to promote high-standard opening-up. The country has announced plans to further expand pilot opening-up programs in sectors such as value-added telecommunications, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, while taking steps to facilitate cross-border trade and investment.
The circular was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the General Administration of Customs. ■

China's longest metro loop line enters full operation in Wuhan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:06 CST
18:23:06 KST

A train runs on the Wuhan Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Oct. 29, 2026. China's longest subway loop line, the Wuhan Metro Line 12, started full line operation on Thursday. The 59.9-km line has 37 stations and stretches across seven administrative districts of the city. By far, the total mileage of Wuhan Metro in operation has exceeded 581 kilometers. (Xinhua/Xiao Yijiu)
WUHAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, the capital of central China's Hubei Province, became fully operational on Thursday, making it China's longest metro loop line, according to the China Association of Metros.
Stretching 59.9 kilometers and serving 37 underground stations across seven urban districts of Wuhan, the line connects the Wuchang and Hankou railway hubs and offers transfers to 18 existing and planned lines. A full loop takes about 96 minutes.
The line opened in two phases. The first phase, 35.3 kilometers long, entered service on May 1 this year. With the second phase now operational, Wuhan Metro's operational length exceeds 581 kilometers, roughly the driving distance between Berlin and Munich or between Rome and Milan.
Wuhan, known as the "river city," has complex geological and hydrological conditions, which posed multiple challenges during construction. The line passes under the Yangtze River twice and the Hanjiang River once. Construction teams overcame a series of technical difficulties, including high water pressure and composite strata.
One cross-river tunnel, in particular, is approximately 4 kilometers long, with its lowest point 71.4 meters below the Yangtze River surface. The project has provided valuable experience for building super-large-diameter cross-river tunnels in China.
Wuhan, home to over 13.86 million permanent residents, is a key transport hub in China and a core city of the Yangtze River Economic Belt. The opening of Metro Line 12 is expected to further facilitate cross-river commuting.
China has issued a plan to comprehensively advance the high-quality development of integrated transport services during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the Ministry of Transport announced in July this year. The plan aims to basically establish a modern integrated transport service system by 2030.
Under the plan, China will improve connections among different modes of transport, make passenger transfers more convenient and enhance freight logistics services. ■

Army standing up a Deep Recce Strike Brigade
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:21:11 GMT
18:21:11 KST

The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to pull intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike together at corps level, including what the department calls novel one-way effectors, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on accelerating the development and deployment of the new Recce-Strike approach set out on page 111 of the Strategic Defence Review.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to provide Corps-level (HQ ARRC) integration of intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike capabilities, including novel one-way effectors. The 5th Generation Land Force programme will increase human-machine teaming, autonomy and decision advantage, further accelerating recce-strike capability across the force.”
A one-way effector is a munition that does not come back, in practice a loitering munition or an attack drone, and the phrase has become the department’s preferred term for a class of weapon that Ukraine has turned into the dominant means of killing vehicles and artillery well behind the line of contact.
The headquarters named is the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks in Gloucester, a NATO corps headquarters Britain provides and commands. The brigade’s output therefore arrives at the level where a corps commander shapes a battle, above divisional and brigade level.
The Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025 set out recce-strike as the organising idea for the future Army, describing a mix of sensors, long-range fires and autonomous systems connected by a digital targeting network. The Defence Investment Plan put £1.8 billion into that targeting web, and the Army has separately acknowledged that its existing drones cannot talk to each other, creating the Uncrewed Systems Centre to deal with that.
The 5th Generation Land Force programme covers the Army’s wider modernisation, including human-machine teaming and the mix of crewed and uncrewed platforms the service expects to field through the next decade.

====================================================================================================

New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:14 UTC
18:20:14 KST

DEFORESTATION INC
New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Two environmental groups have uncovered operational, commercial, personnel and logistical links between First Resources and Indonesian suppliers accused of forest destruction. It’s not the first time the company has obscured its supply chain.
One of the world’s largest palm oil producers allegedly misled investors and corporate customers when it denied links to Indonesian suppliers accused of deforestation, a group of environmental organizations found.
The Singapore-based First Resources group, owned by the billionaire Fangiono family, oversees more than 270,000 hectares of oil palm plantations and is currently under scrutiny as Indonesia and neighboring nations battle a toxic haze caused by illegal fires used to clear land for agriculture.
In 2024, First Resources rejected allegations by the Gecko Project, a partner of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, which had linked the conglomerate to a company now known as Kalimantan Agro Sejahtera (KAS) and palm oil firms allegedly responsible for deforestation on the island of Borneo. The findings were part of Deforestation Inc., a cross-border investigation led by ICIJ that exposed how a lightly regulated sustainability industry overlooks forest destruction and human rights violations when granting environmental certifications.
The Rainforest Action Network and the Environmental Investigation Agency have now uncovered new evidence showing that First Resources, KAS and another company appear to be part of the same corporate group, and have operational, commercial, personnel and logistical connections.
Confidential financial information and court records reveal that, despite marketing its operations as sustainable, First Resources “laundered” into its supply chain palm oil sourced from the suppliers linked to forest loss, according to the reports published today. The company sells its products to Cargill and other major food processing and trading firms.
The researchers also followed trucks and barges and found that a Fangiono-controlled bulking facility was used to offload and transport crude palm oil sourced from mills belonging to First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri — indicating close trade relationships. Companies’ employees interviewed by the researchers also confirmed that the firms were linked to each other, the RAN report said.
Alex Helan, a senior researcher at RAN, said the new revelations show how major players in the forestry sector use “tactics of hide and seek through corporate structures” that weaken authorities’ fight against forest destruction.
“Deforestation in Indonesia has been declining over the last decade, influenced by market expectations for deforestation-free products, together with stronger government enforcement,” Helan told ICIJ. “However, this progress is being undermined by companies using complex corporate structures to hide their continued links to deforestation.”
First Resources denied the allegations, saying it operates according to the law and “does not have coordinated, integrated, and co-mingled Crude Palm Oil (CPO) supply chains” with the Indonesian suppliers mentioned in the report.
‘Related parties’ undercut sustainability claims
First Resources first pledged to end deforestation in its supply chain in 2015. Since then, more than half of its plantations have been certified as sustainable by the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, a voluntary certification organization, according to corporate records.
Companies often use their green certification status to attract lenders, investors and clients committed to “environmental, social and governance” guidelines.
As a publicly listed company on the Singapore Stock Exchange, First Resources is also required to submit a sustainability report, in which it routinely touts its commitment to transparency and environmental standards. The report is not reviewed by an independent third-party — a loophole identified by ICIJ’s Deforestation Inc., which showed how forestry companies use certifications based on flawed audits to advertise products and operations as compliant with environmental standards, labor laws and human rights, misinforming shareholders as well as customers.
The new findings by RAN, EIA and Kaom Telepak raise questions about the company’s sustainability claims — and the RSPO’s and the Stock Exchange’s ability to hold it accountable.
According to the environmental groups, over the last decade, large-scale deforestation has continued in a number of palm oil concessions surrounding First Resources facilities operating under the name KAS Group. The company is controlled on paper by a businessman with a very limited public profile who has been described by researchers as a close associate of the Fangionos’.
The KAS Group operates across several Indonesian provinces with about 15,000 employees, 70,000 hectares of land and six palm oil mills, according to job and training adverts uncovered by the researchers. Information about its ownership is hidden behind shell companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, a secrecy jurisdiction.
Satellite images analyzed for the report reveal that KAS Group and FAP Agri, another palm oil producer allegedly linked to First Resources, were responsible for clearing more than 9,300 hectares of forest between 2021 to 2026, including areas inhabited by the endangered Eastern Grey Gibbons.
Last year, the RSPO found its member, First Resources, in breach of the organization’s transparency rules and suspended it temporarily. It did not, however, require the company to treat the suspect suppliers as part of the same group, and First Resources has continued to deny links to the Indonesian firms.
“The RSPO complaints panel got it wrong,” RAN’s Helan said, “and has thereby allowed apparent laundering of deforestation palm oil to take place.”
Newly uncovered records from a lawsuit filed by KAS Group in 2022 includes employees’ statements describing regular transport of KAS palm oil to First Resource operations, RAN’s report said. Internal accounting files obtained by the researchers and dated April 2024 also appear to identify the three companies – First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri – as “related parties” and show close trading links, the report said.
FAP Agri denied any wrongdoing in a statement to RAN. KAS Group did not reply to requests for comment.
The EIA investigation also found that South Sorong concessions sold by First Resources in 2025 and a First Resources-linked shipping company have the same ultimate owner: an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands. This raises “significant questions about whether the divestment resulted in complete separation from the assets,” EIA’s analyst Ben Melling told ICIJ.
Taken together, Melling said, the findings show that “buyers, investors and certification bodies need to step up their due diligence.”

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
- A European Cockpit Association (ECA) survey found 76.8% of 7,200 pilots across 32 countries had at least one cockpit “microsleep” in four weeks, raising fears about fatigue and safety.
- Only 37.2% usually report when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% do not report it and fly anyway.
- Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information.
AI generated
Three in four pilots have admitted to briefly dozing off or struggling to stay awake while inside the cockpit, a European survey has found.
The report, released on Oct 26 by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), has renewed concerns about overworked and exhausted flight crews that, in turn, present an unseen risk to flying.
The ECA drew on responses from about 7,200 pilots across 32 countries.
Some 76.8% of those surveyed reported at least one cockpit “microsleep” in the previous four weeks, while 38.8% said they usually do not get enough rest to prevent fatigue from accumulating.
They cited brief and uncontrolled sleep, head nodding and fighting to keep their eyes open.
Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
The survey was voluntary and conducted online from Aug 4 to Sept 7.
Reporting fatigue is itself a problem, the ECA said.
Only 37.2% said they usually report themselves unfit when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% said they do not report it and fly anyway.
“When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit,” Captain Coen George, an ECA board director, said in a statement.
‘Alarming number’
Incidents of pilots falling asleep while helming a flight have been reported in Asia.
On Jan 25, 2024, both pilots aboard a Batik Air flight from Kendari to Jakarta fell asleep during the flight, according to Indonesia’s National Transportation Safety Committee. The Airbus A320 was carrying 153 passengers and six crew members.
The captain had been resting when the first officer inadvertently fell asleep. The captain woke up about 28 minutes after the first officer’s last radio transmission, found the aircraft off its intended flight path and woke his colleague.
The plane landed safely, with no injuries or damage.
Investigators found that the first officer’s sleep before duty had been interrupted while helping care for his month-old twins.
In a statement to People magazine, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency said flight-time limits provide a safety baseline, while airlines must actively manage fatigue through reporting systems, operational measures and a culture that allows crews to raise concerns without fear of consequences.
The cockpit association’s president, Captain Tanja Harter, called for stronger oversight and protections for pilots reporting fatigue, saying the lack of meaningful progress since 2023 required action from airlines and regulators.
“Having more than three in four pilots say they reported dozing off while at work is definitely an alarming number, and the industry does need to take note of this,” Bobby Laurie, a Pennsylvania-based travel expert and former flight attendant, told Fox News Digital.
“But it’s not necessarily a warning sign that the flight that you’ve been on had a pilot or both pilots asleep,” he said.

Top Russian official takes US journalists into besieged Ukrainian city ahead of evacuation
Unknown

Russia, Ukraine say Oleshky demining operations complete, humanitarian operation to proceed
Oct 29 - Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine had been completed and that an operation to bring aid and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organise a relief operation for the acutely deprived town's residents, which Russian forces seized soon after Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Both sides have praised US first lady Melania Trump for helping broker a truce in a town where at least one resident who escaped said those remaining feared death by starvation.
Yet any sense of wider relief in a war now stretching beyond 4-1/2 years was rapidly dispelled by a series of attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a strike on the main train station in the southeastern city of Dnipro that killed 14 people.
The ceasefire is confined to the area around the town – opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson on the other side of the Dnipro River.
"Demining operations of routes have been completed for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky," the two sides said in virtually identical statements issued by Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner, and Dmytro Lubinets, her Ukrainian counterpart.
"The humanitarian convoy is ready for departure."
The convoy would head for the district hospital and residents wishing to leave would be permitted to go within a specific time frame. Aid packages would then be distributed, the statements said.
The operation aims to address a crisis in a town marooned inside a war zone since 2022. But it is also part of a diplomatic dance where both sides want to show US President Donald Trump that they back his peace efforts, albeit for different reasons.
Lantratova, Russian human rights commissioner, said she was taking four journalists from the conservative US outlet Newsmax to the area. Lubinets made no reference to specific reporters.
PUTIN SAYS MOSCOW IS MAKING PEACE EFFORTS
President Vladimir Putin told a gathering with African nations in Moscow that relief supplies would begin reaching civilians on Thursday and Friday, "with the support, incidentally, of the first lady of the United States".
Lubinets extended Kyiv's "special thanks" to someone who was "personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky".
Trump has cast Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy as an obstacle to peace while praising Putin, who said on Thursday that Russia was "working on issues relating to a possible peaceful resolution of the Ukrainian crisis itself".
Although Russia, like Ukraine, denies targeting civilians, strikes on trains and other civilian infrastructure have become increasingly common as Ukraine's stocks of air defence missiles have dwindled. Civilian deaths have also increased in Russia.
Although US-mediated peace talks are due to resume next month in Abu Dhabi after a long pause, the two sides are far apart when it comes to terms for ending the war.
But both recognise the ability of Trump, who has another two years in power left regardless of the outcome of US midterm legislative elections next month, to affect the conflict.
Russia still hopes that Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions, such as full Russian control of Ukraine's Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining the NATO defence alliance.
Kyiv wants to ensure that US intelligence sharing continues along with full access to Elon Musk's recently disrupted battlefield communications system, Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, continues to flow.
KHERSON CEASEFIRE DUE TO CONTINUE UNTIL SUNDAY
The truce applies only to Oleshky and the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Some 1,500 of the town's prewar population of 24,000 people are believed to live among the ruins, under regular shellfire amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine has long accused Russia of refusing to let aid in or people out. Russia says it is Ukrainian mines on the approach roads and Ukrainian shelling that have prevented the delivery of aid or the safe evacuation of residents.
By the middle of Thursday, neither Ukraine nor Russia had reported violations of the ceasefire, due to last until Sunday.
Residents wishing to leave and return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government are expected to exit via Russia-controlled Crimea before crossing into southern Russia and being flown to Belarus from where they will be able to cross the border into Ukraine. REUTERS

WASHINGTON – The United States has fired its top military planner, The Atlantic reported on Oct 28, in a surprise shake-up as President Donald Trump appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran.
Army Lieutenant-General Brett Sylvia was removed this week from his role as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the magazine reported, citing unidentified defence department officials.
Sylvia’s ouster would be the latest in a series of high-profile departures from the military since Trump returned to power in 2025.
US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth said in September that the United States has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%, in a move he said is aimed at “accountability”.
He suggested the cuts targeted officers who failed to get on board with his efforts to ensure the military is focused on war-fighting rather than the “woke” policies of previous administrations, describing the reductions as an “accomplishment”.
No reason was given for Sylvia’s departure and no replacement has been named, The Atlantic said.
AFP has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
The reported sacking comes as Trump is widely considered to be weighing fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on Nov 3.
“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said last week, referring to US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war.
He did not give any indication on timing.
Neither the United States nor Iran has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, settling instead into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships.
Sylvia’s previous roles included leading the 101st Airborne Division – the US army’s air assault division – and heading a unit in Iraq. AFP

====================================================================================================

Promises and Perils of Nepal’s India Pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

After months of keeping New Delhi at arm’s length, Nepal’s Balendra Shah government is discovering both the appeal and the political risks of drawing it closer.
Formed after the March 2026 elections, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government did not start on the right foot with the southern neighbor. First, new Prime Minister Balendra Shah declined a one-on-one meeting with then-Indian Ambassador Naveen Shrivastava, in keeping with his policy of not meeting any foreign officials.
What rankled more with the Indians was his subsequent refusal to meet India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who was coming to Kathmandu carrying Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s formal invitation for Shah to visit India. Misri’s trip was called off. India — which continues to emphasize its “unique” relations with Nepal that are unlike its ties with any other country — saw this as a snub, and a breach of trust.
Those were not the only irritants in bilateral ties. The new government in Kathmandu started taxing goods bought by Nepali nationals in Indian border towns, hampering the business of these hubs that rely on Nepali buyers. Entry of Indian vehicles into Nepal was also restricted.
That was the state of affairs for the first five or six months of the Shah government.
But the tide seems to have turned and the government now appears keen to woo the Indians. At the forefront of this effort is Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle.
Even before the March elections, as a top RSP leader, Wagle had repeatedly visited New Delhi with a message that should his party come to power, it would go the extra mile to protect Indian interests.
Of late, Wagle seems to have gotten the government’s green light to boldly assert that the era of “anti-India nationalism” in Nepal is over and his government is ready to turn over a new leaf with the southern neighbor.
Curiously, he and his government also sound accommodative of India’s self-declared red lines. In a recent interview with The Hindu, the Nepali minister said that Nepal now accepts that India’s refusal to buy hydropower from Nepali projects with Chinese investment is a “new geopolitical reality.”
Yet the finance minister is only laying the ground for Shah’s much-awaited India visit in the third week of November. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has also contributed to this effort, outlining potential areas of bilateral cooperation in a recent op-ed. Big deals are being planned during Shah’s visit.
But for any government in Kathmandu, close relations with India come with both costs and benefits. The obvious benefit is that New Delhi pulls many strings in Kathmandu, and it can make life difficult for a Nepali prime minister it does not like. The latest overtures of his government toward India suggest Shah does not want to be one of them.
If Shah can convince New Delhi to, say, secure an additional air route for Nepal during his India trip, it will be a new feather in his bhadgaule cap — and a tangible achievement for his nationalist base back home.
Yet there are also costs of closer ties with India. Whatever Wagle says, the days of anti-India nationalism in Nepal are far from over — as is also evident in the fierce criticism of his remarks in Nepali intellectual circles. Nepalis continue to be suspicious of the oft-meddling regional hegemon that has thrice imposed crippling blockades on the landlocked country.
Shah got an overwhelming mandate, and he can afford to use some of his political capital to push through vital projects with India. But irrespective of how well Shah’s India trip goes, there will still be irritants in bilateral ties.
For instance, a major disagreement remains between Kathmandu and New Delhi on an old border dispute. After India and China unilaterally opened the Lipulekh pass — a trijunction point between the three countries — for trade earlier this year, Kathmandu swiftly dispatched diplomatic notes to New Delhi and Beijing. This issue could again flare up as both New Delhi and Beijing seem to be in a mood to overrule Nepal’s objections and give continuity to their trade through the pass.
It will be hard for the Shah government to stand firm on Lipulekh — something that is in keeping with the Nepali public sentiment — while also pursuing closer cooperation with India. If it does not handle the issue well, a “compromise” on territorial integrity to secure favorable trade terms could even be portrayed domestically as a surrender to the regional hegemon.
Then there is China. The government has signaled that closer ties with India are worth paying the price of narrowing the space for Chinese investment in Nepali hydropower.
Yet if the government pushes Beijing too far through such gestures, it will violate a central tenet of Nepali foreign policy: maintenance of a delicate balance between Beijing and New Delhi. There will thus be a strong opposition to an overt India tilt.
In the end, Shah and his ministers would do well to avoid making sweeping claims that old constraints in India-Nepal ties have disappeared or that the anti-India nationalism in Nepal has run its course. Nurturing this complicated relationship requires sustained diplomacy and setting of realistic expectations. Only then can Nepal protect its interests.

‘Serious suspicions,’ election committee chief orders Shin Bet to investigate foreign funding, election bribery
Sohlberg said he “cannot attest to the nature” of the suspicions but that there is a duty to investigate them. He also says the information that led to the request did not come from a political entity
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet head David Zini to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign entities. According to a letter dated October 28, Sohlberg asked for findings, if any, within the coming week.
The letter followed a briefing in which Zini presented Sohlberg with information described as “exceptionally grave.” The allegations concern improper influence over the elections through foreign funding from outside actors working against Israeli interests.
Sohlberg noted that the information that led to the suspicions does not involve tips received from a political entity, nor is it a response to an inquiry from the Likud party, which alleges fraud and the theft of the election.
“The purity of elections is the heart of democracy,” Sohlberg wrote. “Serious suspicions have been brought before me of improper influence on the elections through foreign funding from foreign entities operating against Israeli interests.”
The committee chairman also stated that he “cannot attest to the nature of the above suspicions,” but said there was a duty to investigate them properly.
Sohlberg told Zini to “do everything in your power to investigate the matter,” and to use the Shin Bet’s powers to locate evidence substantiating the suspicions. “Only in this way can we ensure public trust in the electoral process, and the purity of the democratic process.”
Separately, Ynet reports that Sohlberg sent the letter to Zini following a meeting between them earlier in the week, and claim it may be an attempt by Qatar to influence the elections in Israel. The CEC stated that the information regarding this is “solid.”
Suggested articles
Meanwhile, several additional suspects have been arrested as part of an investigation into alleged bribery in exchange for votes for the Ra’am party.
Following the election, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through bribery, threats, violence, forgery, and prohibited voter mobilization software, and said it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to police, the Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee. Police said they have no investigative or intelligence-based evidence supporting the allegations.
According to police data, 48 complaints of fraud and impersonation had been received nationwide as of last night, compared with nearly 80 during the previous election, a decrease of about 40%.
Political reactions
Several Israeli political leaders from both sides of the political spectrum weighed in on the investigation order.
Current opposition frontrunner and Yashar Party chief Gadi Eisenkot says he is in contact with the relevant authorities and is receiving updates regarding suspicions of foreign interference in the elections. "The State of Israel must rigorously safeguard the integrity of the elections against any attempts at interference, political spin, or bias," Eisenkot said in a statement.

"We have recently received feedback from various quarters regarding the collaborative merchandise with the Japanese television drama VIVANT," Sanrio said in a statement.
"We sincerely apologise for any concern this may have caused."
The project "contains expressions that are inconsistent with the Sanrio Group's corporate philosophy", it said.
Sanrio said it had "decided to cease this collaboration, as well as all subsequent projects and promotional campaigns".
Hello Kitty and other cute Sanrio characters had been depicted as characters from "Vivant" – currently in its second season – in a range of novelty merchandise items.
Read moreFrench-Saudi ‘Dragon Ball’ theme park puzzles Japanese manga fans
Before the apology, Chinese state media outlet the Global Times had accused the show of "smearing China", saying it had "sparked shock and fierce backlash on social media".
The series reflects the "anti-China narrative of the current conservative Japanese right-wing administration, catering to the trend of right-wing extremism in Japanese society", it said.
Long-frosty ties between the countries have worsened since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested last year that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan.
Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as its territory and has vowed to bring it under control one day.
'Beauty and goodness'
The drama "is a completely fictional entertainment work", private broadcaster TBS, which created "Vivant", said in a statement to AFP.
"There is absolutely no intention to deliver messages that disparage any particular nation or hurt public sentiment," it said.
The network's president told Japanese media that TBS "does not in any way take a position that foments conflict between nations or condones the use of force or violence".
Comments posted on Chinese social media platform Weibo before Sanrio's announcement had angrily criticised the merchandise tie-up.
"Sanrio, you are a brand for conveying a message of beauty and goodness, why have you got involved with this?" one post said.
"It's disappointing," read another. "The founder has long taken part in various anti-war activities, and Sanrio was originally founded on the ideals of stopping war and cherishing peace."
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun echoed the complaints at a regular news briefing on Thursday, following Sanrio's statement.
"This television drama once again reveals the persistent existence inside Japan of a force that seeks to use cultural products to vilify and smear China and spread anti-Chinese sentiment," he said.
"This should raise alarm amongst the international community and enlightened individuals within Japan."
The furore follows similar ire from the country over Mbappé's comments.

Restricted airspace now covers fifty defence sites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:09 GMT
18:00:09 KST

Restricted airspace has been applied over fifty defence sites and a further one hundred and seventy are expected to follow in December, part of a wider effort to harden British military bases against drones, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Mark Pritchard, the Conservative member for The Wrekin, asked what additional support is being given to Guardian, the protective security element of Standing Joint Command, in light of increased threats to British military bases.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for security technology and infrastructure. Restricted Airspace has been applied to 50 Defence sites, with a further 170 expected in December 2026, while £15 million has been invested in remotely piloted and counter-uncrewed aerial systems and training over the past 18 months.”
Restricted airspace makes flying a drone over a site unlawful without permission. That does not stop anyone flying, but it gives the police and the Ministry of Defence Police an offence to act on, and it removes the argument that an operator did not know where they were.
The department has set out £240 million for Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system intended to detect and defeat emerging threats, and the Army is running Project Halo Shield to examine what commercially available counter-drone technology could do for site protection. The £15 million figure for remotely piloted and counter-drone systems and training over the past eighteen months is small compared with those programmes and covers work done while they are being stood up.

Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.
The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.
The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.
Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.
Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.
Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.
The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

"No politician is irreplaceable" – Mieriņa delivers a significant message as Latvia's 14th Saeima concludes its work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:56 UTC
17:59:56 KST

As Latvia's 14th Saeima concluded its work on Thursday, Speaker of Parliament Daiga Mieriņa of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) called on lawmakers to maintain respect for the Saeima and democratic values, stressing that the country is always greater than any political party, parliamentary group or parliamentary term.
In her final address to the outgoing parliament, Mieriņa acknowledged that the past four years had not been easy and had required considerable work, patience and compromise. Nevertheless, lawmakers had managed to maintain dialogue even when their opinions differed.
The Speaker recalled that during the 14th Saeima's term, parliament held 219 sittings, conducted 7,911 votes, adopted 1,060 laws and held 3,555 committee meetings.
She emphasised that the Saeima is a mirror of society, reflecting what Latvia has been and what it is today.
Mieriņa thanked lawmakers for their contributions to strengthening parliamentarism, democracy and the Latvian state, noting that every member of parliament had left their mark over the four years, whether through adopted legislation, initiatives or parliamentary debates.
She stressed that in a democracy, there are no small or large mandates, only the trust of voters granted for a limited period.
Addressing lawmakers who will continue serving in the next parliament, Mieriņa encouraged them to retain the ability to listen not only to their own voters but also to those who hold different views.
She also urged them to respect parliamentary traditions and the people on whose behalf decisions are made.
At the same time, Mieriņa noted that society is changing and a new generation is knocking on parliament's doors, bringing its own perspectives and expectations of politics.
She stressed that politicians must be willing to listen to this generation and make room for new representatives.
Mieriņa emphasised that no politician is irreplaceable, as members of parliament serve for a limited time, while Latvia, democracy and the people they serve remain.
Concluding her address, the Speaker wished lawmakers success in both their political careers and personal challenges.
She also quoted author and speaker Neale Donald Walsch, saying that a true leader is not someone who has the most followers, but someone who creates the most leaders.
Mieriņa ended her speech with the traditional Latvian wish: "May Latvia live as long as the sun!"

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:04 UTC
17:59:04 KST

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
American journalists will observe a humanitarian mission under a Russia-Ukraine truce in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia, US First Lady Melania Trump has said. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has confirmed that the reporters are expected there, and that demining operations are already underway.
Alyoshki, located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, was largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege, with drone attacks and remotely laid mines hampering aid deliveries and evacuation efforts from a town where an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remained.
Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukraine of obstructing humanitarian efforts.
However, after US mediation spearheaded by the Slovenian-born US first lady, Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area starting October 27 to allow humanitarian assistance to flow in and evacuations to proceed. As of Thursday, both Russian and Ukrainian officials reported no truce violations. The pause is scheduled to last until Sunday.
Writing on X on Wednesday, Trump said four American journalists from conservative US outlet Newsmax will arrive in Alyoshki and accompany Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders. “Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission,” she said.
Dmitriev confirmed that Newsmax reporters will be there, adding: “Humanity and peace must prevail.”
Speaking to reporters before departing to Alyoshki, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said other foreign journalists are also expected to arrive, without providing further details.
Both Trump and Lantratova confirmed that Russia and Ukraine have begun clearing mines to secure aid routes. “It is now crucial to make the roads safe so that people can leave the town,” Lantratova said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday that most Ukrainian mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones, and that they are predominantly Western-made. It also released a video showing a large-scale demining effort involving remotely-controlled robots.
The Alyoshki crisis was discussed during an October 9 phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the leaders agreed that Russia’s human rights commissioner would maintain direct contact with Melania Trump’s office. US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Putin in St. Petersburg last week to discuss proposals for ending the Ukraine conflict.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The authorities in Spain and Portugal, together with Kiev, are working to develop weapons for strikes against Russia, while their own citizens are grappling with a housing and economic crisis, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the Opposition Platform - For Life party banned in Ukraine, said.

"As a result, the political choices made by Madrid and Lisbon seem highly contradictory. On the one hand, there is condemnation of military actions in the Persian Gulf. On the other hand, these countries are being drawn into the war in Ukraine, which requires funding and cuts to social service budgets. While Spaniards are being forced to live in tents due to the housing crisis, and Portuguese authorities acknowledge the lack of affordable housing as one of the most pressing social problems, the governments of both countries are at the same time allocating state resources, industrial capacity, and technological expertise toward expanding arms production for Ukraine," he concluded.

====================================================================================================

Delhi’s De-Hyphenation Policy is Taking Shape in the South Caucasus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Few would have pictured Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar sharing a stage with his Azerbaijani counterpart, Jeyhun Bayramov, after Baku’s public backing of Islamabad during the India-Pakistan crisis of 2025.
Following the terrorist attack at Pahalgam on April 22, 2025, Azerbaijan was one of the few countries that did not publicly condemn the attack. After a telephone conversation with the Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on April 26, Baku issued a statement, expressing concern over the “recent tensions between India and Pakistan” and stressed the need to “refrain from unilateral actions in such a volatile situation.” Then, after India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, Azerbaijan explicitly condemned the Indian military strikes, saying they harmed civilians. It expressed solidarity with the people of Pakistan.
Against this backdrop, Jaishankar’s visit to Baku on October 23 – the first standalone visit by an Indian external affairs minister since 2018 – when he held talks with Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Bayramov, marks an important step toward repairing strained bilateral ties.
At the joint press conference, Bayramov acknowledged that India and Azerbaijan “had different viewpoints on different issues,” before going on to describe discussions with Jaishankar as “very long and positive and fruitful.” Jaishankar echoed this sentiment, describing the discussions as “focused and forward looking” with both sides exchanging views on “various aspects” of the bilateral relationship and discussing important “regional and global developments from a strategic perspective.”
While no agreements were signed, both sides agreed to deepen cooperation in the oil and energy sector, expand trade and investment, and exchange commercial and business delegations. They also agreed to strengthen regular political consultations and exchange high-level visits. During the visit, Jaishankar reportedly raised the issue of cross-border terrorism, security, and common threats. Notably, including “cross-border terrorism” brought New Delhi’s primary security friction with Pakistan directly into the bilateral conversation, despite Islamabad’s close ties with Baku.
Jaishankar’s visit was not an isolated diplomatic gesture, but rather the latest in a series of moves to accelerate a thaw in India’s ties with Azerbaijan. Jaishankar’s visit to Baku was a follow-up to the meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Aliyev on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit at Bishkek in August-September this year.
Jaishankar’s visit was immediately preceded by a visit by the Indian Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh to Baku, where he led the Indian delegation for the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) held on October 15.
High-level diplomatic contact between New Delhi and Baku was restored in April this year, when India’s Secretary (West) Sibi George visited Baku for the 6th round of the India-Azerbaijan Foreign Office Consultations. The visit came less than a year after Baku condemned India’s military strikes on Pakistan. According to an Indian Ministry of External Affairs media release, the issues discussed included “trade, technology, tourism, pharmaceuticals, energy, culture, people to people exchanges and [the] fight against cross border terrorism.” The previous foreign office consultations were held in 2022.
According to an Indian media report, Azerbaijan resumed crude oil exports to India in September 2025, after a 10-month break caused by pricing issues that led to a halt in supplies. India-Azerbaijan bilateral trade has steadily dropped from $1,882 million in 2022 to $1,435 million in 2023, $958 million in 2024 and just $400 million in 2025. In the first 9 months of 2026, bilateral trade has already reached $600 million, Bayramov said.
It is important to understand the regional geopolitical context in which the thaw in New Delhi-Baku ties is playing out. India’s engagement in the South Caucasus has historically been weighted towards Armenia, Azerbaijan’s adversary in the decades-long Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. This has been a persistent irritant in India-Azerbaijan ties.
Meanwhile, Armenia has emerged as India’s strongest partner in the region – especially through defense cooperation – in recent years, driven largely by mutual concerns over an Azerbaijan-Pakistan-Türkiye nexus. The signing of the U.S. brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict in August 2025 paved the way for New Delhi to separate its relations with Baku from its position on the conflict, without risking derailing ties with Yerevan.
The evolving regional landscape has further accelerated this alignment. Nascent signs of rapprochement between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are evident, with the recent bilateral agreement to promote cooperation in academic engagements.
In September 2025, Armenia and Pakistan also established diplomatic relations after over 30 years of non-recognition by Islamabad. As more extra-regional actors come to play an active role in shaping the South Caucasus’ future, New Delhi is fast realizing it has more to lose by not engaging in multi-directional diplomacy with all actors.
Interestingly, Jaishankar’s visit comes at a time when Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban has strained Baku’s ties with one of its closest partners, Türkiye. After Baku announced a headscarf ban on September 21, Türkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan implicitly criticized the move at the U.N. General Assembly, calling it an assault on fundamental freedoms. The resulting criticism from Erdogan and other Türkish officials prompted a sharp response from Baku, triggering a rare diplomatic showdown between partners who describe themselves as “One Nation, Two States.”
Although Jaishankar’s visit was likely planned well in advance and unrelated to this sudden friction, the trip coincided perfectly with these shifting regional dynamics. It opens a valuable window for rapprochement, granting both nations greater geopolitical maneuvering space in light of New Delhi’s fraught relations with Ankara.
Another reason why New Delhi is looking to revive ties with Azerbaijan is to accelerate work on the International North South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Originally proposed in 2000, the project sat dormant for years until New Delhi recently signaled interest in reviving it, as an alternative to the conventional Suez Canal route amid growing vulnerability in global maritime chokepoints. Azerbaijan, which serves as the land bridge for the Western Route of the INSTC, will play a crucial role if New Delhi wants this route to become a dependable commercial artery. In this context, Baku agreeing to “closer coordination” on INSTC is a welcome development for New Delhi.
Yet, India’s ‘”de-hyphenation” policy may not automatically translate to a reset in ties. Because a formal peace treaty remains absent, the agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia amounts to little more than a fragile truce. If the conflict persists or reignites, New Delhi will find itself increasingly intertwined in turbulent regional security dynamics.
Moreover, whether this relationship broadens or stagnates will also depend to a large extent on Baku’s willingness to accommodate New Delhi’s concerns regarding Pakistan and Kashmir.
Azerbaijan has been a consistent and vocal supporter of Pakistan’s position on the Kashmir issue, most notably at multilateral forums such as the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). Azerbaijan has consistently backed statements and communiques within the OIC and its contact group on Jammu and Kashmir, which condemned India’s actions in Kashmir.
Azerbaijan will be hosting the 2027 OIC Summit, and New Delhi will closely scrutinize how it frames the Kashmir issue in the grouping. Any overtly provocative framing is likely to adversely impact the future trajectory of India-Azerbaijan diplomatic and economic ties.
The trust deficit between the two sides is deep-rooted, and the recent rapprochement seems unlikely to bridge the big ideological differences between the two nations.
Nevertheless, engagement is a positive step, and a practical reflection of New Delhi’s ‘multi-alignment’ approach towards foreign policy.

Washington has gone ahead with the upgrade even as India and the US continue to deepen defense cooperation under a ten-year partnership framework signed last year. India and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, clashed briefly last year with drones and missiles following a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 civilians.
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, in his talks with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, also raised the possibility of sensitive American military technology supplied to Pakistan reaching third countries, the Economic Times reported, citing officials familiar with the discussions. The two officials met on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Philippines.
The proposed package, notified to the US Congress in December, is intended to modernize Pakistan’s aging F-16 fleet and extend their operational life through 2040.
It includes 92 Link-16 tactical communication systems, avionics upgrades, secure communications, navigation equipment, spare parts, and training, according to a US Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification published last month. The package does not involve the sale of new fighter jets, and the US agency said it would not alter the basic military balance in the region.

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023-2025), expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Ukraine joining NATO. That is the most credible option. NATO's deterrence has worked for more than 77 years because no state has ever attacked the Alliance. I do not usually use the word 'guarantee,' but there are benefits to being covered by extended nuclear deterrence from the United States, the United Kingdom and France," the expert said.
At the same time, he cautioned against expecting a nuclear program of one's own to provide absolute protection. Stokes, who headed the Staff Group of NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, outlined his arguments.
According to him, the decision to develop an independent nuclear capability cannot be taken lightly, as no one wants further proliferation of nuclear weapons, which are currently possessed by only a limited number of states. Political commitments, financial costs, the technical expertise and technology required, and the time and money needed to produce a certain number of nuclear weapons must all be taken into account. In addition, a country would need delivery systems, a doctrine, command-and-control procedures, and many other supporting capabilities.
"All of this requires a great deal of effort. I say this as someone who worked for a long time on countering the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Stokes said.
He also cited North Korea as an example of a country that has become a nuclear power. However, the expert noted, North Korea is a pariah state. Ukraine, or any other country, therefore needs to consider whether it wants to become a pariah and potentially face sanctions by withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. "Would that really provide the security they seek?" he said.
At the same time, Stokes acknowledged that he understood those who argue that, from a national security perspective, nuclear weapons offer the ultimate guarantee of national security and sovereignty.
The expert therefore believes it would be better to devote time, money and effort to conventional defense.
"Whether you can be part of a nuclear alliance and reinforce that arrangement, as in NATO or another alliance, or whether there are other ways to obtain some form of security guarantee. There seem to be better options that would be available rather than pursuing a national nuclear weapons program," Stokes concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons, Ukraine should have received a "security umbrella." He described the guarantees the country received at the time as "an unfair game and a major mistake."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Institutes of Applied Research said Tuesday that it worked with Material Science Service Company to use a special coating to stabilize wafers for material analysis.
Shrinking semiconductor processes are prompting manufacturers to develop high-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography. The process uses metal oxide photoresists to produce finer circuit patterns on chip wafers.
NIAR said in a press release that the process is still under development and has high structural requirements. Wafers also need to be dissected to check for possible post-processing defects.
NIAR also said that cutting a wafer open may ruin its nanostructure and material interfaces. The team applied a thin coating before cutting for structural stability.
NIAR President Tsai Hung-yin (蔡宏營) said etching is one thing, but quality checking is just as important. The institute noted that material analysis is crucial to ensuring the wafers meet standards.
The institution said the National Center for Instrumentation Research uses atomic layer deposition (ALD) to form the coating. MSS used the center’s custom-built ALD equipment to test different materials.
MSS also announced that it will partner with NIAR on production verification. MSS Chair Liu Chi-lun (柳紀綸) said he is optimistic, as the firm has received requests from the world’s leading semiconductor equipment makers.

Taiwan warns of forest fire risks as dry season begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:49:58 UTC
17:49:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency warned Thursday that the public should take extra care with fire as the dry season increases the risk of forest fires, particularly in central and southern Taiwan.
The agency said 390 forest fires, or 89% of the total recorded over the past decade, occurred between October and May, before the arrival of the plum rain season. Careless use of fire caused 97% of forest fires, underscoring the importance of prevention, per a press release.
The agency launched a public awareness campaign, “A Single Spark Destroys a Forest,” urging people visiting forests to avoid careless use of fire. To help the public assess local conditions, the agency operates the Forest Fire Risk Assessment System, which provides local fire risk forecasts for the next seven days.
When prolonged drought leaves forest-floor vegetation and other combustible material exceptionally dry, the agency may activate disaster-prevention cell broadcast alerts to warn people in affected areas. The agency urged the public to follow three rules: do not burn weeds, do not discard cigarette butts, and do not burn garbage.
Under Article 34 of the Forest Act, starting a fire in a forest area or forest protection zone without permission is prohibited. Violators can face fines of up to NT$600,000 (US$18,000).
Anyone who deliberately sets fire to another person’s forest faces three to 10 years in prison and may also be liable for civil damages, per the press release.
The agency offers a reward of NT$100,000 for reports of suspected criminal acts involving the burning of national or public forests that lead to the perpetrator being caught. A separate NT$5,000 reward may be given to the first person to report a forest fire, subject to applicable requirements.
Anyone who discovers a forest fire should immediately call the toll-free forest protection hotline at 0800-000930 or the fire department at 119. The agency urged the public to treat forest fire prevention as a shared responsibility and avoid leaving any potential ignition sources behind when visiting the mountains.

Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Following autumn storms Austen and Boelo, cliffs have formed along the coast. On the beaches of the resorts of Blankenberge and Middelkerke, these cliffs are up to 1.2 metres high. The Maritime and Coastal Services Agency (MDK) is pulling them down using machinery. In Knokke-Heist, its was local council workers that levelled the cliffs.
Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
The first autumn storm, Austen, swept across Belgium on Friday 23 October. The Royal Meteorological Institute (RMI) issued a code orange warning for gusts of up to 100 kilometres per hour. A day later, storm Boelo also swept across Belgium. A code yellow warning for wind was issued for the coast.
The effects of the storms are particularly clear on the beaches of Blankenberge and Middelkerke. There, experts identified cliffs up to 1.2 metres high, stretching over hundreds of metres. These are steep, almost vertical walls of sand. They form when waves wash away sand at the high-water mark during a storm.
Higher than 1 metre
The cliffs can be dangerous. They are not always clearly visible, meaning walkers could easily experience a nasty fall. “Sometimes the beach recovers naturally, thanks to the tides. If the cliffs are higher than 1 metre, we have to level them out with a machine,” explains Dries Derudder of the Maritime Services and Coast Agency(MDK). “That is now only the case in Blankenberge and Middelkerke.”
‘The cliffs will be levelled on Thursday or Friday at the latest, so that everything is safe in the run-up to the autumn half-term.’
Cliffs had also formed on the beach in Knokke-Heist. The largest were up to 2 metres high. There local council workers demolished the cliffs. “We’ve created a sort of passageway from the soft sand to the wet sand,” explains Bert De Brabandere, the alderman responsible for beaches. “People can walk there safely. In time, the water will wash away the cliffs.”
