Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what is Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela.
“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martin of the train drivers’ union SEMAF.
“We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again. Everyone should be able to travel without the risk of suffering this kind of accident,” he added at Madrid’s Atocha railway station.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a Nov 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain’s two main parties suspending campaign events.
Spain’s government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed in the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure.
A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said on Oct 28.
Unions have already blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying that talks after the accident in January were abandoned in April.
Meanwhile, the government has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was “inexplicable”.
Pope sends condolences
Pope Leo sent his condolences to the families of those killed, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and conveyed his support and comfort to all affected, the Vatican said, adding he had also encouraged rescue workers to continue their efforts.
Of those injured, 57 remained in hospital, said the authorities.
The crash prompted a major operation, which Spain’s Interior Ministry said involved the deployment of more than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs.
As investigations began, a judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with a 2km exclusion zone in both directions along the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo to take part in a meeting to monitor and coordinate the emergency response, said the authorities were working “day and night” to support the victims and their families and to “get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy”.
Meanwhile, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the centre-right People’s Party, which is currently leading in polls, was due to visit the town of Urda, where local people rushed to help with rescue efforts in the aftermath of the crash.
Foreign nationals among casualties
Spain’s Foreign Ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, information available so far showed. One of them was killed and at least seven were injured.
The Oct 28 accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain’s railways, Europe’s longest network and until recently a source of pride in the country.
Train drivers would go ahead with their strike to press for structural changes in railway safety, SEMAF said, adding that it was studying further action.
Renfe said the strike caused significant disruption to rail services, adding that passengers could change or cancel tickets free of charge and would be notified of affected services. REUTERS

28 October 2026, The Hague – Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Mihai Popșoi held a meeting with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Tom Berendsen.
The discussions focused on Moldova–Netherlands relations and cooperation priorities for the period ahead, with an emphasis on expanding cooperation in various sectors, including support for the Republic of Moldova’s European integration process.
Deputy Prime Minister Mihai Popșoi expressed appreciation for the Netherlands’ support, reflected in initiatives aimed at reforming the justice system, strengthening the rule of law and enhancing the Republic of Moldova’s resilience against hybrid threats, information manipulation and cyberattacks. He also expressed Moldova’s interest in continued Dutch assistance in these areas, including cybersecurity.
The Moldovan Foreign Minister stressed that support from the Netherlands and other partners is essential for strengthening the country’s capacity to ensure the security of its citizens, advance reforms and align with European standards. Mihai Popșoi thanked the Dutch authorities for their support and emphasised that the Republic of Moldova is ready to open the remaining two negotiating clusters: Cluster 4, “Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity”, and Cluster 5, “Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion”.
“Despite the challenges, the Republic of Moldova continues its path towards the European Union with determination. We know that this is a complex process that requires hard work and sustained efforts. We bear an enormous responsibility, but we are confident that, together with reliable partners such as the Kingdom of the Netherlands, we will succeed in completing the transformations our country needs to become an EU Member State,” Mihai Popșoi said.
For his part, Minister Tom Berendsen reaffirmed the Netherlands’ support for the Republic of Moldova’s accession to the European Union and expressed readiness to deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

In this context, Mihai Popșoi invited Tom Berendsen to pay a visit to the Republic of Moldova.

South Korean prosecutor seeks death penalty for Yoon over martial law
The prosecution argues only the death penalty could hold the ex-president fully accountable for a crime as serious as planning a rebellion
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
A South Korean special prosecutor on Thursday demanded the death penalty for ousted president Yoon Suk-yeol, ahead of an appeal court verdict on rebellion charges over his brief imposition of martial law in December 2024.
The Seoul High Court has yet to set a date for a verdict on Yoon’s appeal of a life sentence handed down in February by the Seoul Central District Court. The court found that he illegally mobilised troops and police to seize the legislature, arrest political opponents and establish unchecked rule for a “considerable time”.
Investigators led by special prosecutor Cho Eun-suk also appealed the ruling, arguing Yoon deserved the death penalty because his actions posed a grave threat to the country’s democracy. An execution would be unlikely. South Korea has not executed anyone since 1997, effectively maintaining a moratorium on capital punishment following calls for its abolition.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:43:25 UTC
17:43:25 KST

26 October 2026, Nicosia – Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Mihai Popșoi held a meeting with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Cyprus, Constantinos Kombos, during an official visit at the invitation of his Cypriot counterpart.
The discussions focused on the priorities of Moldova–Cyprus relations, Cyprus’s support for advancing the Republic of Moldova’s European path, expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest, and regional security developments.
The two ministers welcomed the strong cooperation between their countries and reviewed the progress made by the Republic of Moldova in its accession process to the European Union. Deputy Prime Minister Mihai Popșoi thanked the Cypriot authorities for their support, including during the Cypriot Presidency of the Council of the EU, which contributed to the official opening of negotiations on the first cluster, “Fundamentals”, in June this year.
“Accession to the European Union is the Republic of Moldova’s most important national project since gaining independence. The reforms we are implementing contribute to the country’s development and improve conditions for both citizens and businesses by bringing us closer to European standards. We want a stronger and more resilient Republic of Moldova that, in turn, contributes to Europe’s security and prosperity. To advance on this path, we need the support of all EU Member States,” Mihai Popșoi said.
“Cyprus has supported the Republic of Moldova’s European aspirations and will continue to advocate for its accession to the European Union. You have made remarkable progress so far, and we encourage you to maintain this momentum. We also want to deepen bilateral cooperation in areas of mutual interest and strengthen institutional ties between the Republic of Moldova and the Republic of Cyprus,” Minister Constantinos Kombos stated.
The officials discussed opportunities to increase bilateral trade and attract investment to the Republic of Moldova. Mihai Popșoi encouraged Cypriot companies to take advantage of the opportunities offered by Moldova and noted that flights between Chișinău and Larnaca provide direct air connectivity between the two countries.
Another topic of the meeting was the protection of citizens’ rights and the facilitation of their mobility. Mihai Popșoi and Constantinos Kombos discussed the possibility of negotiating agreements on social security, the mutual recognition of driving licences, and the recognition of academic qualifications.
To continue the bilateral dialogue, the Moldovan Foreign Minister invited his Cypriot counterpart, Constantinos Kombos, to pay a visit to the Republic of Moldova.

Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner
Kyiv • UNN
Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed from his position as director of J5 without an immediate replacement. The dismissal came amid possible U.S. strikes on Iran.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. A Pentagon representative said this on October 28, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details
This is the latest in a series of generals being dismissed, and it comes even as U.S. President Donald Trump is considering resuming strikes on Iran in the eight-month war.
U.S. Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff. He became the second general dismissed from the position, known in military circles as "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October last year.
A Pentagon representative said there was no immediate replacement for Sylvia and that no reason for his dismissal had been provided.
A representative of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff said: "The Chairman, Joint Staff and Joint Force express their deep gratitude to Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia and his family for 32 years of distinguished service to our country" and "wish him and his family all the best."
Typically, the J5 director and his staff are responsible for developing and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the U.S. president. Sylvia’s dismissal came amid Trump’s repeated statements about launching new military operations against Iran.
Trump vowed to "finish what was started" in Iran after the war with Israel began eight months ago and said new strikes could take place after next week’s midterm elections.
According to two diplomats familiar with the situation, U.S. officials warned a number of Middle Eastern countries and regional allies that they needed to be prepared for the possible resumption of hostilities after Tuesday’s election, as well as possible retaliatory measures by Iran. They said Trump had not yet made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are heading to the region.
War with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion - NYT28.10.26, 09:38 • 6580 views
Last month, Hegseth said he had ordered the reduction in the total number of senior officer positions to be doubled to 20%, to be completed by January 1, 2027. There are currently about 800 admiral and general positions.
Some members of Congress have criticized the reduction in the number of general officers as a "purge" that will take years to recover from.
"He has some deeply rooted resentment toward the leadership in the Army. He is getting rid of an entire generation of great Army leaders, and it will take a whole generation to recover from this," Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a former U.S. Navy combat pilot who has criticized Hegseth, said last month.

Bulgaria Beats Some Neighbors on Youth Incomes but Trails Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:34:00 UTC
17:34:00 KST

Bulgaria ranks among Southeast Europe’s leading countries for household incomes among young people aged 18 to 24, but remains near the bottom of a 34-country European comparison, with its median annual income at just 40% of the European Union average, according to 2025 Eurostat data.
The median equivalized disposable income of households with members aged 18 to 24 in Bulgaria stands at 8,680 euros per year, exceeding figures recorded in Romania, Serbia, Hungary, Albania and North Macedonia.
However, the EU average reaches 21,482 euros annually, almost 2.5 times the Bulgarian level. The comparison covers 34 countries, including EU members, candidate countries and members of the European Free Trade Association.
Bulgaria’s regional advantage varies considerably. Median annual income for households with young people stands at 8,576 euros in Hungary, 7,754 euros in Serbia and 7,237 euros in Romania. The figures fall to 5,987 euros in Turkey, 5,736 euros in Albania and 4,640 euros in North Macedonia.
Bulgaria’s lead amounts to 1,443 euros a year over Romania and 926 euros over Serbia, but only 104 euros over Hungary. Although the country performs better than several neighboring states, its overall income level remains low.
The indicator measures the disposable income of the household in which young people live, rather than their individual earnings. It includes income remaining after taxes and other deductions, as well as social benefits, while adjusting for household size and composition. Therefore, the figure of 8,680 euros does not mean that every young Bulgarian personally has that amount available each year.
The gap widens considerably when Bulgaria is compared with wealthier European economies. Median annual income for households with young people reaches 23,850 euros in France, 26,330 euros in Germany, 20,315 euros in Italy and 19,338 euros in Spain. France’s figure is 15,170 euros higher than Bulgaria’s.
Switzerland leads the comparison at 52,206 euros annually, followed by Luxembourg at 43,028 euros and Austria at 37,299 euros. The Swiss figure is approximately six times the Bulgarian level.
These differences reflect the unequal financial circumstances in which young Europeans begin independent lives. Income affects their ability to save, meet everyday expenses and secure housing, although it is not the only determinant of quality of life.
The European Youth Forum says income should be assessed alongside access to housing, education, health care and public services. In countries where young adults remain in their parents’ homes longer, household-based figures may make their financial circumstances appear more favorable because they benefit from shared household resources.
Across the EU, the median income of households with members aged 18 to 24 is 21,482 euros per year, equivalent to 93.6% of the 22,939-euro median for the overall population. In 28 of the 34 countries surveyed, households with young people have lower incomes than the general population.
For Bulgaria, the main challenge remains the low absolute level of income. Despite outperforming several Southeast European neighbors, the country’s figures do not by themselves ensure the financial security needed for independent living. Moving closer to European standards requires better-paid jobs, opportunities for professional development and affordable housing that allow young people to support themselves through their own earnings.

Türkiye hosts 13th OTS summit to advance Turkic unity and cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:33:53 UTC
17:33:53 KST

Türkiye is hosting the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara to further “unity in language, thought, and deed” among its member states.
The summit kicked off on Thursday with the Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the OTS.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting, according to diplomatic sources.
Foreign ministers of the OTS posed for a family photo ahead of the meeting.
The two-day summit is hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organisation said on October 24 that the summit will bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said in a statement that the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark Türkiye’s assumption of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organisation’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.
The leaders’ summit will be held on Friday.
‘Unity in deed’
Turan Gafarli, a non-resident fellow at the Baku-based Topchubashov Center, defined support among Turkic states and bolstering their political solidarity as the significant aspect of the Ankara summit.
Noting that they are living through a period in which the world faces “increasing uncertainty,” Gafarli told Anadolu that the Turkic world is evolving into a political structure that is “developing the capacity to act in unison in the face of international developments.”
“Naturally, this is a long-term process. Yet, the true meaning of brotherhood is not just coming together during good times, but standing by one another during difficult ones,” he said, noting his belief that the summit in Türkiye will further solidify the “atmosphere of trust built to date.”
Gafarli highlighted the term of unity used in the summit’s theme as “highly significant,” as well as expressed belief that the summit will give momentum to developments particularly in the realms of economic relations, transport corridors, and political coordination.
He stated the growing strategic importance of the Middle Corridor presented a “historic opportunity” for the Turkic states to become more closely interconnected economically, but that this requires a number of steps, including bolstering trade between member states.
“Furthermore, it is essential that the Turkic states engage in closer consultation on international issues and advocate more robustly for their shared interests,” he said, adding he believes Türkiye’s chairmanship could bring fresh dynamism in this context.
Meanwhile, Shairbek Dzhuraev, the president of the Crossroads Central Asia research institute based in Bishkek, shared the belief that tangible progress has been observed most evidently in the economic sphere, underlining transport and transit in particular.
“The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route depends on the harmonisation of tariffs and the simplification of customs procedures. In this context, results can be measured by the time and cost involved in transporting goods,” Dzhuraev said.
Dzhuraev further underlined digitalisation as a second promising area, which he defined as the focus of the organisation’s informal summit held in Turkistan in southern Kazakhstan in May.
“The most substantial outcome of the Ankara summit would be the establishment of concrete timelines and mechanisms for implementing decisions already reached – particularly those concerning transport and trade,” he stated.
As part of the OTS Ankara summit, sports is also an area where unity is expected to be shown “in deed.”
During a news conference in Ankara ahead of the summit, Kursad Zorlu, the ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party's deputy chair in charge of relations with Turkic states, said the event includes plans for players from Turkic states to be classified as domestic rather than foreign in one another’s leagues, saying the initiative would foster a football ecosystem across the Turkic world.

Drones target one of Russia’s largest chemical complexes in Bashkortostan, media report
This was reported by The Moscow Times, according to Ukrinform.
It is noted that the drones targeted the Bashkir Soda Company (BSC) plant. Smoke began to rise above the plant following the attack.
BSC is one of Russia’s largest chemical complexes and ranks first in the country in the production of soda ash and baking soda.
According to the publication, the enterprise is part of the Roskhim holding company, which holds a controlling stake (57.43%). At the same time, the complex is included in the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade’s closed registry of defense enterprises.
BSC supplies military plants with hydrochloric acid and dichloroethane, and is also the only Russian producer of terephthaloyl chloride.
This is a critically important compound for the production of synthetic ballistic fibers, high-strength polymers, and aramid materials, according to the report.
It is used to manufacture body armor, helmets, and armor components for military equipment and aircraft.
Prior to this, drones had already attacked the BSC on August 27. Smoke was also seen rising above the facility at that time. Authorities did not comment on the attack.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Russian city of Lipetsk was attacked by missile strikes; according to preliminary information, a fire broke out in the area of the Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant.

Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 69 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.

The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.

One of largest air raids on Moscow, 1,214 UAVs: attacks on Russian regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:30:48 UTC
17:30:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Overnight, air defense forces shot down 1,214 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
The attempt by the Ukrainian armed forces to attack Moscow with drones, carried out on Wednesday evening and overnight, was one of the largest of the year so far, according to TASS estimates based on figures published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on his Max channel.
Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a factory in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan. Minor damage was reported, and the plant is operating normally.
TASS has compiled the key details regarding the aftermath.
Scale
- Alert air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions last night, according to the Defense Ministry.
- The ministry reported that enemy UAVs were shot down over the Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Smolensk, Lipetsk, Voronezh, Tver, Oryol, Ryazan, Vladimir, Samara, Saratov, Penza, and Rostov Regions, the Moscow Region, the Republic of Bashkortostan, and the Republic of Udmurtia.
- An attempted drone attack on Moscow by the Ukrainian armed forces, carried out on Wednesday evening and overnight, was one of the largest of the year so far, according to TASS estimates based on data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on his Max channel.
- According to the mayor, between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 28 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) on October 29, a total of 613 enemy UAVs were heading toward the Moscow Region.
- Most were neutralized by the Defense Ministry’s air defense forces at a distance, while 231 drones were destroyed on approach to Moscow, he specified.
- Air defense forces destroyed 170 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 42 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region overnight, Governor Dmitry Milyayev wrote on his Max channel.
- A drone attack was thwarted in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan. Eight drones were shot down, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov reported on Telegram.
- Air defense forces destroyed four drones over the Ulyanovsk Region, Governor Alexey Russkikh wrote on his Max channel.
Consequences
- Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a facility in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan, according to a report by Mayor Emil Shaimardanov on Telegram.
- Minor damage was reported.
- The plant is operating normally.
Airport operations
- Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported that temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures - necessary to ensure flight safety - had been imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports.
- These restrictions have now been lifted.
- Two planes flying from Istanbul to Moscow turned back in mid-flight and returned due to safety restrictions at Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.
- In addition, restrictions were imposed at airports in Bugulma, Izhevsk, Kazan, Kaluga, Kirov, Nizhnekamsk, Orenburg, Penza, Perm, Samara, Saransk, Saratov, Ulyanovsk, Ufa, Cheboksary, Chelyabinsk, Cherepovets, and Yaroslavl.

American weightlifter Morris proud of bronze in Chinese debut, eyes bigger prize
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:30:21 CST
17:30:21 KST

NINGBO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- American weightlifter Hampton Morris said he was proud of his bronze medal at the IWF World Championships despite narrowly missing out on gold after failing his final clean-and-jerk attempt.
Morris, 22, lifted 143 kilograms in the snatch and 185kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 328kg, finishing third in the men's 65kg category behind DPR Korea's Pak Myong-jin, who set two world records with a 187kg clean and jerk and a 331kg total, and Türkiye's Muhammed Furkan Ozbek, who took silver with 330kg on Wednesday.
"I'm very, very proud of what I was able to accomplish today. I had some very, very tough competitors," Morris told Xinhua.
There were nevertheless positives for the American, whose 143kg snatch was a personal best, improving on the 142kg he lifted at a domestic competition six weeks earlier.
However, Morris welcomed the challenge posed by his Asian rivals, who had swept the podium at last month's Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.
"Not nervous, but more excited. It's a really incredible opportunity to be able to compete here," he said. "I'm grateful that they're able to push me as much as they have."
The American's respect for his competitors was evident throughout the competition. During his interview with Xinhua, Morris briefly excused himself to greet Chinese lifters Ding Hongjie and He Yueji, shaking hands with both before returning to answer questions.
Competing in China for the first time, Morris has also embraced his experience away from the platform. He shared his amusement at encountering a food-delivery robot at his hotel in Ningbo in a post on Instagram.
"It's amazing. I've really, really enjoyed being here," he said.
Morris is already a familiar figure among Chinese weightlifting fans, having attracted attention for his cheerful demeanor at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where he won bronze in the men's 61kg category.
His clean-and-jerk lift of 172kg set an Olympic record and helped him become the first American man to win an Olympic weightlifting medal since 1984.
The lifter from Marietta, Georgia, had previously won clean-and-jerk gold at the 2023 world championships in Riyadh, becoming the first American man to claim a world weightlifting title since 1984.
With a 190kg clean and jerk already achieved in training, Morris believes he has the strength to challenge for further records and titles, with the Los Angeles Games his next major target. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia has called for stronger international cooperation to ensure stable global gas markets and reliable energy supplies, emphasizing that energy security is fundamental to industrial competitiveness, investment confidence and sustainable economic growth, the Ministry of Economy said on Thursday.

Spain mourns 68 killed in second deadly high-speed train crash this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:27:33 UTC
17:27:33 KST

Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 68 people and injured over 100, as relatives sought news of missing loved ones.
The crash occurred on Wednesday morning in Castilla-La Mancha when a state-run Renfe train struck the back of a stationary train operated by private company Iryo.
Emergency crews searched the wreckage overnight near the village of Urda, using cranes to lift mangled metal. Police drones resumed flights over the site at daybreak.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said an automatic control system had failed along 69 kilometres of track, stopping trains. The control centre later resumed traffic in what he called “inexplicable circumstances”, despite having time to identify and correct the error.
The disaster has raised fresh safety concerns after a January collision in Andalusia killed 46 people when a derailed train crossed onto an adjacent track. That investigation remains ongoing.
Relatives seek answers
A school in Urda, about 130 kilometres south of Madrid, was opened to relatives seeking information about loved ones.
Red Cross workers and psychologists provided support to families, while the Civil Guard established offices in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to collect DNA samples and help identify victims.
Survivors described the force of the collision and the chaos inside the trains.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian holidaying in Spain, said he had been asleep when he woke up “in the air”.
Pablo Mejia, 42, said a last-minute seat change had saved his life. He described a powerful impact, passengers piled on top of one another and seats ripped out.
“I think I've been born again,” he told AFP.
Flags flew at half-mast as official ceremonies and public events were cancelled or scaled back.

Türkiye marks 103rd Republic Day with ceremonies, nationwide celebrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:26:37 UTC
17:26:37 KST

Türkiye is marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of its Republic with ceremonies in the capital and festivities across the country.
Celebrations in Ankara were set to begin with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and senior state officials visiting Anitkabir, the mausoleum of founder Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. Erdogan will lay a wreath, observe a moment of silence and sign the memorial book, then receive congratulations at the Presidential Complex.
In a video message, Erdogan said Türkiye is stronger today than yesterday and will be more powerful, prestigious and effective in every field tomorrow. He pointed to progress over the past 24 years in defence, energy, transport and diplomacy.
The Republic was declared on October 29 1923, with all 158 lawmakers present in Parliament voting in favour. Ataturk was subsequently elected the country’s first president with all 158 votes.
On Thursday, Türkiye’s senior officials also marked the anniversary.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said the government is working towards the 2053 and 2071 visions under Erdogan’s leadership, aiming to carry its gains further, while Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli said his party was determined to carry the Republic’s legacy into the “Century of Türkiye”.
National Intelligence Organization (MIT) chief Ibrahim Kalin said the Republic embodied Türkiye’s independence, unity and shared future, adding that MIT would continue working to protect national security and sovereignty.
Turkic leaders in Ankara
This year’s anniversary coincides with the 13th Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit, which brings the leaders of the five member states to Ankara on October 29-30.
Erdogan will open the Bestepe National Garden with an equestrian show, then host an official dinner for visiting leaders.
Guests will be welcomed by the Mehter band and by soldiers and flags representing 16 historic Turkic states. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov will receive a state medal, and the president will present this year’s Ali Sir Nevai International Award.
The programme will also feature a concert by Türkiye’s Presidential Symphony Orchestra, a traditional dance performance organised by TURKSOY, an international organisation promoting Turkic culture, and live music by Turkish singer Kirac and Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.
Celebrations across the country
Republic Day events are taking place across Türkiye.
The “Türkiye Pedals” initiative will bring together cyclists across all 81 provinces from October 29 to November 1, ahead of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on November 9-20. Open to licensed athletes, cycling clubs, students, families and cycling enthusiasts, the events aim to promote cycling as a sustainable transport option and raise public awareness of the climate change.
The historic Istiklal Road is being crossed on horseback to mark the Republic’s 103rd year. Organised for the third time by the Equestrian and Culture Association, the ride follows the 95-kilometre route along which weapons and ammunition arriving at Inebolu Port were sent on to Anatolia during the War of Independence. Forty-five riders from across Türkiye are taking part in the two-day journey.
The Osmangazi-Türkiye Century Run on the Osmangazi Bridge is expected to draw around 6,000 participants, with nearly 8,000 applications received and athletes from 19 countries signed up. The event, held for the first time on October 29, features a 10-kilometre race for elite runners and a 5-kilometre public run. Kocaeli Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Tahir Buyukakin said organisers aim to make it a traditional annual event, bringing together people of different generations to mark the Republic Day.
In Corum, residents marked the day with a march carrying a 103-metre Turkish flag.
In Diyarbakir, students unfurled a 54-square-metre Turkish flag at the historic Ickale in the Sur district, in the shadow of the city’s thousands-of-years-old walls and stone structures. The event was led by the provincial education directorate, and the choreography was filmed from the air by drone.

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Public transport apps enterprising developers have come up with are growing in popularity and offer an alternative to Tallinn's official public transport website.
Unlike many European capitals, Tallinn still has no official public transport mobile app, while critics say the official site at transport.tallinn.ee is getting outdated and is not very user-friendly.
"The people who should know how best to do these things haven't done anything. This is the kind of thing that was being done in 2010, and in 2026 we really shouldn't still be dealing with something like this," said Kaspar Sanglepp, creator of the Go Now app, one of the competing products.
"To quickly see bus times, you have to go to different websites and click through a lot of things. I wanted to be able to get that information with one click," Sanglepp said.
"The visual design is 10–15 or more years old. It takes so much time just to get to the route planner," said Sander Pukk, creator of another app, called Mis? Kuhu? ("What? Where to?").
All public transport vehicles in Tallinn and Tartu send their location to the system every 10 seconds. Using this publicly available data, developers have created three different free apps. Despite not being advertised, between them they have amassed over 2,000 daily users.
The newest app on the scene, Tallinn Live, garnered 4,000 views in four days.
"Tallinn Live project, it's very simple: you just are going to the app, you are just using it. That's why it's basic, and that's why people love it," Taha Yasin Erel, creator of Tallinn Live, told "Aktuaalne kaamera".
"I got lots of, hundreds of comments, hundreds of new ideas, and I started with these ideas, and people started to like it more," Erel went on.
Most public transport stops in Tallinn are still old school in that they lack display boards and have only printed timetables. At peak times and with all the ongoing roadworks in Tallinn, there is often a difference between when a bus, trolleybus or tram is scheduled and when it actually arrives, something which apps can help with.
"Real-time information has definitely been the main thing. Many stops still don't have those display boards, so being able to see whether a bus is running late or not has been the subject of the most positive feedback," Pukk went on.
According to Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, however, surveys show that people are satisfied with Tallinn Transport's website. The city nevertheless plans to update it.
"The Transport Department (TLT) is currently carrying out the relevant analyses, and we certainly plan to update it in the coming years to make it more user-friendly, with an app or a mobile view," Jesse said.

Norwegian PM denies claims about conversation with Putin
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre has denied a report by the Financial Times claiming that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin spent almost their entire conversation giving historical explanations for the war. According to Støre, the participants spoke for roughly equal amounts of time.
Source: European Pravda, citing Støre's comments in an interview with Norwegian media outlet TV 2
Details: Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb held a phone call with Putin on Tuesday 27 October. The purpose of this call, according to them, was to explore de-escalation opportunities and establish a European channel for dialogue.
However, the Financial Times published an article stating that during the conversation, the Kremlin leader spent almost the entire time explaining the "initial reasons for the conflict" with Ukraine.
Støre flatly denies these claims.
Quote from Støre: "That is not true. And we asked the Financial Times to correct this information, as it does not correspond to reality."
Details: Støre added that Putin asked to set out his version of the current situation and, in that context, reviewed history from 2014 to the present day.
Quote from Støre: "So the claim that he gave a lecture on Slavic history is simply not true."
Details: Støre also rejected claims that Putin dominated the conversation.
Quote from Støre: "We had an hour and a half. Of course, there was an interpreter, so part of the time went to translation. Therefore, I believe the time was distributed fairly evenly. We probably spent about the same amount of time. But that was also because we set out our positions, on which we requested feedback."
Details: Norwegian newspaper VG, which contacted the Financial Times, reports that it refused to make any changes.
"We stand by our journalism," a spokesperson said.
It is noted that the FT does not wish to comment further on the matter, nor will it clarify the sources of its information.
Background:
- On 28 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that, following a conversation between European leaders and Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, there are indications that Russia is serious about a meeting of the negotiating teams in Abu Dhabi. The Ukrainian president added that the planned trilateral meeting of technical teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US in early November depends on the American side.
- The European Commission's chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, stated that the European Commission had been informed in advance about this phone call.

Ukraine’s military launches one of largest overnight attacks on Russia over year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:21:31 UTC
17:21:31 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Ukraine’s military launched one of its largest overnight drone attacks on Russia over the year when Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 1,214 enemy unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), as follows from TASS calculations based on the data of Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Overnight into October 29, air defenses destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing UAVs over 19 constituent entities of Russia, including the Moscow Region, according to the ministry.
The previous massive attack on Russia was registered overnight into October 18 when air defenses shot down 1,015 Ukrainian UAVs over Russian regions and the Black Sea.
The largest Ukrainian drone attack on Russia was recorded on September 20, the last day of vote at the elections to the State Duma (the lower house of Russia’s parliament) when air defenses intercepted and destroyed 1,951 enemy UAVs and eight missiles.

Former Biden officials who quit over Gaza urge 2028 Democrats to reject his Israel policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:42 UTC
17:20:42 KST

A group of former U.S. officials who resigned over the Biden administration's support for Israel's war on Gaza urged Democratic presidential hopefuls Wednesday to condemn Washington's role in the conflict and exclude officials responsible for the policy from future administrations.
Twelve former officials who stepped down between late 2023 and mid-2024 over former President Joe Biden's handling of the Gaza war issued a joint statement calling on candidates seeking the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 to distance themselves from his administration's policies.
"We call on candidates for the 2028 Presidential Nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel's military actions in Gaza," the group said.
The former officials also demanded that prospective candidates acknowledge what they described as Washington's complicity in Israel's "genocide" in Gaza.
A video accompanying the statement featured images of senior Biden administration figures, including former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, highlighting officials associated with U.S. policy toward Israel during the conflict.
The appeal comes as divisions over U.S. support for Israel continue to shape debate within the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Biden's administration faced sustained criticism from progressive lawmakers, activists and human rights advocates over its continued military assistance and diplomatic backing for Israel despite mounting Palestinian civilian casualties and widespread destruction in Gaza.
Prominent progressive Democrats, including U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have opposed Washington's support for Israeli military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, as well as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Their criticism has also focused on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close political ties with Republicans, amid growing divisions within the Democratic Party over relations with Israel.
Several international human rights organizations, legal experts and United Nations investigations have concluded that Israel's military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide.
Blinken and Sullivan previously voiced concerns over civilian deaths in Gaza, although the Biden administration continued providing military and diplomatic support to Israel throughout the conflict.
The former officials' intervention adds to pressure on prospective Democratic presidential candidates to clarify their positions on U.S. military assistance to Israel and the role of senior Biden-era policymakers in any future administration.

Lithuanian Farmers and Greens tie budget support to family referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

The Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union has warned that its support for next year’s government spending bill could be affected unless parliament takes up a stalled proposal for an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family before approving the budget.
Aurelijus Veryga, leader of the Farmers and Greens Union (LVŽS), said Wednesday that he had raised the issue during budget negotiations with coalition partners, demanding that the referendum proposal be put on the parliament’s agenda before the budget is adopted.
The initiative is an attempt to entrench a conservative definition of family and prevent same-sex couples from claiming equal treatment.
“One of the issues important to us is that, before the budget is adopted, the question of an advisory referendum on the family issue should be brought before parliament,” Veryga told reporters after a meeting of the coalition council.
“This is one of the key issues for us. It will also be a kind of signal about how we should act,” he added.
Veryga said the issue would show whether the Farmers and Greens were being treated as a genuine coalition partner.
“We are not asking our coalition partners to vote in favour of the referendum in any particular way. We know there are differences of opinion,” he said.
However, he argued that deliberately blocking the proposal amounted to a demonstration of political will. He called for an end to what he described as “artificial obstruction” by the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs, saying coalition partners had promised to find a solution at their previous meeting.
Veryga warned that if the referendum proposal is not placed on the parliament’s agenda, it could have a significant impact on how his party’s lawmakers vote on the budget.
“I really cannot say how my colleagues will act then. Since this is a very important issue for us, it will be assessed in the broader context,” he said.
In late September, the parliament’s Committee on State Administration and Local Authorities backed holding an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family alongside next year’s municipal elections.
The draft resolution was approved at its initial presentation in parliament in early April.
Under the proposal, voters would be asked whether they support explicitly stating in the Constitution that legal family relationships arise only from the marriage of a man and a woman, motherhood and fatherhood. Voters would choose between “Yes” and “No”.
Article 38 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that family is the foundation of society and the state and that the state protects and cares for the family, motherhood, fatherhood and childhood. It also states that marriage is concluded by the free consent of a man and a woman.
In a ruling issued in 2011, Lithuania’s Constitutional Court states that non-married couples can also constitute a family.

Russian Doctors Report Widespread Healthcare Cuts as Patients Pay for Basic Supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:13:12 UTC
17:13:12 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Doctors Report Widespread Healthcare Cuts as Patients Pay for Basic Supplies
More than three-quarters of Russian doctors reported cuts to healthcare spending in their regions, with shortages affecting salaries, medicines, supplies, and hospital budgets across the country, The Moscow Times reported on October 28.
The findings were based on a survey by Medvestnik involving medical workers from 74 Russian cities. Among respondents, 75.6% reported declining healthcare spending in their region, while 67.4% stated that cuts were affecting virtually everything, including consumables, wages, and medicines.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Nearly half of respondents, 46%, reported that patients receiving treatment at their institutions had been forced to buy medicines, dressings, or other medical supplies themselves during 2026.
Some doctors noted that patients were formally prohibited from purchasing medicines independently, while state-funded departments still lacked enough money to cover basic needs, The Moscow Times wrote.
The cuts come as Russian regional governments struggle with budget deficits and spending linked to recruiting contract soldiers for the war against Ukraine.
According to Russia’s Accounts Chamber , regional governments allocated 5.8% less to healthcare in the first half of 2026 than during the same period a year earlier.
Healthcare spending was reduced in 42 Russian regions, with cuts exceeding 20% in 11 of them. The sharpest reductions were recorded in the Altai Republic, where spending fell 40.6%, and the Kirov region, where it declined 39%.
The Kemerovo region cut healthcare spending by 33.2%, followed by Orenburg at 32.1%, Tver at 29%, Moscow region at 28.5%, Vologda at 27.2%, and Novosibirsk at 23.4%, according to The Moscow Times.
One of the largest reductions affected Russia’s primary healthcare modernization program, which had been intended to repair aging clinics. Funding for the program fell to less than half of the previous year’s level, while actual spending during the first six months dropped more than fivefold year on year.
The Moscow Times reported that the pressure on regional budgets has already prompted calls for further hospital consolidation. On October 16, Anatoly Artamonov, chair of the Federation Council’s Budget and Financial Markets Committee, stated that regions should consider closing underused hospitals and redirecting patients to larger medical facilities.
“Budget funds are insufficient, and we need to treat these resources carefully,” Artamonov explained.
The pressure on Russia’s regional budgets is also spreading beyond healthcare. UNITED24 Media previously reported that a district in Russia’s Irkutsk region planned to cut 37% of its administrative staff by the end of 2026 as its budget gap widened, with school guards, kindergarten staff, and municipal workers among the positions affected.

17:13:02 KST

A new exhibition opens at the BRUSK arts centre in Bruges on Friday. ‘Hoogtij’ (Figuratively heyday, literally high tide) is an exhibition exploring the impact of the sea and water on people, fashion and art. On display are swimwear by leading designers including Dries Van Noten and fashion houses including Versace and Chanel, as well as sculptures, video art and installations addressing social issues such as climate change and migration.
The sea gives and takes. It is with this idea in mind that the new exhibition ‘Hoogtij’ at the BRUSK art centre aims to challenge visitors. “Bruges’ location on the North Sea has had a major impact on the city’s history. It enabled the city to flourish. Seas and oceans have also had a significant influence on artists and fashion designers, right up to the present day,” explains guest curator Karen Van Godtsenhoven.
The exhibition brings together the work of fashion designers such as Dries Van Noten and contemporary artists such as Rinus Van de Velde. And it does so across a wide range of art forms: from video to photography, sculpture and installations.
On swimsuits...
The exhibition is divided into various themes inspired by the tides of the sea. “The first section, ‘Low Tide’, represents the joy and fertile power of water as the source of human life,” explains Van Godtsenhoven. Swimsuits by designers including Versace, Chanel and Dries Van Noten, alongside Martin Parr’s beach photography, take centre stage here.
To barbed wire
In the final section of the exhibition, ‘High Tide’, current issues such as climate change and migration are addressed. According to Van Godtsenhoven, this section aims to encourage visitors to reflect on, for example, the dual role of the beach. “For some, it is a place of leisure; for others, a place of crossing, offering hope for a different and better life,” says Van Godtsenhoven.
The Palestinian artist Abdul Rahman Katanani, for example, created a wave out of barbed wire, symbolising how he experiences the sea as a life-threatening border.

Bulgarian Firms Fined €310,000 Over Fake German Butter

Bulgarian Firms Fined €310,000 Over Fake German Butter
The Administrative Court of Sofia Region has upheld first-instance sanctions totaling €310,000 against Klas Food and Alpha SD for misleading consumers by selling a product labeled “Deutsche Markenbutter” as cow's milk butter despite containing more than 95% palm fat, soybean oil, sunflower oil and lard.
The court found that the Commission for Protection of Competition (CPC) had acted lawfully and that the financial penalties were proportionate to the seriousness and duration of the violations.
The product was marketed in 250-gram packages throughout 2024 and into early 2025. The case was uncovered earlier this year by the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency (BFSA) and the CPC following a report from the official Bulgarian importer of German butter produced according to the “Deutsche Markenbutter” standard.
The antitrust authority's investigation established that Klas Food and Alpha SD had used misleading labels and packaging to market the product as genuine cow's milk butter meeting the German standard. The product was manufactured by a Bulgarian company specializing in dairy imitations.
The CPC also reported progress in proceedings against Kaufland Bulgaria and Maxima Bulgaria, the owner of the T-Market chain, over suspected unfair commercial practices targeting producers and suppliers. The commission is expected to issue decisions in the two cases within approximately 10 days.
The proceedings against the two major retail chains began at the end of May 2026. During the following five months, the CPC collected a substantial body of evidence.
Under the law, companies can face financial penalties of up to 10% of their total turnover in the preceding financial year for each established violation, the commission noted. Given the revenues of the large retail chains, even a less serious infringement could result in a fine worth tens of millions of euros, while a serious violation could lead to a penalty exceeding €100 million.
The CPC said its sectoral analysis, interim findings from which were presented in December 2025, had highlighted the substantial discounts manufacturers and suppliers offered to large retailers. In some cases, these arrangements could result in products being sold at or below cost.
The findings prompted the commission to step up its scrutiny of pricing policies, discounts, markups and contractual relationships across the sector. At the time, the CPC called on market participants to regulate their own practices, warning that it would launch proceedings under the Law on Protection of Competition if convincing evidence did not show that the identified problems had been resolved.
The antitrust authority is also carrying out a preliminary investigation into possible unfair commercial practices by retail chains following reports from the Commission for Consumer Protection about substantial differences in markups on comparable products supplied by different producers.

Child care sector faces further changes after shocking abuse exposed by Four Corners
In short:
A meeting of education ministers on Monday will consider the creation of a national childcare commission to improve planning and oversight of the sector.
Ministers will also discuss CCTV in child care following a trial involving 300 centres.
Four Corners this week aired shocking CCTV footage of a childcare worker physically assaulting a baby boy at a centre in Far North Queensland.
A proposed national childcare commission will be discussed at a meeting of education ministers next week, as the government faces renewed calls for changes following a Four Corners investigation into Australia's child care system.
Early Childhood Education Minister Jess Walsh told Senate estimates the commission could provide greater national oversight and strategic planning for the $20 billion sector, amid an oversupply of centres in some areas and shortages in others.
"We think a commission could assist with better strategic planning," she said.
Senator Walsh was also grilled about gaps in supervision rules, including why workers who have not completed their qualifications could be left alone with babies.
The questions follow Four Corners exposing shocking CCTV footage of a 13-month-old boy being smothered, kicked, hit and shaken 55 times by a trainee childcare worker, Edwina Ling, inside a Far North Queensland centre.
"Can you explain how a worker studying towards a qualification can be left alone with babies?" Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May asked.
Senator Walsh said state ministers had ordered a review of how the "working towards" rules applied and in what circumstances. She said an update would be provided next week.
"We have asked for a review into how working towards qualifications applies and in the circumstances where it may apply. That review is underway. We will be updated on it at the next education ministers meeting, and it's an important part of the work," Senator Walsh said.
"That service [Injinoo] has responsibilities to ensure that child was adequately supervised and that child was clearly not adequately supervised."
Senator Walsh said there was also broader work underway on adequate supervision in early childhood services.
She told the committee CCTV would be discussed at next week's meeting of education ministers following a trial involving 300 services.
CCTV proved critical in the Injinoo case. Ling originally denied hurting the children and told parents it was another child responsible for the cuts and bruises, but when she was told the footage showed it was her, she pleaded guilty to 82 assaults.
Senator Hodgins-May pressed Senator Walsh on the government's new funding enforcement powers, asking why Little Zak's Academy and Only About Children remain absent from the Commonwealth's enforcement list despite significant compliance histories.
"What does a large provider actually have to do before the Commonwealth intervenes?" she said, pointing to 25 staff ratio breaches last year.
Analysis of the country's 26 largest long-daycare providers found that half of Little Zak's centres had enforcement action in the past two years, the highest proportion of the 26 largest providers analysed.
For Only About Children, another big for-profit provider, the figure was 27 per cent, or one in four.
Liberal senator and Shadow Childcare Minister Matt O'Sullivan said there had been a "massive distrust and breakdown" in confidence in the child care sector and governments needed to do everything possible to rebuild that trust.
Ling was jailed in June for four years with a one-year non-parole period.
Queensland District Court Judge Dean Morzone KC described her offending as "monstrous, cruel and sadistic" and "a gross breach of trust".
The Injinoo Child Care Centre was closed after losing funding.

128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:10:47 UTC
17:10:47 KST

128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Ohio State University
- Summary:
- Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.
- Share:
Deep within an ice cap in northwestern Tibet, scientists have uncovered evidence of a remarkable frozen record that may stretch back more than 128,000 years. The discovery suggests that ice high in the mountains has survived since the last ice age and could provide an extraordinary window into Earth's ancient climate.
The findings extend the known glacial record from the region by more than 100,000 years, making these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet. They also offer rare evidence of how mountain glaciers endured major changes in Earth's climate.
Researchers reached their conclusions by examining ice cores collected from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015. Despite being drilled 23 years apart, the samples revealed strikingly similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, which scientists use to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The close match indicates that the ice has preserved a reliable and reproducible record of climate history.
"Reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important," said Lonnie Thompson, lead author of the study, professor of earth sciences and senior research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center at The Ohio State University. "If you get an identical record a quarter of a century later, it can tell you a lot about the behavior of the ice over time."
How Scientists Dated the Ancient Tibetan Ice
Determining the age of ice that has remained frozen for tens of thousands of years is no simple task. To establish a more accurate timeline, the international research team turned to advanced dating methods involving radioactive isotopes of beryllium and chlorine.
These naturally occurring radioactive forms of elements decay at predictable rates, making them valuable tools for identifying events deep in Earth's environmental history. In this case, researchers used them to detect evidence of the Leschamp Geomagnetic Excursion, a dramatic disturbance in Earth's magnetic field that occurred more than 41,000 years ago and left distinctive chemical signatures in the ice.
The team then compared its findings with oxygen isotope records preserved in nearby Tibetan cave deposits. Together, the evidence suggests that the Guliya ice record may extend well beyond 128,000 years into the past.
"It's a really critical finding, because outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that go back that far," he said. "Records out of Huascarán only go back over 30,000 years, not over 100,000, so that makes Guliya a very unique record."
The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.
A Frozen Climate Record From the Last Ice Age
Ice cores are among scientists' most valuable sources of information about ancient climates. As snow accumulates and gradually becomes compressed into ice, it can preserve chemical clues about the atmosphere and environmental conditions at the time. By examining different layers, researchers can piece together how climate changed over thousands of years.
However, interpreting these records depends on knowing when each layer formed. Without a reliable timeline, even an exceptionally well-preserved ice core can be difficult to understand.
That uncertainty had complicated earlier interpretations of the Guliya ice cap. Previous research suggested that its record reached back only to the middle of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began nearly 12,000 years ago following the last ice age.
The new evidence establishes that at least some of the ice is considerably older than the Holocene. This also has important implications for understanding whether large ice masses in Tibet persisted as the planet emerged from the last glacial period.
"If we only had Holocene-era ice in Tibet, that would mean that the big ice sheets from the last ice age didn't persist through the early Holocene," said Thompson. "But evidence shows that it did."
What the Discovery Reveals About Earth's Glacial History
The Guliya ice cap's unusual geography may help explain why it has preserved such an exceptionally old climate record. Its high elevation and surrounding terrain likely contributed to conditions that allowed ancient ice to remain in place through major environmental changes.
Beyond establishing the ice's age, researchers hope that a more precise timeline will help answer fundamental questions about the history of Earth's glaciers. Knowing when major periods of glaciation began, how long they lasted, and when the ice retreated is essential for reconstructing the planet's natural climate cycles.
"When did ice start forming on the planet and what did those natural processes of loss look like?" said Thompson. "We need to know those things, and the only way you can really demonstrate it is with accurate time scales on these records."
The revised timeline also creates new opportunities to investigate the Guliya ice cores in greater detail. Researchers plan to study additional samples to determine how other indicators of past climate and environmental conditions fit into this much longer history.
Those future analyses could reveal information that was previously overlooked or interpreted differently because scientists did not fully understand the age of the ice.
For Thompson, one of the most encouraging aspects of the discovery is how consistently the different measurements support the same interpretation.
"The big picture is that our results tell a very consistent story," he said. "If you get the science right, it's consistent. It's our understanding of what it's trying to tell us that has to catch up."
The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Ohio State co-authors include Mary Davis and Ellen Mosley-Thompson. Other contributors were Juerg Beer of the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology; Christof Vockenhuber and Marcus Christl of ETH Zurich in Switzerland; Tandong Yao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; and Ninglian Wang and Ling Fang of Northwest University in China.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ohio State University. Original written by Tatyana Woodall. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lonnie G. Thompson, Mary E. Davis, Ellen Mosley-Thompson, Juerg Beer, Tandong Yao, Christof Vockenhuber, Ninglian Wang, Ling Fang, Marcus Christl. Additional evidence supports a timescale exceeding 100,000 years for the Guliya ice cap, Tibetan Plateau. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (40) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2912

AENARA UNVEILS 1:1 MARS HABITAT AT POWERHOUSE PARRAMATTA
Commissioned for Task Eternal at the newly opened Powerhouse Parramatta, Off-World Habitat Wall Section is a full-scale architectural installation designed by space architecture studio AENARA, founded by Melodie Yashar. Opening November 7th, 2026, the exhibition presents a physical cross-section of a conceptual Mars habitat envisioned for the year 2075. Developed from a year-long feasibility study conducted alongside NASA collaborators, university researchers, and industry partners, the installation exposes the structural strata, mechanical utilities, and autonomous manufacturing techniques required to sustain human life in extreme off-world environments.
in situ resource utilization on Mars | image ©AENARA
3D PRINTED SULFUR CONCRETE SHELLS INTEGRATE LIFE-SUPPORT SYSTEMS
Engineered by studio AENARA, the structural assembly demonstrates the coordination between protective outer envelopes and interior life-support infrastructure. The wall cutaway details an autonomous construction sequence utilizing in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), featuring robotic 3D printed outer shells formed from sulfur concrete and local regolith, backing an inflatable pressure membrane, radiation shielding, and high-performance thermal insulation. Integrated conduits route systems for water filtration, atmospheric recycling, data transfer, and power delivery. Balancing critical life-support engineering with crew psychology, the interior module incorporates daylighting strategies and expanded window viewports, translating extreme-environment aerospace research into scalable construction methodologies applicable to both off-world sites and terrestrial circular construction.

A vitamin clue to stroke in the young? Bengaluru study finds low B6 levels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:01:40 UTC
17:01:40 KST

Vitamin B6 is found in liver, fish such as tuna and salmon, chicken, chickpeas, sunflower seeds, pistachios, potatoes, bananas and spinach.
NEW DELHI: A vitamin that helps the body process proteins and regulate important chemical reactions may offer a new clue to why young adults suffer strokes. A study by researchers in Bengaluru has found significantly lower levels of vitamin B6 in young adults who had an ischaemic stroke than in healthy people of a similar age.Ahead of World Stroke Day on October 29, the findings draw attention to a possible factor associated with stroke in young adults. The study compared 171 young adults who had suffered an ischaemic stroke, caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, with 249 healthy controls.Median vitamin B6 levels in stroke patients were 40.9 nmol/L, compared with 65.6 nmol/L in the control group. Vitamin B6 insufficiency, defined by the researchers as levels below 30 nmol/L, was found in 12.3% of stroke patients, compared with just 0.7% of healthy controls.
Vitamin B6 is found in liver, fish such as tuna and salmon, chicken, chickpeas, sunflower seeds, pistachios, potatoes, bananas and spinach.Prof Manjari Tripathi, head of the department of neurology at AIIMS, said vitamin B6 is essential for homocysteine metabolism. “Low vitamin B6 levels can impair this process, allowing homocysteine to rise. Elevated homocysteine can damage blood vessels, promote inflammation and contribute to clot formation, increasing stroke risk.
Maintaining adequate vitamin B6 levels through a balanced diet is important,” she said.The Bengaluru study adds to evidence linking vitamin B6 levels with stroke risk, but whether improving these levels can prevent strokes remains unclear. Dr Pravin Gupta, chairman, Marengo Asia international institute of neuro and spine, said the study was significant because vitamin B6 levels can be measured through a blood test. “However, this study shows an association, not proof that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke. Further research is needed,” he said.The researchers, led by scientists from the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, found that lower vitamin B6 levels were independently associated with higher odds of ischaemic stroke even after accounting for other factors. Among stroke patients, vitamin B6 levels were strongly inversely correlated with homocysteine, an amino acid associated with blood vessel health.
Published in Clinica Chimica Acta in 2026, the case-control study adds to research into factors associated with stroke among younger adults. However, it cannot establish whether low vitamin B6 contributes to stroke, results from other health or dietary factors, or reflects an underlying process. Further studies are needed to validate the findings.The results do not establish that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke or that routine testing for the vitamin should be recommended for young adults.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. China controls key materials for Dutch chips, defence and energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:00:24 UTC
17:00:24 KST

China controls key materials for Dutch chips, defence and energy
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands is heavily dependent on China for seven of the eight raw materials most critical to its economy, according to new research by national statistics office CBS.
The CBS ranked more than 30 materials on the EU’s official list of critical raw materials by three measures: their economic importance to the Netherlands, the risk of supply disruption and the expected growth in demand.
Gallium was top, followed by rare earth metals, germanium, graphite, lithium, cobalt, niobium and silicon metal.
All of those except niobium are mainly processed in China before they’re sent to the Netherlands, either as materials or part of finished products. China handles at least 74% of global processing for each of the seven. The figure is 99% for gallium, 94% for graphite and 84% for rare earths. For niobium, the Netherlands depends mainly on Brazil.
The materials are vital to the semiconductor industry, defence and the energy transition, the CBS said. Demand is growing because of AI, electric cars, faster networks and new defence systems.
Gallium ranks highest because China controls almost all of the world’s production and uses strict export restrictions as political leverage, the CBS said. The metal is also the basis for microchips and other high-tech products made by large companies.
In 2025, the Netherlands imported €17.2 billion worth of critical raw materials from outside the EU, plus €123.9 billion worth of products that contain them – almost a third of the value of all imports from outside the EU.

How IRL Story Lab is Reimagining What Journalism Can Do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:57:00 UTC
16:57:00 KST

The team at the Investigative Reporting Lab (IRL) in North Macedonia carried a frustration familiar to many newsrooms: They would spend months, sometimes a year, unraveling a complex system of corruption and then ask readers to sit through thousands of words to understand it. The information mattered, but the format didn't always do it justice. So they decided to try a new approach.
“We started experimenting with documentary, video, and social storytelling, and we saw very clearly that when you change the way you tell a story, you also change who is willing to engage with it,” says IRL editor in chief Saska Cvetkovska.
That experimentation has now taken IRL somewhere few investigative newsrooms have gone: narrative fiction. Through IRL Story Lab, a production company built inside the newsroom, the team is adapting reporting into film — starting with “The Bench,” a dark comedy inspired by characters in “Spooks and Spin,” a 2017 investigation by IRL and OCCRP into information warfare in the Balkans.
“Fiction can show you what these damaging systems do to people. It can enter a family, a friendship, a marriage, and show how corruption or institutional failure changes the way people live with each other,” says Cvetkovska.
The Power of Fiction
“The Bench” didn't begin as a plan to adapt an investigation. It began with a conversation with her staff, when Cvetkovska described a family she'd reported on years earlier: two brothers, once inseparable, who stopped speaking after ending up on opposite sides of a political divide.
The team brought on Director Trifun Sitnikovski and Chief of Production Gorjan Atanasov — both already with IRL before joining the Story Lab — who immediately saw a film in the story.
“We didn't need the film to reproduce every fact from the investigation. OCCRP and IRL had already done that journalism. The film had a different job,” Cvetkovska explains.
What the team captured was a family divided by media polarization, forced together by a family event, where the tension finally breaks open. The dialogue and humor were written for the screen — compressed, exaggerated, sharpened into dark comedy.
