Failed i-Police project cost the taxpayer over 139 million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

I-Police, the police force’s failed digitalisation project, cost 139.4 million euros of taxpayers’ money. That is almost double the 76 million euros previously reported, according to a report by the Court of Auditors. The report states that millions have been spent on unusable software licences and that the government is structurally dependent on external consultants.
Failed i-Police project cost the taxpayer over 139 million euros
I-Police was launched at the end of 2021 to digitise police operations. As there were still no ‘tangible’ results by 2025, Interior Minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR) pulled the plug on the project.
In the Chamber Home Affairs Committee earlier this year, Quintin had to admit that 75.8 million euros of taxpayers’ money had by then been spent on the failed project. At the time the MPs who fired off questions already suspected that the actual figure would be considerably higher.
At Parliament’s request, the Court of Auditors conducted a thorough review of the entire i-Police project. That report, published Wednesday morning, reveals that 139.4 million euros was spent on i-Police. That is almost double the amount initially reported.
Millions spent on unusable licences
The Court of Auditors, which audits the government’s finances, highlights, amongst other things, the purchase of 30 million euros worth of software licences, the vast majority of which are now unusable.
“Licences worth 21.6 million euros (70 per cent) are now of no use whatsoever to the police: licences worth 7.3 million euros were never used. Licences worth 14.2 million euros were used during the development phase, but the licences have become unusable due to the project being scrapped,” the report states.
“The analyses carried out by the police in 2024 and 2025 highlighted a significant financial risk regarding the licences,” the report continues. “After all, the costs are not limited to the initial purchase, as the costs for maintenance, support and renewal span several years.”
“These costs can become problematic if the solutions in question are not rolled out, are only partially utilised, or if the future of the project to which they belong is uncertain.”
'Quick wins'
The report also highlights the existence of two so-called ‘quick wins’ – milestones that were to be completed as pilot projects within 12 to 18 months of the project’s start. If these ‘quick wins’ were not achieved, the police could have halted the programme.
The Court of Auditors points out that no clear milestones were defined and that the police had already commissioned follow-up projects worth tens of millions of euros, even before the pilot projects had been completed and evaluated.
Structurally dependent on consultants
A third major issue concerns the use of consultants. According to the Court of Auditors, the police – and therefore the government – are structurally dependent on external consultants for critical IT functions.
The report states that “the police’s recruitment conditions were not suitable for recruiting specialised and highly qualified candidates”. “Recruitment was made even more difficult by the shortage of IT professionals in the labour market and their high-salary expectations.”
Judicial investigation
The Court of Auditors emphasises that it has merely scrutinised the case file, without making any judgements as to who is responsible for the debacle.
A judicial investigation is currently underway into the possible misappropriation of public funds and conflicts of interest in the case.
In connection with that investigation, it emerged earlier this week that the spokesperson for Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden (Flemish Christian democrat CD&V) and a spokesperson for the Brussels Public Prosecutor’s Office had been identified as suspects and are being investigated for possibly breaching professional confidentiality.
What is i-Police?
Digitising police processes, bringing together various data systems into a single information platform and thereby enabling the faster detection of risks and criminal networks: these were the ambitious objectives of the i-Police project, which was launched at the end of 2021.
The then Interior Minister, Annelies Verlinden (CD&V), signed a contract worth 299 million euros with the French IT consultancy firm Sopra Steria for this purpose. In December 2025, her successor, Quintin (MR), scrapped that colossal contract because, after years of invoicing totalling nearly 76 million euros, there had been “not a single tangible result”.
Shortly afterwards, the Brussels Public Prosecutor’s Office launched an investigation into the possible misappropriation of public funds and a conflict of interest in the case. Verlinden subsequently came under fire when it emerged that she had acted as a lawyer for Sopra Steria shortly before becoming Minister for the Interior in 2020.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Administration for Cyber Security Director-General Tsai Fu-longe (蔡福隆) said Thursday that the exposure of candidates’ personal identification numbers on the Central Election Commission’s website may have resulted from poorly designed software developed by contractors.
Taiwan Go Go, an alliance of several small political parties, said at a press conference Wednesday that the CEC had exposed the personal identification numbers of 1,573 candidates on its asset disclosure website, per UDN. Taiwan Obasan Political Equality Party Taipei City Council candidate Li Hui-hsuan (李惠暄) said the CEC had violated the law and should notify both affected individuals and relevant authorities of the incident.
The CEC responded that the incident may have resulted from contractors accidentally entering identification numbers into files that were not intended for public disclosure, per Newtalk. The commission said the file appeared as garbled text that ordinary users could not readily read.
The commission said it temporarily suspended the service Tuesday and reopened it at 7 p.m. after correcting the problem.
Tsai announced the preliminary findings of his administration’s investigation, saying the problem may have stemmed from flaws in the contractor’s software design, per TVBS. He added that the Ministry of Digital Affairs would continue working with the CEC to strengthen the security of the entire system.
New Power Party Chair Wang Wan-yu (王婉諭) criticized the CEC’s response, saying the information could be accessed through the browser’s developer tools on the asset disclosure website, per UP Media. She explained that Chinese characters may become scrambled when the wrong character encoding standard is used, but personal identification numbers consisting only of digits and English letters would remain unchanged.
Wang said her team discovered the issue without any engineers or hackers on staff, warning that others may also have noticed the error. She called on the CEC to investigate how many times the information had been downloaded and where it may have been sent.
DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) commented on the incident Wednesday, saying that encoding personal information would not diminish the severity of a data leak, per SETN. He called on the government to provide a more detailed explanation of the incident to restore public trust.
Taipei City Councilor Yang Chih-tou (楊植斗) also demanded answers, adding that affected individuals should seek compensation from the CEC, per China Times. He urged Shen, a national security expert who was also affected by the leak, to pursue accountability through the legislature.

Poland hands Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:55:07 UTC
16:55:07 KST

- Poland will soon transfer two MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine in a new aid package worth about €50 million, Rzeczpospolita reported.
- One jet has reached the end of its service life and may be used for spare parts, while the other is still flying.
Poland will soon hand Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million (about $56 million), Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Oct. 29, in a story quickly picked up by Ukrainian defense outlet Milarnyi.
Reserve Lt. Gen. Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Polish Defense Ministry’s Strategy and Defense Planning Department, confirmed the transfer to the newspaper and said the decision had been made, without giving a date beyond “in the near future.” Only one of the two jets is still flying. The other has reached the end of its service life, and Rzeczpospolita reported that Ukraine may use it as a source of spare parts.
The rest of the package is mostly munitions. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will also send 155 mm and 152 mm artillery shells, 20 mm rounds for the six-barrel cannon fitted to F-16 fighters, which Ukrainian pilots use to shoot down Russian drones, and missiles for the Piorun shoulder-fired air defense system built by Polish manufacturer Mesko. Ukrainian defense officials had said in September that the Polish donation would be worth €50 million and would include air defense equipment. Poland’s Defense Ministry declined to detail the contents, saying only that the package draws on equipment being retired by the Polish armed forces or no longer needed.
The two aircraft are a small addition to a fleet Poland has been feeding since the early part of the war. Poland began openly handing over MiG-29s in March 2023, and by that May then-Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak said Ukraine had received 10 of them, Militarnyi reported. In total, Poland has given Ukraine 14 MiG-29s, Militarnyi said. Rzeczpospolita reported the same figure, adding that the jets were sent in 2022 and 2023 in varying technical condition and with little publicity.
A further transfer has been discussed for more than two years. In July 2024, Poland’s security agreement with Ukraine included a pledge to consider sending at least one more MiG-29 squadron, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw could not simply give up jets still flying air policing missions unless allies supplied replacements. At the time, the Polish Air Force still had 14 MiG-29s: 11 single-seat MiG-29As and three two-seat MiG-29UB trainers.
In late 2025, the two governments began talks on the last Polish MiG-29s. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the handover would benefit Poland because Warsaw would receive Ukrainian drone and missile technology in return. That exchange has not happened. As of mid-June 2026, Poland’s deputy defense minister said no aircraft from that batch had been delivered, and Rzeczpospolita reported the technology transfer stalled at the political level after Ukraine’s president named a military unit after heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a wartime nationalist force whose legacy is deeply contested in Poland.
Poland can spare the jets because their missions are moving to newer aircraft. The MiG-29 has kept a shrinking quick reaction alert role over the Baltic, and Rzeczpospolita reported that its tasks are now handled by Polish F-16s and the first 12 South Korean-built FA-50 light fighters, which reached full operational readiness in 2026.
For Ukraine, every additional airframe matters. The Ukrainian Air Force still relies heavily on the Soviet-designed MiG-29, which it has kept flying through deliveries from Poland, Slovakia and Bulgaria and through cannibalizing retired jets for parts, while losing aircraft to Russian strikes on airfields and in the air.
The new package also follows a separate Polish contribution of Patriot interceptors. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland has given Ukraine 10 PAC-3 MSE missiles in total, five earlier this year and five more through an international donation led by the United States with NATO. Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland’s donations to Ukraine since 2022 were worth about 16.45 billion zlotys, most of them delivered in 2022 and 2023, and the ministry later declassified the full list of transferred equipment.

Pauline Hanson accuses Anthony Albanese of trying to divide One Nation with staffing offer
In short:
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of political meddling after one of its MPs rejected an unsolicited offer of a $200,000 staffer.
The dispute has intensified scrutiny of the prime minister's power to allocate parliamentary resources.
What's next?
Pauline Hanson says the current system is "grubby" and wants an independent body to set staffing levels.
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of trying to use his power to set parliament staffing levels to divide the party after the prime minister offered new MP David Farley extra resources.
The Farrer MP received a letter from Mr Albanese this week authorising him to hire an additional staffer on a $200,000 salary package, an "unsolicited" offer that Mr Farley has rejected.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has criticised the offer as an attempt by Labor to "exert undue political influence" and split her party, which is in the middle of a broader staffing dispute with Mr Albanese.
"We won't be bought or divided by this prime minister,"
Senator Hanson said.
Staffing levels have emerged as a significant point of contention between some crossbenchers and Mr Albanese, who has ignored calls to increase the resources provided to some independents and One Nation.
All parliamentarians are granted five electorate officers, but the prime minister decides additional personal staff levels.
It is understood the extra staff position offered to Mr Farley was the same as the allocation provided to fellow One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce when he quit the Nationals and moved to the crossbench.
Both parliamentarians are in the lower house and have geographically large regional electorates.
Hanson says staffing power 'open to abuse'
In a statement today, Senator Hanson said the staff offer made to Mr Farley showed the system was "grubby".
"This is the type of politics that Australians are sick of," she said.
Senator Hanson has repeatedly asked Mr Albanese to let her hire more staff since One Nation achieved minor party status in the wake of Mr Joyce's defection.
"For months, One Nation has been fighting for fair, transparent and objective allocation of staffing for parliamentarians," she said.
Senator Hanson has called for an independent body to determine staffing levels.
"While this power has always been open to abuse, it has, in our view, been weaponised to an unprecedented extent under this Labor government and this prime minister," she said.
Senator apologises for 'clumsy' Haines comment
Earlier this week, independent West Australian senator Fatima Payman revealed she had apologised to Indi MP Helen Haines for her "clumsy wording" in relation to a staffing stoush with Labor.
During a Senate estimates hearing on Monday night, Senator Payman suggested Mr Albanese was waiting for her to suffer an attack similar to Ms Haines before he would grant extra staff.
Senator Payman refused to withdraw the comment at the time, which Special Minister of State Don Farrell described as an "outrageous statement".
But yesterday, Senator Payman confirmed she had contacted Ms Haines, who is in hospital recovering from a double amputation after an alleged attack last week, to clarify her remarks.
"I have apologised for my clumsy wording on Monday night, and I have conveyed those apologies directly to Dr Haines and her staff," Senator Payman said.
She maintained her need for additional staff, noting the "toll" on her current team.
Crossbench unites in staffing push
Last month, Senator Hanson, Senator Payman and independent Fowler MP Dai Le teamed up to criticise what they described as "unfair" staffing double standards for some crossbenchers.
The trio called on Mr Albanese to provide a "fair" number of staff and later moved a motion attempting to strip him of the personal power to decide personnel allocations.
Data from May this year showed Senator Payman was the only independent in parliament who did not have any additional personal staff allocated.
Ms Le had one extra staff member, as did independent Bradfield MP Nicolette Boele and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet.
The remaining crossbench independents have two personal staff, except Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie, who has three.
The Greens, who have one MP and 10 senators, have 15 personal staff.
One Nation, which has two MPs and four senators, has five additional staff.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's manufactured product prices and domestic supply prices rose in September, driven by higher oil prices and costs of electrical machinery apparatus, including electronic integrated circuits, the Department of Statistics said on Thursday.
The Singapore Manufactured Products Price Index (SMPPI) increased 5.3 percent month on month, accelerating from 4.4 percent in August, marking its third consecutive monthly gain. The oil index rose 7.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 4.8 percent.
The SMPPI surged 47.5 percent year on year, up from 40.1 percent in August. The oil index climbed 58.9 percent, while the non-oil index rose 45.8 percent.
The Domestic Supply Price Index (DSPI) increased 7.3 percent month on month, compared with 4.1 percent in August. Its oil index rose 15.9 percent, while the non-oil index gained 4.1 percent.
On a year-on-year basis, the DSPI jumped 48 percent, up from 38.8 percent in August. The oil index surged 78.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 38.2 percent.
The increases in both indices' oil components were mainly due to higher prices of petroleum and petroleum products, while gains in their non-oil components were largely driven by higher prices of electrical machinery apparatus, the data showed. ■

Командирът на Военноморските сили контраадмирал Кирил Михайлов / Контраадмирал Кирил Михайлов: Не е ясно откъде са дроновете, поразили вчера кораба в Черно море
PHOTO BTA
Font size
None of the 18 crew members - 14 Filipinos and 4 Ukrainians - aboard the container ship CONTSHIP JET, which was struck by maritime drones in the Black Sea around noon yesterday, was injured. They arrived at Varna’s Sea Station last night, and the ship’s owner had already arranged hotel accommodation for them through his local agent. The crew will undergo medical examinations.
Varna Regional Governor Mario Smarkov described the successful rescue operation as “the most wonderful news”, but declined to comment on whether any containers had fallen from the vessel or whether there was a risk to the environment until the relevant authorities had carried out the necessary inspections.
Mario Smarkov
PHOTO Rumen Sarandev
Later, Bulgarian Navy Commander Rear Admiral Kiril Mihaylov announced that the vessel had been carrying 421 containers, 20 of which had fallen overboard and were drifting at sea. He added that, according to the captain of the stricken ship, the containers on board were carrying various fuels and other types of hazardous cargo. The ship sank during the night.
Rear Admiral Kiril Mihaylov said he did not know where the drones had come from, as they could have been launched from anywhere. “We had no forces or assets in the immediate area that could reach them quickly enough to intercept and destroy them”, he stated. According to him, the incident demonstrates that the state needs to invest more in the Bulgarian Navy, as in adverse weather conditions, naval vessels are the only ones that can be relied upon.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Environment and Water has launched an investigation into possible pollution of the Black Sea following the incident, but no visible signs of pollution have been detected so far. According to the ship’s manifest, the cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids, flammable liquids, ethanol solutions, household chemicals and plastics.
Teams from the Basin Directorate will collect seawater samples today at five coastal locations: Durankulak, Shabla, Cape Kaliakra, Byala, and Sozopol.
Teams from the Executive Agency Maritime Administration have inspected the container ship CONTSHIP JET, which was struck by three maritime drones, the Varna Regional Administration announced. Following an assessment of the vessel’s condition, experts informed Varna Regional Governor Mario Smarkov that no significant adverse effects on the marine environment or coastline are expected at this stage.

Beyond Affordable Housing: Integrating Civic Infrastructure in US Mixed-Use Developments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

For much of the twentieth century, affordable housing in the United States was conceived as a distinct residential category, shaped by financing structures and development practices that separated housing for lower-income residents from the broader civic and commercial functions of the city. Federal housing legislation and subsequent urban renewal policies contributed to the construction of large residential developments that were frequently financed and managed independently of surrounding urban infrastructure. The consequences of this approach, including concentrated poverty, deteriorating buildings, unequal access to services, and the eventual demolition of prominent public housing projects, are extensively documented.
Today, the provision of affordable housing is closely tied to economic and regulatory mechanisms that determine feasibility, from land values and construction costs to zoning regulations and public subsidies. Programs for housing credits play a significant role in financing affordable rental housing, while competitive allocation of resources and pressure to maximize housing delivery place considerable emphasis on regulatory compliance.

BRUSSELS, October 29. /TASS/. The European Union’s (EU) next seven-year budget will have to find at least 35 billion euros to repay old loans to Ukraine, the European Commission (EC) wrote in a note seen by the European Politico edition.
The EU will repay last year’s loan worth 90 billion euros after the conflict ends, but the interest rates are already weighing on the next budget. According to the document, the interest amount will reach 41.9 billion euros if interest rates rise by one percentage point.
"The Union budget is equipped to address these costs and has sufficient financial capacities within the headroom [financial cushion]," a Commission official told the publication. But the EU executive wrote in the note that "a source of coverage [for the borrowing costs] is to be defined."
The EC has doled out 171 billion euros in loans to Ukraine since 2014, with most disbursements coming after 2022, according to the note. Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Bulgaria insist that they don’t want to service the borrowing costs for any future loan for Kiev.

Beckman and Melania Trump have worked together for many years on her media and business projects, including the documentary which was released this year and produced with funding from Amazon.

- Lubinets announced that a ceasefire in the Oleshky area would start from 03:00 Kyiv time on 27 October. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed that the ceasefire had been introduced.

- The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in effect until 22:59 on 1 November.

Germany’s Steinmeier says China must avoid one-sided benefits in economic ties
BEIJING – In its pursuit of economic self-sufficiency, China must not create one-sided dependence in other markets, Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged in an address at a top-tier university in Beijing on Oct 29.
Steinmeier, who will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Oct 30, was objecting to the trade imbalance between China and Europe, according to his speech text for delivery at the prestigious Peking University.
“It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences,” he said, but pressed that China’s greater independence must not lead to dependence and vulnerability of others on China.
The European Union has called its widening trade deficit with China unsustainable, and warned in September it will use every possible means to remedy it.
Germany, along with France, has also proposed that the EU enact a new rapid-action measure against countries that harm it, with China likely in focus.
European companies have found themselves with no or little access to the Chinese market, while European markets face large amounts of state-subsidised Chinese imports as well as Beijing’s controls and limits on its raw materials exports, Steinmeier said.
Steinmeier argued that Europe was determined to keep its industrial base, and that he was confident that Brussels and Beijing would be able to find solutions through dialogue.
“We do not want a new bloc confrontation. That would not only be dangerous for international security, but would also be an economic loss for everyone,” said the German president who is on a five-day visit until Oct 31. REUTERS

Canada and EU Drop Associate Membership Plan, Pursue Closer Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:22:30 UTC
16:22:30 KST

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
Canada and the European Union have agreed to pursue closer economic and political cooperation but dropped a proposal to give Canada associate membership in the bloc, according to a joint declaration seen by Reuters ahead of a summit in Montreal hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
The declaration, which EU officials approved on Wednesday evening, is expected to be published on Friday, when the two-day summit concludes. It states that negotiations on defining the future relationship between Canada and the EU will continue until another summit next year.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed associate membership for Canada six weeks ago, but the idea became a divisive issue during negotiations over the summit declaration. Diplomats said Germany led a group of countries opposed to endorsing a concept that has no legal basis under existing EU treaties and had not been sufficiently defined.
Germany, France and Italy were among the countries that raised objections, although they broadly support stronger cooperation with Canada. Governments also expressed concern about insufficient consultation between the European Commission and member states. Another complication was that the term “associate membership” had already been used in discussions about Ukraine's possible accession to the EU.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had previously suggested associate status for Ukraine as an interim step toward full membership, allowing Kyiv to take part in EU summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights. Von der Leyen used the same term to describe a different arrangement for Canada, which has no legal route to EU membership.
An earlier draft of the Canada-EU declaration referred to Canada as an associate member at least twice. It also proposed allowing Canada to participate in consultations on major EU political and regulatory initiatives, with the arrangement's scope to be established by the 2027 summit.
Carney said on Tuesday that this week's meeting marked the beginning of formal negotiations that would take another year. He played down the disagreement over terminology, saying the practical effects of closer cooperation mattered more than the name given to the arrangement.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney told reporters. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
Closer relations with Europe form a central part of Carney's strategy to reduce Canada's economic and security dependence on the United States after President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. However, efforts to strengthen ties with the EU could provoke Washington as Canadian and US officials continue trade negotiations.
Trump previously dismissed the associate membership proposal as “laughable” and warned that, if he regarded the move as a “hostile act,” the United States might stop trading with Europe “on many things.”
The revised declaration instead focuses on an “Alliance for the Future,” a phrase Carney has frequently used to describe relations between Canada and the EU. The initiative aims to remove trade barriers, encourage investment and secure supplies of critical raw materials, medicines and technologies during crises.
The two sides also plan to expand cooperation in energy, climate protection, artificial intelligence, security and education. Canada could gain wider access to EU programs in research, education and defense, while a new economic council is intended to bring together businesses from both sides of the Atlantic.
The declaration proposes a joint feasibility study on increasing Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe. It also includes an initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through “new subsea cable infrastructure,” and plans to make it easier for young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.
However, EU governments diluted several economic commitments included in the original draft. An explicit objective of deeper financial market integration was removed, while a proposed commitment to preferential treatment in economic security measures was replaced with an intention to limit potential negative effects on each other's interests.
Julian Karaguesian, a former adviser at Canada's Finance Ministry, described the summit as “a bit of a show.” He said Canada's efforts to build closer relations with the EU remained poorly defined and questioned whether greater cooperation would necessarily advance Carney's drive to diversify the country's international relationships.
Canada sends nearly 70% of its exports to the United States, while the EU accounts for about 9% of Canada's total trade. Carney's office declined to comment.
The declaration also commits European and Canadian leaders to reaffirming their support for a rules-based international order and says they “deeply regret” US sanctions imposed on the Netherlands-based International Criminal Court.
Barry Appleton, an international trade lawyer and fellow at the Balsillie School of International Affairs in Waterloo, Ontario, said the declaration could anger the Trump administration by emphasizing multilateralism and international law.
“All that talk of multilateralism and support for international law is basically like sticking a finger into President Trump’s eye,” Appleton said.
He also warned that cooperation on economic security could provoke Washington. The declaration commits Canada to aligning its artificial intelligence and digital rules with Europe's, while the US considers EU-style digital regulation a trade barrier.
“This is a highly provocative statement from the EU and Canada,” Appleton said.
The White House said, in response to a request for comment, that US and Canadian trade officials were in talks.
EU officials described the summit at a Tuesday briefing as a “historic milestone,” saying it represented a renewed commitment to Canada and the beginning of an ambitious new chapter in the partnership. They added that all EU member states supported the closest possible relationship with Canada.

India news: 'Cockroaches' back Gandhi's rally against election chief

India news: 'Cockroaches' back Gandhi's rally against election chief
Published October 29, 2026last updated October 29, 2026
What you need to know
- India's Cockroach movement is throwing its weight behind Indian opposition's November 1 rally against the poll body chief
- A group called 'RSS Friends' has registered itself in the US to step up outreach
- Cyclone Arnab leaves devastation behind in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha
This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Thursday, October 29.
Thanks for reading
We will be back tomorrow with the latest news out of India. Thank you for joining us!
Bangladesh sentences ally of former PM Hasina to death in absentia
Bangladesh sentenced another ally of ousted leader Sheikh Hasina to death in absentia on Thursday.
The court also sentenced three more party leaders from Hasina's Awami League to life in prison.
Hasina fled to India after the 2024 uprising that ended her rule. She also faces a death sentence in absentia. This has proved a source of tension between Delhi and Dhaka.
She and leading members of her party face charges from Bangladesh's new government of complicity in the deaths or injuries to protesters during the uprising.
The United Nations estimates that as many as 1,400 people were killed in total between July and August 2024.
The leader sentenced to death on Thursday was Md Mahbubul Alam Hanif, a joint general secretary of the Awami League, who was a government minister during Hasina's 15-year rule.
The charges for all four defendants pertained the deaths of six people in the western Kushtia district durign the unrest.
Prosecutors said the charges were "undoubtedly proved," defense lawyers called the verdict "unacceptable."
Hasina has said she does not recognize the authority of the court that sentenced her to hang. She has also said that, despite the outstanding death sentence, she plans to return to Bangladesh of her own volition in December.
Finance ministry increases 2027 growth prediction, warns of continued inflation and currency risks
The Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.
The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.
India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.
The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."
The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.
However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.
It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.
Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.
But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory.
Opposition bloc promises 'public impeachment' process against election chief
Several leaders from India's opposition alliance, the INDIA bloc, have finalized the "public impeachment" proceedings they intend to carry out against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of voter lists.
They did this in a meeting on Thursday at Indian National Congress (INC) President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence while he himself was in Bengaluru, local media reported.
They now plan to hold a mock Parliament sitting at Kharge's residence on Friday to conduct the "public impeachment" which is purely symbolic.
It will include speeches by opposition leaders, accounts by victims of the electoral roll revision, a motion passed by Kharge and a concluding speech by INC leader Rahul Gandhi. That's ahead of a planned November 1 rally to demand Kumar's removal.
The Election Commission of India began the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in 2025 to remove redundancies from India's electoral rolls including dead voters and those appearing more than once. Since then over 13 crore (130 Million) voter names have been deleted. There have also been reported irregularities allegedly on Kumar's part to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.
The BJP has denied allegations that the SIR exercise has benefited them, arguing it helped weed out "infiltrators" from the voter list.
On Tuesday, the INC claimed it was denied permission to hold the "public impeachment" of CEC Kumar at various venues, the Hindustan Times reported, and accused the government of trying to "silence" the voice of common people after "destroying" the electoral system.
Under law, the CEC can be removed by the Indian parliament through a process similar to the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge. He or she may also resign by submitting a written resignation to the president of India.
Odisha plans air evacuations from marooned villages
The east Indian state of Odisha is coordinating with the central Home Ministry to airlift people from the cyclone-struck Ganjam district where hundreds of villages remain inaccessible after heavy rain.
Ganjam was among some of the worst-affected districts in the state, authorities had earlier said. Some 300 villages there have been marooned due to heavy rain and flash floods, Press Trust of India reported citing a top state official.
Chief Secretary Anu Garg said teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and the Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force have begun rescue operations in the affected areas, but air evacuations could be delayed by low cloud level and continued rain.
Within Ganjam, Sorada village was among the worst affected with the Rushikulya river overflowing due to extremely heavy rainfall over the last three days.
'RSS Friends' registers in US to bolster outreach
A group of "well-wishers" of the India-based Rashtriya Sayamsevak Sangh (RSS) has registered with the US Department of Justice as a foreign agent of the right-wing Hindu nationalist group, news agency Press Trust of India reported on Thursday.
The RSS is a 101-year-old organization with millions of followers across India. It presents itself as the guardian of Hindu values, while critics widely classify it as a paramilitary organization. Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has deep roots in the RSS, its influence reaches to the highest levels of political power. The Group is the ideological parent of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
'RSS Friends,' which provided a Georgia address for itself, listed a Delhi branch of RSS in India as its "foreign principal."
The group said its proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations and community-engagement activities.
"RSS Friends does not have a written employment, consulting, lobbying, public-relations, or agency agreement with RSS containing specified deliverables, compensation, or detailed operational instructions," the group said, adding that the lack of contract did not mean the connection did not exist.
The registration of RSS Friends was submitted two days before RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's outreach program at New York's Madison Square Garden on August 29. The controversial appearance is believed to be part of the RSS' global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.
What else do we know about RSS Friends?
The group's website describes itself as a "dedicated well-wisher organization" seeking to address misrepresentation of RSS by US media or other "politically motivated actors."
Its social media, too, largely covered Bhagwat's NYC Event and has since been inactive.
IN PICTURES: Cyclone Arnab's trail of destruction:
Cyclone Arnab damages homes and farmlands in eastern India
Cyclone Arnab on Wednesday battered Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, damaging homes, farmland and electricity infrastructure, authorities said.
The cyclone made a prolonged landfall early Wednesday as a "very severe cyclonic storm" in the union territory of Puducherry and southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh.
At least three people were killed even as the storm weakened while moving inland. Two women were electrocuted in separate incidents in the port city of Visakhapatnam, while another person was killed when a tree fell in East Godavari district, officials said.
Andhra Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu later said 14 of the state's districts were badly affected, requesting urgent assistance from the central government.
The cyclone damaged 79,000 acres of crops and dozens of homes. The worst hit area was the state's fertile Konaseema district where banana and coconut plantations suffered extensively.
While the eastern state of Odisha seemed to be less impacted initially, heavy rains and winds lashed several districts there on Wednesday evening. State authorities reported landslides, uprooted trees and damaged homes and infrastructure, but zero casualties.
On Thursday morning, Indian Home Minister Amit Shah reiterated the central government's support to the impacted states.
"In the wake of Cyclone Arnab, spoke with the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha and Chhattisgarh and assured them of every assistance to mitigate the hardship of the people in the face of the disaster," he wrote in a post on X, adding that disaster relief teams were continuing operations on a "war footing."
'Cockroaches' back opposition-led rally against election chief
Indian youth-led political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has decided to back the opposition bloc's upcoming November 1 rally, marking a shift in protest strategy.
The CJP said India's election commission has undermined people's right to choose their leaders through the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which allegedly deleted over 130 million names from voter lists across the country.
Election authorities said the list includes people who have died, moved away or were appearing on lists more than once, but critics argue the massive number is also likely to include a large number of eligible voters.
The CJP, several student organizations and opposition parties — with Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi at the helm — have been protesting against the revisions and alleged irregularities purported by India's election chief for over a month now.
What else did the CJP say?
"Gyanesh Kumar has lost the trust required to oversee free and fair elections. His resignation is therefore necessary to restore the credibility and independence of the Election Commission," the CJP said in a statement published on X by founder Abhijeet Dipke.
"Our constitution gave every adult citizen the right to vote. It is our responsibility to ensure that no eligible citizen is deprived of that. The Cockroach Janta Party will therefore support all organizations fighting for free and fair election in our country," it said.
Dipke's caption read: "The Cockroach Janta Party extends its support to the INDIA Bloc's November 1 rally. Nation above all!"
The CJP and Gandhi's Indian National Congress have been running parallel campaigns so far with similar demands. However, they have not expressed direct support or held joint rallies before this, possibly in an effort not to alienate people who may relate to one group but not to the other.
However, the CJP now has limited choices. Its leaders were detained and arrested while protesting earlier this month and made to sign a peace bond which prohibits them from calling for mass protests in central Delhi. Lending their support to someone else's call for protest could be the loophole they needed.

After months of distance, India's Cockroach movement has thrown its weight behind the country's largest alliance of parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
This move came just days before an massive rally led by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, to demand poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and roll back the revision to voter lists.
What remains to be seen is if, when and how the Modi government will respond.
Speaking of chaos, a tropical cyclonic storm dubbed "Arnab" tore through India's east coast on Wednesday.

Moving away from home, India's largest right-wing "Hindutva" organization seems to have new "friends" in the US, looking to improve the group's image and gather support of Indians overseas.

Spain train crash: PM Sanchez calls for investigation as 3 days of mourning begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:22:00 UTC
16:22:00 KST

Spain mourns train crash victims as rail safety questions loom
October 29, 2026
Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday in remembrance of the 69 people killed in one of Europe's deadliest train disasters in recent memory.
On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train run by state operator RENFE slammed into the back of a stationary train operated by private Italian-Spanish company Iryo in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.
A British tourist who was rescued from the RENFE train told the Associated Press that "suddenly, everything started falling apart."
"We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over," the man said.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was on holiday in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the RENFE train when "I woke up and I was in the air."
Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling the AFP news agency that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.
He recounted "a very strong hit ... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos," while wearing a bloodstained jumper and holding a tattered suitcase. "I think I've been born again," he said.
Emergency crews work through the night
Emergency crews continued searching through the wreckage overnight for survivors and bodies, using cranes to move mangled metal.
Relatives of passengers gathered at nearby facilities seeking information about missing loved ones.
Residents of the nearby town of Urda joined emergency workers in helping survivors, providing first aid supplies, water and blankets.
Teams of Red Cross workers offered support.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia told AFP news agency that many people are in shock and "haven't taken on board what has happened."
"The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.
Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to help identify the missing.
Spain's rail network safety in question
Wednesday's crash was Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year and has raised fresh questions about rail safety.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente blamed the crash on an "inexplicable" decision to allow one train to continue after an automatic control system failed along a stretch of track.
He said the RENFE high-speed train had travelled about 25 kilometers before hitting the stationary Iryo train.
Audio recordings reveal pre-crash exchanges
On Wednesday evening, Spanish media published audio recordings revealing confused conversations between the train drivers and the railways control center in the 30 minutes before the crash.
In one recording published by the El Pais newspaper, among others, a control center operator appears to instruct the driver of the RENFE train to resume his journey at normal speed after some technical issues.
"Continue your journey and then proceed ... at normal speed [and] with normal operation," the operator tells the driver.
"At normal speed?" queries the driver, to which the controller confirms: "Yes."
A few minutes later, in another recording, the driver of the Iryo train then informs the control center that she is "stationary in front of the entry signal at [the town of] Urda" — about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) ahead of the RENFE train.
When she is still told to "resume the journey" normally, she says she cannot because of the security system error, reiterating that this is why she is stationary.
The second recording suggests therefore that the control center was aware of the stationary Iryo train having already instructed the RENFE train to travel towards it — but no further action appears to have been taken.
Spanish PM pledges full investigation
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who visited the crash site, pledged a full investigation and measures to strengthen rail safety.
"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sanchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."
In January, 46 people died when a high-speed train derailed and collided with another in the southern Andalusia region.
The latest disaster comes just weeks before Spain's November 29 general election which Prime Minister Sanchez had called hoping to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents — and distract from right-wing attacks on his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which they both deny.
About an hour before Wednesday's crash spread, Sanchez had posted a campaign message on social media reading: "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."
Within 24 hours, Transport Minister Puente was facing calls to resign while Sanchez's main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, demanded a full investigation of the crash and canceled campaign events for the day.
"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Nunez Feijoo said. "But that does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."
There was noticeably less restraint on show from Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, who will be hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives.
"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," he said, refusing to join Nunez Feijoo's campaign pause.
"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.

Police reject Netanyahu party's claims of widespread election fraud in Arab communities

The head of the Central Elections Committee on Thursday asked the Shin Bet domestic security agency to investigate serious allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday's parliamentary election, including suspected overseas funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini urging him to use the agency's investigative powers to determine whether foreign entities had attempted to improperly influence the election. Sohlberg sent the letter to Zini following a meeting between the two on Wednesday.
The suspected foreign interference appears to involve Qatar funneling tens of millions of shekels to influence Israel's election, with Central Elections Committee officials describing the intelligence as "solid."
The Shin Bet had reportedly possessed the intelligence for several days but waited to see whether the suspected vote-buying would actually take place. The agency declined to comment on the ongoing investigation.
"The integrity of elections is the heart of democracy. Take integrity away from democracy, and you deprive it of its vitality," Sohlberg wrote.
He said allegations had been brought to his attention suggesting that foreign actors working against Israeli interests may have sought to influence the election through financial means.
"Serious suspicions have been brought before me concerning improper influence on the elections through foreign funding provided by external actors operating against Israeli interests," he wrote.
Sohlberg acknowledged that he could not independently assess the credibility of the allegations but stressed that their potential implications warranted a thorough investigation.
"I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions," he wrote. "However, given that they concern foreign actors, there is an obligation to investigate them properly to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent unlawful activity intended to undermine the democratic system and subversive activity."
The judge instructed Zini to make every effort to establish whether the allegations were supported by evidence, or whether they could be disproved.
"I ask you to do everything in your power to get to the bottom of these suspicions and to use the powers of the Israel Security Agency to uncover evidence that would substantiate or refute them," Sohlberg wrote, using the Shin Bet's formal name
"Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the electoral process and the integrity of the democratic process."
Sohlberg also requested that the agency report its findings, if any, within the coming week, citing legal deadlines for challenging election results.
"In light of the statutory deadlines for filing election appeals, I ask that you make every effort to present me with findings, insofar as there are any, within the next week," he wrote.
The letter comes amid growing political controversy over the election results after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party accused Arab political parties Wednesday of stealing the vote through widespread criminal activity.
Likud alleged that Arab parties supporting terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state had manipulated the results through serious criminal offenses, including vote-buying, threats against election officials, fraudulent voting and the use of prohibited software to mobilize supporters.
The party said it had submitted evidence of suspected irregularities to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee and demanded an investigation.
Sohlberg's letter did not identify the foreign actors allegedly involved, specify the source of the suspected funding or establish a connection between the allegations of foreign interference and Likud's claims against Arab political parties.
Likud described the suspected foreign interference as a political earthquake, accusing foreign actors of stealing Israel's election to help Arab parties gain power.
"Ra'amgate is an earthquake. Israel's election was stolen!" the party said in a statement. "Justice Sohlberg's remarks about foreign actors interfering in the election and bribing voters to support Arab parties represent an unprecedented political shock."
Likud characterized the alleged interference as "an attack on democracy" aimed at enabling foreign control of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the removal of the right-wing government.
"The goal is to bring about foreign control of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to force an Israeli military withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, first and foremost against Iran," the statement said.
The party argued that the allegations should rule out any cooperation between Jewish-led Zionist parties and the predominantly Arab Ra'am and Joint List factions.
"Now that it has become clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, no Zionist party can be allowed to cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash or establish a government that would endanger Israel," Likud said. "We demand immediate action using every means available to the Shin Bet and police to investigate these crimes," the statement concluded.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the Shin Bet to investigate Arab party leaders. "The suspicion of election manipulation using foreign Islamist money is a test for the State of Israel," he wrote on X. "The leaders of the Arab parties must be questioned by the Shin Bet today. The State of Israel will not be sold to radical Islam with terror money."
Avigdor Liberman, leader of the opposition Yisrael Beytenu party, also weighed in, describing Sohlberg's letter as "a dramatic and unprecedented development."
"I call on law enforcement authorities to act swiftly to establish the truth as soon as possible," Liberman wrote.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar! party, is in contact with the relevant authorities and is receiving updates on allegations of foreign interference in Israel's election, his office said in a statement.
"Israel must safeguard the integrity of its elections against any attempts at interference, political spin or manipulation, and thoroughly investigate every complaint," the statement said.
"At the same time, political actors must not be allowed to exploit the situation to influence the timing of the 26th Knesset's swearing-in."
Police, however, have rejected claims of widespread election fraud, saying there was no investigative or intelligence evidence to support the allegations and that election-related irregularities had declined significantly compared with the previous vote.
"Election Day passed with a small number of exceptional incidents involving election integrity, including in comparison with previous elections," police said. "It should be emphasized that there is no investigative or intelligence evidence supporting the allegations raised in your inquiry."
The dispute comes after a surge in Arab voter turnout helped predominantly Arab parties make significant electoral gains, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining the next government. Neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerged from the election with a clear majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
In a sharply worded statement posted on X, Likud accused Arab political parties of orchestrating widespread electoral fraud.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters," the party said.
Likud said it had collected hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence from polling stations in Arab communities and was transferring the material to police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
The party cited what it described as thousands of envelopes containing cash alongside ballot slips for Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas. It also alleged threats and violence against polling station officials, multiple voters entering voting booths together, people casting ballots under more than one identity and discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and registered voters.
Likud further accused unnamed political operatives of using prohibited voter-mobilization software.
"We demand that the police and Shin Bet conduct a thorough investigation into the theft of the elections by the Arab parties and bring the perpetrators to justice," the party said.
It also demanded immediate action from the Central Elections Committee, arguing that the alleged offenses had compromised the legitimacy of the election results.
"This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens," Likud said. "Law enforcement agencies must act firmly and immediately."
Police, however, said their assessment did not support allegations of widespread irregularities.
"We are not aware of any exceptional incidents concerning election integrity," a police official said. "In fact, during the current election, the number of incidents related to election integrity fell by nearly 40% compared with the previous election."
Likud says authorities ignored 1,183 complaints
Despite the police assessment, Likud officials insisted that their allegations had not received adequate scrutiny.
Sagi Keizler, the party's election integrity director for the Arab sector, said Likud had submitted 1,183 complaints to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day, including descriptions of individual incidents and telephone numbers for polling station officials who could corroborate the allegations.
According to Keizler, the complaints included 38 cases of suspected bribery, 25 allegations of improper police intervention, 66 reports of violence or threats, 115 suspected instances of double voting and 408 complaints involving the extraction of voter information.
The categories he identified accounted for 652 complaints. He did not provide a breakdown of the remaining 531.
"These are the complaint figures we submitted to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day itself, including details of the incidents and telephone numbers of committee members who can testify about the complaints," Keizler said.
He also accused police and election authorities of failing to contact witnesses identified by the party.
"Neither the police nor the Elections Committee called a single witness," Keizler said. "Apparently, the conclusion had already been reached in advance."
Police cast doubt on suspected vote-buying case
The suspects, residents of the Bedouin communities of Segev Shalom and Ar'ara in the Negev desert, were detained during an operation by the Southern District's Central Unit.
Police said searches of their homes uncovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials suspected of being connected to election offenses. Some envelopes reportedly bore Ra'am's logo.
Investigators initially suspected that the money was intended for distribution to voters in exchange for supporting the party.
The suspects reportedly included a doctor, a transportation driver and another political activist. All three denied wrongdoing.
A court subsequently released the doctor despite police objections, while extending the detention of the other two suspects by five days.
The doctor's attorney said his client had organized meetings to encourage support for Ra'am but had not participated in bribery. The driver's lawyer maintained that the cash discovered at his home was intended to cover transportation expenses.
Another suspect said money found in envelopes was intended as charitable donations for needy families on behalf of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am.
Police said that although the investigation remains open, investigators have not uncovered significant evidence of wrongdoing and expect the case to be closed. However, several additional suspects were arrested on Thursday.
Ra'am has rejected the allegations, accusing authorities of politically motivated arrests intended to suppress Arab voter turnout.
The party said its activists were detained at their homes before polling stations opened, rather than while attempting to influence voters. It also accused authorities of selectively targeting its members and reported that Ra'am ballot slips had been removed or damaged at polling stations in several Arab communities.
Police have not alleged that Ra'am's leadership was involved in the suspected bribery scheme.
The arrests prompted a criminal investigation into specific allegations of vote-buying but have not substantiated Likud's broader claims of coordinated fraud across Arab polling stations.
Shin Bet chief praises election safeguards
Police were not the only Israeli security authorities to express confidence in the integrity of the election.
During a visit Tuesday to the Central Elections Committee's command center, Zini said the voting process was secure and properly supervised.
"Elections in Israel are secure, properly conducted and supervised in an inspiring manner," Zini said.
"There are challenges, and there are those who try to undermine the process, but under the leadership of Justice Sohlberg and the Israel Police, we are succeeding," he added.
Arab parties' gains complicate coalition negotiations
The allegations have emerged against the backdrop of a politically inconclusive election in which increased participation by Arab citizens helped strengthen the parliamentary representation of predominantly Arab parties.
Preliminary results Wednesday projected that the Joint List, an alliance of Arab political factions led by Yousef Jabareen, would win 11-12 seats, while Ra'am would secure seven to eight. Together, the two parties were expected to hold 18-19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The gains could prove decisive because neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious allies nor the parties seeking to replace him have secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The results have raised the possibility that opposition parties could seek to form a government with the support of Arab lawmakers, either through a formal coalition agreement or outside parliamentary backing.
Netanyahu and his political allies have repeatedly rejected such arrangements, portraying reliance on Arab parties as a threat to the country's security and political stability.
Ra'am, formally known as the United Arab List, is associated with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement. Under Abbas, the party has pursued a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics, seeking agreements with Jewish-led parties in exchange for commitments to address longstanding problems affecting Arab communities.
In 2021, Ra'am became the first independent Arab party to formally join a governing coalition when it entered the government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
During the latest election campaign, Abbas indicated that he would consider participating in another government if it committed to addressing violent crime, home demolitions, discrimination and other issues affecting Arab citizens of Israel.
The Joint List, meanwhile, represents a separate alliance of Arab political factions with a different approach to participation in Israeli national politics.

U.S. Air Force plans long-term ASARS-2 support for the U-2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:31 UTC
16:19:31 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking companies able to repair and sustain the U-2’s ASARS-2 imaging radar, with industry responses due Nov. 18.
- The notice states the government does not own or have access to the ASARS-2 sensor data.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for companies that can repair and sustain the Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2, or ASARS-2, the imaging radar carried by the U-2 Dragon Lady spy plane, even as the service asks Congress to retire its last U-2s by the end of fiscal 2027.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s U-2 program office posted the request for information on the federal government’s contracting website on Oct. 22 and amended it on Oct. 28, moving the response deadline from Nov. 13 to Nov. 18 at 3 p.m. Eastern. The notice is market research rather than a solicitation, and it gives no contract value, quantity or period of performance.
Under the contract logistics support the Air Force describes, a contractor would provide engineering support, repair spare assets and resolve system failures on the radar and its ground support equipment. Depot maintenance support teams would handle mission software updates, engineering for parts that are no longer manufactured, engineering change proposals, configuration management, technical manuals, specialized in-plant repair, calibration and integration with other ASARS-related systems on the U-2. The work also carries cybersecurity requirements under NIST SP 800-171 and SP 800-53, Intelligence Community Directive 503 and the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification process.
“The Government does not own or have access to the data for the ASARS-2 sensor,” the notice says.
The Air Force has classified the radar as a noncommercial item and has not yet decided what security clearance the work will require or how much of it would be performed outside the continental United States.
Data rights matter here because Raytheon, now part of RTX, has supplied ASARS for the U-2 since the early 1980s, and federal procurement records list the company as the holder of Air Force engineering and sustainment orders for the ASARS-2A version under contract FA8528-20-D-0023. A new supplier without access to the design data would have to show it can still repair and qualify the components.
The notice describes the radar’s job as producing near-real-time, high-resolution, long-range imagery of the ground day or night and in any weather. Synthetic aperture radar builds a detailed, map-like picture from radar returns as the aircraft moves, so clouds and darkness do not block it. Flying above 21,300 meters (70,000 feet), the U-2 can point the radar deep into territory it is not flying over.
The radar has gone through several versions. The baseline ASARS-2 entered service in the 1980s, and the Air Force received the first ASARS-2A as its replacement in 2001. In 2019, Raytheon said the newer ASARS-2B, built around an active electronically scanned array antenna, doubles the surveillance range of the ASARS-2A while keeping its mapping and imagery resolution. The Air Force’s fiscal 2021 budget request said the 2B replaces the 2A’s front-end components, which had become hard to support because parts were going out of production. The new notice refers only to ASARS-2 and does not say which versions the sustainment work would cover.
ASARS-2B is also slated to fly beyond the U-2: a Pentagon budget reprogramming document confirmed that the radar is part of the sensor suite for the U.S. Army’s High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System (HADES) intelligence business jets.
The notice lands in the middle of a long fight over the U-2’s future. In its fiscal 2027 budget, the Air Force proposed retiring its remaining U-2s by the end of the fiscal year, as part of a plan to divest 149 aircraft. Congress has blocked earlier retirement attempts, and House appropriators’ fiscal 2026 defense bill barred the service from divesting more than eight U-2s. The fleet is still flying: in January, maintainers at Beale Air Force Base, California, launched U-2s under simulated attack during Exercise Dragon Shield.

The Central Election Commission (CEC) has ruled that Rumen Radev did not commit an administrative violation of the Electoral Code in a statement he made after attending an event, adopting the decision by an 8-7 vote following several hours of deliberations.
However, some commission members challenged the legality of the ruling, arguing that the complaints concerned the use of the Council of Ministers' official communication channels for election campaigning rather than the statement attributed to Radev. More than 120 complaints were filed with the CEC by citizens, nongovernmental organizations, and the Initiative Committee supporting Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev.
The political coalition Democratic Bulgaria (DB) announced that it would immediately appeal the CEC decision concerning allegations that government communication channels had been used to support the presidential candidacy of Iliana Yotova.
In an official statement, DB said the commission had declined to examine the substance of more than 105 complaints regarding the use of the Government Information Service and the Council of Ministers' official channels for election campaigning. The coalition argued that the CEC majority, backed by representatives of Progressive Bulgaria and Revival, had avoided addressing the central question of whether the government's official website and press office could publish an appeal by Prime Minister Rumen Radev endorsing a particular presidential candidate.
DB accused the commission majority of relying on procedural arguments and misinterpreting the Electoral Code instead of assessing the complaints on their merits. The coalition also questioned the CEC's position that it lacked jurisdiction over certain issues while simultaneously concluding that no electoral violation had occurred.
According to the statement, the arguments presented by the majority changed during the meeting, while the commission continued to avoid addressing the substance of the complaints.
DB stressed that the case was especially serious because it involved neither a political party's website nor a personal account or campaign platform, but the Council of Ministers' official communication channels, which are funded by taxpayers.
“The CEC cannot become an institutional shield that protects those in power from scrutiny. The commission’s independence is not a privilege that allows it to evade difficult decisions; rather, it is an obligation to apply the law equally to everyone,” Democratic Bulgaria said.
The coalition also objected to what it described as the influence of commission members' political affiliations on whether the CEC identifies an electoral violation or declines to do so. “105 reports cannot simply vanish behind procedural maneuvers,” DB emphasized.
The political formation called on the commission to provide a clear ruling on whether state communication resources may be used to promote a particular candidate during an election campaign without breaching electoral law.
“The decision will be appealed immediately. The court must do what the CEC refused to do today - namely, apply the law and determine whether election rules have been violated,” the statement said.
Democratic Bulgaria concluded that election rules must apply equally to everyone, including the prime minister and other officials, regardless of whether the candidate receiving support is Iliana Yotova.

South Korea suspected of rapprochement with Russia amid the war - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:17:45 EET
16:17:45 KST

South Korea suspected of rapprochement with Russia amid the war - FT
Kyiv • UNN
The voyage of a Korean container ship along the Northern Sea Route has alarmed European diplomats. Seoul denies rapprochement with Moscow and fuel exports.
South Korea's "tilt" toward Russia worries European allies. This is reported by the Financial Times, writes UNN.
Details
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung enthusiastically welcomed the crew of the PanStar Acro container ship, which had returned from an Arctic voyage. Praising the crew's "courage and sense of responsibility" in "distant seas," Lee promised to "respond with unwavering action and open a new path for the Republic of Korea."
European diplomats in Seoul were less inspired. Sailing the Northern Sea Route, which runs along Russia's Arctic coast, shortens travel time to Europe via the Suez Canal by 10 days, but requires significant cooperation from Moscow.
The voyage, the first of its kind in South Korean history and completed this month, has become a symbol of what European officials view as Seoul's diplomatic and commercial rapprochement with Moscow, even as the Kremlin deepens its partnership with North Korea and continues its war against Ukraine, the publication writes.
These concerns intensified following reports this month that more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, were shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August, including on tankers subject to sanctions by the United Kingdom and the EU, the publication notes.
Seoul's relations with Moscow have led some European diplomats to question whether South Korea—which they regard as a "like-minded" democracy with shared economic and security interests—remains a reliable partner
"[South Koreans] are not actually 'like-minded,'" said one European diplomat from Seoul. "Their position is that the war [in Ukraine] will not last forever, and they want to restore business relations with Russia as soon as possible once it ends."
Some observers say these concerns have intensified under Lee, who took office in June 2025. Mason Richey, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul, said that South Korean-Russian relations have been "quietly improving" since last autumn.
In a statement to the Financial Times, South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said: "The concerns of some circles that South Korea is leaning too heavily toward Russia are contrary to the facts.
As a responsible member of the international community, the South Korean government supports and participates in global efforts aimed at ending the war in Ukraine and restoring peace."
South Korea's national security official denied reports of diesel fuel, gasoline, and aviation fuel exports to Russia, adding that the authorities were investigating whether false information about the destinations had been declared.
Meanwhile, the publication writes, Seoul's relations with Kyiv have deteriorated following a dispute over information released last month concerning the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war from Ukraine to South Korea.
