Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:12:00 UTC
16:12:00 KST

Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Europe lacks a shared plan for engaging Russia, which makes ending the war in Ukraine difficult, security adviser to the president Rainer Saks said.
Speaking to "Esimene stuudio" following Tuesday's phone call between Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Saks said what matters most is that Ukraine is satisfied.
"I would say that if this phone call is followed by something that brings the peace process closer in a direction amenable to Ukraine, then it can be considered to have been entirely positive. If Ukraine is satisfied that the call went ahead, then this is also entirely positive. We can't say that if Ukraine next asks Romania or Turkey to do something, then everyone else will start waving their arms in offense — that really doesn't work. But the fact that there is no common position on how to engage with Russia is somewhat regrettable," Saks said.
Europe as a whole is not yet mature enough to talk to Putin, since there are no shared discussions and no clear action plan is being drawn up, Saks added.
Saks noted Stubb and Estonia's president at the time, Alar Karis, said in spring talks with Russia at some point were inevitable, but that there was no readiness then as Europe had no common understanding of how the process should work.
Saks said President Ülle Madise, who entered office last month, had no prior warning the call was going ahead; diplomats informed Kadriorg afterwards.
"My advice to the president is that we support these steps if they bring us closer to peace, and we simply need to communicate with each other more. Within Estonia, the first thing is of course for the government to ensure people are on the same wavelength in terms of both information and position," Saks said.
He disagreed with the claim that there is no point in engaging Putin whatsoever. "The question is not whether there is a point in communicating or not, but how you communicate and what it is you want to achieve. [But] there is no point in simply talking for the sake of talking — I agree with that part," he said.
Saks stressed that the concept of Europe being part of the process should not be interpreted as the EU as a whole being part of it, given the multiplicity of institutions and high-ranking figures that would entail. He said a coalition of the willing on support for Ukraine would have the initial moral obligation and right to put something common together. "Until that is done, these potential problems will keep recurring," he said.
Saks said the Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministries briefed diplomats from Estonia and other key partners, but that briefing was of limited value as the content of the meeting had already been splashed across the media in some detail.
As to the claim that Putin delivered a 70-minute monologue, Saks said the Russian president gives such monologues at all meetings, and that the time should be discounted somewhat for translation. "But it also shows that the Russian president took the time, considered it important, and delivered his monologue," he said.
When asked about Russian media attempts to present the call to in a light which gives the Kremlin the advantage, Saks said Moscow is trying to establish two things: first that Europe must eventually join talks, and second that the U.S. alone cannot pressure Ukraine. "That is of course a mistake we all make: we think Ukraine is fighting only because we support them. No — they are fighting because they want to survive, and in the end they decide most of all how long they can hold out, how motivated they are and so on," Saks concluded.
Finland and Norway initiated the 90-minute call from Helsinki in their capacity as states which border Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe. The call was prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the U.S. following last week's Oslo meeting.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) was briefed on Tuesday's call.

U.S. Navy awards $43.7M for F-35 mission data lab upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:11:04 UTC
16:11:04 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $43.7 million modification to upgrade operating systems at F-35 reprogramming laboratory facilities through April 2030.
- F-35 cooperative program partners fund $29.7 million, with the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contributing about $7 million.
Lockheed Martin will upgrade the operating systems running the F-35 Lightning II reprogramming laboratories, which build the threat data the fighter needs for combat missions, under a $43.7 million contract modification the U.S. Navy announced on Oct. 28. Eighty percent of the work will take place in Eglin, Florida, and the remaining 20% in Fort Worth, Texas, with completion expected in April 2030.
F-35 cooperative program partners are paying $29,696,266 of the $43,673,774 total, or about 68%, while the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contribute $6,988,754 in fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, all of it obligated at award. The Navy aircraft procurement account also funds U.S. Marine Corps aviation, and the announcement lists the U.S. Marine Corps among the services the labs support.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued the cost-plus-fixed-fee modification, designated P00025, without competition, adding new contract line items to contract N00019-22-C-0046. The announcement does not name the operating systems being replaced, the laboratories or hardware affected, or how the partner share is divided among countries.
The labs produce mission data files, the libraries of radars, missiles and aircraft that an F-35’s radar, electronic warfare suite and other sensors use to recognize and classify what they detect in a given region. The files are loaded onto each jet before flight from a portable drive.
At Eglin, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps personnel of the 513th Electronic Warfare Squadron, part of the 350th Spectrum Warfare Wing, run the United States Reprogramming Laboratory, which produces mission data for U.S. jets and tests it on a hardware-in-the-loop line against simulated threat signals before release to the fleet. The squadron was activated at Eglin on April 23, 2010, to operate the lab, then valued at $300 million.
A 2017 U.S. Air Force account of the squadron’s work said mission data does not carry over automatically, so the squadron had to rebuild and repackage the files for each new version of the aircraft’s operating system. That refers to the software on the jet rather than the lab computers covered by the new award, but it explains why lab infrastructure gets steady funding as the F-35 moves through successive software releases.
Federal spending records show N00019-22-C-0046 began on April 29, 2022, as a base year plus five years of sustainment support for the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory and surrogate encryption work for the Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory, all for non-U.S. participants. The public announcements do not explain what the surrogate encryption support involves. In April 2025, a $22,126,598 modification (P00014) added maintenance and sustainment of the U.S. Reprogramming Laboratory and the partner support complex for the U.S. military, non-DOD partners and Foreign Military Sales customers. A further $23,312,570 modification (P00022) in April 2026 continued that work.
Lockheed Martin first set up the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory, known as ACURL, at its Fort Worth plant and moved it to Eglin under a $7.5 million modification awarded in 2018. British and Australian officials opened the lab there in February 2020, when it reached initial operating capability, and kept Canada’s name on the facility even though Ottawa had stepped back from the F-35 at the time. British and Australian staff now run the center as the reactivated 80 Squadron, which develops, verifies and validates mission data files for the three allies.
The Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory opened nearby on June 27, 2019, and was formally accepted on Sept. 22, 2021. Israel’s F-35 software work runs under a separate arrangement, and the U.S. Navy added $11.4 million in April for three additional software builds for Israel’s fleet.
Since N00019-22-C-0046 now sustains both the U.S. lab and the partner labs, the operating system work could cover either, and the Oct. 28 announcement describes it only as covering laboratory facilities and systems sustained for the U.S. services and the cooperative partners.
A separate $111.1 million modification to another Lockheed contract, N00019-20-C-0026, funded a minimum viable product of a Common Reprogramming Tool meant to replace the legacy programming tools used across the reprogramming labs. Lot 18 orders also bought multi-ship infrared search and track and Band 5 radar warning receiver hardware for development work at the U.S., ACURL and Norway-Italy labs. Each new sensor on the aircraft needs matching hardware and data in the labs, as will the 432 electronic warfare modification kits the U.S. Navy ordered for $991 million in May.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign said Thursday that cyberattacks using overseas IP addresses had breached a campaign server and flooded a platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups.
CNA reported that Shen’s campaign office said hackers targeted several campaign websites starting last Friday. The attackers exploited a security flaw to gain control of a server, created fake administrator accounts, and installed software to access the system remotely.
The hackers then tried to obtain access to Shen’s main campaign website but failed. The campaign said the website ran on a separate server and its login credentials were not stored on the compromised server.
The campaign team discovered the breach early Wednesday and completed repairs that evening. It removed the malicious software, deleted fake accounts, changed passwords and security keys, and tightened server access, per CTS News.
The second attack targeted a new platform where supporters could sign up for sections of campaign vehicle routes. Within an hour of its launch Wednesday evening, automated programs using overseas IP addresses flooded the platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups, per Tai Sounds.
The campaign said it quickly required users to log in before signing up. The change blocked the automated submissions and allowed the platform to resume normal operations.
Shen said cybersecurity had always been a priority for his campaign. His office said all affected websites were operating normally and that it would continue to guard against further attacks.

Former Taiwan digital minister says AI can help bridge divides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Digital Affairs Minister Audrey Tang (唐鳳) said AI can help people bridge political divides and have a greater say in government decisions, the Financial Times reported Wednesday.
Speaking with Financial Times Innovation Editor John Thornhill, Tang explained how Taiwan uses technology to bring people with opposing views together. Digital platforms, she said, help officials find ideas with broad public support and turn them into policy.
Tang pointed to the country’s efforts to fight AI-generated investment scams in 2024. Fake videos featuring public figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), had spread online to promote fraudulent investments.
As digital affairs minister, Tang sent text messages to 200,000 randomly selected phone numbers to seek public input. Officials then randomly selected 447 people to discuss solutions in small online groups, where AI helped summarize ideas and find areas of agreement.
Participants called for stronger checks on online advertisers and rules holding platforms responsible for losses from scam ads. Tang said more than 85% of participants supported the proposals, which helped shape laws passed within months.
Tang cited official figures showing that deepfake investment scam ads fell by more than 94% in 2025. She argued that the country had shown how public input could help fight online fraud without limiting free speech.
Tang also recalled the 2014 Sunflower Movement, a student-led protest against a proposed trade deal with China that led to the occupation of the legislature. Protesters feared the agreement would give Beijing more influence over the country, and Tang said public discussions helped people develop common proposals despite their differences.
Taiwan used a similar approach in 2015 to address disputes between taxi drivers and Uber over the ride-hailing firm’s services. Online discussions helped both sides reach agreement on proposed rules, offering an early example of how technology could help resolve disputes.
Tang said the country’s approach has drawn interest abroad, and she has visited 29 countries over the past two years to share its experience. In Germany, she has worked on a project that uses AI to help people find shared solutions to problems with transport and public services.
Tang said government action alone was not enough to make public participation work. She urged journalists, educators, and citizens to help turn shared ideas into practical solutions.

Spain Declares Three Days of Mourning After Train Crash Kills 68
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:08:28 UTC
16:08:28 KST

Spain has declared three days of national mourning after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people and injured more than 100, as emergency crews continued searching the wreckage and relatives sought information about missing loved ones.
The crash on Wednesday morning involved a train operated by state-owned Renfe and another run by private company Iryo. Both were traveling in the same direction on the line connecting Madrid with southern Spain when the Renfe train struck the rear of the stationary Iryo service near Urda, in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, sending several carriages off the tracks.
Spanish officials said 107 people had been admitted to hospitals following the collision, including 18 in critical condition, according to regional emergency services and Spanish media. Another 56 people who had been hospitalized were later discharged, leaving 53 still receiving treatment, the Castilla-La Mancha Health Ministry said.
The disaster has renewed scrutiny of railway safety in Spain, particularly after Transport Minister Oscar Puente described an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” surrounding the decision that preceded the collision.
Rescue teams worked through the night to search the wreckage, using cranes to lift twisted sections of metal, Agence France-Presse reported. Emiliano García-Page, head of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, warned on Wednesday that the death toll could rise because “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages.”
The Civil Guard has opened four offices in Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville where relatives can provide DNA samples to help identify victims. Blood donation centers have also been established in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.
A school in Urda, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been made available for relatives seeking information about their loved ones. Red Cross teams provided support to families arriving at the site, some in tears.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia warned that those affected faced a difficult period of grief, saying that “long and hard hours” lay ahead because “every person will manage it in their own way.” She added that the relatives included people who were shocked, angry, sad and worried, and said the grieving process would be complicated.
The collision was Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year. In January, 46 people died and dozens were injured when two trains operated by Renfe and Iryo collided near Adamuz in the southern region of Andalusia.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have.” He said the causes of the latest crash were being investigated and promised that any failures in safety systems or cases of negligence would be addressed with the “utmost severity.”
The first victim identified publicly included José Manuel Chacón, a 31-year-old Civil Guard officer. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media reported that those still missing included a former minister from the People’s Party and several foreign nationals believed to have been visiting Spain on vacation.
Opposition People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called for an immediate investigation into the crash and a “complete and independent review” of the country’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said an automatic control system had failed across a section of track, triggering an order to stop rail traffic. The control center subsequently authorized trains to resume running in circumstances he described as inexplicable.
Puente said the Renfe train was instructed to continue its journey at 8:36 a.m., despite the earlier stop order, and traveled about 25 kilometers before the collision at 8:53 a.m. He said the train may have reached a speed exceeding 100 kilometers per hour.
The control center had sufficient time to check the error but failed to correct it, Puente said. He declined to answer questions about whether he would resign, saying his priority was to establish what had led to the crash and support those affected.
The latest disaster comes one month before Sánchez, who has led the Socialist government for eight years, faces an early general election on November 29 as he seeks to reverse unfavorable polling.

U.S. Navy pays $23 million to shield warship power grids from hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research zero trust cybersecurity for shipboard power systems.
- Integer will work with Florida State University’s Center for Advanced Power Systems, with research running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded South Carolina-based Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research how zero trust cybersecurity can protect the electrical power systems that run its warships, without slowing the split-second controls those systems depend on.
The Office of Naval Research awarded the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for a program called Threat Resilient Integrated Defense for Enhanced Naval Technologies, or TRIDENT, the Department of War announced in its daily contract list this week. Integer is teaming with Florida State University and its Center for Advanced Power Systems, and work will take place in Columbia, South Carolina, through October 2030. The award is a science and technology effort, meaning it funds research and prototyping, and it does not put a new cybersecurity system on any ship.
The contract calls for investigations into “threat-informed” zero trust architecture frameworks tailored to the cyber-physical security needs of shipboard power systems. Zero trust is a security model that drops the old assumption that anything already inside a network can be trusted. Every user, device and command has to prove it is legitimate each time it asks for access. The Navy wants an architecture that lets a ship monitor the cyber and physical state of its power plant, change its defensive posture as threats change, and keep fighting through an attack while the electrical system keeps performing.
The funding structure is more complex than the headline figure. The contract has a 36-month base period and a 36-month option that would begin 12 months after award and run alongside the base, which is why the whole effort ends about four years from now. The Navy obligated $10.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award, enough to pay for the full base period, leaving about $13 million tied to the option. Navy research money is available for two years, so the fiscal 2026 funds expire at the end of fiscal 2027, the government’s current budget year. ONR bought the work through its long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology, an open solicitation that accepts proposals year-round, so the Navy could not say how many bids it received.
The problem TRIDENT is meant to study comes from how warship power has changed. Older surface combatants such as the Arleigh Burke-class destroyers use gas turbines geared directly to the propeller shafts, with separate, smaller generators for electricity. The three Zumwalt-class destroyers were the first U.S. Navy surface combatants built around an integrated power system that generates electricity for both propulsion and weapons. Two Rolls-Royce MT30 main turbine generators and two smaller auxiliary generators produce about 78 megawatts, which feeds the electric motors that turn the shafts and a shipwide grid for sensors, combat systems and hotel loads. The Navy’s planned DDG(X) next-generation destroyer is designed to use a similar integrated power system.
That architecture lets a ship shift power between propulsion and weapons on demand, which matters as electrical loads grow. L3Harris, which builds power distribution equipment for Virginia-class submarines, said this month that advanced radars, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power. Laser weapons such as the 60-kilowatt-class HELIOS installed on USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022 draw their “ammunition” straight from the ship’s electrical system.
It also means a single, software-managed grid now sits underneath nearly everything a warship does. Power is controlled by networked switchboards, power converters, protective relays and a machinery control system that decides how to route electricity and how to isolate a fault before it spreads. Those are operational technology systems: computers whose job is to move physical equipment. If an attacker could send false commands or corrupt the data those controllers rely on, the consequences would be physical, from tripping generators to cutting power to weapons or radars in combat.
The contract identifies two constraints that make zero trust hard to apply aboard ship. The first is latency. Integrated power systems rely on very fast control loops to protect equipment and keep the grid stable, and enterprise zero trust tools typically add checks, such as authentication, encryption and traffic inspection, that take time. A security layer that delays a protective trip or a power transfer by even a short interval could cause the damage it was meant to prevent. The second is the mix of legacy and modern equipment. Ships stay in service for decades and are upgraded in pieces, so a single power plant can contain older controllers that were never designed to authenticate commands alongside newer networked devices. The contract does not say which ship classes or systems the research will model.
Florida State’s Center for Advanced Power Systems is one of the Navy’s main university laboratories for electric ship research. Established in 2000 in Tallahassee, the center operates one of the largest real-time digital power system simulators along with 5-megawatt AC and DC test beds for power hardware-in-the-loop testing, in which real equipment is connected to a simulated ship grid so engineers can stress it under realistic conditions. Cybersecurity for power systems is one of its listed research areas, and it leads the Navy-funded Electric Ship Research and Development Consortium of universities. In June, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the center an $88 million contract for modeling, simulation and testing of advanced shipboard electrical power and energy systems through 2031.
Integer Technologies is a small business founded in Columbia in 2021 by Duke Hartman and Josh Knight. It has built a portfolio of Navy research work focused on cyber-physical systems, often in partnership with universities. In September, ONR exercised a $10.2 million option on a separate Integer contract with Louisiana State University to develop a cyber-physical resilience framework for Navy maritime platforms, with work running through March 2030. The company was also among more than two dozen firms placed on the Navy’s $982 million multiple-award contract for its Unmanned Surface Vehicle Family of Systems in 2024.
The threat the Navy is preparing for has moved from theory to documented activity on land. In a February 2024 advisory, CISA, the National Security Agency and the FBI assessed with high confidence that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon were pre-positioning themselves on IT networks to enable movement into operational technology and disrupt critical infrastructure in a crisis. The agencies said the group had compromised organizations in the continental United States and its territories, including Guam, a key hub for U.S. forces in the Pacific, and had kept access in some networks for at least five years.
Earlier cases showed what attacks on control systems can do. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, sabotaged Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges by manipulating their industrial controllers while showing operators normal readings. In December 2015, a cyberattack on Ukrainian power distribution companies cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers, the first publicly confirmed blackout caused by hackers. Both targeted fixed infrastructure on land, and a warship differs in important ways: its networks are smaller and more tightly controlled, and it often operates with limited outside connectivity. Ships still connect to shore networks in port and receive software and hardware updates from contractors during maintenance, which gives an attacker possible ways in.
The Department of the Navy has led the military services in applying the Pentagon’s 2022 zero trust strategy to enterprise IT, and its officials said in early 2025 that they were preparing zero trust standards for operational technology, the category that includes ship machinery and weapons platforms. TRIDENT is aimed at that harder category, where a security tool has to work within the timing and reliability limits of physical equipment.

CEO of one of Australia's top cultural events becomes French knight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Biennale of Sydney CEO Barbara Moore appointed Chevalier of Ordre des Arts et des Lettres
The CEO of the Biennale of Sydney, Barbara Moore, has been appointed Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, or a knight of the French Order of Arts and Letters.
"I'm pretty shocked by it," she told ABC Arts, ahead of the ceremony at Sydney Town Hall on October 29.
"It's a big deal and admittedly I have a bit of impostor syndrome. Like, I'm still young!
"But these endorsements mean a lot … they say we're doing something that's contributing in a positive way."
Moore, who moved to Australia from Canada in 2007, has been CEO of the festival since 2019.
The French Order of Arts and Letters is one of the country's highest cultural honours, awarded to someone for their contribution to arts and culture in France and around the world.
Past recipients include musicians Nick Cave and Kylie Minogue, actor Cate Blanchett, artist Tony Albert, the late film critic David Stratton, and former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron.
"I think the point of these things is to encourage relationships and bonding," Moore said.
"I'm an untrained diplomat, where I'm just trying to bring people together and break down barriers.
"When the world is so used to shouting at each other and we're losing the art of listening, art helps us connect and learn from each other."
It is a poignant statement in a year when the biennale, curated by Hoor Al Qasimi, was subjected to community, commercial and political pressures, including the withdrawal of sponsors and accusations of antisemitism.
Asked how arts festivals like the biennale should navigate a charged political climate, Moore offered plainly: "Boldly, like warriors."
She continued: "If we operate through fear, if we're part of burning books and over-censoring, we have a problem.
"People are going to have feelings and opinions, especially in divisive times. But that doesn't mean we cancel organisations and we shut projects down.
"We have to remember what we're there for and that's to bring people together."
Taking Australian arts and culture abroad
Earlier this month, Moore was in France for the contemporary art fair Art Basel Paris, which was cut short in response to education and cost-of-living rallies that escalated into rioting.
She was there to take a group of biennale patrons to see a new exhibition by Ghanian artist Ibrahim Mahama. His work featured in the 2020 Biennale of Sydney, which was forced to close after 10 days by the COVID-19 pandemic.
His exhibition opened at the Cartier Foundation gallery, which partners with the biennale to platform First Nations artists and curators.
The partnership has inspired another celebration of Australian artists on the world stage, with Australia announced as guest of honour at next year's Art Paris contemporary art fair.
Art Paris director Guillaume Piens saw the large-scale work of First Nations artists including Kaylene Whiskey and Dylan Mooney at the newly reopened White Bay Power Station during the 2024 Biennale of Sydney.
"He'd never seen anything like that before, and he thought he wanted to bring First Nations artists to the fair," Moore said.
What that means for the place of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art on the world stage, Moore suggests, is more than its popularity with collectors.
"It's a reckoning," she said. "[People are asking:] 'How do we make the world a better place? How do we get through these tumultuous times?'
"Maybe looking at the oldest continuous living culture could be a good start, to think about how to exist on this planet and where the humanity is.
"Maybe there's some things we forgot we need to remember again."
The next Biennale of Sydney is scheduled to start on March 21, 2028, and will be led by Singaporean curator Low Kee Hong.

Where to place a money tree to attract prosperity: folk beliefs and care tips
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:57:43 EET
15:57:43 KST

Where to place a money tree to attract prosperity: folk beliefs and care tips
Kyiv • UNN
The jade plant is recommended to be placed in the southeast, but the main conditions are light, moderate watering, and the absence of drafts. Folk beliefs have no evidence.
The jade plant is often grown at home as a symbol of financial stability and prosperity. According to folk beliefs, the place chosen for this plant may have special significance. UNN explains more about where these beliefs originated, where it is best to place a money tree, and what conditions the plant requires.
Details
The money tree, also known as a jade plant, is easy to recognize by its fleshy, rounded leaves. Their shape resembles coins, which is why the plant has long been associated with the accumulation of wealth, stability, and financial growth. The jade plant gained particular popularity through the traditions of feng shui, in which certain areas of a home are associated with various spheres of life. Supporters of these beliefs consider that a properly placed plant can become a symbol of abundance and a reminder of financial goals.
The southeastern part of the home
According to popular feng shui recommendations, the money tree is most often advised to be placed in the southeastern part of a house or individual room. In Eastern practices, this direction is symbolically associated with wealth and prosperity.
To determine the appropriate area, you can use a compass to check where the southeast is located. After that, you should choose a place that corresponds not only to symbolic beliefs but also to the plant’s own needs. The jade plant is a succulent, so sufficient light and moderate watering are important for its healthy growth. If the southeastern part of the home is dark or a heating appliance is constantly operating nearby, it is better to find another place. The main principle is simple: beliefs may suggest a symbolic location, but the plant’s growing conditions should remain the priority.
Where else you can place a money tree
If the southeastern area is not suitable for growing a jade plant, there are other options mentioned in folk beliefs. For example, the living room, as this is a place where the family often gathers and guests are received. Therefore, popular recommendations on where to place a money tree associate this room with prosperity and harmony in the home.
The pot can be placed on a sturdy stand or a shelf near a window if there is enough light there.
You can also place the jade plant on a desk or in a home office.
In folk beliefs, the money tree here symbolizes professional development, new opportunities, and financial goals. The plant can become part of the workspace and a reminder of plans related to a career or one’s own business. However, it should be placed directly next to a computer or other devices only if there is enough space and light for the pot.
On the other hand, if the money tree is placed near the entrance, one widespread belief holds that it will symbolically help preserve the prosperity of the home. It is believed that in this way the plant seems to greet financial good fortune at the entrance to the house. However, a dark hallway or a drafty spot is not actually the best choice for a jade plant. If you want to place the pot near the entrance, it is better to find a well-lit area away from cold air and sudden temperature changes.
Where you should not place a jade plant
Folk beliefs advise against leaving a money tree among clutter or in untidy corners. Symbolically, disorder is associated with stagnation, which supposedly prevents prosperity. From a practical perspective, the plant also needs a place where it is convenient to care for it. Do not hide the pot in a cabinet, place it in a dark corner, or put it somewhere where it will constantly be knocked or brushed against.
Particular attention should be paid to the following conditions:
-  Lack of light. In a place that is too dark, the plant may become elongated and lose its attractive appearance. 
-  Constantly wet soil. Excessive watering can cause the roots to rot. 
-  A hot radiator. Placing the plant directly next to a heat source can create unfavorable conditions for it. 
-  Drafts and sudden temperature changes. It is better to avoid places where the jade plant is constantly exposed to such changes. 
Therefore, when choosing a place for a money tree, you should consider not only folk beliefs but also the lighting, temperature, and the opportunity to regularly check the condition of the soil.
Do coins under the pot and a red ribbon help?
Some folk traditions involve additional symbolic rituals. For example, a coin is placed under the pot with a jade plant, and the trunk is decorated with a red ribbon, with such actions associated with wishes for financial stability and increased prosperity. Another common custom is to grow the plant oneself from a small cutting. Those who believe in omens consider that this symbolically connects the money tree with the head of the household. However, these rituals belong to the realm of folk beliefs and have no proven effect on one’s financial situation. If the plant’s owners like them, they can be regarded as a personal tradition, without neglecting ordinary care. It is also important to ensure that decorative ribbons do not constrict the trunk and that coins or other small objects do not pose a danger to children or pets.
How to care for a money tree so that it remains healthy
According to folk beliefs, a lush and well-cared-for jade plant symbolizes prosperity. Of course, the plant’s health does not determine one’s income level, but proper care will help it maintain an attractive appearance. A jade plant needs a bright location, while watering should be moderate. Before watering it again, allow the soil to dry out: succulents store moisture in their leaves and do not like constantly wet soil. It is also important to use a pot with drainage holes so that excess water can escape. The plant should be repotted when this is necessary given its condition and the size of its root system, rather than merely because of folk recommendations about frequently changing pots. If the leaves fall off, this does not necessarily mean financial difficulties. The cause may be watering mistakes, insufficient light, or other unfavorable conditions.

China

Chinese warships and aircraft operate around Taiwan overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:51:39 UTC
15:51:39 KST

- Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven navy ships and one official ship around the island in the 24 hours to Oct. 29.
- Five aircraft entered Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, and four fighter and drone sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line.
Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven People’s Liberation Army Navy ships and one Chinese official ship operating around the island in the 24 hours to 6 a.m. local time on Oct. 29, the Ministry of National Defense said on social media.
Five of the six aircraft sorties entered the northern, central and southwestern parts of Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, or ADIZ, a buffer area where Taipei asks approaching aircraft to identify themselves. The zone extends well beyond the island’s territorial airspace, and flights into it are not violations of Taiwanese airspace. The ministry said its forces monitored the activity and responded with combat air patrol aircraft, navy ships and coastal missile systems.
A map released with the report shows two separate groups of flights. Between 9:35 a.m. and 5:20 p.m. on Oct. 28, five sorties of fighters and drones operated along the median line of the Taiwan Strait, the informal boundary between the two sides, and four of them crossed it. A single fighter flew near the northern edge of the zone, north of Taiwan, between 1:55 p.m. and 2 p.m.
The ministry did not identify the aircraft or drone types, the classes of the seven navy ships, or what kind of government vessel the official ship was.
Chinese military aircraft and ships operate around Taiwan almost daily, and Taipei publishes a tally each morning. The figures vary widely from day to day. On busier days the ministry has reported dozens of aircraft, including one 24-hour period when 38 sorties and nine navy ships were detected and 31 aircraft crossed the median line. During large-scale exercises announced by China’s Eastern Theater Command, Taiwan has reported dozens of aircraft and vessels in a single day and put its forces on high alert.
The median line has no legal standing, but for decades both sides treated it as an unofficial dividing line that helped keep military aircraft apart in the narrow strait. Chinese aircraft now cross it routinely, and Taiwan’s ministry tracks each crossing in its daily reports.

U.S. embargo on Cuba draws overwhelming UN condemnation for 34th straight year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:51:27 CST
15:51:27 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The UN General Assembly on Wednesday once again delivered a sweeping rebuke to the decades-long U.S. embargo against Cuba, with 130 member states voting for a resolution demanding an end to the economic, commercial and financial blockade, underscoring Washington's continued isolation over a policy widely criticized for violating international law and inflicting hardship on the Cuban people.
The resolution, adopted with 130 votes in favor, 17 against, and 25 abstentions, expresses concern about the continued promulgation and application of laws and regulations, such as the 1996 Helms-Burton Act of the United States, the extraterritorial effects of which affect the sovereignty of other states, the legitimate interests of entities or persons under their jurisdiction, and the freedom of trade and navigation.
It calls on all states to refrain from promulgating and applying such laws and measures, and urges states that have and continue to apply such laws and measures to take the steps necessary to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible.
Following two days of debate, Wednesday's resolution was the 34th in a row on the necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States on Cuba.
In a rare break from diplomatic decorum during the debate in the General Assembly Hall on Tuesday, the U.S. representative and members of the Cuban delegation were engaged in a shouting match.
Shortly after U.S. Permanent Representative to the United Nations Mike Waltz took the podium and began to show photos of the alleged proof of corruption in Cuba, members of the Cuban delegation pounded their designated table and raised a point of order.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez, joined by members of the Cuban delegation, walked down the hall toward the podium to make his point, prompting a fiery exchange between Waltz and the Cubans. Rodriguez called Waltz a liar, and Waltz demanded the Cubans back off.
The Assembly president briefly suspended the debate before proceedings resumed.
In the two-day debate, the majority of UN member states spoke against the U.S. embargo and called for its end.
The Singaporean representative, who spoke on behalf of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, warned of the "troubling picture of the worsening socio-economic situation in Cuba," underscoring shortages of essential medicines and a decline in food production.
Eritrea's representative, speaking on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defense of the Charter of the United Nations, also condemned the tightening of the embargo as "one of the most serious, prolonged, and systematic violations of international law."
"The Cuban people have the right to build their own future, free from any kind of interference or pressure," said the Eritrean representative.
Uganda's representative, speaking on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, described the tightening of U.S. measures as "a form of collective punishment."
Prolonged power outages have disrupted hospitals, schools, water distribution and food preservation, he said, calling for an end to the embargo against a country that "poses no threat to international peace and security."
Namibia's representative, speaking on behalf of the African Group, recalled Cuba's historic solidarity with African countries. "The position of Africa on this question is settled at the highest level," he said, underscoring that the African Union had renewed its call for the embargo's removal for the seventeenth consecutive year.
Uruguay's representative, speaking on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, criticized restrictions affecting trade, investment and financial transactions involving third countries, warning that they undermine Cuba's prospects for sustainable development.
Introducing the draft resolution titled "Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba" on Wednesday, Rodriguez denounced "the disrespectful, provocative attitude" shown by the U.S. delegation on Tuesday.
"Cuba is not a threat. The (U.S.) blockade is a threat," he said.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first introduced in 1960, a year after the Cuban revolution. In 1962, a full economic, commercial and financial embargo was imposed. The March 1996 Helms-Burton Act of the United States extends the territorial application of the embargo to apply to foreign companies trading with Cuba. The U.S. administration led by President Donald Trump has further heightened pressure on Cuba. ■

Singapore central bank reminds banks to manage environmental risks linked to haze
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:51:11 CST
15:51:11 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's central bank has reminded banks to identify, assess and manage material environmental risks arising from their activities and exposures, including those linked to pollution and deforestation.
Banks are expected to consider relevant information released by the National Environment Agency under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said in a statement on Wednesday.
Where customers may be linked to activities contributing to haze, banks should engage them to understand their involvement and assess whether adequate measures are in place to prevent, detect and stop fires, MAS said.
Banks should take appropriate steps to mitigate heightened environmental risks, including imposing conditions, reviewing financing terms, limiting further exposure or reassessing customer relationships, it added.
"Clear breaches of environmental laws would warrant stronger measures, including limiting exposures or exiting the relationship," MAS said.
It said it supported local banks' clear stance against burning practices and noted that they would take strong action where warranted.
Singapore experienced prolonged haze in recent weeks. The National Environment Agency has issued Preventive Measure Notices under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act to companies that may have contributed to the haze. ■

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's import and export prices rose at a faster pace in September, driven mainly by higher oil and petroleum product prices, official data showed on Thursday.
The Import Price Index (IPI) increased 4.7 percent month on month in September, accelerating from 1.6 percent in August and marking its third consecutive monthly gain, the Department of Statistics said in a statement.
The oil index surged 16.1 percent, compared with the 4.8 percent increase in August, while the non-oil index rose 0.2 percent.
Year on year, the IPI climbed 19.9 percent, up from 15.5 percent in August. The oil index jumped 78.5 percent, while the non-oil index rose 4.4 percent.
Meanwhile, the Export Price Index (EPI) rose 3.6 percent month on month, compared with 1.9 percent in August. Its oil index increased 12.7 percent, while the non-oil index rose 0.9 percent.
Year on year, the EPI gained 19.4 percent, up from 15.2 percent in August. The oil index surged 69.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 8.3 percent.
The increases in the non-oil indices were mainly driven by higher prices of electrical machinery apparatus, including electronic integrated circuits, the department said. ■

Ship Sinks After Drone Strike in Bulgaria's Economic Zone as Defense Chief Says "It Came from the East"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:50:55 UTC
15:50:55 KST

Outgoing Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov told bTV that the maritime drones that struck the container ship CONTSHIP JET near Cape Kaliakra came from the east, while emphasizing that Bulgaria’s military had intelligence about a possible attack and that legal restrictions prevented it from engaging the drones outside the country’s territorial waters.
"Yesterday's drones came from the direction of the sea - from the east," Eftimov said, adding that the armed forces had sufficient information about the unmanned vehicles but did not publicly attribute the attack to a specific country.
He said the military had received advance intelligence about a potential strike and had taken precautions. "We had information, which is why we took appropriate measures. Following the incident in Kardam and the strikes that occurred in early October, this represents a consistent intensification of our efforts - specifically regarding reconnaissance, surveillance, situational analysis, and early warning, which is what took place yesterday," he said.
Asked whether Russia was responsible, Eftimov declined to make a definitive attribution. "I have not heard any Chief of Defense, whether from Romania, Turkey, or any other nation, offer a categorical assessment regarding the origin or attribution of such malicious acts based on the professional intelligence available to them." He said Bulgaria operates as a NATO member and follows the Alliance’s Strategic Concept.
Eftimov said the armed forces had responded appropriately and rejected criticism that Bulgaria had failed to act. Since August, the country has strengthened its air defense and surveillance systems and expanded its air force capabilities, including Su-25, L-39 and F-16 aircraft.
He explained that Bulgaria strictly observes international law and is authorized to engage threats only within its territorial waters. "Do we operate outside our territorial waters? No. We lack the mandate to do so," he said.
Severe weather also hindered the deployment of interceptor assets, although aviation units remained on standby. The drones did not enter Bulgarian territorial waters, where the armed forces would have been able to engage them, Eftimov said. He stressed that Bulgaria was not at war and that the measures taken amounted to stronger security efforts rather than an escalation.
The CONTSHIP JET, a Liberian-flagged container ship sailing from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, sank around midnight east of Varna, according to maritime news outlets and the regional administration. It had been struck by three maritime drones on October 28 within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, about 21 nautical miles southeast of Shabla.
The attack caused a fire and severe damage to the vessel’s starboard side, leaving it listing heavily. All 18 crew members were evacuated onto life rafts and rescued without fatalities or injuries, but the damage proved too extensive for the ship to be stabilized, and it sank overnight into Thursday.
The incident was the fifth attack on a vessel within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. Speaking to Bulgarian National Radio (BNR), shipping agency owner Captain Todor Georgiev said the drones were Russian and described the attack as "a mockery of [Russia's] Black Sea neighbors."
Separately, the Council of Ministers has proposed that the Bulgarian president issue a decree relieving Eftimov of his position as Chief of Defense and discharging him from military service effective January 2, 2027. The proposal follows a formal request from the admiral under Article 163 of the Defense and Armed Forces of the Republic of Bulgaria Act.
Eftimov submitted his request to leave military service on September 30, 2026, with three months’ notice. At the time, he was expected to remain in office until the end of the year.
He has led Bulgaria’s defense establishment since March 2020, following a career in the Naval Forces, the Defense Ministry and NATO structures. In December 2023, the Council of Ministers proposed extending his tenure after his initial four-year term expired. The extension took effect on March 31, 2024.
Born in Varna on August 16, 1961, Eftimov graduated from the N. Y. Vaptsarov Naval Academy in 1984 and subsequently held various command and staff positions in the Naval Forces. He served as commander of the Varna Naval Base and worked at NATO’s International Military Staff in Brussels from 2011 to 2016.
He became deputy chief of defense in 2016 and briefly served as acting chief of defense in early 2017, before returning to the deputy position. He was appointed head of the Bulgarian Armed Forces in March 2020 and received the rank of admiral that same year.
During the final months of his tenure, Eftimov continued to represent Bulgaria’s military leadership in NATO defense policy initiatives and allied commitments. In September 2026, he stressed the need to balance the rapid adoption of innovations with maintaining interoperability. Earlier in the year, he highlighted the importance of NATO’s regional defense plans for security in the Black Sea region.
His departure is to be formalized by presidential decree. Under the proposed timeline, Eftimov will leave office after more than six years as chief of defense and over four decades of military service.

Restored nature hits record 252 million hectares, but still off target: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:50:00 UTC
15:50:00 KST

Restored nature hits record 252 million hectares, but still off target: UN
PARIS – Countries are restoring about 252 million hectares of nature, a record level according to a United Nations report published on Oct 29, but this still falls short of global 2030 targets.
“This report captures the largest documented restoration effort in history,” said Doreen Robinson at the UN Environment Programme in Nairobi at a press conference.
The restored area is equivalent to the size of Argentina or Algeria.
But the report estimates the pace of restoration efforts must “triple” to meet the 2030 target of one billion, and funding will need to increase sharply, particularly from the private sector.
Nature restoration efforts recorded in 149 countries have mostly taken place on land, with 232 million hectares involved, compared with 11 million hectares of inland waters and 5.7 million hectares of marine and coastal waters.
This “lags far behind ambition in both freshwater (inland water) and marine and coastal ecosystems, yet these ecosystems are degrading at the highest rates”, the report warned.
As part of the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration from 2021 to 2030, and an international agreement adopted in 2022 known as the Kunming-Montreal framework, states have committed to taking action to halt biodiversity loss and protect the planet.
The Kunming-Montreal framework aims to protect 30% of terrestrial and marine areas by the end of the decade.
Beyond nature restoration, which can include measures such as replanting trees, the process has also boosted employment with one million related jobs created and a goal of reaching 32 million by 2030.
In terms of restoration on land, China is far ahead of other regions, with 137 million hectares, followed by Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Ethiopia.
The report was published during the key biodiversity COP17 summit in Armenia running until the end of the week. AFP

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has uncovered new cases of Ukrainian intelligence services using the popular Dayvinchik/Leo match bot to recruit teenagers to carry out terrorist attacks, the press office reported.
"The Federal Security Service, together with the Interior Ministry and the Investigative Committee, continues to document instances of Ukrainian special services using the popular Dayvinchik/Leo match bot on Telegram to recruit Russian citizens into sabotage and terrorist activities through deception and psychological manipulation," the statement said.
"In August and September 2026 alone, eight minors (aged 14 to 17) and two adult Russian citizens (aged 19 and 24) were detained in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Omsk, Ryazan, and Sverdlovsk Regions for either plotting or carrying out arson attacks on law enforcement vehicles, gas stations, and energy and transport infrastructure facilities on the orders of Ukrainian special services, as well as for acting as couriers to transfer funds obtained from defrauded citizens to cryptocurrency exchange points," the press office noted. Since July 2025, 56 Russians aged 12 to 24 have been detained in various regions of Russia. They used the Telegram Dayvinchik/Leo match bot and committed crimes under the psychological influence of Ukrainian intelligence agencies, the FSB emphasized.
According to the press office, "Ukrainian intelligence officers posed as young people to make online contact with Russian users via the Telegram match bot. During these conversations, which were intended to develop romantic relationships, the Russian users sent their geolocation data, paid for restaurant reservations in advance, and clicked on phishing links," the statement said. The users were then contacted by impostors posing as representatives of the FSB or Russia’s financial watchdog Rosfinmonitoring, who threatened that the funds they had sent had allegedly been transferred to Ukrainian military accounts and that the geolocation data provided would be used to launch missile strikes or drone attacks.
"After that, the deceived and intimidated citizens, who were unable to critically assess the situation due to psychological pressure, were coerced, under the threat of criminal prosecution, into committing arson to test the anti-terrorism security of the targeted facilities and into participating in other pseudo-operational activities," the FSB noted.
As a result, the deceived teenagers and young adults became defendants in criminal cases involving terrorism, attempted terrorism, or intentional destruction or damage to property. Those who have reached the age of criminal responsibility have been charged. Given the severity of the crimes, they face lengthy prison terms, the press office added.

About 10 missiles were launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea into waters off the country’s east coast, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said. Japan’s Coast Guard said the projectiles apparently had already fallen.
"South Korea, the United States, and Japan are closely sharing information on North Korea’s ballistic missiles while maintaining full combat readiness," South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.
The launches came after a series of ballistic missile tests by North Korea in recent weeks and underscore security challenges in the region, as Kim demonstrates confidence that he can continue weapons testing even after new initiatives by U.S. President Donald Trump to resume dialogue, the publication noted.

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:45:16 UTC
15:45:16 KST

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Opium production in Afghanistan has risen fivefold in a year. According to a UN survey released on Thursday, it’s the first significant increase since the Taliban banned poppy cultivation in 2022.
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) found that the area planted with opium poppy grew by 330 per cent, to more than 43,000 hectares, up from about 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Estimated production rose by 400 per cent, from about 300 tonnes to just under 1,500 tonnes.
Both figures remain well below levels before the ban, when some 232,000 hectares were under cultivation.
For decades, Afghanistan was the world’s biggest source of illicit opium. Before the ban, it accounted for around 80 per cent of global supply.
The Taliban seized power in August 2021. In April 2022, they outlawed poppy cultivation and all narcotics, citing religious grounds.
Hidden in cereal fields
The de facto authorities say they eradicated 22,000 hectares of poppy this year. But UNODC said many farmers appear to have adapted to evade enforcement. Some are hiding small plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds. Others are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to avoid detection.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” said UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma.
She urged the de facto authorities and the international community to work together to support farming communities, by investing in livelihoods, farm infrastructure and access to markets.
Shift to the northeast
Cultivation spread to 16 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, five more than last year. Three in every four hectares were in the northeast, now firmly the country’s main growing area. Before the ban, most poppy was grown in the southwest.
Prices dipped from $570 a kilogramme last year to $500 but remain far above pre-ban levels of under $100. UNODC said large regional price differences may encourage trafficking from the northeast to the southwest.
Stockpiles running low
The survey said traffickers in the region appear to have relied on opium stockpiles to keep supplies moving since the ban.
But recent seizure data suggest those stocks are running down. The 2026 World Drug Report also found early signs that heroin supplies in Europe are falling.
With demand holding up and prices high, shrinking supplies could push cultivation in Afghanistan higher still.
“International cooperation is needed to investigate and dismantle transnational drug trafficking networks both in Afghanistan and the rest of the world,” Ms. Juma said.
UNODC said continued monitoring would show whether this year’s jump is temporary or the start of a resurgence in opium and heroin production.

Bessarabian Bulgarians Day commemorates the consecration of the Holy Transfiguration Church in Bolhrad on 29 October 1838. It was the first major Orthodox church built by Bulgarian settlers in Bessarabia with their own funds and labour. Bolhrad remains a spiritual centre for Bulgarians in the region.

From Atoms to Universes: The Architecture of Everything in the Age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

AI has become a consumer product faster than it has become a discipline. Each week brings new models and more information than anyone can absorb, and the easy response is uncritical consumption. Architecture needs a different strategy, built on criticism and method. AI is now acquiring spatial intelligence, the capacity to understand how physical space behaves, and architects can test a project against its environment while they design it. Used with judgment, AI can bring architects closer to nature and its complexity, and make them better builders. We simulate the world to learn how to inhabit it.
Tool as designer of human
How many times will the present generation have to revolutionize their daily way of being? Historically humanity has experienced drastic reprogramming of a lifestyle once every few centuries. With the industrial revolution it dropped down to once every few generations. AI has compressed this interval in ways we're still bound to find out.
As Jean-François Lyotard wrote, "technology wasn't invented by us humans. Rather the other way around." In a time when humans are being designed by their tools faster than ever, how are we supposed to program our own evolution in order to reach a symbiosis between natural intelligence and the artificial? What are the means of acquiring the necessary skills to allow AI to shape us for the better?
Artificial intelligence is an opportunity to enhance once again the possibilities at hand of every individual. From the first books that allowed broad education, to accessibility to infinite information through the internet, to access to navigation and creation through AI.
Language models to World models
Large language models learned the world through its descriptions. They merely predict text from statistical regularities. They mimic human speech and thought based on large databases and simple probability. World models, on the other hand, are systems that learn how an environment behaves, its physical rules, spatial dynamics, causal states and functional structures, so that they can predict new behaviors. Fei-Fei Li calls current LLMs "wordsmiths in the dark", eloquent about a three-dimensional world they have never had to move through, and argues that spatial intelligence is the field's next frontier. For architecture the difference is decisive. A model of text cannot anticipate how physical and social reality responds to a project, while a model of space enables simulating scenarios, testing how a project responds to gravity, wind, sunlight, wear and human use. Thermal diffusion, moisture absorption, pollutant dispersion and the flow of people become feedback the project responds to, and design proceeds through interaction with these dynamics instead of imposing a form on them.
Simulation can inform a decision. It cannot take over the responsibility of making it. We need now more than ever professionals with criteria, who use AI responsibly as an analytical tool, rather than a mere burst of productivity. The architect becomes less an author of forms and more a designer of knowledge systems, measured by the capacity to anticipate consequences in a dense and often uncertain reality. What remains human is the process.
Mindhub for Intelligent Artificial Worlds
Spatial AI is a call for hybrid profiles that cross design with computational engineering and materials science. The Mindhub for Intelligent Artificial Worlds (MIAWS), at ETSAM, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, is a digital hub for the whole AEC sector built around that change. It combines original research with a worldwide network of practitioners and institutions, and its Foundations program runs online across ten modules that carry one project from AI modeling and simulation to data visualization and integration. The aim is to keep pace with the technology without handing over judgment. We invite you to get to know the program and take part in the change.

North Korea launches missile salvo toward the Sea of Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:42:45 UTC
15:42:45 KST

- North Korea launched suspected ballistic missiles at about 12:36 p.m. on Oct. 29, Japan said, with nothing reaching its territory or exclusive economic zone.
- South Korea said around 10 short-range ballistic missiles were fired from the Wonsan area, North Korea’s first ballistic launch in 17 days.
North Korea launched what may have been a ballistic missile at about 12:36 p.m. local time on Oct. 29, and it is presumed to have fallen near the east coast of the Korean Peninsula without reaching Japan’s territory or exclusive economic zone, Japan’s Ministry of Defense said on social media.
Tokyo said Japan, the United States and South Korea are working closely to analyze the launch, and that so far there have been no reports of damage to aircraft or ships operating nearby. The exclusive economic zone is the band of sea extending up to 200 nautical miles (370 km) from Japan’s coast, where Tokyo controls fishing and resources.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was briefed immediately and gave three instructions: gather and analyze information and keep the public quickly and accurately informed, thoroughly confirm the safety of aircraft and ships, and prepare for any contingency. The government’s North Korea task force at the prime minister’s crisis management center pulled together information from ministries and convened an emergency team to discuss the response.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi then ordered the Self-Defense Forces to work closely with the United States and South Korea on collecting and analyzing information and to keep up surveillance in case of further developments. The Japanese government said North Korea’s repeated missile launches threaten the peace and security of Japan, the region and the international community, and it promised to release more details as they become available.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff gave a fuller picture, saying North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area on its east coast toward the sea at about 12:30 p.m., SBS reported. Neither government has yet said how far the missiles flew or how high they climbed, and North Korean state media had not commented on the launch by Thursday afternoon.
The launch is North Korea’s first ballistic missile firing in 17 days and follows a busy October. On Oct. 3, it fired a missile from near its east coast that Japan’s Defense Ministry said flew about 680 km (420 miles) at a peak altitude of about 90 km (56 miles) before landing outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. On Oct. 12, Pyongyang fired several ballistic missiles from near its capital, some of which flew more than 900 km (560 miles), and later called them tactical ballistic missiles, short-range weapons meant for battlefield targets. Two days later, it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the peninsula.
The launches come as tensions remain high along the inter-Korean border. In early October, South Korea and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had deliberately planted the mines that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone on Sept. 21. South Korea’s National Security Office held an emergency meeting after Thursday’s launch and said the repeated ballistic missile firings violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, which bar North Korea from testing ballistic missiles.

The report, released 11 months after the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po claimed 168 lives, assigned blame to the main contractor for renovations at the housing estate, the project consultant and an inspector for their alleged roles in the tragedy. 'We must learn so that it doesn't happen again': Oct. 7 veterans prepare soldiers for the next war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:39:37 UTC
15:39:37 KST

On Oct. 7, 2023, as Israel awoke to an unprecedented nightmare, these four company commanders were still serving in more junior positions. They rushed from the officer training school, private trips and weekend leave straight into the chaos in communities near the Gaza border, including Be'eri, Kissufim, Nir Oz and the Re'im junction.
They rescued civilians under heavy fire, witnessed scenes they had previously thought existed only in movies and, in some cases, suffered serious injuries. Now, after three consecutive years of intense fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank, they command companies at the Givati Brigade's training base, the Nahal Brigade's training base, the Paratroopers' training program and the squad commanders' course.
The officers are bringing hard-earned operational lessons and insights gained at great personal cost to the training grounds, where they are responsible for educating and shaping the next generation of combat soldiers.
"On Oct. 7, I was a team commander in the Gefen Battalion at Bahad 1," recalled Capt. Y., now a company commander overseeing recruits in the Givati Reconnaissance Unit, referring to the IDF's officer training school.
"We started that morning at 7 a.m., and I drove south with my father to reach the assembly point. I spent my first hours of fighting with two officer cadets, and from there we drove to the Re'im junction area, near the site of the music festival, and then to Nir Oz.
"I separated from the cadets to join my team because I understood that I was responsible for my unit and couldn't let my soldiers fight without me. We brought combat equipment from Bahad 1 and then headed into fighting in Sufa, Nir Yitzhak and the Yesha junction. We spent three or four days restoring control."
One moment from those first days remains particularly vivid.
"There was a moment when we stopped the Humvees, quickly prepared ourselves and the company commander told us to forget what we knew and understand that we were entering a combat zone," Capt. Y. recalled.
"When you're in the Gaza or Lebanon sector and someone tells you that, you understand. But I looked around and saw kibbutzim and Israeli communities. That really struck me. It was a period of tremendous shock and disbelief."
A generation that did not experience Oct. 7
Serious injuries and prolonged combat have become inseparable parts of the commanders' stories.
Capt. N., now a company commander in the Paratroopers' 890th Battalion training program who is set to be promoted to major, fought in Be'eri during the first days of the attack as part of a force known as "Ben-Mosh."
"We ran through Be'eri for two consecutive nights, going from house to house, rescuing residents and fighting in firefights until the community was declared clear," Capt. N. said.
"From there, we moved on to preparations for entering Gaza. A week after the ground offensive began, I was seriously wounded by friendly fire. Shrapnel cut into my windpipe, I was sedated and placed on a ventilator, and I underwent two months of rehabilitation. As soon as I could, I went straight back to my company."
Three years later, the new generation of soldiers is one that did not experience Oct. 7 firsthand as combat troops.
"Today, apart from my deputy company commander, no one serving under me was there on Oct. 7 or at the beginning of the ground offensive," Capt. N. said.
"My job is to help the soldiers imagine what it looked like. We were there, and we remember the initial shock. Our responsibility is to make sure that shock doesn't happen again next time."
Capt. A., a company commander in the IDF's squad commanders' course, puts the cultural and disciplinary lessons in stark terms.
"When I apply Oct. 7 to the training of commanders, I tell my trainees one thing: We must never forget. We must not forget what happened to us and what was done to us, and we must not forget that we failed in our mission," Capt. A. said.
"Alongside heroic battles, there were quite a few professional lessons we must learn so that it doesn't happen again. And it could happen tomorrow morning.
"My trainees were schoolchildren on Oct. 7, and now the responsibility rests on their shoulders. If they forget, we'll fall back into the same assumptions that made us less effective.
"At the tactical level, when I say there could be a war tomorrow morning, it's not a cliché. It's a belief I translate into daily preparations: maintaining constant readiness with ammunition, drills, defensive procedures and readiness at dawn.
"In my view, operational culture is the greatest lesson. Where that culture was lacking, that's where we failed."
'We failed in our mission to defend'
These lessons are shaping the next generation of soldiers from the ground up.
Capt. Y., a company commander at the Nahal Brigade's training base who is currently leading recruits through a week of field training, recalled the moment everything changed for him.
"We entered Kissufim into a full-scale battlefield, with gunfire coming from every direction and rockets in the air," he said.
"As we were driving, a friend who was in the vehicle with me was speaking on the phone with his family in Be'eri, explaining how to tie a shirt into a tourniquet to save their younger brother, who had been shot.
"We went from house to house under fire to rescue families and act as human shields for them. Our mission was to make sure no civilian was harmed, and we failed in that mission."
Capt. Y. of the Nahal training base said today's recruits arrive with a profound sense of responsibility. They understand that they are the country's protective vest, he said, and are eager to learn from the combat experience their commanders have accumulated.
Capt. Y. of the Givati Reconnaissance Unit described his company as part of a "generation of victory," a generation that has fought continuously for three years across multiple fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, and demonstrated levels of resilience and capability rarely seen among soldiers performing mandatory military service.
All four commanders agree that the operational experience gained at such a heavy cost will, in their view, leave the next generation of combat soldiers better prepared to face the most demanding challenges.

Putin and African leaders chart new course for cooperation: As it happened
The third Russia-Africa Summit has concluded in Moscow, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and African leaders adopting a joint declaration and agreeing on priorities for cooperation in the coming years.
The second and final day of the gathering at the Kremlin focused on international affairs, Africa’s growing global role, economic cooperation and security. Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye addressed the summit before holding a joint press conference.
The leaders adopted a declaration covering issues ranging from UN reform and sanctions to maritime security, trade and infrastructure, alongside a cooperation action plan for 2027–2029. The declaration also called for greater African representation in international institutions and opposed neocolonial practices that undermine national sovereignty.
Putin held a series of bilateral meetings with African counterparts, discussing investment, energy, infrastructure and educational cooperation. Speaking to reporters, he also addressed Russia’s relations with Europe, international maritime security and Moscow’s role in resolving conflicts across Africa.
Wednesday’s opening economic forum focused on expanding trade, strengthening financial independence and supporting industrial development across the continent. Putin called for Russia-Africa trade to reach $50 billion, backed reform of the IMF and World Bank, and offered to share Russian digital technologies.
RT followed the summit’s final day, bringing you the key announcements, agreements, and footage from Moscow.
This live feed has now ended.

They tried to persuade some leaders not to come, citing various difficult conditions in Russia,” Ushakov told RT. Despite these efforts, the summit attracted substantial representation, he said, adding that participants were interested in expanding cooperation across multiple sectors.
