Feature: Rising living costs weigh on New Yorkers as midterms approach
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:55:25 CST
14:55:25 KST

A customer shops for produce at a farmers' market in Queens, New York City, the United States, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Ziyu Julian Zhu/Xinhua)
by Ziyu Julian Zhu
NEW YORK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- As the U.S. midterm elections approach, rising living costs are weighing on New Yorkers, shaping their daily spending decisions and influencing what they hope to see from elected officials.
From grocery bills and housing costs to travel expenses and costs of running a small business, financial pressures are being felt across different walks of life. For many voters, the midterm elections offer an opportunity to voice their concerns and seek change.
"The food prices just keep going up," said Sandra W., who declined to provide her full name.
"You need to be more selective in buying meat. The price of steak nowadays or the price of hamburger even is much higher. So if you feel that's something not necessary, you may want to pass on it."
Now in her 70s, Sandra has lived in New York City for decades. Beyond the rising cost of groceries, she said, the election is also about ensuring that voters' choices are respected, and she hopes the newly elected could stem the wave of rising prices.
The U.S. consumer price index rose 3.7 percent year on year in September, with food, shelter and gasoline prices increasing by 2.5 percent, 3.2 percent and 34.2 percent, respectively, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Travel has also become more expensive, adding to the burden on Americans hoping to visit family or take time off. Airline fares rose 22.4 percent year on year in September 2026, according to the bureau.
"Flying anywhere is very expensive. However, it's currently cheaper to fly to Europe than it is to fly anywhere in the United States," said Caleb Schaaf, who was leaving a polling station near Court Square subway station in the borough of Queens.
Missouri-native Schaaf, who is pursuing an acting career in New York City, is concerned that rising airfares could make it more expensive to travel and visit family members.
He recently spent 1,500 U.S. dollars on flight tickets to Southern California, about 500 dollars more than he would normally expect to pay for such a trip, he said. With his wedding scheduled for April 2027, his concern about travel expenses extends to relatives coming from Missouri.
For small businesses, rising costs pose a related challenge, as higher operating expenses can force business owners to raise prices, adding to the burden on consumers.
Richard Nolasco helps run his family's farm business, located about a two-hour drive from New York City. Starting work as early as 3 a.m., he travels each week to between eight and 10 farmers' markets, selling fresh produce directly to urban customers.
Farmers' market sales account for about 75 percent of the family's business revenue, with the rest coming from deliveries and other distribution channels, Nolasco said.
Despite steady demand, rising transportation, labor and other operating costs have made it increasingly difficult to keep the business running. Fuel alone accounts for at least 25 percent of the farm's total budget, he said, forcing the family to raise prices for some products.
"The most expensive thing we raised was the eucalyptuses, which were like 15 (dollars) last year, but now they're 20," Nolasco said, explaining that the crop takes months to grow before it can be sold.
"These squashes were originally two dollars a pound. Now they're three dollars a pound," he added. With costs rising across the board, Nolasco said it had become harder to run the business.
Labor costs have also increased, he said. The family farm relies on seasonal workers, some of whom have sought higher pay this year to keep pace with their own rising living expenses, adding to the family's operating costs.
While economic concerns are top of mind for voters, some New Yorkers are also calling for action on affordable housing, civil rights, immigration and U.S. foreign policy.
Mario Wilson said racial tensions were a particular concern for him, arguing that mutual respect and a safer, more inclusive society should be priorities alongside economic issues.
Wilson also expressed hope that future elected officials would show greater concern for people from different racial backgrounds.
New York state's early voting period runs from Oct. 24 through Nov. 1, allowing residents to cast their ballots ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.
Across the United States, 47 states and Washington, D.C., allow in-person early voting, although the timing and procedures vary by jurisdiction, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
As the midterm elections draw closer, whether they will bring meaningful improvements to people's lives is anyone's guess. ■

Australia has highest rates of anorexia, bulimia: study

14:55:10 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia has the world's highest prevalence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, with an estimated 1,026.5 cases per 100,000 people affected by one of the two disorders, a global study has found.
Global cases of the two eating disorders rose 71 percent between 1990 and 2023, and are projected to continue rising through 2050, underscoring the need to integrate eating disorders into mental health surveillance, prevention, early detection, and care planning worldwide, according to a summary of the study published on the Australian Science Media Center website on Thursday.
The study, based on the Global Burden of Disease 2023 analysis, estimated that about 18.1 million people worldwide had the two disorders in 2023, including 3.92 million with anorexia and 14.2 million with bulimia.
Australia's University of Queensland epidemiologist Damian Santomauro, the study's senior author, told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that Australia's ranking was "surprising and concerning."
Females accounted for nearly 70 percent of global cases, while about 41 percent of all cases affected people aged 10 to 24. The largest increases occurred in East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia, according to the study published in JAMA Psychiatry. ■

Tennessee bids to host the new U.S. Space Academy near Arnold AFB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:53:44 UTC
14:53:44 KST

- Tennessee launched a bid to host the planned U.S. Space Academy at the Coffee County Joint Industrial Park near Arnold Air Force Base.
- A NASA-led presidential commission has 120 days from Trump’s Aug. 28 executive order to recommend a site and structure for the academy.
Tennessee has launched a bid to host the planned United States Space Academy, proposing a campus at the Coffee County Joint Industrial Park near Tullahoma, minutes from Arnold Air Force Base and about 60 miles (97 km) from Huntsville, Alabama.
Gov. Bill Lee announced the bid on Oct. 28 alongside U.S. Sens. Marsha Blackburn and Bill Hagerty and U.S. Reps. Matt Van Epps and Scott DesJarlais, all Tennessee Republicans, WSMV reported. The state is pitching the site’s existing infrastructure and room to expand, and a network of nearby institutions that could support the academy, including the University of Tennessee Space Institute, Middle Tennessee State University, Tennessee Tech University and Vanderbilt University.
“Tennessee offers readily available land, world-class aerospace testing infrastructure, an established academic partner, and a strong network of space, defense, and research institutions,” said Van Epps, a West Point graduate.
The academy does not exist yet. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 28 creating a presidential commission to design what the order calls a NASA-led federal academy, intended to educate future astronauts, engineers, scientists, operators and warfighters. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chairs the commission, whose members include Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, and it has 120 days from the order to recommend how the academy would operate, where it could be located, what service obligations graduates would carry and what Congress would need to approve.
The project breaks with the model of the existing service academies, which are run by the U.S. Department of War or, for the Coast Guard Academy, the Department of Homeland Security. Under the order, NASA would lead the new school, though the commission is also weighing how it would supply officers for the military, including the U.S. Space Force, which now draws most of its officers from the Air Force Academy, ROTC programs and officer training school.
NASA asked every governor on Sept. 10 to submit a single proposal by Oct. 26. The agency wants a permanent site of at least 300 acres near a NASA facility or university, able to house a tuition-free undergraduate program for 1,200 students that could eventually grow to 4,000. NASA has said groundbreaking would come no later than 2027, with about 300 students starting at a temporary location in 2028 and a permanent campus in place by 2031, according to The Center Square. The final site choice rests with the president.
Tennessee faces crowded competition. Alabama has put forward Huntsville, home to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center and the future permanent headquarters of U.S. Space Command at Redstone Arsenal. Texas is backing Houston, home to Johnson Space Center, and Florida lawmakers have introduced bills to place the academy on the Space Coast. Colorado announced its own bid for Colorado Springs on Oct. 23, and officials in Louisiana, Nevada, Ohio and West Virginia have also shown interest.
Tennessee’s pitch leans on its proximity to Huntsville and on Arnold Air Force Base, home of the Arnold Engineering Development Complex, the U.S. Air Force’s largest wind tunnel and engine test site.
“From Arnold Air Force Base to Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Tennessee has powered our nation’s space and defense enterprise for generations, making us the natural home for the U.S. Space Academy,” said Blackburn.
The plan has critics. U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, has called it duplicative and costly, arguing that it overlaps with the Air Force Academy in his state.

Moving trains, broken glass, vigilantes: The chaos delivery robots could face as they arrive in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:48:59 UTC
14:48:59 KST

In brief
- US firm Serve Robotics has launched self-driving robotic food delivery vehicles in Queensland.
- Experts say the coming wave of automation will bring both disruption and benefit.
Australia's first delivery robots have begun their autonomous conquest of the Gold Coast's pavements, with experts saying that they could herald a new era in human-robot relations.
United States-based firm Serve Robotics has partnered with DoorDash to deliver meals on robotic wheels to local residents in Queensland, but the technology still has a long way to go before it becomes commonplace elsewhere in the country.
The robots, which carry takeaway orders on pavements at walking pace, are the same as those used by the company and its competitors in the US. They can access an operations depot at Griffith University.
Japan, Colombia, Germany, and others are also in various stages of rolling out autonomous delivery with other companies; however, the droids have not always been warmly received by residents.
In the US, where resentment towards the construction of data centres and the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence is growing, residents in places like Chicago, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia have filmed themselves attacking the robots.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Retired professor Carolyn Marvin was arrested earlier this month after a campaign of protest in which she deliberately stood in front of the machines to stop them doing their jobs. She said she was concerned that robots could soon replace human workers.
Elsewhere, delivery robots have been seen causing damage and chaos when their programming fails to match up with the environment around them.
There have been reports of broken-down robots blocking pavements, stopping at pedestrian crossings as emergency vehicles try to pass, and even running through glass bus stops.
In one viral incident, a robot was filmed straying onto railway lines before being flattened by an oncoming train.
Australians may hold similarly hostile views about the rise of the machines, given backlash against AI and concerns about data centres.
However, Australia Post's experiments with similar autonomous vehicles in 2017 did not spark major pushback.
Robots must overcome barriers
Professor Michael Milford, director of the QUT Centre for Robotics, told SBS News that an autonomous robotic future is by no means guaranteed.
"There's a number of challenges," Milford said. "There's societal acceptance. There's the perception of hogging precious space on the footpath, getting in people's ways occasionally, occasionally driving into bus shelter windows and all that sort of stuff.
"But ultimately, it's a commercial play by these companies, and there is, as far as I can tell, a very challenging path to being sufficiently profitable."
At present, the use of delivery robots is limited. However, analysts expect to see a spike in their adoption over the coming decade. Research firm Transforma Insight reported last year that 2.1 million could be operating worldwide by 2034.
Although fears about job replacement by technology are widespread, Milford notes that the current food delivery system has its own issues — and is quite efficient.
Without being able to offer some advantage to hand-delivered takeout through price, speed, or otherwise, Milford said the robots face an uphill battle.
Yet, while challenges remain, there are also benefits, such as the removal of cars from the road.
"A lot of [these issues] come down to not the specific technology but to underlying societal things around capitalism and what people will accept," he said.
"This is sort of the pointy end of it, but a lot of this is true of any new technological development."
Productivity gains give robots advantage
While Serve Robotics' vehicles are currently delivering meals from just a single restaurant — Gnocchi Gnocchi, Southport — more are set to join soon.
DoorDash has said the robots are expected to complement its existing delivery drivers by completing short trips in dense urban environments, while humans continue to do longer, cross-city trips.
Professor Hai Vu, head of the Monash Connected Autonomous Vehicle program, told SBS News that automating aspects of the economy is largely inevitable given the productivity benefits on offer.
His team built Australia's first domestically designed and autonomous food-delivery robot in 2025, which they named ARI. Vu said their approach could solve some of the economic issues facing similar machines at present.
"Our approach is actually quite very different," Vu said, explaining that his machines do all of their computing remotely, rather than inside the vehicle as most others do.
"That enables us to have a very simple and low-cost robot," he said. "You could actually scale up thousands of these robots at a fraction of the cost."
Coming to a town near you?
Delivery robots are not automatically legal to operate in Australia and face a raft of regulatory roadblocks, with local councils at the forefront of how they might be regulated.
Gold Coast City Council has been working actively with technology companies and Griffith University to establish how autonomous robots might work on its streets.
Experts at Swinburne University and Monash are also mapping low-speed urban zones where delivery robots and humans might co-exist peacefully.
Milford said that the issues need to be thought through carefully, but that there is little reason Australia couldn't see more robots on its streets soon.
"If you can walk around [a robot], that's fine. But if you're in a wheelchair, for example, that could be catastrophically bad," he said.
"Technically and economically, there is no reason why you couldn't roll out a Waymo service in Sydney tomorrow," he said, referring to the driverless cars operating in the US.
Legally, NSW prohibits the use of fully autonomous vehicles, but Premier Chris Minns has publicly supported the idea, and Waymo — owned by Alphabet, Google's parent company — appears to be preparing to establish a presence in Australia.
"I would not be surprised at all if there was an announcement from Waymo or one of the other organisations that they're going to roll out trials in Sydney in 2027 or 2028," Milford said.
"Elsewhere, I expect to see gradual, steady expansion of these robo-taxis in a lot of places."
While the rollout may be slow, experts say it is coming. Hai cautioned policymakers that they need to play a more active role in addressing how the nation deals with the autonomous future rushing toward it, in order to both mitigate the impacts and reap the benefits.
"If you want to develop the economy," Hai said, "then you need to have the right incentives and provide the right opportunities for people to capitalise on those incentives."

Election night reckoning: pollsters confront their biggest misses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:43:46 UTC
14:43:46 KST

At 10 p.m. Tuesday, as polls closed in Israel's election, all six television news channels released their exit polls. Not all painted the same picture. Channel 12 News, Channel 13 News and Kan 11 projected 50 seats for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, while i24NEWS projected 55, Channel 16 projected 53 and Channel 14 projected 60. There were also differences in the projected strength of individual parties.
As in every election, the exit polls were updated throughout the night as actual results from sampled polling stations came in. Most of the projections eventually moved closer to what are now the preliminary official results.
The differences between the channels are only part of the story. Polls published in the days and weeks leading up to the election sometimes presented a different picture from the exit polls.
One of the most striking examples is Likud. In Channel 13's final preelection poll, published Oct. 23, the party was projected to win just 19 seats. In the channel's initial exit poll, that figure rose to 25, and an overnight update put it at 27. According to the latest official count, Likud stands at 26 seats.
Now, with vote counting still underway, questions are emerging about the gaps between the forecasts, pollsters' ability to identify changes in voting patterns and the professional lessons to be drawn from the election.
In interviews with ynet, two pollsters who were at the center of election night described what they saw in the data, what surprised them and their initial conclusions.
'Likud's strength was something we didn't see in the polls'
Shmuel Rosner, Channel 13's pollster, acknowledged that Likud's strong showing was the biggest surprise for him. Although preelection polls identified several major trends, he said, they failed to reflect the governing party's strength.
"Some things surprised me, and others less so. The main surprise was Likud's strength, something we didn't see in the polls but which appeared fairly early in the exit polls and continued to grow throughout the evening."
And when the actual results began to emerge, were there other surprises?
"Apart from the surprise over Likud, which requires us to think about how it happened and why we didn't see it, we also didn't expect the bloc with a certain advantage to be the coalition bloc rather than the opposition.
"At the same time, some things weren't surprising. For example, we had been seeing for some time that turnout among Arab voters would be high and that the Arab parties would win many seats. We also consistently saw that neither bloc would probably reach 61 seats and that the ultra-Orthodox parties were weakening. Those were things we identified."
What is the professional lesson from this election? Will you do anything differently next time?
"It's still a little early to say what lessons we'll draw. First, we need to understand whether something happened and what it was, and then try to apply the professional lessons accordingly.
"This isn't just about an election campaign. I conduct polls regularly, so obviously, after an event like this, both I and the team I work with need to examine it and understand what happened. We need to try to figure out, as best we can, what went wrong and what we can improve.
"I've only done this once so far, and I'm not sure I'll do it again, so we'll wait and see."
'I was very, very confident in the numbers'
Tzuriel Sharon, founder and owner of the Direct Polls research institute, which conducted the preelection surveys and exit poll for i24NEWS, said he was not surprised by the results of his projection.
According to Sharon, the figures were consistent with trends he had identified throughout the campaign, and his confidence in those assessments had grown in recent weeks.
What went through your mind when the exit polls were released?
"Anticipation. Certainly when you see everyone else's numbers. On the other hand, I was very, very confident in the numbers."
What gave you that confidence?
"The numbers were very consistent with what I had been seeing throughout the entire period. I felt I had a handle on what was happening, that I understood the system, the election, Israeli sociology and the dynamics of Israeli public sentiment.
"I felt very confident in my understanding of the situation throughout the election campaign, and that feeling became much stronger in recent weeks."
How do you explain the large differences between the channels' exit polls?
"First of all, that's a question you should ask them. I believe I have the No. 1 polling system in Israel in terms of technology. I've invested enormous resources in it and its development, particularly over the past year.
"That was partly because of the election, but not only. It was also because of very large commercial clients working with the company.
"Beyond that, I wasn't living in echo chambers. I was very connected to Israeli public sentiment in all its forms. I was highly focused and insulated from background noise. In other words, I understood the mindset of voters across all the different sectors that ultimately make up the political landscape. In that respect, I felt very confident."
One of the main surprises Sharon identified was the high turnout among Arab voters. He said its scale surprised even those who had anticipated significant gains for the Arab parties.
"We knew the Arab sector would probably turn out. Conservative estimates spoke of 14 seats, while the higher estimates were already talking about 15. I think the numbers astonished everyone, and I'm inclined to believe these are figures we won't see again in future elections."
How much did the high turnout affect the exit polls?
"It affects the weight you assign to different population groups. That's something a pollster needs to know how to handle in real time. It shouldn't surprise you once you have the turnout figures.
"In preelection polls, you can estimate turnout. Here, you receive the actual figures and updates from the Central Elections Committee throughout the day."
'Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater'
Sharon also addressed questions about the reliability of polling following the discrepancies between the channels.
He said the results should not be taken as an indictment of the entire polling industry, although he expects the episode to have consequences for the media as well.
After a night like this, the public could lose faith in polls.
"I hope the Israeli public will look at Direct Polls' surveys, because here's a company that has proven itself.
"I don't think we should throw the baby out with the bathwater. It's not as though this entire industry has gone bankrupt. But there are four players who will need to do some soul-searching.
"I expect this episode to have consequences in the short term and perhaps over the longer term as well, not only for the polling industry but also for the media industry."
Still, is there anything you personally would do differently?
"You can always streamline processes and improve them. You learn from everything. There are things we tried that didn't work, and there are things we tried that turned out to be tremendous successes. It's a process of trial and error."
Sharon, like the other pollsters, has completed his work on this election campaign. But with the results failing to deliver a decisive victory to either side, the question immediately arises: Could another polling season be just around the corner, with another election?
Sharon, at least, believes not.
"I don't think we'll go to a second round. I expect we'll see a government with a different composition from the current one.
"Even if I'm going against everyone's predictions here, you saw that I went against everyone during the election campaign, too. I'm not afraid of that."
What do you think was the main message voters sent in this election?
"I think the public has spoken. Netanyahu received a yellow card from voters over his partnership with the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the center-left received a yellow card over its willingness to sit with the Arab parties.
"The public has made it very clear what kind of government it wants to see, and the politicians will have to act."

Russia’s nighttime attacks on Ukraine: explosions in Kharkiv, strikes on Dnipropetrovsk region, and one person killed in Rivne region
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with drones: explosions were heard in Kharkiv, while Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions suffered damage. A man was killed in Rivne region.
During the night of October 29, Russian forces attacked a number of regions of Ukraine with drones. Explosions were heard in Kharkiv, while Dnipropetrovsk and other regions came under attack. There were fatalities and injuries as a result of the attacks. This was reported by representatives of the regional military administrations, local authorities, and the police, UNN writes.
Details
In Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russians attacked three districts with drones nearly 20 times. An enterprise was damaged in Dnipro, and a 35-year-old man was injured. In Nikopol district, Nikopol, the Marhanets, Chervonohryhorivka, and Myrove communities came under attack. An administrative building, infrastructure, and a high-rise building were damaged.
At least three strikes by Russian drones were recorded in Kharkiv overnight. According to Mayor Ihor Terekhov, at around 03:17, the enemy attacked the Kholodnohirskyi district, where a fire broke out.
Later, a drone struck in the Saltivskyi district. According to updated information, an educational institution was hit. At around 07:20, an attack on the Industrialnyi district was also recorded. The consequences are being clarified.
The day before, on October 28, a 60-year-old man was killed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv's Osnovianskyi district. Three other men, aged 41, 46, and 56, were hospitalized. A 48-year-old woman also required medical assistance.
In Zaporizhzhia region, Russian forces launched 849 strikes on 44 settlements in the region over the course of the day. In particular, 20 airstrikes were recorded against a number of settlements, including Komyshuvakha, Zarichne, Veselianka, Vilniansk, and others.
In Rivne region, a Russian drone attacked a civilian enterprise in Sarny district. A 42-year-old man was killed in the strike.
According to the police, vehicles on and near the enterprise's premises, as well as neighboring houses, were damaged. Rescuers extinguished the fire, while bomb disposal experts recovered fragments of the enemy drone.

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead with nearly 90% of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:37:00 UTC
14:37:00 KST

Israel election: Majority remains elusive after final count
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- The final vote count showed Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc finished with 53 seats
- The anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, claimed 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- As neither party won an outright majority, difficult coalition talks are expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election.
Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins
Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.
On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.
However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.
The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.
Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.
He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.
It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.
Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.
Final count released
The final count of ballots from Tuesday's vote has been released by Israel's Central Election Committee.

READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here.
Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon
With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.
- Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
- Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
- Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
- Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
- Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
- Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
- Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
- The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
- Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
- "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says
Oleksandr Karasevych, State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, made this statement in comments to a Ukrinform correspondent in New York.
“Regarding the special tribunal, we are currently actively working to expand its geographic participation,” he noted.
Karasevych recalled that Ukraine already has a legal decision from the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe regarding the tribunal, which was supported by 38 states and the European Union. Now they must implement the agreement at the national level.
“This is no longer a political statement; it is now a legal factor,” the State Secretary emphasized.
He added that, at the same time, Ukraine is seeking to involve more states outside the Council of Europe in the tribunal. In particular, a Ukrainian delegation recently visited Japan to explain the importance of its participation at the political and governmental levels.
Karasevych noted that Japan, Australia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Canada were part of a key group of states that participated in drafting the legal mechanisms for establishing the tribunal, specifically its statute and the relevant agreement.
“They were part of the core group, meaning they participated at the technical level in developing the legal mechanisms, the statute, and the agreement. Now we need to work with them so that they also become participants,” he explained.
The State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also pointed to two areas of work regarding Russia’s accountability: the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression and a compensation mechanism to make up for the damages inflicted on Ukraine.
According to him, more states have formally joined the compensation mechanism, including those that are not members of the Council of Europe. Among them are Australia and Japan, which have joined the Register of Damages Caused by Russia’s Aggression Against Ukraine.
Karasevych recalled that a UN General Assembly resolution adopted in November 2022 served as the basis for developing the compensation mechanism.
He explained that the purpose of his visit to New York is to convey to the legal advisors of partner states—particularly those not yet involved in accountability processes—the importance of establishing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable.
“We must work with those who are not yet involved in our joint efforts, explaining to them what we are doing, why we are doing it, and why it is important not only for Ukraine but for the entire international community,” Karasevych said.
He emphasized that discussing issues of international law and accountability for aggression is particularly appropriate at UN headquarters, since states must adhere to the principles upon which the Organization is founded.
Karasevych also noted that on Tuesday, the Ukrainian delegation participated in a UN Security Council meeting dedicated to the topic “Women, Peace, and Security.” The next meeting involving Ukraine, scheduled for Thursday, will focus on maritime navigation. According to him, it is particularly important for Ukraine to ensure compliance with international maritime safety standards in the Black and Azov Seas.
As reported by Ukrinform, an event was held at the UN on Wednesday dedicated to implementing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable for its aggression against Ukraine.

Unknown

05:31:01 UTC
14:31:01 KST

Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente says a technical failure and a possible breach of safety procedures are being investigated following Wednesday’s collision between two high-speed trains that killed at least 68 people.
Speaking at a press conference, Puente said a technical fault had automatically stopped rail traffic on the affected section of track.
However, a high-speed train operated by Renfe, Spain’s national railway company, was subsequently allowed to continue despite a red signal, Reuters reported.
Puente said the authorization should never have been given and that investigators were examining who was responsible for the decision.
“The decision to resume traffic while the system had not been restored lies with the control center, and the control center made that decision to resume traffic under circumstances that from our point of view are incomprehensible,” he said, according to Reuters.
The minister’s comments suggest investigators are examining both the technical malfunction and the decision to allow trains to resume operating before the system was restored.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez also addressed the accident, promising a thorough investigation into its causes.
“If there has been any negligence, it will come to light, and if there have been errors in the safety system, it will be dealt with with the utmost firmness,” Sánchez said, according to The Guardian.
At least 68 people died when the two high-speed trains collided Wednesday morning.
The accident follows another deadly collision in January, when two high-speed trains crashed near Adamuz in the southern Spanish region of Andalusia.
That accident killed 46 people and injured more than 120 others.
Both collisions occurred this year on the railway route connecting Madrid and Seville.

Albania introduces heavy fines for protesters amid violent anti-government demonstrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:47 UTC
14:30:47 KST

Albania has introduced new penalties for protesters as weeks of demonstrations demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation continue to escalate in the capital, Tirana.
On Wednesday, Rama’s government adopted measures allowing authorities to fine people who remain in crowds where violence or looting occurs, even if they are not directly involved.
Individuals who conceal their identities during demonstrations can also face penalties.
Fines can reach 500,000 Albanian lek, approximately 41,000 DKK, compared with an average monthly salary of less than 7,000 DKK.
Police have also been given powers to temporarily restrict gatherings in areas where they believe violence could occur.
The measures took effect Wednesday but require parliamentary approval within 45 days to remain in force.
Albania has experienced months of anti-government protests, initially sparked in late May by plans to construct luxury hotels in a coastal nature reserve.
The demonstrations were initially peaceful but expanded in mid-October to include concerns about suspected corruption, shortcomings in healthcare and limited opportunities for young people.
Protesters have since gathered daily in Tirana, with recent demonstrations resulting in violent confrontations with security forces.
Authorities estimate that the protests have caused damage exceeding 2 million euros since mid-October, while more than 350 people have been injured in clashes.
Rama said Sunday that the new measures were inspired by French legislation allowing protesters to be held financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.
The prime minister has also repeatedly blamed what he calls “foreign actors” for contributing to the unrest, accusing Iran and Russia of spreading misinformation online.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:41 UTC
14:30:41 KST

Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Written Danish exam grades fall across Denmark’s upper secondary programs
Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.
At general upper secondary schools, known as stx, the average grade in A-level Danish, the highest subject level, fell from 6.8 in 2018 to 6.2 in 2026.
Across upper secondary programs, grades declined both compared with last year and over the longer term.
Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said the figures worried him and raised concerns about students’ use of artificial intelligence.
“Artificial intelligence has in a very short time changed the students’ everyday lives,” he said in a press release.
“And we cannot ignore what it can mean for their academic proficiency. Because if AI becomes a shortcut around the work of writing, analyzing, and expressing oneself, then we risk that the students learn less,” he said.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

“I am very skeptical of this Norwegian and Finnish own initiative. It is not coordinated with the rest of us,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcaster TV 2 during a meeting of the Nordic Council in Finland.
“I think one should keep Europe together instead of going solo,” she added.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also expressed doubts about the call.
“Holding talks that risk dividing the European voice, that is risky,” he said Tuesday, according to Swedish media.
Støre later rejected the criticism, saying the talks were conducted with other countries’ knowledge.
“We do not speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves, but it has been thoroughly consulted, and all our partners and allies were informed in advance and have also received a thorough summary afterwards,” he told Norwegian media outlet VG on Tuesday.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took a more positive view of the talks. In a post on X, he said he was “grateful” for Norway and Finland’s active diplomatic work.
Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.

Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.
With Preben Bang Henriksen’s departure, Venstre loses another one of its vote-magnets, as he received the fifth-most votes in Venstre in the election in March 2026.
Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.
